transcription:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE
FOR WOMEN
The Official Journal of the Electrical Association for Women.
Editor—Miss C. HASLETT, 26 George Street, Hanover Square, London, W. 1.
Vol. I.
JUNE 1926
No. 1
I am proud to have been the first president of an organisation which reflects the practical pioneer spirit of women and their capacity for educational propaganda in new fields. I hope that women will increasingly take this point of view and this spirit into every sphere of industry, commerce and the professions, and that they will succeed in convincing the community that their object is public service, rather than personal advancement. All thinking women long to take their share in building that better world which we believe can be achieved by co-operation, goodwill and unselfish service, and the Electrical Association for Women is one of the interesting and practical ways in which we can express our purpose.
Nancy Astor

transcription:
EDITORIAL

"THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN."
On hearing of the appearance of a new journal, the cynic will exclaim, "What, yet
another!" To the casual observer it would appear that there are far too many periodicals on
the market, but we venture to think that THE ELECTRICAL AGE has a special mission which
has not yet been undertaken by anyone else—that is, to interpret the message of electricity
to the women of this country.
The E.A.W. has grown so rapidly that the need for a medium to express its point of view
and to report its activities has become imperative.
We have been successful, in this first issue, in obtaining articles and expressions of opinion
from some of the most representative people in the electrical and in the womans world.
We are confident of maintaining this high standard in future issues.
For the first year, the magazine will be published quarterly, but if the demand exists, as we
believe it does, for a monthly publication of this sort, then we shall have no hesitation in coming
out as a monthly.

A GLASGOW NUMBER.
This first number of THE ELECTRICAL AGE is to appear simultaneously with the holding of
the thirty-first Convention of the Incorporated Municipal Electrical Association at Glasgow.
This Convention is representative of the electrical authorities in the municipal world, who
have played such an important part in the electrical development of this country.
The E.A.W. have jointly arranged one of the sessions—that of the Special Womens
Meeting to be addressed by Dr. Christina Barrowman on "The Remedial Uses of Electricity"
on June 17th. A full report of this lecture will appear in the next issue of the journal. Women
doctors are increasingly taking up this new departure of medical work, which is proving of
such value in connection with the treatment of diseases and for all kinds of nervous disorders.

HISTORY OF THE E.A.W.
The Electrical Association for Women first saw light of day in November, 1924. Its advent
had been looked forward to by a small band of pioneer spirits who saw in it a great medium
for the expression of womens needs and desires, and in some measure a lever for realising to
women the tremendous potential value of electricity.
For many months its lay-out was discussed and plans carefully projected for its successful
launching.
To Mrs. Matthews, of the Womens Engineering Society, belongs the credit for the outline
of the scheme, although many developments have since taken place which were not foreseen or
even anticipated at the inauguration.

Unnamed: 9: President of British Electrical Developments Association welcoming the new journal.
transcription:
6 The Electrical Age

A Welcome to "The Electrical Age " from

Mr. R. P. SLOAN, C.B.E., M.I.E.E.,
President British Electrical Developments Association,
and Chairman Newcastle-on-Tyne Electric Supply Co.

It gives me great pleasure to contribute a note for inclusion in the first issue of your journal, THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN.
There may be some who will view with mixed feelings the advent of yet another

MR. R. P. SLOAN, C.B.E., M.I.E.E.

periodical, as there are so many publications available nowadays dealing with practically every subject of general and trade interest.
As, however, this new publication of the Electrical Association for Women will
possess many features of peculiar interest, I feel confident that it will appeal to a growing class of serious readers.
THE ELECTRICAL AGE should act as a much needed link between the women who are studying electricity and its many uses, and those who will benefit by its application, particularly in the home.
Many of the present-day publications are produced for the benefit of those "within" the industry itself and to keep them abreast of development from day to day. Much of the information so produced is of such a highly technical character that it is seldom produced in the ordinary journals perused by the general public, and when reproduced is often unintelligible to the non - technical reader.
It is here that your journal may fulfil a unique purpose — those who are fully acquainted with the construction and use of electrical appliances, and the cost of and benefit accruing from their use will, through the columns of THE ELECTRICAL AGE, have an opportunity of bringing such information before possible users in simple and non-technical language.
I would urge all those associated with the electrical industry, whether suppliers of electricity, manufacturers of appliances or engaged in fitting up installations and retailing apparatus, to support your Association in its efforts and to enhance the value of your journal by providing the Editor with information on the "service" they have to offer the public and its benefits ; I feel sure that the little trouble involved will be more than repaid by the results achieved.
I wish your journal every success.

Unnamed: 9: Sends a welcome greeting to the new journal for women.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 7
Greetings from other public Men and Women
From Dame Millicent Fawcett—
I heartily welcome THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN, and wish it every success.
* * * * *
From Sir Hugo Hirst, Bart.—
Indications are plenty showing that electri-
city is bound to change our industrial, social
and home lives. Nothing seems more
natural than that women should play an
important part in this gradual transforma-
tion.
Your new venture, THE ELECTRICAL AGE
FOR WOMEN, the object of which is to enlist
women’s sympathies and collaboration in
this common effort, has a great mission. My
best wishes for a long and prosperous career.
* * * * *
From Major-General Sir Philip Nash—
I have always thought that Great Britain
possesses not only first-class electrical brains,
and facilities equal to them for the produc-
tion of electrical material, but it also
possesses a first-class electrical technical
press. It wants, however, more and more
articles in the public press to educate the
people of this country to the great advan-
tages which a greater use of electricity can
bring in the domestic lives of the people.
THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN aims at
work of this description, and I feel sure that
it has before it a very useful function and I
wish it every possible success.
* * * * *
From Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley—
I welcome the advent of an electrical paper
for women. Women have “pulled wires”
throughout the ages — now electrical wires
should also claim their attention.
* * * * *
From Lady Cowan (President of the British
Women’s Patriotic League)—
I welcome THE ELECTRICAL AGE, which
should do much to accelerate the arrival of
the age of electricity in this country and put
British housewives on a footing of equality
with their Canadian sisters, half of whose
housework is done for them by electricity.
* * * * *
From Lady Emmott—
Delighted to hear of your new journal.
The uses of electricity in the house need
much explaining to become popular.
* * * * *
From The Hon. Lady Shelley-Rolls—
A word of warm welcome to THE
ELECTRICAL AGE, and may it awaken the
women of England to the many possibilities
of electrical development.
* * * * *
From Viscountess Rhondda—
THE ELECTRICAL AGE promises to revolu-
tionise the homes of millions of women, and
your new paper should be invaluable as a
means of assisting development along the
right lines. Success to you.
* * * * *
From Lady Snell—
May THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN
bring greater comfort, health, leisure and
happiness into the homes of British women.
* * * * *
From Lady Paxton (Glasgow)—
My heartiest welcome to our new paper,
ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN. Electricity
has come like the Waverley pen, “a boon
and a blessing” to women. So good luck to
our new venture.
* * * * *
From Mrs. G. Z. de Ferranti—
I wish your new paper, ELECTRICAL AGE
FOR WOMEN, every success. I think it is a
paper that is much needed. It seems to me
that a great number of women have no idea
how much electricity used entirely in their
houses can save them the great difficulties
of running their homes nowadays.
I think housework, as it used to be—the
hardest and most tedious work a woman
can do—electricity can now make so easy
and pleasant that no woman can object to it.
If only your paper can reach every woman of
every class, and explain and make them
interested in finding out how they can all get
electricity and use it, it will have done a great
work for women.

The Electrical Age

E. A.W. Branch Activities

Glasgow and District Branch.

By The Lady Belhaven and Stenton.

When I was approached in October, 1925, and asked if I would be President of the first Branch of the Electrical Association for Women, I very gladly accepted, because I felt that here was good work to be done for women by women.

The aim of the Association held such a strong appeal for women of all types—from the purely domestic woman, who does every scrap of her housework, right on through all the types to the modern bachelor woman who has a tiny flat, and in her endeavour to pursue her business life must also live a reasonable domestic one.

The Association is the offspring of the Women’s Engineering Society and, as such, has for its object the teaching of labour-saving to the woman in the home, the shop and the factory.

During the short time in which our Glasgow Branch has been in operation, we have had a variety of ideas offered to us through lectures and visits.

At our inaugural meeting on 19th November, 1925, held in the Banqueting Hall of the City Chambers, Glasgow, we had a very good assembly in spite of the dense black fog and heavy frost which prevailed. I gave my presidential address to the ladies and gentlemen present; then Bailie W. B. Smith (chairman of the Smoke Abatement Committee, Glasgow,) was on the platform and spoke in praise of the object for which we are working. We also had Treasurer Carmichael (Greenock), Bailie Balderstone of Paisley, with us, and Miss C. Haslett (London), director of the Association.

Miss Haslett spoke on “Electricity in the Service of Women.”

After the meeting, tea was served by kindness of the Glasgow Electricity Department, and we enrolled about 45 members.

During our Winter and Spring session we had many visits and lectures of interest. The first was a visit to the super-generating station at Dalmarnock (of the Glasgow Corporation Electricity Department), including an inspection of their all-electric canteen. A delightful tea was served in the canteen. The next visit was to the Scottish Electric Lighting Service Bureau, at which Mr. Hughes and his demonstrator, Miss Lindsay, gave a lecture on “Good and Bad Lighting in the Home.”

Later, we attended a lecture at the Royal Technical College, by Professor Parker

THE LADY BELHAVEN AND STENTON.

When I was approached in October, 1925, and asked if I would be President of the first Branch of the Electrical Association for Women, I very gladly accepted, because I felt that here was good work to be done for women by women.

The aim of the Association held such a strong appeal for women of all types—from the purely domestic woman, who does every scrap of her housework, right on through all the types to the modern bachelor woman who has a tiny flat, and in her endeavour to pursue her business life must also live a reasonable domestic one.

The Association is the offspring of the Women’s Engineering Society and, as such, has for its object the teaching of labour-saving to the woman in the home, the shop and the factory.

During the short time in which our Glasgow Branch has been in operation, we have had a variety of ideas offered to us through lectures and visits.

At our inaugural meeting on 19th November, 1925, held in the Banqueting Hall of the City Chambers, Glasgow, we had a very good assembly in spite of the dense black fog and heavy frost which prevailed. I gave my presidential address to the ladies and gentlemen present; then Bailie W. B. Smith (chairman of the Smoke Abatement Committee, Glasgow,) was on the platform and spoke in praise of the object for which we are working. We also had Treasurer Carmichael (Greenock), Bailie Balderstone of Paisley, with us, and Miss C. Haslett (London), director of the Association.

Miss Haslett spoke on “Electricity in the Service of Women.”

After the meeting, tea was served by kindness of the Glasgow Electricity Department, and we enrolled about 45 members.

During our Winter and Spring session we had many visits and lectures of interest. The first was a visit to the super-generating station at Dalmarnock (of the Glasgow Corporation Electricity Department), including an inspection of their all-electric canteen. A delightful tea was served in the canteen. The next visit was to the Scottish Electric Lighting Service Bureau, at which Mr. Hughes and his demonstrator, Miss Lindsay, gave a lecture on “Good and Bad Lighting in the Home.”

Later, we attended a lecture at the Royal Technical College, by Professor Parker

transcription:
The Electrical Age 9

Smith, on "The All-Electric House." This was a joint meeting with the Institution of Electrical Engineers.
Next we visited the Glasgow Corporation Tramways—saw their power station at Pinkston and the repair works at Coplaw-hill. The whole process of the manufacture of a tramway car was demonstrated, from the melting of the metal to the finished paint and varnish on the completed car.
Then followed several useful and instructive lectures by Mr. A. P. McKim, on fuses, plugs and sockets, and simple electrical practices in the home. These were of the most delightfully simple kind and greatly appreciated.
Next came a talk on different forms of house wiring by Mr. Alexander Lindsay, I.E.E., which was also offered in a simple way so that we lay women could listen, mark and inwardly digest everything to our ultimate benefit.
We have also had a delightful lecture and demonstration by Mr. Greig, of the Singer Sewing Machine Co.
Our second inspection of a generating station was to the Greenock power station in May. We went by char-à-bancs from Glasgow on a perfect day, saw the present station and the former station (which houses a turbine ordered originally for Moscow but acquired by the Greenock Electricity Department). We had a most interesting peep at the showrooms there, had our photograph taken and a most delightful lunch at the Tontine Hotel, and finished up a truly royal day by driving round the new Hunter Street Housing Scheme, then round the Inverkip Valley and home.
All the lectures have been well attended and very much enjoyed by every member.
We have aroused the electrical interest of the Glasgow and West of Scotland College of Domestic Science, and have enrolled a large number of the staff and pupils there.
We hope to continue on these simple lines after the Summer meeting of the I.M.E.A., which is being held in Glasgow this year.
This is just a brief résumé of what we have done. Our membership stands at 183 to-day.
As I am a large user of domestic electricity for heating and cooking in my own home, at "Wishaw House," Wishaw, I have the interest of the Association very near to my heart in what it can do for the housewife and business woman of to-day.
My sincere greetings to Headquarters and the other Branches which have been formed, and best wishes that they may all do good work in our joint "adventure."

The Birmingham and Midlands Branch.

By Lady Brooks, C.B.E., J.P.

The Birmingham and Midlands Branch was inaugurated on February 23rd last, at the British Industries Fair, where a meeting was convened by Miss Haslett, who spoke on the aims and objects of forming a Womens Electrical Association in the Midland Area. Mr. R. A. Chattock also spoke on the useful purpose that such an Association could serve, giving us his promise of help and co-operation in our efforts. A Council was then formed of representatives from the local and many surrounding districts. Mrs. Lawson kindly accepted the work of Hon. Secretary, and our President was also elected.

Mrs. Chattock (the wife of our Chief Engineer) and Mrs. Beale (the wife of the chairman of the Electric Supply Committee of the City Council) were elected Vice-Presidents. From a painting by Bernard Munns.
LADY BROOKS, C.B.E., J.P.
President, Birmingham and Midlands Branch,
E.A.W.

Lady Brooks (President, Birmingham and
Midlands Branch) was for three years Lady
Mayoress of Birmingham, and is immediate
past-President of the National Council of Women
(Birmingham). Her many activities include
County Commissioner for Girl Guides, Chairman
of Anglo-French Society, and a Justice of the
Peace. The photograph which we produce is one
of a portrait that has just been painted and hung
in the Birmingham Spring Exhibition, and is by
the well-known artist, Bernard Munns.

kindly came to Birmingham to address the
meeting, and Professor Burstall (Vice-
Principal of the Birmingham University)
delivered an interesting and fascinating
address on "Science in the Home," pointing
out the need for women to advance scienti-
fically in the business of home-making, com-
paring home-building with business-building
and the contrast of womans outlook with
mans outlook, in the matter of discarding
wasteful labour and utilising labour-saving
devices.
On April 22nd, a visit to an all-electric
house on Messrs. Cadburys Woodlands
estate was arranged, which gave rise to
many interesting discussions, such as
economic water heating and efficient ventila-
tion in chimneyless rooms. Tea was kindly
provided by Messrs. Cadbury Bros.
On April 28th, we had a most interesting
lantern address at the University by Mr.
Macdonald, the Power Engineer of the
Birmingham Post Office, on "Lighting,"
showing the growth and development of the
various methods and pointing out the wise
and unwise use of the different kinds of
lamps. This was very helpful from the
womans point of view.
Various other visits to showrooms and
works have been arranged for our members
in the hope of arousing a live educational
interest, and in the near future it is hoped to
arrange lectures and demonstrations in the
surrounding districts, such as Walsall and
Wolverhampton.
We already have a membership of 65, and
we are hopeful that our enterprise may
develop and be of real value to the com-
munity at large.

showing the growth and development of the
various methods and pointing out the wise
and unwise use of the different kinds of
lamps. This was very helpful from the
womans point of view.

works have been arranged for our members
in the hope of arousing a live educational
interest, and in the near future it is hoped to
arrange lectures and demonstrations in the
surrounding districts, such as Walsall and

develop and be of real value to the com-
munity at large.

transcription:
12		The Electrical Age

Glasgow City Electrical Engineer
Mr. R. B. Mitchell, M.I.E.E.
(also President of the Incorporated Municipal Electrical Association)
Sends a Welcome

I have been asked to address a few words in this, the first number of THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN, to the women members attending the Convention of the Incorporated Municipal Electrical Association, and to the members of the Scottish Branch of the Electrical Association for Women, who, during the Convention week, are having a joint meeting in Glasgow, to acquire further knowledge of the subject in which they are all so greatly interested.

Mr. R. B. Mitchell.

I do so with great pleasure, and let me say at the outset that I believe, and I am sure you will cordially agree with me, that electricity in the households of the future will prove to be as great a boon and blessing as it has already done in the workshop and factory.
It is only after some thirty years of development of electricity supply that its use in the home, and all that it can do there to make it beautiful, more comfortable, and at the same time to ease the burden of the housewife, are really beginning to be thought about.
For lighting, there is now no question at all as to which is the best illuminant. Electricity can be applied at any point and in any quantity. Paper, paint, and decorations generally last four times as long, and the saving made due to this advantage is not often given due recognition.
The fact that electric lighting does not exhaust the air in a room has only to be mentioned, and its merits in this connection are so apparent, that in any new building no other form of illumination is now ever considered.
Lighting, however, is only a beginning, and it is the many other uses in the home to which electricity may be applied which are to make it the real boon to the housewife of which she is so much in need.
Cooking.—I know I am preaching largely to the converted, but it may be said again that electric cooking is carried on under more pleasant conditions than with any other method. No longer do we cook the cook, no longer is her health endangered by the inhalation of deleterious fumes, and no longer is the food cooked in what may be a poisonous atmosphere. These new conditions should weigh greatly with educated and intelligent people, and much more so than the comparative costs, although even these are now quite favourable to electricity.
Heating.—Electric heating bases its claims on convenience, portability of appliances, and cleanliness. It gives out a warm, cheerful glow—creates no smell—

person_entry: President of the Incorporated Municipal Electrical Association
Unnamed: 5: President of the Incorporated Municipal Electrical Association
Unnamed: 9: Welcomes women attending the Convention meetings in Glasgow in 1926.
transcription:
14	The Electrical Age

now 2,000 cookers and nearly 8,000 fires on hire in the city.

Mention must also be made of the work in the city of the Scottish Branch of the Electrical Association for Women.

It is very desirable that women, interested in and aware of the benefit to be derived from the use of electricity, should become familiarised with the devices which are used in ordinary installation work and have a general idea of its generation at the power station, and its transmission and distribution to the consumers.

The fear of this mysterious force, which we call electricity, which has been so common in the past, especially among women, has to be got rid of, and it is only by means of such Associations as the Electrical Association for Women that we can hope, within a reasonable time, to bring this about.

I have been very pleased to learn of the enthusiastic way in which the women of Glasgow have taken up this new enterprise.

Thanks in great measure to an energetic secretariat, the membership is now approaching the two-hundredth mark. Much has been done in the way of lectures and demonstrations to instil that knowledge and create that familiarity with what has been termed this beneficent fairy which comes into the house, does its work silently and unseen, and leaves just as silently.

I have every confidence that it may be during the Convention week, and more certain during next Winter season, the membership of the Scottish Branch will be largely increased. I trust that the example set by London and Glasgow will be followed in many other parts of the country.

To conclude, it may be said that twenty-five years ago electricity was a luxury only to be enjoyed by the rich and well-to-do—the ordinary householder could not afford it. To-days conditions are very different. It has now come to be a necessity, and ordinary people cannot afford to be without it. If we are not ready yet for the quite smokeless city and the automatic home, yet there is no reason why our wives and their helpers should not at once be relieved of at least half of their worries and dirty work by means of electricity. The means exist to-day, and anyone living in this, and many other cities, who can afford a house, can afford a partly electrified one.

As time goes on, and electricity supply is extended over all parts of the country, it will be within the reach of everyone.

Someone has said that in a few more years it will only be the very rich—if any are left—who can afford to be without an electrified home.

As president of the Incorporated Municipal Electrical Association, I have to extend a very hearty welcome to women attending the Convention meetings in Glasgow. I trust that they will have a very enjoyable time and that the Womens Meeting to be held on the afternoon of Thursday, 17th June, will be a great success.

Snippet from Glasgow.

Some little time ago, a few cooking experiments were carried out by a gentleman who used to say that with an electric cooker in one hand and a decent recipe book in the other, no man need starve.

The results of the meat-cooking experiments in his fairly large household proved that after a slight increase in the consumption of meat per person per day (when the cooker was new), the portions fell slowly to about 10 per cent. decrease on the former consumption and remained at that, which seemed to indicate that there was more nourishment in electrically cooked meat; therefore, a smaller portion sufficed for the individual need.

Unnamed: 9: Author of the article How Electricity is Made. Part 1.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 15
How Electricity is Made. Part 1.—The Power Station
By J. W. Beauchamp, M.I.E.E.

There are, perhaps, few of the great natural agents enlisted in the service of man concerning the nature of which we really know less than is the case with electricity. More and more we realise to-day that individual knowledge must, to a large extent, be limited to starting where others have left off, and that in most of the activities of life we can have little more than an intelligent comprehension of the way to handle or employ the resources of modern science, leaving to the specialist such actual knowledge of their way and being as is so far available.

Everyone to-day is interested in electricity and no one need be entirely without an accurate, if superficial, knowledge of the way in which it is produced, distributed and used—in fact, a little knowledge of that kind is essential to a clear understanding of the economic laws which govern its sale and purchase.

Incidentally, the pursuit of this knowledge is doing a great deal to bring about a more correct appreciation of the use and abuse of light, heat and mechanical power, a knowledge becoming more valuable and important to the welfare of the individual and of the community year by year as life becomes more complicated, civilised communities more dense and the struggle to get the last ounce out of every expenditure more keen.

ELECTRICITY FROM COAL.
Broadly, it may be stated, at least so far as these islands are concerned, that electricity is made from coal, the amount of water power is small and employment of gas or oil for the production of electric power is quite limited.

Dismissing for the moment the potential power of falling water, the tides, or the wind, our great reserve lies in the deposits of coal, the most abundant and powerful of fuels available to us.

The modern system of producing and using electrical energy on a large scale for artificial lighting, heating, cooking food, driving machinery, trains, carrying out industrial processes of any kind, is based upon discoveries made early in the last century which brought to light the fact that mechanical power and electricity are mutually convertible, that a machine of a very simple character, generally referred to as "dynamo" or "generator," could be made to produce a continuous flow of electrical energy if it were driven by some suitable engine, water-fall or other source of power and that similarly such a machine supplied with a continuous flow of electrical energy would produce a reverse effect, that is to say act or rotate, giving off power which in its turn could be applied to driving other machines.

Now for us the most efficient method of driving these large dynamos or generators of electricity is by means of steam engines or steam turbines; this brings us back to the consumption of coal in the furnaces of boilers to provide the necessary steam and we perceive the complete chain of process from the heat of burning coal under the boiler to the heat given off by the electric cooker in a consumers house. We have, however, with the electrical energy supplied to the consumer the immense facility that he or she can at will make it appear or serve either as artificial light, heat for any purpose, or as power for driving a machine which may vary in size and capacity from the unit necessary to work a sewing machine up to the most powerful electric motor as employed to drive a train or operate a large factory.

This flexibility and the ability to convert

Unnamed: 9: Author providing suggestions for bringing lighting schemes up to date.
transcription:
18
The Electrical Age
Light for the Modern Home
Some Suggestions for Bringing Lighting Schemes Up-to-date
By Florence Hodge
The woman of to-day, however "advanced"
she may be, still possesses a goodly supply
of house-pride. Probably she keeps it tucked
away at the back of the top shelf in her
mental store cupboard, not labelled for all
the world to see, but quietly and surely
holding its own with all her other varied
interests. Apart from the joy of possession
natural to every woman whose home is the
centre of her life, there is the ambition to
create a home which is not merely a reflec-
tion of good taste in the choice of furniture
and decorations, but which also gives subtle
evidence of the owners personality. The
setting which she has chosen for the stage of
her life is one in which she needs to appear
at her best; being vain, but wise at the same
time, she will welcome any addition to
comfort and beauty that may come within
her reach. Such additions may be obtained
at little financial outlay through a careful
consideration of the possibilities of light as a
contribution to the home beautiful.
To many housewives the possession of
electric light means a form of illumination
which, from the point of view of cleanliness
and convenience, is a vast improvement on
previous methods. Beyond that-well-its
advantages are not outstandingly obvious;
in fact, it might even be criticised on account
of its harsh brilliancy and cause a sigh of
regret for the days of soft, mellow light
which, though inefficient, was at least a more
kind and sympathetic light. The fact that
electric light, of all forms of illumination, is
the most adaptable has not been brought to
the notice of the average housewife, and she
does not realise that the longed-for "kind"
light can be obtained just as well with
electric light as with the mediæval candle;
not only light which deals equally well with
complexions and the favourite colour
scheme, but one which will give bright light
just when and where it is wanted without
any disconcerting glare.
With the aid of broad vision, a touch of
imagination and a few fundamental and
common sense lighting rules, much may be
done to create light in a home which is an
integral part of its comfort and beauty, and
at the same time a fitting background for
the woman whose artistic hand has at last
touched the medium of light.
The room which more than any other
invites the touch of the lighting artist is the
drawing-room or lounge. With its multi-
plicity of uses as a modern living-room, it
calls for an illumination which fulfils the re-
quirements of many and diverse occupations.
The housewife whose critical lighting eye is
well opened to the defects of her own lighting
system will probably find that the present
installation is limited in two ways; either it
is too bright or too gloomy. We can
imagine a typical system obviously installed
with a minimum amount of imagination.
We are all familiar with the "electrolier"
type of fitting with a varying number of
arms spread out to make the best (or worst)
of some clear glass electric lamps of uncom-
fortable brilliancy, and an attempt at
decoration with clear glass shades which do
not lessen the glare from the lamps. Of
course, it is an indisputable fact that the
light directly underneath this type of fitting
is bright enough for any purpose, but one is
not always seated under a fitting, and when
one finds the chair at the fire-side more
inviting the trouble starts. Needlework or
a book has to be held at a certain angle to

Unnamed: 9: Author of a series of articles on home lighting topics.
transcription:
20 The Electrical Age

said, and a later article will deal more fully with it.
In the language of illumination, the lighting obtained from an electrolier type of fitting is called "direct"; that is, light which falls from the lamp directly on to the object to be illuminated. Other forms of lighting, "indirect" and "semi-indirect," are often preferred, but certain conditions are necessary for their complete success. The principle of both these methods is that the lamp, the actual source of light, is hidden, and the rays of light are sent on to some reflecting medium and from thence diffused throughout the room. A practical application for the drawing-room is the use of a decorative bowl—popular taste trends towards those of alabaster or treated glass ware, hung a few feet from the ceiling with one large lamp suspended above it but hidden by the bowl itself. By this means, the light from the lamp is directed upwards so that ceiling and walls, provided they are light in colour, act as reflecting mediums and illuminate the whole room. Here is the ideal "kind" light, but one which may become monotonous in effect if not relieved by other lighting touches, and it is now that the portable lamp comes into its own and proves its worth. Especially to the woman of many moods, and the exception is not the rule in this case, will they make an irresistible appeal. Is it not reasonable to expect that a woman expressing a change of mood by a change of dress should not also change her room as a suitable background for any particular mood; and the easiest and most effective way to transform the appearance of a room is with the use of an adaptable lighting scheme. A quiet mood will require an atmosphere of restfulness, and a floor standard or table lamp standing out as a glowing touch of colour in its own radiant circle of light, undoubtedly satisfies such a mood.
Of the many types of portable lamps, mention may be made of one which gives very useful service both as decorative addition and as practical means of general

lighting, apart from the usual local illumination demanded from a portable lamp. In the accompanying diagram it will be seen that by an ingenious arrangement of a single lamp within a scientifically designed reflector, light is radiated downwards for reading or working, and upwards on to the ceiling and walls, and thus acts as an indirect lighting

REFLECTOR WHITE LAMP
DIFFUSING BOWL— SILK SHADE

DIAGRAM OF INDIRECT LIGHTING FITTING

fitting. The shade is shown to the very best advantage, for it veritably glows with light and has not the patchy effect which results when a single lamp shows as a point of light through the silk.

NOTE.—This is the first of a series of articles by Miss Hodge on Home Lighting. The second article will appear in the September issue.— Ed., "E. A."

transcription:
22 The Electrical Age
E. A. W. Luncheon at the Hotel Cecil, June 4th, 1926
Nearly three hundred persons sat down to the luncheon arranged by the E.A.W. to celebrate its first birthday.
Amongst those present were many outstanding figures, including the Right Hon. Lt.-Col. Wilfrid Ashley, M.P. (Minister of Transport) and Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, Lady Cowan, Sir Hugo Hirst, Bart. (Chairman, General Electric Co.) and Lady Hirst, Lady Brooks (President, Birmingham and Midlands Branch, E.A.W.), Mr. R. P. Sloan (Chairman, Newcastle-on-Tyne Electric Supply Co., and President of the British Electrical Developments Association), Alderman Mrs. Hammer (Chairman, E.A.W., and Vice-Chairman, Hackney Electricity Committee), Mr. Chattock (President of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, and City Electrical Engineer, Birmingham) and Mrs. Chattock, Major-General Sir Philip Nash (Chairman, Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical Co.), Lady Snell (Vice-President, E.A.W.), Mr. J. H. Stephens (British Thomson-Houston Co.), Mr. Ll. B. Atkinson (Cablemakers Association) and Mrs. Ll. B. Atkinson, the Hon. Lady Shelley-Rolls, the Earl of Bective, Mr. Cramb (Hon. Secretary, Incorporated Municipal Electrical Association), Mr. J. W. Beauchamp (Director, British Electrical Developments Association), Mrs. George Cadbury (Vice-President, E.A.W.), Mr. Blake (President, Batti-Wallah Society), Mr. Elgar (Electrical Contractors Association), Mr. G. W. Sully (Electric Lamp Manufacturers Association), Mrs. M. L. Matthews (Vice-President, E.A.W.), Mrs. I. E. Bray; the company being made up of E.A.W. members from all parts of the country.
The chair was taken by Lady Cowan, a Vice-President of the Association, in place of the President (the Viscountess Astor, M.P.) who was unable to be present.
The Right Hon. Lt.-Col. Wilfrid Ashley, M.P. (Minister of Transport), in proposing the toast, Electricity in the Service of Women, said:—
Lady Cowan, Ladies and Gentlemen,—I understand that the baby, The Electrical Association of Women, is only eighteen months old. Well, when I look round this big dining-room and see the hundreds of ladies and gentlemen who have come to attend the first annual banquet, I must say that I am almost afraid of the dimensions which this luncheon will assume in four or five years time.
Seriously, ladies and gentlemen, it is most gratifying to all those associated with this movement that in so short a time, under circumstances referred to by Lady Cowan of general strikes and coal strikes, so vast an assembly should have come together on a Friday afternoon to further the excellent objects of this Association.
Your Association has been very active in the few months since its inception. It has branches in Manchester, Birmingham, Glasgow; you are extending your services to South Wales, and by speeches and lectures you are putting to the women of Great Britain that electricity in the home is the hope of the housewife. Above all, you are not connected with any trade organisation and, thank God, you are not political—(hear, hear). It is so pleasant to speak to a non-political organisation, because political organisations in their essence must be partial and obviously must see only one side of the case. A politician who could see both sides of the case would cease to be a politician.
So I come here this afternoon greatly honoured by your invitation to say a few words to a large number of experts on electricity. When I see the distinguished gentlemen connected with the electrical industry seated on my right hand and seated on my left hand; when I have Lady Snell, the wife of the Chairman of the Electricity Commission, on my right, then I feel I am greatly daring when I venture to say a few words on electricity to all these experts. But I

The Electrical Age 23

hope and trust there are many ladies and gentlemen in this audience who are as ignorant of electricity as I am, and, therefore, the subsequent speeches of the electrical experts will be a liberal education to us.
Electricity, as far as commerce is concerned, as far as public utilities are concerned, can, I think, as in the past, be not inappropriately left mainly to the male sex. But in the home, obviously woman has always reigned supreme, should reign supreme, and will, even with the spread of womans rights, always remain the predominant factor. Therefore, what we have got to do, or what you are doing, is to ensure that the women in this country appreciate the advantages of electricity and electrical gadgets in the household.
In connection with this, generation of electricity is important, but I think the experts will agree with me that merchandising, the selling of the electricity when generated, is of equal importance. That is where I respectfully suggest that we in this country have not pushed that branch as well as, let us say, in America. We have been largely content in this country to generate the electricity, to say, "Here is power, here is current," and hope the consumers will come. That is not, in my opinion, the way to approach it. You ought to generate your electricity, and then go out into the highways and byways, and by propaganda, by articles in the Press, by Associations such as yours, appeal to them to come in, appeal to the housewives to buy, point out the advantage of electrical apparatus from the health, cleanliness and labour-saving point of view—(applause). The more extended use of electricity in the home will certainly show the housewife how to be happy though servantless.
Lady Cowan, who has just returned from America, will, I am sure, bear me out when I say that electricity in the home is a commonplace in America and in Canada, and is an exception, unfortunately, in this country. There is no reason why it should be an exception in this country. We are just as progressive, just as enlightened as any other country in the world, and it is only because we are super-cautious in approach to new subjects that we are lagging behind.
In this respect, I think the electrical industry can learn a good deal from the gas industry. The gas industry in this country has shown great initiative in pushing its wares, given great advantages to the consumer, and the hire system apparatus can be secured. Let the electrical industry do the same, and I am sure the advantages of an all-electric home will be so obvious, that, electricity for heating, electricity for lighting, electricity for cooking will be far more extensively used than it is at the present day.
With respect to America, I came across this quotation from The Landmark the other day—"I understood the whole of America better after I had seen a fireless cooker, an electric sweeper and a dish-washer, and a washing, drying and ironing installation. I realised in one moment why American women can do their own house-work, wear beautifully pressed skirts, and go to lectures with manicured nails"—(applause).
That is true. If you have an electric fire, you do not dirty your hands. You have cleanliness. You have an even temperature in the room if somebody is ill. You can turn it on or turn it off with no trouble. Think what it means to lay a coal fire, and above all—if you are a man—to light it. I remember when I was a fag at Harrow, the harrowing and agonizing whacks I got from my fag master because I could not light his fire—I had no fire of my own to light! I was all thumbs.
Women can light a fire, and keep it alight if the husband is there to put the coals on and to remember about keeping the fire in, but though you can light this coal fire it is a great trouble. It is very dirty and the electrical fire is immeasurably superior.
THE ELECTRICITY BILL.
We have before the House of Commons now a Bill to improve the supply of electricity to the people of this country. Some such

Unnamed: 9: Lady Cowan, Vice-President of E.A.W., speaks about womens service.
transcription:
24
The Electrical Age
measure, all are agreed, has been necessary for years past. All are not agreed as to the wisdom of all the provisions in this Bill. It would be strange if everybody did agree, because in so complex an industry, in an industry which has now been established firmly in this country for twenty or twenty-five years there must be diversities of opinion as to the best way of approaching this very, very important subject; because whatever diversity of opinion there may be, all are agreed, I think, that the approaching age will be the Electrical Age. All are agreed, I think, in broad principles that we are lagging behind, in this country, our chief commercial competitors, in consumption per head of the population. That is wrong. We cannot afford in this country to give away one ounce of weight to any of our commercial competitors. We have a hard fight before us in this country to maintain our overseas trade. We have keen commercial rivals, who are doing their best to take away from us that overseas trade by which we must live and move and have our being.
Therefore, everything that can be done to help our manufacturers to secure easier weapons for our working classes must be an object which should be supported by all of us, and I would appeal to those who do not see eye to eye with all the provisions of the Bill to let me know what are their main objections, and having done that to try and co-operate in putting this Bill through, which is going to be put through, in the best possible form, and to endeavour to bring this Bill to an Act of Parliament at the earliest possible moment. Because, remember this, the longer the discussion of this Bill lasts, the longer must be the uncertainty in the electrical industry in this country, which is not good for the electrical industry and is not good for the country as a whole. The Government is not unreasonable. The main principles of the Bill must be preserved, but any alteration which may be proved to be good we are quite willing to consider, and should welcome the whole-hearted co-operation of anybody or any body of institutes
who are concerned in this great and important measure—(cheers).
Lady Cowan (Vice-President, E.A.W.).
—Service with women has grown up with women, and as womans services for the men and for the world are as old as the Garden of Eden, the whole idea of service in a womans life has become embodied even in the legends and sagas of our own race.
So that we women are well accustomed to the idea of service in that way, but it is left to these later days to find that the great forces of Nature are being commandeered for the first time in the service of women, and that we are for the first time in the history of civilisation in control of a tremendous power and energy which, if properly directed and utilised, will not only ease the burden of womens lives but of the weary lives of the vast majority of workers, not only in this country but throughout the whole world.
England has always been a leader, and often the leader, in the great unfolding and in the great amelioration and progress of the human race, but, as Colonel Ashley has just told us, we have somehow lagged behind, particularly in the development of electrical appliances and mechanical devices, and have been outstripped in the race in this particular development by other countries, and even by the daughter States of our own Empire.
I think that this Association is going to do an immense deal to make up that leeway, and is going to give that necessary encouragement to patriotic-minded manufacturers by creating a demand for these mechanical and electrical devices, for the want of which we are suffering so much in our homes to-day.
England has always been a pioneer, and the splendid spirit of our race, I feel sure, is not going to leave us at a moment when it is almost imperative that we should come up with the other nations, not only in order to assure greater leisure for ourselves, but that opportunity which is not granted to the vast majority of women of enjoying those legiti-

mate pleasures which life surely is intended
to provide for us all.
Having returned recently from Canada
and America, and with the impressions which
I received there still very fresh in my mind,
I realise to what an extent electricity is used
there in the homes of the people. I am fired
with a great ambition to bring about in the
homes of this country the same state of
things, and to emulate our sisters overseas,
so that we can also get provision of these
good things. We keep hoping, and I think
that we are now, through the interest which
women are beginning to show, as evidenced
by this great gathering here to-day, much
nearer realising the dream of an all-electric
house, which is a common form in Canada
and the United States.
I saw in my travels in Canada and the
United States, electricity used in the home
and in everyday life to an extent which
would be surprising to many of us here. We
are accustomed to use electricity for amuse-
ments here; we have our electrically pro-
pelled piano player, our wireless, our means
of communication through the telephone,
but we do not really realise here how it can
ease us in our homes and lighten our
burdens, and I am determined to do all in my
power to increase and to popularise the use
of electrical devices in our homes. What is
called "help" is very scarce on the other side
of the Atlantic, and necessity became the
mother of invention with them. It became
absolutely necessary, because of the shortage
of domestic service in the homes of the
Canadians and Americans, to create a
species of electrical robots to perform the
work of the homes.
Not only do we find these electrical robots
in the houses of the wealthy and of the well-
to-do middle classes in the trans-Atlantic
Republic and in her sister state, the Dominion
of Canada, but we find these labour-saving
apparatus in the humble homes of the
working men. I have seen them myself.
No Canadian or American woman would
dream of lighting, tending and minding a
coal fire, blackleading the grate, and clean-
ing the flues. Nor yet would she dream of
using her own muscular energy in washing,
ironing or sweeping.
The woman in the Canadian home sits
down to her ironing with a smiling face. She
puts the clothes into an up-to-date washing
machine, and adds water and soap. She
presses a button and puts the lid on, and
goes away to attend one of these lectures or
one of those very attractive concerts at
11 oclock in the morning (at which I have
also had the pleasure of being present), and
comes back to find her washing done.
She sits down to do the ironing, with a
smiling face, at a wonderful ironing machine.
The tablecloths, pillow-cases and sheets drop
into a basket on the other side, and she has
finished her ironing without any fatigue
whatever.
The days of "blessed be drudgery" are
ended for our American and Canadian
friends. Here the woman does the work.
There she presses a button, and electricity
does the rest. That is one of the reasons why
the workers in America and Canada are so
much happier, more prosperous and con-
tented than here, because they have less
drudgery and more time and leisure for
outdoor life and for those amusements and
pleasures which are their legitimate right.
It is because I firmly believe that this
association of women for the propaganda
work in electrical appliances and labour-
saving devices is going to be a success, is
going to lighten and ease the burdens of the
women in this country, that I have great
pleasure in responding to the toast proposed
by Colonel Ashley, to whom we owe a deep
debt of gratitude as Minister in charge of the
Bill which is going through the Committee
stage of the House of Commons to-day, and
to whom we look to be the herald of that
millennium of feminine emancipation from
drudgery, to which we look forward with
such unspeakable relief—(applause).
Sir Hugo Hirst, Bart., proposing the
toast, The Electrical Association for Women.

26                                     The Electrical Age

made it easy for me to propose this toast, which I am sure you will receive with approbation. They have enumerated the various activities with which your Association can occupy itself in the future. I need not do it again. You are going to see this afternoon a number of appliances more than have been enumerated.

I really think Colonel Ashley asked a question which he forgot to answer. He said, “Why is it that the Americans and Canadians are so much ahead?” I always hate the reproach being made to the British manufacturer. I always feel that I must stand up and make an excuse. If a country has a system of electricity supply that embraces some forty or fifty systems, it is impossible for the manufacturer to go into mass production, and therefore it is equally impossible for the supply of goods to be cheap enough. Whilst, therefore, on the one hand current is not supplied as cheaply as it could be supplied under certain conditions, and whilst the apparatus cannot be manufactured as cheaply as might be under other conditions, the manufacturer cannot accept the blame. That is why, I believe, Colonel Ashley is busy with this Electricity Bill. We wish him every success. I am one of those who welcomed his Bill, and I am certain, in due course, it will produce the results that we all hope and that are so important to this Association.

Men are not properly qualified to sell all the apparatus in a domestic home for utility and for comfort to the ladies of the house. Man never understood woman, and will not understand her now. It requires a woman to get at the heart of another woman for this purpose. Look at our drapery establishments ; they always employ women to sell bargains to other women.

I feel, however, in proposing the toast of this Association, that I might strike one serious note. This is not going to be a mere question of selling. It is going to be a question of service. I feel the embryo of a new science is showing itself, which I call domestic engineering science. I think your members, if they are to reap the opportunities which have been held out by Lady Cowan, will have to go in for a serious training, studying not only the way to use but the characteristics of those machines which are doing service in the house, be they refrigerators or washing machines, or dishwashers or sewing machines. They have to give constant service, and a staff of people—whether independently, attached to manufacturers or distributors, or at central stations—a staff of ladies will be wanted in due course.

I feel almost it requires, as I have said on a previous occasion, some kind of institution, may be university, may be technical college, to disseminate the knowledge necessary for that purpose. I am certain, if you look at it from that point of view, if you take your objective seriously, you will find opportunity for remunerative employment, not only in the way of salesmanship, but in other respects.

The servant question, so pronounced in America, is going to be no less pronounced, in due course, in this country. Women in the future will have to take a great deal more interest in their domestic household affairs than they did in the past. They will want this labour-saving apparatus, not only to do good service, to be easily cleaned, but to be ornamental, and the knowledge which you gain by contact with the housewife is wanted in the business houses and the factories in which these articles are produced. I see opportunities for employment coming in that direction.

I am satisfied you are going the right way to work. The women of England helped us to win the war, and they will do a big part in the reconstruction of our social life in the future. You are on the way to doing your share towards it. You have not only given a wonderful report of last years activity, but I feel confident that you will succeed under the Presidency of Lady Astor, under the Vice-Presidency of Lady Cowan, and under

a Chairman for a local section like Lady Brooks.
It is my privilege, Lady Brooks, to couple your name with the toast. As a manufacturer in Birmingham, I have known of the activities of Lady Brooks for a great many years. Anything that has been for the advancement, the betterment, the social condition of almost any grade of society which affects women, Lady Brooks has given a leading and helping hand to.
I feel you will be certain of the success you wish, and I hope that this assembly will rise to join me in wishing you that success.
Lady Brooks, C.B.E., J.P., responding, said: I feel that we are exceedingly lucky in this Association in having such splendid women to go forward in the early days of the movement. We owe these pioneer women an intense debt of gratitude for the work that they have done, and I think that we ought to be grateful that an Association like this has come into being at such a psychological moment as that of to-day. I do not think we could have come into being at a better moment, for I think, perhaps, one of our greatest difficulties is going to be that of eagerness. Everyone seems just to be bursting to go forward and to help, and therefore my one thought that I want to go out this afternoon is that of patience and co-operation. Those two thoughts are going to help us all enormously if our men friends will back us in the way that they give promise of doing, and as I am sure they will. If we help headquarters in a loyal and steadfast way, as we should, I feel sure that the Association is going to help enormously the whole country.
Alderman Mrs. Hammer, in proposing the toast, Our Guests, thanked all those who had helped to celebrate the first official birthday of the Association.
The picture of the all-electric house was not quite unique, she said, even in England. There were many of them for the working woman as well as for the middle class woman.

R. P. Sloan, Esq., C.B.E., M.I.E.E., in response, expressed his strong desire as President of the Incorporated Association of Electric Power Companies, that some legislation should be put through, provided it was on proper lines. He had been accused of obstructionism, but his opposition was constructive and not destructive opposition. It was necessary for the success of this country that some Bill should go through Parliament, but it would be disastrous if it were not on the proper lines. One of the greatest disadvantages under which they had laboured in this country had been an excessive legislation. Since the 1919 Act was passed, they had had no less than five Electricity Bills before Parliament, including the present one. This had meant that the industry had been living under very uncertain and indefinite conditions for all that time, which had led to difficulties in raising capital.
They did not want interference with private enterprise. This industry owed a great deal to private enterprise, and if the Bill were passed into law in its present form, it would hamper instead of helping development.

VISIT TO METRO-VICK SHOWROOMS
A happy termination to the first days birthday party was a visit to the beautifully designed new showrooms of the Metro-Vick Electrical Co. A delightful and dainty tea had been arranged by Mr. Crinks (the Managing Director), who welcomed the large company of visitors. Great interest was shown in the up-to-date domestic electrical equipment on view.

R. P. Sloan, Esq., C.B.E., M.I.E.E., in response, expressed his strong desire as President of the Incorporated Association of Electric Power Companies, that some legislation should be put through, provided it was on proper lines. He had been accused of obstructionism, but his opposition was constructive and not destructive opposition. It was necessary for the success of this country that some Bill should go through Parliament, but it would be disastrous if it were not on the proper lines. One of the greatest disadvantages under which they had laboured in this country had been an excessive legislation. Since the 1919 Act was passed, they had had no less than five Electricity Bills before Parliament, including the present one. This had meant that the industry had been living under very uncertain and indefinite conditions for all that time, which had led to difficulties in raising capital.
They did not want interference with private enterprise. This industry owed a great deal to private enterprise, and if the Bill were passed into law in its present form, it would hamper instead of helping development.

The Electrical Age

Electrical Refrigeration of Food
By Kilowatt

The refrigeration of food comes down to us through the centuries from the time when Alexander the Great stored wines in snow-filled trenches.
The need for keeping food cold in Summer led to the use of ice blocks for the purpose, which were brought from Polar and other regions, until the production of ice in factories made it more accessible.
An advance upon this procedure was the production of ice at home, and a Frenchman, Abbe Audiffren, in 1900, is supposed to have designed the first electric refrigerator for this purpose.
A refrigerator may be regarded as a cold cupboard for the preservation of food at constant low and unvarying temperature. In a mild, damp atmosphere such as ours, food spoils quickly through the action of bacteria ; but between 45o and freezing point germs cease to exist, and food kept at these low temperatures is thus preserved in a scientific manner.
Electrical refrigeration is entirely automatic ; you have only to switch on. It requires no other attention.
There will shortly be restrictions in the use of chemical preservatives in food, and "cold" as a preserving agent will be in great demand both at producing factories, wholesale distributors and at the consumers premises also. Refrigerators in the home will come into more general use, and as the food will be untainted by harmful chemicals, the result will eventually be manifest in better health of the nation.
Very large ice-making plants are needed for the cold storage of meat, fish, fruit and eggs, and on ships for the ocean carriage of food of all descriptions.
Complete temperature control of these large plants is very important, as different food products require different temperatures for their satisfactory preservation. Bananas, for instance, need a temperature of 50o F., while oranges and citrus fruit in general
require from 38o to 45o F. Apples and pears need 27o to 29.5o F., and eggs between 31o and 35o F., just over the freezing point, which for eggs is 30.8o F. Eggs, therefore, are "chilled," not actually frozen.
In the Spring of 1925, in addition to all the imported eggs, there were three million British eggs put into cold storage for delivery in Autumn and Winter. There is

also the fish industry, which has large cold storage plants.
The main interest to women in electrical refrigeration is, of course, in the home equipment, how it works and how much does it cost. The working is perfectly simple, you switch on and that is all. The cost of running a modern equipment is very low. In a typical refrigerator the current consumed is 300 watts an hour. Eight hours operation a day would be sufficient for the general house requirement of cold storage, therefore 2.5 units of electricity per day would be the total cost of having all your food kept fresh and preserved, and having as much ice available as you are likely to need.

Electric Cooking
Some Dainty Dishes. The Modern Way for the Maidless Mistress.
By Mary MacKirdy (College of Domestic Science, Glasgow).

The virtues of the electric cooker still fascinate me; its cleanliness, itself, surroundings, and its pans no dirtier than ordinary dishes; and above all these outstanding advantages, there is the housekeeper at the end of a morning in the kitchen fresh and without that feeling of limpness which almost invariably follows cooking.

Quick Savoury Dishes in the Oven.
A Meat Dish:
Switch on the oven to “full” for about twenty minutes, then to medium. While the oven is heating, have ready a thick piece of tender steak, such as is used for grilling or frying (it should be about 1 1/2 inches thick), put it under the grill, cooking one side only for five minutes.
Spread a fireproof dish with butter, set the steak on it (cooked side down), put a piece of butter on top and put into oven.
When it has had time to firm on surface, pipe round it, using a large rose pipe, sieved cooked potatoes mixed with a piece of butter, salt, pepper and enough beaten egg to moisten slightly. Place so that they form a garnish, some tiny tomatoes; continue the cooking.
The steak taking in all about twelve minutes.
Serve very hot on the dish on which it was cooked.

A Casserole of Vegetables.
A variety of vegetables may be used for this dish.
The following make a good mixture:— Onions cut in thin slices, carrots and turnips

A delightful dish, and especially so with new vegetables.

A Savoury Dish of Fish.
Spread a fireproof or aluminium dish thickly with butter, and place on it a whole haddock that has been skinned and boned but with the shape preserved.
Place some strips of fat bacon over it and bake for fifteen to twenty minutes, according to size.
A few minutes before serving, arrange some small or halved tomatoes round, and complete the cooking. Sprinkle with finely chopped parsley, and serve hot.

A cut of cod or other fish might be substituted for haddock; a Finnan is excellent done this way. Another way—this is not quite so speedy, but is particularly good.
Pour some good tomato sauce over the fish, bake, then serve with a little more sauce poured over and parsley sprinkled on. In this case the bacon is omitted.

transcription:
34 The Electrical Age

A Page for Girl Guides

When The Light Failed

By Margaret Partridge, B.Sc.

"And the wicked fairy flew away, and they all lived--" Phip!--Darkness--right in the middle of the story.
There is something remarkable, almost uncanny, about the sudden silent change from light to dark when electric service fails. Gas, oil, candles, all show signs of distress--sputterings, flickerings or gradual fading away--which robs the sudden plunge to darkness of much of its impressiveness ; but when electric light fails, it does it so suddenly

DISMANTLED LAMP-HOLDER

that it is not unusual for weak-nerved people to scream and lose their heads.
Not so, of course, the well-trained guide or amateur electrician. She will not dash for outside help, nor will she sit patiently suffering in the dark. She will don her thinking cap and start reasoning something in this wise. "Something is wrong or the light would not have failed. How wrong? Is it the whole town, the whole street, the whole house, part of the house, or this room only ?"
A little investigation will soon answer this question, and in nearly every case it will be either about half-a-dozen lights off or just the one room. If it is in one room only, the question is where is the fault--in lamp, holder, flex, ceiling rose or switch.
The lamp is the weakest link in our chain, so that is where we may expect the fault first. Try another lamp, and if it is found that this lights, inspect the old one for a broken filament. Sometimes it is possible to get an old lamp to work again by tipping it and tapping it gently till the broken filaments fall across each other. It seldom lives long after this treatment, and it burns with an increased brilliancy for the remainder of its life, but it is interesting to try.
If the lamp is not the sinner, we must inspect the lamp-holder, with the switch off. It is possible that the spring of the plungers is weak with old age or some other cause, and is not butting hard against the back of the lamp.
If lamp and holder are both all right, take the cap of the switch off and inspect it with care. If contacts are bad, or a screw has shaken loose, it will be quite clearly seen on inspection.
If neither lamp nor holder nor switch are at fault, re-wire the holder with a new piece of flex, or take off the old piece, examine it and re-clean the ends and re-connect. The illustration shows clearly how this can be done. Make sure the screws are in tightly and the ends of the flex are cleaned of all insulation and screwed up tightly, and that no stray bits of copper wire are left loose, likely to wander out of the terminal hole in which they are meant to be.
Now suppose that several lights have gone out. The secondary reason has to be sought for in the fuse box, where the fuse will be found to have melted. The primary reason needs a little consideration. A melted fuse indicates one of two things--either too heavy a current (say, too big a piece of

The Electrical Age
Artificial Sunlight for Babies
By Len Chaloner

Sunshine is as important an agent as food in the building of the proverbial " bonnie babies." It is scarcely less important for the mother in the months before her baby is born. Largely is it due in fact to the wealth of sunshine in certain parts of Australia that the normal birth-weight of babies there is so much above our own in England. If there were more sunshine we should even have less rickets, less tuberculosis and less anaemia.
That is why the discovery and development of artificial sunlight is so important. It helps to make healthy babies, and healthy mothers, but in addition it is already being found useful in the treatment of diseases, and lesser ailments, to say nothing of the tribulations of obesity.
In the great rays of the spectrum, or sunlight, which are discernable by prism as seven different colours, the most health giving is the ultra violet. It is by means of electrical apparatus that we are able to produce "artificial sunlight," that is that we are able to capture and control the ultra violet rays, regulating and focusing their operations through a special lamp, somewhat after the manner that we are able to use the better known X-ray.
At present the discovery is too new, and too little is known of the diversity of its possible application, for us to use advisedly on our own initiative in the home, as we turn on and off our electric light or avail ourselves of the natural sunlight on a fine day. But assuredly in a by no means remote future, artificial sunlight will come into our everyday home curriculum as naturally as our hot bath.
Meantime, if we wish to see the effect and its actual operation, there is no need to resort to the one-time famous method of "trying it on the dog." We can instead begin with a visit to the Zoological Gardens in Regents Park, where it was tried last winter in the monkey house with great success.
From the little huddled family of previous winters the occupants became speedily transformed into their lively and contented summer selves, merely by reason of the lamp diffusing its ultra violet ray amongst them.
But much more interesting still is a visit to some of the clinics where its effect on babies can be observed. The treatment can of course only be carried out under medical supervision and trained assistance. With due protection for their eyes the babies lie out free from any clothing that could impede the force of the rays, and literally bask in artificial sunlight, filling out their tiny frames and acquiring the firmness and colouring of health day by day. Treatment for the mother before her baby is born is of the same order, and by this means she nourishes not only herself but the child also.
Just as in Switzerland, at the Winter sports resorts, the bright sunshine makes us warm even when the snow is deep beneath our feet, so the artificial sunlight keeps the baby warm, compensating it for clothes, even though the instant it leaves the treatment room it will be wrapped in blankets.
Yet there is no discomfort, no scorching sensation of a heat wave, and nothing to strike terror into the heart of an imaginative child. Only the lamp, diffusing its brilliant light by means of the quartz mercury vapour, or the Tungsten arc, affords us any idea that an immensely important and health-giving treatment is in progress.

The Electrical Age 37

The First Annual General Meeting of
The E.A.W.

This meeting was held at the Hotel Cecil, London, on June 4th, immediately preceding the public luncheon.
Alderman Mrs. Hammer, as chairman, welcomed the members. The first Annual Report of work carried out was submitted by Miss C. Haslett (the director), and the annual accounts by Mrs. I. E. Bray (Hon. Treasurer).
The present Council was re-elected en bloc,
with the addition of Miss Marx (Pioneer Club) and Mrs. Gregory (West Ham Electricity Committee).
After passing a number of resolutions making slight adjustments to the constitution of the Association, the meeting listened to a very interesting address by Mr. J. W. Beauchamp on the Government electricity proposals.

"The day must come when electricity will be for everyone, as the waters of the rivers and the wind of heaven. It should not merely be supplied, but lavished, that men may use it at their will, as the air they breathe."—Emile Zola.

transcription:
40
The Electrical Age
The Social Service of Electricity
By Alderman Mrs. Hammer
Electricity has "made history" fast during the last forty years or so. This new power, as many another great discovery did in the past, has revolutionised the daily life of the people in work, in amusement, in travel, in home life. The great minds of such men as Faraday, Edison, Parsons, Ferranti, and a host of others early visualised and made immediately possible the use of this great power in the service of mankind. They have harnessed this mighty giant and made him obedient to the touch of even a little child.
The events of the last few days must have made many of us realise to a greater extent than before what this social service of electricity is, and to what success its mission has already attained. It has bridged the ocean by telegraph cables.
Space is eliminated by its telephones. It has dotted its mighty power stations over the earth — these "great hearts" with their numberless arteries and articulations; the "power behind the worker" in workshops, factories, mines; the source of energy for lifts, cranes, machines; in answer to a press of the switch, giving light, power, traction; aye, and affecting more intimately the every-day life of the great army of home workers, supplying the energy outside the worker to bake, boil, grill, sweep, wash, iron—slowly but surely eliminating drudgery.
In the railways, electricity is changing and bettering traffic possibilities, and helping much to solve the smoke and fog problems.
For propelling ships, too, electricitys mission is to "wash out" the slavery of the stoke-hole, and "all-electric ships" are increasing in number yearly. To "those who go down to the sea in ships," the wireless S.O.S. has given a new weapon to fight the perils of the deep—thousands of lives are saved every year by its means—and no ship, even thousands of miles from home, need lose touch with the every-day world and its ways, and the whereabouts of the ship need be a mystery no longer. Broadcasting of to-day has ended isolation for ever — if we will it so—for no dweller in the uttermost parts of the earth or sea need be beyond the sound of human voices, and with the phone or loud speaker can obtain amusement and true knowledge hand in hand. What a triumph for the social service of electricity was the broadcasting of the news bulletins just lately when other news distributors were not functioning!
Electricity has lent its aid to the doctor and the surgeon, and wonderful light and other instruments are now being used which save the once necessary exploratory operations and help conserve health and strength. In our hospitals and clinics, electricity now plays a great part in healing the sick. The housing problem of to-day has a great friend in the new labour-saving schemes made possible by electricity. "All-electric houses" have come to stay. Why?
Electricity saves money—no chimneys and flues required. Saves space; women and child welfare problems (urgent problems) are solved by electricity; the new maid in the servantless home; the workers mate in the cottage; the great supply of domestic labour-saving appliances now available is the means by which drudgery may be brought to an end, and time and leisure and energy be left to the mother to keep fit, and through her, the child.
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter—so aptly put by Mr. V. W. Dale. "Electricity in her social service adds one more stone to the eternally growing edifice of human brotherhood."
By courtesy of The Electrician
ALDERMAN MRS. HAMMER

It has dotted its mighty power stations over the earth — these "great hearts" with their numberless arteries and articulations; the "power behind the worker" in workshops, factories, mines; the source of energy for lifts, cranes, machines; in answer to a press of the switch, giving light, power, traction; aye, and affecting more intimately the every-day life of the great army of home workers, supplying the energy outside the worker to bake, boil, grill, sweep, wash, iron—slowly but surely eliminating drudgery.
In the railways, electricity is changing and bettering traffic possibilities, and helping much to solve the smoke and fog problems.
For propelling ships, too, electricitys mission is to "wash out" the slavery of the stoke-hole, and "all-electric ships" are increasing in number yearly. To "those who go down to the sea in ships," the wireless S.O.S. has given a new weapon to fight the perils of the deep—thousands of lives are saved every year by its means—and no ship, even thousands of miles from home, need lose touch with the every-day world and its ways, and the whereabouts of the ship need be a mystery no longer. Broadcasting of to-day has ended isolation for ever — if we will it so—for no dweller in the uttermost parts of the earth or sea need be beyond the sound of human voices, and with the phone or loud speaker can obtain amusement and true knowledge hand in hand. What a triumph for the social service of electricity was the broadcasting of the news bulletins just lately when other news distributors were not functioning!
Electricity has lent its aid to the doctor and the surgeon, and wonderful light and other instruments are now being used which save the once necessary exploratory operations and help conserve health and strength. In our hospitals and clinics, electricity now plays a great part in healing the sick. The housing problem of to-day has a great friend in the new labour-saving schemes made possible by electricity. "All-electric houses" have come to stay. Why?
Electricity saves money—no chimneys and flues required. Saves space; women and child welfare problems (urgent problems) are solved by electricity; the new maid in the servantless home; the workers mate in the cottage; the great supply of domestic labour-saving appliances now available is the means by which drudgery may be brought to an end, and time and leisure and energy be left to the mother to keep fit, and through her, the child.
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter—so aptly put by Mr. V. W. Dale. "Electricity in her social service adds one more stone to the eternally growing edifice of human brotherhood."
By courtesy of The Electrician
ALDERMAN MRS. HAMMER
