MRS. WILFRID ASHLEY
As one of the Vice-Presidents of the Electrical Association for Women, I feel that women have a new sphere of usefulness placed in their hands—a new branch of knowledge with which to occupy their minds, and yet another method of displaying their desire to further public service.
In these days women have equal chances with men to be pioneers, and in matters pertaining to the development of electricity in home life, their help and co-ordination are essential. Their desire for labour-saving devices, through the medium of electricity, should provide the impetus—if such an impetus is necessary—towards the application and further practical use of this great and as yet little developed power.

46 The Electrical Age

The All-Electric Home
Practical Hints to the Housewife

By Gladys F. Sharp

In view of the fact that the heating of water is so important, I think that any hints on how to do this, electrically, in the most economical way, will be acceptable to the housewife with the all-electric home who wishes to keep her bills down to an absolute minimum.
I expect it will come as a distinct surprise to the majority of housewives to hear that water for almost all washing-up can be heated without any cost at all. It certainly sounds impossible, but here is my hint.
For a hot meal you will almost certainly have your oven and, at least, one hotplate in operation for a considerable time. When you have switched these off ready for serving up the meal, put in the oven a bowl, as big as possible, of cold water. On each hotplate that you have used, place a good-sized saucepan, also full of cold water. You will be surprised to find when you come to wash-up that the water in the utensils is quite hot, certainly hotter than you can bear your hand in—and all without any current being consumed.
My second hint is with regard to the heating of water for cooking boiled puddings, green vegetables, etc. Many people I know put the water into a saucepan cold, and boil it up on a hotplate. By far the quicker and more economical method is to boil the water in an electric kettle, switch on your hotplate a few minutes before the kettle boils, then put the boiling water from the kettle into the saucepan, and so on to the hotplate. Hot- plates are dreadfully slow for boiling water as compared with a kettle.
For the housewife who does her own washing, either by electricity or hand, here is a useful hint with regard to drying.
Taking an average household where there are no electrically heated drying cupboards and where, if the weather is bad, the clothes have to be dried indoors, it is as well to bear in mind that an electric fan will perform this duty quicker and much more economically than an electric fire. The fan consumes only
COSMOS ELECTRIC FAN
about one-twelfth of the current taken by a 3 kw. fire. The fan should be placed fairly high up on the wall to be thoroughly effi- cient. In addition to the quickness and economy of this method, the clothes tend to have that fresh sun-and-air smell which is so difficult to get anywhere but in the garden. How much more pleasant, too, it is to enter a room where a fan has been going for several hours, as compared with one in which a 3 kw. fire has been full on for the same time !

The Electrical Age                                     49
Aylesburys Rural Electricity Scheme
Our picture shows Mrs. Llewellyn Atkin-
son, a valued member of the Council of the
E.A.W., cutting the first sod of the
Aylesbury Rural Electricity Extension.
For a number of years, Aylesbury has
been considering a scheme for supplying
electricity to its outlying districts, in order
that the man and woman on the farm and in
the country might benefit from the advan-
tages of electricity.
The Mayor of Aylesbury, in giving the
scheme his blessing, said that electricity had
proved a great success in the town, and they
now felt that they would like to extend to the
rural districts within 10 or 13 miles of
Aylesbury the same benefits.
In a very charming speech, Mrs. Llewellyn
Atkinson expressed her pleasure at taking
part in the ceremony, and stated she was
pleased a woman should have been asked to
perform such a duty which would bring some
of the comforts of the town into the beautiful
countryside of Buckinghamshire.
Women who had seen and experienced
what electricity can do in their homes, knew
how it would lighten their daily tasks—
working sewing machines, churns, milk
separators and dust removers, and brighten-
ing homes by better and cleaner lighting.
In the name of the women of the country-
side round Aylesbury, she wished all success
to the new enterprise.
The ceremony took place at Chequers
Court Park, within a short distance of the
country home of the Prime Minister.

[Photograph]
Mrs. Ll. Atkinson Cutting the First Sod of the Aylesbury Rural Electricity Extension Scheme

Mr. Borlase Matthews, the well-known
expert on electric farming, gave some very
interesting particulars of the value of elec-
tricity to the farmers.
Viscount Stopford proposed a vote of
thanks to the Mayor, which was seconded
by Mr. A. C. Gerrett.
We wish Aylesbury every success in its
enterprise!

Institute

The E.A.W. is arranging a series of
six lectures, at the special request of Dame
Henrietta Barnett, for the above Institute,
on various aspects of electricity.

“That Iron!”_x000D_
By Margaret Partridge, B.Sc._x000D_
“I can’t come to the party this evening. My dress is all crushed and ’tis Saturday afternoon. The iron won’t work and there is no possibility of getting it mended till Monday, and everyone is cross and the world is horrid”; and if Eva had lived in the last century she would undoubtedly have wept, but being a 1926 miss, she merely set her lips very tight and proceeded to “tidy up” with disconcerting vehemence._x000D_
’Tis always the little things that count, and when Eva’s troubles are analyzed they will probably be found to have all their origin in some trivial displacement of a bit of metal—as easily remedied as sewing on a button—if only we knew where to find the ill._x000D_
Let’s have a look at this defaulting iron. More likely than not the fault isn’t in the iron at all, but somewhere in the flexible connection._x000D_
We’ll start from the lamp-holder. It is quite certain the “juice” is there all right,_x000D_
THE COSMOS ELECTRIC HOME IRON_x000D_
as the lamp we have just taken out lights up (By the way, a two-way adaptor which would allow lamp and iron both to be on at once would be very useful here.)_x000D_
Now the easiest way of testing for “open circuits” is to wire up a lamp-holder to a piece of flex—untwist the ends a bit, and bare them back and then, with lamp in socket, apply the two bare ends to two points where we expect the electric supply to be._x000D_

Our last number showed how to wire up a lamp-holder, and if the lamp lights we know that all is well thus far._x000D_
If we had such a thing as a spare lamp-holder just now, we should be quicker clearing up Eva’s troubles, because we should apply our test lamp to the iron end of the flexible connection and switch on._x000D_
If the lamp lights, it proves conclusively that the fault is in the iron, not the flex. If it fails to light, but the lamp in the original lamp-holder lights, then the fault must lie somewhere between the permanent lamp-holder and the test lamp._x000D_
In this case, we are expecting that the fault lies in the flexible connection. Feel this carefully for kinks or sharp bends, which may indicate a break in the wire inside. Then take a small screwdriver and take off, first, the attachment which is usually plugged on to the iron, and examine the ends

transcription:
The Electrical Age 51

of the flex carefully. In nine cases out of
ten, when an iron wont work, you will find
that the copper of the flex has broken off a
little way from this attachment. If this is
the case with Evas iron, we will just cut off
the broken bit, clean back the flex a little
way, and screw it up again in the attachment
exactly as before. As we have just taken
this all to pieces, it is quite simple to reverse
the operation and to put it all together again
in exactly the same way as it came to bits.
Remember, as always, to keep the bared
ends of the flex clean and well screwed up
together.
If the break is not here, the next most
likely place to find it is close to the adaptor,
which goes into the lamp-holder. Treat this
in the same way.
If, as sometimes happens, the broken wire
is in the middle of the flexible connection,
the proper thing to do is to put in a new
flexible cord, but as it is Saturday afternoon,
and we must get Eva to that party if it is
humanly possible, we must be satisfied with
a temporary joint for the time being.
Clean back the covering braid, cotton,
rubber, or whatever it may be, and pull out
the two ends of the broken wire.
The break may have affected both sides of
the flex, or only one. In any case, when the
ends of the broken wire are drawn out, clean
the copper strands well and join them
together again with a very tight twisted
knot. If you twist tightly enough it is not
necessary or advisable to solder the joint,
but it is very necessary to insulate it, i.e., to
cover it with some cotton, or silk, or rubber,
or any non-conductor, so that there is no
chance of wandering copper strands touch-
ing any other metal, or human being and,
especially, no chance of the two sides of the
flex touching each other.
Rubber or rubberised tape makes the
easiest, quickest covering, but if this cant
be procured, make a bandage of sticking-
plaster, or tape, or string, or any non-con-
ducting material that is handy, and dont lay
the two flexes together, but keep them well
apart, with plenty of insulation between
them. It will look bad, but on Monday we
shall be able to do the job properly and,
meanwhile, Eva can go on with her ironing.
If the fault really lies in the iron itself and
not in the connection, our chances of being
able to effect a temporary repair are not so
good, but we wont despair yet.
Take the iron to pieces. Usually, this
only means unscrewing two screws, and the
whole iron will come to bits. Careful hand-
ling and light fingers are very necessary

Unnamed: 9: Eva might get to the party if iron is fixed.
transcription:
52		The Electrical Age

able to effect a repair. First ascertain, by careful examination, how the connection is made—see the wire, screws, nuts, etc., and you should soon find the fault. If the resistance wire has broken off just by the terminal, draw out an inch or so more, and screw that in tight.
If the little strip of tinned copper which presses against the bottom of the terminal is cracked or flattened with much use, carefully bend this a bit further up and replace the top, and put the iron together exactly as you found it.
Quite a slight jar sometimes causes this last fault, and just lightly levering up the strip of copper with a penknife will put things to rights.
Now put everything together and try again, and if Eva gets to the party to-night, we may go to bed satisfied that our good deed for this one day has been carried out all right.

* * *

E.A.W. Bookshelf

ELECTRICITY FOR EVERYBODY, by R. Borlase Matthews, A.M.I.C.E., M.I.E.E., published by the Electrical Press, Ltd., price 7s. 6d.
The Editor can confidently recommend this book to any who wish for simply written up-to-date knowledge on matters electrical.
Whilst containing a wealth of information, the book is so very well arranged that it could be easily carried about in a handbag, and is sufficiently artistic to leave on the drawing-room table.
A description of various electrical terms is given without the usual technical dressing. Advice is given with regard to systems of wiring, the best kind of electric fitting for different kinds of rooms, useful information with regard to electric cooking, cleaning and other domestic apparatus.
In addition, there are chapters on Electricity as Used on the Farm, in the Factory, and a very excellent chapter on Selling Electricity.
The book is profusely illustrated with very excellent diagrams, and a number of excellent tables are given for reference purposes.
In order that the book should be made a complete guide and friend to the housewife with an all-electric home, we hope that Mr. Matthews, in a future edition, will devote a short chapter on some simple hints re the maintenance and upkeep of domestic electrical apparatus in the home.

HOUSEHOLD ENGINEERING and THE NEW HOUSEKEEPING, by Christine Frederick.
We have received these two very interesting books from Mrs. Christine Frederick, of U.S.A.
Mrs. Frederick is a lecturer and domestic science expert of some repute in America, and she is hoping to visit this country next year to carry out a number of important lecturing engagements.
Mrs. Frederick writes in a very clear and interesting way of the need for planning the woman’s workshop (the kitchen), just as carefully and as scientifically as the man arranges his own workshop.
She points out how that by the scientific planning of a kitchen much unnecessary labour might be saved, and much energy preserved for more useful and interesting work for the home-maker.
Her plan is to standardise as many of the activities, as possible, for the home-maker, and the text of her book is that “the need and aim of home efficiency is not a perfect system of work or scientific scheduling, or ideal cleanliness and order; it is the personal happiness, health and progress of the family in the home.
These books are published by Messrs. Doubleday, Page & Co., of New York.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 53

E.A.W. Branch Activities

Glasgow and District Branch
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251 Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

Miss R. F. Kennedy, whose picture we show, is the indefatigable Honorary Secretary of the Glasgow and District Branch. It is due in no small measure to her enthusiasm that the Branch has already achieved so much success.
Miss Kennedy has been in the service of the Glasgow Electricity Department since 1915, gaining administrative experience in the office and costing sections and, subsequently, being appointed demonstrator to the department when the Corporation opened their showroom.
Right from the time of her girlhood, Miss Kennedy has been associated with engineering work, her father being an architect and engineer, and she was thus able to gain a good foundation for the work which she is now carrying out.

BRANCH NEWS
The Officials and Committee of the Glasgow and District Branch are to be congratulated on the very fine meeting which they helped to organise during the I.M.E.A. Convention in June, when a very interesting address was given by Dr. Christina Barrowman.
The chair was taken by Mrs. Dewar, and the vote of thanks proposed by the President, the Lady Belhaven and Stenton.
The Glasgow Branch is busy arranging a very attractive programme for its members during the Autumn.
The idea is to arrange one lecture and one visit each month. The fixtures include visits to the Paisley Generating Station, and to Beatties Bakery and All-Electric Canteen, which has recently been opened and is in operation day and night.
The new Metro-Vick Showrooms will also be visited, and an opportunity given to members to see the up-to-date fittings manufactured by this firm.
A carpet factory is to be included in the list of visits, and members will also have an opportunity during the session of seeing the Corporation Showrooms and again visiting the Dalmarnock Power Station.
The lecturers include Mr. R. B. Mitchell (the City Engineer), Mr. Cochrane (of Glasgow University), who will speak on the "Fundamental Principles in Electricity," and Mr. Buckle is to give a talk on "Colour and its Effect on Human Beings." Miss Holm, of Newcastle, who is an expert on electric cooking, will visit Glasgow during the session.
It is hoped that during the Autumn there

MISS R. F. KENNEDY,
Hon. Secretary, Glasgow and District Branch

The Birmingham and Midlands
Branch
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. Lawson, 19 Southam
Road, Hall Green, Birmingham.

Mrs. Lawson, the Honorary Secretary of
the Birmingham and Midlands Branch, is a
native of Birmingham, and was educated at
King Edward’s Grammar School, Birming-
ham. Here she obtained a scholarship and
won another at the Birmingham School of
Art, where she studied for five years, chiefly
modelling and carrying out illustration work
for books. She has exhibited at the
Birmingham Society of Artists.
Mrs. Lawson has, for a long time, been
closely associated with the electrical world,
her husband, Mr. W. Lawson, M.I.E.E.,
being a past Chairman of the South
Midlands Centre of the Institution of Elec-
trical Engineers.
During her husband’s year of office, the
Summer meeting of the Institution of Elec-
trical Engineers was held at the South
Midlands Centre, and in this and many other
ways, Mrs. Lawson has come in contact with
many well-known personalities in the elec-
trical world, and is thus very well fitted to
act as the Honorary Secretary of the
Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the
E.A.W.
In addition to her many other accomplish-
ments, Mrs. Lawson is a distinguished
linguist, speaking fluently French, Italian
and Russian.

BRANCH NEWS
The Autumn season received a good send-
off with two lectures, on September 9th and
15th, at the Smoke Abatement Conference at
Bingley Hall, to which our members were
invited. The lectures were given by Mr.
Francis, of the B.E.D.A., the first being on
“Electricity and Health” and the second on
“Electricity in the Home.”
Lady Brooks took the chair on the latter
occasion, and a large audience of more than
300 was present. After the lecture, several
ladies asked practical questions, and the
burning question of price per unit was
raised.

MRS. WALTER LAWSON
Hon. Secretary, Birmingham and Midlands Branch

For the next three months, a varied
programme has been arranged, commencing
with a lecture, by Mr. Francis, at the home
of Mrs. Beale, one of our Vice-Presidents,
and wife of the Chairman of the Birmingham
Electric Supply Committee. It is hoped to
get a big meeting here, as Mrs. Beale can
seat and provide tea for over 60 people.
Our other Vice-President, Mrs. Chattock,
is also giving a drawing-room meeting in

October, and several smaller ones will be fixed later.
Singers Sewing Machine Co. have promised to give us a demonstration of electric sewing on October 14th, and a visit to the showrooms of the General Electric Co. is fixed for November 25th.

Lighting-Up Time for Sport!

By Len Chaloner

Daylight-saving gave us a glimpse into the joys of extra hours for outdoor recreation after the days work had been completed. All through the Summer we could bathe until dusk, play tennis after dinner, or manage a full round of golf, even if the last putt on the eighteenth green hung on the flickering uncertainties of a match.
But the end of September saw the end of such freedom in the past, even if the return to "sun time" pleased the cows who were "called" for milking at a more normal hour, and relieved the anxiety of the hens about the mornings eggs for breakfast.
The illuminating engineers of to-day, however, are offering us even greater possibilities than daylight-saving, for extending outdoor sport to all hours, in all seasons, and without any disturbance to the agricultural community. By means of electricity, they are offering us what is, literally, artificial daylight!
In a hot Summer, we shall soon be able to have games like football, or hockey, by moonlight (plus artificial light). On a cold Winters evening we shall be able to enjoy tennis after leaving the office or, as the Autumn days draw in, if our Summer holiday has been delayed, we shall be able to enjoy bathing when the sea is at its warmest, after the days sunshine has left it and dusk has made beach bathing for the average public not a very safe pastime.
A glorious picture, but how is it all done? Any one who has played indoor games by artificial light knows the importance of even lighting that yet avoids glare. In an uneven light, an object travelling between a light and dark space appears to alter its speed, and becomes almost impossible to judge correctly. Glare, on the other hand, makes it impossible to watch a ball throughout its journey, while in shadows between bright light we lose it altogether.
These were the problems the illuminating engineer had to overcome, and he has done it in three different ways, to accommodate different needs in different games, which inevitably occupy very different areas.
For a bathing beach, or a golf course,

Unnamed: 9: Miss Hodge will give a demonstration on "Good Home Lighting."
transcription:
The Electrical Age 57

where posts would be impracticable and a large area has to be lit, flood-lights with projectors are used — set up to throw the beams from the shore or the club-house. They can be arranged to give either a wide beam or a narrow beam. In the case of a clock golf game, it is, of course, easy to use posts and reflectors. For games like hockey, angle reflectors may be used, lighting the field from the sides, but this is only useful for games that do not need vision at upper angles, where it would be impossible to avoid glare. The third type of lighting is by means of reflectors of enamelled steel, and this is useful for tennis, as the reflectors are designed to give a good distribution of light downwards. Lighting must, of course, be arranged sufficiently high not to interfere with the play or cause glare to the players. The units may be suspended from a central cable strung between poles at opposite ends of the ground or, if the court is surrounded by netting, they may be mounted on brackets attached to the framework. Roughly, it may be appreciated that the higher the mounting the fewer the units required ; at the same time, if they are placed too far apart the lighting will be uneven and spoilt by shadows. About twenty to twenty-one feet high is the best level for the lighting of a tennis court, and six units will be found adequate. In America, the idea is by no means new, for the vast water supply, standardisation of current, and other conditions have helped to develop the use of electricity and made it cheap. But in England, we are only just beginning to realise that these ideas are not merely "ideas," but practical business propositions deserving our personal investigation, remembering always that it is demand which creates not only supply, but cheap supply also. If the lighting of a golf course is yet rather a luxury, to arrange for the lighting of a modern tennis court or hockey field is becoming very nearly a necessity.

An Easy Wiring System
The Selfix Electric Company have recently put on the market an installation which can be used by amateurs for wiring homes. A book of instructions is issued with each installation, and it is claimed that the whole arrangement is so designed that no special knowledge of any sort is required to carry out the work.

Streatham Womens Local Government Association
The Director is giving an address to this Association during October on "Womens Influence in the Development of Electricity," and on November 9th, the Association will visit the E.L.M.A. Lighting Service Bureau, when Miss Hodge will give a demonstration on "Good Home Lighting."

Special Kitchen Lighting Fitting
The kitchen has, hitherto, not had sufficient attention paid to it from the point of view of good lighting. 58	The Electrical Age

*How Electricity is Made. Part 2.—Putting
Electricity “On Tap”

By J. W. Beauchamp, M.I.E.E.

We have already explored, in a rather
sketchy manner, the main principles which
underlie the production of electricity for
public service. The electric power produced
in bulk at the generating station, has to be
conveyed over long distances and, ultimately,
distributed in large or small quantities to a
great number of points in the district.
Electricity cannot be manufactured, put
up into handy packets and stored for retail-
ing across a counter when wanted, as is the
case with most familiar commodities. The
works where the electricity is made must be
linked, by means of cables, to each and
every one of its customers, so that they can
call upon the service at any moment, day or
night.
Electricity is easily conveyed through
metals, whilst a great many other sub-
stances either oppose its passage or prevent
it altogether; for example, paper, glass,
china and many non-metallic materials,
which for this reason are generally referred
to by electrical people as “insulators.”
*The first article of this series appeared in
the June issue

Around this idea the distribution of elec-
tricity is centred. Cables, or wires of metal,
covered with one or other of the insulating
materials, permit power to be conducted in
any direction without escape. Of all the
metals in general use and reasonable in
price, copper is the one which conducts
electricity with the least loss of power, and
for that reason, together with its flexible and
non - rusting characteristics, is mostly
employed in the making of electric cables.
Vast quantities of copper are used each year
for electrical conductors along the streets,
in houses, and as component parts of the
apparatus used to convert electricity to the
requirements of the consumer.

THE LAYING OF ELECTRIC CABLES.

The laying of electric cables along roads
is a familiar sight to-day. The narrow
trenches, so quickly cut and covered in
again, in which flexible cables are drawn or
laid, remind us continuously of the rapid
progress being made by the electric supply
undertakings and the extent to which the
people are depending upon electricity for the
many services which it can render.

The Electrical Age 61

As with the case of gas and water, the cable networks can be sub-divided at convenient points. This is effected by switches in underground boxes, or in the so-called "feeder pillars," which are to-day a familiar object along our roads.
The art of making and laying electric cables has reached a very high pitch of perfection, and trouble with them is very rare to-day. A cable made of pure copper, surrounded with oiled paper, and tightly encased in pure lead, is practically imperishable, barring some accident, which may destroy the protective casing. Such accidents are guarded against by covering the cables with tiles or boards or, in some cases, drawing them into iron pipes; and in the event of the cables being destroyed by men digging in the road, or by other violent means, nothing more serious than temporary extinction of the supply takes place. The destruction of the cable and its insulating sheath naturally leads the electricity to escape at once to the earth, through which it finds a return path to the generating station. These sudden rushes of electricity can be destructive to the machinery, but on modern cable systems are kept in check by automatic devices which switch off or disconnect parts of the cable network, when the current flowing into them becomes greater than a pre-determined amount, so leaving that section deprived of its electric supply until the damage in the cable has been located and remedied, generally an easy matter, and promptly attended to by the maintenance men who are employed by Supply Undertakings for that purpose.

Electrical Progress !
Things We Hear

That a recent application of electrical heating is for the sterilization of eggs. Sterilization is accomplished by passing the eggs through an oil bath at 235° F.; the oil fills the pores in the egg-shell and prevents air from entering. It is said that tests have been made which indicate that eggs so treated will keep odourless and fresh for years.—Electrical Review (September 3rd).

That an electrically operated device for dealing playing cards has been registered at the Berlin Patent Bureau.—The Electrician (September 3rd).

That a remarkable advance in bricklaying, in connection with home building, has been made recently, according to Charles R. Taylor, of New York — an electric brick-laying machine, which lays bricks at a rate far greater than that of a mason under ordinary conditions. — Popular Science Monthly (August).

That electric steaming-irons, with a water reservoir and tiny holes in the ironing surface for the emergence of steam, are now being produced in America. It is claimed that this device obviates the need for damping clothes before ironing.—The Electrician (July 23rd).

That to Calais belongs the distinction of having the first crystal-controlled "Sound-house." At the end of the sea-wall is a vibrating quartz crystal wireless valve device, which sends out an under-water sound-beam that can be received by ships better than a light-beam, through fog, blizzards, etc. It is possible that these sound-beams will, in time, replace light-houses altogether.—Popular Wireless (Aug. 28th).

Correspondence

Cooks and Electric Cookers
Dear Madam,—If you will allow corre- spondence in your columns, may I ask a question and give my experience?
People tell me they cannot have an electric cooker because the cook will not use it.
I should like to say that I have an all- electric flat, and have had a series of maids in the last ten years, mostly daily women, and have had no real objections from them. Before coming, one or two have said, " Do you think I can manage it? " I always re- assure them.
As soon as they come, and before they have had time to get into difficulties, the Borough Council demonstrator has appeared and given the first lesson. I leave the cook to find out the times things take to cook, but am about to remind her that heat continues after switching off.
The joy of the cleanliness and absence of smell, and the confidence that you will always get the same result, soon make them- selves felt and valued, and after a few days the work is well and economically done. Why cant others get this result?
Yours, etc.,
C. M. Marx.

A Bachelor Womans "Electrical" Difficulties
Dear Madam,—The Electrical Age has been a joy to me. I read it through, from cover to cover, and then went over it again to see I had not missed any little "tit-bits" with which it abounds. There are very many people like myself who must have enjoyed this first number; now do you think we dare ask you to make it even more interesting by letting us write and ask you points we are anxious to know; it is going to be a tremen- dous help to some of us bachelor women if you will. For instance, I am at present seething with discontent over the fact that I have tried to aspire to an electrically-worked flat on a small scale that an ordinary working woman, like myself, could afford, and—have failed. A well-known company whom I approached want me to pay a sum of £33 0s. 8d., payable on the hire purchase system, within nine months, for bringing the power to points arranged in the flat; this irrespective of the usual hire charges for the apparatus. I have the lighting in my flat already. Well, now, isnt that making it prohibitive for the ordinary working woman, to whom the advantage of electricity is going to be of such value? Before I can have that advantage, which I am willing to pay for, I have to find a sum of £33. We working women cant do it. The purport of my telling you of this is to ask you—" Is there going to be any chance for us workers to have the benefit of the wonders of electricity —or is it only to be for the opulent ones? "
Yours truly,
F. E. Jones.
[We agree with Miss Jones; this is a real difficulty which many women have to face, both bachelor and married. It clearly demonstrates the need for the womans point of view in all electrical adminis- tration.—Ed., " E.A."]

68 The Electrical Age

Radio and Furnishings
Receiving Apparatus Designed to Harmonise with
Drawing-Room Surroundings

By F. H. MASTERS, O.B.E. (Editor of "The Electrician")

In the four years in which radio broadcasting has been in existence in this country, the whole trend of receiving apparatus design has changed. In the early days, the penalty to be paid for listening-in was an unwieldy mass of wires and switches in alliance with a crude-looking box, the exterior of which was sprinkled with knobs and other "gadgets." Although there is still a certain demand among "experimenters" for this type of apparatus, the public generally call for something that can be switched on as easily as electric light, and, above all, something that will take its place inconspicuously amongst the normal furnishings of the home.

This demand has been met in two ways. Firstly, in the refinement of the shape and finish of apparatus, the function of which remains obvious to all; and, secondly, in disguising the apparatus in such a way that it appears to be something entirely different. In the first class, British makers have some very interesting designs available, a noticeable improvement in many sets being the replacement of the old black ebonite panel by a panel of polished wood. In some cases, ebonite is still used, but the material is specially treated to resemble mahogany, oak and even marble. Many sets are now made with very well-finished and polished cases of various kinds of wood, and carving and inlay work is sometimes introduced with pleasing effect. Exterior fittings on these sets are reduced in number, and one manufacturer supplies receiving sets with fittings of either oxidized bronze or oxidized silver. Some novel effects are also obtained by enclosing the sets in one-piece cases moulded from an insulating compound.

Loud speakers of the familiar horn type are presented in more attractive shapes and finishes, and one instrument seen at the Olympia Radio Exhibition was plated all over and very highly polished. Crystalline

JACOBEAN STYLE CABINET

enamel is used on some models, and a new chocolate shade is distinctly pleasing.

On the whole, then, it can be said that the "non-disguised" types of receiver and loud speaker have now been greatly improved in appearance, and their efficiency has not been impaired but, rather, improved by these modifications. From an object which was only admitted to the drawing-room on sufferance, and even then had to be hidden behind furniture or pushed into a corner when visitors were about, the wireless receiving set has developed into a neat and,

70
The Electrical Age
development of the gramophone suffered a temporary check for this self-same reason, and it was not until it could be produced in hornless models, enclosed in handsome wooden cabinets, that it was considered worthy of inclusion among the other furnishings of the home.
The need for the similar treatment of wireless receiving apparatus was early recognised by British radio manufacturers, who can now provide sets which resemble anything but that which they are.
One maker has evolved the "Corner Cabinet" set, in oak, which is illustrated on page 69. A handsome piece of furniture, worthy of its place in any old-world room, it in no way betrays to the eye that it is the last word in modern amusement devices. There are no wires or other paraphernalia to be seen, the whole apparatus being hidden behind the attractive panelled doors.
Sets of this type can be had in various guises, and though, in many of its forms, the cabinet or container resembles a familiar article of furniture, it has been specially designed to accommodate the receiving apparatus in such a way as will enable it to give the most efficient service possible. A popular form of cabinet resembles a bureau, made in dark oak in the Jacobean style. The desk flap opens to give access to the panel of the set, and two doors below enclose compartments for the accumulators or high-tension batteries. Other models also have provision in the lower part of the cabinet for a loud speaker.
Closely resembling the spinet, after which it is named, a cabinet set, in mahogany, is a pleasing addition to a drawing-room, particularly as it houses, very inconspicuously, an efficient loud speaker near the top of the case. Another firm makes a very handsome mahogany sideboard, the top of which can be lifted to reveal the panel of a four-valve set. On slightly more conventional lines is a cabinet in mahogany or oak, practically identical in appearance with the cabinet model gramophones. A loud speaker is accommodated behind double swing doors,
which can be used to regulate the volume of sound.
Where it is not desirable or convenient to have floor cabinets, there is a good selection of attractively designed models made to stand on a table or sideboard.
Some very decorative forms of loud speakers are also available, one of the most popular being the type designed after the style of the bracket clock. One maker supplies these in various pleasing polished woods, and also in fine oriental lacquer. They look very well on a mantelpiece, and can also be stood on a wall bracket supplied by the manufacturers.
A novel production is a loud speaker which is entirely concealed in a picture which hangs upon the wall. Not only is the sound-producing instrument entirely hidden, but there is nothing to indicate that it is anything more than a framed picture. The makers supply any type of picture frame, and there is a large variety of etchings, oil and water-colour paintings, etc., to choose from. If desired, the purchaser may have a portrait of some relative or friend mounted and framed in this way.
ATTRACTIVE SMALL RADIOLUX WITH THE LACQUER FINISH.
Fuse Wire Holder
Usually when fuse wire is required in an emergency, it cannot be found anywhere. Mr. James Duncanson, A.M.I.E.E., has brought out a very excellent little fuse wire holder, which can be conveniently hung in the kitchen near the electric stove. The holder contains fuse wire both for lighting and heating. The holder is aptly termed "The Gleam," and is priced at 1s. 6d. This can be obtained from electrical stores or shops throughout the country.

The Electrical Age 71
What Birmingham is doing Electrically
By R. A. Chattock, M.I.E.E. (City Electrical Engineer)
As so little appears to be known of the great public services being rendered by our Electrical Undertakings, we propose to publish a series of illustrated articles showing the activities of some of the large Company and Municipal Enterprises.—ED., "E.A."
At the present time, the rate of progress in the use of electricity in Birmingham is increasing very rapidly. This development is not confined to electric lighting, which is now universally recognised as the most convenient and economical form of artificial illuminant, or to current used for industrial power purposes, but is also spreading to the domestic heating and cooking load.
This satisfactory increase in the use of electricity is shown by the fact that, whilst in the year immediately preceding the war, the new consumers connected in Birmingham totalled 1,300, the new consumers connected last year alone were nearly 9,000. The number of units sold during the same period has grown from 73½ million units to 224 million units. The demand is increasing so rapidly that, although the new Princes Generating Station was only opened by H.R.H. The Prince of Wales so recently as June 1923, the Electric Supply Committees scheme for the erection of a super-generating station at Hams Hall, near Birmingham, has been approved by the City Council. This site is a most suitable one for the purpose, with an ample supply of water available. There is no doubt that before Hams Hall Station is in commission, the plant at Nechells will be working at its full capacity.
ELECTRIC LIGHTING PROGRESS.
So many people realise, nowadays, the important part that electricity plays in the modern home, that it is difficult for us to appreciate that a few years ago it was looked upon as a luxury to be enjoyed by the wealthy classes only. Largely as a result of the progressive policy pursued by Supply Undertakings in offering current at substantially reduced rates, together with the placing on the market by manufacturers of artistic lighting fittings and efficient electrical heating and cooking apparatus at quite moderate prices, the use of electricity has been extended to the small villa residences and, finally, to the home of the artisan.
There is an air of comfort and convenience in every home where electricity is installed, which was formerly the principal reason for its adoption in the residences of the well-to-do.
Houses require redecorating at much longer intervals than where other forms of lighting are installed, and the saving thus effected is an appreciable and indisputable one. Figures on a large private estate, after conversion to electric lighting, showed a saving of, approximately 30 per cent. in the cost of decorating.
Electricity improves the value of property, and is especially suitable for houses with low ceilings, so many of which are, as a result of high building costs, being erected at the present time. It does not vitiate the atmosphere, a point of great importance during the long Winter evenings when artificial lighting is chiefly used.
The fact that tenants live under far healthier and cleaner conditions when their homes are electrically lit, is being increasingly realised by the responsible public

As so little appears to be known of the great public services being rendered by our Electrical Undertakings, we propose to publish a series of illustrated articles showing the activities of some of the large Company and Municipal Enterprises.—ED., "E.A."
At the present time, the rate of progress in the use of electricity in Birmingham is increasing very rapidly. This development is not confined to electric lighting, which is now universally recognised as the most convenient and economical form of artificial illuminant, or to current used for industrial power purposes, but is also spreading to the domestic heating and cooking load.
This satisfactory increase in the use of electricity is shown by the fact that, whilst in the year immediately preceding the war, the new consumers connected in Birmingham totalled 1,300, the new consumers connected last year alone were nearly 9,000. The number of units sold during the same period has grown from 73½ million units to 224 million units. The demand is increasing so rapidly that, although the new Princes Generating Station was only opened by H.R.H. The Prince of Wales so recently as June 1923, the Electric Supply Committees scheme for the erection of a super-generating station at Hams Hall, near Birmingham, has been approved by the City Council. This site is a most suitable one for the purpose, with an ample supply of water available. There is no doubt that before Hams Hall Station is in commission, the plant at Nechells will be working at its full capacity.
ELECTRIC LIGHTING PROGRESS.
So many people realise, nowadays, the important part that electricity plays in the modern home, that it is difficult for us to appreciate that a few years ago it was looked upon as a luxury to be enjoyed by the wealthy classes only. Largely as a result of the progressive policy pursued by Supply Undertakings in offering current at substantially reduced rates, together with the placing on the market by manufacturers of artistic lighting fittings and efficient electrical heating and cooking apparatus at quite moderate prices, the use of electricity has been extended to the small villa residences and, finally, to the home of the artisan.
There is an air of comfort and convenience in every home where electricity is installed, which was formerly the principal reason for its adoption in the residences of the well-to-do.
Houses require redecorating at much longer intervals than where other forms of lighting are installed, and the saving thus effected is an appreciable and indisputable one. Figures on a large private estate, after conversion to electric lighting, showed a saving of, approximately 30 per cent. in the cost of decorating.
Electricity improves the value of property, and is especially suitable for houses with low ceilings, so many of which are, as a result of high building costs, being erected at the present time. It does not vitiate the atmosphere, a point of great importance during the long Winter evenings when artificial lighting is chiefly used.
The fact that tenants live under far healthier and cleaner conditions when their homes are electrically lit, is being increasingly realised by the responsible public

transcription:
The Electrical Age 75

The Economics of Home Lighting

Part II.
Reflecting Powers of Various Coloured Walls.—Maintenance.—
Importance of Using Correct Voltage Lamps

By Florence Hodge

No matter how carefully a lighting scheme
may have been planned with due regard to
the choice of service-giving and decorative
fittings, correct lamps and shades which give
the finishing touch of beauty to the whole
room, the final result will be disappointing
if the surroundings are not adapted to reflect
adequate light.
The question of the proper painting of
walls and ceilings is of great importance.
The ceiling and wall surfaces in a room are
secondary sources of light, that is, they
receive and reflect light from the lamps
themselves and they should, therefore, be as
light as possible. A pure white ceiling is an
excellent reflecting medium, but for a more
artistic effect a slightly creamy tint is recom-
mended; any white which at all approaches
blue or grey is cold and cheerless. Not only
is the colour of the ceiling important, but the
actual finish must also be considered. A
glossy surface reflects images of the lamp
filament and introduces glare, causing eye-
strain; either a flat or matt surface is
essential. A well-painted ceiling, finished
with several coats of white paint, will also
reflect more light, since a thin coat of white
paint through which a dark surface can be
seen will allow the light to get through and
become absorbed. With any type of indirect
fitting, such as an alabaster bowl, it will be
found that a well-painted ceiling reflects 84%
light as compared to 68% from a buff finish.
When it comes to a question of wallpaper,
there is the same general rule to follow. If
it is of such a colour that it does not reflect
the light satisfactorily, only an unusually
lavish supply of lamps will make the room
appear brightly illuminated. For instance, a
dark green paper will only reflect 21% of
light, while a red one is even worse, reflect-
ing only 16%. Then a room finished in deep
brown woodwork, or with a good deal of
dark wood panelling, is often uncomfortable
when lighted by ordinary methods; no
matter how much precaution is taken to
shield and diffuse the light, the whole equip-
ment and lamps (especially with the elec-
trolier type of fitting) show up as annoying
bright spots in contrast to the dark back-
ground.
A satisfactory method of lighting such an
interior—apart from installing costly and
elaborate indirect lighting — is by using
plenty of table and floor standard lamps to
give good local illumination for reading and
working, with bright tinted shades to give
the necessary colour note, and leaving the
rest of the room in comparatively subdued
light.
On the other hand, a combination of
creamy white ceiling and a wallpaper of a
little deeper tint—in fact, any tone ranging
from cream to golden yellow—will make an
excellent reflecting medium, sufficient to
reflect, at least, 75% of the light given from
lamps in a fitting.
Bearing all these facts in mind, the con-
clusion drawn is that when decorating or re-
decorating a room, a woman needs to think
in terms of light (and her lighting bill) when
choosing a scheme of decoration. If she is
not prepared to double either the existing
number of her lamps or their power, she will

transcription:
The Electrical Age 77
What I Saw in Switzerland
Novelties in Electrical Appliances
By Mrs. Walter Lawson (Hon. Sec., Birmingham and Midlands Branch, E.A.W.)
During my stay in Basle, I spent part of two days visiting some works where many interesting electrical appliances are made, some of which are not generally known to the English public. For instance, an automatic boiler is made here, which is used by farmers chiefly. It serves three purposes; it steams the farmers potatoes (these with smoked bacon being the main article of diet amongst the country people), or it will cook the pigs food, and when not needed for cooking, it does the family wash equally well. This boiler works at night on a cheap tariff.
Electric water-heaters are also made at this factory, in varying sizes, to hold anything up to 40 gallons. These are considered indispensable in every Swiss house, and the first question a prospective tenant asks a landlord is whether an electric water-heater is installed. If the answer is not in the affirmative, the house generally remains empty, Switzerland apparently being one of the few places left where one may pick and choose.
Their method of installing a water-heater is to fix it in the basement, from where it automatically supplies the whole house with hot and cold water, no other water supply being necessary.
We also saw the apparatus for electric floor heating in process of construction at these works. This method of heating is especially suitable for banks or other big buildings, but many private houses which are now being built are having it installed. In this system, many flexible cables are run under the tiled or tesselated floor at regular and frequent intervals. These are encased in metal and packed with pebbles for several feet underneath in order to throw the heat up. Certain tiles are made removable in case of repairs being necessary, and the cables being flexible it can easily be drawn out and pushed back again. transcription:
The Electrical Age 79

The E.A.W. Visits the B.T.H. at Rugby

A few years ago, no one would have believed that a party of between 50 and 60 women would travel long distances to visit a works where machinery was being made. It could, perhaps, be better understood if such women were intending entering upon an engineering career, but the majority of the women who formed the party which visited the B.T.H. Works at Rugby, on July 22nd, were mainly women concerned with household management and Public Affairs. The idea of such a visit was first suggested by the Committee of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the E.A.W., and such is the enthusiasm of Mrs. Lawson, the Hon. Secretary, and the Committee, that representations were quickly made to the officials of the B.T.H. and a warm and cordial invitation was soon forthcoming from the Company. A small group of members from London joined the Birmingham party at Rugby just before one oclock, and were met at the station by Mr. Price-Hughes who appeared to have thought out every small detail for the comfort and convenience of the party. On arrival at the works, the party was met by Mr. and Mrs. Sporborg and other officials of the company. A very delightful lunch was served in one of the staff dining-rooms, and the party at the outset had an opportunity of experiencing the very generous hospitality, which is an indication of the way in which the B.T.H. carries out duties of this kind. In a word of welcome to the party, Mr. Sporborg remarked that this was the first occasion on which the company had entertained a party of ladies unattended by gentlemen. He thought that this was an interesting indication of the great interest which women were now taking in everything

During our walk through the works, we had a chance of talking to Mrs. Sporborg, and learnt from her and Miss May of the wonderful work which is done under the name of welfare. One got the impression that Mrs. Sporborgs interest was not of the old-fashioned "grandmotherly" type, but was based on an earnest wish to give the women employees a chance of a full and interesting life. Here and there one got a glimpse of the splendid team spirit which seems to exist throughout the B.T.H. organisation.
As one spoke to different members of the staff, one realised that there was a common aim and ideal underlying the work of every one.
Before leaving the works, the party was shown over the special exhibition, where the Company has displayed a sample of its products manufactured in different parts of the country. Here there were to be seen up-to-date lighting methods, switchboard and switch-gear, motors for all purposes, and a demonstration of the latest type of electric cooker, which claimed the attention of most of the members.
At 4.30, a weary, but very happy and interested party returned to the staff dining-room, where tea had been provided.
Lady Brooks, the President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the E.A.W., expressed the thanks of the party for such generous hospitality and for so interesting an afternoon.
Alderman Mrs. Hammer, the Chairman of the E.A.W. Council, in her usual witty manner, added her quota of thanks, and at the close of the afternoon, the Director took the opportunity of telling the assembled company that the British Thomson-Houston Company had been one of the first to realise the great educational value of such a body as the E.A.W.
Thus ended one of the pleasantest afternoons in the annals of the E.A.W.

transcription:
82 The Electrical Age

The New Cooking

By Olive Lauth

Mrs. Lauth and her husband, who is an engineer, have recently introduced an entirely new and revolutionary idea in electric cooking. In the next issue of THE ELECTRICAL AGE, Mrs. Lauth will describe fully the new Electric Induction Cooker, which, undoubtedly, has a very great future.—ED., “E.A.”

The following quotation from the Editorial in the first issue of this journal shows us that one of the chief causes which has hindered the perfecting of domestic labour-saving appliances in the past, has been the lack of intimate co-operation between man (inventor and manufacturer) on the one side, and woman (user) on the other :—
“The work of women is best known to women. Men have, as inventors and manufacturers, tried to discover what they have understood to be women’s requirements. For cooking, heating and cleaning we have much to thank the engineer and manufacturer for, but much more remains to be done.
“It is to bring together the maker and the user which is one of the immediate aims of the Electrical Association of Women.”
This hiatus between the woman user and the male inventor and manufacturer was nowhere wider than in the sphere of cooking.
For centuries, cooking stoves were made by men who did not understand the requirements and deficiencies of the woman’s kitchen. Not that the man was, by any means, wholly to blame! In how many kitchens would the penetrating enquiries of an inventive male be tolerated while the housewife had her culinary operations in full swing? In one kitchen, toleration grew into co-operation. Two heads were laid together to investigate the kitchen problems to their very roots, and out of this combination emerged the new Electric Induction Cooker, of which a photograph is herewith shown, and a short description of the

THE ELECTRODUCERS RANGE
Inventor’s Original Model

cooker, with some account of the new methods of cooking which it has made possible, will be given in the next issue of THE ELECTRICAL AGE.

This hiatus between the woman user and the male inventor and manufacturer was nowhere wider than in the sphere of cooking.
For centuries, cooking stoves were made by men who did not understand the requirements and deficiencies of the woman’s kitchen. Not that the man was, by any means, wholly to blame! In how many kitchens would the penetrating enquiries of an inventive male be tolerated while the housewife had her culinary operations in full swing? In one kitchen, toleration grew into co-operation. Two heads were laid together to investigate the kitchen problems to their very roots, and out of this combination emerged the new Electric Induction Cooker, of which a photograph is herewith shown, and a short description of the

Vol. I. JANUARY, 1927 No. 3
Photo by Lenare
LADY SNELL
“The Electrical Age for Women” claims that one of its main objects is “to help the Woman in the Home,” and all women interested in the improvement of the conditions of life among the wage-earning sections of the community will sympathize with the endeavour to make more widely known the possibilities of electricity in its domestic applications, and its advantages in regard to health, cleanliness, the lightening of manual labour and economy, both direct and indirect.
It seems incredible that large housing schemes should be proceeding in this country to-day without any provision being made for the supply of what, in many other countries, is looked upon as an indispensable necessity of modern life.
I wish “The Electrical Age for Women” every success in its mission.
Anne Snell

transcription:
EDITORIAL

THE PROGRESS OF THE E.A.W.
May we take this opportunity of wishing all readers of THE ELECTRICAL AGE a very Happy and Prosperous New Year ! The year 1927 is, we feel, full of immense possibilities for the Association, and by the end of the year we hope that there will be very few women in the country who have not heard something of our activities and have not benefited from the work which we are doing.
Since our last issue, one further Branch has come into existence at Cheltenham, and preliminary arrangements have been made for the formation of a Branch on the North-East Coast.
On every hand we find tremendous interest in the work which we are doing, and the difficulty we are faced with is to make our organization develop as quickly as the demand arises.

THE NEED FOR MORE COLOUR AND BEAUTY IN OUR NATIONAL LIFE.
Sir Leo Chiozza Money, writing recently in the Sunday Observer, gave an interesting description of the function of electricity in Italian life, describing especially the beauty in architecture of the Italian Power Stations.
When visiting our great Industrial Centres in the Winter months, one is struck by the gloomily dreary aspect which they present, and one wonders when we may hope for more colour, beauty and light in these areas. Surely this is what we might expect from electricity ! A lifting of the tremendous pall of smoke and dust which hangs over our towns in the Winter months, and the possibility of more harmony and comfort in our homes.

THE WOMANS POINT OF VIEW ON ELECTRICAL MATTERS.
All our readers will join in congratulating the Chairman of the E.A.W., Alderman Mrs. Hammer, on her election as Chairman of the Hackney Electricity Committee. Mrs. Hammer is the first woman in the country to hold such a position, and we can think of no one more deserving or suitable, and we think Hackney is fortunate in having found such a Chairman.
Another member who is doing yeoman service in her district for electricity is Councillor Mrs. Gregory, who is a member of the West Ham Electricity Committee.
Further evidence of the value of the womans point of view was shown in the Report recently issued by H.M. Stationery Office, giving the conclusions of the Advisory Committee set up by the Electricity Commissioners on Domestic Supplies of Electricity and Methods of Charge. Two members of the E.A.W. gave evidence before this Committee, this being the first occasion on which the Government had heard the womans point of view on the Uses of Electricity in the home.

THE ELECTRICITY (SUPPLY) ACT, 1926.
The long journey of the Electricity (Supply) Bill through the Houses of Parliament has now come to an end. The Bill received the Royal Assent on December 15th, and, after many vicissitudes, becomes the law of the land. Its effect on Electrical Development in this country will be keenly watched by women of all sections of the community.
86

EDITORIAL

THE PROGRESS OF THE E.A.W.
May we take this opportunity of wishing all readers of THE ELECTRICAL AGE a very Happy and Prosperous New Year ! The year 1927 is, we feel, full of immense possibilities for the Association, and by the end of the year we hope that there will be very few women in the country who have not heard something of our activities and have not benefited from the work which we are doing.
Since our last issue, one further Branch has come into existence at Cheltenham, and preliminary arrangements have been made for the formation of a Branch on the North-East Coast.
On every hand we find tremendous interest in the work which we are doing, and the difficulty we are faced with is to make our organization develop as quickly as the demand arises.

THE NEED FOR MORE COLOUR AND BEAUTY IN OUR NATIONAL LIFE.
Sir Leo Chiozza Money, writing recently in the Sunday Observer, gave an interesting description of the function of electricity in Italian life, describing especially the beauty in architecture of the Italian Power Stations.
When visiting our great Industrial Centres in the Winter months, one is struck by the gloomily dreary aspect which they present, and one wonders when we may hope for more colour, beauty and light in these areas. Surely this is what we might expect from electricity ! A lifting of the tremendous pall of smoke and dust which hangs over our towns in the Winter months, and the possibility of more harmony and comfort in our homes.

THE WOMANS POINT OF VIEW ON ELECTRICAL MATTERS.
All our readers will join in congratulating the Chairman of the E.A.W., Alderman Mrs. Hammer, on her election as Chairman of the Hackney Electricity Committee. Mrs. Hammer is the first woman in the country to hold such a position, and we can think of no one more deserving or suitable, and we think Hackney is fortunate in having found such a Chairman.
Another member who is doing yeoman service in her district for electricity is Councillor Mrs. Gregory, who is a member of the West Ham Electricity Committee.
Further evidence of the value of the womans point of view was shown in the Report recently issued by H.M. Stationery Office, giving the conclusions of the Advisory Committee set up by the Electricity Commissioners on Domestic Supplies of Electricity and Methods of Charge. Two members of the E.A.W. gave evidence before this Committee, this being the first occasion on which the Government had heard the womans point of view on the Uses of Electricity in the home.

THE ELECTRICITY (SUPPLY) ACT, 1926.
The long journey of the Electricity (Supply) Bill through the Houses of Parliament has now come to an end. The Bill received the Royal Assent on December 15th, and, after many vicissitudes, becomes the law of the land. Its effect on Electrical Development in this country will be keenly watched by women of all sections of the community.

88 The Electrical Age

The existence of this problem has already been recognized by a group of Head-mistresses, and the question of putting into operation the necessary teaching is being seriously considered. In this work, the E.A.W. is playing a very important part, and we hope before long to be able to announce the fact that at least two centres have commenced this instruction.
It is an extraordinary fact that up to the present time so few people have seen the need for instructing the girls of this genera-tion in the many uses of electricity, but we believe that, with the work which the E.A.W. is doing in various quarters, the time will not be far distant when every Girls School will afford an opportunity to the scholars to learn more of the applications of this science to housecraft.

ELECTRIC WASHING DAY
By Dorothy Vaughan

Women, to-day, are taking increasing advantage of the developments in domestic science and of labour-saving appliances with the thought always in mind that the great and wonderful business, or profession one might say, of keeping a home may be more easily accomplished.
The drudgery of family laundering has become more of a problem each year as the sphere of woman has broadened and outside interests have made greater demands upon her time.
The laundry easily qualifies as the room where the hardest work is done.
It is in the home laundry that the family clothes each week must be washed and made ready to wear again—clothes stained with the grease of the workshop or the dust of office or store ; garments soiled in the course of household tasks, and the childrens things all spotted and spattered with stains and splotches picked up goodness knows where.
Removing all this miscellaneous dirt, getting the cleaned garments dry and then ironing them, is a task of tremendous pro-portions when the whole burden falls upon human muscles.
It was probably because of this fact that among the first electrical household appliances that were placed on the market were devices to lighten the labour of launder-ing. And because every woman realises that laundry work is the hardest work she has to do, she usually starts in the laundry to equip her home electrically. Four electrical appliances are used in modern home laundries—the washer, dryer, ironer and hand-iron.
THE ELECTRIC WASHER.
Every process of washing makes use of the principle of forcing water through the meshes of the fabric. Clothes have always been washed this way, and probably always will be. Washing by hand amounts to nothing more nor less than this. All wash-ing machines employ this principle. Methods of obtaining the water action vary, of course, but the fundamental principle is always the same.
There are many designs of washing machines on the market, each possessing special characteristics, but the latest is one where the "washing" is effected by the creation of a highly energized turbulence in the soapy water, which forces the latter through the meshes of the fabric of which the clothes are made. The washing tub is made of cast aluminium, and is fitted with a four-bladed gyrator which agitates the water and clothes.
Above the tub is a fixed swinging wringer, designed to swing in a complete circle and arranged so that it can be locked securely in seven positions. The wringer has fitted an

after having watched a demonstrator, can use one of these devices expertly, cutting to one-third the time required for her ironing.
THE ELECTRIC HAND-IRON.
The electric hand-iron is the most widely used of all electric appliances. Its popularity is well deserved—it has obviated the necessity of continually walking to and from the stove or fire to keep the iron hot, the handle is always cool and easily grasped, and once the iron is heated (which takes but a few seconds), ironing can be continued uninterruptedly.
The six-pound iron is the best size for general household use. In many homes, the hand-iron is used for the entire ironing, but an increasing number of electric ironing machines are being introduced, and the
hand-iron is reserved for very small pieces and exceptionally dainty pieces of negligée or other very delicate garments.
When purchasing appliances such as have been described, there should be no uncertainty. They represent an important investment. They are not an everyday purchase—you are buying for the years to come. You ought to be certain that ten years from now you will be just as enthusiastic about the appliances you select as you are to-day.
If any doubt exists, take no ones word for it — insist upon a demonstration being given by the manufacturer under your own conditions. Then select the appliance that meets your ideas of what it should do. For, after all, performance—the ability to do your work as you would have it done—is what counts.

Electrical Progress
Things We Hear
One of the most interesting applications of ultra-violet rays is in obtaining a legible photograph of the ancient writings, so carefully erased from parchment in mediæval days, in order to make room for new records. There was no cheap paper then, so this act of vandalism may be understood though not excused, but the fact remains that the older writings were often by far the more interesting and valuable. By means of ultra-violet rays, they may be resurrected after centuries of oblivion.—The Arc (October).

* * *

Vita-glass, the new substance discovered by Professor F. E. Lamplough, which allows the ultra-violet rays of the sun to pass through, has been fitted to a score of educational and hospital buildings, and an interesting test recently was carried out at the Council School at Smethwick between two classes of children, each class consisting of
about twenty children. One class worked in a room fitted with ordinary glass, the other being in a room glazed with vita-glass. At the end of six months, the children in the former class had made the normal increase in height and weight, but the vita-glass class had gained no less than 60% over and above the increase gained by the other class.—The Builder (November 5th).

Electric generating plant is to be installed in the "Implacable," the only warship still afloat which took part in the Battle of Trafalgar.
A daily paper reports that the pavements of Vienna streets are to be heated electrically during the Winter. — The Electrician (November 26th).

Birmingham and Midlands
Branch
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. Lawson, 19 Southam Road,
Hall Green, Birmingham.

Mrs. Forrest, who comes from a family of sea-going engineers, was born at Tynemouth, in Northumberland.
She is the wife of Mr. F. Forrest, the Chief Assistant to the City Electrical Engineer at Birmingham, and, therefore, has through her husbands interests been associated with electrical development in a very definite form.
She was trained as a professional musician, and music is still one of her greatest hobbies. In addition, she is also a great croquet enthusiast and holds the championship of her club for the current year.
Mrs. Forrest has displayed great enthusiasm and interest in the work of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch, and is in every way a very excellent Treasurer.

MRS. FORREST.
Treasurer, Birmingham and Midlands Branch

BRANCH NOTES
The Autumn programme has proved very interesting, and resulted in a gratifying increase of membership.
The first item was a Drawing-Room Meeting at the house of Mrs. H. K. Beale, one of our Vice-Presidents, and wife of the Chairman of the Birmingham Electric Supply Committee.
Mr. Francis, of the E.D.A., lectured to a company of about 60, and a demonstration of various electric appliances was given. Altogether, it was a very instructive afternoon. Lady Brooks, Mrs. George Cadbury and many other well-known Birmingham ladies were present.
On October 14th, the members, including Lady Brooks and Mrs. Chattock, attended a demonstration of electric sewing by the Singer Sewing Machine Co., preceded by a short lecture on the development of the sewing machine from its earliest stages. Everyone was delighted with the artistic results which can be obtained without any physical effort.
On October 21st, the members were invited by Mr. Joseph H. Riley to a musical recital at the Queens Hotel. This concert was given to demonstrate an electrically driven pianola. Reproductions of masterpieces, as played by some of the most celebrated pianists of the day, were heard and enjoyed by a large audience.
This was a most delightful afternoon, and Mr. Riley has promised to give us another in the Spring.
A most successful meeting took place on October 28th, at the residence of Mrs. R. A. Chattock, our Vice-President, when about 60 guests assembled to hear Miss Griff lecture on "The Housewife: Her Own Electrician." Afterwards a cooking demonstration was given by Mrs. Williams, of the Electric Supply Showrooms, followed by an electric washing demonstration. Other electrical appliances were also exhibited and explained, including a vacuum sweeper.
On November 2nd, a meeting took place in the Council House, Walsall, the Mayor of Walsall presiding. Lady Brooks explained the aims of the Association, and Mr. G. S. Francis, of the E.D.A. lectured on "Electricity and Domestic Efficiency."
A meeting was held on November 16th at Moseley Presbyterian Hall. Lady Brooks presided, and Miss Griff gave a lecture, entitled, "Electricity, the Domestic Magician." A demonstration of cooking, sewing, cleaning, etc., by electricity followed, and subsequently Mr. E. J. Jennings, Secretary of the Birmingham Electric Supply Department, gave a short address. There was a large attendance at the meeting.
On November 25th, members of the E.A.W. visited the showrooms of the Birmingham Branch of

transcription:

the General Electric Co. The party was welcomed by the Branch Manager, Mr. F. Boyes, and Mrs. Boyes, and then conducted round the showrooms, where a selection of artistic electric light fittings was exhibited.
An interesting talk on "Colour Lighting" was given by Mr. Unwin. The use of colour screens to produce daylight effects in illuminating shop windows was exemplified by a model shop window dressed with silks of various colours. The latest method of lighting factories was demonstrated, in contrast with the inefficient older methods. A mining signalling system was also shown in opera- tion. This was a most instructive and enjoyable afternoon.
The last event on our programme was a Drawing- Room Meeting at the house of Mrs. Forrest, on Thursday, December 2nd.
A party assembled to hear Miss Griffs lecture, and to see a demonstration of electric sewing, heat- ing and lighting, etc. The audience was very enthusiastic, and the success of these drawing-room meetings shows how much can be learnt by social intercourse, with practical exponents, of the advan- tages of electricity in the home.
A successful meeting was held at Harbury, on December 9th, a village eight miles outside Leaming- ton, which has just been installed with electricity. Miss Haslett spoke on this occasion to a crowded audience in the Village Schoolroom. Mr. W. Lawson, M.I.E.E., also spoke on "Electricity in the Home and on the Farm."
We have several items arranged for the Spring programme. Our main activities will be concen- trated on the Conference which we shall hold for three days, commencing on February 23rd with a luncheon at the Queens Hotel, at which Lady Cowan will preside, followed by a visit to Nechells Power Station.—G.I.

Manchester District Branch
Hon. Sec.—Miss G. L. Entwisle, A.M.I.E.E.,
5 Holmfeld, Sale, Manchester.

BRANCH NOTES
The Manchester District Branch is now thoroughly in being and shows signs of progress. It has, in fact, been found necessary to duplicate some of our meetings, as it is not always possible to find room for all those who want to come. Another reason for duplication is that the Association appeals to all types of women and some, therefore, can come only in an afternoon and others only at night.
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti very kindly spoke to us at the first public meeting, held in the Lesser Free Trade Hall, on October 26th. He dealt especially with the necessity for introducing labour-saving methods into the home and with the need for an adequate and cheap supply of electricity to make these possible. Mrs. Lamb, the Chairman of the local Committee, gave interesting anecdotes, from her experience, to bring home the same points. Following this, Miss Haslett explained the work the Association was doing and showed how, by becom- ing members, those present could get useful informa- tion for themselves, and also help to get the womens point of view considered in the country generally. Miss O. M. Forbes, the Honorary Treasurer of the Manchester Branch, is a native of Helens- burgh, Scotland, and since 1915 has acted as Welfare Superintendent at the Hollinwood works of Messrs. Ferranti, Ltd., Electrical Engineers. Miss Forbes has always been keenly interested in electrical engineering, and is an enthusiastic advocate of womens work in this direction. the General Electric Co. The party was welcomed by the Branch Manager, Mr. F. Boyes, and Mrs. Boyes, and then conducted round the showrooms, where a selection of artistic electric light fittings was exhibited.
An interesting talk on "Colour Lighting" was given by Mr. Unwin. The use of colour screens to produce daylight effects in illuminating shop windows was exemplified by a model shop window dressed with silks of various colours. The latest method of lighting factories was demonstrated, in contrast with the inefficient older methods. A mining signalling system was also shown in opera- tion. This was a most instructive and enjoyable afternoon.
The last event on our programme was a Drawing- Room Meeting at the house of Mrs. Forrest, on Thursday, December 2nd.
A party assembled to hear Miss Griffs lecture, and to see a demonstration of electric sewing, heat- ing and lighting, etc. The audience was very enthusiastic, and the success of these drawing-room meetings shows how much can be learnt by social intercourse, with practical exponents, of the advan- tages of electricity in the home.
A successful meeting was held at Harbury, on December 9th, a village eight miles outside Leaming- ton, which has just been installed with electricity. Miss Haslett spoke on this occasion to a crowded audience in the Village Schoolroom. Mr. W. Lawson, M.I.E.E., also spoke on "Electricity in the Home and on the Farm."
We have several items arranged for the Spring programme. Our main activities will be concen- trated on the Conference which we shall hold for three days, commencing on February 23rd with a luncheon at the Queens Hotel, at which Lady Cowan will preside, followed by a visit to Nechells Power Station.—G.I.

Manchester District Branch
Hon. Sec.—Miss G. L. Entwisle, A.M.I.E.E.,
5 Holmfeld, Sale, Manchester.

BRANCH NOTES
The Manchester District Branch is now thoroughly in being and shows signs of progress. It has, in fact, been found necessary to duplicate some of our meetings, as it is not always possible to find room for all those who want to come. Another reason for duplication is that the Association appeals to all types of women and some, therefore, can come only in an afternoon and others only at night.
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti very kindly spoke to us at the first public meeting, held in the Lesser Free Trade Hall, on October 26th. He dealt especially with the necessity for introducing labour-saving methods into the home and with the need for an adequate and cheap supply of electricity to make these possible. Mrs. Lamb, the Chairman of the local Committee, gave interesting anecdotes, from her experience, to bring home the same points. Following this, Miss Haslett explained the work the Association was doing and showed how, by becom- ing members, those present could get useful informa- tion for themselves, and also help to get the womens point of view considered in the country generally.
