Miss Haslett spoke on this occasion to a crowded audience in the Village Schoolroom. Mr. W. Lawson, M.I.E.E., also spoke on "Electricity in the Home and on the Farm."
We have several items arranged for the Spring programme. Our main activities will be concen- trated on the Conference which we shall hold for three days, commencing on February 23rd with a luncheon at the Queens Hotel, at which Lady Cowan will preside, followed by a visit to Nechells Power Station.—G.I.

Manchester District Branch
Hon. Sec.—Miss G. L. Entwisle, A.M.I.E.E.,
5 Holmfeld, Sale, Manchester.

BRANCH NOTES
The Manchester District Branch is now thoroughly in being and shows signs of progress. It has, in fact, been found necessary to duplicate some of our meetings, as it is not always possible to find room for all those who want to come. Another reason for duplication is that the Association appeals to all types of women and some, therefore, can come only in an afternoon and others only at night.
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti very kindly spoke to us at the first public meeting, held in the Lesser Free Trade Hall, on October 26th. He dealt especially with the necessity for introducing labour-saving methods into the home and with the need for an adequate and cheap supply of electricity to make these possible. Mrs. Lamb, the Chairman of the local Committee, gave interesting anecdotes, from her experience, to bring home the same points. Following this, Miss Haslett explained the work the Association was doing and showed how, by becom- ing members, those present could get useful informa- tion for themselves, and also help to get the womens point of view considered in the country generally. BRANCH NOTES
The Cheltenham Branch was formally inaugurated on November 25th, 1926, a meeting being held in the Drawing-Room of the Town Hall.

On introducing Miss C. Haslett (Director of The Electrical Association for Women), the Mayoress gave a short resume of Miss Hasletts activities both in connection with The Electrical Association for Women and the Womens Engineering Society, and of her work during the war.

Vice-President, Cheltenham Branch.

Lady Cowan concluded her interesting speech by referring to the revolutions which have taken place in the lives of the Canadian women by the introduction of electricity in the home.
Other speakers at the Luncheon included the Lord Provost (Mr. David Mason), who welcomed the work of the Association and said he looked forward to the time when, through the use of electricity, Glasgow would have no smoke, no black fog, fewer lung troubles, and only rosy-cheeked children. Mr. W. L. Winning (President of the Scottish Centre of the Institution of Electrical Engineers) spoke in support of the good work of the Association, and speeches

"Emma! — you read THE ELECTRICAL AGE. Do be a sport, and come and do something to our vacuum cleaner. It wont work, and Aunt Jane is coming to-morrow, and mother says we must have the house ab-so-lutely spotless and polishy before she comes."
"Right-oh! I expect you have blown a fuse in your energy. Wait till I get my screw-driver and pliers. Have you got a bit of 5-amp. fuse wire in your house or shall I bring some?"
"Oh! weve bags of fuse wire. What do you take me for? But I dont think it is a fuse, because I put the lamp back when I found the vacuum wouldnt vac, and the lamp is quite all right."
"Hum! That means the fault lies on the vacuum or its connections. Do you know if there is any current at all through it?"
"No. How do you find that out?"
"Thats easy. Take off the switch cover and see if there is a slight spark at the switch blades when the circuit is broken. Here we are—lets try that first."
Emma nipped off the switch cover with the speed of a practised "Guider," and demonstrated the sparkless switch blades to the round-eyed Anne.
"That proves there is an open circuit somewhere," she explained. "And we know it must be somewhere beyond the lamp-holder. Lets follow the path of the current
from the lamp-holder on, and see if we can find the break."
Emma, proud of her training in matters electrical, started a systematic examination
"CROYDON" ELECTRIC CLEANER
of the apparatus, keeping up a running commentary which was very illuminating to Anne.

Unnamed: 9: Emma identifies a corroded adaptor while repairing a vacuum cleaner.
transcription:
The Electrical Age	97
thing itself. I dont see any obviously weak spot in your trailing flex, but well have to feel it all down, starting from the lamp adaptor. It isnt unusual for a break to occur right up close to a plug or adaptor. Hallo, though! I believe Ive got it." And Emma held out the adaptor, showing the two brass contacts badly corroded.
"That does look mouldy!" exclaimed Anne. "Ill rub that up with a bit of sand-paper while you examine the rest."
"Thanks, that will save time. The flex is certainly all right. Now the switch in the cleaner is the next link. Lets open that up and see if it is making good contact. On our cleaner at home you take off a little plate, with two screws, to get into the switch. With this one, it seems, the whole top unscrews. Yes, thats it—look, there are the contacts, but they look in perfect condition. If they werent, we could easily push them up closer together so as to make tighter contact."
"I see," said Anne. "Suppose we try to work the thing again now Ive cleaned the adaptor, before you research any more."
So the two girls plugged in and switched on the vacuum again, and were rewarded by the well-known hum. "Bravo!" cried Anne. "Now I wonder how the adaptor got in that state."
"Age partly, and partly, I expect, it has been used in a lamp-holder where the plunger spring has grown a bit weak. When that happens and contact is not very good, it starts slight sparking, and that makes matters worse."
"I understand. Now tell me—suppose you hadnt spotted the fault so quickly, where else would you have looked for it?"
"The motor brushes," replied Emma promptly. "Lets unscrew these little ebonite knobs on the motor and examine them."
They did so, and tipped out first a coiled spring and then a little black cylinder, which Emma explained was the brush which passed the current to the rotating armature.
"Occasionally, one of the brushes gets stuck up in the holder so it isnt pressed down on the commutator as it should be, but both these brushes slide in and out quite easily—so thats all right."
"Is there anything else you would have examined?" queried Anne.
"Nothing very easy. I have taken one of these motors to pieces and cleaned up the commutator, but that was after a lesson on motors, and I shouldnt advise you to try that without assistance."
"Very well, I wont. Thank you for your help. Now Ill get on and prepare for Aunt Jane. I wish, though, we didnt always have to put the vacuum in where the lamp is. For one thing, we sometimes want to use the cleaner after dark and, for another, it seems silly to have wall plugs quite handy and yet not be able to use them."
"My dear child, what you need is to join the E.A.W. immediately," said Emma with some superiority.
"Didnt you know you could get a two-way lamp adaptor so that both a lamp and
[Illustration of adaptor]
"MAGNET" 2-WAY ADAPTOR
any other gadget could be plugged into one lamp-holder? About the plug—if you will give me one of your plugs I will wire it up for you on to a lamp-holder, so that you can use any of the plug points for your vacuum, or iron, or any of the appliances that are usually fitted with a lamp adaptor."
"Thanks," said Anne meekly. "Ill let your words of wisdom sink in, and Ill be awfully glad to have the plug-lamp-holder appliance, and I know mother will be delighted."

The Electrical Age
How The American Housewife Achieves Leisure
Through Electricity
By Mrs. Christine Frederick
It may surprise many British women to learn that 98 per cent, of all American home-makers do their own housework! Long before the recent war, we were faced with a serious shortage of help, and had our own "servant problem," because domestic workers were tempted away by higher wages and greater independence to work in shops and factories.
Therefore, as much as 25 years ago, the American home-maker had only two choices — (1) to entirely abandon private family living and to substitute forms of boarding house and hotel life; or (2) to continue the private home, but to entirely re-organize it, both in building construction, methods and the equipment used to maintain it.
Mrs. Christine Frederick
will be visiting this
Country in February,
1927, and will lecture
for the E.A.W. in
London, at Glasgow,
Birmingham and
Manchester.
Since, fortunately, the majority of home-makers saw the advantages of continuing home life, there has been a constant progress in the United States along the movement for "Reconstruction in the Home." And this "reconstruction" has taken practical and concrete shape to the end that the private home may be retained, while at the same time women are freed from the former drudgery, yes, even slavery, of old-fashioned housekeeping.
I am merely stating facts when I say that the average American home-maker does her own cooking, keeps her house clean, cares for her children, and often does the laundry work, assisted by only a little extra "day labour," and often not that.
Electricity has been practically applied to the re-modelling of the house, to the improvement of home installations, and the operation of household labour-saving appliances. There have been three main lines of development along which this important "reconstruction" has proceeded in the United States. And these are:—
(1) The designing and erection of smaller, more compact and step-saving houses, involving less maintenance and service.
(2) The manufacture and installation of more efficient systems of general heating, water supply, lighting, and power for household needs.
(3) The adoption of countless electrical labour-savers which have reduced the effort and time required in the special operations of the home — notably the electric cooking unit, the power washer, the ironer and vacuum cleaner.
Since the American woman is doing all or most of her own housework, and since even the "new-fashioned" servant when obtainable, refuses to perform the heavy work previously considered part of her duties, American builders have been forced to recognise these special conditions. There have been developed, consequently, many excellent designs and models of what we call "the servantless house" or "the self-service house." It is specially designed for the woman who herself manages the home, or where a single servant only is employed. In

Unnamed: 6: American Household Efficiency Expert; Founder; Director; Author
Unnamed: 9: American household efficiency expert who wrote about modern kitchen design.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 99

general, this house is small, compact, and
with few corridors, halls, or detached
pantries. Where it used to be almost a half-
hours journey for the servant to carry the
roast from range to table, there is now built
the convenient dining alcove but a step away
from the kitchen, or the kitchen itself is so
re-modelled that the work of preparing any
meal is lessened and lightened.
The American kitchen, 1927 model, is a
marvel of step-saving and electrical con-
venience. A floor space of about 10 feet by
12 feet has been found sufficient in which to
prepare foods for from six to eight persons.
Each of the main pieces of equipment can be
so placed that the worker may proceed from
one task to the other, making a chain of
steps or " routed work." Thus, the food
storage, the preparing table, and the elec-
trical range should be located adjacent or in
one group. It will then be possible for the
worker to move expeditiously and easily
from one cooking process to the other, and

The Electrical Age
101
An All-Electric House in Switzerland
By Mrs. Walter Lawson (Hon. Secretary, Birmingham and Midlands Branch)
Mrs. Lawson is writing a series of articles giving her impressions and a description of the various interesting Electrical Appliances and Equipment which she saw on a recent visit to Switzerland. The first article on the subject appeared in the October issue of this Journal.
In this Utopia electric light appears to be used in every home, and many houses are all-electric. We visited one charmingly arranged all-electric house in which several appliances were installed which we had seen in process of manufacture. The kitchen was supplied at two points with cold and boiling water. In addition to an electric oven there was a metal-topped table with electric boiling rings fitted into the top and a large drawer underneath. The drawer accommodates the pans, which have detachable handles to economise space. On the dining-room table electric chafing dishes, one specially designed for fish and another for joints, were used; also an electric coffee percolator. For warming the room a heat accumulator stove was used. I described this method of heating in the October number of THE ELECTRICAL AGE. The stoves use the current at night at a cheap rate, and the heat is stored in stone blocks. The special stone which composes the blocks is called steatite, and has the property of absorbing a great amount of heat. The heating elements which carry the current are placed between the blocks. The heat is given off during the day, and can be regulated by turning a handle which opens and closes the ventilator at the top.
The breakfast-room was very prettily arranged to imitate the living-room of a Swiss farmhouse, with high-backed settles. Behind an old carved bench the stove, which was of blue tiles, formed the wall supporting a solid looking shelf of blue porcelain on which were arranged an assortment of large pewters, mugs and pitchers. The stove formed a partition between this room and the lounge, heated both and was constructed on the same principle as the one described above. These stoves are fumeless, odourless, do not need cleaning, and are cheap to run.
After seeing the electric bath-room with nickel fittings and complete with shower-bath (with thermometer to gauge the exact heat) and two large washing-bowls of Cararra marble, hot water supply in each bedroom, the electric refrigerator in the store cellar and the 40-gallon electric water-heater in the basement which supplied the house, one came away full of envy, and feeling how delightful it would be if all-electric Swiss châlets could be shipped here complete.

transcription:
102 The Electrical Age

Electricity and Silk Stockings!

By Len Chaloner

Though we may be quite ready to thank electricity for lighting, heating, labour-saving devices, and many of the amenities of civilisation generally, it is still something of a surprise to learn that electricity played a part in the discovery of artificial silk.
Many scientists had foreseen that artificially produced silk would, some day, become a possibility, but though Chardonnet, a Frenchman, was the first to take out a patent for an artificial silk in 1884, the early efforts of Sir William Crookes and Mr. Swan in 1882-1884, in experiments to produce a structureless thread for lamp filaments, led them to the observation that a thread for textile purposes, with the appearance and characteristics of silk, could also be made.
Artificial silk has paid its debt to electricity however, for by the latest methods of production, known as the acetate process, it is much used for the insulating of electric wires, particularly telephone wires, on account of its quality of absorbing very little moisture from the atmosphere.
It may be added that, from a decorative point of view, artificial silk is also used for electric lighting flex in some of the beautiful colours which up-to-date dyeing methods have made possible.
But in addition, just as electricity in its many services about the home, and our cities, gives us that clean, civilised feeling of luxury, so our electrically inspired artificial silk affords even the most modestly exchequered of us the self-respect, the charm, that was once only within the reach of those who could afford real, silk-worm silk. In its civilising value, this child of electricity is surely almost as valuable as its parent.
The curtains at the window, the carpets—like silken Persian rugs—on the polished floor, the cushions and the upholstery, the bedspread or the net casements; all, to day, are artificial silk, even if allied with wool or cotton.
And for ourselves, our personal selves, whether it is our cobweb stockings (a double delight since they are without the pangs of conscience for extravagance that would be attached to real silk) or undies that are so modestly priced that the thought of years of enforced darning does not depress us, or whether it is the jumper, proud product of our knitting needles, or a frock of silk that gives us the much-to-be-desired "slim silhouette" of an all-commanding fashion, we may thank electricity as a sort of fairy godmother. But, perhaps, being merely human, we shall at the same moment switch on the electric light in order more comfortably and serenely to admire ourselves in our new possessions!

Chalk and Electricity

In the process of burning chalk for the manufacture of lime, sufficient electricity is being produced at Heathfield, Sussex, to light the village. It is claimed that this process could be employed in chalk or limestone districts to supply, at infinitesimal cost, a large proportion of the electricity needs of the nation. The Heathfield experimental plant has been erected for the inventor, Mr. T. A. Reid, a chemical engineer, who states that in the making every week of 5 1/2 tons of lime, he obtains power sufficient to generate 5,000 Board of Trade units of electricity. The process consists mainly in utilising the gases given off when chalk or limestone and fuel are burned together to make lime.—The Dyer (October).

years ago, in the first year of the Borough Council taking over the work of the old Vestry.
The great comments at the time of the opening were upon the enormous expenditure of ratepayers money in an undertaking which, being municipally managed, was doomed to failure, and on the extravagance of putting in such large machinery, the capacity of which would surely never be used in the supply of electric light to Hackney.
At this time, Mr. L. L. Robinson was appointed Borough Electrical Engineer, and put in charge of the undertaking, together with Mr. J. R. Bowden as Distributing Engineer, both these engineers having previously been on Mr. Robert Hammonds staff, and having supervised the erection of the generating station and the laying down of the mains.
From the very commencement, the undertaking has been an unqualified success, and it is interesting to note that from the commencement the Borough Electrical Engineer has visualised the enormous importance of keeping Hackney electricity prominently before the ratepayers.
In most undertakings, in those early days, the Corporation used to supply electricity to those who came to fetch it, but right away from the commencement Hackney has operated a pushing sales policy, and in 1906 went to Parliament and was one of the pioneers in obtaining full powers for the municipality to wire installations and supply all sorts of apparatus for sale, on easy purchase or on hire, and be in a position to render a full service to their consumers, so that they were able to supply not merely electricity but the finest possible service for light, heat, power and cooking.
From the full operation of this policy in 1906, the output of this important undertaking has progressed by leaps and bounds. Instead of 1,800 kilowatts, the installed capacity of the works to-day is 39,000 kilowatts, and instead of an output of 1,614,968 units in the year 1902-3, the output for the year ending 31st March last was no less than 27,369,426 units, while the capital expenditure upon the undertaking has increased from £215,191 to £1,166,694.
It is obvious to those who know anything about the subject that this enormous business could not have been attempted with the system of supply originally put down in 1901.
About 1912, the Electricity Committee recognised the urgent importance of making a change, and on the advice of their engineer they started building an addition to their old generating works, which generated electricity by direct current at low voltages. This contains the most modern turbine plant, generating electricity at the high pressure of 6,000 volts at 50 cycles per second, so that the energy may be transmitted to distant points very cheaply through small mains and there converted for the consumers use. It is significant of the foresight of Hackney that this type of current has been standardised by the Electricity Commissioners as the standard for the whole country.
After the electricity has been generated at the works in its crude form at about 6,000 volts, it is sent from Millfields Road by small, but very heavily insulated, cables to sub-stations at Northwold Road, Dalston Lane and Balcorne Street, and at these it is altered to direct current at the pressure of supply desired by consumers, namely, 240 volts for lighting and 480 volts for large power.
Already these stations are becoming insufficient for the growing demands of the Borough. Two new stations have recently been built, which are automatic, or semi-automatic, being started up or stopped under remote control from the nearest old sub-station. Three more similar sub-stations are badly wanted, and will shortly be commenced.
What will happen as to further extensions it is rather difficult to prophesy, but it is quite certain that an old 5,000 kilowatt turbo-alternator will have to be taken out of the works next year and replaced by a 10,000 kilowatt set, and after that there is room left on the site for a station of 40,000 kilo-

Instead of 1,800 kilowatts, the installed capacity of the works to-day is 39,000 kilowatts, and instead of an output of 1,614,968 units in the year 1902-3, the output for the year ending 31st March last was no less than 27,369,426 units, while the capital expenditure upon the undertaking has increased from £215,191 to £1,166,694.
It is obvious to those who know anything about the subject that this enormous business could not have been attempted with the system of supply originally put down in 1901.
About 1912, the Electricity Committee recognised the urgent importance of making a change, and on the advice of their engineer they started building an addition to their old generating works, which generated electricity by direct current at low voltages. This contains the most modern turbine plant, generating electricity at the high pressure of 6,000 volts at 50 cycles per second, so that the energy may be transmitted to distant points very cheaply through small mains and there converted for the consumers use. It is significant of the foresight of Hackney that this type of current has been standardised by the Electricity Commissioners as the standard for the whole country.
After the electricity has been generated at the works in its crude form at about 6,000 volts, it is sent from Millfields Road by small, but very heavily insulated, cables to sub-stations at Northwold Road, Dalston Lane and Balcorne Street, and at these it is altered to direct current at the pressure of supply desired by consumers, namely, 240 volts for lighting and 480 volts for large power.
Already these stations are becoming insufficient for the growing demands of the Borough. Two new stations have recently been built, which are automatic, or semi-automatic, being started up or stopped under remote control from the nearest old sub-station. Three more similar sub-stations are badly wanted, and will shortly be commenced.
What will happen as to further extensions it is rather difficult to prophesy, but it is quite certain that an old 5,000 kilowatt turbo-alternator will have to be taken out of the works next year and replaced by a 10,000 kilowatt set, and after that there is room left on the site for a station of 40,000 kilo-

watt capacity, designed on the most modern lines, with very high pressure steam, high super-heat, powdered fuel, and every modern device, so that Hackney will always be able to generate for itself much cheaper than it could buy from one of the modern power stations.
About 1905, the Head Offices of the Department were situated in a small shop. In 1923, the staff had grown so much owing to the increase of the business that they were almost pushing out the walls of the building and were working under most unhealthy and insanitary conditions.
The result was that the Committee was forced to find increased office accommodation, and Hackney should be thankful that in so doing they took the bull by the horns and decided to build Head Offices and Showrooms worthy of so wonderful an undertaking.
For this purpose they bought the whole of the land in Lower Clapton Road, now occupied by the Head Offices. These offices are showrooms, repairing shops, sub-station—and are amongst the most modern and fully equipped of any in the United Kingdom.
They were opened to the public on the 8th October, 1925, since which date, owing to the greater facilities which these premises give for educating the public in the use of electricity, the progress of the business has gone forward with still greater leaps and bounds.
Every Tuesday and Friday afternoons there are special lecturettes and demonstrations in the use of electricity in the home, especially for washing, cooking, and for water heating.
These Demonstration Halls belong to the ratepayers of Hackney, and they are for the ratepayers to use, and the officials there are always glad to greet any and to give every sort of information which they have at their disposal in reference to the Undertaking. Throughout the Winter months, on Tuesday evenings, interesting lectures on all sorts of subjects are given free of charge, and these are usually illustrated with most interesting lantern slides and cinematograph films.

Press Button Wireless
The Felcourt Products, Ltd., of Greater Felcourt, East Grinstead, have recently put on the market a very ingenious wireless receiving set. There is an entire absence of the usual array of gadgets on the front panel, all that has to be done to get reception is to press the loud speaker plug into the required “loud” or “soft” hole on the right of the panel.
The set is arranged to receive from two places—the nearest local B.B.C. Station and Daventry, so that dual programmes are always available.
For the advantages it offers, the set is very moderately priced, and can be obtained from any stores or wireless dealer, and is known as the Felcourt Press Button Set.
Mr. Borlase Matthews, of the All-Electric Farm, East Grinstead, is one of the patentees.

Unnamed: 9: Fictional child character sitting by the nursery fire.
transcription:
The Electrical Age
111
KIDDIES KORNER
BRIGHTER LAND
"Hello! hello! everybody pay a visit to Brighter Land," said the big loud speaker in the nursery.
"But how do we get there?" asked Baby Molly, seated in the glow of the fire.
"Dont be silly!" said Bobbie, her twin brother, turning a somersault on the carpet. "The man who said that cant hear you."
"Oh! cant he," said a voice, and sure enough out of the loud speaker came two black feet, next a pair of blue trousers, a red jacket and, last of all, a black, merry face and a mop of fuzzy hair.
"Why, its Jimmy, the gollywog, I saw in Oxford Street," exclaimed Molly; and so it was.
"Now you two, hurry and follow me; I cant wait." And the gollywog walked straight into the loud speaker, which grew and grew until it was just a long black passage. "Oh! but its so dark," said the twins, and just then Jimmy touched a little button near him, and, as if by magic, there appeared all along the passage hundreds of electric lights. "Its so easy to switch on these kind of lights and so much nicer than candles or gas; no striking matches to burn our fingers."
"Come along, I have only just time to show you a corner of Brighter Land, as I am meeting Mr. and Mrs. Rical, known so well as the Elect-Ricals. Ah! but here they come."
"How strange, they are just like the bulbs on the lectric lights we have at home," said Bobbie.
The Ricals seemed to be in a great hurry. Mr. Rical told Jimmy he was sorry he could not see him as arranged, owing to the sad disappearance of Mr. Lamp, as he had been asked to try and throw more light on the mystery; he (Mr. Rical) was the leading power. So saying "Good evening," he hurried off.
The passage ended all at once, and the twins found themselves in a big hall so large they were unable to see the other end. There were thousands of people just like Mr. Rical running here and there as if something very exciting had happened.
"This is a small part of Brighter Land, where your people get all their bulbs from to make their homes brighter; all these are so pleased to know they are going into your world to live and shine, making hearts lighter and homes brighter. We must hurry home now, for your mother will be wondering what has become of you, but I will come and fetch you another day." The sound of the loud speaker made the twins know they were back by the nursery fire once again.

Unnamed: 10: Pioneer of the wireless communication technology discussed in the article.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 113

A brief reference to what may be called the business side of radio communication may serve to emphasise what a wonderful thing is this miraculous agency which, merely as a side line, gives music on tap in countless thousands of homes.
As a means of communication between ships at sea, it has figured in many an epic story of lives saved through the ability of a distant vessel to hear the wireless distress signal. For flashing the latest news and important business messages from one end of the world to the other, and even beyond this sphere—for did not a super-optimist only recently pay for the transmission of a message of greeting to Mars?—radio communication finds its most useful application.
In this field, however, new developments are constantly taking place, one of the most important being the new beam system of wireless transmission discovered by that radio pioneer, Mr. Marconi. Five years ago, most radio engineers imagined that they knew all about their subject, but the beam system meant a radical change of principle, and all the cut-and-dried theories of that time had to be replaced by others founded on the new discovery.
Under the old arrangements, the sending of wireless messages over long distances would have been so costly that very little profit would have been made on the services so conducted. The big transmitting stations were very costly; those built in this country, as at Rugby and Carnarvon, cost something like £500,000, and used enough power to supply a small township. The wave lengths used for this long distance work were of the order of from 8,000 to about 30,000 metres.
Mr. Marconi conceived the idea that by using very short waves, of only a few metres in length, considerable economies could be effected. After many experiments on these short wave lengths, the system was found to be a practical success, and already we have short wave communication in operation between this country and Canada.
With these short waves, very high working speeds are possible. Our high-power long wave stations were capable of transmitting and receiving each way at an average speed of 20 words per minute during a daily average of 18 hours. Already, the beam stations have been proved capable of working at an average speed of at least 100 words a minute during 18 hours out of every 24.
Another great advantage of the short waves is that their use allows the choice of a very much larger range of wave lengths than before. Now the long waves come between 5,000 and 30,000 metres, and the short waves between 5 and 100 metres; but when two long wave stations are working on wave lengths which are very close together, each of the stations is liable at any time to interfere with the messages sent out or received by the other. In fact, in the seemingly wide range between 5,000 and 30,000 metres, it has been found that there are only 90 practicable wave lengths. With the short waves between 5 metres and 100 metres, however, there are no fewer than 3,700 suitable wave bands which can be used without any danger of interfering with the work of other stations.
Already beam stations have been built by the Marconi Company for the Governments Imperial wireless communication system. There is a transmitting station at Bodmin for communication with Canada and South Africa, the receiving station for those countries being at Bridgwater. There are also similar stations at Grimsby and Skegness for communicating with India and Australia, and stations of the same type are being built in the Dominions.
One of the most interesting facts about this beam system is that it is actually a return by Mr. Marconi to some discoveries made during his earliest experiments about 30 years ago, when he found it was possible to transmit and receive signals when working on short waves. As it happened, the long wave system developed rapidly and the earlier discovery was brushed aside, and but for the high cost of the long wave, this development might never have taken place.

114 The Electrical Age

The Electrical Development of Great Britain

The Steam Age—Electric Age—Britain Pioneer in Generating Electricity for Public Use—Some Difficulties to be Overcome—The Aim of the Government Electricity (Supply) Bill

By George S. Francis

As conceived by the scientist and engineer, the vision of power for the future involves large scale electrical development, which will tap the cheapest sources of power, extract energy from waste, and transmit the power thus generated to effectively co-ordinated areas of distribution extensive enough to embrace the city and the country-side, linking the varied life and activity of the whole into an effective unit by the inter-communication of its telephone and transport services, and providing light, heat and power to every person who lives within the network of its wires. Such a conception involves a break with conventional thought and practice ; it demands a national outlook on power problems, an outlook that implies planning for the future instead of floating along on a policy of drift ; an outlook that will avoid regrets for missed opportunities by looking ahead. If courageously planned and greatly conceived, electricity can provide us with a power cheaper, more widely distributed and more extensively useful than any other form of power known to man.
From the dawn of history till about a hundred years ago, all the work of the world was done by the power of human and animal muscle, slightly assisted by the pressure of wind and the weight of falling water. This inability to use Nature forces limited human activity to an extent that is difficult for us of to-day to realise, and if the men of the ancient world did great things (and remains indicate that they did), it must have been at a cost in time and toil which we find it hard even to imagine. Into a world thus limited, was introduced the power of steam. For the first time in the history of man, goods could be produced in lavish abundance and transported quickly and cheaply over the whole world. That stands to its credit, but there is a debit side that must not be overlooked. Owing to the fact that steam power could only be used at or near the point where it was generated, and the additional fact that the steam engine was too big and costly to be used except by large numbers of workers under skilled supervision, steam power drew production from the home into the factory, and people from the country into the towns, created the problem of urban congestion, and covered large areas of town and country with a pall of smoke and dirt. The economics of steam power were such that industry, in its competitive struggle for markets, was continually striving to combine a high standard of human efficiency with a low standard of life in its effort to keep costs down, and thus increased, if it did not initiate, the historic struggle between capital and labour, the end of which we have not yet seen.
The discovery of steam produced a revolution, but because its revolutionary nature was not perceived and prepared for, a heritage of social and industrial problems was left in its train. But if the change from muscle power to steam power was revolutionary, the change from steam power to electricity will be more so. We must not let it break upon us unawares ; we must think out the problems it is likely to create, and take measures in advance to avoid the chain

The Electrical Age 117

Quick and Tasty Dishes—on an Electric Table Stove
By Mary MacKirdy (Glasgow and West of Scotland College of Domestic Science).

I can safely say that the most popular dish is the one that is tasty and quickly made with the least possible number of implements, and the appeal of this type of dish is naturally strongest to the bachelor of either sex or the woman of many duties.
With a little table stove, astonishingly good results can be obtained with the minimum of expense and time.

A VERY SIMPLE TASTY DISH.
Toast a fairly thick slice of bread on one side under the grill, turn it, and arrange on it some nice pieces of ham or bacon ; grill until cooked. The bread will absorb the fat and at the same time become crisp, and while this is cooking the tea or coffee is being prepared. Slices of tomato or apple may be cooked at the same time as the ham.

UNDER THE GRILL.
For the solitary one, this is an ideal method, as all kinds of little things cook well by this method, which is supposed to be the oldest and the best.

SOMETHING TO GRILL.
Kippers, Finnan haddocks, fillets of white or other fish—a fresh herring is excellent, split open and grilled—a chop, piece of steak (but it must be tender and thick)—a piece of chicken, a half one does well, and keep it basted with a little butter.

TWO TASTY SAVOURIES.
(1.) Toast a slice of bread and cut it in four, each piece being large enough to hold a sardine. Butter the pieces and dip one side in grated cheese, lay a sardine on top, sprinkle cheese over, and grill for a few minutes. Serve very hot.
(2.) Toast a slice of bread, then cover it with thin shavings of a rich cheese, I mean one that will melt easily when the cheese is toasted, but not too much ; lay over it some very thin slices of bacon or ham ; grill for a few minutes and serve very hot. The toast might first be spread with a little mustard.
These dishes are all so simple ; some will wonder why they have never made them, but they are good—try them.

“Wiring the Homes of Britain” Campaign
This Campaign, which we referred to in our last issue, has now been running for about twelve weeks, and has, we understand, been successful far beyond the hopes of its originators.
There have been 32 special Electric Exhibition Houses arranged in connection with the Campaign, and over 800,000 copies of the Competition Booklet have been disposed of.
Many thousands of competition vouchers have already been received and dealt with, and there is very distinct evidence that the Campaign is creating a tremendous amount of activity amongst all sections of the Electrical Industry and also of the General Public.
The more electricity is used and the more electrical apparatus is demanded, the more efficient and cheap will our electrical service in this country become. We would, therefore, urge members of the E.A.W. to take the greatest possible interest in helping the Campaign everywhere ; in particular, we hope that members of the E.A.W. will not fail to send in their competition vouchers in order that they may have an opportunity of winning one of the many excellent prizes which are offered.
As readers will remember, these Competition Booklets may be obtained from any Electric Shop or Showroom without fee or obligation of any sort.

transcription:
118          The Electrical Age

Correspondence

All-Electric Flats for the Bachelor.
Dear Madam,—I feel certain that many of your readers will be interested in some one-room "American" flats that are being made in Liverpool. Each room of a rather large house, convenient to the city, has been fitted with a double bed (which folds into a cupboard), a beautifully upholstered window seat, a dresser, several cupboards, and the whole finished in delightful shades of brown, gold and buff, toning in with the oak Chesterfields.
An electric fire, cooker and vacuum cleaner are fitted with every flat, and the washing is done by an electric washer in the possession of the caretaker. Chintz curtains hanging from the ceiling hide both the cooker and the sink.
The rental is from £1 to £1 5s. per week, an amount which must be regarded as more than reasonable.
The owner is reckoning to obtain 10% on the money he has sunk in the venture, and has used electricity because the resulting cleanliness will keep his property from deteriorating in value. The best of good wishes to THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN.
Yours truly,
PATRICIA HALL.

Advantages of Electric Cooking.
Dear Madam,—You may be interested in my experience of an electric cooker. I have an eight-roomed house which, when I came to it, had a big "kitchener" with two side ovens, requiring a large amount of coal to heat them.
I had this taken out and the space lined with glazed bricks, building it up waist high, thus forming a shelf for oven and hot plate.
The electric oven (Jacksons), which has been in constant use for 5 1/2 years, has given entire satisfaction, and the only attention it
has required has been the renewal of two of the elements, and even this did not throw the oven out of use.
In 15 minutes, after switching on, it is up to 400° Fah., and the heat can easily be regulated.
Last week, when baking Christmas cakes, the temperature remained at 250° for five hours, with the switch at low.
I have two maids, and my cook was quite inexperienced when this oven was put in, and though at first rather diffident, she quickly got used to it and has now nothing but praise for its good qualities, and I, of her good results in using it.
The price of electricity here for cooking is 1 1/4 d. per unit, and I find it most economical and have been unaffected by the recent shortage of coal.
Yours, etc.,
(Mrs.) I. C. HINTON.

transcription:
120	The Electrical Age

The New Cooking
By Olive Lauth

"The New Cooking" was introduced to our readers by Mrs. Lauth in the October issue of THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN. Further reports will be given from time to time of the progress of this new method of cooking.

The characteristic of previous methods of boiling has been that the necessary heat was produced in one appliance—the fire, stove or boiling ring—and then transferred by radiation or conduction to the other appliance—the pan. This division of function had three disadvantages, involving loss of time in heating up the stove ; loss of heat, for only a fraction of the heat produced in the stove penetrated into the food ; and difficulty of regulation, because to change the degree of boiling the cook usually altered the heat in her stove, which, after an uncertain period of time and to an uncertain degree, made itself felt in the pan.
The Electric Induction Cooker works on a new principle. A large induced current is made to pass through the bottom and sides of the pan, thereby producing heat directly in the pan, while the cooker itself remains cool. Although this current is large, it is at a very low tension, making it impossible for it to produce the slightest shock.
Current is induced into the pan by the cooker, which is therefore called an " Inducer," and is controlled quite simply in a graduated range of eight to ten heats by means of switches mounted on the Inducer.
The domestic apparatus is designed to bring water to the boil at the rate of one pint per minute on the highest heat—" very fast " ; and the lowest heat—" slow simmer " —will keep food hot in the pan for an indefinite period without spoiling or requiring attention. The intermediate heats are proportioned to keep the contents of the pan at a fast, quick, or slow boil, or a quick simmer. The moment a switch is operated the corresponding degree of heat is set free in the pan ; there is no waiting for one heat to gradually augment or diminish into another, the change is immediate and visible. No one but the cook herself can fully appreciate the saving of thought, time and worry which this ease of control and practically perfect heat regulation gives, especially at times of unexpected pressure in the kitchen.
If water in the pan be replaced by fat, the

THE INDUCER AND ITS UTENSILS

Unnamed: 9: Owner of the All-Electric Farm visited by E.A.W. members.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 121

temperature will vary instead of the degree of boiling. With the switch at "quick boil," the temperature will be about 400° to 450° F. when pan-baking and frying can be performed. This pan-baking or braising gives delicious cooking results for a very low current consumption, and is specially useful for tough and inferior joints, rendering the meat quite tender and juicy, while preserving the full flavour and giving a nice roasted appearance to the exterior. Deep frying—so often disliked and shirked by the cook—holds no terrors for those who use an Inducer, but is a quick, clean and certain operation. For instance, 4lbs. of cold lard, or other fat, will be "smoking" hot in from 6 to 7 minutes after switching on to "very fast," and five or six fillets of plaice, sole or haddock may then be fried in a wire basket every minute without waiting to re-heat the fat between the rounds. Potato chips, meat cutlets and thicker fillets of fish will take

from 2 to 5 minutes a round, so that the entire operation (for, say, six people) will be completed in from 10 to 16 minutes.

The same ideals of serviceability, durability and beauty which inspired the development of the Inducer itself have been extended to the utensils which are used in connection with it. All the pans are made of a strong, stainless metal, making them very easy to clean, and practically impervious to damage arising from such accidents as overheating, or being dropped and knocked, while in addition they have a pleasing if somewhat unique appearance.

The oven is as flexible in use as the boiling apparatus, a notable feature being that it requires no preliminary heating up. Single operations, such as baking a sheet of 16 to 20 scones, pastries or sponges, are accomplished within 7 to 15 minutes from the time of switching on the cold oven, and for energy consumptions as low as a quarter unit.

E.A.W. Activities in London

The London Autumn Programme commenced on Saturday, October 2nd, with a very interesting visit to the All-Electric Farm of Mr. Borlase Matthews. On arrival the party first had an opportunity of inspecting the modernized residence of Mr. and Mrs. Borlase Matthews, which, although 400 years old, had all the up-to-date conveniences which electricity can give.

In the conservatory there was a 2,000 candle power lamp used for concentrating artificial light on flower seedlings, which, by the continued stimulation of light for 24 hours per day after planting out, during the four or five days they benefited by it, became so invigorated that they bore flowers in about one-third the usual time.

Close at hand was the modern apiary, without hives, which was very popular both with the bees and the bee-keepers, as operations could be conducted in any weather and at any time.

Before proceeding to the farm a little distance away, the party had an opportunity of inspecting a delightful school, set in beautiful country surroundings and run on Montessori lines, this being the idea of Mrs. Matthews, who wished to give children in the country the same advantages of modern methods of teaching as the children in the towns.

On the farm it was discovered that there are now sixty-seven different applications of the uses of electricity, such as haymaking without sunlight and in any weather, applications in the poultry farm, electric ploughing, electro-culture of crops and many other uses in the dairy and milking sheds. VISIT TO LONDON ELECTRIC WIRE WORKS.
In October, the members visited the
Leyton Works of this Company, where they
saw all the processes in connection with the
manufacture of wire for electric purposes.

A CORNER OF THE ALL-ELECTRIC FARM

The party was especially interested in the
large number of girls who were employed on
different processes, including the covering of
fine sizes of wire in silk and enamel.
Tea was afterwards provided in the Works
Canteen, and an interesting resumé of the
history of the Company given by Mr. Hawke,
the Works Manager.

The two lectures given respectively by
Mr. W. C. Jeary and Miss Partridge were
much appreciated, and will be reported
in THE ELECTRICAL AGE at a later date.
The visit to Good Housekeeping Institute
was a favourite item, and the final visit of

the session to the Electric House at Croydon
was undoubtedly amongst the most popular.
Members were received, on arrival, by Mr.
Cramb (the Croydon Electrical Engineer),
Mrs. Cramb, and members of the Electricity
Committee. During the afternoon, an in-
teresting lecture was given on “Electric
Water Heating.”

VISIT TO LONDON ELECTRIC WIRE WORKS.
In October, the members visited the
Leyton Works of this Company, where they
saw all the processes in connection with the
manufacture of wire for electric purposes.

A CORNER OF THE ALL-ELECTRIC FARM

The party was especially interested in the
large number of girls who were employed on
different processes, including the covering of
fine sizes of wire in silk and enamel.
Tea was afterwards provided in the Works
Canteen, and an interesting resumé of the
history of the Company given by Mr. Hawke,
the Works Manager.

The two lectures given respectively by
Mr. W. C. Jeary and Miss Partridge were
much appreciated, and will be reported
in THE ELECTRICAL AGE at a later date.
The visit to Good Housekeeping Institute
was a favourite item, and the final visit of

the session to the Electric House at Croydon
was undoubtedly amongst the most popular.
Members were received, on arrival, by Mr.
Cramb (the Croydon Electrical Engineer),
Mrs. Cramb, and members of the Electricity
Committee. During the afternoon, an in-
teresting lecture was given on “Electric
Water Heating.”

North-East Coast Branch of
the E.A.W.

Arrangements are in hand for the forma-
tion of a North-East Coast Branch of the
E.A.W., with headquarters at Newcastle.
An inaugural meeting will be held early in
February, and, in the meantime, Miss Anna
Holm, a Founder Member, has agreed to act
as Hon. Secretary. Those wishing for
further information may write to—Miss
Anna Holm, at Dial House, Northumberland
Street, Newcastle-on-Tyne.

transcription:
EDITORIAL

THE NEW ELECTRICITY BOARD.

With the passing of the new Electricity Act, and the setting up of the Central Electricity Board, comes a great opportunity to the women of the country. All kinds of interests will claim recognition, but none surely more representative of national well-being than the woman who runs the home.

Factories and Shipyards, Foundries, Steel and Cotton Mills, will all of them demand, and very properly demand, a large share of the time and energy and capital at the disposal of the new Board, but in all these electrical services and development the fact must be ever kept in mind that the real basis of our national life and prosperity begins at an earlier period than in any industry, however great and important.

A REVIVAL OF RURAL LIFE AND INDUSTRIES.

The great feeder cables are going to stretch out their arms over the country-side; we may expect, in course of time, that no corner of England will remain unexplored. This, we hope, will mean the revival of the Life and Industries of our rural districts.

Facts force themselves upon us from all sides that already the towns are overcrowded, and the problem of maintaining a healthy community can only be solved as more and more facilities are provided for the people to spread themselves out over the country-side.

THE WOMANS DEMAND.

It is an old adage, but surely a true one, that what a woman really wants she can always get. Surely the desire of members of the E.A.W. is to see, as quickly as possible, all women relieved from the slavery of household drudgery, and we must not rest content until an adequate electrical service is within reach of every woman in the home.

Similarly, we must demand that all the necessary electrical apparatus is more and more accessible to all women, and especially the working woman who bears so large a share of household drudgery.

Excellent hiring facilities and easy-purchase schemes are already available in many of our large centres, and we may hope that as the demand for domestic appliances increases, the facilities for obtaining them will become easier and less costly.

As Mrs. Frederick so truly said in one of her recent very stimulating addresses—"We shall only get cheaper electrical apparatus when the demand from the women is sufficiently great to induce the manufacturer to introduce mass production methods in the factory."

126

Unnamed: 9: Sir John and Lady Shelley-Rolls conceived the idea of electricity.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 127

Electricity on the Avington Estate

A wonderful piece of pioneer work has been carried out at Avington, the country home of Sir John and Lady Shelley-Rolls. Here, about 45 years ago, a water wheel was in use for grinding corn, and this was later displaced by an early type of water turbine which drove a pair of stones for grinding corn. Sir John and Lady Shelley-Rolls conceived the idea of applying this power for producing electricity on the Avington Estate, with the result that, to-day, not only has the

In the farm near by, electricity is being used for lighting the dairy and cow byres, and it is intended before long to use electricity for milking and other farm operations.

In passing through the villages of Itchen Abbas and Easton, one may see beautiful old thatched cottages radiant with electric light.

The special interest attached to this scheme is that, with a nett working fall of 2 feet 11 inches, the electrical engineers employed have obtained energy sufficient to

[Illustration: THE OLD MILL, NOW THE POWER STATION. (This shows the Small Fall available.)
(By courtesy of "Country Life"]

Avington Estate an adequate supply of electricity, but a large number of surrounding villages have also been supplied. The whole scheme of using this water power to supply electricity to the surrounding districts was carried out under the advice and instructions of Messrs. A. W. Sclater & Son.

Avington House is beautifully situated on the River Itchen — famous for its excellent fishing — and the house itself is of great historic interest. Rumour has it that Nell Gwynn stayed here during one of her visits to Hampshire.

supply a large mansion house and its estate with all electrical facilities, together with two villages and their public buildings.

Sir John and Lady Shelley-Rolls have always been interested in any enterprise which will benefit the lives of those with whom they come in contact, Sir John having started many years ago one of the first co-partnership schemes on his farm. A wonderful piece of pioneer work has been carried out at Avington, the country home of Sir John and Lady Shelley-Rolls. Here, about 45 years ago, a water wheel was in use for grinding corn, and this was later displaced by an early type of water turbine which drove a pair of stones for grinding corn. Sir John and Lady Shelley-Rolls conceived the idea of applying this power for producing electricity on the Avington Estate, with the result that, to-day, not only has the

In the farm near by, electricity is being used for lighting the dairy and cow byres, and it is intended before long to use electricity for milking and other farm operations.

In passing through the villages of Itchen Abbas and Easton, one may see beautiful old thatched cottages radiant with electric light.

The special interest attached to this scheme is that, with a nett working fall of 2 feet 11 inches, the electrical engineers employed have obtained energy sufficient to

[Illustration: THE OLD MILL, NOW THE POWER STATION. (This shows the Small Fall available.)
(By courtesy of "Country Life"]

Avington Estate an adequate supply of electricity, but a large number of surrounding villages have also been supplied. The whole scheme of using this water power to supply electricity to the surrounding districts was carried out under the advice and instructions of Messrs. A. W. Sclater & Son.

Avington House is beautifully situated on the River Itchen — famous for its excellent fishing — and the house itself is of great historic interest. Rumour has it that Nell Gwynn stayed here during one of her visits to Hampshire.

transcription:
128

The Electrical Age

*Electric Water Heating

By P. C. HONEY
(Of the Croydon Corporation Electricity Department)

So many requests have reached us as to how the problem of securing an adequate supply of hot water can be solved by electricity, that we feel this article will be of very practical interest to many earnest enquirers. Croydon is leading the way in giving to its consumers an Electric Hot Water Service.

Hot water has been one of the necessities of life from ancient times. History does not tell us much in this direction, but the question of water heating was probably settled in the days of our forefathers by immersing red-hot stones, previously heated in a wood fire, in a convenient pool, a fore-runner, one might say, of the present-day immersion heater. It is only within the last forty years that the Englishmans home has been fitted with water heating apparatus of sorts and the mystical symbol, "bath, h. and c.," began to appear in estate agents circulars. In the early days, the coal range heated a simple little boiler at its side, where hot water on tap was sometimes obtainable. As time went on, pipes and storage tanks were added, and the modern bathroom appeared with its hot water brought right up to the spot. This system worked quite well while coal was 20s. a ton and maids were plentiful, especially as the coal range was in use for cooking purposes as well as for hot water. Since the war, there has been a constant demand for a really reliable apparatus to heat the household hot water system simply and economically. The gas geyser and the coke boiler have, to a certain extent, supplied that want, but the same inherent trouble, lack of cleanliness, has not been removed by these methods, and, furthermore, attention is still necessary either to stoking or combustion of the heating medium.

The "instantaneous" type of water-heater was first tried, but was not adopted for hiring purposes on account of the rapid furring of the elements and consequent failures experienced with most of these types. Furthermore, the maximum loading of 3 kw. we allowed for this class of apparatus made it useless for bath purposes. After testing many different makes of electric water-heaters, calorifiers, geysers, etc., we came to the conclusion that the thermal storage type of water-heater, with elements loaded from 500 to 1,000 watts, was most suitable for our purpose.

The thermal storage water-heater, such as the "Sadia" and "Inventum," is nothing more than a big "thermos flask," if I may borrow the term, always full of water and heated by a gentle heat which is about that of an electric kettle. An ingenious automatic switch keeps the water from actually boiling, cutting off the current as soon as the temperature is approximately 200° F., and switching on again after some hours to replace the heat lost during that period. As soon as hot water is drawn, cold water begins to take its place, and once again the automatic switch operates, keeping the current going until the water reaches 200° F. again. It will therefore be appreciated that this gives a service of hot water which is available, within reason, at all times.

During the last eighteen months, nearly four hundred electric water-heaters have been installed in Croydon houses, some

*Abstract of an Address given by Mr. Honey before the E.A.W., at Electric House, Croydon.

Unnamed: 9: Speakers will include Viscountess Astor, M.P. (President) at the meeting.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 131

safe from frost, but, naturally, the length of piping to the taps is the deciding factor. This water-heater is also loaded to 1,000 watts and has its automatic features.
We now come to the question of running costs. This is not approached from the point of view of so many gallons of hot water for so many pence. We press the claims of service first and foremost. We tell the housewife that this electric hot water service is exactly the same as if she had her fire going day and night, all the coal supplied and put on for her, all the stoking and damper manipulation done and, finally, all the ashes swept up and taken away. That service is so valuable, and yet so simple and so safe, that one cannot compare the cost of water heating by electricity in this way with other methods of hot water supply simply on a costs basis.
We have, however, taken careful tests on a number of installations in various districts in Croydon, and find that consumption does not vary very widely. To take two examples :
In a six-roomed house in Addiscombe, an 11-gallon "Sadia" water-heater is installed to supply hot water, available at all times to scullery and bathroom taps, and the consumption per quarter, allowing for four baths a week and usual domestic purposes, averages thirty shillingsworth of electricity.
In another case, a 17-gallon "Sadia" water-heater is installed in a similar manner, and hot water is used for two baths a day, for the lavatory basin, in the scullery, for clothes washing and house cleaning, and for culinary purposes; in short, for every possible use in the home, and the consumption varies between fifty to sixty units per week, or round about three pounds per quarter. The service alone is worth that.
There is one fundamental point with regard to the electric hot water, and that is the relation of consumption to output. One unit of electricity will raise two gallons of
cold water to approximately 195° F., and it can be safely assumed that if electricity is being consumed by a water-heater it must be making water hot. We know that little heat can escape from the outside of the water-heater, because the cork lagging used is so efficient that the outside is cold to the hand when placed on its surface. The only other waste would be by boiling, and if the automatic switch fails to prevent that, the steam generated soon acquaints us by its presence that boiling point has been reached. So you can therefore feel quite safe with the electric water-heater both as regards cost and operation.
I am glad to state that Croydon has been one of the pioneers of Electric Hot Water Service, and already there are many Supply Authorities in the British Isles who have commenced to hire electric water-heaters after hearing of our success, and it is safe to say that the day is not far distant when electric hot water service will be one of the chief uses for electricity.

The Electrical Age

Sound Scenery

Broadcasting Calls for New Kinds of Stage "Prop"

By BERNARD C. HOLDING (Editor of "The Electrician")

Not the least important of the problems to be faced in wireless broadcasting is the provision of realistic incidental "noises." In the cinema, the spectators can actually see the thundering express train, and the sounds produced in the orchestra do not need to be absolutely accurate to emphasise the effect. On the stage, too, the "noises off" are not of outstanding importance. With wireless broadcasting, however, the listener is without any visual guide, and relies entirely for his mental idea of the setting of a play on the words spoken by the actors, and on noise effects or sound scenery. The old "props" of the theatre and the cinema are generally useless before the sensitive microphone, which demands that the passing train must make a noise like a train, and not like a motor-cycle or a tug.
In the building of scenery out of sound, the radio producer can either use "props" or bring the actual sounds into the studio by means of a supplementary land line. Some time ago, the B.B.C. successfully employed the second method, placing a microphone at the corner of a busy London thoroughfare, and using the sounds thus collected as "scenery" for a play which was being broadcast from the studio.
Many effects are, however, difficult to secure in this way, and such a fine effect as a forest fire might not always synchronise with the production of a radio play requiring it as a background. At WGY, the Schenectady broadcasting station of the American General Electric Co., some time ago, a realistic forest fire was created by means of an ordinary plumbers blow-lamp (which reproduced the sound of wind and roaring flames) and by breaking up matches to imitate the noise made by the cracking and breaking of burning branches.

As the listener cannot yet see the entrance of a character in the broadcast play—although, with the development of television, he well may before very long—the entry is usually marked by the closing of a door, and that is why the doors in radio play settings are inclined to be squeaky, and their users slam them, with or without provocation.
Mr. T. E. Clay, who directs the plays broadcast from the WGY station, finds that in producing radio drama the noises are easily the most difficult problem. The actors, not needing to memorise their lines, only require one or two rehearsals, but the sounds are quite another matter, as the obvious one is not always found to be the most suitable for producing a certain effect, and many hours are sometimes spent in devising and rehearsing realistic effects.
One of the most stubborn of the "sound" problems tackled by Mr. Clay was the production of the sound of an express train travelling at a high speed. The train in question was supposed to be on a roughly laid single line, where the track was, consequently, none too smooth, and a flat wheel or two might be expected to contribute to the medley of sound.
This producer first made a thorough study of the sounds made by railway trains, learned them all in their proper sequence, and then set about reproducing them so faithfully that listeners could have no doubt that they were listening to the passing of a steam engine drawn train.
A real locomotive bell and a creditable whistle were readily produced. To these were added two boards covered with sand-paper, which were rubbed one against the other to make the chug-chugging noise of the engine. A flour sieve helped to define the sharp first sound heard as the engine puffs.

134
The Electrical Age
Wedding Presents!
By Len Chaloner
In what must assuredly have been the "good old times" from the bridegrooms point of view, there was no question of what to do with the "white elephant" wedding present, for there were none! We have it, on the contrary, on the best authority, that about eight hundred and fifty years ago, a little before the Norman conquest, loans were raised for the newly married ones to start them in their "Paradise enow." What better precedent could be found for the making of practical wedding offerings, and what more practical form could they take than electrical equipment for the home? If
Another thoroughly up-to-date present is wired furniture, such as a dining-room table, a tea waggon, or a dressing-table, complete with accessories.
But supposing that we are not relations, merely "friends" of the kind ushered into the left or right-hand pews, under the guidance of a rosetted sattelite who murmurs "brides or bridegrooms?" There is still a fine selection for us among the details of complete equipment.
No bride will want to appear at breakfast till her hair is duly waved! Or, perhaps, we might offer an electric brush, a refreshing vibro, or a "drier" to make shampooing a joy instead of labour.
ELECTRIC COFFEE PERCOLATOR
"Universal" ELECTRIC TABLE STOVE
we chance to stand in the serviceable capacity of aunts and uncles to one of the young couple, who will look for us to come down handsomely on the auspicious occasion, we may offer to provide light for the establishment, or what is no less important, wiring for power... so many points, giving the bride and groom a chance of placing these where they will, our own share of the business ending with the contractors. More entertaining to ourselves, however, may be to choose their electrical fittings for them, and in this direction of shades quite the last word in charm and luxury lies with the new English and also Bohemian (Czecho-Slovakian) glass.
Then comes breakfast. How chummy, in the simple household, to have everything done on the breakfast table by means of a griller, a toaster, percolator, kettle, egg-boiler, etc., complete! Dare one suggest that it is even good for *himself* to see what a lot of little items go even to the preparing of a mere breakfast?
And the days work? Even in these days of limited staff, it need produce no grey hairs and wrinkles if some thoughtful friend has presented the happy pair with a vacuum cleaner—electrically driven, of course—and

Unnamed: 9: Constructional Engineer whose initials match the Electrical Association for Women
transcription:
The Electrical Age 135

an electric washer wherewith to save laundry bills. Incidentally, of course, this makes an electric iron quite indispensable... a modest but most acceptable gift. Dinner à deux ends the days work in the ideal menage, and it will, of course, have been cooked by an electric range. And, at this juncture, it might be added that though an electrical range looks a little complicated at first sight, the bride need neither boil over a saucepan or burn her fingers even once, if she will but read the instructions carefully.

But in this practical offering of the most "everyday" presents, comes the queer little afterthought that we are harnessing up for the newly married ones one of the most tremendous forces in the world as we know it yet—a force that in its unknown quantities is as great and mysterious as love itself—and, by strange irony, a force that is capable of keeping a heart beating for many years long after the owner of the heart has passed away to a sphere where, traditionally speaking, there are no more problems to solve.

An Appreciation of Our Journal
Reprinted by kind permission of Kahncrete Engineering

By a remarkable coincidence, the writer of the article, who is a Constructional Engineer, has the same initials as our Association.

“It has sometimes been said that the truest test of the degree of civilisation to which any age or country can claim to have attained is to be found in the position of women at that time or place.
“At all events, we must allow that as nations have escaped from their primitive conditions and achieved an increasing culture, so also the value which has been placed upon women has steadily risen and the sphere of activity allotted to them has widened and increased, until at length there would appear to be emerging an entire equality with men in every department of life.
“The growth of education among women, which has been such a feature of the last fifty years, has not been without its opponents. The home life, that central pivot upon which our civilisation turns, has, some would have us believe, been threatened by the increasing number of women who find their chief interests in intellectual spheres hitherto only explored by men. For those who have watched, either with sympathy or with apprehension, the growth of the intellectual movement among women, THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN must present a challenge of the very deepest interest; for here would seem to be present not only the attainments of specialised education among women, but also the application by women of those attainments in no small measure to the problems of the home life, a sphere which must remain, at any rate in the minds of men, as the central feature of a woman’s life.
“In the subject-matter of its contents, no less than in its general production, this journal would seem in every way to be worthy of the cause of which it must be regarded as a pioneer.
“The service which electricity has already been able to render to the home life of this country has indeed been very great, and it must surely be all to the good that they who are the real experts in home requirements should in this way be working to progress by its aid still further in labour-saving devices and increased cleanliness in domestic work.
“THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN is a periodical which should be closely studied by everyone who is interested in up-to-date methods of home management, and also in the increasing sphere of intellectual activity which is the heritage of women, as it is of all mankind.”—E.A.W.

transcription:
136
The Electrical Age

London’s New Electric Restaurant

Dining and Dancing in Delightful Surroundings

The “Tricity” Restaurant, recently opened at the top of Savoy Street, in the Strand, is a natural development of Tricity House in Oxford Street, a pioneer Electric Restaurant in London.
The new restaurant is situated in the most central position and is easily accessible from all parts of the Metropolis. Our London members will have the opportunity of seeing it on April 6th, by kind invitation of Mr. A. F. Berry, and we hope our country readers will pay it a visit when they are in town. We are sure everyone will be delighted with the architecture, the decoration, the comfort, and the cooking. Excellent chefs and cooking staff have been engaged, under the direction of Mr. George Stone, and all the kitchen equipment is the last word in improved electrical apparatus — all-electric cooking, heating, lighting and ventilation. Most of our restaurants specialise in either old English or French cooking. Here we find a cuisine that will supply both, so whatever you want—an English grill or roast, or a French table d’hôte—you can always get it at what, we are sure, will be a very popular rendezvous. We must also add that the restaurant is fully licensed.
The lighting scheme is restful and harmonious, and excellent effect is obtained by the use of “Tricity” Sun-Ray Lamps. The soft warmth and light of these lamps is most comforting and refreshing, especially after the rush and turmoil of the streets and present-day business.
For the dancing enthusiasts there is a very delightfully sprung floor and a first-class dance band—attractive Dinner Dances are a feature of the restaurant.
Mr. A. F. Berry and the management are to be congratulated on providing such a charming and comfortable modern restaurant, and we hope they will get the support they deserve for helping to bring in the Electrical Age.—V.N.

THE “TRICITY” RESTAURANT

The Electrical Age 137
Useful Hints for the Home-Maker
By "ELECTRA"
"ELECTRA" will be pleased to give information regarding any electrical apparatus mentioned in the Journal. She has had practical experience herself in the use of domestic electrical appliances and will be pleased to place her experience at the disposal of our readers. In writing to her at Head Office of the E.A.W., kindly enclose stamped addressed envelope.
ELECTRIC TOWEL RAILS
I have recently seen a towel-airer, which every woman who cares for a well-appointed bathroom would like to have. It consists of a tubular rod heated by electricity, and the element is totally enclosed. The consumption is very small, being only 40 watts, and it can be run for 25 hours for one unit. A further advantage is that it can be used on any plug or lamp-holder. Single or double rods and brackets are fixed about 15 inches above the heated rod, thus eliminating the annoyance of wet towels.
The heated rod is nickel-plated and the airing rack is of crystal, so cleaning is
"GENII" TOWEL-AIRER
reduced to a minimum. They are easily screwed on to the wall, and the price of this useful and ornamental combination is very moderate.
THE VOLTA VAC.
With the Spring sun come thoughts of Spring cleaning, but with the increasing popularity of the Electric Vacuum Cleaner, I notice less dread of it even among our men-folk.
There are several excellent machines on the market, but a new one is always interest-
THE VOLTA VAC.
ing, is it not? In this one, the dust-bag is fixed inside the metal body, and all the attachments are connected to the hose, even the large one for carpets; so there is no need to push the whole machine along. It has a very convenient foot-switch, and the consumption of electricity is low. The accessories enable you to clean every corner of the house, and the Volta Vac. is as neat as its name.
"UNIQUE" SHADE CARRIER
We have all experienced the difficulty of keeping our lamp-shades, especially glass ones, really clean, because of the trouble with the shade carrier ring. Getting it off
