The Electrical Age 139

How Electricity Is Made. Part 4—The Unit
and Its Use

By J. W. Beauchamp, M.I.E.E.

The preceding three articles have given an outline of the process of producing electricity, distributing it to the housewife, and the metering and selling procedure which takes place in her home.
It may be worth while, in concluding, briefly to sketch the modern way of using electricity in the home, its limits of usefulness as they exist to-day, and the possibilities offered in different districts.
This article, at least, may be guaranteed to get out of date quickly owing to the rapid development taking place in the extent and variety of appliances put forward by the electrical engineer for the use of his housewife customer, and more particularly by reason of the commercial development which is leading suppliers of electricity, who a few years ago considered their duty to end with reading the meter, to offer a “full service” in many districts, helping the users to get wiring easily, obtain appliances on attractive terms and learn how to use them.
In districts where few, if any, of these “extra” facilities exist and electricity may be comparatively dear, there is no need for complete discouragement; there are few domestic users who could not, with advantage to themselves, employ a little more power or use it in a different and better way. The journal of the E.A.W. is doing a most useful work in bringing to its readers simple and accurate information on every aspect of power use in the home.
It is a favourite slogan of the industry that “electricity saves more than it costs,” and whether this little string of words has any particular merit as a slogan it, at least, contains one of the essentials of every good slogan—it is substantially true, and that truth is particularly noticeable in some of those uses of electricity where the amount of energy consumed in the year is small. Even in districts with a rather restricted supply, the small labour-saving appliances can generally be used without difficulty and if the rate per unit is high; on the other hand, the units used are few and the annual cost trifling compared with the release from drudgery which follows their employment.
Comfort and easy work in the home depends greatly upon a combination of two essential features—the architectural lay-out of the interior (shape, size and interdependence of rooms); and the equipment for lighting, heating and mechanical work, and particularly the way in which that equipment is brought together into a homogeneous house-work machine.
Even a new house is often imperfect in regard to the lay-out of the service and kitchen portion; it is difficult for the architect to square all the conflicting claims—big living-rooms, good natural light, pleasing aspect—and yet to give to those important parts where the work is done that amount of space and the form which they should have.
In any case, it falls to few of us to realise the almost universal ideal of building or finding exactly the house we want, and it is encouraging to remember that where that is not possible a liberal use of electricity will go further than anything else to mitigate the ingrained drawbacks of an ill-planned interior, to reduce the labour associated with a house of many stairs, and to cut out what the railwayman calls “idle mileage,” the miles, literally, which the housewife or her helpers have had to walk in the course of the year because one thing is awkwardly situated with regard to another; and all that treadmill-like procedure which starts when the

Unnamed: 9: Author of the article "The Domesticated Motor" for girls.
transcription:
142 The Electrical Age

A Page for Girl Guides
“The Domesticated Motor”
By Margaret Partridge, B.Sc.

“Many happy returns, Pat! Ive brought
you a few tools in honour of the day. Have
you had many nice things?”
“Oh! Molly, I am glad youve come. Ive
got the most wonderful present from mother
and father—and youve got to come and try
it with me. Father calls it ‘Electric Sally,’
and it really seems as though it can do any-
thing any person could do.”
“But what is it, really?”
“Just a little electric motor with all sorts
of gadgets you can fix on for cleaning and so
on. Its got a few now, but Im going to
think out a whole lot more we can make for
it, so that it will do just anything.”
So off went the two girls, Pat radiating
enough excitement and energy to run a train,
and Molly more soberly but very curiously
following.
They lifted the treasure from its box, a
small heavy object about as big as two fists,
and a number of small wheel-like attach-
ments for it and one cake whisk.
“What does the label say? One-tenth
B.H.P.—thats horse power, isnt it? 230V.
—thats volts; A.C. or D.C.—now thats
what beats me. A.C. or D.C. means alter-
nating current or direct current, I know—
but Jim says that a motor which will run on
one wont run on the other, so how can mine
be all right on both?”
“Oh! I have heard that, because I asked
the same question about our vacuum cleaner.
There is just one kind of ‘winding’ which
does as a motor for alternating current and
direct current. The funny thing is that it is
the same kind they use for vacuum cleaners
and motors like yours as they use for trams
and trains; at least, thats what dad says,”
said Molly dubiously.
“Well, then, there is another question.
The other day we heard that a dynamo was
a machine you put movement into and got
electric current out of, while with a motor
you put current in and got movement out,
and that the same machine could be used for
either job. Now, what I want to know is—
could this machine play the same tricks?
Could I get light out of it if, say, I drive it
round with the sewing machine?”
“Not this kind,” said the well-informed
Molly. “There is some difference about the
way the coils are connected up that dad did
try to explain to me, but I just couldnt grasp
it without a motor to demonstrate on.”
“Well, lets try this. Oh! look; what
does 3,000 R.P.M. mean?”
“Three thousand revolutions per minute
—almost as fast as you can talk, old girl.”
Pat contented herself with making a face
at her friend, and made preparations to plug
the lamp-adaptor connector into the lamp-
holder.
They found a nice little press-button
switch in the cord close up to the motor, and
first held the motor tightly and switched on.
The first start was very surprising, and
nearly made Pat drop the motor, but once it
was running, the motor was as steady as a
rock.
Then they fixed up the little motor on its
proper stand and fixed on the emery wheel.
“What shall we sharpen? I know, my
screw-driver has a blunt edge.”

Unnamed: 9: Molly learns to use an electric motor for household tasks.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 143

It needed a little practice to learn how to hold the “driver,” but they soon learnt, and then all the scissors and knives in the house received the most magnificent rejuvenation.

[Illustration of a motor]
B.T.H. ONE-TENTH HORSE POWER MOTOR

Next they tried one of the polishing buffs. It didn’t make much mark on the stained eggspoon when dry, so they dipped the buff (a bunch of calico circles threaded on a shaft) into some silver polish, with dire results.

When the motor started, the centrifugal force at high speed hurled plate polish all over the girls and the room, and made a mess.

“Molly,” said Pat, seriously, “it is now clear to my limited intelligence—and I hope to yours, too—that the correct way is to put the polishing matter on the thing to be polished and not on the buff.”

So that was settled satisfactorily, and soon the spoons looked like new.

“Now, my child, will you tell me how to polish the fender? Must we take ‘Sally’ to the fender or the fender to ‘Sally’?”

Molly gurgled, but failed to produce any better solution than that ‘Sally’ must try to have a go at polishing the fender.

Pat, however, wouldn’t try till she had done some more thinking.

“It isn’t really sensible to cart around ‘Sally.’ She is too heavy to hold easily, unless we can steady her in some way. Look here, Molly, you are usually ingenious enough—can’t you devise some kind of contraption that we could use to hold the motor in?”

“I think a sort of flexible drive would be better,” said Molly. “Your motor doesn’t seem to have one, but I’ll ask dad when he comes home and see if we couldn’t get one.”

“I see, something like a speedometer drive on a car—yes, that’s the idea. Well, let’s try the sewing machine attachment and cake mixer now.”

The trouble with the cake mixer was that, at first, they mixed the whole cake all over the place, but after a little practice, they learnt that, too.

“Now, Molly,” said Pat, “we have learned how to sew, polish, sharpen, and mix

[Illustration of motor attached to washing machine]
MAGNET FRACTIONAL MOTOR attached to Washing Machine, which, amongst other things, makes Ice Cream, Minces Meat, and Sharpens Knives

cakes with this motor—can’t we make it do anything else? Clean boots, or work Jim’s lathe, or—oh! I’m tired of thinking. Do let’s each prepare a list of all ‘Sally’ could do, and see who makes the longest.”

“It isn’t really sensible to cart around ‘Sally.’ She is too heavy to hold easily, unless we can steady her in some way. Look here, Molly, you are usually ingenious enough—can’t you devise some kind of contraption that we could use to hold the motor in?”

“I think a sort of flexible drive would be better,” said Molly. “Your motor doesn’t seem to have one, but I’ll ask dad when he comes home and see if we couldn’t get one.”

“I see, something like a speedometer drive on a car—yes, that’s the idea. Well, let’s try the sewing machine attachment and cake mixer now.”

The trouble with the cake mixer was that, at first, they mixed the whole cake all over the place, but after a little practice, they learnt that, too.

“Now, Molly,” said Pat, “we have learned how to sew, polish, sharpen, and mix

144	The Electrical Age

Electricity Behind the Scenes

By Blaise Wyndham

Nowhere has electricity wrought greater changes than "behind the scenes"; it is responsible, directly or indirectly, for almost all the wonderful effects seen in the modern theatre.
At the London Coliseum (where last November members of the E.A.W. witnessed a stage demonstration) electric power is everywhere. The famous revolving stage, the giant cyclorama and panorama, and the cradles for hauling heavy weights above the stage, are all dependent upon it, to say nothing of lighting, cleaning and heating, and the numerous telephones and microphones.
A brief description of the more important appliances may interest readers not present at the demonstration.
The revolving stage, driven by 14 motors, is in three concentric circular sections. These sections can be interlocked or revolved separately. When locked, they form a huge table 75 feet in diameter, which can be driven in either direction at any speed up to 22 miles per hour.
The immense value of the revolving stage for racecourses, railway tracks and similar spectacular scenes is obvious, but perhaps the greatest advantage it possesses over the stationary stage lies in the fact that noisy scene shifting during the performances and "waits" between the items are almost entirely eliminated. The stage being 225 feet in circumference, only a portion of it is required for each scene, i.e., the segment directly facing the auditorium, so that scenes which are to follow may be set quietly and at leisure while the current turn is performing; particularly heavy scenes, however, are usually set before the performance begins. Immediately an item is concluded, the stage is revolved until the "set" for the next item is brought into position; simultaneously, a back-cloth is lowered from the flies and the electrically operated proscenium curtains move forward — within a few seconds the next turn is performing.
In a semi-circle, around the stage, stand the cylinders of the cyclorama (a huge moving scene embracing the back half of the revolving table); other cylinders provide for panoramic scenes extending right across the stage. The cylinders are driven by electric motors and some of them are 40 feet high.
Built into the wall at the rear of the stage is a cinematograph operating box, so that if necessary a film can be projected from the stage instead of from the auditorium.
Down by the footlights is a tiny square box — the stage microphone. It carries every word spoken on the stage up to the stage-managers office at the back of the theatre. There is also a rehearsal microphone enabling the stage-manager or his assistant to conduct the important lighting rehearsal without interfering with any other rehearsal in progress at the same time.
To the right of the stage is the prompt corner. Here are controls for the three sections of the revolving table, for the act drop (which, by the way, is the largest in this country, being nearly 55 feet wide), the proscenium curtains and the revolving roof.
At the Coliseum even the call-boy has been superseded by electricity, and a dictagraph enables the assistant in charge to call up not only the stage-manager, musical director, fly-men, stage doorkeeper, and other members of the staff, but also the artistes in their dressing-rooms. In passing, it may be noted that deference has been paid to the superstition of many theatrical folk — no dressing-room is numbered "13"!

Unnamed: 9: Stage-manager at London Coliseum considering electric power for scene setting.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 145
Beyond the prompt corner is the main switchboard where, in addition to rows of lighting switches, are the dimmer wheels. It is by manipulating these wheels that the delicate lighting effects are obtained, and the subtle changes from daylight to sunset, and sunset to dawn made. The wheels, when turned, actuate copper rods contained in the dimmer jars beneath the stage, and the principle of resistance is called into play; when the rods are raised in the jars, resistance is increased, and vice-versa.
Under the stage is the control room, the intake rooms (containing the main change-over switch, the dimmer jars referred to, and large automatic clapper switches), and the huge circular vault enclosing the motors and metal framework of the revolving stage.
Forty feet above the stage are the flies, where are cradles capable of hauling weights totalling 14 tons and no less than 130 sets of scene-lines. At present, scene setting is done in the usual way by hand, but Mr. Crocker, the stage-manager, tells me that he contemplates introducing electric power even here.

Unnamed: 9: Mrs. Lawson writes about electric water-heating benefits in Switzerland.
Unnamed: 10: Author of the article "Electric Water-heating in Switzerland"
transcription:
146	The Electrical Age

Electric Water-heating in Switzerland

By Mrs. Walter Lawson

In this third article, Mrs. Lawson tells how Electricity has given the Swiss Housewife
a cheap supply of constant Hot Water for all Domestic Purposes.

Of all the electrical apparatus I saw in Switzerland, the water-heater interested me most. Electric water-heaters have been in use in that country for ten years, and the type almost universally used is that which works on the heat-accumulation principle. We are just beginning to realise their possibilities and convenience in this country, and those who like to be up-to-date either have, or intend to have them installed. There is already quite a colony of them at Chichester, where over 100 electric water-heaters are installed on the hire system, as well as many houses in Eastbourne, Portsmouth and various towns in the country, and a London theatre has just had two water-heaters of 6,000 gallons each installed.
In Basle, where they are in general use, the average house has one of 40 gallons capacity installed on the floor in the basement, which supplies the house with hot water, i.e., laundry, scullery, bedrooms and bathrooms, etc., but smaller ones can be had to fix on the wall above the bath, wash-bowl or sink.
The initial cost of the fixing of the latter type would be much less, but the supply is more limited.
They can be had with shower-bath attachments and a tap to supply a mixture of hot and cold water which can be regulated by hand according to requirements; a douche for shampooing the hair can be had also.
These water-heaters on the Continent use the current during the night at a cheap rate. In England, there seems to be some difficulty over the initial cost of an extra meter for registering night load; if we could remove this objection, electric water-heating would become quite common and would prove very remunerative for supply undertakings.
I saw these water-heaters being manufactured, and noticed that they have to go through many very careful processes.
The boiler is made of rust-proof sheet steel; the outside is iron enamelled. The heating elements are fixed at the bottom of the tank and project upwards into the water. The space between the boiler and the other case is packed with granulated cork, which prevents the escape of the heat; the water will thus remain hot for hours after the current is switched off.
I have been experimenting with a small water-heater myself for the last nine months, and as an adjunct to an unsatisfactory kitchen range, with its inefficient hot water system, I have found it so convenient as to be now indispensable. Used in this way, the cost in current is quite reasonable even on an ordinary power tariff.

The Viscountess Grey has consented to become President of the North-East Coast Branch, the inaugural meeting of which has unfortunately been delayed, but will be held in the near future.

Unnamed: 9: Author of article about Manchesters electricity developments and industry impact.
transcription:
The Electrical Age
147
What Manchester is Doing Electrically
By J. D. Peattie, B.Sc., A.M.I.E.E.
(Member of the Staff of the Manchester Corporation Electricity Department)
We are apt to think in this country that Electricity is much more expensive than in the United States of America. As is shown in this article, Manchester has been able to disprove this theory.
In point of size, the Manchester Corporation Electricity Department, with a yearly output of more than 300 million units (or kilowatt-hours), and a maximum load of over 140,000 kilowatts, takes a high place among electricity undertakings in this country.
So far as efficiency is concerned, Barton Generating Station ranks with the half-a-dozen most efficient stations of the world. At the moment, the station is developed to only half its ultimate capacity, and, when the extensions now in progress are completed, it is expected that a still higher efficiency will be obtained. Although considerably older than Barton, Stuart Street Station is still one of the largest in this country.
Electricity is distributed directly over an area of 43 square miles and, in addition, bulk supplies are given to six adjacent authorities. Three of these—Middleton, Cheadle and Sale—take the whole of their supply from Manchester, while the others take a part supply only.
INDUSTRY.
Although Manchester is usually only regarded by the general public as the centre of the cotton industry, its activities are by no means confined to this industry and its innumerable ramifications. Engineering and chemical works of various descriptions—to mention two classes only—are to be found within its boundaries, and it is interesting to note that, of the units sold by the Electricity Department in 1926, twenty per cent. were used in engineering works of various descriptions, 11 per cent. by textile mills and factories, and 8 per cent. by chemical works.
The indirect influence of such applications is of enormous importance to all dwellers in an industrial area such as Manchester, where the smoke from thousands of factory chimneys and hundreds of thousands of domestic fires shuts out the sun for so many hours in the year.
At one time the Department claimed to have been responsible for felling over three hundred chimney stacks. Since then many more have fallen, but there are still thousands to fall before we can be satisfied with that phase of development.
The frontal attack to bring more sunshine into the city is a slow, and, at times, irritating struggle, but recently a side attack has developed on new lines. Public and private artificial sunlight clinics, taking supply from the electricity mains, are now a feature of the city, and large numbers of patients, especially children, are receiving treatment with gratifying results.
In industry, electricity supply has not only brought increased material prosperity, but it has assisted very considerably in improving the conditions under which the employees work. The electric drive makes possible the provision of airier and cleaner workshops and factories, while electric lighting provides illumination on a scale not dreamt of a few years ago, thereby easing strain and increasing production, especially in the fine work required in so many branches of the cotton industry. In several of the more up-to-date factories, electric cooking has also been introduced into the works canteens.

Unnamed: 9: Read a paper on The All-Electric House at Buxton convention.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 151

SHOWROOMS.
In order to provide a centre for demonstra-
tions, where consumers can also obtain
independent advice and information about
electrical equipment, the Department have
showrooms in the heart of the shopping
centre of the city. An expert staff is in
attendance to demonstrate the uses of the
various lighting, heating, cooking, and other
domestic appliances. Until recently, these
showrooms were used for demonstration pur-
poses only, but the Corporation have now
decided to make use of their powers and to
proceed with the sale of appliances.
Visitors are always welcome, and special
cooking demonstrations are given on alter-
nate Wedoesdays and Fridays.

FUTURE DEVELOPMENT.
Although the Department has every reason
to be proud of its past record, there is still a
vast field for expansion before it. Taking
domestic consumers only, the figure of 18,000
has already been mentioned, and sounds im-
pressive until one remembers that, according
to the 1921 Census, there are, in Manchester
alone, over 136,000 dwellings of four or more
rooms occupied by private families. Even
after a liberal allowance is made for houses
which are never likely to be wired, there
remains a very substantial balance of poten-
tial consumers—many times greater than
the present total on the mains. So far as the
new houses now being built are concerned,
the position is, of course, more satisfactory.
We are often reminded in this country of
our backwardness in the applications of elec-
tricity in the home, but it is well to bear in
mind that competent electrical engineers
from the great cities of the United States
agree that they are unable to offer so low a
tariff for domestic power as is now available
in Manchester and other large cities in this
country.
We have been told, recently, that we are
living in the midst of another industrial
revolution. The development of steam power
was one of the most powerful influences in
the industrial revolution of last Century, in
which Manchester played a leading part, and
we believe that electricity will have an
equally important influence in the revolution
now in progress. It offers opportunities of
making good some of the omissions of the
past, especially in matters which concern the
welfare of the people, and provides one of
the most powerful tools for the building of
the city beautiful and prosperous.

Electrical Convention at Buxton
The Incorporated Municipal Electrical
Association is holding its Convention at
Buxton this year, from May 30th to June 4th.
The special Womens Day is being
arranged on Thursday, June 2nd, when a
paper will be read in the morning on "The
All-Electric House," by Mr. H. H. Berry,
and in the afternoon members will visit
Baslow Hall, at the kind invitation of Dr.
and Mrs. Ferranti.
Baslow Hall is a delightful example of a
beautiful country home fitted with all the
modern conveniences which electricity can
give.
We shall hope, in a future issue, to give a
description of Mrs. Ferrantis home.

News of Members
We learn that one of our new members,
Mrs. A. Atkinson, of Newcastle, is very
pluckily carrying on the work of her late
husband, Mr. Thomas Atkinson, an electrical
contractor. She was left with two little girls
to provide for, and the only thing for her to
do was to try and carry on the work of her
husband. The work of the firm is mostly
concerned with shop and house wiring.
Miss Edith Beesley, who has been an
active supporter of the E.A.W. from the
early days, has now been appointed Manager
of the West End Branch of the Southern Life
Association. We are pleased to learn that
Miss Beesley has an all-electric office.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 151

SHOWROOMS.
In order to provide a centre for demonstra-
tions, where consumers can also obtain
independent advice and information about
electrical equipment, the Department have
showrooms in the heart of the shopping
centre of the city. An expert staff is in
attendance to demonstrate the uses of the
various lighting, heating, cooking, and other
domestic appliances. Until recently, these
showrooms were used for demonstration pur-
poses only, but the Corporation have now
decided to make use of their powers and to
proceed with the sale of appliances.
Visitors are always welcome, and special
cooking demonstrations are given on alter-
nate Wedoesdays and Fridays.

FUTURE DEVELOPMENT.
Although the Department has every reason
to be proud of its past record, there is still a
vast field for expansion before it. Taking
domestic consumers only, the figure of 18,000
has already been mentioned, and sounds im-
pressive until one remembers that, according
to the 1921 Census, there are, in Manchester
alone, over 136,000 dwellings of four or more
rooms occupied by private families. Even
after a liberal allowance is made for houses
which are never likely to be wired, there
remains a very substantial balance of poten-
tial consumers—many times greater than
the present total on the mains. So far as the
new houses now being built are concerned,
the position is, of course, more satisfactory.
We are often reminded in this country of
our backwardness in the applications of elec-
tricity in the home, but it is well to bear in
mind that competent electrical engineers
from the great cities of the United States
agree that they are unable to offer so low a
tariff for domestic power as is now available
in Manchester and other large cities in this
country.
We have been told, recently, that we are
living in the midst of another industrial
revolution. The development of steam power
was one of the most powerful influences in
the industrial revolution of last Century, in
which Manchester played a leading part, and
we believe that electricity will have an
equally important influence in the revolution
now in progress. It offers opportunities of
making good some of the omissions of the
past, especially in matters which concern the
welfare of the people, and provides one of
the most powerful tools for the building of
the city beautiful and prosperous.

Electrical Convention at Buxton
The Incorporated Municipal Electrical
Association is holding its Convention at
Buxton this year, from May 30th to June 4th.
The special Womens Day is being
arranged on Thursday, June 2nd, when a
paper will be read in the morning on "The
All-Electric House," by Mr. H. H. Berry,
and in the afternoon members will visit
Baslow Hall, at the kind invitation of Dr.
and Mrs. Ferranti.
Baslow Hall is a delightful example of a
beautiful country home fitted with all the
modern conveniences which electricity can
give.
We shall hope, in a future issue, to give a
description of Mrs. Ferrantis home.

News of Members
We learn that one of our new members,
Mrs. A. Atkinson, of Newcastle, is very
pluckily carrying on the work of her late
husband, Mr. Thomas Atkinson, an electrical
contractor. She was left with two little girls
to provide for, and the only thing for her to
do was to try and carry on the work of her
husband. The work of the firm is mostly
concerned with shop and house wiring.
Miss Edith Beesley, who has been an
active supporter of the E.A.W. from the
early days, has now been appointed Manager
of the West End Branch of the Southern Life
Association. We are pleased to learn that
Miss Beesley has an all-electric office.

152
The Electrical Age

Electrical Progress !
Things We Hear

That one of the research engineers of the General Electric Company of America has evolved an inside frosting process for incandescent lamp bulbs, which leave the bulb rigid instead of weak. Lamps made by this process can be dropped on to a wooden floor without smashing; tests have shown that the bulb will bounce when dropped from a height of a few feet, without any detrimental effect. All "Mazda" lamps are being made by this process, for the inside frosting not only reduces the glare but gives more light. —English Mechanic.

* * * * *

That a striking improvement in modern typewriters is the Mercedes Electric Type-writer, in which most of the physical operations usually carried out by the typist are performed electrically and automatically. For example, keys, shift key, space bar, carriage and return, and line space mechanism are all operated electrically by means of a small electric motor running off ordinary lighting mains.

The average typewriter key requires a tapping pressure of about 10 ounces, acting through a distance of about 3/4-inch. The amount of work performed by a typist working for several hours a day can readily be worked out. In the case of the machine in question, the finger pressure requires only 1/2 oz., the movement being 1/4-inch. The electrical machine, therefore, requires only 1/200th of the effort of the ordinary typewriter.

Another point worthy of notice is that the ordinary carriage requires a force of 5 lbs. to shift it, whereas in the present case it is shifted automatically by merely touching a certain key. —English Mechanic.

The Electrical Age 153

The Central Electricity Board

(By courtesy of "Electrical Times")
SIR ANDREW RAE DUNCAN, M.A., LL.B.

No sooner had the Electricity (Supply) Bill become an Act of Parliament than Colonel Wilfrid Ashley, the Minister of Transport, set to work to appoint the new Board which is to carry out the provisions of the Act.
Sir Andrew Rae Duncan has been chosen as the Chairman of the Board, and it is the general opinion of all those concerned that no happier choice could have been made. As his name implies, Sir Andrew Duncan is a Scotsman, and has had a very successful and interesting career.
Sir Andrew has already shown his interest in progressive womens organisations by allowing his name to appear on the Advisory Committee of the big Wembley Womens Conference, and we hope that in his new work he will not overlook the tremendous part which women can play in making the new Act a success.
Among the members of the Board, the E.A.W. has already a number of friends in
Alderman Walker, Sir Duncan Watson, Sir James Devonshire, and Mr. Frank Hodges.
The Board commenced its duties on March 1st, and its work will be closely watched by all interested in electrical development in this country.
The task they have before them is by no means an easy one. As Sir Henry Fowler remarked at the Annual Dinner of the British Electrical Development Association on March 17th, the duty of the Board will be, by means of co-ordination and co-operation, to give the country mass production of electricity.

transcription:
154
The Electrical Age

E. A. W. Branch Activities

Glasgow and District Branch
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251 Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

Lady Paxton, Vice-President of the Glasgow and District Branch of the Electrical Association for Women, is a popular local personage whom various Associations like to have on their platforms. During the three years her husband, Sir Thomas Paxton, occupied the Lord Provosts chair, it fell to her lot to play a leading part in numerous important local events, and each one as it came found her equal to the occasion.

Lady Paxton has a certain natural delight in life and the duties expected of her—her activity and energy are unfailing, and she has one unusual merit that, notwithstanding that her engagement book is almost always full, she keeps her engagements. Lady Paxton is an effective public speaker, and her bright manner is always a valuable asset. It was, therefore, natural that the Glasgow and District Branch, when formed, promptly asked Lady Paxton to be a Vice-President. On several occasions she has had to take the Presidents chair, and has always filled it with acceptance and success. She is keenly interested in the Electrical Association for Women, and has done everything that lies in her power to make it an important institution which must be reckoned with in the electrical world.

BRANCH NOTES

We had our first meeting at Greenock in February, and on that occasion Mrs. Christine Frederick was the speaker, with Councillor Mrs. Laurie, J.P., Greenock, in the chair, supported by Bailie Miss Isabelle Kerr, Greenock, and Bailie Mrs. Bell, J.P., senior magistrate of Glasgow. It was a packed and enthusiastic audience who listened to Mrs. Frederick.

Our next meeting in Greenock will be on "Good and Bad Lighting in the Home," by Miss K. St. Clair Lindsay, of the Scottish Electric Lighting Service Bureau, Glasgow.

Mrs. Christine Frederick had a very rousing reception in the Cadoro, when she spoke to the Glasgow and District members on "How the American Housewife has Achieved Leisure through Electricity."

The General Electric Company have invited us to visit their Showrooms, and are giving cooking demonstrations and a short intimate talk on the beautiful Electric Bungalow which is fitted up within their showrooms.

The Richmond Park Laundry Co., Cambuslang, have also invited us to inspect their Laundry, which is one of the most modern and well equipped in the country.

This Spring we are holding a meeting of enquiry on Electric Cookers, at which we hope to have a large attendance.

[By courtesy of the Glasgow Citizen and Lafayette]
LADY PAXTON
(Vice-President, Glasgow and District Branch)

transcription:
The Electrical Age 155

In the early Summer we are visiting the Glasgow
Corporation Water Department Estate at Loch
Katrine. This is a very large engineering accom-
plishment, and the portion in which the members of
the Association are most keenly interested is the
Electric Power House, which supplies current to the
houses on the Estate for lighting, heating, cooking,
sweeping, ironing, etc., replacing coal and oil power
with all its attendant drudgery.
One of the most delightful meetings we have had
this Session was the one on "Colour in Lighting,"
presented by Mr. Buckell, of London. We were a
very small audience, but a very deeply appreciative
one. Mr. Buckell is a Founder-Member of the
E.A.W., and was the fifth member to give a lecture
to the Glasgow and District Branch. Do we hold a
record in this matter?
Four lady members and one gentleman member
have given us lectures and demonstrations.

Miss Mary MacKirdy

Miss Mary MacKirdy, who has already written recipes for THE ELECTRICAL AGE, has
promised to continue to do so in the future. Miss MacKirdy has recently returned
from a visit to America, and she should, therefore, have some interesting news to
tell. The next batch of recipes will appear in the July issue.

Miss Mary MacKirdys name needs no introduc-
tion in Glasgow, or in fact throughout Scotland.
For many years she has been one of the head
teachers of Cookery in the Glasgow and West of
Scotland College of Domestic Science, and teachers
throughout the length and breadth of Scotland to
the furthermost isles have had cause to bless the
day they had the opportunity of training under her
most practical guidance.
Miss MacKirdy has a broad grasp of her subject,
attractive personality, an ever ready interest in her
audience, students and subject which compels
attention and ensures faithful allegiance.
Her Saturday cookery articles in the "Glasgow
Heralds" are read by both men and women and are
eagerly looked for. She has quite recently added
to her fame by producing an excellent cookery
book entitled "Recipes for you."
She is a niece of the late Mrs. Black, of Cookery
School fame, and has inherited her talent and
perhaps surpasses that well known pioneer in her
own field.
Miss MacKirdy is intensely interested in elec-
tricity in all its applications to the home, particu-
larly in regard to Cookery; her inclusion on the
Committee of the E.A.W. shows much acumen on
the part of the Executive.
MISS M. MacKIRDY

transcription:
156
The Electrical Age

Birmingham and Midlands Branch

Hon. Sec., Mrs. Hayes, 1 Bloomfield Road,
Moseley, Birmingham.

Mrs. Chattock, one of the Vice Presidents of the
Electrical Association for Women, of the Bir-
mingham and Midland Centre, has been closely
associated with the electrical world for the past
21 years.
Her husband is Mr. R. A. Chattock, the City
Electrical Engineer of Birmingham, and she is
therefore brought into intimate contact with all
the latest developments.
This is especially the case with domestic
appliances, in which she is greatly interested.
Mrs. Chattock takes a prominent part in the life
of the city, her chief interests being music and art.

BRANCH NOTES
Since writing our Branch News for the October
issue of the Magazine, we have had several very in-
teresting meetings.
On December 16th, a visit was paid to the Show-
rooms of the British Thomson-Houston Co., where
Mr. F. Hughes Caley entertained 40 of our members
with a wireless concert and a lecture on cathedral
lighting, and conducted the party over the hand-
somely fitted and well-arranged showrooms.
Our members were invited to visit the works of
Messrs. J. H. Tucker & Co., Tyseley, on January
25th. On this occasion, owing to extremely bad
weather and the influenza epidemic, our party was a
small one, but the 15 members who ventured were
rewarded by a thoroughly enjoyable visit, thanks to
the excellent arrangements made by the firm, who
showed them over the works and explained the
manufacture of switches and switch-gear.
A meeting was held on January 28th at the Baths
Assembly Rooms, Wolverhampton. Lady Bird
occupied the chair, and V. W. Dale, Esq., of the
Electrical Development Association, lectured to 200
people. Lady Brooks also addressed the meeting.
Water-heaters and other electrical apparatus were
on show, and Mrs. Morgan, wife of the Borough
Electrical Engineer, provided tea—altogether a very
successful meeting.
In addition to the above meetings, one of the
members, Mrs. Perford, of Erdington, gave a
Drawing-Room Meeting on January 29th at her
house, where a very good demonstration of many
domestic electrical appliances was given, together
with a short talk by Mr. Ginno, of the Birmingham
Electric Supply Showrooms.—G.L.

For report of Annual Meeting, see pages 158, 160 and 162.

SUBSCRIPTION.—The Electrical Age Annual Subscription is 2/6, which includes postage.

MRS. R. A. CHATTOCK
Vice-President (Birmingham & Midlands Branch)

Unnamed: 7: E.A.W. South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch; Electric Service Bureau
Unnamed: 9: Hon. Sec. of the South Wales and Monmouthshire E.A.W. branch.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 157

The South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Sec.: Mrs. J. Tyler, Electric Service Bureau, Royal Chambers, Park Place, Cardiff.

BRANCH NOTES
The inaugural meeting of the South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch of the E.A.W. was held at the Lesser Hall, City Hall, Cardiff, on Thursday, March 24th, 1927, at 6.30 p.m., the chair being taken by Mrs. M. A. Jenkins (Lady Mayoress of Cardiff). Owing to a previous engagement, the President of 

(Photo by Facundo)
THE VISCOUNTESS RHONDDA, J.P.
(Pres., South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.)

the South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch (Viscountess Rhondda, J.P.) was unable to attend. The speakers included Councillor Rhoda Parker, J.P. (Cardiff), Mr. C. G. Morley New, M.I.E.E. (City Electrical Engineer, Cardiff), and Miss C. Haslett (Director of the Association). 

The meeting was in every way successful, and augurs well for the future prosperity of this, the Fifth Branch of the E.A.W. 

It was announced that the programme of local fixtures would include a visit to the Power Station of the Cardiff Corporation; a lecture on "The Reme-dial Uses of Electricity," by Mrs. L. E. Wright, at the Institute of Engineers, Park Place, Cardiff; a visit to the G.E.C. Showrooms, with a talk on "Illumination" by Mr. James; and a visit to the Upper Boat Power Station of the South Wales Elec-trical Power Distribution Company.

----

Viscountess Rhondda, J.P., who has been elected President of the South Wales Branch, is a woman of outstanding prominence in the Industrial and Feminist World. She succeeded to the title in 1918, being the only child of the late Lord Rhondda. A woman of tremendous energy and business ability, she is on the Board of 27 companies, in-cluding many colliery companies.

She is also Editor of "Time and Tide," the weekly review, and is President for the current year of the Institute of Directors.

Her work for the full enfranchisement of women is an outstanding characteristic, and during the pre-war days she suffered imprisonment for this cause, with many other prominent women. In 1922 she tried by Petition to the Committee of Privileges to obtain a Writ of Summons to the House of Lords, but failed on the interpretation of Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act, on which her claim was based.

The South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch is indeed fortunate in its President.

...

Manchester District Branch
Hon. Sec.: Miss G. L. Entwisle, A.M.I.E.E.,
5 Holmfield, Sale, Manchester

BRANCH NOTES
The Manchester Branch, handicapped in its early days by the General Strike, has gone ahead rapidly since the first public meeting in October, and has had a varied and entertaining Spring programme. In January, a demonstration was held by the Singer Sewing Machine Co. in the Y.M.C.A. Lecture Hall, and proved full of interest. The opportunity was taken of visiting an all-electric house open for inspection during this month, and it was extremely interesting to see how much the use of electricity added to the comfort, appearance and efficiency of a house of this type (five moderate-sized rooms and kitchen-scullery) now being erected in such large numbers.

transcription:
158		The Electrical Age

[Photograph of Mrs. Lamb standing in a doorway wearing a fur-trimmed coat and hat]

MRS. LAMB
(Chairman, Manchester District Branch.)

At the Lighting Service Bureau later in the month, Mr. Hawkins kindly repeated his November lecture on "Home Lighting," and also gave one on "Lighting Fundamentals," both of which were very much appreciated. A visit to the General Electric Companys Showrooms was arranged early in February, and was most enjoyable; and an evening lecture by Dr. Langley, on "Electricity and Medicine," was very well attended, and Dr. Langleys account of the part played by electricity in medicine evoked an interesting discussion on the merits of vita-glass and artificial sunlight treatment.

The Annual General Meeting was held on February 22nd in the Lord Mayors Parlour, and after reports had been read and officers, Committee and Council re-elected for the next year, Mrs. Christine Frederick held us enthralled while she described the methods adopted by the American housewife to solve the shortage of domestic help—a shortage very much more acute even than in Great Britain. Her account of the labour-saving devices, mostly run by electricity, and the methods by which an old-fashioned, badly planned kitchen could be converted at little cost into a step-saving, efficient workshop for the preparation and cooking of food, inspired more than one member of her intent audience with a passionate zeal to be home again and reorganising her own kitchen without the loss of a single second. There were probably more cupboards pushed about, more boxes moved to adjust heights of sink or table, more maids muttering "‘undred and thirteen, ‘undred and fourteen," as they counted
their steps that evening than ever before in the history of Manchester.

The March programme included an extremely enjoyable visit to the Showrooms of the British Thomson-Houston Co., where demonstrations of cooking, laundry work and R.K. loud speakers were given, and films illustrating various applications of electricity were also shown.

Mr. Hawkins gave a most helpful afternoon lecture on wiring, the mending of fuses and plugs, etc., which is to be repeated as an evening talk on March 17th. On March 22nd, we hope to pay a visit to the Metropolitan-Vickers Works at Trafford Park, an account of which will appear in our next issue.—D.M.P.

Our picture shows Mrs. Lamb performing the formal opening of the "All-Electric" Demonstration House at Denton this year in connection with the W.O.B. campaign. Mrs. Lamb is the very active chairman of the Manchester District Branch and since its inception has worked untiringly for the success of the Branch.

As the wife of the City Electrical Engineer of Manchester, she is able to exert influence and interest on behalf of the work of the E.A.W. in Manchester.

At the large public meeting arranged by the Manchester District Branch in October last year, the outstanding feature of the meeting was the very witty speech given by Mrs. Lamb almost at a moments notice. For many years, Mrs. Lamb has been very actively engaged in all work that is concerned with the complete emancipation of women.

Cheltenham Branch
Hon Sec.: Miss A. A. Stemp, 1 York Terrace, St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.

BRANCH NOTES
The Winter programme opened well with two very interesting meetings. The first of these was in the form of a Lecture by Miss C. Griff (Vice-Chairman of the Birmingham Branch) on "Every Woman Her Own Electrician." The lecture was illustrated by lantern slides and various electrical devices and appliances. An interested audience of members and friends attended, most of whom have asked for a similar lecture to be given again at a later date. This we have arranged to do.

Our second meeting was a visit to the Spa Medical Baths, to view the electro-medical treatments given there. Two eminent physicians, the sister in charge and two nurses were indefatigable in demonstrating the various treatments. Goggles were donned for the artificial sunlight cure. Birmingham and Midlands Branch First Annual General Meeting
The Three Days Conference Report (February 23rd—25th inclusive)
By Mrs. Hayes (Hon. Sec., Birmingham and Midlands Branch)
The Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the E.A.W. arranged a very ambitious three days programme to celebrate its first Birthday. With what success, the following account will show.
The Conference of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch opened with the inaugural meeting at Queens College on Wednesday, February 23rd, 1927. Mrs. Cary Gilson presided over a good attendance and congratulated Lady Brooks (President of the Branch) on the success attained by the Association in its first year, and remarked, "The air is electric with our work as women." Mrs. Christine Frederick, an American lady, who was described by Mrs. Cary Gilson as the premier scientific exponent of housekeeping, gave an address and modestly disclaimed any desire to hold up the housewives of the States as more clever than those in Great Britain. All she wished to do, she said, was to point out how American housewives had grappled with a situation which might soon arise in this country—that was, having to do without servants. This problem had been faced twenty years ago, and the solution to the difficulty had meant entire re-organisation of the house and changing of conditions surrounding it. Large family houses gave place to tenements or flats. Thus it was that the kitchen and its arrangement should be given much thought. Mrs. Frederick explained, by means of diagrams, how a well-arranged kitchen meant the saving of time and labour; and all unnecessary walking could be eliminated by the placing of sink, larder, table and cooker in places relative to their use. Then, too, the American housewife, realising that she spent seventy-five per cent. of her working time there, always insisted on well-lighted and brightly coloured kitchens. It kept the mind from suffering from depression. Mrs. Frederick then pointed out how much time could be saved in the ordinary household work by

Birmingham and Midlands Branch First Annual General Meeting
The Three Days Conference Report (February 23rd—25th inclusive)
By Mrs. Hayes (Hon. Sec., Birmingham and Midlands Branch)
The Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the E.A.W. arranged a very ambitious three days programme to celebrate its first Birthday. With what success, the following account will show.
The Conference of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch opened with the inaugural meeting at Queens College on Wednesday, February 23rd, 1927. Mrs. Cary Gilson presided over a good attendance and congratulated Lady Brooks (President of the Branch) on the success attained by the Association in its first year, and remarked, "The air is electric with our work as women." Mrs. Christine Frederick, an American lady, who was described by Mrs. Cary Gilson as the premier scientific exponent of housekeeping, gave an address and modestly disclaimed any desire to hold up the housewives of the States as more clever than those in Great Britain. All she wished to do, she said, was to point out how American housewives had grappled with a situation which might soon arise in this country—that was, having to do without servants. This problem had been faced twenty years ago, and the solution to the difficulty had meant entire re-organisation of the house and changing of conditions surrounding it. Large family houses gave place to tenements or flats. Thus it was that the kitchen and its arrangement should be given much thought. Mrs. Frederick explained, by means of diagrams, how a well-arranged kitchen meant the saving of time and labour; and all unnecessary walking could be eliminated by the placing of sink, larder, table and cooker in places relative to their use. Then, too, the American housewife, realising that she spent seventy-five per cent. of her working time there, always insisted on well-lighted and brightly coloured kitchens. It kept the mind from suffering from depression. Mrs. Frederick then pointed out how much time could be saved in the ordinary household work by

the use of electrical appliances, but in using these it was essential that a full universal supply of electricity, at moderate rates, was necessary.
THE LUNCHEON.
Lady Brooks subsequently presided at a Luncheon, in place of Lady Cowan (who was a victim of the prevalent influenza), at the Queens Hotel. Alderman H. K. Beale (Chairman of Electric Supply Committee) proposed the toast of "Electricity in the Service of Women." He said women were beginning to realise the convenience and cleanliness of electricity. He was going to add economy, but if economy had not yet come, it was coming. At present, they had only touched the fringe of the question of electricity in the house. The best way to obtain cheaper electricity was to install appliances, because the greater the demand the cheaper electricity would become. Mr. Chattock, M.I.E.E. (City Electrical Engineer), responded, and he was convinced that the women of this country would not only become more interested in the great possibilities of electricity, but would eventually insist upon having their homes equipped with it.
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti proposed the toast of "The Electrical Association for Women," and remarked that the great thing that stood in the way of electrical development was a general want of knowledge in the handling of the commodity and the apparatus connected with it. Miss Haslett responded, and remarked on the work of the Association and its Branches.
Lady Brooks proposed the toast, "Our Guests," and Dr. Railing, of the General Electric Company, responded.
During the afternoon, members of the Conference paid a visit to Nechells Power Station, where they were received by Mr. Forrest (Chief Assistant City Electrical Engineer) and other guides, who escorted them round the station. A card was presented to each member with the plan of the station and explanation of same. Tea was kindly provided by the Electric Supply Department.
PROFESSOR CRAMPS LECTURE.
The Annual Meeting of the Branch was held at the Birmingham University, Edmund Street, Mr. Chattock presiding. After the business part of the meeting was concluded, Professor Cramp gave an address. He said that the problem of cheaper electricity in this country would not be solved until that of electrical storage was solved. But until this was overcome, much might be done to maintain the load of the Electricity Department. Where, at present, there was very light load on the generating station between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m., the load might be increased by the installation of apparatus for water-heating by electricity. This had been adopted on the Continent with success. The idea was to heat water during the night for use during the following day, and it had been discovered that this could be done at
the cost of three-eighths of a penny per unit or a total of 5d. per night. This was equivalent to the lowest price of coke heating and knocked out the gas-heater altogether. He suggested that the slogan for women in this matter should be—Heat while you Sleep.
A DAY WITH THE GENERAL ELECTRIC COMPANY AT WITTON.
On Thursday, the members of the Conference visited the General Electric Companys Works at Witton for the whole day. Buses conveyed the party from Birmingham to Witton, where they were met by Mr. Whitford (Commercial Manager) and Mrs. Welbourne (Welfare Superintendent). When the whole party had arrived, the members adjourned to the gymnasium, where Mrs. Frederick gave her second lecture on "Food Values in connection with Electric Cooking," Lady Brooks presiding. Foods were divided into classes according to their composition and the work they did in the body. Thus it was found that to keep the body healthy, different kinds of foods were necessary, and to acquire perfect health a perfectly balanced menu was essential. As a general rule, an adult needs twice as much mineral foods as body builders and heat producers. But one must always remember the occupation of the person. Thus a clerk would not need the same diet as a miner. Now, when cooking a perfectly balanced meal, the electric method is the best, as it is most uniform. All fine fibre meats cook quickly, but the coarser fibre meats cook slow in a casserole, as the simmering method tends to break up molecules in the fibre and makes the meat tender. On the other hand, the quick method of cooking tender meats closes the pores to keep in juices which are so good to the body. All vegetables should be steamed in little or no water—then there is no chance of losing goodness of same in water in which they are boiled. Many questions were asked and answered at conclusion of the lecture, and members were highly interested in the whole subject.
After the lecture, members adjourned to the Rest Room, where all kinds of electrical gadgets for the home were displayed.
At 1 p.m., Dr. Railing (Director of the General Electric Company) escorted Lady Brooks to the staff dining-room. Here the members were lavishly entertained to lunch. After lunch, Dr. Railing, in a very appropriate and humorous speech, heartily welcomed the visitors and explained what could be done in an all-electric house to save time and labour. Lady Brooks responded on behalf of the visitors, and thanked the General Electric Company for their kind hospitality.
After lunch, the members were divided into parties, each with guides, and set off to visit many parts of the works. All parties paid a visit to the Development Department, Small Motor and Transformer Department, Turbo Shops, Power House and Foundry, Vacuum Cleaner Shop, Switch-gear Works

Unnamed: 9: Provided a message about the benefits of electricity for households
transcription:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE
FOR WOMEN
The Official Journal of the Electrical Association for Women—Issued Quarterly.
Editor—Miss C. HASLETT, 26 George Street, Hanover Square, London, W.1.
Vol. I. JULY, 1927. No. 5
Every woman must realise the benefits electricity does and should increasingly bring to her household. It is the most cleanly producer of all that is essential for comfort, the abolition of the use of coal for cooking and heating purposes and its efficiency for domestic power supply. The lighting of rooms without pollution of the atmosphere and its ready application to our many and varied every day needs.
The most recent development is for household refrigeration to keep food pure and wholesome without chemical preservatives, but—the one thing essential to bring all these benefits into our daily life is cheap electricity and may the day soon come when we can use it freely without having to think of these costly units.
LADY MOIR, O.B.E.
Margaret Moir

transcription:
EDITORIAL.

THE E.A.W. SECOND ANNUAL MEETING.
If proof had been needed of the growth and progress of the E.A.W. it was amply given at the Second Annual Meeting of the Association, held on May 11th and 12th.
It was good to see the large body of members from all parts of the country mingling with distinguished and representative people in Public Life and in the Electrical Industry.
The spirit of confident progression pervaded all the speeches, and no doubt existed in the minds of any that the E.A.W. had come to stay.
The final words in the Annual Report summed up the whole position:—" Goodwill and co-operation have been the two outstanding characteristics of the past years work, and we may hope that next year may see an even greater increase in our usefulness and in our membership roll.  The E.A.W. is obviously filling a very greatly needed niche in the life of the community, and especially amongst women folk.  We are serving the Nation by giving knowledge and understanding which will eventually lead to healthier and more efficiently run homes and to a brighter and more knowledgeable community."

* * *

WOMEN AT THE I.M.E.A. CONVENTION.
At the Womens Day during the Convention of the Incorporated Municipal Electrical Association at Buxton, the E.A.W. members acquitted themselves admirably.  During the discussion on Electrified Homes, opened up by Mr. H. H. Berry, some practical and valuable contributions were made by the women speakers.  Lady Brooks urged a closer co-operation with architects and builders in order that houses should be so designed as to be suitable for the application of electricity for all purposes.
Mrs. Hayes drew attention to the difficulty of adapting existing types of houses for the purpose of the use of electricity for all purposes.
Mrs. Lamb, of Manchester, delighted the audience with one of her very witty speeches.  Mrs. Howie, of Walsall, pointed out the need for a new outlook on the design of houses to meet the real needs of the housewife, and a vote of thanks to the speaker was given by Alderman Mrs. Hammer, who extended her thanks to the I.M.E.A. for its invitation to women to be present.  We hope that more and more there will be an opportunity at these gatherings of electrical engineers for the Home-maker to express her point of view.

* * *

THE NEED FOR MORE WOMEN ON ELECTRICITY COMMITTEES.
Councillor Mrs. Gregory, of West Ham, in a splendid fighting speech at the Convention, suggested that there should be at least one woman on every Electricity Committee to put forward the womans point of view.
In her experience, she found that the men were more concerned about the technicalities of the subject than about the human aspect of the problem as applied to the homes of working people.
This suggestion received warm applause, and as pointed out by The Electrical Review, " Women can be co-opted if they are not available as Councillors, and the inclusion of women on a Committee would no doubt prove beneficial to domestic consumers."
We would draw the attention of all Electricity Authorities to this excellent suggestion.

During the discussion on Electrified Homes, opened up by Mr. H. H. Berry, some practical and valuable contributions were made by the women speakers.  Lady Brooks urged a closer co-operation with architects and builders in order that houses should be so designed as to be suitable for the application of electricity for all purposes.
Mrs. Hayes drew attention to the difficulty of adapting existing types of houses for the purpose of the use of electricity for all purposes.
Mrs. Lamb, of Manchester, delighted the audience with one of her very witty speeches.  Mrs. Howie, of Walsall, pointed out the need for a new outlook on the design of houses to meet the real needs of the housewife, and a vote of thanks to the speaker was given by Alderman Mrs. Hammer, who extended her thanks to the I.M.E.A. for its invitation to women to be present.  We hope that more and more there will be an opportunity at these gatherings of electrical engineers for the Home-maker to express her point of view.

* * *

THE NEED FOR MORE WOMEN ON ELECTRICITY COMMITTEES.
Councillor Mrs. Gregory, of West Ham, in a splendid fighting speech at the Convention, suggested that there should be at least one woman on every Electricity Committee to put forward the womans point of view.
In her experience, she found that the men were more concerned about the technicalities of the subject than about the human aspect of the problem as applied to the homes of working people.
This suggestion received warm applause, and as pointed out by The Electrical Review, " Women can be co-opted if they are not available as Councillors, and the inclusion of women on a Committee would no doubt prove beneficial to domestic consumers."
We would draw the attention of all Electricity Authorities to this excellent suggestion.

THE E.A.W. SECOND ANNUAL MEETING.
If proof had been needed of the growth and progress of the E.A.W. it was amply given at the Second Annual Meeting of the Association, held on May 11th and 12th.
It was good to see the large body of members from all parts of the country mingling with distinguished and representative people in Public Life and in the Electrical Industry.
The spirit of confident progression pervaded all the speeches, and no doubt existed in the minds of any that the E.A.W. had come to stay.

transcription:
168			The Electrical Age

		The Electrical Equipment
				of
			Baslow Hall.
	Electric light, electric cooking, and a few
electric fires were installed at the Hall a

[Image: THE DINING ROOM.]

number of years ago. It was only, how-
ever, two years ago that complete electric-
fication was achieved. Since then every
requirement of heat, light and power has
been filled electrically. There is no electric
supply yet available at Baslow, and Dr.
Ferranti is therefore obliged to generate
his own electricity.
When considering the installation, every
provision was made for a complete plant,
and it was arranged in such a manner that
at a later period supply could be taken from
the public mains. There is reasonable
hope that this may be accomplished in
about a years time.
The fundamental feature underlying the
installation is HEAT STORAGE.
In order that electricity may be cheaply
supplied, it is necessary that it should be
used over the longest possible time during
each day. This involves storage, and as
electricity cannot be stored at a low cost
at present, it is necessary to do the equiva-
lent of this in another way. With the
exception of lighting and a small amount
of power, domestic requirements are
entirely for heat. Now heat can be very
economically stored in the form of hot
water, and this is what has been done in
the Baslow installation.

[Image: THE KITCHEN]

The capital cost of hot water storage is,
of course, much less than that of direct
electrical storage, and Dr. Ferranti finds
that with his particular plant he gets all
the hot water that is required for baths
and washing and house-heating. The
system of heating the house is by radiation.
All the principal rooms have invisible
panels in the ceilings, consisting of pipes
bedded in the plaster below the surface.
The general heating is therefore taken care
of by radiation at low temperature from the
ceilings of all the principal rooms, and not
by heating the air by convectors, which
are wrongly called radiators. The reason
for placing the panels in the ceiling is that
they shall not heat up the air; the idea is

[Image: THE COW HOUSE.]

Unnamed: 9: Invited a party of interested people to visit the farm.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 169

to have in the top of every room a layer of constant hot air which keeps the surface of the ceiling reasonably warm, i.e., which does not take away by convection from the heat in the ceiling. The heating is produced by radiation at low temperature from the warm surfaces. The temperature at the surface of the ceiling, where one wants the heating, is 110°—120°F. The high grade radiant heat is produced by electric radiators. Every room has one or more electric radiators of various kinds in it. The heat efficiency of the whole installation is extremely high; something over 75 per cent. of the heat in the oil used by the engine is usefully employed in one form or another in the house from the high temperature form of light to the low temperature form of low grade heat radiation.
There are four bathrooms, ten lavatory basins and five sinks in the house, so that the demand for hot water is considerable. This is obtained from a tank contained within the large storage tank previously described. Electric lighting is amply provided for. In the cellar there is an electric washer, an electric ironer motor driven, and a large drying and airing cupboard. There is also an electrically driven cream separator in the dairy, and an electric fan to keep the air moving in the cellar and the dairy.
The kitchen is provided with a complete cooking range, and an old electric oven made in the early days of electric cooking is still in use and perfectly effective. There are also a number of cooking appliances with self-contained heater elements, for which a special table and switch and plug board is provided.
The cow house is fitted with an electric chaff cutter, and food cutter, and other apparatus necessary in this respect. The floor of the garage is heated by means of the exhaust gases taken in piping through the floor prior to their being discharged into the atmosphere.
A large electric lawn mower is used for mowing the lawn. Power plugs are connected at different points in the garden for the electric lawn mower, and at the tennis courts for teas.
CELLARS.
All dirt has been eradicated by the installation of electric light, since the storage of coal and coke has been obviated and the space that was once used for coal and coke and the heating boiler has now been adapted for electric washing.
It has been estimated that by introducing a complete electrical system nearly 50 per cent. has been added to the accommodation of the house, and it is significant to note that where it was necessary, before the installation was complete, to employ five maids to work and keep the house clean, the whole of the work is now being done by two helpers. It will be seen, therefore, that electrical equipment materially lightens the work, reduces the labour costs, and increases the floor space available for useful work.
* * *
An All-Electric Farm.
At the invitation of Mr. Alderson-Smith, of "Electro-Farming," a party of interested people paid a visit to the All-Electric Farm of Mr. Borlase Matthews, at East Grinstead, on May 20th.
During a tour of the Farm it was learned that there are now some 67 different applications of electricity, which is more than on any other Farm in the world. Extensive experimental work is being carried out, which undoubtedly will result to the benefit of the farmers in this country.
Throughout the country farming is at present an unprofitable business, and it is necessary to change the conditions under which it is being carried out—to mechanise and electrify the industry. Hence the importance of the work being done on this Farm.

Unnamed: 9: Gave a lecture on public health and food preservatives regulations.
transcription:
170 The Electrical Age
* Refrigeration and the Preservation of Food.
The new "Public Health, Preservatives in Food, Regulations" must claim the special attention of women, and hence the lecture delivered by Dr. Porter, Medical Officer of Health, Marylebone, and that of Mr. H. W. Roberts on "Refrigeration" will, we are sure, merit the special interest of our readers.
Probably, said Dr. Porter, this country, of all the more progressive countries, is the only one which has no Pure Food Act; other countries that have Pure Food Acts have them because we want them to. This country is the largest food-importing country in the world, and our custom is competed for by all food-exporting countries in the world. We are good customers and must therefore be well looked after. We want the best and are only going to have the best—and that is the reason why all other countries have Pure Food Acts.
Those countries that have Pure Food Acts have included in them provisions with regard to preservatives, particularly chemical agents used as preservatives of food, and I rather think that they have these provisions with regard to chemical agents as preservatives because we have forced it upon them. The reason for this is, I think, that we have not as a country up to now objected to foods containing preservatives. Countries exporting foods, because they have to send them a considerable distance to reach us, take precautions against wastage by putting in chemical agents to preserve them. But the manufacturers, I imagine, did not limit the putting in of preservatives into food Our Government said we should have to take steps to stop putting preservatives into the foods which are sold here, and made Regulations accordingly.
Why it is only comparatively recently that we have placed an embargo on the putting of preservatives into food it is rather difficult to say. As a matter of fact, the people of this country take comparatively little interest in what is done with their food. The reason why we have an embargo on preservatives is not because people object to them, but because various official people, like myself, for example, and other Medical Officers of Health, also a few members of the Medical Profession,

Unnamed: 9: abuses of chemical methods of food preservation, said Mr. Roberts
Unnamed: 10: speaker advocating for refrigeration over chemical preservatives; advisor
transcription:
The Electrical Age 171

did not like the idea of preservatives in food, and thought some efforts should be made to stop them or control them. It was a very difficult task.

UNNATURAL PRESERVATIVES.
One of the things which I wish to emphasise is the harm that is done, and particularly the diseases that are caused, by the presence of chemical preservatives in food. Unfortunately, we have no figures, and that is the great trouble with which people like myself and members of the Medical Profession are faced, as they cannot produce anything in the shape of figures. They cannot say: " Here is Scarlet Fever," or " Here is Consumption," or " Here is this and that," and other diseases, and cannot give the number of deaths that have occurred from these diseases—due to the fact that people are eating food containing preservatives. We can only say we are convinced that damage is done by foods containing chemical agents. Foods should not be treated with chemical agents, as these are unnatural things.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES.
Another general principle is that if these things are being put into food, you are interfering with the nature of the food. You are interfering with the vital principle in the food. The food cannot be so fresh if you put these things in, and therefore you are interfering with the vital principles. We are convinced that if you interfere with the vitamines in the food you interfere with the nutriment of the people, and therefore these things should not be allowed. We had hopes of people from the other side coming forward to convince us that it did not do us any harm to put in these things. The Ministry of Health and the Government determined to take action on the statements that we made and the advice which we gave, that there should be a law forbidding the addition of chemical agents to foods. Certain chemical agents, such as Boric Acid and Formaldehyde, were considered distinctly harmful, but other chemical agents were allowed in small quantities in certain articles. Otherwise our advice was taken, and the law was passed. These Regulations are known as " Public Health, Preservatives in Food, Regulations." We were able to suggest alternative methods of food preservation. We said there is no use and no necessity for the addition of chemical agents in food. Physical-natural methods can be used. It may mean expense to manufacturers and dealers, but physical means can be found to preserve food.
Two physical agents used for preservation are, of course—heat and cold. We decided for cold in the place of chemical agents. There were certain objections, chiefly because of the expense involved. But of the value and advantage of cold in the preservation of food, there can be no possible doubt whatever. If electricity is capable of producing cold which can be used in connection with the preservation of food, all I can say is " God Bless Electricity," because it is going to do away with the necessity for agents of a chemical nature, which are harmful to the human body and should not be allowed.

REFRIGERATION : WHAT IT MEANS, AND WHY.
The abuses of chemical methods of food preservation, said Mr. Roberts, has led, in the interests of health, to legislative restriction and control, and although the restrictions authorised by the Public Health Regulations were purposely designed to be put into operation gradually, the provision of alternative methods of conservation and preservation became immediate as each class of food was brought within the scope of the regulations.
Apart from the chemical additions to food, there were several methods by which preservation could be effected, such as pasteurization, for example, but most of these were in effect processes of cooking or partial cooking, so that Refrigeration stood out well from the other methods, in that it was the only means of attaining the desired end without causing changes of flavour, texture, or, most important of all, of food values.

Unnamed: 9: Author of article on a Swiss hydro-electric power station.
transcription:
174	The Electrical Age

Hydro-Electric Power Station at Augst on the Rhine.
By Mrs. Walter Lawson.

In her fourth article on Switzerland, Mrs. Lawson gives a fascinating picture
of a Super-Generating Station on the Rhine.

During my visit to Switzerland I spent
three days in Basle, and whilst there I was
fortunate enough to have the opportunity
of being taken over the Hydro-Electric
Power Station at Augst, on the Rhine, by
the Chief Engineer.
This Power Station is situated a few
miles out of Basle, in a most interesting
spot, as the Rhine at this point, and for
several miles in each direction, forms the
frontier between Switzerland and Germany,
the Germans having a large Power Station
of their own immediately opposite the
Swiss Station.
We walked half-way across the bridge
to look at the dam, but were not allowed
to go further, as the other half of the bridge
is in Germany.
A tremendous force of water is kept back
at this point, and having accumulated more
than they needed, it was being let out at
the side of the dam, causing a surging and
noise of rushing waters like a miniature
Niagara.
We then went down into the underground
corridors. Through trap-doors we looked
up and could just catch a glimpse of the
shaft of the hydraulic wheel at work. The
noise here was deafening, the pressure of
water being all around us.

© © ©

Entering the Power Station, one was
struck by the extreme simplicity of the
design of the building, and the apparent
absence of human beings. In the long
narrow room ten generators were in full
swing, the man in charge controlling the
activities of the entire Station from a
switchboard in the gallery. Apart from
him, we only saw one workman, whose
duties were to oil and clean the machinery,
otherwise the Station appeared to run
itself.
From rooms leading off the gallery, the
power is transmitted to the City by means
of underground cables, a few overhead
cables being used in times of extra pressure.
We were told that in winter there is not
always enough water to work all the
generators, when the mountain torrents
which feed the Rhine are frozen, but
Switzerland is supplied with a network of
over eighty Power Stations, linked up in
such a way that they can help one another,
and as there is always a plentiful supply
near Lake Geneva, where the weather is
not so severe, the supply is always main-
tained, although the amount of current
used in the country is stupendous.

E.A.W. Membership Campaign.
While the membership of the E.A.W.
already runs well into four figures, it is the
aim of the Association to double its mem-
bership before the next Annual Meeting if
possible. With the object of encouraging
each member to get as many new members
as possible, it has been suggested that a
set of electrical terms should be drawn up
somewhat on the lines of those adopted by
our friends the Frothblowers. At the
moment, as far as London is concerned,
Mrs. Llewelyn Atkinson holds the "Peak
Load." Suggestions for a suitable set of
titles will be welcomed from our readers.

The Electrical Age				175

Nursery Magic!!

By Len Chaloner


A visit to a modern nursery is prone to make us feel a little like the traditional Rip Van Winkle, so amazing are the changes that have taken place in the last few years. Almost it seems like the work of fairies, were it not so scientific that one half fears whether the entire world of fairies may not have been consumed in the onslaught of " units " ; for it should be said at once that the modern nursery is an electric nursery.

THE ELECTRIC SCREEN
Necessary to the Equipment of a Modern Nursery

An electric fire has taken the place of the erstwhile open grate, and the nursery is scrupulously clean in consequence; besides, is it not treated to a daily audience of the electric vacuum cleaner? Perhaps one is tempted to wonder, faintly, where the fascinating shining blackness of the coal-box has gone to, but Nannies spirit lamp and kettle have undoubtedly been superseded by an electric milk warmer, and a peep into her cupboard shows us an electric iron. Hard by, in the bathroom we find an electric geyser, and towel airer, while a bath water heater is lying ready to heat babys bath in the nursery.
More wonderful still is the gentle warmth that radiates from the screen, by the nursery door. It is so decorative one would never have suspected it of more
