176 The Electrical Age

it can be switched on without recourse to matches. It is, moreover, estimated to consume 1/200th of a unit per hour. Taking it that our current is as high as 8d. per unit, that means that our dimmer costs us 1d. for twenty-five hours. Distant memories tell us that a box of nightlights, each of which lasted about eight hours, cost us around ten pence; it came out about a penny a night light. There is a distinct saving in favour of the dimmer even probably if the cost of renewing the bulb is included.
If, however, in July, when night and day seem very much the same, we are more concerned with cooling than heating problems, the electric fan has much to offer the modern nursery, while that seemingly irreducible piece of labour, the constantly recurring laundry problem, can be dealt with comfortably, and with unheated brow if we possess an electric washing machine. The economy point with all such labour-saving devices rests merely on the numbers of our family, which make for what is known in industrial circles as short or long, runs of work, repaying us by degrees for our initial outlay.
Yet in this efficiency, this very spick and spanness, we are left a little wistful. What happens when there is no Nannies work-basket to tidy, or when there are no red coals to look into the fire, and discover wonderful glowing castles which fall into new and fantastic shapes even as one gazes! Dare one even wonder whether fairies dance round the electric dimmer as they danced round our pink shaded nightlight?
We whisper to ourselves, questing a little like Aladdin: "New lamps for old!" but the truth is that we are looking for the fairies through our glasses, and alas, by that time one does not discover them. Fairies are the prerogative of youth, and youth will be served, fairies and all, to-day, to-morrow or in days years hence.
But youth to-day needs no ring to rub, for the summoning of an obedient genii. He presses a bright brass switch, or pushes
in a plug, with sturdy little hands, and magic is to his order; even the vacuum cleaner is but a fascinating and all absorbing giant, more vivid than any discovered between the scarlet or yellow covers in the bookshelf. Youth is as ever triumphant, gorgeously supreme over each obstacle that comes his way. Imperiously he presses the switch to summon his geniis services, and the name of the genii to-day is Science.

The Electrical Age 177
£2,000 Prize Won by a Bristol Girl.
The £2,000 prize offered by the British Electrical Development Association in the recent National Ballot Competition was won by Miss Edna Gardiner, of Bristol.
As our readers will remember, the first prize was a freehold house, fully wired and equipped with electric lighting, cooking, heating and labour-saving appliances, or alternatively a cheque for £2,000.
Miss Gardiner, who is employed on the commercial staff of a large firm in Bristol, has decided to accept the cheque.
Amongst the prize winners of this competition there was a large proportion of women.
We cannot help feeling sorry that Miss Gardiner did not decide to accept the All-Electric House.
* * *
The Standard Telephone & Cable Co. have presented to the office a beautifully enlarged framed edition of the photograph of E.A.W. members taken at their Works on May 12th, 1927.
MISS GARDINER.
* * *
School Girls Visit Power Station.
At the request of the Headmistresses Employment Committee of the Ministry of Labour, the E.A.W. arranged for over 60 girls from London Secondary Schools to visit the Hackney Power Station.
The party was received by Mr. L. L. Robinson, Borough Electrical Engineer, and Alderman Mrs. Hammer, Chairman of the Electricity Committee.
After inspecting the Showroom, the party was conveyed to the Works in motor coaches, returning afterwards to the Showrooms for a talk by Mr. Robinson on the film "From the Coal Heap to the Consumer."
Considerable interest was shown by the schoolgirls, and Mr. Robinson has offered three prizes for the best three essays giving a description of the visit, to be judged by an E.A.W. Committee. We shall hope to publish extracts from these essays in "The Electrical Age."

178

The Electrical Age

The Work of The Electricity Commissioners.


The record of the Electrical Industry and its service to the Nation cannot be told completely without reference to the scope and work of the Electricity Commissioners. This work is carried out to a large extent " behind the scenes," and the public is, therefore, often unaware of the manifold duties and responsibilities of this very important body.
With the tremendous interest which the general public, and women in particular, are taking in all matters appertaining to the electrical welfare of the country, we feel that our readers would welcome a closer acquaintance with the functions of the Electricity Commissioners.
The Commissioners were appointed in 1920 under the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1919, "to Promote, Regulate and Supervise the supply of electricity." At that period the great need of the time was for co-ordination, not only for the concentration of Generation in larger Stations with larger units of plant, but in respect of Voltages and Frequencies and Systems of Supply. The complex position at this period arising from past development on an individualistic basis is now seen to have resulted in unnecessary expenditure of capital, wasteful consumption of coal, and high charges for current.
Electrical energy for power purposes in Industry was in great demand, and the lack of concentration and co-ordination of public supply, and consequent high charges, was the direct cause of many manufacturers installing their own Generating Plant and adding thereby to the multiplicity of small Stations. The absence of any correlating agency had its effect on the manufacture of electrical plant, and the consequent necessity for many types of plant instead of a few standard types deprived those concerned of the advantages that otherwise would have accrued in the shape of less costly apparatus and easier running. It is obvious, too, that such diversity and lack of cheapness must have interfered with the development of the home market and also have been a great handicap in the securing of markets abroad.
Thus the time was ripe for bringing about a comprehensive system of Generation, Transmission and Distribution; during 1918 the Board of Trade set up important committees, upon whose recommendation the next step was taken to ensure an adequate and economical supply of electrical energy for all classes of consumers, special regard being paid to the need of those Industries dependent upon a cheap supply of power for their development.
By the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1919, the general supervision of the supply of electricity in the country was placed in the hands of five Commissioners, and the Chairman appointed by the then Minister of Transport was Sir John Snell. The Commissioners were men of great electrical or financial knowledge and experience, and the Chairman brought with him also much goodwill, which proved of great value in the many delicate tasks confronting him and his colleagues. The Secretary to the Electricity Commission is Mr. R. T. G. French.
The work of the Electricity Commissioners since 1920 is one of great progress and of undoubted benefit to the Electrical Industry and the Public generally. Their value as a co-ordinating and controlling agency cannot be over estimated. Their statutory powers and duties covered a tremendous field, and were, inter alia:—To appoint Advisory Committees; to determine Electricity Districts; to make Orders for the Formation of Joint Electricity Authorities; to deal with the question of constructing new Generating Stations and of extensions to existing Generating Stations or Main Transmission Lines; to sanction the

Electricity and Everywoman.
Being a brief indication of the contribution of the Cable Industry to the progress of civilisation, given by Mr. Martin (Works Manager) of the Standard Telephone and Cable Co., during a visit of the E.A.W. to the Cable Works of this Firm at North Woolwich.
I will commence my few remarks to you this afternoon with a truism—"Womans work is never done." This well-known saying is often, I fear, uttered in jesting fashion by those members of the male sex who lack the imaginative sympathy to realise its truth.
Now if there is one agency or form of energy which can do—and has done—a great deal to lessen the truth of that saying, it is electricity. Electricity must be carried from the site where it is generated to the place where it is to perform useful work, and the channels through which we carry this energy are cables. This, in brief, is the connection between the cable industry and the home, for the house is the chief place where the benefits of the cleanest and most easily used form of energy are most appreciated.
Probably all of my listeners have at some time or another glanced at a cable gang at work in the town streets or along country roads. You have seen the big wooden drums slowly unreeling their lead tubes into the ducts beneath the road, but has it occurred to you at that moment that these "Tubes" are the networks of electric power supply to your homes, and to countless other homes, offices and factories? transcription:
182	The Electrical Age

One of the most important problems con- cerned with this work was the production of cables capable of carrying electricity at the very high pressures now required. The Woolwich Power Station supplies energy through main cables of 33,000 volts, which were actually made in this factory, and as the requirements of power transmission become more exacting it may interest you to know that we have manufactured lengths of cable capable of working at the extremely high figure of 66,000 volts. As you are aware, the ordinary lighting circuit operates at about 200-220 volts. The work of generating electricity and the work of transmitting it from place to place moves parallel, and there are always new prob- lems to be faced and solved.
The contribution of this industry to the progress of civilisation is not, however, confined to light, heat and power.
The radio industry, that popular and wonderfully cheap form of entertainment, uses a great deal of cable of various kinds. The supply of power to the high power transmitting station is made through cables, the assembly of radio sets demands a large supply of insulated wires, and the trans- mission of many broadcasts is made over telephone lines.
We now come to a very important section of the cable industry, the manufacture of telephone cables. The telephone is one of the most useful inventions ever given to the world, especially to the business world, and the gradual perfection of telephone systems has moved hand in hand with the perfection of design and manufacture of telephone cables. The technical demands for perfection in uniformity and balance over the metallic circuits in the modern long distance cable are such as would have been thought ridiculous only ten years ago. The improvements in trunk cable design, together with the use of amplifying devices, have made possible clear and strong speech over ever increasing distances, and the development of international communica- tion is steadily moving ahead.
There has been in the past a tendency to look upon the telephone mainly as a
business sid, while forgetting its great value in the home. The telephone in the home saves time, money and often need- less worry. Through its inter-connected lines you can call up the doctor for an urgent illness, you can call up tradesmen and have food sent in to meet an unex- pected demand, you can call up friends and make or cancel appointments—the uses of the home telephone are manifold— and now the miracle of calling up friends and relations across the Atlantic Ocean is an accepted fact of normal existence. We are gradually acquiring more fully the telephone habit in this country as we realise its potentialities.
I have covered briefly the main lines of usefulness in which the cable industry plays its part in regard to everyday exist- ence, and I hope you will take away with you the impression that this industry, in common with its partners in the Engineer- ing World, is helping all of us in its small way to find life more comfortable and more pleasant.
We do not claim to be altruists, but we claim to be carrying out a useful and necessary function in the organisation of our everyday world.
* * *
Inauguration of Electrolux Works.
On May 18th an interesting ceremony took place at Luton, when the Right Hon. Sir Robert Horne, M.P., opened the new Works where the Electrolux Refrigerator is to be made.
We were interested to note, in passing through the Works, the large number of women employed in the manufacture of this refrigerator.
We discovered, too, in the course of journeying round the Works, that the fac- tory had previously belonged to Hewlett & Blondeau; it may be remembered that during the War Mrs. Hewlett carried on very extensive Aircraft Works, and trained her own son as an aviator. We wish this new Industry every success in its very interesting surroundings.

The Electrical Age

A Page for Girl Guides.

“Fancies in Fans.”

By Margaret Partridge, B.Sc.

Bessie and Helen had been friends and playmates from their earliest years, and it was a wrench when Bessie went off to a School of Domestic Science, while Helen expended her energies at a College of Engineering. On the first day of their first holidays what a lot they had to say to each other! It took some hours of rapid talking

A SIEMENS ELECTRIC FAN SHOWING OIL HOLES.

before the obvious questions: “Do you like it?” “What do you do?” “Are the other students all right?” etc., etc., had been asked and answered on both sides, and then reminiscences!
“Do you remember that railway accident you had on the dining room floor!”
“Yes—we must have been about five years old then. How I enjoyed those toy ‘puff-puffs.’ It was good of you to sacrifice your best doll for my love of trains,” replied Helen.
“Oh, my pleasure in it was nursing Evangeline after the accident. I have her still, poor darling, but she has lost a lot of her stuffing. I believe that if we had been a bit older you would have insisted on X-raying her.”
“Perhaps I might,” laughed Helen.
“Do you remember how I lighted your doll’s house with electric light? We must have been ten then.”
“Rather,” said Bessie. “And how one light would never go out till you had to call in Dad to help you. And do you remember your Meccano, and how you would have cranes and building extensions all round about my doll’s house, and wanted to make a lift inside, but there wasnt room?”
“There was room, only you wouldn’t let me cut out a bit of the landing. Really, I’d like to put in that lift now.”
“You’ll have to ask Babs. It’s her

REVO DESK FAN.

doll’s house now, but she wants an electric fan put in. I’ve been commissioned to ask you about it ‘instant minute you come home, please.’”
“I’ll see about it,” answered Helen.
“But why does Babs want a fan?”

transcription:

" We have got one at home, now—a desk type—and Babs is not happy unless her dolls house has everything Mothers house has. By the way, Mother is like Babs. She also wants your attention to her fan, because she says it sparks a bit.
" Brush pressure or dirty commutator, replied Helen. I think I can titivate that all right. Lets see?
" The girls got the fan, and found it true that there were sparks, but worse on one brush than the other. Helen unscrewed the two little black ebonite milled caps which held the brushes in place and tipped out first two coiled springs and then two small round carbon brushes.
" The springs, she quickly noticed, were of equal length and equal strength, and as the brushes were comparatively new they were also of equal length, but she soon saw that whereas one brush showed a smooth clean surface where it pressed on the commutator, the other was uneven, and showed signs of burning.
" Probably a bit of grit or hard carbon, was her verdict. If we rub this up with glass paper I expect it will be all right.
" A very few rubs on a bit of glass paper effected the needed repair, and Bessie and Helen proceeded to examine the rest of the fan.
" Mother says that a drop of oil once in a blue moon does lots of good.
" I expect it does, said Helen. The two oil holes are easy to get at. Better than some machines I know. Look here, Bessie, tell me this: What is the real good of a fan of this sort. It doesnt make any fresh air, just stirs up the air already in the room?
" I know, assented Bessie. But the pores of the skin seem to be more active in moving air than in still air. If you really want to remove fumes or odours or to introduce real fresh air to a room you must have a big extract fan in the wall. We have one in the kitchen at the school, and if you pass outside it you can judge how useful it is. The cooking fumes it emits are too awful!
" Dont they ever use intake fans for the same purpose? asked Helen.
" Yes, sometimes. It seems to depend on the natural facilities for ventilation and the opinions of the engineers, said Bessie. I think extract fans are more usual. Of course, the little desk fans are sometimes put near an open window in ordinary houses.
" Thats true, said Helen. They can be used like that and really help to ventilate. At home, you know, we havent a proper fan, but we sometimes take the bag off the vacuum cleaner and use that as a fan. Before last term I used the vacuum to dry my hair, and it did the trick jolly well, too.
" Wasnt there any dust with it? said the careful Bessie.
" Not a particle. Of course, I let it blow hard for a bit first to clear itself, but it was all right.
" Bessie didnt look as though she was attending, and after a pause she said slowly: Do you know, the harder I think the more certain I am that the fan the Principal has on her desk at the school has no little black caps like you took off to find the brushes. Is that possible?
" Quite possible. Heaps of fans are driven by squirrel cage motors instead of commutator motors, if they are on an A.C. supply.
" Why dont you say Alternating Current? Your engineering slang is most confusing?
" Thats not slang, protested Helen. Merely abbreviation. D.C. means Direct Current, and K.W. means Kilowatts, and R.P.M. means Revolutions per ——.
" For heavens sake, stop, shouted Bessie. If you go on like that Ill give you the chemical abbreviations for all the food we eat.
" Pax, murmured Helen.
" Thats all right. Tell me, though, is Squirrel Cage an abbreviation too, or slang?
" It sounds like slang, said Helen, but its used in all engineering books. Really,

Four Distinguished E.A.W. Glasgow Members.
Three out of the four women Magistrates of Glasgow, who are all active members of the E.A.W., attended in their official capacity at the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland in Edinburgh, on Tuesday, May 24th. This is the first time in history that this has occurred, and we are proud that these ladies are members of the E.A.W. It is a curious fact that each of the four women bailies bear the same Christian name, namely: Mary—Bailie Mary Bell, Bailie Mary Snodgrass, Bailie Mary Craig Roberton, and Bailie Mary Barbour. Bailie Mrs. Bell is the Senior Magistrate of Glasgow, and as such invested the new Lord Provost with his symbol of office in November last.
She has created still another Municipal record by presiding at the Licensing Court, and may also be remembered as the first lady Magistrate to attend an execution. Bailie Mrs. Bell is proud of the fact that she was one of the first women to bring Electricity into her home in Glasgow.

"THERMOID" FLEXIBLE CORD.
Everyone has experienced the annoyance of suddenly being stopped just in the middle of ironing, or getting tea, and at many other inconvenient moments, through breaking of the flexible cord at the point of entry at the plug or at the apparatus, and these accidents seem to be most frequent when ironing.

192			The Electrical Age

A Cookery Page.

Conducted by Miss Mary Mackirdy,
Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow, (who has recently returned from a visit to America).

A Cold Lunch.

The very wide scope of Salads as a prominent feature in a Lunch, Dinner or Supper menu is scarcely appreciated as it deserves to be by the British cook. In a country which boasts of the naturalness of its cookery and which therefore ought to hold the salad in highest honour, gives it instead an inferior place with often a spoilt result.

This proved to me the most interesting and enlightening branch of American cookery, with its almost endless variety of delicious salads, consisting of vegetables, fruits, separate and in combination with meat and fish, and delightful dressings.

With all the good things necessary at 
[Illustration of a grill]
A BELLING "BOILER GRILLER" suitable for
the preparation of the Dishes described
by Miss Mackirdy.
this season, I would put in a strong plea for the greater use of these for dietetic reasons, and apart from this very important reason there is the saving of labour and current, and last, but not least, the real delight of seeing and eating a well got up salad.

The dishes introduced here are suitable for various meals, including a Picnic.

A Cold Fish Savoury with Salad.

Some cooked fish, which may be salmon, white fish or lobster, or it may be a mixture of white fish and prawns or shrimps, one or more hard-boiled eggs, some good salad dressing, lettuce, radishes, few cooked potatoes, some large raisins, gherkins.

Take all skin and bones from the fish and break into flakes, add to it the eggs chopped roughly, some chopped gherkin if desired, and make all savoury with dressing; pile up roughly in the centre of a dish.

Arrange round the fish nice-looking leaves of lettuce, fixing the stalk end under the fish, fill in the leaves with potatoes cut in dice, some stoned raisins and dressing, and by way of decoration stick a fringed radish in each pile of potato.

This dish lends itself to various treatments; for example, meat may be used in place of fish, various vegetables may be used, or it may be served simply as a salad omitting the fish in the centre.

A Good Salad Dressing.

One raw yolk of egg, 1 hard-boiled yolk, 4 tablespoons salad oil, 2 tablespoons vinegar or lemon juice, at least 1/4 teaspoon each of salt, pepper, mustard and sugar.

Bruise the hard-boiled yolk with a wooden spoon till smooth, add the other and mix till smooth; fix a wet towel round the bowl to keep it steady, and add the oil very slowly, stirring it constantly and always the one way. After the oil, add the vinegar or lemon, then the other things, adding more seasoning to suit the taste. A delicious sauce is made by adding one or two tablespoons whipped cream to this dressing.

To Fringe Radishes.

Cut the radishes from the narrow end down to the leaf end in eight sections, but do not separate; keep in cold water till required.

194	The Electrical Age

E.A.W. Branch Activities.

North East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm, Dial House,
Northumberland Street, Newcastle-on-Tyne.

The North East Coast Branch is particularly
fortunate in having secured as its President
the Viscountess Grey of Falloden, who is
known to the public as an indefatigable worker
in many good causes. Amongst her other
interests, Lady Grey is a member of the Society
for Physical Research. She also sits on the
Committee for the National Society for the
Prevention of Tuberculosis, and takes a great
interest in Infant Welfare and the work of the
Westminster Health Society on behalf of
Mothers and Babies.
She is a writer of articles of a varied nature,
and amongst subjects on which she has con-
tributed may be found " Winter Woods,"
"The Greenfinch," "The Rook," "The
Sayings of the Children," "Shepherds
Crowns," "Windlestraw," and many other
books.
One of her great hobbies is birds, as her
beautiful aviaries at Wilsford Manor, Salis-
bury, will testify.
She also takes a great interest in the work
of the League of Nations Union, and her
acceptance of the office of President of the
North East Coast Branch of the E.A.W. will,
we feel, surely claim the same sympathetic
interest from her as many other movements to
which she has devoted her time.

BRANCH NOTES.
The Sixth Branch of the Association was
inaugurated at Newcastle-on-Tyne on April 28th,
1927, and is known as the North East Coast
Branch.
The Inaugural Meeting, which was held in the
Lighting Service Bureau, Dial House, Northum-
berland Street, Newcastle, was very well
attended.
In the absence of the President, the Viscountess
Grey of Falloden, the chair was taken by Mrs.
Norbert Merz. The aims and objects of the
Association were outlined by the Director, and

VISCOUNTESS GREY OF FALLODEN.

Mr. R. P. Sloan, Managing Director of the
Newcastle-on-Tyne Electric Supply Co., addressed
the meeting.
He pointed out that with the increasing
development of the domestic uses of electricity
on the North East Coast it was essential
for the women to have an opportunity of
learning more of the fundamental principles
underlying the use of electricity in the home.
He was certain that the E.A.W. would feel this
need, and he wished the Association every success.
In its inaugural meeting the E.A.W. had the
support of the local E.D.A. Committee and also
members of the Institution of Electrical
Engineers. A representative committee was
formed, with Miss Anna Holm, a Founder
Member, as Secretary and Treasurer.
A number of invitations have already been
received for members to visit the works in the
area, and an attractive programme is being
drawn up for the autumn.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
The Glasgow and District Branch are slowing down for the Summer Season, no more visits and lectures until the Autumn.
The Summer Outing took place on Monday, June 20th, to Loch Katrine, the estate of the Glasgow corporation. The level of one of the minor Lochs has been raised considerably, and the resultant head of water has been used in the generating of electricity for lighting, heating and cooking for the various houses on the estate.
The Branch has set out on a new venture until September; Greenock, Gourock, and Port Glasgow members have been formed into a sub-section with Councillor Mrs. Laurie, J.P., as Chairman of a small local committee. The sub-section has had two cookery demonstrations, a lecture on "Good and Bad Home Lighting," and a talk on House Wiring and Minor Repairs. Now a visit has been arranged to the Greenock Electricity Station, a Co-operative Dairy, and the X-Ray and Sunlight Dept. of the Royal Infirmary.

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. L. Hayes,
1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
After the air had been fully charged with electricity by the Spring Conference, we have now settled down to fully appreciate the results of that electrification. This undoubtedly has been very fruitful, as may be realised by the fact that our membership increased by 69 members in less than a week.
The first meeting to follow the Conference was a visit to the General Post Office. The members thoroughly appreciated this visit and have expressed a desire to know a little more about the intricate workings of such systems. This we hope to do in the near future.
Mrs. Christine Fredericks films were shewn (having been kindly lent by Mr. Beauchamp, of E.D.A.) by the Manager of the Gaumont Studio in Birmingham. They were short but good, and the members who saw them enjoyed them thoroughly.
One of the best meetings of the Branch was the discussion of the Cooker. Members were

IDEAL for use in small modern households for grilling, roasting and baking.
The efficiency of the "Protos" is so great that a little more current than for an electric iron is used, viz., 3/5ths of a unit per hour. The small amount of fat or water necessary ensures retention to the full of flavour and nutritive value. The special construction effects greatest economy in respect of shrinkage of food.

actively interested and a very lively discussion took place, especially on the Hot-Plate.
Following this meeting, members were invited to a demonstration of the Hoover suction-cleaner. Tea was provided and members thoroughly appreciated the work of the cleaner, when they were allowed to participate in the cleaning of a carpet brought specially for that purpose.
One of the most enjoyable meetings during the Session was the lecture-recital given by Messrs. Priestleys on their "Duo-Art Pianola " Piano. The triple accomplishments of this instrument thoroughly amazed everyone, and many members wished that such instruments were more within the reach of the ordinary person.
The activities of the Branch are being noised further abroad, by arranging a meeting in West Bromwich, at which Her Worship the Mayor will preside. Here we hope to enrol new members.
This Branch is closing its Session with an inspection of electrical activities in rural areas. This meeting will take the form of a summer outing, in which members will travel in buses from village to village where such electrification has taken place, and details will be pointed out and explained.
It was with much regret that the members received the resignations of their Hon. Secretary—Mrs. Lawson, and Hon. Treasurer—Mrs. Forrest. Their work during the first year of the Branch was most trying and arduous, but neither spared time or energy to give the Branch a good footing. All members of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch are most grateful to them for the effort they put forward, and are happy in the fact that though they have resigned as officials, they are still actively engaged in our Association.
A.L.H.

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss G. L. Entwisle, A.M.I.E.E.,
5, Holmfield, Sale, Manchester.

The Manchester Branch has had the misfortune to be deprived temporarily of two of its Hon. Secretaries in succession. Miss G. Entwisle, who has been the energetic and indefatigable Secretary of this Branch from its inception, has been forced to take a rest from her duties for a time, and Mrs. Robertson, who undertook the Hon. Secretaryship temporarily, has just passed through an operation which will necessitate complete rest for some months. Miss Entwisle has nobly stepped into the breach till a new Secretary can be appointed, and we hope to be able to record in the next issue that all offices are filled once more.

actively interested and a very lively discussion took place, especially on the Hot-Plate.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 197

The Spring programme opened in April with a visit to the Metropolitan-Vickers Co.s Works in Trafford Park, and to those who visited it for the first time it must have seemed more like a town than a factory, with its roads, railways, huge buildings, and great variety of manufactures.
Small groups, each in charge of a guide, followed each other round the works, and in turn emerged from the offices to wonder at the view of the main Machine Shop, with its glass roof, galleries and cranes above, and its long aisles of whining machinery below. From turbines, punching machines, insulating and winding departments we made our way to the more familiar electrical appliances of the household, where so great a congestion was caused round the radiators, irons, fans and workers that for a time guides found themselves party-less or in charge of an alien group till we were persuaded to leave this fascinating corner.
The last of the departments visited was the canteen, where over a most welcome tea warm thanks were expressed to Captain Hilton for the firms hospitality, and we discussed whether it was eight or ten miles that we had walked since entering the gates.
In May, a visit was paid to the Pendlebury Childrens Hospital, where the remedial effects of electricity on the little patients was clearly shown. By the courtesy of the Matron, we were shown over many of the wards before seeing the departments for special treatment by artificial sunlight, X-Rays, etc., and so ended our visit on a more hopeful note.
On June 2nd, we were invited to the I.M.E.A. Convention at Buxton, and arrived by motor coach in time to hear Mr. Berrys paper on the electric house, and noted that our members did their share in the interesting discussion that followed. After lunch came the delightful drive to Baslow Hall, which Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti had so kindly thrown open to us all. Each one of the 220 guests must have carried away slightly different pictures of the afternoons enjoyment: the delightful old hall, stone built as all good Derbyshire houses should be, open to all the winds and yet sheltered by trees; the wonderful views of hill and valley framed by the windows that made every room a delight; the fine portraits in the hall; the ceilings that invisibly radiated heat to the rooms; the cupboards and wash bowls so cunningly contrived out of the old disused fireplaces; the countless electrical appliances from the floor-polisher to the sleek cow in the model cow-house so lazily enjoying its electrically-chopped hay, and the electric lawn mower that guided us to the big marquee for a delicious tea. To each of us it wore a slightly different aspect, but two things we all carried away in common: first, the delightful photograph and account of the hall which was handed to each guest on arrival; and second, the kindness and wonderful organising powers of Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti, who could welcome 220 guests to their home undismayed and send them home, after seeing so much, still unfatigued and longing for more.
D.M.P.
* * *
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Stamp, 1, York Terrace, St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.

Our Branch is forging steadily ahead and making good progress. The various meetings have been much appreciated and have been the means of bringing together our members and of giving them an opportunity to voice their ideas and problems.
Our visit to the Cheltenham Electricity Works in March was, as mentioned by our President, Mrs. Atwell Lake, at the conclusion of the tour of the Works, a complete revelation. Our Electrical Engineer (Mr. W. J. Bache), before escorting the members round the Works, gave them a short description of the various processes involved in the generation of electricity. The electrical equipment in use for the tea, thoughtfully provided by Mr. Bache, was of great interest to the members.
On April 6th, an illustrated lecture on "Lighting in the Home and School," given by Mr. W. E. Bush, Manager of the Lighting Service Bureau, was very much appreciated by those present, some of whom confessed that they intended having the lighting in their own homes altered after seeing the illustrations shown by Mr. Bush.
The visit to the Gloucester Wagon Works on May 8th was a popular one. Beginning at the forges, we passed on to the timber departments, where from rough tree trunks, the progress of the timber was followed, to end at the beautifully finished coaches, many of which were destined for abroad.
On May 16th we visited the Electrolux Showrooms, Promenade. Mr. Davis, of "Electrolux," Bristol, gave us a most interesting lecture on "Refrigeration and the Food Act." The discussion which followed whilst tea was served was ample evidence of the interest created by the lecture.
The last meeting on the seasons programme will be in the form of a lecture demonstration by our Electrical Engineer, Mr. W. J. Bache, on "Simple Faults and Where to Find Them."
A.A.S.

The Spring programme opened in April with a visit to the Metropolitan-Vickers Co.s Works in Trafford Park, and to those who visited it for the first time it must have seemed more like a town than a factory, with its roads, railways, huge buildings, and great variety of manufactures.

The last of the departments visited was the canteen, where over a most welcome tea warm thanks were expressed to Captain Hilton for the firms hospitality, and we discussed whether it was eight or ten miles that we had walked since entering the gates.

Convention at Buxton, and arrived by motor coach in time to hear Mr. Berrys paper on the electric house, and noted that our members did their share in the interesting discussion that followed. After lunch came the delightful drive to Baslow Hall, which Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti had so kindly thrown open to us all. Each one of the 220 guests must have carried away slightly different pictures of the afternoons enjoyment: the delightful old hall, stone built as all good Derbyshire houses should be, open to all the winds and yet sheltered by trees; the wonderful views of hill and valley framed by the windows that made every room a delight; the fine portraits in the hall; the ceilings that invisibly radiated heat to the rooms; the cupboards and wash bowls so cunningly contrived out of the old disused fireplaces; the countless electrical appliances from the floor-polisher to the sleek cow in the model cow-house so lazily enjoying its electrically-chopped hay, and the electric lawn mower that guided us to the big marquee for a delicious tea. To each of us it wore a slightly different aspect, but two things we all carried away in common: first, the delightful photograph and account of the hall which was handed to each guest on arrival; and second, the kindness and wonderful organising powers of Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti, who could welcome 220 guests to their home undismayed and send them home, after seeing so much, still unfatigued and longing for more.

Bush, Manager of the Lighting Service Bureau, was very much appreciated by those present, some of whom confessed that they intended having the lighting in their own homes altered after seeing the illustrations shown by Mr. Bush.
The visit to the Gloucester Wagon Works on May 8th was a popular one. Beginning at the forges, we passed on to the timber departments, where from rough tree trunks, the progress of the timber was followed, to end at the beautifully finished coaches, many of which were destined for abroad.
On May 16th we visited the Electrolux Showrooms, Promenade. Mr. Davis, of "Electrolux," Bristol, gave us a most interesting lecture on "Refrigeration and the Food Act." The discussion which followed whilst tea was served was ample evidence of the interest created by the lecture.
The last meeting on the seasons programme will be in the form of a lecture demonstration by our Electrical Engineer, Mr. W. J. Bache, on "Simple Faults and Where to Find Them."

Mrs. Atwell Lake, President of the Cheltenham Branch, is a well-known member of many public organizations in Cheltenham.

Her many activities include Vice-President of Mothers Union Gloucester Diocese, President of Prestbury, Cirencester and Tewkesbury Conservative and Unionist Association, President of the local Branch of the British Sailors Society, member of the Executive Committee (local Branch) of the National Council of Women, also of the Council of the Charity Organization Society, the Girls Orphanage and the Branch Committee of the National Citizens Union.

***

South Wales
and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Tyler, Electric Service Bureau, Royal Chambers, Park Place, Cardiff

Since the Inaugural Meeting on March 24th, we have had several very interesting and well attended meetings, the first being a visit to the Cardiff Corporation Electric Power Station. The members were shown over the Power Station by Mr. C. G. Morley New, the City Electrical Engineer, and Mr. S. Hosgood, after which they were entertained to tea. A thoroughly enjoyable afternoon was spent.

The second fixture was a lecture, at the South Wales Institute of Engineers, on "The Remedial Uses of Electricity," by Mrs. L. E. Wright, a member of the Committee of the South Wales Branch. This was most interesting and descriptive. Mrs. Wright demonstrated and explained the different appliances used by the medical profession. This was greatly enjoyed by all the members and friends, over 100 being present, including many well known gentlemen.

The next fixture was a lecture and demonstration by Miss A. Bissett, of the Jackson Electric Stove Co., on "Cooking by Electricity." This proved a very popular and interesting meeting, being much appreciated by members and visitors. At the close of the demonstration, members and friends were entertained to an all electric tea, and several new members were enrolled.

On May 25th, the members were received by Mr. W. E. Hobbs, District Manager of the General Electric Co., at their Cardiff Showrooms, when a very instructive talk on "Home Lighting" was given by Mr. D. C. James. Many questions were put to Mr. James by the members, showing the keen interest taken in the

MRS. ATWELL LAKE.

subject. At 4 oclock, greetings were received by wireless from the Cardiff B.B.C. Station, wishing all success to the South Wales Branch. Tea was then provided and members were afterwards shewn over the showrooms and stores. More members were enrolled at the close of the visit.

The Committee have arranged for two further meetings to take place before closing down the present session, one being a "Clean Milk" demonstration at the farm of Mr. G. H. Merrett, arranged by Mr. J. D. Davidson, Director of Agriculture for Glamorgan, and the last will be a visit to the Upper Boat Power Station of the South Wales Electrical Power Distribution Co., on June 29th.

Many enquiries are being received as to whether classes are being formed for obtaining general information and practical knowledge.

Arrangements are being made for very interesting lectures for our next Session, which opens in September.

In less than three months our membership has reached 100, including 14 Founder members.

The Branch Secretary is giving instruction on the uses of the Electric Cooker to several members. J.T.

The Electrical Age 201

The Second Annual Meeting
of the
Electrical Association for Women.

No more impressive testimony to the rapid growth of the E.A.W. could be found than the scene at the Hotel Cecil on May 11th. Our President, Lady Astor, presided over a company of more than 400 people, including many distinguished names.
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti proposed "The Electrical Association for Women," and said the Association was a comparatively new one, but in its present state of development it had come into being at the right time. Its growth was a measure, in his mind, of its utility; nothing could have been better for the progress of electricity to-day than the formation of such an Association. He was an electrical enthusiast and believed that the greatest possible benefit would result to the community by means of doing everything electrically. But without knowledge this state of affairs could not come about. There were great electrical developments going on in the country at present; they were to have a much more widespread supply of electricity than heretofore and they were to have electricity at a much lower price, but none of these things could bear fruit without they had the knowledge which would turn them to useful account. They were just now entering on a new phase in the life of the community when electricity and electrical appliances were beginning to be introduced into the home, so that with a given amount of labour a much better result might be produced. The drudgery of the work of the home was proverbial. Electricity was the greatest labour saver they knew of, and now it was beginning to be introduced into the home and later on would be very generally available so that the work of the house might be accomplished with much less labour. It was obvious, therefore, that they required a general knowledge amongst the community of mechanical and electrical things, for otherwise the benefits which could be derived from doing things electrically could not be brought about. Engineering had been a profession generally practised by men, and had served a wonderful purpose in the world. Now engineering and especially electrical engineering, was going into a different field. It was going into the homes all over the country, a very wide field indeed, and it was his opinion that outside the professional classes it was more important for woman to have electrical engineering knowledge than a man. It was very obvious why this should be so. Houses in the future would be full of various labour-saving devices, which involved mechanism and electricity, and to work them properly they wanted engineering and electrical application. They had already in many homes that modern marvel, wireless, which was beginning, or had already, educated people to a large extent with regard to things electrical. Unnamed: 9: Director of the Electrical Association for Women mentioned for success.
transcription:
The Electrical Age
203
plex piece of mechanism, taught people to be engineers and they certainly want to have a fair amount of electrical knowledge as well if they wanted to take care of themselves. The sewing machine had done a great deal to teach women to be mechanics. Personally, he thought one of the highest forms of engineering was to be able to cut out a dress and make it up. The Association which had developed so splendidly and which he felt was such an asset to the community, would be more important as it went on. He had followed the Association from the beginning with the greatest interest, and congratulated them upon the success achieved. The movement had been started by a number of women with vision, who had no thought for themselves, but were concerned to bring knowledge and understanding to other women. He would especially offer his congratulations and admiration to their Director, Miss Haslett. Their success was due partly to the necessity for the existence of such a society and largely due to their good organisation, and for this they had to thank the Director very much. They had also their local centres and a number of able and earnest people working for the good of the Association, and this was a vital factor. He hoped they would long keep up their enthusiasm and keenness in all they did in the Association.
Viscountess Astor, M.P., replied to the toast in a characteristic speech. She disclaimed having any knowledge of electricity but was proud of being the first President of the Electrical Association for Women. It sent a warm feeling into her heart when she saw what the women had done. She had been thinking of the men who were always saying that womans place was in the home, and wondered if some of them would live to realise that if every woman had never thought of any home but her own, what a poor world it would be for the great mass of other women who lived in less favoured homes. The women who started the Electrical Association for Women were inspired to help other women. She remembered when these women were laughed at, and when she said she was going to take it up people said women could not do it. She never said a man could not do a thing, for she had seen such curious men who did such curious things. The history of the last twenty years had shown what women were able to do, and that the Association was a wonderful inspiration to all of them who were interested in women. When it was said that electricity would reduce the drudgery in the home she believed it was perfectly true. Women suffered so cruelly for their mistakes that she thought they had far greater balance in many ways than men. Now this future development of electricity was going to help men, too, for any woman would tell them that it would be quite easy to keep the home if there were no men about; the minute they got a man in the home the trouble began. She was inspired by the great work the Association had done and the greater work it would do.
Sir Philip Nash, in proposing "Electricity in the Service of the Community," said he believed it was recorded in the year 600 B.C. that a Greek philosopher first discovered electricity; but it was not until about 100 years ago that the world was given the opportunity of making practical use of electricity. Faraday showed the world how to do it, and since
then great scientists and great engineers had made further discoveries and shown possible further developments: men like Sir Oliver Lodge, and Rutherford, and others, and they had with them that day Dr. Ferranti, one of the greatest pioneers. Electricity had entered now into almost every phase of modern existence. In the domestic service the application of electricity as an illuminant was well established. It was not so well established in other directions of domestic requirements, like cooking, heating and washing, but it was becoming more popular. In industry they could see that electric power was essential. In railway work electric power was becoming every day more and more important in their existence. In medical science he thought it would be correct to say that the greatest discoveries in surgery, at any rate, in modern days, would not have been possible without electricity. The most modern discovery was the light-ray, which made it possible to bring health to those who lived under conditions where they had not the priceless gift of sunlight. They saw that electricity was the main-stay of the telegraph and telephone, and probably the most spectacular part of that development was broadcasting. A few years ago broadcasting was a luxury, but about a year ago broadcasting in a national crisis enabled them to allay rumours and maintain the stability of the nation. Electricity was beginning to be used in agriculture, and there was a great future for it in connection with the chemical industries. Modern science showed that the structure of all forms of matter was electrical in origin, which showed what a great future lay before that science and the industry. There was another thought which always passed through his mind in connection with electricity, and that was that as such invention was handed down to the people, the horizon, instead of becoming smaller, became broader, because each discovery disclosed more and more possibilities whereby electricity could help them. They were passing through a transition period: through a period when fuel was wasted, and raw material and man power were wasted. They were passing to an age when greater use would be made of raw materials and man power would be saved and production would bring a higher standard of living to those who lived by it. They read that in the organisation of the League of Nations there was a body called the International Economic Council, which sat regularly and at which the various nations of the world discussed questions of international tariffs and trade. He thought that in a few years it would be impossible to discuss any question of an international character without this question of electricity dominating the discussion. After all, electrical energy was merely a commodity exactly the same as wheat and iron ore or anything else. When they looked at the circumstances of the day, they saw Germany transmitting power to Holland and Austria, and she was importing power from Switzerland and France. Denmark was importing power from Norway, and Italy was electrically connected by high tension transmission lines with both France and Switzerland. Last year, when a great hydro-electric installation failed owing to an unusual drought, Italy was able to keep her industries going by importing power from France and Switzerland. In these circumstances surely it was not a dream to say that the development of

Europe was to create a network of high tension electric transmission lines from one country to another; just as they had seen a great network of international railways connecting the centres of consumption with the centres of production and the centres of production with centres of raw materials, as they were going to see electrical transmissions connecting the centres for the economic production of power with the places which required that power. In those circumstances were they dreaming when they said that electricity must dominate the discussions in the future of questions of international tariffs and trade? If they were to maintain their industrial supremacy they must take steps to bring themselves into line with what others were doing, and he ventured to say the first great step had been taken, and they had in one of their guests, Sir Andrew Duncan, the Chairman of the new Central Board. That Board was charged with the duty of scientifically co-ordinating the sources of supply in this country, and above all its duty was to give them a cheap supply of electricity. No greater help could be given to the electrical industry than to increase the domestic load, and the more the Electrical Association for Women could do to make people clamour for electricity the more they would be helping their neighbours and the more they would be doing to improve the conditions in many a dismal home.

Dame Henrietta Barnett responded to the toast, and recalled the work she and Canon Barnett had done amongst the workers in Whitechapel and the Hampstead Garden Suburb in providing better homes for the people.
It was just over twenty years ago that she cut the first sod of the Hampstead Garden Suburb, in which there now lived 12,000 people of all classes.
When overlooking East London and seeing its long, dreary streets, its crowded tenements, its congested population, the thing that claimed her admiration was not the devoted philanthropist, or the overburdened clergy, but the working woman, who, loved by her children, slaves and plans and prays to be able to be home maker. Above the chimney pots also stands, a spiritual force, but too often physically broken by labour. It is to her relief that this Association will come, bringing in its kind hands appliances to ease her household tasks and leave her time, strength and courage to face her childrens problems, to consider their education and guide their tendencies.
Silently, electricity will come to her aid, and then the classes that already have the privilege of greater knowledge and a wider outlook must see to it that the working woman is supplied with opportunities for acquiring knowledge.

Lady Snell gave the toast of "Our Guests," who, she said, were many and distinguished, and included representatives of the Professional Institutions, various Government Departments and the Electrical Industry.
One guest she must make special reference to, Sir Andrew Duncan. They welcomed him as the Chairman of the Central Electricity Board, which was the latest addition to the family. "I believe," continued Lady Snell, "is to be the general opinion in the Electrical Industry that the Minister of

Transports choice of Sir Andrew has been particularly happy and auspicious. I know that is most emphatically my husbands opinion, and I would like to quote, if I may, from the letter he wrote to our Director when much to his regret he felt compelled by reason of his present very heavy duties to decline our invitation to this luncheon. After referring to the schemes for the whole country which are being designed and prepared by himself and his brother Commissioners, he goes on to say: It will be for Sir Andrew Duncan and his colleagues on the Central Electricity Board to carry out the executive work in connection with these schemes. A very onerous task, in which the Commissioners hope the whole Electrical Industry will give the Board very material assistance and thus enable to be put into the highest state of efficiency a great Industry, which can and will confer much benefit upon the people of this country."

Sir Andrew Duncan said that in coming to the luncheon he had a private and unofficial undertaking that he was to be allowed to remain a silent observer of the proceedings, and he believed Lady Snell took the view that this understanding would not be breached, for she ascribed to the popular belief that Scotsmen had such vast experience in receiving hospitality that they were able at any moment to return thanks for it. All he would say was that he advised them not to build their hopes quite so high as Sir Philip Nash had recommended them to do. The new baby was only two months old, but he hoped when it was slightly older it would meet with success. He knew they would be patient, and in the meantime, until they got under weigh, there was no reason why attention should not be directed to organisations such as Sir Philip Nash represented. He felt that economy was not to be had only in the generation of electricity. There were many other economies to be found, and he hoped it was part of the functions of that Association to keep up the pressure. He hoped that the first scheme of the Central Board would set the pace for other areas.

The Lands Improvement Company.
It may be of interest to our readers to know of this Company, which exists for the purpose of assisting owners of land to improve their properties. Advances are made by the Company for such agricultural and general improvements as are sanctioned by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries (which administers the Companys special Acts of Parliament), and include the following:—
The erection and improvements of farm houses and buildings, drainage, water supply, afforestation, electric light and power.
Those who would like further information of the activities of this Company should write to the Secretary, Miss M. B. Barry, 58, Victoria Street, S.W.1.

transcription:
204 The Electrical Age

Europe was to create a network of high tension electric transmission lines from one country to another; just as they had seen a great network of international railways connecting the centres of consumption with the centres of production and the centres of production with centres of raw materials, as they were going to see electrical transmissions connecting the centres for the economic production of power with the places which required that power. In those circumstances were they dreaming when they said that electricity must dominate the discussions in the future of questions of international tariffs and trade? If they were to maintain their industrial supremacy they must take steps to bring themselves into line with what others were doing, and he ventured to say the first great step had been taken, and they had in one of their guests, Sir Andrew Duncan, the Chairman of the new Central Board. That Board was charged with the duty of scientifically co-ordinating the sources of supply in this country, and above all its duty was to give them a cheap supply of electricity. No greater help could be given to the electrical industry than to increase the domestic load, and the more the Electrical Association for Women could do to make people clamour for electricity the more they would be helping their neighbours and the more they would be doing to improve the conditions in many a dismal home.

Dame Henrietta Barnett responded to the toast, and recalled the work she and Canon Barnett had done amongst the workers in Whitechapel and the Hampstead Garden Suburb in providing better homes for the people.
It was just over twenty years ago that she cut the first sod of the Hampstead Garden Suburb, in which there now lived 12,000 people of all classes.
When overlooking East London and seeing its long, dreary streets, its crowded tenements, its congested population, the thing that claimed her admiration was not the devoted philanthropist, or the overburdened clergy, but the working woman, who, loved by her children, slaves and plans and prays to be able to be home maker. Above the chimney pots also stands, a spiritual force, but too often physically broken by labour. It is to her relief that this Association will come, bringing in its kind hands appliances to ease her household tasks and leave her time, strength and courage to face her childrens problems, to consider their education and guide their tendencies.
Silently, electricity will come to her aid, and then the classes that already have the privilege of greater knowledge and a wider outlook must see to it that the working woman is supplied with opportunities for acquiring knowledge.

Lady Snell gave the toast of "Our Guests," who, she said, were many and distinguished, and included representatives of the Professional Institutions, various Government Departments and the Electrical Industry.
One guest she must make special reference to, Sir Andrew Duncan. They welcomed him as the Chairman of the Central Electricity Board, which was the latest addition to the family. "I believe," continued Lady Snell, "is to be the general opinion in the Electrical Industry that the Minister of

Transports choice of Sir Andrew has been particularly happy and auspicious. I know that is most emphatically my husbands opinion, and I would like to quote, if I may, from the letter he wrote to our Director when much to his regret he felt compelled by reason of his present very heavy duties to decline our invitation to this luncheon. After referring to the schemes for the whole country which are being designed and prepared by himself and his brother Commissioners, he goes on to say: It will be for Sir Andrew Duncan and his colleagues on the Central Electricity Board to carry out the executive work in connection with these schemes. A very onerous task, in which the Commissioners hope the whole Electrical Industry will give the Board very material assistance and thus enable to be put into the highest state of efficiency a great Industry, which can and will confer much benefit upon the people of this country."

Sir Andrew Duncan said that in coming to the luncheon he had a private and unofficial undertaking that he was to be allowed to remain a silent observer of the proceedings, and he believed Lady Snell took the view that this understanding would not be breached, for she ascribed to the popular belief that Scotsmen had such vast experience in receiving hospitality that they were able at any moment to return thanks for it. All he would say was that he advised them not to build their hopes quite so high as Sir Philip Nash had recommended them to do. The new baby was only two months old, but he hoped when it was slightly older it would meet with success. He knew they would be patient, and in the meantime, until they got under weigh, there was no reason why attention should not be directed to organisations such as Sir Philip Nash represented. He felt that economy was not to be had only in the generation of electricity. There were many other economies to be found, and he hoped it was part of the functions of that Association to keep up the pressure. He hoped that the first scheme of the Central Board would set the pace for other areas.

THE ELECTRICAL AGE
FOR WOMEN
The Official Journal of the Electrical Association for Women—Issued Quarterly.
Editor—Miss C. HASLETT, Palace Place, Kensington Court, London, W.8.
Vol. I. OCTOBER, 1927. No. 6
It will be a glad day for Scotland when next year the supply of electric power comes to our hills and dales on Tweedside.
We women want to get an intelligent knowledge and an understanding of our new luxury.
To all rural communities throughout the country I would say, "If you want Electric Light in your homes investigate the availability of water or coal supply in your district—explore the advantages that could accrue to you and your neighbourhood should Electricity become available, and preach always the gospel of cheap Electric current and the wisdom of combined demands for it."
THE VISCOUNTESS ELIBANK.
Ermine Elibank

transcription:
EDITORIAL.
ELECTRICAL DEVELOPMENT IN RURAL AREAS.
This is the title of a very interesting and useful Memorandum which has just been issued by the Electricity Commissioners, with a view to making more widely known the principal considerations which govern the successful commercial development of rural places, and of enlisting the co-operation of all who are in a position to assist in facilitating such development.
If the people of our countryside are to enjoy the same amenities as the town dwellers, it is to the advantage of all to encourage the Suppliers of electric power to run their power lines or cables liberally across the countryside.
The Suppliers of electricity are all, whether Municipal or Company, working under Statutory limitations and ample provision is made for the protection of the public against any aggressive or monopolistic attitude on the part of the Undertaking.
As Miss Partridge points out in an article in this issue, where owners of property fail to recognise that way-leaves are required primarily for public utility purposes, and with-holding facilities for way-leaves, this represents a dis-service to the community.
We have heard recently in the Daily Press of one or two unfortunate casualties connected with overhead lines. It is refreshing to learn from the Memorandum issued by the Electricity Commissioners that during the past seven years only six cases have been reported to them of accidents through the breakage of overhead lines or of the posts sup-porting them. In comparison with the large number of road accidents which occur daily in the streets of London, the casualties due to any fault arising from the use of electricity in our daily life, are infinitesimal.
* * *
KENSINGTON COURT.
The new home of the E.A.W., at Kensington Court, will, we hope, open up a new era of usefulness and activity for the Association.
It is fitting that our new home should be on the same site as one of the oldest genera-ting stations in the world, and that one of the veterans of the Electrical Industry should be our landlord and next door neighbour. Colonel Crompton, whose memory is, perhaps, the longest living one in the Electrical Industry, will, we hope, in the near future entertain us with some of the many anecdotes and reminiscences for which he is so widely renowned.
By a curious coincidence, our new telephone number will also have an electrical ring about it—Kelvin 9468.
* * *
E.A.W. AUTUMN ACTIVITIES.
News reaches us from all our Branches of great preparations for lectures and visits during the coming autumn.
In each Branch there pervades an intelligent electrical atmosphere, full of the energy which has a definite mission to fulfil and yet, withal, the enthusiasm and idealism which spurs on to great endeavour.
Not only are these lectures of great educational value in themselves, but the Associa-tion is providing a training ground for many women in public work and service.
Our women are learning to become articulate in their demand for an efficient electric service, and for this the Association is largely responsible.
A great effort is being made to increase membership, and we hope that 1928 will witness an even longer list of Branches and a greatly strengthened membership roll.

transcription:
210 The Electrical Age

these new premises should, if possible,
provide accommodation for a Club Room.
A very attractive offer of suitable
premises has now been secured at Kensing-
ton Court, W.8, which although not quite
so central as the present offices are situated
in a very pleasant and very good shopping
district.
In addition to office accommodation,
provision is being made for a large Club
Room where members may rest, write
letters and meet their friends.
Our Branches and many friends are
making generous offers to furnish the Club
Room, which we hope will be officially
opened some time during October.
In addition to the Club Room a small
room is being set aside as a model electric
kitchen where lectures and demonstrations
will be held from time to time.
The whole place has been wired through-
out for light and heat and will represent
all that is modern in office lighting and
heating.
Many friends in the Electrical Industry
have generously assisted in the wiring and
provision of electrical equipment of the
building. A full list of names of donors
will be given in the next issue of the
Journal.
The history of our new home is particu-
larly interesting, and we are indebted to
Mr. G. S. Britton, Manager, and Mr. G.
E. C. Western, Chief Engineer, of the
Kensington and Knightsbridge Electric
Lighting Company, for the following
information:—
On this site forty years ago, under
a temporary structure, a small steam
generating plant was erected for the
purpose of giving a supply of electricity
for lighting a few houses forming the
adjacent Kensington Court Estate.
The Company responsible for this
early experimental undertaking was
known as the Kensington Court Electric
Light Co., the engineers and contractors
being Messrs. R. E. Crompton & Co.,
which firm was founded by Colonel
Crompton, who will be our next door
neighbour and who has already under-
taken a great interest in our new home.
This initial effort was on a very small
scale, and it is interesting to note the
rate of progress in such early days.
Records show that the supply was com-
menced on January 1st, 1887, and by
October of that year the number of
lights supplied was 360, at the end of
May, 1888, it had risen to 1,440. The
connection of a few additional lamps
was a great event in those times.
Confident in the future of electricity,
however, the Company sought and
obtained consent to extend its area, and
in June, 1888, a larger undertaking, the
present Kensington & Knightsbridge
Electric Lighting Co., Ltd., was formed
to take over the original one and secured
powers to supply electrical energy in the
Kensington and Westminster districts.
The erection of the present building
was commenced in 1889, the equip-
ment consisted of Babcock Water Tube
Boiler, Willans High Speed Engines
coupled to Crompton Dynamos.
The upper premises now occupied by
the E.A.W. were for many years the
Engineering Offices and Test Rooms of
the Company and, consequently, have
witnessed much that has been done in
the advancement of electricity supply.
Later, a second generating station
was established in the Westminster
District at Cheval Place, and until quite
recently the Company’s supply has only
been direct current.
Many changes have necessarily oc-
curred on this site during the progress
of the undertaking. Increasing

Radio in the Home.

By Bernard C. Holding
(Editor of "The Electrician").

Many housewives whose menfolk were
bitten early by the wireless craze, under-
standably took a dislike to the litter of
wires and the various untidy looking pieces
of apparatus which struck a discordant
note amongst the furnishings of the home.
Even now that the litter and incongruity is
no longer essential to the reception of
broadcast programmes, a certain amount
of prejudice still exists in the minds of
house-proud women against the installation
of wireless in their homes. Such progress
has, however, been made in recent months
in the simplification of the receiving
apparatus itself, and in the cabinet and
other receptacles devised to hide "the
works," that complaints of this kind no
longer hold good, and even those ladies who
complain of stained carpets due to spilt
accumulator acid can insure themselves
against further damage of this kind by
installing one of the many battery elimin-
ators which are now available.

Loud speakers, formerly the reverse of
elegant, now take a variety of forms, the
most efficient being the cone type, which
not only occupies less space than the horn
type, but also lends itself admirably to
effective incorporation in attractive cabinets
which would grace any room. In cases
where a utilitarian-looking loud speaker of
the horn type is already in existence, the
artistic housewife can often improve its
appearance by various forms of painting
and decoration which will bring it more in
accord with the other appointments of the
room. For this purpose, gold paint,
certain kinds of transfers and stencils, and
the new types of quick drying cellulose
lacquers offer interesting possibilities.

For those who are absolutely against the
use of any interior wiring in their homes,
and indeed, for those who are not so par-
ticular on this score, the portable wireless
receiving set—which requires no separate
aerial or earth connection, and contains its
own batteries and loud speaker in the same
cabinet—is a piece of apparatus which can

Unnamed: 9: Author of the article discussing overhead lines and rural electrification.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 213
Overhead Lines and Rural Electrical Development.
By Margaret M. Partridge, B.Sc.
Miss Partridge is in her happiest and most graphic vein in dealing with some of the many difficulties attached to the problem of Rural Electrification.
English people, strange to say, still hold two totally opposed views about the electrification of rural districts.
The vast majority believe that the alleviation of rural conditions by a supply of electric power to improve domestic and hygienic conditions is a matter of vital importance to the whole nation. Many also hope that when sources of energy are readily available, rural industries, such as were once wont to be carried on in the home, will be encouraged and revived, and that the dreadful housing problems of the great industrial centres will be solved in the villages and country towns.
Others, near relations of Mr. Ruskin, believe that "Country" means some sort of primeval forest, and that anything which is really useful sounds a discordant note. One dear old lady, in a village we lighted, quite gleefully had her house wired, and then she sent for me and said sadly, "My dear, I have been so silly. I have always lived in towns before and I quite forgot that, of course, one doesnt have electric light in the country. I am afraid I cant use it now I have it in; it wouldnt be the thing."
This is, perhaps, an extreme instance, and few people would express themselves so honestly as my old lady, but there are many who have vague feelings or beliefs very much like this.
Many more have quite emphatic views about the undesirability of overhead electric mains, and talk about their unsightliness and the destruction of rural amenities, and make as much fuss about a line of overhead mains passing through a village as they would if we suggested planting an acre of the black country in the middle of the village green.
True, it must be confessed that there are unsightly electric poles. Speaking as an engineer, Ill allow that I have seen overhead lines whose unsightliness could make me weep, but they have nearly all been erected by unskilled workmen, and more often than not at least half the tears are drawn forth by inattention to engineering principles. On the whole, though, modern practice does not produce the unsightly atrocities which justify the aesthetic grumblers.
In several instances I have known people the most loud in denunciation, who are quite unaware which villages in their neighbourhood have, and which have not, electric mains. Tidy, evenly spaced lines, nearly always pass unnoticed. Only last week a friend stayed with me who was particularly emphatic in her denunciation of "those hideous electric wires," so I took her to two small towns with recent installations and drove very slowly through, pointing out the various characteristic features. At the end I said, "What do you think of the electricity mains there?" and in each case the answer was, "I never noticed there were any," so I drove back again, pointing out the poles—showing how even spacing and careful choice of position—evenly strained wires, and inconspicuous colouring had helped to minimise any jarring notes. Anyway, I won one convert to rural electrification by means of overhead mains, and I hope that she will help to convert her friends and relations.

Unnamed: 9: Member of E.A.W. showing handicraft work done in her studio
transcription:
The Electrical Age 217
merely temporary—either a bird or a fault in someones house, which will have blown his own fuse and cut out the offending section, and he will make one or two efforts to make the line alive again—which would be excessively uncomfortable to anyone touching the wire at the moment.
Overhead electric wires, in company with trees, houses and telegraph wires, serve to make flying more difficult and dangerous, but the Air Ministry cant expect a monopoly of the land, and it is surely up to them now—before it is too late—to peg out their claims to such open spaces as will be needed for the Air Traffic of the future.
Overhead mains cost from one-half to one-third the price of underground, and as it is distribution and transmission of electricity far more than generation which governs the cost, it is quite essential that villages and rural districts should be served overhead. Local governments and local authorities are, I am glad to say, beginning to awake to the advisability of holding out a helping hand to electricity undertakings, but in many districts there is still much room for improvement. One has only to read the Memorandum issued by the Electricity Commissioners in August of this year to realise how village pump squabbles and local government fussiness may tend to hamper and hinder the progress of rural electrical development.
We hope that at no very distant date there will be members of the E.A.W. on the large majority of local councils. There are already several members in Parliament, there are members on the directorate of supply undertakings—not many, but the thin edge of the wedge has been inserted. If we work together with purpose and intelligence we shall soon be in a position to offer well-informed members as candidates for Councillorships in all parts of England. Good luck to the E.A.W., and may that day be quick in coming.

A Handicrafts Exhibition.
A very attractive Exhibition will be held at the Lyceum Club, 138, Piccadilly, S.W.1, on Tuesday and Wednesday, November 29th and 30th, 1927.
Mrs. Francis-Lewis, who is a member of the E.A.W., will be showing the beautiful work done in her studio, and our readers will be able to see the results of Electricity as applied to Handicrafts. This Exhibition will provide a choice of many charming Christmas gifts at all prices, from a shilling to a guinea, and Mrs. Francis-Lewis will be pleased to forward tickets and further particulars; application should be made to her at The Studio, 18, Soho Square, London, W.1.

218 The Electrical Age

* Ultra Violet Rays and Health.

" Natural Sunlight, not always being readily available, science has stepped in and provided apparatus which produces the Ultra-Violet Rays . . . ."
