A Cookery Page.
Conducted by Miss Mary Mackirdy
(Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow).

In the following notes Miss Mackirdy tells us how to cook quickly, easily and cheaply in the Electric Oven.

Economy in the Use of Electricity.
The best possible value at the least possible cost is the desire of most folks, although the attainment may be somewhat difficult; to get this from an Electric Cooker, one must have an intelligent understanding as to the least amount of current or no current required for the satisfactory cooking of food. It is astonishing how much can be cooked in an oven that has only stored up heat after the current has been switched off, provided the oven has been well heated to begin with and there is no direct draught to cool down the stove. I shall try to illustrate this later. The same applies to the modern covered boiling plate, where I have found it possible to keep a stew simmering with the current off for 20 minutes.
There are two outstanding economies not always considered when Electric versus other stoves are being discussed, and these are cleanliness and comfort. There is no soot, no flues to clean, no ash, no blacklead, dust, fumes, smell, grease, matches or paper, pots and pans are no worse to clean than dishes, and walls are not discoloured.

A Dinner all in the Oven.
Roll of Veal.
Two or 3 lbs. veal suitable for rolling, some pieces of thinly cut fat ham or bacon, 1 teacup breadcrumbs, 2 ozs. finely chopped suet, 1 teaspoon chopped parsley, salt, pepper, nutmeg, 1 egg or a little milk. Have the veal boned; mix all the other ingredients, adding enough egg or milk to bind them. Lay thin strips of ham on the veal then the forcemeat, roll and tie.
Put on tin and cover with a thickly greased paper.
Put into a quick oven at first then reduce heat and cook for about 1 1/2 hours. Serve with gravy, baked tomatoes or other vegetables, and if desired, rolls of bacon.
Oven.
Meantime, put oven switch to full and heat for 20 or 30 minutes or till 350 degrees.
While the oven is heating prepare the sweet.
Lemon Pie.
This is a delightful sweet, and is good either hot or cold; it should be baked quickly, so put in oven with the veal.

The Electrical Age 223

A Page for Girl Guides.
Electricity.

As Miss Partridge is writing on a very grown-up subject this time, we are reprinting on this page the winning Essay in connection with the recent visit of over 60 London Secondary School Girls and their Mistresses to the Hackney Power Station. Mr. Robinson, the Engineer, offered three prizes, and Miss Hilda Taylors article, entitled "Electricity," won the first prize. All the Essays were of a very high order.—Ed. E.A.

By Hilda Taylor
(Godolphin and Latymer Girls School).

On June 9th, our party, consisting of one mistress and six girls, left school at 1.30 and proceeded by train and tram to Hackney Electricity Show Rooms. Here we were made welcome and entertained until a charabane arrived to take us to the electricity works. We were shown round the "Electric House," an ideal home, such as we all long to possess. The dining room was fitted with an artistic and ingenious lamp, which could be switched on so as to illuminate the table or the ceiling, giving a soft, diffused light all over the room.
The bedroom was furnished with wired furniture, the dressing table fitted with wavers and comb and a hair drier, which supplied hot or cold air. The bed had a switch in the head panel, from which the lighting of the room could be controlled: one switch controlled a radiator under the bed, and another an electric bed warmer.
The kitchen contained an electric cooker and a geyser, which gave a constant supply of hot water just below 100° C. When the current was switched on, the water was heated by means of coils. When the temperature was about 94° the current was automatically switched off by means of a thermostat. The coils were heavily lagged to prevent loss of heat. As the temperature gradually fell, a point was reached at which the current was automatically switched on again, and thus the water was kept hot. The bathroom was supplied with a similar geyser.
From the Showrooms, we were taken by charabane to the "Electricity Works." The first place we visited was the least pleasant, for there they were sorting household rubbish and removing all the incombustible things, such a fruit tins, trays, and metal goods of all descriptions. These were taken away, and the tin removed to make tin-foil. The iron parts were then compressed and sold to other concerns. The combustible parts of the rubbish were then burnt as fuel under steam boilers.
From there we were taken to the river bank, where water was being drawn into the cooling pipes by great pumps. The water was first passed through a slowly revolving sieve, which removed from it all rubbish which would spoil or choke the machinery. After passing through this sieve, the water was chlorinated, to kill all sorts of fish or living organisms that might have escaped the first cleansing. This water then condenses the steam that escapes from the turbines and which passes through a condenser, consisting of long lengths of tube immersed in water. The river water heated in this way is poured back into the river higher up the course.

transcription:
The Electrical Age

225

If the district supplied is at all large, as is the case at Hackney, the supply far off would not be as great as that in the immediate neighbourhood. The electricity is therefore sent at high pressure to relay stations, from where it is sent at low pressure to the surrounding districts. The relay stations that we saw contained transformers to reduce the pressure of the current sent to them from the power station and relay it to the public. When more electricity is needed, the engineer has only to set another transformer going.

USES OF ELECTRICITY.
The electricity supplied to our houses can be used in all manner of ways. Besides being convenient, it is safe and clean. There is no smell, no smoke, and no open flames. The only risk is that too much current may pass and the wires may get very hot. This is provided for by fuses. These are pieces of wire, often tin, which have low melting points, so that if the wires should get hot the fuse melts before a dangerous temperature is reached.
Electricity can be used for all heating purposes. Radiators, geysers, ovens and boilers are all simply enough worked by electricity. Besides producing heat, electricity is used indirectly to produce cold. In the Kelvinator refrigerators there is an electric motor. This is used to compress a gas such as sulphur dioxide or ammonia, which can be liquefied by pressure alone. The liquefied gas passes through a coil of tubing immersed in brine, which is contained in a tank containing a recess into which trays of water, divided by a lattice of metal strips, are placed. The liquid gas takes heat from the brine as it expands, and lowers its temperature. The freezing point of brine is below that of water, so that the brine remains liquid while the water freezes. The current is automatically controlled by a thermostat, which switches off the current when the water has frozen, that is, when the temperature is at 40° F., but as soon as the temperature has risen to 45° C., the current is switched on again, and the work of compression and cooling goes on again until the temperature is at 40° F. The temperature of the inside of the refrigerator is thus kept within narrow limits as long as the current is switched on.

▣ ▣ ▣

Training in Electrical Housecraft.
As a result of the number of Conferences between the Headmistresses Committee of the Ministry of Labour and Miss Haslett, Director of the E.A.W., a new course in Electrical Housecraft will be commenced at the Chelsea Polytechnic and the Battersea Polytechnic in the near future.
The training will include the usual course in domestic science, together with a series of lectures on simple electrical knowledge.
This course will, we hope, provide a training for girls who wish to enter the Electrical Industry in connection with the Development of the Domestic Uses of Electricity. The Electrical Association for Women will, as far as possible, in the future keep a register of trained women, so that supply engineers and manufacturers may communicate with the Association as and when they have a vacancy on their staff.
The training will commence first at Chelsea Polytechnic, and full particulars may be obtained from Miss Kempson, Domestic Science Department, Chelsea Polytechnic.
The course at Battersea Polytechnic will be under the supervision of Miss Masters.

226 The Electrical Age

West Ham Electricity Service.
Its Schemes for Assisted Wiring—Hiring of Electric Cookers and other Apparatus.

By Councillor Mrs. Gregory, West Ham
(Member of the E.A.W. Council).

Having only been a member of the West Ham Council since 1923 and a member of its Electric Lighting and Tramways Committee for the past two years, I am not in a position to tell your readers much about the history of the West Ham Electricity Undertaking before I was elected to my present position, but thanks to the courtesy of Mr. F. W. Purse, the Engineer and Manager of the Electricity Department, who has supplied me with the necessary data about it. I am enabled to give my fellow members of the Association the following interesting particulars about this great and progressive service of which the Council is so justly proud.
I was very glad to be elected a member of the Electricity Committee, because, knowing the tremendous advantages of electricity in my own home, I am most anxious that the time will soon arrive when it will be in the home of every working woman as a matter of course, and I naturally think the Electricity Committee the place to stress this point of view.
I am glad to say in West Ham we are quite progressive in this respect, and the use of electricity for domestic purposes is increasing very rapidly.
A FEW FACTS AND FIGURES ABOUT THE WEST HAM ELECTRIC SERVICE.
It was toward the end of the year 1896 that the initial plans were drawn up and the necessary plant ordered for providing a public supply of electricity in the Borough of West Ham.
The first switching on to consumers premises took place on December 11th, 1898, from the Generating Station at Abbey Mills, Stratford, which was the original source of supply for the whole borough. The generating section of the Undertaking was, however, transferred in 1904 to the present station on the River Lea at Canning Town, where, from time to time, considerable extensions to both plant and buildings have taken place.
The total supply arranged for at the beginning only amounted to the equivalent of 15,000—8 c.p. lamps in use at one time, the merest fraction of the supply available to-day for lighting purposes alone.
For some time past, the principal power and lighting needs of the borough have been dependent on the Councils Electricity Service; whilst for heating, cooking, ironing and many other domestic purposes, the demand for a supply is rapidly and daily on the increase.
Just one contrast of figures is here given to illustrate the extraordinary expansion that has taken place in the electricity output of West Ham.
1900 Units sold (for all purposes) ... 572,793
1927 Units sold (for all purposes) ... 74,097,934
an increase of 12,836 per cent.
As a Councillor I would take this opportunity of reminding my fellow citizens that as this great Undertaking is owned and controlled by the burgesses of West Ham, it is their duty, and in their own interest, to support it in every possible way; as it is also the duty of every woman who uses electricity to carry on the propaganda work for the benefit of the community.

transcription:
230    The Electrical Age

Useful Hints for the Home-Maker.
By "ELECTRA."

" ELECTRA " will be pleased to give information regarding any electrical apparatus
mentioned in the Journal. She has had practical experience herself in the use of
domestic electrical appliances and will be pleased to place her experience at the disposal
of our readers. In writing to her at Head Office of the E.A.W., kindly enclose
stamped addressed envelope.

A NOTE ON LAMPS.
We are very delighted to note a decrease
in the price of many of the Standard or
E.L.M.A. Lamps, and we are sure our
readers will be equally pleased; but it will
still be said that some other makes are
cheaper. The reasons are not far to seek.
All lamps made according to British
Standard, have a guaranteed life of about

MAZDA LAMP FACTORY.

1,000 hours, and the consumption of elec-
tricity is also certified. If you buy a 40 w.
or 100 w. lamp, you are sure the lamp uses
only 40 w. or 100 w., with a very narrow
margin. Much careful and expensive
research has been necessary in order to
attain this high standard, and the manu-
facturers are not even now resting on their
laurels, but are working to improve still
further the life and the efficiency of the
lamps.

Other lamps are often marked a certain
wattage, and when tested are found to burn
considerably more. The duration of the
lamp, too, is a matter of conjecture, and
thus the saving of a few pence proves a
costly proceeding in the end. In lamps, as
with other commodities, Quality stands for
Economy. If any of our readers would like
to know more about their lamps and their
cost compared with the amount of electric-
ity consumed, they will find much to inter-
est them in a leaflet, E.D.A.664, issued by
the British Electrical Development Associa-
tion, 15, Savoy Street, Strand, London,
W.C.2, who will be pleased to forward a
copy on request. Will you kindly mention
"The Electrical Age " when writing?

A PIANO HEATER.
This is something really new among elec-
tric gadgets, and will prove a boon to our

"INVENTUM" PIANO HEATER.

pianos during the damp weather, especially
in rooms not used daily and in new houses.

Unnamed: 9: Author of the article describing a visit to power station.
transcription:
The Electrical Age

233

Visit of the
International Electro-Technical Commission to the
Hydro-Electric Power Station of Mese.

By Mrs. Walter Lawson.

On September 9th, a party of about 300
people from all over the world set out from
Bellagio, where the Commission is being
held, on a three-hours journey by boat and
train to Chiavenna, north of Lake Como, to
visit the biggest Hydro-Electric Power
Station in Italy, which has only been
opened within the last month.
All the inhabitants stood in the sunshine
at their doorways in the sleepy village of
Colico to watch the party walk from the
boat to the train, which completed the
journey to Chiavenna. Certainly no such
crowd of foreigners had ever before pene-
trated to this remote corner of Europe.
Like all the villages in Italy, electricity
is supplied to the residents and shop-
keepers, there being full evidence of this
from the overhead wires which criss-crossed
the streets at frequent intervals.
The Hydro-Electric Power Station of
Mese was constructed to utilize the water
power of Liro, a tributary of the River
Mera, which flows into Lake Como.
The plant supplies electric power at
130,000 volts pressure to Turin, Bologna,
Milan and other places.
The generators work at 8,000 volts, which
are transformed to the higher pressure.
The Liro is a mountain torrent, conse-
quently the pressure of water coming from
a great height is tremendous. A special
type of turbine, which is made in Milan.
and called the Pelton Turbine, is employed
to withstand the force of the water.
This water-wheel is entirely different
from those used at Augst, on the Rhine,
the latter being the shape of a marguerite
with tilted petals, suitable for dealing with
the water in shallow rivers or lakes, where
the pressure of water is much lower.
On the contrary, the Pelton wheel has
a double row of cup-like paddles, or
buckets, which revolve with the force of
two jets of water which pour into them.
The force of the water is regulated by a
machine brake, and is conducted to the
turbine through a very thin corrugated steel
pipe, reinforced by three layers of thick
steel wire, wound like cotton on a reel.
The buildings of this power station are
palatial, the architecture being most artis-
tic, harmonising with the old church and
the houses of the village and the glorious
amphitheatre in which it is set. The
interior is paved with mosaic, the lower
part of the walls consisting of slabs of
Verona marble, golden brown in colour, the
higher portion of the wall being cream
washed, surmounted by a pale yellow
frieze, which camouflages the iron girders
which act as rails for the overhead crane.
All the corners of the interior are slightly
rounded, to facilitate cleaning, cleanliness
being essential where electricity is generat-
ing at high tension, because if particles of
dust penetrated the generators sparking
might ensue, and would wear out the
machinery very quickly.
We were told that the additional cost of
all the beautiful decoration was only 2 per
cent. of the whole expense, and was of dis-
tinct commercial value in impressing
capitalists with the dignity and importance
of electrical undertakings and causing the
workpeople to take a pride in their work.
We were entertained to lunch by the
Società Generale Italiana Edison di Elet-
tricità in a part of the station which was
temporarily partitioned off from the plant
and decorated with the flags of all nations.
After lunch, we left for the station of
Chiavenna in cars, amidst the cheers of the
station staff.

The Electrical Age 235
Electric Communal Laundries.
The Womens Co-operative Guild, which has always shown a very active interest in electrical labour-saving appliances, has recently taken part in an international discussion at Stockholm on "The Family Wash."
A report has been prepared on this subject by housewives from Great Britain, Germany, Sweden and many other countries, the principal object being to find a solution for the dismal wash day, which is one of the black spots in the life of the working housewife.
National Electric Week.
The British Electrical Development Association, which so successfully organised last year the W.O.B. Campaign, has this year initiated an even larger and more ambitious scheme in order to help bring before the public the many advantages of electricity in the home.
In addition to the arrangement for lectures, local luncheons and electric demonstration house, there is to be a
By courtesy of the I.M.E.A.
A GROUP OF E.A.W. MEMBERS AT THE BUXTON CONVENTION.
Reading from left to right
COUNCILLOR MRS. GREGORY, MISS C. HASLETT, MISS A. A. STUMP, MRS. RYCROFT, MRS. LAMB.
A solution which was put forward by Mrs. Webster, the President of the English Guild, and was endorsed by women from many other countries was the desirability of arranging a communal wash-house which would be equipped electrically. Such wash-houses would be attached to blocks of buildings for the common use of the tenants.
This seems a very commonsense solution and one which the members of the E.A.W. would do well to study, if electricity is really to be the servant of the working woman.
National Electric Week from December 3rd to 10th, 1927.
In all parts of the country all kinds of electrical activities will be taking place during this week, and we hope that members of the E.A.W. will lend their assistance in this splendid movement.
Further particulars can be obtained from Mr. J. W. Beauchamp, Director, E.D.A., 15, Savoy Street, Strand, W.C.2.

Electric Communal Laundries.
The Womens Co-operative Guild, which has always shown a very active interest in electrical labour-saving appliances, has recently taken part in an international discussion at Stockholm on "The Family Wash."
A report has been prepared on this subject by housewives from Great Britain, Germany, Sweden and many other countries, the principal object being to find a solution for the dismal wash day, which is one of the black spots in the life of the working housewife.
National Electric Week.
The British Electrical Development Association, which so successfully organised last year the W.O.B. Campaign, has this year initiated an even larger and more ambitious scheme in order to help bring before the public the many advantages of electricity in the home.
In addition to the arrangement for lectures, local luncheons and electric demonstration house, there is to be a

Unnamed: 9: Hon. Secretary of the E.A.W. North East Coast Branch.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 237

E.A.W. Branch Activities.

North East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm, Dial House, Northumberland Street, Newcastle-on-Tyne.

The North-East Coast Branch turned up in good force at the visit to the Carville Power Station, by kind invitation of the Newcastle Electric Supply Co. Mr. J. Cusworth, head of the Power Station Organisation, conducted the party round the houses, and cheerfully undertook to answer all questions that were not too technical for him! The members were keenly interested in picking out their own district sub-stations on the wonderful diagram of the whole N.E.S. Co.s system of over 1,000 square miles, which they saw in the control room. Before leaving, members were kindly entertained to coffee, and it was much appreciated.
On July 9th, at the invitation of Mrs. Osbaldiston-Mitford, one of its Vice-Presidents, members of the North-East Coast Branch of the Electrical Association for Women paid a visit to the beautiful grounds of Mitford Hall. An unaccustomed sun shone brightly and appropriately, for, in addition to the attractions of ruined Castle and Manor House and old-world gardens, a large audience had the privilege of listening to Dr. Saleeby, the eminent lecturer, who gave a most interesting address on "Sunlight and Health." The marvellous effect of sunlight treatment on tuberculosis and other diseases was shown in a series of slides, and through the kindness of the Newcastle Electric Supply Co. who had fitted up one of the newest types of Violet Ray lamps, Dr. Saleeby was also able to demonstrate the value of artificial sunlight in a country like England, where the real article is so elusive.
Our programme for the coming session is now complete, and a visit to the British Broadcasting Co.s Station at Newcastle-on-Tyne is arranged for Saturday, September 17th.
In October there will be a Reception by the Lady Mayoress of Newcastle-on-Tyne, at the Lighting Service Bureau, Dial House, Northumberland Street, and during the following months we are to have conferences on "Electricity in the Home," "Electrical Apparatus—Its Use and Misuse," "Electricity, the Doctors Aid to Health," and "The Decorative Value of Electric Light," by such well-known people as Mr. Geo. S. Francis, Mr. J. R. W. Rae, Dr. Christina Barrowman, and Mr. G. S. Evans.
We should be pleased to send particulars of our programme to anyone interested.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy, 251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

While there were no visits and lectures during the summer, we have been very busy arranging our programme for the autumn and winter session.
Our first meeting is a visit to the Housing Exhibition at Kelvin Hall, and then there are regular fixtures until April of next year.
The programme includes visits to the Lighting Service Bureau, the Clyde Valley Electric Power Co.s new showrooms, the Paisley Royal Alexandra Infirmary X-Ray Dept., and the Dalmarnock Generating Station. Lectures will be given on such varied subjects as the "History of the Sewing Machine," "Electric Cookery," and "House-wiring, Switches, Fuses, Plugs, etc."
The social side is being catered for by a luncheon, a whist drive, and a dinner-dance, and so the coming session promises to be a very full and interesting one.

* * *

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. I. Hayes, 1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.

The Birmingham and District Branch, after two meetings, closed down until September. These two were held in June. The first was an inaugural meeting for the West Bromwich District. This was a splendid meeting and new members were enrolled—including Her Worship the Mayor. Mr. Francis, of the Electrical Development Association, gave a very interesting lecture on "Electricity and Domestic Efficiency" to a most appreciative audience, and this was followed by many questions and much discussion; and many were the problems discussed over the very welcome cup of tea, which was kindly provided by the West Bromwich Electricity Committee.
The second meeting—our Summer Outing—took place on June 30th. This was a visit by omnibus from Birmingham to the new Stourport Power Station, and the Electrification of the Rural Areas was pointed out en route. In spite of the pouring rain, 70 members took part in this visit—hoping for the best. They were not

disappointed, for after the rain had continued to pour for another half hour the clouds rolled away, the sun shone and everyone was smiling and happy when they arrived at the Power Station. This is one of the latest super-Stations—on a river—and has all the very latest equipment and machinery. Truly a very fine station. After touring the station all members were assembled on the steps of the main entrance and a photograph was taken, which turned out to be a very good one indeed. Every member thoroughly enjoyed this visit, especially the welcome cup of tea which was kindly provided by the Shropshire, Worcestershire, and Staffordshire Electric Power Company. The visit concluded with a drive home in open cars, in beautiful sunshine, through charming scenery, and all marvelled at the small cottages en route which were enjoying the comforts of electricity, owing to the energy and enterprise of their Power Company. A.L.H.

*  *  *

Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Stemp, 1, York Terrace, St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.

At the concluding meeting of last seasons programme the attendance was beyond our expectations.
The lecture demonstration, "Simple Faults and Where to Find Them," attracted most of our members, and is a sign of their keenness to understand and obtain knowledge of the emergency repairs which might at any time be required for the electrical appliances in their homes.
Mr. W. J. Bache (Borough Electrical Engineer) had had constructed a miniature house, where the entrance of the main cable was shown, followed by the rest of the wiring and various accessories all complete. This lecture demonstration greatly enlightened many of the members present, and we hope that Mr. Bache will give us another lecture of a similar nature at some future date.
We are now looking forward to October 4th, when Mr. G. S. Francis, of the Electrical Development Association, has promised to give us a lecture on "The Domestic Applications of Electricity."
A visit to the Cheltenham Automatic Telephone Exchange has been arranged for November, also a lecture demonstration on "Domestic Electrical Appliances."
Early in December we are to have a demonstration of "Cooking by Electricity."
Our membership is increasing, but, like Oliver Twist, "we want more." A.A.S.

We regret to learn, as we go to Press, of the sad death of Mr. Charles Marshall, of Cheltenham.
Mr. Marshall was a well-known engineer, and he took a great interest in all matters social and educational.
Mrs. Marshall is a Vice-President of the Cheltenham Branch of the E.A.W., and she and Mr. Marshall have taken a keen personal interest in their Branch.
We should like to express our deepest sympathy with Mrs. Marshall and her family in their sad bereavement.—(Editor, E.A.)

transcription:
The Electrical Age 241
enrolled a few more members, who are eagerly
looking forward to our coming session.
The last two fixtures on our Spring Syllabus
were very popular, one being a Clean Milk
Demonstration, given by Miss V. D. Harrison
(organised by the Director of Agriculture) at the
farm of Mr. G. H. Merrett, Cyncoed, Nr. Cardiff,
on June 16th.
The last fixture for the session was a visit to
the South Wales Electrical Power Distribution
Companys Power Station at Upper Boat, on
Wednesday, June 28th, when over 50 members
met together. They were escorted in groups of
ten over the Power Station by members of the
Power Station Staff (under instruction of Mr. R.
Roper, Resident Engineer), after which Mr. W.
A. Chamen, General Manager, and Mrs. Chamen
kindly entertained all to tea. Mr. C. T. Allan,
Assistant Manager, was also present. A brief
address was given by Mrs. C. T. Allan, Chairman
of the Committee of the South Wales and Mon-
mouthshire Branch, in which she appealed to the
members present to get keen about enrolling new
members. She also advised them to take our
Journal, "The Electrical Age," and so gain some
helpful knowledge. A very happy afternoon
ended with a hearty vote of thanks to Mr.
Chamen and the Power Station Staff.
Our autumn programme promises to be almost
overwhelming with its store of "good things to
come," as we have been fortunate enough to
secure the promise of a lecture from such well-
known celebrities as Miss M. Partridge, Mr. J.
W. Beauchamp, E.D.A., Mr. W. E. Bush,
E.L.M.A., a visit to Messrs. Chivers Vinegar
and Pickle Factory, Cookery Lectures and
Demonstration, etc. We are also arranging a
visit to a gathering of the Newport Womens
Citizens Association, Newport, Mon., where we
hope to sow seed for a go-ahead Sub-Section.
A very special event was the Garden Party
held at Melrose Hall, St. Mellons, by the very
kind invitation of Mr. and Mrs. G. Fairfield, to
raise funds for the E.A.W. Headquarters Club
Room.
Melrose Hall is a most interesting house, having
been converted from an old monastery, and the
grounds are delightful.
A Bridge Drive was arranged, and prizes were
kindly given by Mr. W. Hobbs (District Manager
of the General Electric Co., Ltd.) and Mrs.
Morley New, and there were, besides, tennis,
croquet, badminton and clock golf matches.
There was a large number present, and a most
enjoyable afternoon was spent. Everyone appre-
ciated the kind hospitality of our host and
hostess, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded
Mr. and Mrs. Fairfield, proposed by Mrs. C. T.
Allan, and seconded by Mrs. L. A. Snow. J.T.

Unnamed: 9: Assistant Manager present during the visit to the power station.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 241
enrolled a few more members, who are eagerly
looking forward to our coming session.
The last two fixtures on our Spring Syllabus
were very popular, one being a Clean Milk
Demonstration, given by Miss V. D. Harrison
(organised by the Director of Agriculture) at the
farm of Mr. G. H. Merrett, Cyncoed, Nr. Cardiff,
on June 16th.
The last fixture for the session was a visit to
the South Wales Electrical Power Distribution
Companys Power Station at Upper Boat, on
Wednesday, June 28th, when over 50 members
met together. They were escorted in groups of
ten over the Power Station by members of the
Power Station Staff (under instruction of Mr. R.
Roper, Resident Engineer), after which Mr. W.
A. Chamen, General Manager, and Mrs. Chamen
kindly entertained all to tea. Mr. C. T. Allan,
Assistant Manager, was also present. A brief
address was given by Mrs. C. T. Allan, Chairman
of the Committee of the South Wales and Mon-
mouthshire Branch, in which she appealed to the
members present to get keen about enrolling new
members. She also advised them to take our
Journal, "The Electrical Age," and so gain some
helpful knowledge. A very happy afternoon
ended with a hearty vote of thanks to Mr.
Chamen and the Power Station Staff.
Our autumn programme promises to be almost
overwhelming with its store of "good things to
come," as we have been fortunate enough to
secure the promise of a lecture from such well-
known celebrities as Miss M. Partridge, Mr. J.
W. Beauchamp, E.D.A., Mr. W. E. Bush,
E.L.M.A., a visit to Messrs. Chivers Vinegar
and Pickle Factory, Cookery Lectures and
Demonstration, etc. We are also arranging a
visit to a gathering of the Newport Womens
Citizens Association, Newport, Mon., where we
hope to sow seed for a go-ahead Sub-Section.
A very special event was the Garden Party
held at Melrose Hall, St. Mellons, by the very
kind invitation of Mr. and Mrs. G. Fairfield, to
raise funds for the E.A.W. Headquarters Club
Room.
Melrose Hall is a most interesting house, having
been converted from an old monastery, and the
grounds are delightful.
A Bridge Drive was arranged, and prizes were
kindly given by Mr. W. Hobbs (District Manager
of the General Electric Co., Ltd.) and Mrs.
Morley New, and there were, besides, tennis,
croquet, badminton and clock golf matches.
There was a large number present, and a most
enjoyable afternoon was spent. Everyone appre-
ciated the kind hospitality of our host and
hostess, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded
Mr. and Mrs. Fairfield, proposed by Mrs. C. T.
Allan, and seconded by Mrs. L. A. Snow. J.T.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 243

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. Harcourt Williams,
"Woodville," Ack Lane, Bramhall, Manchester.

Mrs. Harcourt Williams has kindly undertaken the duties of Hon. Secretary in succession to Miss G. Entwistle, and in consultation with the Committee is well on with the winter programme.
Although the Committee has met several times since the last report, only one open meeting has been held, when members of the Manchester Branch were invited to see her all-electric house, by the kind invitation of our Chairman, Mrs. Lamb.
On that delightful afternoon it was difficult to say which we enjoyed more—the house with its marvellous electrical fittings, planned with such care and judgment, or the beautiful garden with its shady paths, exquisite rose garden and wide lawn, where Mrs. Lamb added to our deep sense of gratitude by providing tea. No other meetings will be held until the winter activities begin in October.
D.M.P.

Since receiving the above Notes, we have heard of the following interesting fixture, which we have pleasure in announcing:—

Programme for Manchester Conference.
Thursday, October 13th, 1927.

10.30 a.m. Lecture—" Electricity, the Hand-maiden in the Home," by Dr. Christine Barrowman. Followed by an address by Mr. J. W. Beauchamp (Director of the Electrical Development Association). To be given at The Lighting Service Bureau, 4, Fountain Street, Manchester.

1.15 p.m. A Luncheon at the Midland Hotel, Manchester. The Rt. Hon. The Lord Mayor (Alderman J. H. Swales), accompanied by The Lady Mayoress, will preside, and the Mayor and Mayoress of Salford, Dr. R. Veitch Clark, Miss Ellen Wilkinson, M.P., Mr. J. W. Beauchamp, Mrs. Eliott Lynn, will also be present.

2.30 p.m. Invitation to Lady Members and Friends to visit Messrs. Ferrantis Works, Hollinwood. Transport will be provided for which there will be a charge.
Mrs. Harcourt Williams, " Woodville,"
Ack Lane, Bramhall. Tele.: Bramhall 264.

transcription:
244

The Electrical Age

Electrical Enterprise !

Our readers will be interested to hear of a practical attempt to bring the service of electricity to a number of small towns on the East Coast. Electrical Enterprise, Ltd., is a new Company which has just been registered, the Directors of which are Dr. John Purves, Mrs. L. A. Willson, Mr. Alan Johnston, Miss Margaret Partridge, Miss C. Haslett, and Mr. Houblon. We cannot do better than reprint the objects of the Company:—
" It is now generally understood that the scope of the scheme initiated by the Government under the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1926, provides for the co-ordination and encouragement of Bulk Supplies, the distribution or retailing being largely left to private enterprise. The Directors, realising this, and appreciating the fact that development of Electricity Supply in rural districts and small towns of up to 15,000 population has been very slow in the past, owing to the difficulty of making such investments attractive and marketable, believe that there is a considerable field for the acquisition of Distributing Powers in such districts and for the retailing of electrical energy when Bulk Supplies are available. In districts where Bulk Supplies are not yet available, it is proposed to establish generating stations—where possible in conjunction with existing gas undertakings—designed to give a supply, which stations can readily be changed over if and when supplies in Bulk can be obtained on reasonable terms. This will meet a need that is daily becoming increasingly insistent, as the benefits of such supplies for the improvement of domestic and hygienic conditions are more and more realised."
The Directors hope to provide openings for women in the business of electricity supply, and by that means to encourage women to enter a calling which is most important from the point of view of public service, and is essentially one of equal interest to men and women. They feel that the services of women will be particularly valuable in introducing to rural homes the benefits to be derived from these modern services. They also believe that, if sources of energy can be made readily available, rural industries such as used to be carried out in the home will be encouraged and revived."
Any readers who may be interested in this enterprise should write for a copy of the Prospectus to Miss R. Haslett, 13, Victoria Street, Westminster, S.W.1.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 249

The Electric Kitchen and Club Room
At 46, Kensington Court, W.8.
By The Editor.

"A dream come true," was how Alderman Mrs. Hammer described the new premises at Kensington Court when Lady Astor formally declared them open on November 14th, 1927.

THE NEW CLUB ROOM.

The old engineering test room and the hard, cold stairway of the sub-station had been converted into a veritable fairy palace. Blue curtains edged with primrose pattern against sun coloured walls and blue-edged carpet on the stairs gave a cheery welcome to the visitors.

Blue tinted woodcuts and paintings by Miss Molly Hickin relieved the hardness of the walls, and the well diffused pink glow from the electric lamps and fittings gave just the right touch of warmth, aided by the merry glow of a variety of electric fires.

An original note was introduced to the proceedings by an electrically

lighted bouquet of shell flowers which was presented to Lady Astor by Miss Dorothy Cramb. This beautiful gift had been designed by Mrs. Francis-Lewis in her electrical handicrafts studio.

Upstairs in the offices, Sun-ray fires spread their warmth and cheeriness in rooms which were perfectly illuminated with no sign of shadow and no glare to irritate the eyes of the worker.

The kitchen presented a fairyland of delight to the home-maker. Here was a washing machine which could also be used to mince meat, clean knives and perform many other useful but uncongenial household tasks. The electric cooker claimed its share of attention, as also did the water heaters, refrigerator and that most useful of all appliances, the suction cleaner. A dainty electric silver grill came in for much admiration,

THE MODEL ELECTRIC KITCHEN.

    With the aid of electricity such a trans-
formation had taken place in this old,
somewhat uncouth, building that our
grandmothers would have declared that
nothing short of a miracle could have
brought it about.
    Visitors from all parts of the country
come to see and learn of this new servant
—Electricity—and its use in kitchen,
office and club room.

* * *

Electricity on the Farm.

By courtesy of Electro Farming
Electric Ploughing, one of the modern uses of
Electricity on the Farm.

    The two schemes which have re-
cently been issued by the Electricity
Commissioners in connection with the
work of the Central Electricity Board
have created great speculation as to
how far and how soon the farmers and
the country folk will begin to get a
supply of electricity, and the lectures
on this subject which have been given
to the E.A.W., one by Mr. Borlase
Matthews in London, on the "Small-
holding," and one on "Rural Elec-
trification," by Mr. S. T. Allen, at
Wolverhampton, have proved of
special interest.
    Mr. Borlase Matthews pointed out
the many and varied uses of electricity
not only on the Smallholding, but
in the larger domain of farming. In
addition to the uses of electricity in
the poultry house and the bee house,
experiments are now being carried out
on the uses of Ultra-Violet Lamps for
the treatment of farm stock.
    Mr. Allen, who has recently visited
several European countries, pointed
out how in these countries they are
solving their unemployment problem
by the revival of rural industries,
which have been made possible by a
supply of electricity in the country
districts.

transcription:
The Electrical Age
251

Fused Quartz or Silica—and Some of its Uses.

In view of the great interest which is being taken in the use of Ultra-Violet Ray Lamps for remedial and other purposes, the part played by fused quartz in the manufacture of Mercury Vapour Lamps will prove of special interest to our readers.

By R. W. Clark, A.M.I.E.E.

One of the most interesting products of the modern electric furnace is fused quartz or silica.
This material possesses unique properties, and is of great value for Scientific, Medical, Industrial, and even household purposes. Silica, or to give it its chemical name, silicon-dioxide, goes to make up more than one-half of the solid crust of the earth, and occurs in an almost pure form in flint and rock crystal. The pebbles of natural rock crystal were used by opticians for making spectacle lenses and such lenses were called pebbles.
In its pure natural state it is hard and crystalline, and requires a very high temperature to melt it.
When mixed with soda, compounds of lead, and other materials, it melts much more easily and is made into the ordinary window and table glass which is in such universal use. Pure natural quartz, either in the form of rock crystal or silica sands, if heated to a sufficiently high temperature, fuses into a glass-like material, which unlike ordinary glass, can be made red hot and quenched in water without damage and will withstand the action of acids. It has also other characteristics which are made use of in optical and industrial applications. Unlike ordinary glass, fused silica cannot be melted to a liquid condition, because if any attempt be made to heat it above the temperature at which it becomes thickly viscous, like toffee, it passes off as a vapour. To melt it even to the viscous condition it is necessary to heat it to a blinding white temperature, from which it cools very rapidly, thus rendering manipulation very much more difficult than is the case with ordinary glass, which can be worked at a dull red heat and cools relatively slowly.
For a long time after it had been discovered that silica could be fused, it was impossible to utilise it commercially, although its valuable properties had been investigated. The difficulty of heating it to a sufficiently high temperature and of working it after actual fusion had been accomplished, appeared to be insurmountable. It was only the advent of the electric furnace that rendered possible the production of articles of commercial size, and even then many manufacturing difficulties had to be overcome before fused silica became available as an article of commerce.
At the present time two varieties of fused silica are available which are quite different in appearance. The first, which looks like ordinary glass of an unusual transparency, is made from rock crystal. The second, having a milky-white appearance, is made from a very pure quality silica sand. If this latter fused material be examined with a lens it is found to consist of a transparent structure interspersed with an enormous number of air bubbles. The shape of the air bubbles, originally spherical, depends on how the material has been worked during the process of manufacture. They may have been flattened, or drawn out into long threads,

Unnamed: 9: Man shown in the process of manufacturing fused quartz material.
transcription:
252 The Electrical Age

and it is upon their form that the appearance, and in some cases the beauty, of the material depends. For instance, when the fused silica has been drawn out into long lengths of tubing it has a satin-like sheen, such as is seen, for the same reason, in toffee when it has been drawn out repeatedly in making confectionery.

Fig. 1.
A Process in the manufacture of Fused Quartz.

a suitable mould and blown out to fill it, just as the inner tube of a bicycle or motor tyre is blown out to fill the outer cover, or it is drawn out into long lengths to form tubing.
Now that the manufacture of fused silica has been touched upon briefly, we will turn to some of its more common every-day uses. Before doing so, the unique characteristics of this material must be borne in mind. They are as follows:— Fused Silica will withstand intense heat without softening, and, unlike other vitreous material, it can be either heated or cooled rapidly without cracking. It is not attacked by acids, and the clear quality is remarkably transparent to rays invisible to the human eye, which lie beyond the red end of the visible spectrum, known as the infra-red rays, and to those

The effects obtained from Electric Light Bowls made of Fused Quartz are extremely beautiful.

The process generally employed in the manufacture of fused silica is to embed a rod of carbon or graphite in the sand and to pass a very heavy current of electricity through it. This raises the rod to a very high temperature and causes the surrounding sand to melt around it into a cylindrical mass. When sufficient sand has been fused the rod is withdrawn and the hollow sausage shaped mass now called a fusion is removed from the furnace. One end is then closed by the simple method of cutting it off, the other is seized with a pair of tongs which, while gripping it, introduces a tubular nozzle, into the hole at the end of the fusion. into which the violet coloured rays merge at the other end of the spectrum, known as the ultra-violet rays.

256    The Electrical Age

Londons Electric Shopping Facilities.

. . . It is an extraordinary fact that apart from the large Stores such as Selfridges and Waring and Gillows, few facilities exist in the great shopping centres of Oxford Street and Piccadilly to acquaint the home-maker with the use of this most wonderful of all modern conveniences. . .

London, the heart of the Empire, with its many and varied attractions and its great shopping centres, still leaves much to be desired in the facilities which it offers to the home-maker to see and learn of the many uses of electricity in our home life, in medicine, in the factory, in the office, on the farm and in innumerable other spheres of our modern life in which this fascinating force is taking so great a part.
It is possible to walk the whole length of Oxford Street and Piccadilly without coming across an electric shop, apart from the large stores such as Selfridges and Waring & Gillows, and one or two shops devoted solely to the sale of lamps and shades.
Certainly, turning off Oxford Street into Newman Street one may wander into the electrically displayed period showrooms of Touchbutton House, where the work of the engineer and the artist have been combined, or a visit may be paid to the showrooms of the British Thomson-Houston Co., where all that is latest in electric lighting and fittings may be seen in choice profusion.
The Strand is becoming associated with "Tricity" attractions and, in addition to the restaurant which has become so famous for its electrically cooked food, there are now provided attractive showrooms where one can see all the various adaptations of the "Tricity" Sun-ray; as someone has aptly described it, "September sunshine that clouds cannot dim."
Kingsway, which is the home of many of our large electrical organisations, always affords something unique electrically, and one may learn from the shop windows all about such questions as electric refrigeration and country house lighting.
A visit to Magnet House and the new showrooms of the General Electric Company is well worth while. Here is seen a wonderful array of electrical domestic apparatus to delight the heart of the home-maker - easier methods of washing
Reading Hour in the "Sun-ray" Nursery in the Strand.
and cleaning, cleaner methods of cooking and better methods of lighting the home. The shop is lighted throughout with the new Pearl Osram Lamp.
A few minutes walk from Kingsway takes one to the Showrooms of L. G. Hawkins and Co., where lovely modern Satsuma ware is displayed. Instead of the hard wooden standard lamp one may have beautiful bowls, hand made and hand decorated, with silk shades of exquisite colourings.
A little farther on in the Charing Cross Road, at the Headquarters of the Metro-

A new electrical restaurant has recently been opened in the City at Ludgate Hill, where attractive displays of electrical apparatus may be seen, for those who use St. Pauls Churchyard as a shopping centre.
Another recent addition to Londons electric shops is the new showrooms of the Westminster Electric Supply Corporation in Victoria Street, which is well worth a visit.
The Boroughs lying immediately outside the heart of the West End are very well served and attractive, and architecturally beautiful showrooms may be seen at such places as Hackney and Battersea.
Many of the electrical contractors are now beginning to open electric shops, but, apart from such pioneers as Troughton & Young and Rawlings Brothers, the West End of London is still very badly in need of such shops.
While we have referred to a few good examples of places in London where the manifold applications of electricity can be studied by the home-maker, prompt and energetic action is needed on the part of the Electrical Industry to ensure that greater and better facilities are offered to the public in the near future.
It should be just as possible for women to get the electric shopping habit as they have, say, the millinery shopping habit!
It would seem, too, that here is scope for the energies of women with artistic ability and some knowledge of electrical methods, to consider the opening up of electrical shops.

The Electrical Age 259
Electric Lighting and Starting Sets on Motor Cars.
By C. Griff
(Chairman Womens Engineering Society).
It is probable that few women motorists realise that, on modern cars, they carry with them what is practically a miniature Electric Light and Power Station. The lighting and starting units are such an important part of a cars mechanism that women owner drivers will be well advised to learn something of the systems.
There are various makes of these sets, with consequent variations in their "lay out," but we will take for example a well-known set for medium powered cars.
We have the engine of the car, the storage battery, the electric motor and dynamo, which can be roughly compared with the Supply Power Station. Then there is the cut-out and fuse box, which corresponds somewhat to the main switch and fuses in our houses; and the wiring and distribution of the current to the lights on different parts of the car, is equivalent to the lighting of the rooms of a house.
We get the current for the electric starter motor from an accumulator (storage battery). On pressing the starter switch the motor rotates and is thrown into gear with a toothed ring on the flywheel of the engine. When the car starts, the starter is thrown automatically out of mesh. The wiring for this is simple: a lead from the position (marked +) terminal of the accumulator goes to the one terminal of the motor, from the other to the starter switch, and from that back to the negative (—) terminal of the battery.
The lighting circuit is more intricate, but as briefly as it is possible to describe it, it follows a pathway thus . . . From the Battery to the Ammeter, which we see on the dashboard. This is a Meter, or register, of the amount of current passing through the circuit, and a means whereby we can tell whether the battery is being charged or discharged. From the Ammeter the current flows along its wire pathway to the switches, which close or open the road to the lamps, from each of which the return is made direct to a connection on the switchbox; from this terminal a single wire is carried back to the negative one on the accumulator. This also takes the return circuit, or in other words, is the backdoor path for the dynamo, cut-out and fuse box circuits, which simplifies the wiring.
The Dynamo, driven usually by belt or chain off the driving or carden shaft of the car, creates the current for charging the accumulator, and is

Until we all become highly skilled elec-
tricians, there are only certain things
which it is wise for the ordinary owner
driver to attend to herself. We will briefly
run through these. All other adjustments
and repairs are best left to the makers of

The BATTERY must be regularly
attended, noting that the acid level is kept
well above the top of the plates; it can
be filled up by adding distilled water, never
tap water. The specific gravity of the acid
as given by the makers of the battery for

meter, which can be purchased at most

use of it. It is most important to measure

and tightened up, and those on the accu-
mulator smeared with vaseline.
FUSES. To replace a blown fuse,
remove the nut D shown in illustration
Fig. 2, place a spare fuse strip over the
projecting screw, then replace and tighten
up nut. The principle is exactly the same
as the house fuse, but instead of fuse wire
it is a thin strip of metal.
LAMPS. New bulbs sometimes have to
be focussed. In the type of lighting set
that we are considering, there are three
notches at the back of the holder, allowing
the bulb to be tried in three positions.
The reflector is of great importance, and if
tarnished must be cleaned carefully with
chamois leather and rouge wet with petrol,
unless it is of stainless steel, in which case
it must NOT be touched with rouge, but
cleaned with a damp cloth and dried and
rubbed with a very soft chamois leather.

starter motor should be done very
sparingly. It is sufficient to give a few
drops of oil through the lubricators only
every 1,000 miles. Do not put oil in every
opening like so many have done to their
vacuum cleaners, with consequent disas-
trous results.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 261
A Page for Girl Guides.
How We Wired a House in Paradise.
By Beatrice Shilling and Mona Willis.
So many people we find are quite ignorant as to how their house is wired for an Electric Service. Beatrice and Mona, who are apprenticed to Miss Partridge, in Devonshire, have therefore written for our Girl Guide readers a humorous description of the way a house is wired for electric light.
Wiring a house in Paradise should be one of the nicest wiring jobs possible, but our Paradise was an earthly Paradise! It was a court in the town of South Molton.
The house should have had a large roof space and lath and plaster walls. It should have been newly built, clean and unoccupied. It was very old, very dirty, the walls of cob and the roof space, at its highest, a bare three feet. Very fortunately, when we wired it, it was unoccupied. If we had had linoleum to take up and furniture to contend with in its small rooms, it would have been still more like a house in Purgatory.
The job took us three days and consisted of installing eight lights with two-way switching for one.
In the house-wiring the wires are laid between the floorboards and the ceiling below and the wires for the switches are either dropped down inside the walls, if these are hollow, or clipped neatly down the surface if they are solid. For the top floor the wires are laid along underneath the roof.
The first thing to do is to decide the exact position of the lights and make holes in the ceiling for the wires to come through. Then you knock upwards through the hole to the floor above with a stair-rod, or its like, so that your mate can see, or rather hear, which boards must be taken up.
We next started on the upstairs. Of course, there was no way of getting into the roof, so in the darkest corner at the end of a passage we made a small hole in the ceiling and cut out, with a keyhole saw, a piece of ceiling about two feet deep by eighteen inches. We lit a candle and had a look round the roof. It was the worst roof we had ever been in, full of cobwebs and thick black dust. We climbed into the roof with many contortions, and hoisted up the cable. Crawling about, poking wires down holes, we got more dirty than seemed possible. Our landlady was horrified when we returned that evening (we waited until it was dark) and got the bath ready immediately.
All the wires are put in first and the ceiling roses, lampholders and switches connected up afterwards.
Connecting up the switch is simple, there are only two wires and two terminals. The ceiling roses are more difficult, for several wires will be poking through the ceiling. However, if the twin switch wire has been marked it is fairly simple. All the + wires go into one terminal; except for the — switch wire, the — wires all go into another, while the — switch wire goes all by itself into the third. The lamp-holder is connected to the terminals with — wires in them.
Having got all the cables laid in, we did the bonding, that is, connecting all

chain goes through fairly easily if it is well shaken in, and once the chain is through, the flex can be firmly attached to one end and drawn through without much further loss of breath. The drawing through must be done with great care, though, for the flex is very apt to slip from the chain just at the last moment, and the whole business has to be done again. 
House wiring is very interesting work, particularly, we think, this last part of fitting lamps and shades. It is so very important to get for each room the shades and lamps which are right, both from an illuminating point of view and also from the point of view of artistic effect. 

* * *

Electric Railways in Italy.
By Mrs. Walter Lawson.

Over a thousand miles of Italian Railways have been converted from Steam to Electricity. Not only is expense saved by this change, but the improvement in travel comfort cannot be exaggerated—no noxious fumes from inferior coal to worry the passenger and blot out the beautiful landscape.

Owing to the paucity of coal and oil fuels in Italy (which necessitates the importation of 12,000,000 tons of coal into the country annually) and, on the contrary, the richness of their water supply, Italys great electrical engineers have devised means of utilising this marvellous resource, transporting the water long distances and transforming it into power for the most varied uses. 
Their urgent need caused them to solve the problem of electric railways as early as 1897, when the Engineer of Public Works nominated a commission to deal with the difficulty, and in 1901 and 1902 a practical solution was arrived at with the electrification of the Varesine and the Valtellinesi Railways, respectively. They claim that the latter was the first big step in railway electrification in the world for passengers and goods.
Since that time till the present day, the electrification of Italian railways has proceeded with intensity (only interrupted partially by the War) and now extends over a thousand miles, and one of the last lines to be converted from steam to electricity is the one connecting Genoa with Leghorn. It is worth mentioning that not only is expense saved by this change but the improvement in comfort cannot be exaggerated when one realises that there are 67 tunnels between Genoa and Spezia, and, speaking from personal experience, the fumes from inferior coal, in the old days, were enough to asphyxiate the passengers.
In France, in Central Europe, and in Norway and Sweden, electric railways are largely in use. In England we have some electric railways, but these by comparison are on a small scale. At this time of the year, when parties for both old and young are the order of the day, Miss Mackirdys delicious new cake recipes will be welcomed.
A Few Cakes.
Cake-making as a branch of cookery has made rapid strides in the last half-century, and the delicious combinations of the present-day have little resemblance to the cakes of Shakespeares time described as "small masses of plain dough, baked," and on this assumption we no longer wonder at the want of respect given to them by Shakespearean characters.
Heat of the Oven.
The baking of the cake is the most difficult part in the process of cake-making, but obviated by a little experience and some idea of oven temperatures. The oven should be heated to 400°, and when the cake is put in, the switch is turned to medium; then when the cake shows signs of browning the temperature should be still further reduced, the current being ultimately switched off. The heat at this stage is usually sufficient to complete the cooking and drying of the cake.

flavouring. Beat butter and sugar till
creamy, beat in the eggs, adding them
one by one; when the second egg has been
added begin to beat in the flour time about
with the eggs. Add baking powder then
fruit; mix thoroughly, put in greased tin
and bake for about 2 to 2 1/2 hours, accord-
ing to thickness.
Other fruit or a mixture of fruits may
be substituted for sultana raisins. The
tin may be lined with paper.

A Walnut Cake.
Seven ozs. flour, 6 ozs. castor sugar,
2 ozs. butter, 3 yolks, 2 whites, 1/2 teacup
milk, 1/2 teacup chopped walnuts, 1/2 teaspoon
cream of tartar, 1/4 teaspoon carbonate of
soda.
Cream butter and sugar, add yolks,
milk, soda, cream of tartar and walnuts;
beat the mixture well and fold in the
whites stiffly beaten. Bake in a greased
tin—the tin may be lined with paper, in
which case do not grease.
A walnut cake will take about 1 1/4 hours.
When the cake is cool it is improved if
coated with American Cream Frosting.

American Cream Frosting.
One small teacup castor sugar, a small
1/2 teacup water, 1 large white of egg, lemon
juice, any flavouring desired; colouring
may also be used. Put the sugar and water
in a small saucepan and heat very slowly
at side of stove plate till the sugar is dis-
solved, then boil steadily for 5 minutes,
when the syrup should look slightly thick,
have the white whisked in a bowl till dry-
looking. Whisk the boiling syrup quickly
into the white and continue whisking until
the frosting is thick and creamy and of a
consistency to remain on the cake. While
whisking, add gradually lemon juice and
any other flavouring or colouring.
Pour over the cake and decorate with
walnuts or finely chopped pistachio nuts
that have been blanched to remove the
skins.

The Best Sponge Cake I Know.
Five eggs, the weight of 4 eggs in castor
sugar, the weight of 3 eggs in flour. Whisk
the eggs and sugar in a large bowl for 1/2 an
hour, then fold in very carefully the flour
which should be sifted, mix only until all
traces of the flour disappear. Put into
three greased sandwich tins and bake
quickly for about 8 minutes. Put together
with preserve, cream or whatever may be
liked. The top may be covered with the
American Frosting, which might be varied
by the addition of some melted chocolate.
The secret of the success of the sponge is
steady beating then careful folding, not
beating in of the flour. The result is a
delicious layer cake varied with all sorts
of fillings and coatings.

transcription:
270
The Electrical Age
Useful Hints for the Home-Maker.
By "ELECTRA."
"ELECTRA" will be pleased to give information regarding any electrical apparatus mentioned in the Journal. She has had practical experience herself in the use of domestic electrical appliances and will be pleased to place her experience at the disposal of our readers. In writing to her at Head Office of the E.A.W., kindly enclose stamped addressed envelope.
ELECTRIC SHAVING MIRROR
Our men-folk are never happier than when shaving can be done expeditiously and without undue worry. I am very glad, therefore, to have come across this Electric Shaving Mirror recently.
This is the table type of the "Electric Shaving Mirror."
A little hole is made in the mirror, and over this is fixed a special frosted "bulls-eye" lens which throws an even distribution of light over the face, with no shadows. Any standard make of lamp may be used—a 20-watt is generally sufficient—and it is easily put into the lamp-holder behind the mirror.
The position of the lamp gives this mirror another advantage, and that is the glass gets just sufficiently warmed to prevent any condensation of breath on it while shaving.
Incidentally, the "Electric Shaving Mirror" also serves as an excellent "making-up" mirror.
The silver frame makes it very attractive, the price is quite moderate, and the mirror can be obtained for hanging on the wall or standing on the table.
"JACKSON" ELECTRIC FIRES.
I am sure my readers will be interested in the new "Jackson" Fire, with the plug-in elements. If you move from one place to another where the voltage is different, you have only to take out the elements, have them re-wound, and you can replace them again yourself in a few seconds. The advantage of this will be quickly appreciated.
The one-bar "Jackson" Fire may be used for both heating and cooking. Note the Plug-in Element in the Centre.

transcription:
The Electrical Age
275

E.A.W. Branch Activities.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy, 251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

The second birthday of this Branch took the form of a very interesting luncheon, when over 300 ladies and gentlemen were present.
In the afternoon a visit was paid to the show rooms of the Clyde Valley Electrical Power Company, when a delicious electrically cooked tea was served to the members.
The next item on the syllabus is a joint meeting with the Royal Scientific Society, who have granted us a limited number of tickets for a lecture on "Television," by J. L. Baird, Esq., to be held in the Royal Technical College, Glasgow. This will be followed in February with a lecture on "Electric Sewing Machines," by Mr. W. Greig, of the Singer Sewing Machine Co., Ltd., who is continuing the history of the electric sewing machine with demonstrations of all kinds of work by his lady demonstrator. This lecture was one of the outstanding events of last year.
Later in the month we are having a most useful and instructive lecture on "House Wiring, Fuses and Plugs"; this is the kind of lecture that the members flock to in great numbers.
The membership is steadily increasing, due, in a great measure, to the Membership Campaign and mutual exchange of ideas which comes as the result of each successful meeting.
We also had the pleasure, through the E.D.A. Circle Campaign, of enjoying a delightful lecture and demonstration on an Electric Cooker, by Miss Holm, of Newcastle. The menu was a Christmas dinner, and greatly appreciated by the ladies and gentlemen present.
The Sub-Section at Greenock has started off their winter session with a splendid talk on "Electricity in the Home," and a delightful lecture on "Smoke, Sunshine and Electricity," by Dr. Dorothy Chalmers Smith.
Last week the E.D.A. Circle Campaign had a demonstration house on view, to which the E.A.W. members at Greenock and environs were invited: about 2,500 people visited this very alive piece of propaganda work, where they saw every house appliance, and in the kitchen a young lady baking on an electric cooker.

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. L. Hayes, 1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.

The Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the Association have this session had a programme of evening and afternoon "Talks" and afternoon visits. The first "Talk" was given by Mr. Berry, of "Magicoal Fire" fame. This was a very interesting talk on the "Colectric" system and was followed by discussion on the "Colectric" System v. Electric Fires.
A lecture (we could hardly call this a "Talk") by Prof. Cramp, of the Birmingham University, took place next, on "The Fundamentals of Electricity," and was one of the finest we have ever had. The wonderful yet simple experiments he performed, leading from one point to another, taught the members some of the most essential points, which they had never understood before.
This was followed by a visit to Tuckers Switch Works. Here over 50 members saw how switches were made. All the intricate detail that is necessary in the making of a switch was viewed with wonder, and the idea conceived was that in spite of all the many processes the switch goes through before it is complete, it is comparatively small in price. Here the members were entertained to tea, and it was thoroughly appreciated after the tour round the works.
The next meeting was a "Talk" by Dr. Sumpner, Principal of the Technical College. This was a very simple explanation of the principle of the electric motor. A skeleton model of a motor in wood was used, and from that members learned how the current drove the motor. This was a "Talk" from which members gained real knowledge, and was very aptly arranged to follow the most interesting lecture by Prof. Cramp, and all who were present thoroughly enjoyed the whole meeting.
One of the most popular "Talks" was given by Mr. R. Rook-Jones, on the Ultra-Violet Ray, in the afternoon. "The Uses of the Ultra-Violet Ray, Infra Red Ray, and High Frequency as Applied for Health Purposes in Self Treatment in the Home" were fully explained, and the members were so keen about it all that it was with much reluctance that they wended their

Baird, Esq., to be held in the Royal Technical College, Glasgow. This will be followed in February with a lecture on "Electric Sewing Machines," by Mr. W. Greig, of the Singer Sewing Machine Co., Ltd., who is continuing the history of the electric sewing machine with demonstrations of all kinds of work by his lady demonstrator. This lecture was one of the outstanding events of last year.
Later in the month we are having a most useful and instructive lecture on "House Wiring, Fuses and Plugs"; this is the kind of lecture that the members flock to in great numbers.
The membership is steadily increasing, due, in a great measure, to the Membership Campaign and mutual exchange of ideas which comes as the result of each successful meeting.
We also had the pleasure, through the E.D.A. Circle Campaign, of enjoying a delightful lecture and demonstration on an Electric Cooker, by Miss Holm, of Newcastle. The menu was a Christmas dinner, and greatly appreciated by the ladies and gentlemen present.
The Sub-Section at Greenock has started off their winter session with a splendid talk on "Electricity in the Home," and a delightful lecture on "Smoke, Sunshine and Electricity," by Dr. Dorothy Chalmers Smith.
Last week the E.D.A. Circle Campaign had a demonstration house on view, to which the E.A.W. members at Greenock and environs were invited: about 2,500 people visited this very alive piece of propaganda work, where they saw every house appliance, and in the kitchen a young lady baking on an electric cooker.

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. L. Hayes, 1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.

The Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the Association have this session had a programme of evening and afternoon "Talks" and afternoon visits. The first "Talk" was given by Mr. Berry, of "Magicoal Fire" fame. This was a very interesting talk on the "Colectric" system and was followed by discussion on the "Colectric" System v. Electric Fires.
A lecture (we could hardly call this a "Talk") by Prof. Cramp, of the Birmingham University, took place next, on "The Fundamentals of Electricity," and was one of the finest we have ever had. The wonderful yet simple experiments he performed, leading from one point to another, taught the members some of the most essential points, which they had never understood before.
This was followed by a visit to Tuckers Switch Works. Here over 50 members saw how switches were made. All the intricate detail that is necessary in the making of a switch was viewed with wonder, and the idea conceived was that in spite of all the many processes the switch goes through before it is complete, it is comparatively small in price. Here the members were entertained to tea, and it was thoroughly appreciated after the tour round the works.
The next meeting was a "Talk" by Dr. Sumpner, Principal of the Technical College. This was a very simple explanation of the principle of the electric motor. A skeleton model of a motor in wood was used, and from that members learned how the current drove the motor. This was a "Talk" from which members gained real knowledge, and was very aptly arranged to follow the most interesting lecture by Prof. Cramp, and all who were present thoroughly enjoyed the whole meeting.
One of the most popular "Talks" was given by Mr. R. Rook-Jones, on the Ultra-Violet Ray, in the afternoon. "The Uses of the Ultra-Violet Ray, Infra Red Ray, and High Frequency as Applied for Health Purposes in Self Treatment in the Home" were fully explained, and the members were so keen about it all that it was with much reluctance that they wended their

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams,
" Woodville," Ack Lane, Bramhall, Cheshire.
The winter programme, which opened with
the one day conference on October 13th, des-
cribed elsewhere, has included four visits and four
lectures before Christmas. In October we visited
the showrooms of Metropolitan-Vickers, Ltd., in
Long Millgate, and spent a most interesting after-
noon inspecting the household appliances shown to
us by the demonstrators, and standing fascinated
round the cooker where a joint sent forth savoury
smells when the oven door was opened. Tea
was served upstairs to the strains of wireless,
and our hearty thanks are due to Mr. White
and his colleagues for their courtesy and kind-
ness.
Later in the month, a lecture by Mr. N. E.
Barber, on " Refrigeration," was much appre-
ciated, and we realised more vividly than ever
how much refrigeration is to be preferred to the
pleasant little " improvements " that used to be
added to make stale food palatable: as Dr.
Veitch Clark, Medical Officer of Health for Man-
chester, said as he presided, refrigeration is the
only system of food preservation by which food
remains in its natural state.
Our first visit in November was to the
Co-operative Laundries Association in Levens-
hulme, one of the largest electrically equipped
laundries in the district. Some of the electric
washing machines made us very envious, but,
unfortunately they were too bulky to be easily
smuggled.
Later in the month we visited Messrs. Berrys
showrooms in Deansgate, where we inspected the
lighting fitments, cookers and washers, etc., and
admired the " Magicoal " fires, including replicas
of the ones supplied to H.R.H. the Prince of
Wales and the Duke and Duchess of York.
After a most enjoyable tea at the Victoria
Hotel, Mr. Shilton, A.M.I.E.E., gave his simple
explanation of " Electrical Units in Domestic
Supply," which threw fresh light on our ignor-
ance of the fundamentals of electrical power in
the home. We are very grateful to Mr. Shilton
for the care he had taken in adapting his know-
ledge to our elementary needs.
Two more lectures were held in November:
Mr. E. R. Taylor spoke on " Industrial and
Medical Applications of X-Rays," emphasising
the splendid work done at the Infirmary and else-
where, and the care needed in using these rays.
Mr. Hawkins gave another of his interesting
talks on the various aspects of lighting;
with beautiful lamps, sprayed bulbs, and with
his own infectious enthusiasm he showed us
how exquisite colour schemes could be built up
in large and small rooms: how " daylight "
lamps were made, and a most useful demonstra-
tion on the correct blending of colours.
The last visit of the autumn was to the Man-
chester Corporation Electricity Showrooms,
where all the demonstrators vied in adding to
our knowledge and enjoyment. The demonstra-
tion of cooking was watched with keenest
interest, and we thoroughly appreciated the
delicious tea that was provided later. A
flashlight photograph was taken at the end of
an extremely pleasant afternoon, and we offer
our thanks to the Electricity Department for
arranging so enjoyable a visit. D.M.P.
One-Day Conference
at Manchester.
At 10.30 a.m. on Thursday, October 13th, the
room in the Lighting Service Bureau was filled
to the last chair: late-comers perched (uncom-
fortably, one fears) on edges: Dr. Christina
Barrowman rose to give her lecture on " Elec-
tricity, the Handmaiden in the Home "; our
One-Day Conference had begun.
It was, I think, an enjoyable day for all: even
those who had borne the beat and burden of the
fray, coping with last-minute absences of pro-
spective speakers, must have felt soothed by the
attentive audience in the morning and the sight
