Unnamed: 9: presided over by the Lord Mayor at luncheon in Midland Hotel
transcription:
The Electrical Age 279
of their 250 guests at luncheon in the Midland Hotel, presided over by the Lord Mayor: must have heaved a sigh of relief as saloon bus after bus was loaded up at the Hotel door with visitors to Messrs. Ferrantis Works at Hollinwood, and finally realised as they sat down gratefully to the delicious tea that Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti had so kindly provided that the day had been a success and that nothing could now spoil it.
Dr. Barrowman covered a wide area in her stimulating talk: she spoke of the common uses of electrical domestic appliances, and of some not quite so common, as the use of the hair dryer for drying dogs and films. She described the remedial uses of electricity and the boon it is in hospitals all over the country: of the advantage to health of refrigeration over other methods of food preservation: on simple safeguards that prevent accidents: and lastly, a vision of the future use of television, in which the wife will put on the potatoes when she sees her husband take down his hat from the office peg.
Mr. Beauchamp, Director of the Electrical Development Association, in his interesting address, made a distinction between the woman who only wants to use electricity, and the woman training as a demonstrator who needs to understand it more fully. Referring to the price of current, he reminded us that it is the millions of users that make cheap current, and sometimes the wise policy was to buy dear units to gain cheaper units.
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, opening the discussion, said that meetings of this kind were to the advantage of the individual, of the industry, and of the nation as a whole, as electricity affected all. He mentioned the use of "servicing" in some towns of U.S.A. for repairs and renewals, where stations send out teams of men who take a pride in seeing how soon they can be on the spot and set right what is wrong.
Several members spoke, including Mrs. Ferranti, who spoke of the satisfaction her electric cooker had given, and a doctors wife who showed that a cooker could be run at a cost of 2s. 2d. in current for a family of three adults and two children, all cooking and baking being done at home. The difficulties met with owing to lack of standardisation of voltage were also touched on.
At 1.15, the Lord Mayor presided at luncheon in the Midland Hotel, where the chief speakers were to have been Mrs. Elliot Lynn and Miss Ellen Wilkinson. But marriage detained the former and influenza the latter, and we were lucky indeed to have Mrs. E. D. Simon, who, in spite of her numerous engagements, at a moments notice stepped into the breach. In her wise and charming speech she emphasised the greater happiness that must come to the whole nation where the women have more leisure to be real companions of their husbands.
Mrs. Lamb, who replied to the toast of the Association in an excellent speech full of the dry humour that we anticipate so eagerly, must have prepared it almost entirely during the luncheon itself, as she deputised for Miss Wilkinson at extremely short notice and had been busy up to the last moment.
Although about 150 members and friends were the guests of Messrs. Ferranti, Ltd., who so kindly provided transport out to Hollinwood, we were divided up into parties so neatly, and conducted through the works so ably, each one of us felt she had been shewn and informed about every point of interest. The new building with its windows of vita-glass was a source of interest, and it may, of course, have been imagination, but we fancied that the draughtsmen here were pinker, more alert and perhaps a trifle heavier than any that we saw working elsewhere. A fine sight was that of the great transformers lined up ready for shipment, their destination written on a card. A mighty bulk towered above us - it was for New Zealand: at its side was one almost as large for Oldham. Niagara, Leeds and Buenos Ayres elbowed each other for the last time.
It was strange to pass from these monsters to the fine, delicate work of the girls on wireless or metal work, where even their nimble fingers seemed too clumsy for the tiny parts they had to assemble. Tea in the fine girls canteen ended a very enjoyable visit, and the thanks of all of us were happily voiced by Miss Haslett, who had travelled from London to give us her support that day.
We are grateful to all who helped to make the conference a success, and our thanks are specially due to our Hon. Secretary, Mrs. Harcourt Williams, and to Mr. Harcourt Williams, whose help was invaluable and who performed yeoman service in a multitude of ways. D.M.P.
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Stemp, 1, York Terrace, St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.
Our first year has passed, fortunately, without any untoward happenings. We have to congratulate ourselves that our meetings have been so much appreciated and so well attended. The Association has been the means of bringing together a number of Cheltenham housewives

The Electrical Age 279
of their 250 guests at luncheon in the Midland Hotel, presided over by the Lord Mayor: must have heaved a sigh of relief as saloon bus after bus was loaded up at the Hotel door with visitors to Messrs. Ferrantis Works at Hollinwood, and finally realised as they sat down gratefully to the delicious tea that Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti had so kindly provided that the day had been a success and that nothing could now spoil it.
Dr. Barrowman covered a wide area in her stimulating talk: she spoke of the common uses of electrical domestic appliances, and of some not quite so common, as the use of the hair dryer for drying dogs and films. She described the remedial uses of electricity and the boon it is in hospitals all over the country: of the advantage to health of refrigeration over other methods of food preservation: on simple safeguards that prevent accidents: and lastly, a vision of the future use of television, in which the wife will put on the potatoes when she sees her husband take down his hat from the office peg.
Mr. Beauchamp, Director of the Electrical Development Association, in his interesting address, made a distinction between the woman who only wants to use electricity, and the woman training as a demonstrator who needs to understand it more fully. Referring to the price of current, he reminded us that it is the millions of users that make cheap current, and sometimes the wise policy was to buy dear units to gain cheaper units.
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, opening the discussion, said that meetings of this kind were to the advantage of the individual, of the industry, and of the nation as a whole, as electricity affected all. He mentioned the use of "servicing" in some towns of U.S.A. for repairs and renewals, where stations send out teams of men who take a pride in seeing how soon they can be on the spot and set right what is wrong.
Several members spoke, including Mrs. Ferranti, who spoke of the satisfaction her electric cooker had given, and a doctors wife who showed that a cooker could be run at a cost of 2s. 2d. in current for a family of three adults and two children, all cooking and baking being done at home. The difficulties met with owing to lack of standardisation of voltage were also touched on.
At 1.15, the Lord Mayor presided at luncheon in the Midland Hotel, where the chief speakers were to have been Mrs. Elliot Lynn and Miss Ellen Wilkinson. But marriage detained the former and influenza the latter, and we were lucky indeed to have Mrs. E. D. Simon, who, in spite of her numerous engagements, at a moments notice stepped into the breach. In her wise and charming speech she emphasised the greater happiness that must come to the whole nation where the women have more leisure to be real companions of their husbands.
Mrs. Lamb, who replied to the toast of the Association in an excellent speech full of the dry humour that we anticipate so eagerly, must have prepared it almost entirely during the luncheon itself, as she deputised for Miss Wilkinson at extremely short notice and had been busy up to the last moment.
Although about 150 members and friends were the guests of Messrs. Ferranti, Ltd., who so kindly provided transport out to Hollinwood, we were divided up into parties so neatly, and conducted through the works so ably, each one of us felt she had been shewn and informed about every point of interest. The new building with its windows of vita-glass was a source of interest, and it may, of course, have been imagination, but we fancied that the draughtsmen here were pinker, more alert and perhaps a trifle heavier than any that we saw working elsewhere. A fine sight was that of the great transformers lined up ready for shipment, their destination written on a card. A mighty bulk towered above us - it was for New Zealand: at its side was one almost as large for Oldham. Niagara, Leeds and Buenos Ayres elbowed each other for the last time.
It was strange to pass from these monsters to the fine, delicate work of the girls on wireless or metal work, where even their nimble fingers seemed too clumsy for the tiny parts they had to assemble. Tea in the fine girls canteen ended a very enjoyable visit, and the thanks of all of us were happily voiced by Miss Haslett, who had travelled from London to give us her support that day.
We are grateful to all who helped to make the conference a success, and our thanks are specially due to our Hon. Secretary, Mrs. Harcourt Williams, and to Mr. Harcourt Williams, whose help was invaluable and who performed yeoman service in a multitude of ways. D.M.P.
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Stemp, 1, York Terrace, St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.

transcription:

of their 250 guests at luncheon in the Midland Hotel, presided over by the Lord Mayor: must have heaved a sigh of relief as saloon bus after bus was loaded up at the Hotel door with visitors to Messrs. Ferrantis Works at Hollinwood, and finally realised as they sat down gratefully to the delicious tea that Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti had so kindly provided that the day had been a success and that nothing could now spoil it.
Dr. Barrowman covered a wide area in her stimulating talk: she spoke of the common uses of electrical domestic appliances, and of some not quite so common, as the use of the hair dryer for drying dogs and films. She described the remedial uses of electricity and the boon it is in hospitals all over the country: of the advantage to health of refrigeration over other methods of food preservation: on simple safeguards that prevent accidents: and lastly, a vision of the future use of television, in which the wife will put on the potatoes when she sees her husband take down his hat from the office peg.
Mr. Beauchamp, Director of the Electrical Development Association, in his interesting address, made a distinction between the woman who only wants to use electricity, and the woman training as a demonstrator who needs to understand it more fully. Referring to the price of current, he reminded us that it is the millions of users that make cheap current, and sometimes the wise policy was to buy dear units to gain cheaper units.
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, opening the discussion, said that meetings of this kind were to the advantage of the individual, of the industry, and of the nation as a whole, as electricity affected all. He mentioned the use of "servicing" in some towns of U.S.A. for repairs and renewals, where stations send out teams of men who take a pride in seeing how soon they can be on the spot and set right what is wrong.
Several members spoke, including Mrs. Ferranti, who spoke of the satisfaction her electric cooker had given, and a doctors wife who showed that a cooker could be run at a cost of 2s. 2d. in current for a family of three adults and two children, all cooking and baking being done at home. The difficulties met with owing to lack of standardisation of voltage were also touched on.

In her wise and charming speech she emphasised the greater happiness that must come to the whole nation where the women have more leisure to be real companions of their husbands.

A mighty bulk towered above us - it was for New Zealand: at its side was one almost as large for Oldham. Niagara, Leeds and Buenos Ayres elbowed each other for the last time.
It was strange to pass from these monsters to the fine, delicate work of the girls on wireless or metal work, where even their nimble fingers seemed too clumsy for the tiny parts they had to assemble. Tea in the fine girls canteen ended a very enjoyable visit, and the thanks of all of us were happily voiced by Miss Haslett, who had travelled from London to give us her support that day.
We are grateful to all who helped to make the conference a success, and our thanks are specially due to our Hon. Secretary, Mrs. Harcourt Williams, and to Mr. Harcourt Williams, whose help was invaluable and who performed yeoman service in a multitude of ways. D.M.P.

Unnamed: 9: Gave an illustrated lecture on domestic applications of electricity.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 281

who are anxious to save time and labour in their homes and who have had the opportunity of discussing this objective at the various meetings. The autumn seasons programme has been more practical than the preceding one.
We commenced with an illustrated lecture, given by Mr. G. S. Francis, E.D.A., on "The Domestic Applications of Electricity." Both the lecture and lantern slides were much enjoyed; Mr. Francis was lucid and convincing and gave the members and their friends much food for thought on the many ways in which electricity can be applied in the home. Mrs. Atwell Lake (President) passed a vote of thanks to Mr. Francis for his extremely interesting lecture. This lecture prepared the way for the practical lecture demonstration which followed a few weeks later on "Domestic Electrical Appliances," given by Miss Stemp, of the Electricity Department. The members were able to see the many appliances, which they had viewed on the screen, put into actual use. This was a very popular meeting and attracted a good proportion of members.
Our visit to the Automatic Telephone Exchange had to be split up into two consecutive days, more applications being received than could be arranged for at one visit. We all felt very grateful to the engineers, who conducted us over the Exchange, for demonstrating the many intricate workings of the "dialling" system in such an interesting manner. Our members had a thirst for knowledge and no effort was spared to satisfy them. The lady supervisor also gave us some very helpful hints.
Our last meeting, held on December 1st, was a seasonable one, being a lecture demonstration on "Cooking Christmas Fare by Electricity." This practical demonstration was much enjoyed by the members present. Mrs. Atwell Lake (President) passed a vote of thanks to the demonstrator (Miss Stemp) for the very useful and enjoyable demonstration.
We are now fixing up the various items for our Winter Programme. A.A.S.

Unnamed: 9: Honorary Secretary for the South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 281

who are anxious to save time and labour in their homes and who have had the opportunity of discussing this objective at the various meetings. The autumn seasons programme has been more practical than the preceding one.
We commenced with an illustrated lecture, given by Mr. G. S. Francis, E.D.A., on "The Domestic Applications of Electricity." Both the lecture and lantern slides were much enjoyed; Mr. Francis was lucid and convincing and gave the members and their friends much food for thought on the many ways in which electricity can be applied in the home. Mrs. Atwell Lake (President) passed a vote of thanks to Mr. Francis for his extremely interesting lecture. This lecture prepared the way for the practical lecture demonstration which followed a few weeks later on "Domestic Electrical Appliances," given by Miss Stemp, of the Electricity Department. The members were able to see the many appliances, which they had viewed on the screen, put into actual use. This was a very popular meeting and attracted a good proportion of members.
Our visit to the Automatic Telephone Exchange had to be split up into two consecutive days, more applications being received than could be arranged for at one visit. We all felt very grateful to the engineers, who conducted us over the Exchange, for demonstrating the many intricate workings of the "dialling" system in such an interesting manner. Our members had a thirst for knowledge and no effort was spared to satisfy them. The lady supervisor also gave us some very helpful hints.
Our last meeting, held on December 1st, was a seasonable one, being a lecture demonstration on "Cooking Christmas Fare by Electricity." This practical demonstration was much enjoyed by the members present. Mrs. Atwell Lake (President) passed a vote of thanks to the demonstrator (Miss Stemp) for the very useful and enjoyable demonstration.
We are now fixing up the various items for our Winter Programme. A.A.S.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 283

Our visit to the Jam and Pickle Factory of Messrs Chivers, Ltd., Ely, was very enjoyable, over 50 members being present, each of whom was given a souvenir jar of Chivers famous O.W. Pickle.

The next item was a lecture, which, owing to Mr. J. W. Beauchamps unavoidable absence, was given by Mr. V. W. Dale, Business Manager of E.D.A., on "Electricity, Its Uses and Abuses." This meeting was greatly appreciated by the members, Mr. Dale explaining in detail many of the uses of electricity in the home.

Our visit to the Co-operative Wholesale Societys Biscuit Factory was very satisfactory, nearly 100 members turned up, and all were delighted to see the very interesting process of making and baking biscuits, especially as we were asked to sample them as they came from the ovens, crisp and piping hot.

The last fixture to date was a very instructive Cookery Lecture and Demonstration by Miss E. M. Roff, Demonstrator to the Cardiff Corporation Electricity Department. I think most of our members enjoy these lectures more than any other.

The last fixture on the syllabus was a lecture by Mr. W. E. Bush, of E.L.M.A., on the "Principles of Good Lighting in the Home," which proved very interesting.

A very interesting programme has been arranged for the Winter Session, including three E.D.A. lectures, one on the "Electrical Supply Act for 1926," one on "Transforming the Homes of Britain," and "Lighting the Homes of Britain," a visit to Messrs. Falk, Stadelmann, Ltd., a visit to the South Wales News Printing Works, and a visit to the Avana Cake Works, also a Cookery Lecture Demonstration.
J. TYLER.

The winter Conference opened with a reception by the Lady Mayoress, in the Lighting Service Bureau, Dial House, on October 6th. About 95 were present, mostly members, and as a Committee Meeting had been called previously, most of the members of the Committee were also present.

Tea was provided by the Committee and prepared by the Demonstrators Staff of the Newcastle-upon-Tyne Electric Supply Company, and served by Girl Guides.

The British Thomson-Houston Company connected up a Panatrope and provided an excellent musical programme. Miss Balls, Chairman of the North-East Coast Branch, and Miss Boot, played in an amusing sketch.

Houseproud!
ELECTRICITY opens the door to better lighting, to labour-saving appliances and a host of other conveniences. It increases pride in the home because of the beauty and comfort it provides. Wiring the house is now a simple matter if the Callender Wiring System is used. No damage to walls, no disturbance to the decorative scheme. That is the key-note of this most up-to-date Wiring System. Your local Electrical Contractor will be pleased to furnish full particulars.

Unnamed: 9: Hosted the winter conference reception at the Lighting Bureau.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 283

Our visit to the Jam and Pickle Factory of Messrs Chivers, Ltd., Ely, was very enjoyable, over 50 members being present, each of whom was given a souvenir jar of Chivers famous O.W. Pickle.

The next item was a lecture, which, owing to Mr. J. W. Beauchamps unavoidable absence, was given by Mr. V. W. Dale, Business Manager of E.D.A., on "Electricity, Its Uses and Abuses." This meeting was greatly appreciated by the members, Mr. Dale explaining in detail many of the uses of electricity in the home.

Our visit to the Co-operative Wholesale Societys Biscuit Factory was very satisfactory, nearly 100 members turned up, and all were delighted to see the very interesting process of making and baking biscuits, especially as we were asked to sample them as they came from the ovens, crisp and piping hot.

The last fixture to date was a very instructive Cookery Lecture and Demonstration by Miss E. M. Roff, Demonstrator to the Cardiff Corporation Electricity Department. I think most of our members enjoy these lectures more than any other.

The last fixture on the syllabus was a lecture by Mr. W. E. Bush, of E.L.M.A., on the "Principles of Good Lighting in the Home," which proved very interesting.

A very interesting programme has been arranged for the Winter Session, including three E.D.A. lectures, one on the "Electrical Supply Act for 1926," one on "Transforming the Homes of Britain," and "Lighting the Homes of Britain," a visit to Messrs. Falk, Stadelmann, Ltd., a visit to the South Wales News Printing Works, and a visit to the Avana Cake Works, also a Cookery Lecture Demonstration.
J. TYLER.

Unnamed: 9: Giving a lecture of broadcasting fame on the 18th April.
transcription:
EDITORIAL.

THE 1928 CONFERENCE is to be held in London after all.  Owing to unforeseen circumstances which would make it difficult for the Conference to be a success in Glasgow at the present time, the Council, in consultation with the Glasgow Branch, decided that the Conference should be held in London.  While the programme has had to be arranged somewhat hurriedly, it is none the less full of interest.
    The Institution of Electrical Engineers has kindly placed its Lecture Theatre at the disposal of the Association, the Annual General Meeting being held there on the morning of April 17th, and a lecture by Captain Eckersley, of broadcasting fame, on the afternoon of the 18th April.  Visits have been arranged to the London Light Clinic and the Electrical Installation at the Zoological Gardens.
    The Ball at the Hotel Cecil to which T.R.H. The Duke and Duchess of York have graciously given their patronage, promises to be an outstanding social success.

▪ ▪ ▪

THE ELECTRICAL "OUTLET" CAMPAIGN.—Those who were responsible for bringing the Electrical Association for Women into existence had two definite objects in mind; the first, to provide facilities for the woman in the home to obtain a more intimate knowledge of the uses of electricity in our modern civilisation and especially in its relation to the home, and, secondly, to provide a platform for the expression of the womans point of view on any question relating to electricity which may affect her private or public interests.
    Up to the present time we have been mainly concerned with educational work amongst our members.  This inaugural work has enabled our women to gain considerable knowledge of electrical economies and methods, and the time now seems ripe, with the knowledge thus gained, to begin to express the womans point of view to the responsible authorities.
    One of the most crying needs of the day is the lack of electrical "Outlets" in the average house.  In the existing house it is too often true that the unfortunate householder has to bear the cost of installation and to put up with the inconveniences which a little foresight in building would minimise or definitely anticipate.
    The "Electrical Outlet Campaign," which has been devised by the E.A.W., has for its object the provision of an adequate number of "outlets" during building.

▪ ▪ ▪

THE NEED FOR STANDARDISATION OF ELECTRICAL FITTINGS has also been realised by the E.A.W., and the new Campaign will urge upon the responsible electrical authorities the need for the use of standardised plugs and sockets for all domestic purposes.  Everyone has experienced the annoyance of a badly fitting plug and socket and the difficulty of interchangeabilty.
    Very good work in connection with the standardisation of plugs and sockets has already been carried out by the British Engineering Standards Association, which has issued a number of specifications for the manufacture of standardised fittings.
    While our new Campaign is still only in its infancy, very definite and practical interest has already been shown in our efforts with promise of co-operation.  The first practical result has been an invitation from the British Engineering Standards Association to appoint a woman representative to serve on the Electrical Accessories Committee of this Association to represent the womans point of view.
288

transcription:
The Electrical Age 289

How Many "Outlets" Have You
in Your Home?

By The Editor.

THE "OUTLET."

When will the British housewife grow
more impatient with the badly equipped
houses in which she is expected to live and
work and when will she cease to accept
inefficiency as a necessary part of house-
keeping?
We are told on all hands that electricity
is to be the servant of the woman in the
home, but how can we have a real electric
labour-saving home unless we have the
means whereby to use all those many
useful appliances which are the real savers
of labour.
Every modern woman has had the
experience of going into an up-to-date
Store and seeing displayed useful electric
table fittings, vacuum cleaners, polishers
and charming standard lamps; she may
decide that these are within her purse limit,
but then, having decided to purchase, she
suddenly wonders how she is going to use
them.
There is, perhaps, one lighting point and
one heating point in the room, but then
she may require to use the newly purchased
coffee percolator at the same time as the
electric light and electric radiator are also
in commission.
True, there are numerous adaptors on
the market which can be used, but how
much better if in each room there were
provided a number of "Outlets" or, as they
are sometimes called, "Wall Plugs"?
How much easier it would be to plug in
the vacuum cleaner, the polisher and the
extra standard lamp exactly where they are
needed.

With the coming of the warm weather
the prudent housewife may decide to invest
in a refrigerator, but on further reflection
she will ask herself the question—"Where
can this be plugged in?"

The risk of falling over innumerable flexes,
added to the annoyance of the light being
in the wrong position, makes dressing a
tiresome matter.

The joy of a bedroom fitted with a number
of "Outlets."

useful appliances which are the real savers
of labour.
Every modern woman has had the
experience of going into an up-to-date
Store and seeing displayed useful electric
table fittings, vacuum cleaners, polishers
and charming standard lamps; she may
decide that these are within her purse limit,
but then, having decided to purchase, she
suddenly wonders how she is going to use
them.
There is, perhaps, one lighting point and
one heating point in the room, but then
she may require to use the newly purchased
coffee percolator at the same time as the
electric light and electric radiator are also
in commission.
True, there are numerous adaptors on
the market which can be used, but how
much better if in each room there were
provided a number of "Outlets" or, as they
are sometimes called, "Wall Plugs"?
How much easier it would be to plug in
the vacuum cleaner, the polisher and the
extra standard lamp exactly where they are
needed.

With the coming of the warm weather
the prudent housewife may decide to invest
in a refrigerator, but on further reflection
she will ask herself the question—"Where
can this be plugged in?"

The risk of falling over innumerable flexes,
added to the annoyance of the light being
in the wrong position, makes dressing a
tiresome matter.

The joy of a bedroom fitted with a number
of "Outlets."

Unnamed: 9: Expert in electric bells and batteries writing for Girl Guides.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 291

A Page for Girl Guides.

Bells and Batteries.
By Mr. W. C. Jeary.

So many Guides have written to us from time to time enquiring about Electric Bells and Batteries that we asked Mr. Jeary, who is an expert in these matters, to write us the following article, which not only tells you all about Electric Bells, Batteries and Indicators, but how to locate faults and mend them.

It is hardly necessary to describe an electric bell in detail, as everyone must be acquainted with this everyday article and know the principle on which it works.
Electric bells may be divided into three classes which are in general use, Trembling, Single Stroke, and Continuous Action.
The one in most general use is the trembling bell, which continues ringing as long as the circuit is closed by means of a push or switch.
Single stroke bells are mostly used for signalling, and when the circuit is closed the hammer strikes the bell once.
Continuous action bells are generally used for fire and burglar alarms, when the circuit is closed the bell rings continuously until a lever is pulled down.
In recent years a large percentage of houses which have electric light installations supplied from an alternating current supply have used small transformers instead of batteries. These transformers are made with four terminals—two the primary circuit which receive the mains from the electric light, say 200 volt; the second set of terminals, or secondary, are then connected to the bell circuit in the same manner as the ordinary primary battery. This is a very convenient and efficient method, and does away with the cost of battery renewals. Where a bell installation is employed with an indicator showing where the signal emanates from, the bell must be selected so that it is the same resistance as the indicator movement, otherwise the bell will ring and the indicator remain stationary, or vice versa. For seaside towns and humid atmospheres, a good quality bell with platinum contacts, seasoned woodwork, preferably of teak, and well lacquered terminals should be used, otherwise oxidation will cause premature failure.
Since the War a large number of State subsidy houses have been erected, and owing to the high rentals and general housing shortage, a number of houses have been converted into flats, and there has been a demand for an electric bell which can be operated from the hall door, the bell to ring just inside the door. As this class of property is generally compact, and a bell can be heard in every room, it is fortunate that a combined bell and battery to meet this demand has been put on the market.
There are no wires or staples required. The push is fixed outside the hall door and the bell and battery opposite the push inside the door and connected with a short bar which makes contact when the push is pressed.
Another special feature, which has been introduced owing to the bank robberies which have taken place in districts where a small country bank is situated in an isolated position, is what is termed an emergency indoor alarm system.

continuous action bell, batteries and a

The Leclanche Cell.

There are a number of Primary Batteries
on the market, all useful for their respec-
tive purposes, but there are only two types
which we need trouble about in connection
with electric bell installations. The Wet
Leclanche Cell and the Dry Cell.

The Leclanche type consists of a glass jar
painted about 1 1/2 ins. from the top to prevent
creeping—when these cells were first intro-
duced, this margin was heavily coated with
paraffin wax instead of paint—but, owing
to commercial needs is now merely painted.

Then there is a porous pot fitted with
carbon plate which is finished with a carbon
or lead top and terminal—this carbon plate
is surmounted by crushed carbon and
manganese dioxide. These pots should be
of high porosity, otherwise the existing
solution of chloride of ammoniae, commer-
cially known as Salammoniae, would not
soak through and bring the cell into action.
The zinc, which is placed in the Glass Cell
outside the porous pot should be best drawn
solid, commercially pure and well amal-
gamated with mercury solution, otherwise
it would soon be eaten away. Exciting
fluid—3ozs. Salammoniac dissolved in water
two pint size.

Dry Batteries.

Although dry batteries cannot have the
part replaced as in the case of Leclanche
cells, owing to their cleanliness and con-
veniences they have, to a large extent,
taken the place of wet batteries. It is as
well, when purchasing dry batteries, to see
that these are made by a reputable English
firm and are guaranteed to give a high
current output with a long life and will
not unduly deteriorate when standing idle.

The dry cell consists of a zinc case form-
ing the negative pole, which surrounds and

contains the positive pole in the form of a
carbon plate, terminating in a screw
connection, as in the case of a wet cell.
This is surrounded by a depolarising
mixture of carbon and manganese dioxide,
the electrolyte being in the form of a paste,
which lies between the positive pole and
the zinc—the whole cell then being con-
tained in a cardboard case.

the fore as a combination of the wet and

The Electrical Age 297
Yes, our jobs are very different. A young 200-volt Watt I met recently had been exciting a crane motor hoisting joists to the top of a new building. The view was wonderful, he said, which shows there is compensation in exalted positions, after all Very different is the lot of another gang I know, who spent two years under a tube train between the Bank and Shepherds Bush with nothing but the passengers feet to see, through a crack in the floor.
* * *
Anyway, things are going to get levelled out for us, I hear. Were going to be a lot cheaper, and do more for our hire than ever before. Better conditions, and all that ... Zipp!—thats the kitchen switch on the cooker— Im wanted for bacon grilling—sorry, I must be going. Tootle-amp.
[Cartoon illustration of a stick figure electrical character]
Books Received.
"Electro Farming." By H. Borlase Matthews, Wh.Ex., A.M.Inst.C.E., M.I.E.E. Published by Ernest Benn, Ltd. Price 25s. net.
With the spread of electricity to rural districts, the appearance of a book on "The Application of Electricity to Agriculture" is very timely.
Innumerable articles have been written on the deplorable state of our farming industry and the need for a remedy.
Mr. Borlase Matthews, who is an engineer-farmer, tackles this problem in a very practical manner, showing how electricity may come to the aid of the farmer, basing his idea on the practice gained on his own six hundred acre farm in Sussex, where there are now about sixty-seven different applications of electricity—only two horses being employed.
The book is profusely illustrated and contains much useful data, not omitting a chapter of special interest to the farmers wife.
We can heartily recommend this book to all those interested in the application of electricity to rural England.
Seventh Annual Report of the Electricity Commissioners. Published by H.M. Stationery Office. Price 3/-.
Those who are interested in the more serious side of electrical progress as shown by statistics and official reports will find much valuable information in this, the latest, report of the Electricity Commissioners.
After referring to the future organisation of the industry which will take place under the new Electricity Act, the Report proceeds to show the many improvements which are taking place in electrical generation and transmission, including the important economies which have been effected in the utilisation of coal for the production of electricity.
Every improvement and increase in efficiency which the engineer can effect will eventually show its result in the revised price of electricity to the housewife.

298 The Electrical Age

Domestic Electrical Service on the North-East Coast.
By W. F. T. Pinkney, M.I.E.E.

Showing the progressive policy adopted by a large electricity undertaking, where the people in the villages are catered for on the same terms as the town dweller.

The North-East Coast has always been regarded as an area humming with industrial mechanism, and it is true enough that the extensive system of electrical transmission in that area, erected by the Newcastle-upon-Tyne Electric Supply Company, Limited, and its associated Companies, was designed primarily with the object of distributing electrical power to the many collieries, shipyards, factories, and innumerable other industrial activities.

Domestic Supplies.
Encouragement of the uses of electricity for domestic and other purposes not purely industrial has not been neglected, however, and in later years special attention has been given towards development in this direction. Not only has the use of electricity greatly increased in the cities and towns, but the benefits of its availability have been carried into a large number of villages over a very wide area, by "tapping" the power distribution system and laying out village networks.

VILLAGE OVERHEAD DISTRIBUTION.
An Old World Village where Electricity has been introduced, without marring the beautiful surroundings

Some idea of the extent of this may be gained from the fact that within an area of 1,600 square miles there are some 93 separate low tension networks in towns and villages, and 24 additional networks are in course of erection or under consideration.

Unnamed: 9: Author of article on electricity supply to rural districts.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 301

How Electricity is Supplied to Rural Districts.

By Margaret M. Partridge, B.Sc.

So many enquiries have reached us recently as to how a supply of Electricity can be obtained in Rural Districts, especially from Womens Institutes, that we have asked Miss Partridge, who has had considerable experience in such matters, to write an article setting forth the position.

What a lot of ink has been spilt, what volumes of hot air have been expended on the subject of electricity for country districts. Abuse has been heaped upon everyone by everyone else because there is not enough of it, or too much of it, or because it is not made use of where it is supplied, or because it is not supplied where it might be made use of ; and now our worthy Editor has instructed me to spill more ink and perhaps earn more abuse by writing an article on the subject.
She tells me that frequent enquiries are made by our country members asking how they are to obtain a much-needed electricity supply and she thinks I should be able to satisfy some of the enquirers.
I only wish I could. I wish, indeed, that there was anyone in England who could, but the truth is that conditions are in such a state of transition that no one can really give information with any certainty.
The history of the subject is interesting.
In the old days, electricity in the country was considered a luxury for the very few who were wealthy enough to own private plants.
Then a time followed when some few villages, through the enterprise and energy of a few public spirited enthusiasts, acquired small local undertakings which struggled hard against many difficulties and gave good service in very limited areas.
At first the enthusiasts who promoted these little schemes were ridiculed on the one hand for being unpractical idealists and condemned on the other for being unscrupulous adventurers, robbing the village communities of their savings to finance little companies which were certain not to pay.
In course of time, however, as the village electricity companies proved their worth and their capacity to keep their heads well above water, rural electrification was undertaken in some districts by much larger companies which took in an area of two or three counties and transmitted electrical energy from one large central generating station through a network of high voltage mains to all the small towns and villages within their area. These companies, which are technically described as "Power Companies," have nearly always been situated in districts where a number of mines or factories gave the Companies a good " day load " which enabled them to keep their generating stations working productively throughout the greater part of the twenty-four hours.
The essentially agricultural districts remained uncatered for to any material extent, and every investigation proves that much more might be done—though investigators disagree about the reasons for the slow progress.

transcription:
302 The Electrical Age

the use of electricity. Others blame our
system of local government which gives the
power of electricity supply into the hands
of District or Borough Councils, and conse-
quently private enterprise is somewhat
handicapped.
Parliamentary Acts and regulations come
in for a fair share of abuse, and finally,
the ever useful undefined " They " repre-
senting all authorities or public bodies of
any sort are accused of leaving undone all
those things which they ought to have done,
and having done quite a lot of things which
they ought not to have done.
In this state of affairs, Mr. Baldwins
Government decided to take a hand, and
the 1926 Electricity (Supply) Act was
passed. By this Act, the Central Elec-
tricity Board was created whose duty it is
to build a large 132,000 volt network of
primary transmission mains over the whole
country to link up the greater generating
stations and sell electricity in bulk to all
the smaller stations which require it. This
huge network is hardly likely to help the
rural districts very much, as the main
routes chosen merely link up the larger
towns, and no tapping points will be avail-
able in between ; by enabling the larger
towns powers to buy electricity in quantities
not limited by any considerations of the
size of their own plant or their ability to
increase it, they should be able to sell
electricity to the surrounding country at
quite good terms.
This state of affairs has started a whole-
sale system of land grabbing. Companies
and individuals on all hands are making
application to the Electricity Commis-
sioners and to Parliament for powers to
distribute electricity, either wholesale or
retail, in large and small areas.
Meanwhile, to return to my opening
remarks—how are we to know who to turn
to for our electricity supply?
In general, my advice to members need-
ing electricity in a country home is first to

canvass their neighbours. If you live in
cold isolation with no neighbours your
chances of being linked up with any Supply
Companies mains are very small indeed. If,
on the other hand, you can demonstrate
that ten or a dozen houses within a small
area want current then you can do some-
thing. I should suggest the following
course:—
Sit down quietly and read the parable
of the importunate widow and let it sink
well in.
Then enquire from the Town Clerk or
Clerk to the Local Council, if anyone owns
the lighting rights over your district. If
no one owns it, or has staked out any

Unnamed: 9: Earliest and most energetic member of the E.A.W., budding authoress.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 303

Our Portrait Page.

Interesting Personalities in the E.A.W.

Miss Gladys Sharp is one of the earliest and most energetic members of the E.A.W., and probably holds the record for having attended more meetings than any other member. Knowing this, it is all the more surprising that she is a budding authoress, her first novel, "The House of the Lighted Window," having been published at the end of March by Everleigh, Nash and Grace, Ltd., price 7/6.
Before the War, Miss Sharp worked in the office of the Jackson Electric Stove Company as shorthand typist, after which she went to Stockholm, where she taught English to the Secretary of State for Commerce and his wife.
It was while in Sweden that she gained some of the interesting knowledge which she uses in her new book.
May we wish Miss Sharp every success and that this novel may be the first of a long list of successful publications.

MISS GLADYS SHARP.

Mr. Llewelyn B. Atkinson, an engineer, philosopher and great friend to the E.A.W. Our picture is a reproduction of the portrait which has been painted by Mr. George Harcourt, R.A., and was presented to the Institution of Electrical Engineers in Feburary, 1928, by Mr. Ernest Leete, on behalf of the Cable Makers Association.
The great work which Mr. Atkinson has done for all sections of the electricity industry, both on the scientific and industrial sides, would require many pages for the telling. Some day, we hope to persuade Mr. Atkinson himself to write for this Journal some of those delightful reminiscences for which he is so famous, and to tell in his own inimitable way the difficulties, trials and humours of the early days and of the pioneers of great electrical industry.

The portrait of Mr. Ll. B. Atkinson, which now hangs in the Institution of Electrical Engineers.

transcription:
304                                        The Electrical Age

Electricity at the Zoo.

By Mrs. Walter Lawson.

Londoners have always been proud of
their Zoo, though, looking back, the old
arrangements for heating and lighting
seem archaic in comparison to the present
day when electricity has been introduced
and such striking improvements made that
they can now safely claim that the London
Zoo is the finest in the world.
Specimens of animal life from tropical
latitudes used to suffer in health from the
difficulty of reproducing the right atmos-
pheric conditions for them, but in the last
year or two, the G.E.C. Research Depart-
ment, in co-operation with the Zoo
authorities, have succeeded in their
experiments and have contrived to repro-
duce and control at will the tropical
temperatures and sunlight required by the
various occupants to enable them to think
they are in their own native wilds.
The new Reptile House, Monkey House,
and Baboon Terrace are all-electric, and
the new Aquarium mostly electric, the
current being supplied from St. Maryle-
bone Power Station.
The average heat maintained is 80 deg.
Fahrenheit. The greatest difficulty lay in
regulating the heat to suit the individual
requirements of each inmate. This was
overcome by having separate control for
each cage, and indicating lamp-boards
behind the scenes show by tiny coloured
lamps if the temperature rises or falls as
much as 5 deg. If it falls, owing to a
broken fuse or element, or severe climatic
conditions, a bell rings in the Keepers
Room and a green light shows. If a red
light appears, this signifies that the tempera-
ture has risen. Numbers corresponding to
the cages by the side of the lamps make
it easy to locate the trouble and an operator
immediately attends to it.
The Reptile House is roofed with green
Spanish tiles which give the right exotic
touch to the exterior.
The interior has been designed by
scientific and artistic geniuses.
The crocodile lives in an all-electric
swamp, the rocks and sand being also
heated. About 200 connections are neces-
sary to heat and control the temperature of
the water alone. A painted creek forms a
natural-looking background. Ultra-violet
rays and radiant heaters placed out of sight
in the roof flood the cage with sunshine
and prevent steam forming on the glass
front.
In other dens, scenic artists have painted
wonderful jungle scenes, where lianas and
scarlet orchids hang from the banyan trees,
or African deserts full of prickly pear give
the right setting to snakes and giant lizards
from every clime.
The tropical humid heat is confined to
the cages, which are also ventilated
separately from the public corridor.
Twenty miles of electric cable are used
in this Reptile House measuring 180 feet
by 80 feet.
The Monkey House is roofed with vita-
glass, which allows the ultra-violet rays of
the sun to penetrate. Part of the floor
surface of each cage is heated by a tray of
electric elements inserted beneath, which
can be drawn out complete in case of
repairs being required.
The monkeys sit on a swinging perch
underneath the ultra-violet ray lamp which
is fixed in the roof of each cage, to enjoy
their treatment for stated periods every
day.
Bowl fires to warm the air are also fixed
in the roof out of the reach of their investi-
gating paws, and tails. Each cage has
outdoor accommodation reached through a
swing door which the monkeys operate

306
The Electrical Age
Art and Electricity.
By Henry Hyams, F.R.I.B.A., M.I.Struct.E.
(Architect for the new Electric House, Battersea).
An electric lamp might form a fitting symbol of this modern age, and in taking up the problem of designing showrooms for electricity there would seem to be a good opportunity to strike a blow for modernity against tradition. But as the work of designing proceeds, ideals and principles, one after another, are forced aside-
By courtesy of "The Builder"
An example of the Marble Niche, Electrically Lighted from the top, showing Inlay Marble Work.
freedom is fettered on all sides by requirements, materials, workmanship, expense, lack of time, site and so on. To do anything original, too, needs weeks of experiment, and in the rush of modern building operations there is no time for this. However, there still remains the detail designing of the decorative work. In this work, at least, the architect may remain firm to principles to a great extent. It is true, commercialism steps in and insists on requiring a setting for imitation burning logs which give no heat, and imitation candle-sticks made of glass. Yet these things are small details which the architect sometimes successfully abolishes.
At Electric House the aim has been to show the use of electricity as far as possible in an aesthetic manner as well as in a utilitarian. Aesthetically, we are all influenced more than we know by fashions. Absurdly shaped garments, for instance, actually appear beautiful to a person if they are fashionable. The crinoline, the bussel, the hobble skirt, the bee-hive hat and the Oxford trousers have all seemed beautiful to some people at some time or other.
It is the same in architecture and art. We have a period of Neo-Greek architecture, or a season of "The Merry Widow" waltz.
To-day we are all influenced by fashions, and, moreover, we have complexes which make us dislike a thing, however beautiful it may be, simply because it awakens a certain unpleasant, unconscious memory. For this reason a person may dislike a definite shade of orange-or a pointed arch, or a certain perfume. Another point about our sense of beauty is that it changes with the growth of our development. Savages and primitive people require a blow, as it were, on their sense of beauty to awaken it: zig-zag stripes, brilliantly coloured feathers, beads, and patterns; while the more highly evolved people find subtle beauties in things unassuming. In judging a thing aesthetically, therefore, we should

Unnamed: 9: ornament mars many of our electric light fittings—Adams heads
transcription:
The Electrical Age 307
be on our guard against prejudices, caused by fashions or complexes, and we must remember that because a thing does not appear beautiful to us, it does not necessarily follow that it is lacking in beauty : it may be our sense of beauty that is at fault. All things that fulfil their function must really be beautiful. Thus a slender steel column, if it be strong enough to serve its purpose, must be beautifully proportioned. If it appear not so, then it is our association with stone columns of the Greek order which warp our aesthetic sense. Proportion in a column is based on strength and varies according to the material.
Useful questions which one may ask in judging a thing aesthetically are :--
Is it a sham? Does it fulfil its function? Is there anything meaningless or superfluous about it? What kind of emotion does it create in us?
Standards for electric light in many cases are still made after the old candle-stick models with the rim around the socket to catch the candle wax. Electric fires are still made on the gas fire pattern. Meaningless ornament mars many of our electric light fittings—acanthus leaves, Greek fret patterns and egg-and-tongue mouldings, Adams heads, and so on. Ornament in the beginning had a symbolic as well as a functional meaning. It is absurd to repeat it, parrot-like, centuries after it has served its purpose.
On the other hand, there exists to-day a movement in decorative work which seeks truthfulness, suitability, simplicity, cleanliness, and the elimination of the superfluous. Heavy enriched cornices and florid carving are disappearing and in their place we find a simple coved or splayed cornice : the furniture of a smooth surface of inlay-wood.
Wood inlay is a wonderful material for giving different light effects : it has the
THE DRAWING ROOM AT ELECTRIC HOUSE.
nature of mother-of-pearl. The panels here illustrated are photographs from Electric House. The colours vary according to the quality, angle, and quantity of light which reaches them. Silver leaf, slightly lacquered, and gold leaf reflect the light in an attractive manner. The drawing-room at Electric House is an example of its use : the furniture is silvered wood and the cornice, silvered too, is a simple splay designed to reflect the light which is thrown up from behind the picture rail.
Thus in this new Electric House at Battersea, we have endeavoured to introduce a modern note in design.

Unnamed: 10: Author of the article; Conductor of the cookery page
transcription:
308 The Electrical Age

Miss Mackirdy gives a delightful Assortment of dishes for various Meals—
A Cookery Page.

Conducted by Miss Mary Mackirdy
(Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow and Author of "Recipes for You").

It is a pure delight to bake pastry in an electric oven provided the cook does her part, for although the ingredients for pastry are of the simplest—flour, water and some- thing greasy—what an endless variety of atrocities may be the outcome! To the French cook is generally accorded the credit of the perfection of modern pastry, but with a little care we, too, may work wonders which our electric oven completes.

A Sausage Pie.
The filling:—1 lb. pork or other sausages, 1 or 2 tomatoes, 2 or 3 ozs. macaroni boiled till tender, salt, pepper, chopped parsley, stock or water. Cut the sausages in short lengths, put in pie dish in layers with the other ingredients filling the dish well above the level of the rim; fill up with stock or water. When tinned tomatoes are used the stock may not be required.

The cover:—½ lb. flour, 6 ozs. butter or margarine, small ½ teaspoonful baking pow- der, water.

Sieve the flour on to a board, add the fat and cut in rough pieces but do not chop it; add baking powder. Turn all into a bowl, add enough water to make a stiff paste, turn out, press into shape and roll very lightly. Fold the paste in three, turn half way round, press the ends, roll again; repeat this process four times altogether, the last time rolling the paste to the required size. Cut narrow bands, line the rim of the dish, brush it also with water and lay on the cover; trim the edges, cut a hole in centre, brush with egg, mark out leaves with sharp-pointed knife and put into oven heated to 350° or 400°. Switch off the current and cook the pie until the paste is a good brown, possibly about 30 or 40 minutes.

Pineapple Puffs.
Make double the amount of paste when preparing it for the pie, roll it to about 1 inch in thickness, cut in rounds about 3 inches in diameter, brush with egg and bake quickly at same time as pie.

Boil the liquid of a tin of pineapple with 3 or 4 ozs. sugar and the rind and juice of a lemon, add the pineapple and cook for a few minutes. Put a slice of pineapple on each piece of paste, reduce the syrup, colour with a few drops carmine, pour it over the fruit. The puffs may be decorated with chopped pistachio nuts, walnuts, coconut or whipped cream, the latter only if to be served cold. Other fruits might be substituted for pineapple and the result is a very good and easily managed sweet for dinner or lunch.

Almond Biscuits.
Have these ready to put into oven when the pastry is cooked or at the end of a baking, they cook quickly.

½ lb. flour, 3 or 4 ozs. castor sugar, 4 or 5 ozs. butter, ½ teaspoonful baking powder, 1 egg. Some rough sugar and chopped almonds.

Rub the butter into the flour, add sugar and baking powder also the egg beaten; the mixture will at this stage be very crumbly but do not add more liquid, knead it until it is smooth then roll thinly. Cut the biscuits with a cutter, brush the tops with egg and dip the tops only in the sugar and almonds. Bake till a light brown. Various spices and flavourings may be added.

Something Quick for Supper or Lunch.

Something Under the Grill.

Take the skin and bone from a "finnan" and cut in neat pieces, put butter on top, put under grill or in oven with small or halved tomatoes, cook for about 8 or 10 minutes. Serve very hot.

A Spiced Loaf for the Kiddies.

While the vegetables for dinner are cooking this could be steaming at side of plate. Mix 1 lb. good brown meal with 1 teaspoonful bi-carbonate of soda, and 2 teaspoonfuls cream of tartar, salt, 3 or 4 tablespoonfuls currants, a few chopped nuts. 1 teaspoonful cinnamon, 2 tablespoonsful treacle and enough milk to make all into a soft dough. Put into a greased tin and steam for 1 1/4 hours; it may be baked, but is best, I think, steamed. It is very wholesome and is an excellent substitute for cake.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 311
Useful Hints for the Home-Maker.
By "ELECTRA."
THE " AJAX " NURSERY LAMP.
The question of sunlight—both real and artificial—has become so much a leading problem of the day, that I was delighted to come across this mild power Ultra-Violet Ray lamp. It can be used in the home without supervision and with absolute safety, as it is specially designed for children and invalids.
The Ultra-Violet Rays are emitted by the Tungsten filament through the generating bulb which is made of Vitaglass. It is a 300-w. unit, and the light is modified to a lovely golden sun-colour effect. An extra comfort when using this lamp is the very appreciable heat which is radiated from it.
In addition to the " On " and " Off " switch, a " Strong," " Mild," and " Weak " regulator is provided, so that even young babies can enjoy a " Sun Bath," while the same lamp will serve for sun-lighting the nursery or any other room, as well as for close application for invalids and general toning-up.
The design of the "Ajax" Nursery Lamp may be seen from the accompanying illustration, and I need only mention that the copper hood is nickel-plated, as is the tubular rod which can be moved up and down as required in the tube running to the white-enamelled base.
The whole apparatus is very well balanced and supported on this solid base.
" AJAX " NURSERY LAMP. Note the "on" and "off" switch, and Power Regulator.
THE " ULTROZONE " OZONISER.
The beneficial effects of ozone are almost as well-known as the benefits of sunlight, and the small portable model of the " Ultrozone " Ozoniser will prove to be a very useful piece of electrical apparatus. The outstanding feature of this system is that the ozone produced is absolutely free from all oxides of nitrogen.
The small Domestic Model of the " ULTROZONE " OZONISER.
Smoke and stuffiness are banished as if by magic, and 20 minutes will be sufficient to ozonise the atmosphere for about three hours. The consumption of electricity is very small—60 hours for one unit.
The " Ultrozone " portable machine is very neat in a beautifully made mahogany case, and it is moderately priced. Another interesting feature is that it can be obtained with High Frequency Violet Ray attachment.

Unnamed: 9: Inventor of the Square Saucepans and a new Cookerette.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 313

A NEW COOKERETTE.
Women’s inventions naturally have a special interest for us, particularly one by a member of our Association.
Mrs. Holt is already well-known as the inventor of the Square Saucepans, and she has now brought out a small Cookerette specially designed to fill the requirements of flatlets, and for the business woman who has to cook a meal on her return home at the end of the day.
This Cookerette is also just the thing for the square saucepans, and Mrs. Holt claims that she can balance a 6-pint saucepan, a 4-pint, a 3-pint and a 1 1/2-pint saucepan on it at the same time and they will keep boiling, while simultaneously a fair-sized roast is being cooked in the oven.
The enamelled hob is hinged, and it is fitted with a 9in. x 7 1/4in. Hotplate loaded to 1800 watts. A 3-heat switch is supplied, and the oven is provided with several runners so that the shelf can be used where desired, and this Cookerette certainly provides for one of the most efficient uses of heat we have come across.
MRS. HOLTS NEW COOKERETTE.
Note the drop down door, and the arrangement of the saucepans
The Cookerette is made for Mrs. Holt by the Jackson Electric Stove Company, and it is sold at the very reasonable price of £4 19s. 6d.

Unnamed: 9: Honorary Secretary of the Leeds and West Riding E.A.W. branch.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 315

E.A.W. Branch Activities.

NEW BRANCH.
Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o. Ingleby Motors, Sweet Street, Leeds.

A Leeds and West Riding Branch of the Electrical Association for Women has now been formed, and a very successful inaugural meeting took place on January 27th in the Philosophical Hall, Leeds, the speakers being Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, Mr. W. B. Woodhouse, Mrs. L. A. Willson, and Miss C. Haslett.
Dr. Ferranti, who has taken a great interest in the Association since its commencement, spoke of electricity as the great labour saver, and said it was the business of the women of the E.A.W. to realise its advantages.
Mr. Woodhouse said that lighting was not only a matter of health but also of beauty, and here womens artistic sense had a chance of expression. Mrs. Willson and Miss Haslett gave interesting addresses on the objects of the Association and wished the new Branch every success.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 317
"Television." Mr. Baird explained in simple language the operation of the televisor. The lecture was much appreciated by all present.
1st February.—Lecture by W. Greig, Esq., on "Electric Sewing Machines." This was a repetition of a most successful lecture that was given two years ago and was found very helpful, especially by the newer members of the Association.
22nd February.—H. E. Hughes, Esq., of the Scottish Electric Lighting Service Bureau, gave a lecture and demonstration on lighting. The subject of his lecture was "The Magnetism of Light." Visits have been made on several occasions to the Electric Lighting Service Bureau, and this was principally intended for new members of the Association.
29th February.—A. E. Coombs, Esq., District Manager of the Post Office Telephone Department, gave a lecture on "Telephone Service from Within." Mr. Coombs explained the difficulties and trials encountered in the telephone service, and his lecture and demonstration was of very great interest to the members who attended.

■ ■ ■

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. L. Hayes, 1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
A very successful second Annual General Meeting was held at Queens College, Birmingham, on February 23rd, presided over by the President, Lady Brooks.
In the absence, through illness, of Mrs. Hayes, the Honorary Secretary, the arrangements for the Annual Meeting had been capably carried out by Mrs. Hyde.
After the Treasurers report, given by Mrs. Howie, the President introduced Sir Charles Grant Robertson, Vice-Chancellor of the University, who, in an exceedingly interesting and witty speech, referred to the growth of the "scientific mind" amongst women.
He thought that the E.A.W. was doing splendid work toward this end, and wished the Association every success.
Professor Cramp, in supporting what the Vice-Chancellor had already said, stated that he was very pleased to learn that the Association was concerned in the training of young girls in electrical housecraft.
Mr. R. A. Chattock, the City Engineer, in moving the re-election of the President, paid a very well-deserved tribute to the work and influence of Lady Brooks in maintaining a very high level for the Association in Birmingham and District.
In spite of the fact that The King and Queen were visiting Birmingham that day, a very large party sat down to the luncheon.
"Electricity in the Service of Women" was proposed by Colonel Vignoles, the new Director of E.D.A., who gave the meeting some interesting facts and figures concerning the use of electricity for domestic purposes in this country.
Mr. J. T. H. Legge, in proposing the toast, "Electrical Association for Women," referred to the excellent work which could be done by such a body as the E.A.W. in helping to solve the problem of rural electrification.
Mr. Legge expressed his gratification that the E.A.W. had already done such splendid work, and hoped that they would at an early date turn their attention to the question of helping the women in the country districts.
A vote of thanks to the guests was proposed by Mrs. H. K. Beale and responded to by Mr. G. R. J. Parkinson.
An interesting programme is now being arranged for the late spring and early summer.

■ ■ ■

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, "Woodville," Ack Lane, Bramhall, Cheshire.
Our first visit this year was to inspect the electrical apparatus at the Royal Infirmary, and among the host of new impressions received one or two stand out in particular. The throng in the demonstration room—the only demonstration room in the world devoted entirely to X-rays—intent on Dr. Barclays interesting talk on methods and processes, and the two interesting X-ray photographs of a penny in a patients throat and the incredible assortment of pins, screws and needles that had been relished by some child: the tubes that hung poised over the beds for electrical treatment of various kinds; and a grisly memory of the engine room where the enthusiastic electrician showed us how neatly meat (one hoped it was beef) could be cut and cauterised during an operation, and how the tiniest electric lamp could be made to light up the dark tunnel of the throat far into the body.

■ ■ ■

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. L. Hayes, 1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
A very successful second Annual General Meeting was held at Queens College, Birmingham, on February 23rd, presided over by the President, Lady Brooks.
In the absence, through illness, of Mrs. Hayes, the Honorary Secretary, the arrangements for the Annual Meeting had been capably carried out by Mrs. Hyde.
After the Treasurers report, given by Mrs. Howie, the President introduced Sir Charles Grant Robertson, Vice-Chancellor of the University, who, in an exceedingly interesting and witty speech, referred to the growth of the "scientific mind" amongst women.
He thought that the E.A.W. was doing splendid work toward this end, and wished the Association every success.
Professor Cramp, in supporting what the Vice-Chancellor had already said, stated that he was very pleased to learn that the Association was concerned in the training of young girls in electrical housecraft.
Mr. R. A. Chattock, the City Engineer, in moving the re-election of the President, paid a very well-deserved tribute to the work and influence of Lady Brooks in maintaining a very high level for the Association in Birmingham and District.
In spite of the fact that The King and Queen were visiting Birmingham that day, a very large party sat down to the luncheon.
"Electricity in the Service of Women" was proposed by Colonel Vignoles, the new Director of E.D.A., who gave the meeting some interesting facts and figures concerning the use of electricity for domestic purposes in this country.
Mr. J. T. H. Legge, in proposing the toast, "Electrical Association for Women," referred to the excellent work which could be done by such a body as the E.A.W. in helping to solve the problem of rural electrification.
Mr. Legge expressed his gratification that the E.A.W. had already done such splendid work, and hoped that they would at an early date turn their attention to the question of helping the women in the country districts.
A vote of thanks to the guests was proposed by Mrs. H. K. Beale and responded to by Mr. G. R. J. Parkinson.
An interesting programme is now being arranged for the late spring and early summer.

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, "Woodville," Ack Lane, Bramhall, Cheshire.
Our first visit this year was to inspect the electrical apparatus at the Royal Infirmary, and among the host of new impressions received one or two stand out in particular. The throng in the demonstration room—the only demonstration room in the world devoted entirely to X-rays—intent on Dr. Barclays interesting talk on methods and processes, and the two interesting X-ray photographs of a penny in a patients throat and the incredible assortment of pins, screws and needles that had been relished by some child: the tubes that hung poised over the beds for electrical treatment of various kinds; and a grisly memory of the engine room where the enthusiastic electrician showed us how neatly meat (one hoped it was beef) could be cut and cauterised during an operation, and how the tiniest electric lamp could be made to light up the dark tunnel of the throat far into the body.
In the same month, Miss Fitzgerald gave a lecture on "Smoke Abatement" that was at once an indictment of the past generation, a challenge to the present and a hope for the future. Her inspiring talk ought to have

resulted in a 10 per cent. reduction of the guilty chimneys among her audience.
Every member of the party that visited Messrs. Glovers Cable Works at Trafford Park will in future swell the crowd of children, errand boys and unemployed that is always found wherever men are uprooting the roadway and laying dark gray sinuous shapes into the trench prepared. Thanks to the kindness of the management and the skill of our guides, we feel we are experts on cables for ever.
The title of Dr. Catherine Chisholms lecture, "Electricity and Sunlight," seemed a doubly attractive one on the damp, cold evening on which we crowded into the demonstration room of the Manchester Corporation Electricity Showrooms, so kindly lent for the occasion. In her enthralling lecture, Dr. Chisholm covered a wide range, from a description of the movement of waves of light to the miraculous change wrought in the deformed and wasting bones of rickety children by artificial sunlight. In the discussion that followed, the Doctor laid emphasis on the need for proper medical supervision of treatment by artificial sunlight.
Our Annual General Meeting was held in the Lord Mayors Parlour at the Town Hall on Feb. 28th, the Lady Mayoress presiding.
Lady Arthur Grosvenor was elected our President, Miss Ellen Wilkinson, her predecessor, kindly consenting to become a Vice-President.
Dr. Veitch Clark, Medical Officer of Health, gave a most interesting and practical talk on "Food Preservation," and after hearing of the advantages and disadvantages of drying, canning, smoking and pickling—not to mention the pleasant practice, recently forbidden, of adding small doses of poison to the food, we were unanimous that the best way of food preservation, the only way for perfect health, is by refrigeration—rhetorically, of course.
D.M.P.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 319

resulted in a 10 per cent. reduction of the guilty chimneys among her audience.
Every member of the party that visited Messrs. Glovers Cable Works at Trafford Park will in future swell the crowd of children, errand boys and unemployed that is always found wherever men are uprooting the roadway and laying dark gray sinuous shapes into the trench prepared. Thanks to the kindness of the management and the skill of our guides, we feel we are experts on cables for ever.
The title of Dr. Catherine Chisholms lecture, "Electricity and Sunlight," seemed a doubly attractive one on the damp, cold evening on which we crowded into the demonstration room of the Manchester Corporation Electricity Showrooms, so kindly lent for the occasion. In her enthralling lecture, Dr. Chisholm covered a wide range, from a description of the movement of waves of light to the miraculous change wrought in the deformed and wasting bones of rickety children by artificial sunlight. In the discussion that followed, the Doctor laid emphasis on the need for proper medical supervision of treatment by artificial sunlight.
Our Annual General Meeting was held in the Lord Mayors Parlour at the Town Hall on Feb. 28th, the Lady Mayoress presiding.
Lady Arthur Grosvenor was elected our President, Miss Ellen Wilkinson, her predecessor, kindly consenting to become a Vice-President.
Dr. Veitch Clark, Medical Officer of Health, gave a most interesting and practical talk on "Food Preservation," and after hearing of the advantages and disadvantages of drying, canning, smoking and pickling—not to mention the pleasant practice, recently forbidden, of adding small doses of poison to the food, we were unanimous that the best way of food preservation, the only way for perfect health, is by refrigeration—rhetorically, of course.
D.M.P.

Unnamed: 9: Proposed a vote of thanks during the U.C.A.L. works visit.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 321

Our next meeting was one of the most popular of the visits yet arranged. We were agreeably surprised on visiting the Works of the United Chemists Association, Ltd., Cheltenham, to find such a busy and up-to-date works in our own town. Here, amid ideal surroundings, the U.C.A.L. products have been steadily becoming famous. The electrical machines in use were varied and numerous, one machine alone turning out 450 tablets a minute. We were indeed grateful to the Works Chemist and others of the staff for their instructive descriptions and demonstrations. Miss A. M. Andrew proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. H. Miller, Managing Director, for the opportunity afforded us of viewing the Works, also for the dainty tea and souvenir box of U.C.A.L. products presented to each member. Miss E. Woodward seconded.
On February 23rd, a small party of our members joined the Birmingham members in their visit to "The British Industries Fair." There were so many interesting exhibits to view, that the time was all too short. We very much enjoyed meeting the Birmingham members at tea.
Our Annual Meeting and Luncheon, which is fixed for March, is the next fixture on our programme. After the luncheon we shall visit the new Domestic Science Centre, by the invitation of the Cheltenham Education Committee.
A.A.S.

South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Tyler, Electric Service Bureau, Royal Chambers, Park Place, Cardiff.

Our Autumn Session closed with a very successful whist drive held during E.D.A. All-electric Week. Prizes given by the different manufacturers included two bowl fires, "Litlux" bed fitting, table standard and shade, a toaster and kettle. 165 people were present.
The first item on the winter programme was a cookery lecture and demonstration by Miss L. Chapman, of the General Electric Co., Cardiff, this being thoroughly appreciated by all present.
A lecture by Mr. L. Owen, B.Com., "The Electricity Supply Act of 1926," drew forth many questions from the members.
On the 20th January, a very enjoyable dance was held, this being promoted to enable the members to get to know each other better. It proved very satisfactory in every way.

Unnamed: 9: Gave an address during a visit to showrooms in Cardiff
transcription:
The Electrical Age 323
A visit was paid to the new Showrooms of Messrs. Falk, Stadelmann, Ltd., Cardiff. An address was given by Mr. C. G. Morley New, City Electrical Engineer, after which we were entertained to a sumptuous tea.
A lecture by Mrs. R. A. Clement, on "Transforming the Homes of Britain," was very instructive and enjoyable.
Our visit to the South Wales News Printing Works was most interesting, and we are still wondering how it is possible to produce our "Daily" for one penny per copy. After a two hours "tour" of the different departments, we were entertained to tea, a fitting climax to the courtesy and kindness shown to us by Messrs. Duncan and Son, and members of their staff.
The first of a series of lectures arranged by the Electrical Contractors Association was given by Mr. R. L. Booth, Chairman of the E.C.A., on Thursday, 1st of March. Members were shown the correct way to put on a lamp adaptor, plugs, connectors, replace a fuse wire, etc. It is needless to say how very much the members appreciated this.
Our first Annual General Meeting will take place on Wednesday, 28th March. Miss Haslett, our Director, has promised to be with us, so we are looking forward to this meeting with great pleasure.
J.T.
North East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm, Carliol House, Newcastle-on-Tyne.
The Winter Conferences for the North-East Coast members of the E.A.W. are almost at an end. The last Conference is to take the form of an afternoon or evening in the Cinema at Carliol House, when a varied programme will be shown.
A lecture in December, given by Mr. J. R. W. Rae, on "The Use and Misuse of Electrical Apparatus," was instructive and aroused a very helpful discussion.
On January 26th, Dr. Barrowman dealt with the subject of "Electric Therapy in Its Relation to Public Health." The lecture was made interesting by the display of lantern slides and some medical appliances.
Mr. J. S. Cooper, of the Lighting Service Bureau, gave a delightful lecture on the "Decorative Value of Electric Light," on February 9th. Mr. Cooper demonstrated in the model rooms new ways of lighting, and how the value of such lighting schemes could be enhanced by the introduction of colour. An indication that the lecture was appreciated may be gathered from the fact that numerous questions were asked having reference to individual lighting problems, and it was Mr. Coopers pleasure to furnish all the information asked for.
