Unnamed: 9: Architect of the House of the Future giving a talk.
Unnamed: 10: Architect of the House of the Future
transcription:
324 The Electrical Age

E.A.W. London Activities.

The Spring Programme arranged for London members has been very popular and all the fixtures have been very well attended.
Since January we have been to the B.B.C. Studios; the Underground Railway Company’s Power House at Lots Road; The Hurley Machine Co., who gave a lecture and demonstration on “The Home Electric Laundry”, and the new Showrooms of The Westminster Electric Supply Corporation.
Then we had a special day at the Ideal Home Exhibition, when over 100 members availed themselves of the kind invitation of the British Thomson-Houston Co., who conducted us in small parties over the “House of the Future.”
The party then proceeded to the stand of the Hotpoint Electric Appliance Co., where members were particularly interested in, among other things, the Floor Polisher Attachment for the Premier-Duplex Vacuum Cleaner.
Our hosts very kindly provided refreshments for the party at the Grill Cafe, and it is hardly necessary to say how much this interval was appreciated. Everyone was delighted, too, with the opportunity of hearing Mr. Duncan, the architect of the much-talked of “House of the Future,” who gave a most interesting explana-
tion of some of the ideas expressed in this house, and the vote of thanks proposed by Alderman Mrs. Hammer to Mr. Leevers, of the B.T.H. Co.; Mr. Rawlinson, of the Hotpoint Electrical Appliance Co.; and Mr. Duncan, was enthusiastically given.
During the afternoon the E.A.W. met again at the stand of the General Electric Co., where we were met by Mr. Jeary and Major Leith. After an interesting tour of inspection round this beautifully arranged exhibit, the party was entertained to tea at the Pillar Hall by the kindness of the G.E.C. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded by Mrs. Ll. B. Atkinson on behalf of the members.
In addition to these fixtures, the Social Sub-Committee have held three very successful “At Homes” in the Club Room, at 46, Kensington Court, W.8, and two further “At Homes” have been arranged to take place in May and June.
The three lectures for cooks, given by Miss Dorothy Vaughan and Mr. A. H. Hunter, in the E.A.W. Model Electric Kitchen, were most successful, and in response to the many requests received, a further lecture-demonstration on “Electric Cooking” was given by Miss D. Vaughan on March 29th.

Colonel Crompton, who has been
aptly described as "the grand old
man of the electrical industry," has
just published his reminiscences under
the title of "R. E. Crompton—
Reminiscences."
In this book, which is dedicated
to his wife, who has been "during
almost 60 years my courageous fellow
worker and devoted companion," we
learn something of the life of a
pioneer, not only in the electrical
world, but in motoring and mechanical
road transport.
A friend of the late Emperor of
Austria, he relates many interesting
adventures in Vienna, and also in Paris
in connection with his early electrical
work on the Continent.
This "Grand Old Man" of 83 is still hale and hearty, taking a
great interest in all matters pertaining to the progress of the electrical
world and keeping a kindly eye on the youngest recruit—the E.A.W.

transcription:
EDITORIAL.
THE THIRD ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING which was held at the Institution of Electrical Engineers, on April 17th, was a great success, although it showed very clearly that much more time must be left in future for discussion with the Branches regarding the business of the Association.
A pleasant surprise was the presence of our new President, Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, who later in the day received the guests at the very successful Ball which was held at the Hotel Cecil.
Amongst the new officers who were elected were Mrs. Llewelyn Atkinson, Hon. Treasurer, Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti, Vice-Chairman, Alderman Mrs. Hammer remaining as Chairman for a further year. We were pleased to elect as Members of the Council Mrs. Hollis, of West Ham, and Miss Gladys Sharp, who will represent a new interest on the Council, that of the woman worker in the electrical industry.
The invitation from the North East Coast Branch to hold our Annual Conference in 1929 at Newcastle-on-Tyne during the North East Coast Exhibition, was accepted.
* * *
THE ELECTRICAL CONVENTION AT BATH.—The Womens Day at the Incorporated Municipal Electrical Associations Annual Convention now seems to have become an institution, and the special day set aside this year at Bath proved a very happy affair.
Contingents of E.A.W. Members arrived for the Womens Day from London, Birmingham, Cheltenham, South Wales and Gloucestershire, in addition to the many women who were attending the whole Convention from Scotland, Ireland, and the North East Coast.
At the discussion which followed the reading of the Papers in the morning, Mrs. Lamb, of Manchester, brilliantly led the way with one of her witty and clever speeches which are becoming a feature of such gatherings.
The luncheon arranged by the I.M.E.A. proved to be a great success and was followed by a visit to the Electrical Exhibition, where we were pleased to see that many of the suggestions put forward in our Cooker Report had been adopted by the manufacturers.
The special interest of the day was centred in the Reception given by Madame Sarah Grand, the Mayoress of Bath, who is so well-known as a great novelist, and who took part in many of the early battles for womens emancipation.
A visit to the Roman Baths concluded a very happy and memorable day at Bath.
* * *
THE ELECTRICAL OUTLET CAMPAIGN.—Unfortunately there was not sufficient time to discuss the Outlet Campaign at the Annual General Meeting of the Association, and the drawing up of the Special Womens Specification has, therefore, been deferred until the Council Meeting in July.
It was generally agreed, however, by all the Branch representatives that this was a Campaign that could not be hurried, as there was so much for the members to discuss and also to learn about this all-important question of electrical outlets.
Meetings on the campaign are being held throughout the country, and a most enthusiastic meeting was held at the new Club Room on May 17th, when the point of view of the London members was taken. A report comes to hand of a well-attended meeting on the subject in Glasgow, with Miss Mary Mackirdy in the chair, when over 60 members took part in the discussion.
The valuable suggestions already received from Glasgow, Manchester and Birmingham will be incorporated in the National Womens Specification which will be issued after the July Council Meeting, when arrangements will be made for the second stage of the campaign to be entered upon in the early autumn.

The Electrical Age 329

The New President.

Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley.

___________________

The E.A.W. is very fortunate in having secured as its second President, Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, whose interest in all matters electrical is so well-known.

As wife of the Minister of Transport, we have every reason to believe that she took a very active interest in the passage of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1926.

Of special interest to women is the fact that she works for a firm of decorators in London, and her advice in connection with house decoration is sought for by many well-known people. To listen to a lecture by her on colour schemes and house decoration is a sheer delight. She has always taken a great interest in the British Film Industry and has recently joined an English film company, where her activities lie in working with the producer in the production of films.

In a somewhat different field she gives her practical support to such excellent movements as the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and she is particularly interested in the National Orthopaedic Hospital, being the Chairman of Buttercup Day.

During her busy life she finds time to interest herself in many charities, and works energetically on the committees for many balls and functions for raising money for needy and worthy objects.

One frequently sees articles from her pen in literary and society papers, and always one can depend upon that freshness of outlook and originality for which Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley is so universally known.

Politics, too, claim some of her time, and she is President of the New Forest and Christchurch Womens Conservative Association, and Vice-Chairman of the South-West Area National Union of Conservative and Unionist Associations.

In addition to her beautiful house in Westminster, she has a lovely country home at Romsey, Hampshire, where she takes an intimate interest in the affairs of the district, acting, amongst other things, as a Member of the local Board of Guardians.

We are happy indeed in having as our President one of those busy and capable women who can always find time to help just one more worth while association.

Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley on Electric Cooking:---

It has come to my knowledge that certain persons are making capital out of the statement which is purported to have been made by me in regard to the cost of Cooking by Electricity. The statement entirely misrepresents my point of view.

My declaration was "that when the Electricity Act was fully in power, every woman would be able not only to light and heat her house by electricity but also to cook by it."

Already in a large number of districts to-day, Electric Cooking compares favourably on the score of cost with other methods and is much to be preferred on the ground of cleanliness and ease of operation.

Molly Ashley

330

The Electrical Age

A Page for Girl Guides.

That Good Deed. By Gladys F. Sharp.

Author of “The House of the Lighted Window,” one of the best sellers of the season.

Through the reverie-producing monotony of the whirring suction-cleaning motor there came to Patrol-Leader Jane Smith a cry of distress, faint yet hauntingly mournful. She hastily switched off the current and listened. Again the cry sounded through the house, this time a little louder, more compelling. She distinguished her own name and, recognising her mother’s voice, stood rooted to the spot, her mind running over an appalling list of accidents which might have happened. Her first-aid training would be useful at last and, as for the third time that heartrending call came from the kitchen, Jane Smith ran to her room, collected her medical outfit and hastened down the stairs.

Her mother turned as she entered and the expression on her face prepared Jane for the very worst. It came:

“The cooker is quite dead and I have just put in a fruit cake.”

Undismayed at this unsuspected calamity, Jane tossed her first-aid box on to the table, gathered a screw-driver, pliers and fuse wire, studied the diagram of circuits for a moment and mounted the ladder. The main switch crashed off, the fuse was withdrawn, new fuse wire substituted; another crash and the element wires pinged as the heat surged through them.

“Possibly the fault will have blown itself clear,” said Jane. “If, however, the fuse blows again then we must find the fault.”

Drawing by Miss W. D. Sharp, Captain, 2nd Battersea Rise Girl Guides.

Patrol-Leader Jane Smith studying the diagram of Circuits.

334 The Electrical Age

Electric Light in the Poultry House.

By R. Borlase Matthews, Wh. Ex., A.M.I.C.E., M.I.E.E.

who conducts his own Electric Farm in Surrey, where many new and novel experiments on the application of electricity to Farm Work have been carried out.

The use of electric light in the poultry house to give the birds a longer working day during the winter months is an interesting and novel way of increasing the winter egg supply. Experiments conducted by the author have proved to his complete satisfaction that by using electric light at a total cost for the whole period of 2 1/2d. per hen (i.e., the value of one egg in the winter) and giving the hens a day of from twelve to fourteen hours (with ten hours sleep every night) it is possible to obtain an increase of from ten to fifty per cent. in the winter egg supply, and this at a time when eggs bring in the highest prices.

This experience is not by any means unique, in fact, the practice has now passed the experimental stage, and is becoming one of the most important commercial innovations introduced into the poultry world during recent years.

It should be remembered that the only object of lighting the poultry houses is to increase the feeding and exercise time. This does not strain the birds in any way, in fact, their health is not affected, as the hen is of sub-tropical origin, where the winter days are much longer, and accordingly the digestive organs are probably better suited to longer winter hours. What the writer always marvels at, is that the hen lays as many eggs as she does when in an unlighted house during the winter months, considering that she must be in a half starved condition during part of the long winter nights.

The lighting of poultry houses should not be carried out in any haphazard manner. Experience shows that when the following rules are observed no trouble is experienced with the birds and excellent results are obtained:—
(1) The intensity of the light over the feeding and scratching area should not be less than one foot candle.
(2) The lamps should be hung about six feet from the floor.
(3) All rays of light should be reflected on the feeding spaces.
(4) Suitable reflectors should be used. The best types are the vitreous enamelled dispersive type and the glass industrial prismatic dispersive type.
(5) The lights should not be suddenly switched off, as hens cannot see in the dark. There are a number of ways of dimming the lights to produce an artificial dusk and dawn. Special wiring schemes may be introduced or cheap alarm clocks can be used to switch off certain lights at a pre-arranged time, or elaborate automatic self-winding electric time clocks with astronomical attachments, to enable them to follow the varying time of sunrise and sunset, (in fact, clocks that do everything but talk) can be set to control all the lights on the farm. On very large poultry farms, these automatic clocks are very suitable, as their cost, when spread over a large flock of birds, is not excessive.
(6) The hours of lighting should be regular. Birds subjected to irregular lighting fall into an early moult.
(7) The birds should be allowed from ten to eleven hours sleep.
(8) Lighting should commence in October and stop in March.

An outstanding feature of this type of incuba- tor is its ability to permit of continuous hatching, that is, the trays can be filled in turn, and hatch in turn. In fact, they become regular chicken factories, chicks being removed regularly every Monday and Thursday. This type of incubator is ideal for the small holder who wishes to specialize in the day-old chick business, for though

Hoovers and Foster Mothers.
The chief advantage of the electric hoover is the even distribution of heat, which is such a simple matter to obtain with electric heaters, whereas a badly regulated central heat, disturbed by every change of air current is all that is possible with the older types of oil and coal burners. A clear, fresh atmosphere is also difficult to obtain when using coal or oil, but with the electric heater there is nothing to contaminate the air, and the chicks breathe pure fresh air all the time.

Ultra-Violet Ray Treatment.
What is, no doubt, one of the latest developments in the electrified poultry house is the use of ultra-violet lamps for treating fowls. During the past few years the Rowett Research Institute of Aberdeen have conducted a series of valuable experi-
ments to determine the effect of treating poultry with the rays.

Young chickens, especially those born in the early part of the season, are very susceptible to leg weakness, which is a disease closely related to rickets. As ultra-violet radiation had already proved effective in the case of young children suffering from rickets, it was tried on chickens suffering from leg weakness, with the result that it was found to act as a supplement to the antirachitic factor of foodstuffs and thus minimise the tendency to this disease.

The experiments carried out on laying hens have also shown very promising results. By treating hens in this way more eggs have been obtained during the winter months, and the hatchability of the eggs thus obtained was considerably improved. Another important factor from the market- ing point of view was, that the quantity of lime in the shell of the eggs of irradiated hens was much greater than in the eggs of untreated hens.

Miss Merz, who is a member of the well-known firm of electrical engineers bearing that name, devotes her life to innumerable good causes in Newcastle.
In her capacity as Justice of the Peace, she takes a special interest in the Juvenile Courts which she attends every week, and is a member of the Probation Committee.
In addition, she runs and manages two lodging houses for women and girls and is honorary treasurer of the Burslem Grove Settlement which she was practically instrumental in starting.
To know something of all the excellent
movements which Miss Merz is helping forward, mostly those connected with the "lower dog," would leave one wondering how she ever finds time for rest or leisure.
Even so, she was one of the first women to realise the importance of such an organi- sation as the E.A.W. and to give it her practical support.

The Electrical Age 337

The Swindon Road Domestic Subjects Centres,
Cheltenham.

It is mainly due to the progressive policy of Miss G. M. Dawson Caves that so many domestic electrical appliances are in use at the Cheltenham Domestic Subjects Centres.
The elementary school to which the Domestic Subjects Centres are attached is a modern one with a definite practical bias.
There are four distinct Centres in a separate building for cookery, laundrywork, needlework and combined domestic subjects; they consist of a flat, with kitchen, sitting room and bedrooms.
Girls attend the Centres from 11 until 14 years of age; 2 1/2 days weekly are devoted to domestic subjects, the remainder of the work is spent in the school where special emphasis is laid on the three R’s. The Centres are exceptionally well equipped with electrical appliances, including electrical cookers, washboiler, boiling ring, irons and kettles, in addition to the usual coal range and gas cooker.
Both practical and experimental work receive proportionate time, and it is found that the girls soon understand the use of electrical apparatus.
There is close co-operation with the Electricity Department, whose Demonstrator, Miss A. Stemp, has given short lectures to the staff and the girls.
Miss Dawson Caves, whose picture appears on our Portrait Page, is an active member of the Cheltenham Branch of the E.A.W., having been elected this year as Honorary Treasurer.

Unnamed: 9: Author of the article and inventor of Synchronome electric clocks.
transcription:
338

The Electrical Age

Electric Clocks.
Uniform and Accurate Time in the Home.

By F. Hope-Jones, M.I.E.E., F.R.A.S.

Few have done more to improve the punctuality of the community than Mr. Hope-Jones. He was Chairman of the British Horological Institute for some years, also one of the founders and Chairman of the Radio Society of Great Britain. Inventor of the "Synchronome" System of electric clocks, he introduced the six dot seconds which gives us Greenwich time by wireless.

No two clocks in our homes ever tell the same time. Each one is striving to achieve the impossible and does its little best, but as independent units, their task is hopeless.
Is there not something pitiable in this happy-go-lucky method of time-keeping, something pathetic in the idea of thousands of separate and independent clocks all attempting the impossible? They cannot keep correct time for any considerable period, much less can they succeed in keeping together, and it is absurd to expect them to do more than they already accomplish. The real mistake lies in asking them to do as much.
Absolute accuracy of time-keeping is impossible of attainment. Until three years ago, when the "Synchronome" Free Pendulum was installed at Greenwich, even the most perfect clocks in our observatories were usually found in error if two or three cloudy nights occurred in succession and the astronomers were unable to correct them by the stars. How then can we expect to obtain accuracy from the ordinary mantelshelf clock, with its short pendulum and the quality of its works so often made subservient to the ornamentation of the case?
The more one thinks of this, the more one is forced to the conclusion that mere improvement in the quality of clocks generally used will not prove a satisfactory solution of the matter, and that it is necessary to strike at the root of the whole evil, their individuality and independence.
If ever there was a job for electricity, this is it. Just a single wire concealed by the picture rail from clock to clock throughout the house, and you may have uniform and accurate time in every room; incidentally, the clocks will not require winding up, because clock-works are dispensed with.
The master clock, which we illustrate in the margin, is in the Club Room. It is the only one which measures time, and is, therefore the only one which has a pendulum. Its duty is to send an impulse to the other clocks, which, however, can hardly be called clocks, because they are only faces with one wheel and a magnet behind each.

Photo of the New Electric Clock in the E.A.W. Club Room.

transcription:
340
The Electrical Age
The Value of Refrigeration in Winter.
By A. H. Hunter.
The value of Refrigeration during the Summer months is quite obvious to every house- keeper, but the question might arise: "Of what use is a Refrigerator in the Winter?" To this question, Mr. Hunter, who is an expert on the question of Refrigeration, gives a very convincing reply.
During the past few years the factor in our home lives which has undergone the most change, the most marked advance- ment, is the standard of hygiene observed by families in their domestic routine.
A few years ago, the menace of flies, the dangers of dust from old-fashioned stoves, the effects of humid atmosphere and the ravages of bacteria in the air and in food- stuffs were largely ignored or, at least, not properly understood. In cleaning, brooms and dusters were the universal distributors (not collectors) of bacteria infected dust from all parts of the house.
Foodstuffs lay about in badly ventilated larders which formed the paradise of flies and the settling place of dust chased from floors or hangings by the action of the ferocious broom. Perishable foods lay exposed on plates, perhaps protected by a piece of muslin and perhaps not, open to the effect of our humid atmosphere which incubated bacteria in the most perfect manner possible. In the summer or in a super-heated kitchen in winter, meat and such like things went bad in half a day— and were thrown away. Milk went sour within a few hours of its being delivered— and had to be made into junket or bread- cakes. Otherwise it had to undergo that pernicious process, "scalding." Salads wilted, meat pastes "went off," fruit rotted, and a dozen other unpleasantries beset the anxious housewife.
In those days very few gave a thought to the fact that all these dire calamities were due simply and solely to the growth and activity of bacteria.
People did not realise that much of such bacteria was within the foodstuffs as a natural constituent and that the naturally humid heat of the atmosphere encouraged it rapidly to develop beyond the limits of a certain "safe" standard.
The post-war period, however, started with a general employment in the home of many of the new factors of hygienics revealed to us in the hard school of experience.
The virulence of bacteria and their menace to a healthy existence became more thoroughly appreciated and refrigera- tion was sought to combat it.
The public wakened to the fact that cold storage of some kind was absolutely necessary, if only for the purpose of avoiding waste. Conditions of living had changed and it was no longer possible casually to throw away meat, vegetables, fruit or milk which had "gone off." Such extravagance could not be afforded.
Important as the factor of refrigeration in the home has become, however, there seems still to be a proportion of the public who do not yet know exactly what refrigera- tion really is.
The term as usually applied means the actual freezing of perishable foodstuffs to enable them to be marketed at a great distance from the source of supply. In ordinary domestic use, however, this complete freezing is not only unnecessary but is actually harmful to certain classes of foodstuffs, as it causes undesirable changes to take place in their physical and chemical structure. We must look upon Household

Unnamed: 9: Subject of a correction regarding her age in the journal.
transcription:
342

The Electrical Age

In the winter, meals are more substan-
tial and more serious affairs. The hostess
is more likely to stand or fall by their
condition. Foodstuffs have to be bought
well in advance and must be served in the
very pink of condition. Out of season
fruits and delicacies have to be provided
and much highly perishable matter has to
be handled as though its nature were
stable and unaffected by heat and time and
humidity.

For these reasons the hostess herself
frequently has to work fast and hard
within a few hours of the arrival of her
guests. Nothing must be left to chance.
But nothing can be prepared at leisure
beforehand because much of it would not
keep. In addition to the hostess being thus
prevented from attending to the more per-
sonal matters which crave attention at the
time of any function in the home, her
domestic staff is frequently driven off its
legs on account of the same condition which
can only spring its urgency at the last
moment.

This is where the refrigerator is a boon
in the relief of the situation.

Consider for the moment the giving of a
dinner on a certain day—Wednesday for
instance. On Monday or Tuesday soup
stock, having been boiled even earlier
than this, can be placed in the refrigerator
and forgotten until it is wanted. Fish and
joints and seasoned meats can be pur-
chased a week previously, if necessary.
Salads can be prepared on the Monday or
Tuesday. Mushrooms can be peeled, sand-
wiches cut, sauces of all kinds prepared,
sweets—even iced sweets—made, fresh fruit
drinks prepared, eggs shelled and chopped,
and a dozen other things.

Obviously, when it is thus possible to
make such preparations in advance a
tremendous personal responsibility is taken
from the shoulders of the hostess. Fur-
thermore, it is much more fair to the
domestic staff who are thus relieved of the
necessity for achieving the almost impos-
sible—the feat of doing properly about
half a dozen things at once only an hour
or so before the function is due to
commence.

From this it will be appreciated that
refrigeration in the home is not a purely
seasonal thing to be considered only when
we are favoured with brief intervals of
summer weather. Its application to all
the year round housekeeping becomes
perfectly obvious to anyone who thinks for
a moment upon the subject.

The Electrical Age 343
Useful Hints for the Home-Maker.
By "ELECTRA."
A COMBINED CLEANER AND POLISHER.
Housewives have long been asking for a machine that could be used both as a vacuum cleaner and as a floor polisher, and it is obvious that for people of moderate means the outlay necessary for two pieces of apparatus is considerable.
The makers of the "Premier-Duplex" Vacuum Cleaner have now solved this problem by making a polisher which can easily and in a few minutes be attached to the cleaner.
Showing simple method of converting the "Premier-Duplex" Cleaner into a Floor Polisher.
All you have to do is to remove the brush and belt from the cleaner, and close the brush guard. Next remove the bag and close the exhaust orifice with the attachment provided.
Then you place polisher over the nozzle of the cleaner, and it is adjusted and kept in position by turning a screw.
Finally, you fix the belt over the shaft in the same way as for the revolving brush when doing the carpet, and the polisher is ready for use.
To all fortunate possessors of "Premier-Duplex" Vacuum Cleaners I would recommend their Floor Polisher as well.
THE "XCEL" TOURIST IRON.
It is now generally agreed that an iron is a necessary and indispensable item when travelling, whether it be for business or on holiday.
I think the "Xcel" Tourist Iron illustrated here satisfies practically all possible requirements.
Showing the Iron ready for use. Handle folded down for packing
It is light in weight, only 2 1/4 lbs., it can be used on any and every supply voltage, from 90 v. to 250 v., and it is fitted with a folding handle which turns down neatly and compactly on to the body of the iron when not in use.
The measurements of this "Xcel" Iron with the handle folded for packing are interesting: 5 1/2 ins. long, 2 1/8 ins. wide, and 1 1/8 ins. deep. It is heavily nickel-plated, mirror finish, and the price is moderate.
(A further note by "Electra" appears on 351.)

344
The Electrical Age
Our Portrait Page.
Interesting Personalities in the E.A.W.

Miss Q. F. COPPEN, as we have always known her in the E.A.W., has now become Mrs. George E. Green, and we would offer her our sincere congratulations and all good wishes for her future happiness.
Miss Coppen, who is a Founder Member of the E.A.W., commenced her career as a shorthand typist with Messrs. Purcell & Nobbs, electrical engineers, eventually becoming secretary both to the firm and in a private capacity to Mr. Walter Nobbs, M.I.Mech.E., consulting engineer.
It was during her seven years with this company that she gained her knowledge of domestic electric water heating methods.
Since leaving this firm she has held a similar position with Messrs. George Green & Co., where her work has resulted in the happy position of becoming Mrs. Green.
The Members who attended the last Sessions Evening Classes will remember the charming and informative paper which Miss Coppen gave on Domestic Water Heating; later on she gave a similar address to the Ashford Branch of the E.A.W.
By courtesy of "Electricity."
Miss Q. F. Coppen, whose marriage to Mr. George E. Green took place recently.

MISS DAWSON CAVES, who is the Organiser of Domestic Subjects and Needlework for the Cheltenham Education Committee, is a woman whose vision and personality has been translated into very practical channels in the work which she has done in connection with the Swindon Road Domestic Subjects Centres, Cheltenham.
Trained at the Battersea Polytechnic, she holds 1st Class and Honours Diplomas in Domestic Subjects, Needlecraft and Hygiene. She is Examiner for the Union of Educational Institutions and Superintendent of the Womens Training Class for the Ministry of Labour.
She is also one of those leaders who is able to command the loyalty and respect of her staff, and in addition she is an enthusiast for the electrical method of housekeeping.
MISS G. M. DAWSON CAVES, M.I.H., A.R.San.I

Our Portrait Page.
Interesting Personalities in the E.A.W.

Miss Q. F. COPPEN, as we have always known her in the E.A.W., has now become Mrs. George E. Green, and we would offer her our sincere congratulations and all good wishes for her future happiness.
Miss Coppen, who is a Founder Member of the E.A.W., commenced her career as a shorthand typist with Messrs. Purcell & Nobbs, electrical engineers, eventually becoming secretary both to the firm and in a private capacity to Mr. Walter Nobbs, M.I.Mech.E., consulting engineer.
It was during her seven years with this company that she gained her knowledge of domestic electric water heating methods.
Since leaving this firm she has held a similar position with Messrs. George Green & Co., where her work has resulted in the happy position of becoming Mrs. Green.
The Members who attended the last Sessions Evening Classes will remember the charming and informative paper which Miss Coppen gave on Domestic Water Heating; later on she gave a similar address to the Ashford Branch of the E.A.W.
By courtesy of "Electricity."
Miss Q. F. Coppen, whose marriage to Mr. George E. Green took place recently.

MISS DAWSON CAVES, who is the Organiser of Domestic Subjects and Needlework for the Cheltenham Education Committee, is a woman whose vision and personality has been translated into very practical channels in the work which she has done in connection with the Swindon Road Domestic Subjects Centres, Cheltenham.
Trained at the Battersea Polytechnic, she holds 1st Class and Honours Diplomas in Domestic Subjects, Needlecraft and Hygiene. She is Examiner for the Union of Educational Institutions and Superintendent of the Womens Training Class for the Ministry of Labour.
She is also one of those leaders who is able to command the loyalty and respect of her staff, and in addition she is an enthusiast for the electrical method of housekeeping.

The Electrical Age 345
A Home-Makers Views on the "Outlet" Campaign
By Mrs. Walter Lawson.
Women who use electricity for domestic purposes are finding that the wiring of their homes is inadequate, and that without incurring considerable extra expense, they must remain outside the magic circle of those whose aim is to do everything electrically.
in the domestic uses of electricity, and except by virtue of some specially drawn up specification, just provide for the lighting circuits and leave it at that. 
The female mind, however, is very practical when it is a question of household fittings and what we desire is something
A Picture of the E.A.W. Model Electric Kitchen at Kensington Court, which has just been re-equipped with all the latest domestic electric appliances. The Kitchen is well provided with Electrical "Outlets" which are placed waist-high on the wall.
The "Outlet" Campaign has been instigated by the E.A.W. in order that women may band together and proclaim their grievances, so that the authorities will lend an ear to their outpourings, and henceforth see fit to meet their requirements.
Evidently the architects, builders, wiring contractors, or others, responsible for household electrical arrangements, have not kept pace with modern developments
to produce warmth, light, and power, how, when and where we need it.
It sounds very easy till one goes into the question and then one realises there are difficulties.
The conditions vary in different localities according to the cost of current, and, of course, individual requirements vary to some extent. Tariffs which encourage the free use of current are rapidly being adopted by supply departments, and where

Unnamed: 9: Mr. Stanley Baldwins residence, Astley Hall, has been recently wired.
Unnamed: 10: Owner of the residence mentioned in the advertisement
transcription:
346	The Electrical Age

these tariffs exist there is no excuse for leaving out a sufficient number of large and small outlets in planning installations of dwelling houses, and architects should be induced to recognise this.
Where the cost of current is high, and is likely to remain so, large outlets will not be much in demand, but there are certain uses to which electricity can be put within the reach of everyone irrespective of the price at which the current is sold, and it is here that the demand for outlets should be invariably satisfied.
It is, for instance, most inconvenient in using a vacuum cleaner to have to remove a lamp from its holder at the risk of damaging it, and plug in an adaptor.
Outlets at convenient positions would obviate this.
The electric iron which is now used universally, whatever the price of the current, should always have an outlet provided for its use. The kettle and the toaster are other examples which call for convenience in connecting up when and where required. Lighting fittings are often found to be irrevocably fixed in the wrong places, and the absence of extra outlets prevents the housewife from supplementing the centre light by portable reading lamps, or gaining an artistic effect by the use of a standard lamp.
The conclusion one comes to is that no house that is wired should be without outlets for the use of small portable power consuming devices.
Many houses are being planned, or are in course of building which will be wired in a manner totally inadequate to the ultimate requirements of their future tenants. Why resign oneself, and accept their shortcomings with the fatalism of the East?
Let us, then, be up and doing with the " Outlet " Campaign, and try to move forward with the spirit of progress so well expressed by the E.A.W., which I am convinced will go ahead and can be relied upon to achieve its object.

The Electrical Age 347
A Cookery Page.
Conducted by Miss Mary Mackirdy
(Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow, and Author of "Recipes for You").
Some Delicious Summer Dishes.
The very decided trend of the present
day, for the greater use of uncooked fruits
and vegetables is one to be encouraged by
the housekeeper; there is the physical as
well as the monetary saving, the latter
represented by the greater bulk of food
with its constituents conserved and its
elusive vitamins untampered with.
The other side to the question is the low
consumption of current, which does not seem
to fit in with the name of our Journal
but I am certain that no housekeeper will
complain when she has tried and sampled
these dishes and totalled expenditure of
heat.
Mayonnaise of Fish.
Many kinds of fish may be used for this
dish—fillets of sole, whiting, pieces of
cooked salmon, etc. Some good mayonnaise
sauce, lettuce, tomatoes, cress,
cooked potatoes.
When fillets of sole or other similar ones
are used, season them and squeeze over a
few drops of lemon juice, fold them to form
a fan-shape, put on a buttered tin and bake
for a few minutes.
Put some finely shredded lettuce down
the centre of a dish; coat the fillets when
cold with mayonnaise, arrange them overlapping
on the lettuce and garnish with
little tomatoes and cress.
Sprinkle the centre of each fillet with red
pepper and put a bunch of potatoes cut in
dice at each end of the dish.
They might be dished in a circle and the
potatoes piled up in the centre. The cook
with initiative will manage to work out
many ideas with various vegetables, fish,
and meat.
The sauce:—I consider this recipe the
best I know: 1 raw yolk, 1 hard boiled
yolk, 4 tablespoonfuls salad oil, 2 tablespoonfuls
vinegar or lemon juice, at least
½ teaspoonful each of salt, pepper, mustard
and castor sugar.
Beat the yolks in a small bowl with a
wooden spoon till smooth, then fix a wet
cloth round the bowl to make it secure.
Drop in slowly the oil, stirring constantly
and stirring one way; next add the acid
being doubly careful at this stage not to
reverse the stirring, then season. The
addition of 1 or 2 tablespoonfuls whipped
cream to this sauce before serving makes it
delicious.
Banana and Orange Salad.
Take the skin with all the white pith from
1 or 2 oranges, cut in thin slices across and
take out pips; arrange in the centre of a
dish. Peel as many bananas as may be
required, cut in long pieces and roll in
chopped nuts; place these round the
oranges.
Finish off the dish with lettuce finely
shredded or in little leaves; when the
latter is used put some of the sauce in each
leaf.
Cucumber Cups.
Cut a cucumber in lengths of about 1½ or
2 inches, hollow them leaving sufficient
space to hold the mixture.
Mix some chopped cooked lobster, salmon,
chicken, white fish or whatever may be
at hand, with enough mayonnaise to
moisten, fill up the cups, fringe a long-shaped
radish and fix it in the centre with
a little fine cress. The cups are then
served on a bed of shredded lettuce. The
result should be a very attractive dish

The Electrical Age 351
Books Received.
“Women’s Work in Modern England,”
by Vera Brittain.
Miss Brittain, one of our foremost
women journalists, has given us an inter-
esting and very readable book on the
different kinds of professions and businesses
which are open to women at the present
time.
For those who are interested in careers
for their daughters or for themselves, the
book will give some very useful information.
It contains a very complete and detailed
bibliography, and at the same time treats
the whole problem of women in industry
and commerce as a very human and under-
standable subject.
Miss Brittain refers very sympathetically
to the work of the Women’s Engineering
Society and the Electrical Association for
Women, which she thinks is doing much
to bring happiness and health into our
homes.
We heartily recommend this book to all
our readers. It is published by Noel
Douglas, 38, Great Ormond Street, W.C.1.
Price, 6s.
DAME HENRIETTA BARNETT has
sent us a charming booklet, entitled, “The
Story of the Growth of the Hampstead
Garden Suburb, 1907/28.” The book,
which has been dedicated to H.M. The
Queen “in evidence of Her Majesty’s
interest in the ideas realised in the Hamp-
stead Garden Suburb,” is written to
celebrate the “Coming of Age” of the
wonderful piece of social work for which
Dame Henrietta Barnett is so largely
responsible. The booklet can be obtained
at the modest price of 6d. from the Secre-
tary, Hampstead Garden Suburb Institute,
London, N.W.11.
Useful Hints for the Home-Maker—(Continued from page 343)
THE “LITLUX” BEDLIGHT FITTING.
I wonder if there is anyone who does not
enjoy that last half-hour’s reading in bed,
even now when the wireless may be listened
to in every room.
Everyone has also suffered from the dis-
comfort of holding the book at an angle
convenient for the light. The latest bed-
light fitting, the “Litlux,” is just the very
thing required for comfort in use, beauty
of appearance and simplicity. It is placed
on the rail at the head of the bed, as shown
in the illustration, and it can be slid along
the rail to any position most comfortable to
the posture of the body and to the focus of
the eyes. Its position is maintained auto-
matically by weighted tags and it, therefore,
needs no fixing.
Another convenience is the hanging
switch, which enables you to switch on or
off without rising.
The light is scientifically screened and
the shades are made in a variety of artistic
shapes and colourings.

plete with lampholder, switch, 3 yards of

by Vera Brittain.
Miss Brittain, one of our foremost
women journalists, has given us an inter-
esting and very readable book on the
different kinds of professions and businesses
which are open to women at the present
time.
For those who are interested in careers
for their daughters or for themselves, the
book will give some very useful information.
It contains a very complete and detailed
bibliography, and at the same time treats
the whole problem of women in industry
and commerce as a very human and under-
standable subject.
Miss Brittain refers very sympathetically
to the work of the Women’s Engineering
Society and the Electrical Association for
Women, which she thinks is doing much
to bring happiness and health into our
homes.
We heartily recommend this book to all
our readers. It is published by Noel
Douglas, 38, Great Ormond Street, W.C.1.
Price, 6s.
DAME HENRIETTA BARNETT has
sent us a charming booklet, entitled, “The
Story of the Growth of the Hampstead
Garden Suburb, 1907/28.” The book,
which has been dedicated to H.M. The
Queen “in evidence of Her Majesty’s
interest in the ideas realised in the Hamp-
stead Garden Suburb,” is written to
celebrate the “Coming of Age” of the
wonderful piece of social work for which
Dame Henrietta Barnett is so largely
responsible. The booklet can be obtained
at the modest price of 6d. from the Secre-
tary, Hampstead Garden Suburb Institute,
London, N.W.11.
Useful Hints for the Home-Maker—(Continued from page 343)
THE “LITLUX” BEDLIGHT FITTING.
I wonder if there is anyone who does not
enjoy that last half-hour’s reading in bed,
even now when the wireless may be listened
to in every room.
Everyone has also suffered from the dis-
comfort of holding the book at an angle
convenient for the light. The latest bed-
light fitting, the “Litlux,” is just the very
thing required for comfort in use, beauty
of appearance and simplicity. It is placed
on the rail at the head of the bed, as shown
in the illustration, and it can be slid along
the rail to any position most comfortable to
the posture of the body and to the focus of
the eyes. Its position is maintained auto-
matically by weighted tags and it, therefore,
needs no fixing.
Another convenience is the hanging
switch, which enables you to switch on or
off without rising.
The light is scientifically screened and
the shades are made in a variety of artistic
shapes and colourings.
The “Litlux” Bedlight Fitting in position.
Every “Litlux” fitting is wired com-
plete with lampholder, switch, 3 yards of
flexible cord and wall plug or adaptor.

Unnamed: 9: Hon. Secretary of the Glasgow and District Branch E.A.W.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 353

E.A.W. Branch Activities.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

March 7th—One of the members of the
Branch, Miss Monro Nicol, attached to the staff
of the Glasgow and West of Scotland College of
Domestic Science, gave a lecture and demonstra-
tion of electric cooking. There was a large and
appreciative audience.
March 14th.—A most interesting visit was
paid to the X-ray Department of the Paisley
Royal Alexandra Infirmary.
April 24th.—Lecture and demonstration of
electric refrigerator, by B. G. A. Staples, Esq.,
of Electrolux, Ltd. There was a good turnout
and Mr. Staples gave a very interesting lecture.
May 8th, 10th, and 14th.—Visits to the Works
of the Singer Manufacturing Co., Ltd. About
100 members of the Branch participated in these
visits and keen interest was shown in the various
processes connected with the manufacture of
sewing machines, particularly electric sewing
machines.
May 29th—Delightful weather favoured the
annual Summer Outing of the Branch. The
party proceeded by motor coaches to Peebles and
had lunch at the Hydro, and on the return
journey a halt was made at the Clyde Valley
Hydro-Electric Scheme at Falls of Clyde where
the ladies spent a pleasant hour seeing over the
station. The conditions were perfect and the
outing was much enjoyed by everyone.
June 5th.—About 100 members visited the
Works of the Scottish Co-operative Wholesale
Society, at Shieldhall, and found much to
interest them in the numerous activities and
processes connected with the various products
and the electrical aids employed.

Birmingham and Midlands
Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. F. W. Hayes,
1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.

On March 29th the members of the Birming-
ham and Midlands Branch held one of their
meetings in Kidderminster, for the benefit of
members in those districts. A very interesting
cookery demonstration was given by Miss
Lockley, Demonstrator for the Shropshire,
Worcestershire and Staffordshire Power Co.,
and the members also paid a visit to a large
carpet factory run entirely by electricity. This
was much appreciated and highly instructive.

The members paid a visit to Nechells Power
Station, Birmingham, on Tuesday, April 24th,
by kind invitation of Mr. Chattock, the City
Electrical Engineer. Here they had the
privilege of viewing the up-to-date system of
firing the huge boilers from which the steam so
generated passes into the turbine. The new
method, now called pulverised fuel firing, was
indeed an education, our members having
explained to them the whole system, from where
the coal refuse is received in barges, picked up
therefrom by mechanical grabs, conveyed elec-
trically inside the building to discharge its load
of ten tons into the hoppers of the pulverising
unit. From this point, as powdered fuel, it is
forced into the firing compartment, so heating
the pipes which carry the steam into the boilers
which again feed into the turbine, to which is
mechanically coupled an alternator which
generates the electricity of our City of Birming-
ham. The controlling feeder panels were then
viewed, and also the huge plan showing the
numerous sub-stations with their connecting
cables to the main generating station. After
their delightful tour of the station, the members
thoroughly enjoyed a welcome cup of tea,
kindly provided by the Electric Supply Depart-
ment.

On Thursday, May 3rd, the members were
privileged in hearing Mr. Cary Gilson, M.A.,
Headmaster of King Edwards School, New
Street, give a lecture on "How Electric
Energy is Bought, Sold, and Used—Volts,
Amperes, Watts, etc." The lecture was one
which dealt with a subject the members knew
little or nothing about and certainly explained
the difficult points in a very clear and simple
fashion. All members were unanimous in their
appreciation of the whole lecture and feel they
are wiser after the hearing of it.

On Wednesday, May 9th, the members visited
the showrooms of Walker Bros., Quality House,
Temple Row, Birmingham. The members here
divided into groups each with a guide who
escorted them round the showrooms and
explained details of all the various exhibits
there. Members were most interested in the
electric clock, which runs for 800 days before
the battery needs to be renewed, the electric
fires, violet ray apparatus and the many wash-
able shades that are now being shown. The
refrigerator was a particular point of interest.
After the members had enjoyed a welcome cup
of tea, Mr. Walker gave a very practical talk
on the best methods of wiring houses, with
special reference to the prevention of fires.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 355

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, " Woodville," Ack Lane, Bramhall, Cheshire.

The five meetings arranged for the spring months have been varied in character. In March we visited the City and Central Telephone Exchange of the Post Office, in York Street, where we were impressed with the skill of the operators in handling the maze of switches and plugs. It was for many of us our first experience of the " what-number-please?" end of a telephone, and we found the visit both interesting and salutary.
The lecture given on March 13th by Mr. A. P. M. Fleming, entitled " The Romance of Electricity," was a delight to the large number of members who were privileged to hear it.
On March 29th, we saw a demonstration of electric cooking by Miss M. Rees, of the Hot-point Co., at Hotpoint House, Corporation Street, when we had an opportunity not only of seeing an excellent demonstration of cooking by electricity but of bombarding the demonstrator with questions as she worked.
The writer felt very keenly the advantage a woman may have over a man engaged on this work: the man demonstrator can show off the good points of an electric cooker or washer. He can answer with accuracy every question about resistances, current consumed and the problem of spilt milk. He can even tell us (sometimes) the inside measurements of the oven. But with rare exceptions he has never used it himself. His are not the hands that have mixed the batter or trimmed the joint or tried to fit the one little extra pudding dish into an overcrowded oven. He is the maker and the technical expert; the woman demonstrator is the cooking expert with some technical knowledge; and the person who will in the end use and judge that appliance is the cook herself, whether mistress or maid. There is ample scope for both in this field, but this advantage of the woman demonstrator should be stressed.
Our last visit was on April 17th, to Messrs. Bannermans Brunswick Mill, Ancoats, where electricity has been put at the service of one of Lancashires oldest industries. The visit was full of interest, and planned so that we followed the cotton from its arrival as a greyish fluffy mass through all the processes of cleaning, carding and spinning, and finally the passage of 108 thicknesses of material under electric knives that cut out nine dozen shirts at once!
The visit to Bath on June 14th, at the invitation of the I.M.E.A., is described elsewhere.
D. M. Peattie.

Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Stemp, 1, York Terrace, St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.

The first annual General Meeting and Luncheon was held at Georges, Ltd., Restaurant in March. Our President, Mrs. Atwell Lake, presided at both meetings, and each was carried through in a most successful manner.
Our guests at the luncheon included the Mayor and Mayoress of Cheltenham (Alderman and Mrs. C. H. Margrett), Miss C. Haslett (Director), Mr. F. H. Corson (Gloucester City Electrical Engineer), Mr. W. J. Bache (Cheltenham Borough Electrical Engineer), Mr. W. T. Long (Cheltenham Education Secretary), Dr. J. S. Kellett Smith, Dr. C. W. Marshall, Mr. L. Scott Langley, Mr. J. Marshall and Mr. J. A. Hogg.
The Mayor in proposing the toast of " The Electrical Association for Women," mentioned that the Cheltenham Domestic Science Centres were among the first to introduce the use of domestic electrical appliances. Miss Haslett, in responding, said that the Association was the outcome of a spontaneous desire of the women of the country to know more about electricity.
Mrs. Atwell Lake proposed the toast of " The Visitors," to which Mr. Scott Langley replied.
After lunch we visited the latest Domestic Science Centre. The Organiser, Miss Dawson Caves (our newly-appointed Hon. Treasurer), explained the scheme of instruction. The girls were all seen working in a practical manner at their various tasks, and we were able to sample some good specimens of their work in the dainty tea which they and the instructresses had prepared. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. W. T. Long (Education Secretary), Miss Dawson Caves and the instructresses for the enjoyable visit.
The next meeting was a practical class on the repair of fuses, kettle and iron connections, etc., for which we had the services of three of the Electricity Departments staff, and so were able to divide into groups, convenient for seeing and handling the various accessories.
A lecture on " The Medical Uses of Electricity " was given by Dr. Kellett Smith, F.R.C.S., D.M.R.E., in an extremely interesting and lucid manner, interspersed with touches of humour. The display of diagrams and films illustrating the use of X-rays added considerably to the interest of the lecture. A vote of thanks was proposed by the President for the valuable instruction afforded to members and their friends.

Our guests at the luncheon included the Mayor and Mayoress of Cheltenham (Alderman and Mrs. C. H. Margrett), Miss C. Haslett (Director), Mr. F. H. Corson (Gloucester City Electrical Engineer), Mr. W. J. Bache (Cheltenham Borough Electrical Engineer), Mr. W. T. Long (Cheltenham Education Secretary), Dr. J. S. Kellett Smith, Dr. C. W. Marshall, Mr. L. Scott Langley, Mr. J. Marshall and Mr. J. A. Hogg.
The Mayor in proposing the toast of " The Electrical Association for Women," mentioned that the Cheltenham Domestic Science Centres were among the first to introduce the use of domestic electrical appliances. Miss Haslett, in responding, said that the Association was the outcome of a spontaneous desire of the women of the country to know more about electricity.
Mrs. Atwell Lake proposed the toast of " The Visitors," to which Mr. Scott Langley replied.
After lunch we visited the latest Domestic Science Centre. The Organiser, Miss Dawson Caves (our newly-appointed Hon. Treasurer), explained the scheme of instruction. The girls were all seen working in a practical manner at their various tasks, and we were able to sample some good specimens of their work in the dainty tea which they and the instructresses had prepared. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. W. T. Long (Education Secretary), Miss Dawson Caves and the instructresses for the enjoyable visit.
The next meeting was a practical class on the repair of fuses, kettle and iron connections, etc., for which we had the services of three of the Electricity Departments staff, and so were able to divide into groups, convenient for seeing and handling the various accessories.
A lecture on " The Medical Uses of Electricity " was given by Dr. Kellett Smith, F.R.C.S., D.M.R.E., in an extremely interesting and lucid manner, interspersed with touches of humour. The display of diagrams and films illustrating the use of X-rays added considerably to the interest of the lecture. A vote of thanks was proposed by the President for the valuable instruction afforded to members and their friends.

The Electrical Age 355

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, " Woodville," Ack Lane, Bramhall, Cheshire.

The five meetings arranged for the spring months have been varied in character. In March we visited the City and Central Telephone Exchange of the Post Office, in York Street, where we were impressed with the skill of the operators in handling the maze of switches and plugs. It was for many of us our first experience of the " what-number-please?" end of a telephone, and we found the visit both interesting and salutary.
The lecture given on March 13th by Mr. A. P. M. Fleming, entitled " The Romance of Electricity," was a delight to the large number of members who were privileged to hear it.
On March 29th, we saw a demonstration of electric cooking by Miss M. Rees, of the Hot-point Co., at Hotpoint House, Corporation Street, when we had an opportunity not only of seeing an excellent demonstration of cooking by electricity but of bombarding the demonstrator with questions as she worked.
The writer felt very keenly the advantage a woman may have over a man engaged on this work: the man demonstrator can show off the good points of an electric cooker or washer. He can answer with accuracy every question about resistances, current consumed and the problem of spilt milk. He can even tell us (sometimes) the inside measurements of the oven. But with rare exceptions he has never used it himself. His are not the hands that have mixed the batter or trimmed the joint or tried to fit the one little extra pudding dish into an overcrowded oven. He is the maker and the technical expert; the woman demonstrator is the cooking expert with some technical knowledge; and the person who will in the end use and judge that appliance is the cook herself, whether mistress or maid. There is ample scope for both in this field, but this advantage of the woman demonstrator should be stressed.
Our last visit was on April 17th, to Messrs. Bannermans Brunswick Mill, Ancoats, where electricity has been put at the service of one of Lancashires oldest industries. The visit was full of interest, and planned so that we followed the cotton from its arrival as a greyish fluffy mass through all the processes of cleaning, carding and spinning, and finally the passage of 108 thicknesses of material under electric knives that cut out nine dozen shirts at once!
The visit to Bath on June 14th, at the invitation of the I.M.E.A., is described elsewhere.
D. M. Peattie.

South Wales and Monmouth-
shire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Tyler, Electric Service
Bureau, 27, Newport Road, Cardiff.

Our first annual General Meeting was held at
the Royal Hotel, Cardiff, on Wednesday,
March 28th, over which Mrs. C. T. Allan
(Chairman of Committee) presided.
The annual report, which was read by the
Hon. Secretary, was adopted on the proposition
of a very old friend of the E.A.W., Mr. J. W.
Beauchamp, General Manager of the South Wales
Electrical Power Distribution Co., Ltd.
The report given by Mrs. J. H. Dinham
(Hon. Treasurer), was adopted on the proposi-
tion of Mr. R. L. Booth, Chairman of the Cardiff
Branch of the E.C.A.
A most interesting address by our Director,
Miss C. Haslett, on the “New Outlet Cam-
paign,” was much appreciated.
The luncheon following the general meeting
was a great success. Mr. C. G. Morley New
(City Electrical Engineer) was in the chair.
There were nearly 170 people present.
Our fixtures during the session have been
instructive and of great interest, and include a
visit to the “Western Mail” Printing Works,
a visit to Messrs. Woolworths Ltd., Kitchen
and Catering Department. The efficiency and
cleanliness in the kitchens was remarkable, and
the tea provided was most enjoyable.
A very interesting talk was given by
Mr. B. L. Booth. He dwelt on the Outlet Cam-
paign as expounded by Miss C. Haslett at the
General Meeting; and the members afterwards
bombarded him with questions. A visit to
Messrs. Electrolux, Ltd.; the lecture by Mr. J.
Davies, Manager of the Cardiff Branch, was
extremely good, after which we were entertained
to a most sumptuous tea.
We all enjoyed very much the visit to the
I.M.E.A. Convention at Bath on Womens
Day, Thursday, June 14th.
There will be a Cookery Lecture by Mrs. J.
Tyler, Demonstrator to the South Wales Power
Co., Ltd. A visit to the Lydney Power Station,
Gloucester, by charabanc on July 18th, is the
last item on our fixture card for this session,
after which we close down for the summer
months, re-opening during the first week in
October.
Our membership is gradually increasing.
J.T.

North East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm, Carliol
House, Newcastle-on-Tyne.

The first Annual General Meeting was held in
the Lecture Theatre, Carliol House, on April
25th.
Miss Balls was in the chair, and a representa-
tive audience of members, delegates from the
Womens Institutes and Womens Co-operation
Guilds numbering 80, gathered together.
Miss Balls, in introducing Miss Haslett, said
that she thought the annual report was very
satisfactory and that the North East Coast
Branch had done a great deal in educating
themselves, and now we were required to do
something to bring the use of electricity to the
help of the intelligent women workers, as it was
not only a question for the rich, but was a
necessity to everyone.
Miss Haslett officially accepted the invitation
of the North East Coast Branch to hold the
Annual Conference of the E.A.W. in Newcastle
during the North East Coast Exhibition.
Miss Haslett gave a résumé of the work done
by Headquarters of the E.A.W. This year
there were signs that it was likely to become an
international organisation. The Director also
explained the “Outlet” Campaign and asked
the members to send suggestions to Head-
quarters, so that the National Specification
should be of help and worthy of the E.A.W.

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o., Ingleby Motors, Sweet Street, Leeds.

The membership of the Leeds and West Riding Branch is rapidly growing, and interest in this new Branch is steadily increasing. On March 28th, over 50 members and friends paid their first official visit to an electricity works.
They were invited by Mr. Woodhouse, of The Yorkshire Electric Power Company, to inspect the new Ferrybridge Power Station, one of the most up-to-date power stations in the country, and one which will eventually be linked up to the grid in the scheme of the Central Electricity Board.
The members left Leeds at 2.15 p.m. in buses kindly provided by Mr. Woodhouse, and after a pleasant country ride on a bright afternoon they arrived at the power station in very good spirits.
The party was divided into four separate groups, and gentlemen of the Power Company conducted them on a tour of inspection round the Works, giving instructive accounts of the working of the machinery. The tour ended in the Companys all-electric canteen, and very great interest was shown in the various cooking appliances.
The guests were kindly invited to tea, and returned home by bus, having thoroughly enjoyed this very interesting outing.
On May 7th, Mr. Dale, of The British Electrical Development Association gave the members a very instructive and enjoyable address on "The Generation and Distribution of Electricity," and this following immediately after the visit to the Power Station proved very adequate.
Mr. Dale thoroughly explained how current is generated at power stations and then distributed through cables to sub-stations and thus to distribution boxes in our own homes.
A summer outing is now being arranged, and it is proposed that a visit should be paid to an all-electric farm in the Yorkshire Dales.

New "Sunlight" Apparatus
for Home Use.
Switch on your own Sunshine.
Functions on all House Lighting Circuits.
Nursery Sunshine Lamp.
The apparatus here illustrated and described has been specially designed for Home use in accordance with the specification of Dr. Albert Eidinow, of the National Institute for Medical Research ("British Medical Journal," Dec. 10, 1927).
The wonderful effects obtained by the application of Artificial Sunlight have been widely commented upon in the Public Press recently.
The Nursery Model illustrated has been most enthusiastically received, because it enables parents to give weak and ailing children a beneficial Sun Bath on any sunless or wintry day whenever desired.
It has been specially designed for use for Children in the Nursery or bedroom, but it is equally suitable for Adults, Invalids, and Convalescents. The Ultra-Violet Rays emitted are of long wave length and the light produced is practically the same as real Sunlight.
The Light and Ultra-Violet Rays are obtained by an incandescent Tungsten Burner, the bulb of which is made of Vitaglass, which allows of the passage of Ultra-Violet Rays. It is adjustable to any height and has a proper guard to prevent children from reaching the burner.
It is fitted with a "regulator" by which the strength can be reduced at will so that even babies can be placed in the Rays on sunless, dark days. Children can play about within the rays of this lamp all day long with highly beneficial results, and, in fact, feel the same as if they were in natural Sunshine.

The membership of the Leeds and West Riding Branch is rapidly growing, and interest in this new Branch is steadily increasing. On March 28th, over 50 members and friends paid their first official visit to an electricity works.
They were invited by Mr. Woodhouse, of The Yorkshire Electric Power Company, to inspect the new Ferrybridge Power Station, one of the most up-to-date power stations in the country, and one which will eventually be linked up to the grid in the scheme of the Central Electricity Board.
The members left Leeds at 2.15 p.m. in buses kindly provided by Mr. Woodhouse, and after a pleasant country ride on a bright afternoon they arrived at the power station in very good spirits.
The party was divided into four separate groups, and gentlemen of the Power Company conducted them on a tour of inspection round the Works, giving instructive accounts of the working of the machinery. The tour ended in the Companys all-electric canteen, and very great interest was shown in the various cooking appliances.
The guests were kindly invited to tea, and returned home by bus, having thoroughly enjoyed this very interesting outing.
On May 7th, Mr. Dale, of The British Electrical Development Association gave the members a very instructive and enjoyable address on "The Generation and Distribution of Electricity," and this following immediately after the visit to the Power Station proved very adequate.
Mr. Dale thoroughly explained how current is generated at power stations and then distributed through cables to sub-stations and thus to distribution boxes in our own homes.
A summer outing is now being arranged, and it is proposed that a visit should be paid to an all-electric farm in the Yorkshire Dales.

Nursery Sunshine Lamp.

It is fitted with a "regulator" by which the strength can be reduced at will so that even babies can be placed in the Rays on sunless, dark days. transcription:
The Electrical Age 361
London Activities.
The outstanding event since the last issue of our Journal, was, of course, the Third Annual General Meeting and Conference, which took place on April 17th and 18th.
We were privileged to hold our business meeting at the Institution of Electrical Engineers. Alderman Mrs. Hammer, Chairman of Council, presided over a large gathering. The adoption of the Annual Report was proposed by Lt.-Col. W. A. Vignoles, who expressed great pleasure at the educational work the E.A.W. is carrying out; this was seconded by Mrs. Atwell Lake, the President of our Cheltenham Branch.
The Financial Statement was read by Mrs. I. E. Bray, and adopted on the motion of Mrs. Ll. B. Atkinson and Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti, who were later elected Hon. Treasurer and Vice-Chairman respectively. Alderman Mrs. Hammer was re-elected Chairman.
We were all delighted to welcome Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, who gave a very charming speech on her election as President.
Excellent reports were read from all the Branches, and the appreciation of the meeting was expressed by Lady Snell.
At the conclusion of the Business Meeting, a very hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Institution of Electrical Engineers.
During the afternoon, quite a large party of members visited the London Light Clinic, where Dr. Deck gave a most interesting talk on "Artificial Sunlight and the Uses of Electricity for Treatment by Light and Inhalation," in this most up-to-date centre.
In the evening, the E.A.W. held its first Ball at the Hotel Cecil, and Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley received the guests, who numbered over two hundred and forty. The Cabaret was much appreciated; everyone who was present will agree that the Ball was a most enjoyable and successful function.
The morning of the second day of the Conference was spent in a visit to the heating and lighting installation at the Zoo. The party was shown round by the Zoo Engineer, Mr. Davolles, Mr. Settle of the G.E.C., and Mr. Wyld, who represented Mr. Selley of the St. Marylebone Electricity Supply Dept.
In the afternoon, a most appreciative audience was held spell-bound for over an hour by the fascinating and witty lecture of Captain P. P. Eckersley, who spoke on "Some Technical Problems of Broadcasting."

transcription:
The Electrical Age 361
London Activities.
The outstanding event since the last issue of our Journal, was, of course, the Third Annual General Meeting and Conference, which took place on April 17th and 18th.
We were privileged to hold our business meeting at the Institution of Electrical Engineers. Alderman Mrs. Hammer, Chairman of Council, presided over a large gathering. The adoption of the Annual Report was proposed by Lt.-Col. W. A. Vignoles, who expressed great pleasure at the educational work the E.A.W. is carrying out; this was seconded by Mrs. Atwell Lake, the President of our Cheltenham Branch.
The Financial Statement was read by Mrs. I. E. Bray, and adopted on the motion of Mrs. Ll. B. Atkinson and Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti, who were later elected Hon. Treasurer and Vice-Chairman respectively. Alderman Mrs. Hammer was re-elected Chairman.
We were all delighted to welcome Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, who gave a very charming speech on her election as President.
Excellent reports were read from all the Branches, and the appreciation of the meeting was expressed by Lady Snell.
At the conclusion of the Business Meeting, a very hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Institution of Electrical Engineers.
During the afternoon, quite a large party of members visited the London Light Clinic, where Dr. Deck gave a most interesting talk on "Artificial Sunlight and the Uses of Electricity for Treatment by Light and Inhalation," in this most up-to-date centre.
In the evening, the E.A.W. held its first Ball at the Hotel Cecil, and Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley received the guests, who numbered over two hundred and forty. The Cabaret was much appreciated; everyone who was present will agree that the Ball was a most enjoyable and successful function.
The morning of the second day of the Conference was spent in a visit to the heating and lighting installation at the Zoo. The party was shown round by the Zoo Engineer, Mr. Davolles, Mr. Settle of the G.E.C., and Mr. Wyld, who represented Mr. Selley of the St. Marylebone Electricity Supply Dept.
In the afternoon, a most appreciative audience was held spell-bound for over an hour by the fascinating and witty lecture of Captain P. P. Eckersley, who spoke on "Some Technical Problems of Broadcasting."

Unnamed: 9: Editor of the journal The Electrical Age for Women.
transcription:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE
FOR WOMEN
The Official Journal of the Electrical Association for Women—Issued Quarterly.
Editor—Miss C. HASLETT. 46, Kensington Court, London, W.8.
Vol. I. OCTOBER, 1928. No. 10
My husband and I have always been interested in the application of Electricity to domestic use. I think we must have been one of the first to install it in a private house, which we did 38 years ago. The Electricity was generated by means of a steam engine heated by a coal fire, as my husband had a strong dislike to gas; our house was previously illuminated with oil lamps.
In those early days my husband also had electric power applied to the sewing machine, and laundry implements, thus being a pioneer in introducing labour saving appliances for womens work in the home.
Later on, when the village of Bournville was developed, we introduced electric lighting in the public buildings, in the schools, etc. It was supplied from the Power Station at the Bournville Works.
A few years ago, the Corporation of Birmingham extended their cables to outlying districts; most of the houses already built in the village were wired, and it was provided for all new houses. It is now almost universal, the two thousand houses included in the Bournville Housing Schemes being nearly all supplied with electricity. There is one all-electric house, but we find that practically everyone prefers a coal fire.
MRS. CADBURY.
Eliz M. Cadbury

The Electrical Age 369

Our Portrait Page.

Interesting Personalities in the E.A.W.

MISS NORAH BALLS, of Newcastle.

The North East Coast Branch of the E.A.W. is fortunate in having secured Miss Norah Balls as Chairman of Committee.
Miss Balls is well-known in Newcastle, probably chiefly for her work as Divisional Commissioner for the Newcastle Girl Guides, being also Vice-President and County Secretary for the Northumberland Girl Guides.
She also extended her activities to the Newcastle Juvenile Organisations Council, and is Job Mistress in the Toe H League of Women Helpers.
Those of us who had the pleasure of listening to her at the Annual Conference in London last April were charmed with her beautiful voice and manner. It is not, perhaps, surprising to learn that Miss Balls is interested in English folk song and dancing, and, in fact, all kinds of dramatic work.
She is a perfect chairwoman, gracious and yet firm in handling her committees.
She has unbounded enthusiasm for the work of the E.A.W., which she will undoubtedly use in making our 1929 Conference at Newcastle a success.

The photograph which we show of Miss Dicks was taken by Mrs. Llewelyn B. Atkinson at the Electrical Contractors Conference at Cheltenham this year.
Miss Dicks is a member of the Electrical Contractors Association, being responsible for carrying on the contracting business of Messrs. Dicks, Ltd., of Winchester.
Miss Dicks had for a long time been the helpmate of her father in his business, and when he died some years ago she took over complete control.
She will become an active member of the Hampshire Branch of the E.A.W., which is about to be formed, being already well-known amongst the Electrical Contractors circle in that district.

Described by Mrs. Lamb, Chairman Manchester District Branch, E.A.W

The members of the Electrical Associa-
tion for Women welcome the Electrical
Outlet Campaign because it is constructive
work which is much needed, and, if suc-
cessful, there can be no doubt that it will
be the means of helping to lessen the toil
of housework for many women.

The object of the Campaign is to influ-
ence those who are responsible for building
houses, so that the installations will be
carried out in such a way that the occu-
piers will be able to make full use of
electricity for domestic purposes.

Architects and members of Housing
Committees, unless they happen to be
women, cannot understand the necessity
for more electrical outlets in houses, but,
as they are always anxious to bring about
improvements in building, they will, we
hope, give careful consideration to our
arguments.

PRIESTNALL LODGE, HEATON MERSEY.
