transcription:
The Electrical Age			373

A Page for Girl Guides.

Running a Country Showroom.
By Mona Willis.

Miss Willis, who is apprenticed to Miss Margaret Partridge, is now getting some experience
in running a showroom in a Country Town, an amusing description of which she gives below.

Electricity in Bun-Town is now approach-
ing its second birthday, so the combined
Showroom and Office standing in the old
Market Place, has lost its first flush of
novelty. It is now sufficiently well-known
for the consumers to bring their grumbles
up here directly they discover them, instead
of waiting until the meter is read at the
end of the quarter, to tell you in an
aggrieved voice that the sitting-room lamp
broke two days after it was put up, and
they have had no light from it since.
The work of running the Showroom is not
heavy. It consists of looking after the
Showroom itself, keeping check of the
stock of wiring materials, lamps and
shades, entering up the few necessary books
and taking out the lighting accounts and
collecting the money, at the end of every
quarter.
The stock-keeping is the least interesting
side—simply a matter of keeping check of
all the material used on a house-wiring job,
or the number of lamps sold, entering into
various books, pricing and checking—all
very impersonal and mechanical.
The Showroom, by contrast, has many
sides and possibilities. Many of the goods
we have on view, such as electric irons,
toasters, kettles, and coffee percolators, are
of bright metal and require careful dusting,
and at some seasons of the year, even dry-
ing, every day. Window dressing, another
of the necessary activities of the Show-
room, is not as simple as it might appear
to the uninitiated outsider. It is often
most amusing, and sometimes almost
tragic, the way in which quite simple
displays are cruelly misinterpreted. On
one occasion the dressing consisted of a
breakfast table set out with cup, plate,
electric coffee percolator, toaster and
hot plate, the two last being complete with
toast, and a dish of eggs and bacon. This
was taken rather too literally by a small
party, obviously in from the country for
the weekly shopping, who came in and
asked with perfect confidence, for " Tea
for three, scones and butter, and a few
cakes." Another time, an electrically
driven sewing-machine was put in the
window, but the only harvest that we
reaped from the effort, was a roaring trade
in machine needles that lasted for several
months.
The types of shades and fittings that
attract the largest sales are often the most
unexpected. Shades with a conventional
basket of flowers or fruit are always popu-
lar, as are also those with that awful shade
of blotting-paper pink as a basic colour.
One small, simply-moulded and very
slightly tinted shade that was the first
to take my fancy, was despised by many
generations, but was finally chosen, with-
out a moments hesitation or query as to
price, by a small boy of about ten, who was
sent in by his mother to make his choice.
I was rather surprised at his discrimina-
tion, so told him that if his mother did
not care for it, we would change it for
him. He smiled up at me with perfect
and apparently justified self-confidence,
and said, " Shell like this one, Miss."
At the end of every quarter comes the
task of taking round the lighting accounts.
Many, of course, can be slipped into
letter-boxes, but some people prefer to pay

Unnamed: 9: Took the photograph of the London members in the garden.
transcription:
374                                        The Electrical Age

the bill at once, and so save themselves the trouble of walking up to the office with the money another time. Their methods of indicating this “preference” are not, however, always very obvious. One old dame always begins with the same phrase, “What, you coming round asking for money again? WICKED, I calls it!” She takes the bill, and begins again, “What, you charge me all that for the little bit of light I’ve used? WICKED, I calls it. I haven’t enough money to pay you.” She then proceeds to dive into various pockets in numerous aprons, skirts, and petticoats, and at length produces a greasy note from the pocket of the fifth or sixth layer counting from the outside, inwards. Once the money is on the surface, she begins to cheer up, and by the time the receipt is handed over, the tone of her conversation might almost deceive you into believing yourself her life-long friend. Another rather unusual method of shewing a desire to pay, is employed by a certain butcher,
who waves his long knife about in the air, less than a foot away from your nose, and shouts “Go away, I don’t want you here to-day.” If you take him at his word and turn to go, the knife comes even nearer, and when at last you stand petrified and unresisting, he retires to the back of the shop, produces the money and shoos you out, with the knife still twirling dangerously in his hand.
These two, I am glad to say, are specimens of the minority. Many people smile a cheerful welcome to you, and even do their utmost to keep you gossiping by showing you the latest baby, or asking your opinion on the best way of taking geranium cuttings.
Oh, there’s no doubt about it, though “London shops are rare shops, where gallant things are sold,” for sheer personal interest and constant amusing incidents, a showroom in a small country town cannot be beaten.

Where Dr. and Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti have converted an ordinary house into a modern fairy-land. As the pictures will show, they have been wise in the number of Electrical "Outlets" installed.

Described by Doris M. Peattie, B.A.

I want an all-electric house!
At first, I wanted it vaguely:
Then I wanted it wistfully:
Now I want it fiercely!
Ive seen Dr. and Mrs. Ferrantis seaside home at Deganwy, and Ive realised the possibility of converting an ordinary house — your house, anybodys house, into the kind of place that gets four full page photographs to itself in "Ideal Homes."
Till that visit I thought that having an all-electric house might mean that you were a city engineer with the faith and courage to practise what you preached, but their numbers were too few to alter the landscape. In most cases it meant the building of a brand new house, a bottomless purse, and an architect whom one could lead like a little child.
Little Haldon, at Deganwy, when Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti first saw it, was an ordinary house, roughly square in shape, of the two reception, four bedroom, kitchen and scullery type, common in all residential suburbs. Its inadequate windows, flat to the wall, made little of the glorious views of river and mountains close by. It was filled to the brim, of course, with gas pipes, inverted mantles and coal scuttles. Hot baths were a painful subject. One said, as hundreds of us are saying nightly, "Will you put on the kitchen fire earlier to-night, please? Id like my bath at 9." And from 6.30 p.m. till 9, night after night, whether blazing July day or cold December evening, bucket after bucket of coal was tipped into that rapacious maw.
For the single bath and wash-basin there was the usual family scramble from 7.20 till 8.40 every morning. Thousands of steps a week were wasted passing from the roomy kitchen where food was prepared to the roomy scullery where it was cooked and the dishes washed. On Monday mornings the arm energy wasted in rubbing clothes by hand would have swum the channel. The house, in fact, was rather like the ones that we have all lived in at some time in our lives.
The situation however was delightful, the house the right size and Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti bought it. In a few weeks time there emerged from the chaos of wires and ladders the delightful seaside home

Once the household has been
well organised for the daily
routine work, often deadly in

the help that electrical energy
can give so easily. Few women
realise how much hard physical
work they do in a normal days
housework. Few men would
stand by and see a woman

crank up a car, but there are many wringers
and mangles that involve far greater strain
on women than the starting handle of a
car.
Every woman needs electrical help in
her home : that is, she needs her house
wired for power as well as for electric light
and she needs plenty of outlets, in the
right places, so that she can make use of
the power when it is installed. All over
the country municipalities are building
houses; private contractors are building
houses. In nearly all we find electric
light; in scarcely any do we find power
outlets. Anyone—municipality or private
builder—who builds a house to-day with-
out wiring it for power, is denying the
women who live in it of effective electri-
cal help not only now but probably for
many years.

what can be done by the pioneers in the
adoption of electrical energy to household
use. It is our task, in the new Outlet
Campaign of the E.A.W., to see that this
help is brought within the reach of those
who need it most.

transcription:
378	The Electrical Age
A Visit to the Highest Kitchen in Europe.
A Kitchen all Electrically Equipped.
By Alice R. Bisset.
Miss Bisset, who was accompanied by her friend, Miss Waterman, both experts in electric cooking, gives a fascinating description of a visit to an All-Electric Kitchen situated amid the eternal snows in Switzerland.
Of all the interests and pleasures of a glorious holiday in the Bernese Oberland this summer, not the least and certainly one of the most unique and marvellous was a visit to the highest hotel in Europe—the noted "Hotel Berghaus" on the Jung-fraujoch, 11,342 feet above sea level. Veritably a house among the clouds, situ-ated as it is far above the snow line, in the region of eternal snow and ice. The hotel itself is a marvel of modern enter-prise, built into the rocks, overlooking the largest glacier in Europe—the wonderful Aletsch Glacier. It is reached by the Jung-frau Railway, one of the most daring engineering achievements of modern times, being at the same time the highest railway in Europe. It lies for almost the whole of its length, in the interior of the mighty snowclad Alps and took fourteen years to build, at an expenditure of something like twelve million francs.
On our ascent we left the train at various viewpoints, probably the two most interest-ing being the Eigerwand Station and the Eismeer Station. The station terrace of the former, 9,405 feet up, is cut out of the rock and commands a magnificent view of the Grindelwald Valley and of northern Switzerland as far as the Jura, Vosges and Black Forest. The next station, Eismeer Station, 3 1/4 miles further on is reached in ten minutes. Its marvellous construction is a masterpiece of blasting and one gazes from its halls of rock with awe-inspired wonder on the wildest Alpine scenery. The snow-clad Wetterhorn, Schreckhorn, Fiesherhörner rise majestically into the clouds above the glaciers. From Eismeer
the last portion of the line, 1 1/4 miles long, changing shortly before the end from an adhesion to a rack-and-pinion line with a gradient of 25%, brings us to the Jungfrau-joch Station 11,342 feet, with its restaur-ant (all electrically equipped) and its postal and telegraph office. From the station a gallery through rocks leads to Europes highest hotel—the famous "Hotel Berg-haus" with its spacious salons, dining room and thirty pleasant bedrooms with bath-rooms.
An all-electric hotel, the appointments of which, at such an altitude can only be regarded as marvellous, for here the visitor can enjoy the most luxurious up-to-date comfort with all the courtesy of a perfect hospitality so marked in Swiss hotels. This was extended to my friend Miss Waterman, and myself in the most pleasing manner, and when our interest in electricity as re-gards the domestic side and especially the cooking side was realized, the manager evinced the greatest interest in showing us all he could, and conducted us to the all-electric kitchen, with apologies for its con-dition after one of the busiest luncheons of his season. We marvelled at its order and realised with fresh appreciation the splendid organising ability and mastery of detail in all domestic practice of the Swiss in general and the Swiss hotel proprietor in particular. In the kitchen we found two Master Chefs with their assistants and apprentices and noted the systematic and excellent training the latter were receiving. The two Master Chefs having finished the rush of their luncheon (for with true system-atic Swiss outlook so had the manager

The Electrical Age 381
Useful Hints for the Home-Maker.
By " ELECTRA."
A DOMESTIC WATER HEATER.
Water heating is always one of the most urgent problems of the housewife, and the " Ferranti " Storage Tank is specially designed to meet practically all difficulties.
It is a large capacity tank, well lagged, and with automatic heat control; a thermometer is also provided to show the temperature of the water at any time.
The tank is easily connected to the existing pipework, and it can also be fixed to work in conjunction with a coke boiler.
SECTIONAL VIEW OF " FERRANTI " STORAGE TANK.
A few special features which will appeal particularly to our women readers are: 1.—The incoming cold water does not mix with the water stored in the tank. The whole supply of hot water is therefore always available for drawing off at its full temperature. 2.—The heating elements and thermostat can be withdrawn without interfering with the water system. 3.—Simple provision is made for emptying the tank for the purpose of cleaning. Finally, the " Ferranti " Storage Tank costs little to run, and is therefore economical as well as efficient.

transcription:
382
The Electrical Age
The Electric Blanket.
Made by Ex-Service Men at Leatherhead.
During the summer one of the most interesting visits paid by the London members of the Electrical Association for Women, was to the Frederick Milner Home at Leatherhead, where ex-Service men are being employed under ideal conditions in a beautiful country factory. Most of the men are suffering from shell shock and it would be very difficult indeed for them to compete in the open market; but in this model, light and airy factory, they are able to earn quite a good living. It is also interesting to know that the undertaking is run on an economic basis.
The chief product of this factory is the  Thermega  Electro-Radiant Blanket.
The Blanket is light, soft and flexible and the wire is made and protected by a special patent process which makes accidents practically impossible.
The object of the Electric Blanket is not to provide heat, but regular, adjustable warmth, which is so necessary in this generally damp climate of ours. It airs and dries and warms the bed evenly throughout and so promotes sound and healthy sleep. It is very useful in bedrooms without fires, and a blanket with Universal voltage will very soon be considered as an essential item in every travellers equipment, for who has not experienced the dread of the strange bed being damp?
In the sick-bed too, where artificial warmth is so essential, the  Thermega  is recommended not only to aid a cure, but to promote convalescence. For cases where purely LOCAL heat is required, the ex-Service mens factory is making electric pads, which are adjustable to three different degrees of temperature.
It is advised that these pads should not be used as bed warmers, as this creates the same unhealthy temperature contrasts as hot water bottles do.
There is yet another use for the  Thermega  Electric Blanket and that is for a very important person, who needs a great deal of care and attention, namely the Baby. The little one in our illustration evidently appreciates the comfort of his electric blanket, which gives him the warmth so necessary to his well-being.
Both medical men and nurses are enthusiastic in praise of  Thermega  Blankets and Pads.
Baby finds comfort in the Electric Blanket
 Thermega  Blankets and Pads.
Useful in the Bedroom.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 387
of Overhead Lines which the Central Electricity Board will administer under the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1926.
Thus the North Wales Power Companys net-work of lines which has been designed for almost infinite expansion into the remoter rural areas, is fed from the Carnarvonshire end by the Hydro-Electric Generating Stations at Cwm Dyli and Maentwrog and (by arrangement with the Aluminium Corporation, Ltd.) at Dolgarrog. At its eastern end it is connected to the selected Steam Super Station at Runcorn and will soon be connected to the Central Electricity Boards Grid at Crewe. In addition, certain collieries at which modern steam turbine plant was already installed, are also connected to the net-work into which they can pour their surplus energy which is available to them by keeping their turbines running at constant full load and therefore of highest efficiency. So far as these collieries are concerned, the passing of their surplus energy into the North Wales network of overhead lines merely represents the sale of so much coal which is won and stoked by them at the collieries.
Every coast town in North Wales is drawing its bulk supply from this network of lines and so also are other towns such as Wrexham, Oswestry and Crewe, and numbers of smaller villages and hamlets, and by degrees these lines will be extended into still more remote districts where already some of the more enterprising townships and villages are proceed-
ing with local developments in anticipation of the coming of bulk supplies.
In addition to bulk supplies to towns, the demands for industrial power are being met to an ever-increasing extent. The great railway works at Crewe draw their power supplies from this system whilst the quarries and collieries which form the staple industries of North Wales are very large users of electric power.
New industries are also finding their way to North Wales and the outlook for large increases of output are very favourable.
It is a noteworthy feature of electric supply that the more it is used the cheaper it becomes, and this is perhaps particularly understandable in the case of schemes which are largely dependent upon water-power and extensive transmission lines.
These represent a very large capital expenditure and the interest charges upon this expenditure have to be met out of the price per unit sold. If these charges can be met with an average bulk price of 1¼d. per unit in the early days it is clear that we can look forward to at least the halving of this figure when the present output is doubled.
There is one feature of the North Wales Scheme of transmission lines which is worthy of note an d it may be that some day credit will be acknowledged to the foresight of those who had the vision and the enterprise to proceed with this fine development far in anticipation of the National Grid Scheme with which it will so admirably unite.

transcription:
388
The Electrical Age
A Cookery Page.
Conducted by Miss Mary Mackirdy
(Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow, and Author of "Recipes for You").
Scotch Scones.
Scones and oatcakes, the latter a survival of what was probably the primitive bread of the country, made before there was any knowledge of raising materials, were and still are cooked on a girdle. A girdle or griddle is essentially Scottish with a pedigree dating back many centuries; it is a simple contrivance composed of a circular piece of iron with a handle that enabled it being swung over an open fire. With restricted space and the more concentrated heating of smaller stoves, the girdle has fallen considerably into disuse. In many country districts where home-baked scones were a necessity, the bakers motor van relieves this need, a relief which unhappily will tend to make scone-making a lost art.
When I began to use an electric cooker I had some difficulty reconciling it with a girdle, but to my great satisfaction I found that the boiling plate made an excellent substitute provided the heat was carefully regulated.
To prepare the boiling plate for scones turn the current on to "low" just before mixing the dough, then the plate should be sufficiently hot by the time the scones are shaped; if the heat should be so strong as to overbrown the scones turn off the current. In my experience the current need never be increased beyond "low."
Plain Girdle Scones.
Half lb. flour, pinch salt, ½ teaspoon carbonate of soda, 1 teaspoon cream of tartar, about 1 teacup sweet milk.
Mix the ingredients, with the exception of the milk, using a broad-bladed knife or the fingers, then very quickly, mixing as little and as lightly as possible, stir in the milk, using a knife. The dough should be much softer than for pastry, but not so soft as to be difficult to handle.
Turn the dough out on a floured board, halve, form each piece into a round, roll to about ½ in. thick, cut in four and cook on hot plate first one side then the other till a very pale brown. When the edges of the scone are cooked the centre should be; they are placed one on top of the other in a cloth, this is called "steaming" the scones, the steam passing through softens the surface and may complete the cooking.
With experience, a larger scone may be made, one round with ¾ lb. flour.
Other Scones.
A variety of scones may be made from the above recipe and directions:-
(1) Add 2 teaspoons fine sugar or syrup.
(2) Rub 1 or 2 teaspoons butter into the flour.
(3) Add a few currants or raisins to the flour.
(4) Substitute wheaten meal for flour or for part of the flour.
In the country districts of Scotland scones are usually made with buttermilk. If this is done, use only half the amount of cream of tartar, the acid of the milk supplying the remainder.
This rule also applies to scones made with milk that has soured.
Treacle Scones.
Mix 2 teaspoons treacle or more to the milk for ¾ lb. flour, a very slight reduction is made in the amount of cream of tartar, treacle having an acid action.
Oatmeal Scones.
These are delightful for breakfast. They may be made in the same way as wheaten scones, but I consider it an improvement to steep the meal in the milk, allowing 6 ozs. meal to 2 ozs. flour, the other ingredients as in first recipe. The flour and raising materials are added when the meal has steeped for about 20 minutes, with, if necessary, more milk.
It will be seen from the recipes given that they are all worked from a foundation. If this foundation of ¾ lb. flour, with its correct proportions of raising material is observed, there should be little difficulty ringing the changes and having an interesting variety.
Oven Scones or Teacakes.
These are easily managed by anyone who has made the others. Use the foundation as given for plain scones, adding to the flour 1 oz. butter and 1 oz. fine sugar, with fruit as desired.

The method of making is the same, but the dough should be at least 1 in. thick before cutting: the scones may be cut with a small cutter. Put on an oven tin, dusted with flour or brushed with egg, and bake in the top shelf of a quick oven.
A large pancake may be made by forming the dough into a large round, flattened slightly on the tin and scored or not, as the fancy dictates.
Dropped Scones.
As the name indicates, these are dropped on to the girdle or hot plate, therefore the dough must be softer than for scones proper. They are usually made richer than scones.
Mix 1 lb. flour with 1 teaspoon fine sugar or syrup, 1 small teaspoon carbonate of soda, 2 small teaspoons cream of tartar, 1 beaten egg and 1 1/4 gills sweet milk. The ingredients should be mixed thoroughly, not beaten.
Prepare the boiling plate or girdle as for scones, rub with a piece of suet, then with a dry cloth
or paper. Drop out the mixture from a jug or a spoon, brown first one side then the other.
They are excellent split open while hot and heated apricot or other preserves put between, served hot.

The Electrical Age 393

E.A.W. Branch Activities.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

The Branch has arrangements in hand for a number of very interesting Autumn Lectures and Visits.
A supply of tickets has been sent for the Housing and Health Exhibition, which is being held in the Kelvin Hall from September 19th to October 13th. These tickets are available at a special price for members of the E.A.W.
Miss Kennedy, the indefatigable Secretary of the Branch, has had a very serious illness, from which she is now recovering.
During her illness she has had many expressions of the appreciation of the members for the wonderful way in which she has conducted the Branch affairs.
* * *
Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. F. W. Hayes,
1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.

On Thursday, May 24th, the members attended a "Talk" by Mrs. Williams (the Birmingham Electric Supply Demonstrator of Electric Cooking), in the Electric Supply Showrooms, Birmingham, on the "Construction and Control of an Electric Cooker."
All members thoroughly appreciated this talk, and absolutely enjoyed seeing the Cooker taken to pieces and every part explained as to the why and wherefore of its position. They understood much that had been puzzling before, and the sampling of the cakes and tarts cooked in their presence, with a welcome cup of tea, was an ideal finish to such an afternoon. The members were enthusiastic in their praises of Mrs. Williams and thanks to the Electric Supply Department
The members of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch were privileged to hear a most interesting Lecture given by Dr. Alexander Bryce, M.D., on "Sunlight, Artificial and Natural - in Health and Disease," at Moseley, on Thursday, June 7th. Many demonstrations of the Ultra-Violet Ray Apparatus were given, and the Violet Ray Apparatus which tells good and bad eggs, margarine from butter, etc., filled members with amazement. Altogether this was a most interesting lecture, and we hope to hear another on the same subject in the very near future.
On Tuesday, June 12th, at 3 p.m., members visited the Lightfoot Refrigeration Works in Digbeth, and Cheapside, Birmingham. In the latter works, the party visited "Chilling"

IMPORTANT ANNOUNCEMENT.
We are actual manufacturers of all types of Ultra-Violet Ray (Artificial Sunlight) Generators for all purposes.
We supply large numbers for Hospital, Medical and Dental use, and each Lamp supplied is designed for the specific purpose for which it is intended, but many have a wide range of utility.
Such lamps are specially designed for giving curative treatment, to be used only by skilled operators under the supervision or prescription of qualified Practitioners.
They are powerful Units and the dosage and technique have been definitely established by eminent Specialists in Actinotherapy.
There are, however, many other purposes for which such apparatus can be used; one of the most important fields, in our opinion, is to derive the tonic effect from low power units in the home.
A Medical apparatus must not be used by lay persons, but we have designed certain other Ultra-Violet Ray Lamps, provided with shields that prevent the passage of the short wave length and certain chemical rays.
We have been guided in designing these apparatus by the most competent Medical opinion and advice and the spectrum of the light of our lamps for Sun-bathing in the home is very similar to that of natural sunlight.
Twenty minutes or half-hour, or even one hours Artificial Sun-bathing can be indulged in without hesitation, but the same respect should be paid to Artificial Sunlight as to natural Sunlight. One does not expose ones eyes to the full glare of the sun, nor yet ones body clothed or unclothed to cause discomfort and exactly the same principles apply to Artificial Sunlight, produced by a lamp that is specially designed for Sun-bathing.
We will quote as follows:-
Albert Eidinow, M.B., B.S., L.R.C.S., L.R.C.P. (The National Institute for Medical Research): "For home use and general treatment, lamps emitting ultra-violet rays 4,000-3,000 A.U., which are similar to the extent of the ultra-violet rays of the sun, should only be employed. This can only be obtained by the use of carbon arc lamps containing Vitaglass screens."
W. Kerr Russell, M.D., B.S.: "In regard to the most suitable form of ultra-violet lamp for use in the home, the obvious choice is the carbon arc."
Leonard Hill, M.B., F.R.S.: "If you wish to make an artificial source like the sun, put on a Vitaglass screen. In that way it is possible to cut down the power of the lamps and render them like sunshine."
The screens provided with the Ajax "Sunray" Lamps for home use are of Vitaglass and we supply both the Carbon Arc and Mercury Vapour Quartz Burner types of apparatus.

Unnamed: 9: Honorary Secretary of the Manchester District Branch of the organization.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 395

Rooms, always kept at 36° to 37°F. They saw a refrigerator under test for India, and were amazed to know that machinery for ice-making in the tropics was tested in rooms at a temperature of 120°F.

The Research Room was highly interesting, and members would have liked to stay longer to hear about the experiments which were carried out here. The party also visited the Testing Department, where small motors are thoroughly tested before being sent out, and were amazed to see snow in June here.

The whole tour was most interesting, and members were unanimous in voicing thanks for one of the most interesting visits of the season, when they were entertained to tea at the conclusion of the visit.

On Friday, June 29th, at 6.30 p.m., the members visited the Co-operative Bakery, Gt. Brook Street, Birmingham. This is one of the most complete Electric Bakeries in Birmingham, and here members saw dough mixed and cut, rolled and put into ovens, all by Electric Machinery.

This certainly is a Bakery to be appreciated, and members thoroughly enjoyed their visit, and were most pleased to receive a sample loaf from the All-Electric Bakery.
A.I.H.

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, "Woodville," Ack Lane, Bramhall, Cheshire.

The only visit made by the Manchester Branch since the last report was the delightful one to Deganwy, near Llandudno, to see the seaside home of Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti. So many members applied for tickets that the visit was extended to two days, July 10th and 11th, and through the great kindness of Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti over 60 people had a most enjoyable day.

As their guests, we left Manchester by charabanc about 9 a.m., had lunch with Mrs. Ferranti at the Castle Hotel, Deganwy, and in the afternoon made a most interesting inspection of her all-electric house, "Little Haldon." Tea was thoroughly appreciated on that sunny day, and about 5.30 the charabanc returned to Manchester. Our warmest thanks are due to Dr. and Mrs. Ferranti for all their kindness. The house is described in some detail on another page.

The Committee has met several times during the summer, and the winter programme is now almost complete. At our first meeting, on October 4th, we are hoping to open by a Civic Reception in the Lord Mayors Parlour of the Town Hall, when Mr. Llewellyn Atkinson has promised to come and speak. D.M.P.

Unnamed: 9: Hon. Secretary of the Cheltenham Branch of the E.A.W.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 397

Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Stemp, 1, York
Terrace, St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.

The concluding meeting of last seasons pro- gramme was a lecture demonstration on "Elec- tricity and Motor Cars." The number of members who assembled at Mr. H. E. Steels spacious Motor Showroom fully illustrated the interest taken by modern Eve in the subject. Mr. H. E. Steel described and demonstrated the various electrical apparatus used on a modern car. A stripped car chassis enabled everybody to follow more closely the position and function of each device. Many points were raised at the con- clusion, and much useful information was given.
The Electrical Contractors Association kindly invited our members to the various meetings of their Annual Conference, which was held at the Cheltenham Town Hall during the first week of July. We were fortunate in enrolling several new members at this Conference.
Our list of fixtures for the Autumn Programme is practically complete. It includes a Medical Lecture, a Cookery Demonstration, a Discussion Meeting, a Lecture Demonstration on "Ultra- Violet Rays and Health," and a visit to one of our Printing Works. Full particulars will have been received by members and will be sent on application to anyone interested.

* * *

South Wales and Monmouth- shire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Tyler, Electric Service
Bureau, 27, Newport Road, Cardiff.

A Cookery Demonstration was given by Mrs. J. Tyler, of the South Wales Electrical Power Distribution Co., on June 26th, and as the number wishing to be present could not be accommodated, the Demonstration was repeated the following day. Altogether 97 members turned up for these Demonstrations (showing the popularity of "Cooking by Electricity.") Each day the members were welcomed by Mr. J. W. Beauchamp, Engineer and General Manager of the Power Co., and afterwards entertained to tea.
July 18th brought to a close one of our most interesting Sessions. On this date we were invited by Mr. Harry Ellis, Chief Engineer and Manager of the West Gloucestershire Power Co., to visit the Power Station at Lydney. The extensions taking place there brought home to us the vastly increasing popularity of electricity, and our members thoroughly enjoyed hearing about the miles of overhead lines that were being carried from one district to another. transcription:
The Electrical Age
399
impossible to describe the happy time we had there, but the members (numbering 51) were unanimous in the opinion that it was quite the most successful fixture we have had.
Our Autumn programme includes a Lecture on "The Preservation of Food"; a visit (at the invitation of the Newport Womens Citizens Association) to the Ideal Homes Exhibition at Newport, with an address by Mr. A. Nichols Moore, Borough Electrical and Tramways Engineer, Newport, Mon.; a Cookery Lecture and Demonstration; a visit to Messrs. Santon, Ltd., Electrical Engineers, Newport; a visit to Messrs. Metropolitan-Vickers New Showrooms.
A film on "How a Lamp is Made," will be shown by Mr. L. A. Snow, Manager of the Cardiff Branch of Messrs. British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd.
Mr. R. L. Booth, Chairman of the Electrical Contractors Association (Cardiff Branch) has very kindly promised to continue to give his "lessons" on the "Small Repairs in the Home." We appreciate this very much indeed, as we find these instructions very helpful. J.T.

▣ ▣ ▣

North East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm, Carliol House, Newcastle-on-Tyne.

The North East Coast Branch have utilised the summer months by visiting Tyneside Industries—the object being to create an interest in commodities made locally and to see electrically driven machinery used in factories.
The first visit, in June, was to the Cremona Toffee Works. The cleanliness and efficiency of the whole work of the factory was wonderful, and the members were amazed at the good quality of the ingredients used.
In July a visit was paid to Messrs. Davidsons Glass Works, and every process in the making of moulded glass was observed.
The visit in August was to the Team Valley Paper Mills, and again the process from mechanical and synthetic pulp to the finished notepaper was watched.
At every factory our reception was most cordial, and the firms concerned took pains to explain everything to the members—and we are all grateful for the hospitality we received. Our last visit was made in September to Messrs. Hedleys Soap Works, and this promises to be most interesting.
The winter programme is almost complete, and it is to consist of some visits, the School of Cookery, an electrical Therapy Nursing Home and a Colliery and some Lectures. The first event for the Winter Session is a Reception and Social, and we are anticipating with great pleasure the presence of our President, the Viscountess Grey of Fallodon. We hope at this function to raise the nucleus of a Hospitality Fund for use at the Conference in 1929.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 401

Ashford and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. B. M. Wilson, " Gleniffer
Brae," Vicarage Road, Kennington, Nr. Ash-
ford, Kent.

Since the last issue of the E.A. we have spent
our time on the lighter side of the Aims and
Objects of our Association before we take up our
work in earnest in October. July found us enjoy-
ing a delightful trip to Mr. Borlase Matthews
All-Electric Farm. The welcome we received
from our host and hostess will long be remem-
bered by each one of us. It was also an added
enjoyment to meet there a contingent from
London. August: the non-holiday makers paid
a visit to the Ashford Power Station. September
5th was a red letter day, when we enjoyed a most
successful garden party at " Gleniffer Brae."
Mr. A. J. Southam, Chairman of the Ashford
Urban Council, presided at the opening ceremony,
which was performed by Mrs. H. W. Blackburne.
A presentation to Mrs. Blackburne of an Elec-
tric Smoke Absorber was made by Mrs. F. Hay-
ward (President of the Ashford and District
Branch).
Mrs. I. E. Bray spoke on the tremendous
future of electricity in the country.
The entertainment provided was most varied,
and included tea stalls, side shows, dancing and
a tennis tournament, and the co-operation and
help of a number of enthusiastic workers resulted
in a most enjoyable and successful garden party.
B.M.W.

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o., Ingleby Motors, Sweet Street, Leeds.

The Leeds and West Riding Branch will be
re-opening for the Winter Session in October,
and an interesting and attractive programme has
been arranged.
On October 9th, Mrs. Francis-Lewis, well-
known for her skill in making charming elec-
trically illuminated flowers, will lecture and
demonstrate on " Electricity as Applied to Arts
and Crafts," and on October 24th, Mrs. W. B.
Woodhouse (one of the Vice-Presidents) has very
kindly invited the members to tea at her home
at Bramhope to see some special features of
" Interior House Decoration," and hear a lecture
on this subject.
During November, Mr. B. C. Holding, Editor
of " The Electrician," will lecture on " Elec-
tricity in the Home: the Labour-Saver and Com-
fort Bringer," which is a subject that should
appeal to all members, and on December 12th,
Miss Haslett has kindly promised to pay a visit

Astley Hall,
Worcestershire.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 403

to Leeds and fully explain the objects of the
new " Electrical Outlet Campaign." Many
other interesting lectures and visits are also
arranged for the New Year.
The Branch is hoping to raise much enthusiasm
this Winter, and to be successful enough to, at
least, double its membership before the end of
the season.
* * *
London Activities.

Our Summer Programme concluded with an
extremely popular visit by motor coach to
Ashtead and Leatherhead. At the Ashtead Pot-
teries the party was received by Major Moore,
who gave a most interesting talk on the making
of the pottery. Everyone admired the lovely
work, which is all done by ex-Service men.
The Frederick Milner Home, too, was most inter-
esting, and Mr. Key conducted the party through
the workshops, where "Thermega" Blankets
were being made.
Then we all had a delightful tea in Mrs.
Jacksons lovely garden at her home in Leather-
head. The weather was all that could be desired,
and it was everywhere agreed that this was one
of the happiest fixtures of the year.
Our programme for the Autumn and Winter
includes a meeting arranged by the Mayoress of
Kensington, Mrs. R. Dudley Baxter, at her
home, where members of the E.A.W. will meet
representative women of Kensington. Other fix-
tures include a lecture on the Electricity Supply
Act, 1926, by Mr. E. E. Hoadley, at which Mrs.
Wilfrid Ashley has promised to take the chair.
Visits to the "Model Dairies of the London
Wholesale Dairies, Ltd.," and to the new "Elec-
tricity Showrooms at Battersea," three Lecture-
Demonstrations at the Model Electric Kitchen,
46, Kensington Court, and Social Afternoons and
a Social Evening arranged by the Social Sub-Com-
mittee. In addition, a series of Evening Lec-
tures has been drawn up specially for those en-
gaged in the Electrical Industry and in Domestic
Science, and the lecturers include Colonel
Vignoles, Mr. W. J. Jones, and two such well-
known women as Miss Gladys Burlton and Miss
Nora E. Miller.
Particulars of these Lectures will be sent on
application to the Director.
V.N.

transcription:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE
FOR WOMEN
The Official Journal of the Electrical Association for Women—Issued Quarterly.
Editor—Miss C. HASLETT, 46, Kensington Court, London, W.8.
Vol. I. JANUARY, 1929. No. 11
I look forward to the day when the majority of the people will take an intelligent interest in electricity, and what is more important, know what they want of its services, so that they may benefit by the many labour-saving and comfort-bringing devices recently invented.
The Electrical Association for Women was formed with the object of interesting and instructing the women of the country on this subject. I hope the Association will make rapid strides and will before long be able to open branches all over the country.
After creating the desire to know more of the power of modern electricity, it is to be hoped this will be followed up by a strong public demand for cheap current, so as to bring these amenities within the reach of as many as possible.
A great increase in the use of electricity will surely result in a decline of smuts in our cities—may we live to see that happen!
Photo by Bertram Park. THE DOWAGER LADY SWAYTHLING.
Gladys Swaythling

transcription:
The Electrical Age 409
Our Portrait Page.
Interesting Personalities in the E.A.W.

Photo by Ethel M. Eadon.
MRS. S. Z. DE FERRANTI.

Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti has been elected President of the newly-formed N. Wales Branch of the E.A.W.
Of all the women in this country who believe that Electricity can bring emancipation from drudgery to the woman in the home, Mrs. Ferranti would undoubtedly be placed first.
Not only is she a wonderful preacher of the value of Electricity, but she has applied all her principles in a practical way in her own homes. Both at the lovely old Derbyshire Hall at Baslow and at the more modern seaside home of Deganwy, there will be found Mrs. Ferrantis practical application of her belief.
Her point of view and experience are the more worth while when it is known that she herself in the early days had to battle with coal fires and the resultant dust and smoke. Knowing the difference in the home life when Electricity is installed, Mrs. Ferranti is impatient for all women in this country to benefit as she has done herself.
During the wonderful career of her husband, Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, F.R.S., she has been his constant companion, and together they have radiated such belief and confidence in Electricity as one of the most wonderful forces of emancipation in civilisation, that a friend laughingly referred to it as the " Ferranti Faith."

Lady Bird, who is an active Vice-President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the E.A.W., is very interested in all Electrical labour-saving devices. She is the wife of Sir Robert Bird, Bart., M.P. for West Wolverhampton, and in her busy life manages to take an interest in all kinds of important movements.
We learn that she has just been elected Vice-Chairman of the Womens Advisory Council for the West Midlands Area of the National Union of Conservative and Unionist Associations for the coming year.
Lady Bird is a lover of Music and all the Arts, and is Chairman of a Music and Entertainment Sub-Committee which promotes Choir Singing, Folk Dancing and Acting, and which produced in 1926 the Pageant of Queen Elizabeths visit to Charlecote. The Womens Institutes, which are doing such excellent work in the country districts, also claim a portion of Lady Birds time, she being a member of the Executive Committee of the Warwickshire Federation. Her interests extend to the younger generation and find expression in the Girl Guide movement. She was recently appointed Division Commissioner for the Tamworth Division of Warwickshire, and has been Division Commissioner for the Stourbridge Division of Worcestershire for the last five years.
A member of H.M. Queen Marys Committee of the Queens Institute of District Nursing, she takes a great interest in many hospitals and nursing associations. Like so many busy women, Lady Bird is a sportswoman, finding time to play both tennis and golf.

Photo by Lenare.
LADY BIRD.

The Electrical Age 409
Our Portrait Page.
Interesting Personalities in the E.A.W.

Photo by Ethel M. Eadon.
MRS. S. Z. DE FERRANTI.

Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti has been elected President of the newly-formed N. Wales Branch of the E.A.W.
Of all the women in this country who believe that Electricity can bring emancipation from drudgery to the woman in the home, Mrs. Ferranti would undoubtedly be placed first.
Not only is she a wonderful preacher of the value of Electricity, but she has applied all her principles in a practical way in her own homes. Both at the lovely old Derbyshire Hall at Baslow and at the more modern seaside home of Deganwy, there will be found Mrs. Ferrantis practical application of her belief.
Her point of view and experience are the more worth while when it is known that she herself in the early days had to battle with coal fires and the resultant dust and smoke. Knowing the difference in the home life when Electricity is installed, Mrs. Ferranti is impatient for all women in this country to benefit as she has done herself.
During the wonderful career of her husband, Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, F.R.S., she has been his constant companion, and together they have radiated such belief and confidence in Electricity as one of the most wonderful forces of emancipation in civilisation, that a friend laughingly referred to it as the " Ferranti Faith."

Lady Bird, who is an active Vice-President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the E.A.W., is very interested in all Electrical labour-saving devices. She is the wife of Sir Robert Bird, Bart., M.P. for West Wolverhampton, and in her busy life manages to take an interest in all kinds of important movements.
We learn that she has just been elected Vice-Chairman of the Womens Advisory Council for the West Midlands Area of the National Union of Conservative and Unionist Associations for the coming year.
Lady Bird is a lover of Music and all the Arts, and is Chairman of a Music and Entertainment Sub-Committee which promotes Choir Singing, Folk Dancing and Acting, and which produced in 1926 the Pageant of Queen Elizabeths visit to Charlecote. The Womens Institutes, which are doing such excellent work in the country districts, also claim a portion of Lady Birds time, she being a member of the Executive Committee of the Warwickshire Federation. Her interests extend to the younger generation and find expression in the Girl Guide movement. She was recently appointed Division Commissioner for the Tamworth Division of Warwickshire, and has been Division Commissioner for the Stourbridge Division of Worcestershire for the last five years.
A member of H.M. Queen Marys Committee of the Queens Institute of District Nursing, she takes a great interest in many hospitals and nursing associations. Like so many busy women, Lady Bird is a sportswoman, finding time to play both tennis and golf.

Anti-Flash "Outlets" and Interlocked Switchplugs.

We all know that at times a flash has appeared when using our switch in connection with electrical equipment. While there is usually very little danger in this, it is apt to be rather trying for the specially nervous person.

Recently a completely new departure known as the "Anti-Flash" socket has been placed on the market by the "M.K." Electric Company. The sockets are completely covered by an insulating housing. On the insertion of the plug head these housings automatically open, and on the withdrawal, they automatically close. This completely cuts off the flash and renders them practically shock-proof.

The Interlocked Switchplug is designed in such a way that the switch cannot be "on" when the plug is out and the plug cannot be removed when the switch is "on." Thus the mother need have no fear that the "outlets" will be a source of danger to the children should they decide by any chance to play with the switch.

Lampholders & Lampholder Adaptors.

In these days when people are apt to use bowl fires, electric kettles and other similar apparatus from the lampholder, it is necessary to see that not only the flexible is safe to carry this over load but that the lampholder and the adaptor will also do so.

This can only be ensured by purchasing lampholders and adaptors manufactured by well-known firms. The new "Tucker" Adaptor is designed to make the lamp contact stem and the wiring terminal out of one solid rod thus eliminating any possibility of heating up owing to bad screwing, or any part revolving, as all the parts are actually moulded into the adaptor and so form one-piece contacts.

Another question which should claim the attention of the home-maker when having the house wired is the subject of the two-way switch. This is quite a simple matter which avoids the necessity of constantly going upstairs or downstairs to switch a landing light on.

Childrens mischievous pranks need give rise to no alarm when "M.K." Interlocked Switchplugs are installed.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 413
On Choosing an Electric Fire.
By Mrs. Walter Lawson.
A certain percentage of electrical people still believe in a good old coal fire. This is heresy. We all know that wood and coal have always been used for firing, and so carry with them a certain tradition, which has great weight with the conservative mind, but in these advanced days why cling to the usages of our forefathers?
Coal is primitive and dirty.
Two questions I should like to ask. Do you like cleaning out ashes? Do you know any-one who does? No, neither do I!
Having once become used to the idea of heating houses without coal, the adoption of electric fires follows naturally, and their advantages appeal to one forcibly. They can be carried where they are wanted. They make no fumes, dust or smoke, thus saving pounds in doctors and decorators bills. The saving of labour is so obvious that there is no need for me to dwell on it. One point which is often overlooked is the benefit to plants and flowers. In a room where only electricity is used, freshly cut flowers will last three weeks, and longer and plants in pots which are difficult to rear will thrive and flower.
Among the would-be users of electric fires are many newly married people with limited incomes, living in small villas already wired for lighting, who long for the additional convenience of electric fires, but who hesitate to take the plunge because they are in the dark as to the cost of running them.
If they can obtain electricity for this purpose at 1d. per unit, the cost will be moderate if they train themselves to use them economical-ly, by judicious switching. As with gas fires big bills can be run up by careless people overheat-ing rooms, or for-getting to switch off when the rooms are not in use. There are generally two or three controls so that electric fires can be regulated to any require-ments.
Even where the cost of current is considerably more than 1d. per unit, electric fires can still be used with great advantage, and are not too costly to run in bedrooms or anywhere else when they are only in occasional demand.
There are so many admirable designs on the market that it is possible to suit all tastes.
The two main things to consider are what are you prepared to pay, and what kind of room do you wish to heat?
If you want to transfer your fire from one room to another, there are multitudes of inexpensive, light, portable types to

select from, but if you need one for con-

log fires, but the price is rather high.

The G.E.C. have many good styles to suit varied requirements, besides stocking Magicoal fires, and make a special one to be mounted on the wall in bathrooms. Bowl fires in the ceiling are also suitable for this purpose. Electric fires in bathrooms should be permanently installed by a competent contractor, and not placed on the floor.

Veritys Maxlume fires are very neat in Jacobean and Adam designs at reasonable prices.

Amongst many good models at the B.T.H. Showrooms, one called the Sheet Metal Fire appealed particularly by reason of its quaint style which reminded one of a turret window. This could be had in four sizes at very moderate prices.

Some of the fires I have mentioned have stands on which a kettle can be kept boiling. An article on Electric Fires would not be complete without a reference to the well-known "Tricity" Sunray Fires, with which we are all familiar, and which give not only a pleasant warmth but also an appearance of sunlight in the room.

I will conclude my list with a description of the Vesper Fire Screen. This is very useful, for it combines a very pretty metal fire screen and an electric fire, the latter of small round shape placed in the centre of the screen and covered with a decorative metal cap, when not in use. These are specially recommended to warm the rooms when summer evenings have turned chilly, and are just powerful enough for that purpose. There are two or three similar designs on the market.

transcription:
416    The Electrical Age

Some New Ideas on House Lighting.

A Horse and Cart put in their Right Order.

By MARY E. PROCTOR-GREGG.

It has long been acknowledged that to build a house first and to add light afterwards, is to harness the light to the right end of the house. But it is now being suggested (and the suggestion bears looking into) that the most workmanlike and satisfactory way is to reverse the procedure,

Photo by courtesy of The Electrical Times.
A Corner giving a glimpse of Cornice Lighting at the London Showroom of Troughton & Young.

and to begin by a "Let there be Light" dictum, followed by "Let a House be built round it." In other words, the right moment to consider the lighting question in a house is before it is built, not afterwards.
This perhaps sounds fantastic, but there are the practical reasons to support it . . . reasons so practical, in fact, that it would seem nothing more than commonsense to accept and act upon them.

In the first place, one has to concede that in the house that is built first and lighted afterwards, there is always the problem as to whether it is better to place the furniture so that it suits the room, or so that it can benefit by the lighting facilities. To comply with both these considerations at the same time and in the same place is rarely possible. The usual solution of this insoluble problem is either to compromise or to sacrifice utility alternately with comfort.
But that is no satisfactory way out of the difficulty. The obvious remedy is to have a house-full of rooms built to conform to a pre-determined and all-adequate system of lighting. This is also to argue that such rooms will be eminently suited to the purposes for which they are to serve, since ideal lighting will always allow of more than one method of furniture arrangement.
The ubiquitous and generous light given by the sun, sets a standard to which our humanly devised lighting systems can attain and even enhance. Our artificial lights can be turned off and on at will, and need never go down. Yet the most admirable characteristic of the sun as a light-giver, which is Impartiality, can only be copied below our roofs if the position and number of our counterfeit suns is assured before the house is built. To Bring the Sun Indoors, is a pleasant little catch-word and an excellent idea, but the only way to carry it out is to carry it in—before the walls are up and the

roof is on. Introduced by makeshift devices, heating and lighting power is half frustrated before it is released.
Before talking the subject threadbare, there are many other points of interest to take into consideration concerning this new idea of house-lighting. The time-honoured electric lamp with its globular bulb partially covered by its conventional parchment or fabric-covered shade, is due to die the death. In its place comes the new glass cover whose purpose is to hide the

[Illustration of a light fixture]
Photo by courtesy of "The Electrician."
A recent French Design by Jean Perzel.

bulb light, diffuse it fairly (and often squarely!), and to make the lamp, whether it be ceiling-hung, wall-bracketed or portably adjustable, a point of interest and beauty, strikingly noticeable or quietly unobtrusive. The accompanying photographs are suggestions as to the form and shape of these shades, which hide the bulbs that run

through their length and breadth, may take.
The colour, shape and plain or patterned glass that can be used for the shades offers almost unending alternatives and combinations of design and effect. This Art has come from Paris, but the Showrooms in this country, where these modern fittings for modern lighting can be seen, are those of Messrs. Troughton and Young, of 143, Knightsbridge, London, S.W.1. This firm is designing and carrying out lighting schemes all over the country and undertaking the branch of that work which forms the final subject of this discussion.
This subject has reference to the houses already built, whose owners may feel that it is too late now to mend their obsolete lighting systems, or for it to be possible for them to benefit by the latest ideas on the matter. But so far from settling down to that attitude commonly known as "being resigned to our lot," householders should foster a healthy discontent concerning their "lot," and seek advice as to how their houses may be converted and adapted to well-laid schemes for improved lighting on the lines of the new system. One would liken the already-standing house with the finally-installed lighting system to the cart that was put before the horse. But it is generally possible to cut the harness and put the horse at the other end of the cart, and in the same way to correct the relation of house to lighting. It means scrapping the old harness, but those wise in their generation will now be able to have their horse and cart in their right order—from the word "Go."

Unnamed: 9: Author providing recipes for an evening party on electric cooker.
transcription:
418		The Electrical Age

On the Electric Cooker.
By Miss Mary Mackirdy.
(Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow, and Author of "Recipes for You").

Suggestions for an Evening Party.

Little Chicken Shapes.
Savoury Eclairs.
Peach Baskets.
Meringue with Chocolate Mousse.

The addition of sandwiches, coffee and other drinks will be required to make the menu complete; there need not necessarily be two savouries and two sweets, one of each is sufficient.

Little Chicken Shapes.
1 fowl, a small knuckle of veal, 1 or 2 ozs. bacon, 2 bay leaves, 1 blade mace, salt, pepper, 1 or 2 cloves, a few peppercorns.
Cut the chicken in joints and put in pan with all the other ingredients, adding 2 pints water; simmer till the chicken is tender, then take all flesh from the bones, return the bones to the pan and simmer for two or three hours longer. The stock is strained and measured, there should be about 5 gills, the amount varying slightly with the size of the fowl. Mix the stock, the pieces of fowl and seasoning, put into little moulds and set aside to firm. When set, turn out.
The moulds are served on individual dishes, garnished with shredded lettuce, cress, endive or whatever may be desired. A fringed radish is placed at the side of the mould, and on top a rose of whipped cream made savoury with salt and a few grains of cayenne. The shape may be entirely covered with a good mayonnaise to which has been added a little whipped cream.

Savoury Eclairs.
The cases: 1/2 pint water, 2 ozs. butter, 4 ozs. flour, 3 eggs.
Boil the water and butter; sift the flour on a paper, then quickly "dump" it into the water, beating vigorously until the whole is converted into a thick paste that comes away from the sides of the pan. Let the paste cool, then beat in one egg at a time, dropping them right out of the shell. When the paste is smooth put it into a bag with a large plain pipe, press out in finger shapes on a greased tin, bake quickly till the whole surface is brown and firm. Split the eclairs with a knife or scissors and fill with a savoury mixture; the tops are brushed with glaze and sprinkled with chopped pistachios.
The filling: Two or three tablespoons chopped cooked chicken, sweetbread, lobster, etc., 1 oz. butter, 1 oz. flour, 1 gill stock or milk, a little cream, salt, pepper, few grains cayenne, few drops lemon juice.
Melt the butter, add the flour, and mix, add the liquid and cook till there is a thick paste, add the other ingredients, seasoning carefully. A mixture of chicken and ham or tongue is good.

Peach Baskets.
Make some little pastry cases with very good short crust pastry, bake them and cool.
Drain some tinned apricots—they are smaller and look better for this dish—mix some chopped dates, cherries, walnuts and prunes with a few sponge cake crumbs and enough red currant jelly or fruit syrup to bind the whole into a paste. Form the mixture into small balls, fill the hollow of the apricots, put two pieces together to make a whole apricot, stick a thin shred of angelica in each for a stem and place neatly, one in each case. Boil the syrup from the apricots with 2 tablespoonfuls sugar and the juice of 1/2 lemon, boil till thick, add a few drops carmine; glaze the apricots with the syrup and when cold decorate with whipped cream.

Meringue with Chocolate Mousse.
Whisk 4 whites of eggs, adding while whisking two or three pinches of castor sugar; when the whites are stiff and dry-looking fold in carefully 8 ozs. castor sugar. Rub a hot oven shelf with white beeswax, put the meringue out in two, form these into rounds or ovals according to the dish on which it is to be served—they must be made of a size, sprinkle with sugar and put in a cool oven to harden. When firm they should come easily from the shelf. Meringues will keep indefinitely if sufficiently dry and kept in an air-tight tin.
Put one piece on the top of the other with whipped cream between, and coat the whole with Chocolate Mousse, sprinkle with chopped pistachio nuts or any decoration that may suggest itself. This sweet is delightful, and lends itself to almost endless variety.
The Mousse: 2 eggs, 2 bars of plain chocolate, 2 ozs. sugar. Heat the chocolate in a cup in hot water till soft. Beat the yolks and sugar till thick and creamy, beat in the chocolate then fold in the whites, beaten till very stiff. This Mousse may be served as a sweet alone: it is excellent chilled in a refrigerator or simply on ice.

We should like to assure our readers that all goods advertised in our pages are made by firms of repute, and are thoroughly reliable and strongly recommended.
When replying to advertisers, kindly mention "The Electrical Age."

Unnamed: 9: Gladys Sharp authored this article about electricity in country workshops.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 419

A Page for
Girl Guides.

Electricity in the
Country Workshop.

By . .
Gladys
Sharp.

Lovers of the English countryside are sad people in these enlightened days for, as time goes on, it becomes apparent that seemingly civilisation and beauty cannot go hand in hand. Every few miles along our

Turning a "Thrown" Pot.

highways the unsightly petrol stations have leapt into existence; every few minutes during the summer char-a-bancs rumble along our by-ways, however narrow and overhung, turning the greenness into a dusty reproduction of London. Posters on hoardings leer at us from fields, trains thunder through the quietest glade and steadily the ever-increasing populace of our overcrowded cities is spreading into the surrounding country and settling in houses for the most part ill-suited in appearance to the beauty which surrounds them.
For the London Girl Guide particularly, who has enjoyed many a hike in the lovely country of Surrey, it will come as a shock to know that at Ashtead, in the popular district round Guildford and Leatherhead, there exists a factory for the manufacture of pottery.
But electricity has stepped in so that the factory is far from being a blot on the land-
scape. Indeed the delightful exterior might well belong to a country mansion, a little isolated from the world by its pleasant drive up to the main entrance.
Inside this model factory electricity rules, the only fuel used being for firing the kilns in which the pottery is dried and for heat-
ing purposes. Everything else goes at the touch of a switch.
The potters wheel, which many of you may have watched with fascinated eyes when it occupied the centre of the stage in "Chu Chin Chow" and which is older than history, is here linked with one of the newest discoveries of civilisation and whirls merrily without effort of the potter.
The jolleys, those magical machines which fashion cups, saucers and plates,

Shaping a Pot on the Wheel.

the aerographs which spray colour evenly and thinly, the compressors and lathes, each playing a part in the wonderful busi-
ness of making pottery, are all driven by electricity.
The sliphouse boasts its switches which give instant control of the machinery with-
out any more effort than it takes for you to switch off the electric light in your home.

Unnamed: 9: Hon. Secretary shown in the centre forefront of the photo.
transcription:
420	The Electrical Age

One could wish this state of affairs to exist in all factories but in this particular one it is of vital importance for the Ashtead Potters are all men who have been disabled by the war and who, incapable of taking up their old avocations, have been trained to this new one and have become self-supporting citizens in a real money-making firm. And in watching beautiful vases and dainty pottery of every description shaped, hardened, coloured and glazed by their own efforts they have forgotten their disabilities and so taken a long stride towards health and happiness.
Electricity has helped in this as surely as it does in hospitals through the medium of ultra-violet ray lamps, for electricity creates a clean, cheerful atmosphere, which must have its effect on the minds as well as the bodies of those who call it in to help with their work.
Leaving the Ashtead potters busily making things to delight our eyes and brighten our homes we will take a short journey to another, smaller workshop in Surrey where electricity is doing its good turn every day.
The Frederick Milner workshop for disabled ex-service men is a large airy room in which about a dozen men, all of them declared totally unfit for any occupation, work under the very best conditions making electrically-heated blankets and stocking driers.
When our unhappy climate fails to pour health-giving sunshine through the many windows it is only necessary to switch on and from the lofty ceiling artificial sunlight is diffused from evenly-spaced lamps which also light the room and, of course, help to warm it.
The electrically-heated blankets are made entirely by the men and there is no fatigue attaching to it for the sewing machines are driven by electricity.
As in the case of the Ashtead potters these men are doing a full days work, are self-supporting and away from the grime and noise of cities, are quickly becoming class A citizens once more—helped two-fold by electricity. And the countryside is not spoiled by unsightly buildings, tall chimneys and clouds of black smoke!

Photo by Mrs. Benyon Stout.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 421
Colour and Health in the Home.
By W. G. Raffé, A.R.C.A., M.I.E.S., etc.
The subject of light and colour is one that is vast and complex, and many of its secrets are being but slowly revealed. Certain phases of the problem are so obscure that their great importance is not impressed upon us it should be. Light is health, light is life, light is vigour and vitality. And colour, being a specialised or sectionalised part of the light range of etheric vibrations, offers a special phase of vigour with a more definite reaction.
We are coming back to sunlight in therapeutics, and we are coming back to the wise and deliberate use of colour in the home. We have realised that light is beating upon us and our environment for all our waking hours. This light has an unceasing action upon us, for good or for bad. But we can scarcely say that any light is bad: it is insufficient light or the wrong coloured light, the glaring and badly designed light, that is wrong, because it upsets our delicate bodily balance.
Light exercises its power whether we are aware of it or not. It is by no means essential that our eyes should take in light and colour, or that we should consciously observe it. Blind people are influenced much the same. Even though they may not enjoy colour in the same visual manner, they get most of its benefit. Plants respond to light and to selected colour, though they have no eyes.
The clever woman knows much of this instinctively, and her physical sensitiveness to colour leads her to care for the choice of colour in the home. In daylight hours, it is more difficult to arrange or to modify the action of sunlight or skylight (two different hues, one yellow, and one bluish) as it enters the windows. By skilful selection and arrangement of furnishing and decoration, in hangings, floor covering, wall finishes, much can be done to produce a thoroughly healthy colour environment. It is, of course, impossible within the short space of an article to describe exactly what to do to get anywhere the right effect. And even in lectures where practical demonstrations are possible, only the general principles can be given. Each of our rooms must be taken on its merits. A practical artist, who is familiar with light and colour and knows their subtle effects, can do much by criticism, elimination of certain items or the introduction of others, to produce (often at little or no actual expenditure) charming results in a room which now fails completely to satisfy its usual occupants. A survey is made, a diagnosis is developed, and a prescription is completed, but always in due relation to the owner and occupier who is to use the place, and whom it must satisfy.
With artificial light, the clean, brilliant and flexible electricity, the best results are attainable. Almost anything that can be thought of can be done, though some ideas are very expensive to carry out. Others are equally as simple. Not only do we need the right lamp in the right place, but also the right colour in relation to environment. The right hue and intensity in illumination is as important decoratively as the right hue and shape in costume, and it is just as much worth while to take some trouble to ensure their correctness. Every woman is aware, for instance, that an evening dress of blue or mauve may easily be a failure, in certain circumstances, because the yellowish light from some lamps causes the hue of the frock to become "greyer" to the eye, and the true shade of the colour is lost. The same thing occurs in relation to domestic decoration. We often enter a room at night, which previously we have

Unnamed: 10: President of the Electrical Association for Women presiding at the luncheon
transcription:
422 The Electrical Age

seen only by daylight, and we remark on
the apparent change, sometimes better and
sometimes worse. Surely it is worth while
taking trouble to have it arranged so that
the colour looks just as nice at night, as it
does in the daytime, even if it is allowed
to be different.
Definitely we may now assert that a rest-
ful and harmonious colour scheme as our
environment tends to make us personally
restful and quiet. We cannot escape the
enduring effect of colour on our health.
Our bodies are as sensitive as any plants,
our emotions and minds much more so.
We should not endure for a moment an
unpleasant odour as part of our daily en-
vironment, but we should take steps to
remove it. We use flowers for their sweet
scent as well as their pleasant colour. Why
then do we neglect so often the equally
important question of definite colour
harmony? We resent unpleasant sounds.
They offend the ear, and cause annoyance,
even to the unmusical person. Why allow
the equally sensitive eye to be subject to
continual chromatic assault—for it is
nothing less?
Every part of the house, from attic to
cellar, should be made pleasant in colour
and efficiently lighted. It is not an expen-
sive proposition. Paint and lighting can
harmonise with and complement each
other. This electric age can bring clean-
liness and health by its light and its colour.
Our kitchens and cellars should be as
clean as our bathrooms. They should be
well lighted and cheerfully coloured. In
these days of few servants—or perhaps
none at all—we spend no inconsiderable
time in the kitchen. Even our friends—
perhaps just a few privileged ones—pene-
trate to our kitchens to bring some mes-
sage. Why should home workshops be less
important than the modern workshops of
a great factory? They are kept clean, well
coloured and adequately lighted because
the educated modern employer knows very
well that all these things make for true
efficiency and genuine economy, helping
greatly to eliminate waste and accidents.
A kitchen may be made a very pleasant
place to work in, or it may be a constant
source of irritation. That is a matter which
is very largely in our own hands. Having
banished raw coal with all its attendant
worries of dirt, smoke and soot, let us
banish also the black and unlovely iron-
work which was thought necessary to coal
burning. We can use instead white or light
tinted enamels and introduce pleasant
draperies without the need of endless wash-
ing and frequent renewal.
In all, we can remember that electricity
never fails us if we use it properly. Its
light and its colour are at our call, and if
we do not derive the greatest benefits, it
is our own fault for not making the ex-
periment.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 423

The
Manufacture of Electric Cookers.

The New
“Magnet” Works
at Birmingham.

In these days when women are taking
such interest in Electric Cookers, and in
all Domestic Electric Appliances, we are
pleased to know that manufacturers are
taking the matter very seriously, and are

Showing the Oven Interior being withdrawn
for cleaning.

giving consideration to the woman’s point
of view. New works are being erected,
and Science and the Laboratory are being
called in to help.
We recently visited the General Electric
Company’s new works at Birmingham,
where “Magnet” Cookers are being con-
structed.
To follow the history of the “Magnet”
Electric Cooker from its beginning, we
must go back for some of the parts to
some of our Iron and Steel Industrial
Centres, where the Iron Ore is made into
Pig Iron; this is further made into Steel,
and in turn is rolled into Steel Plates,
and after these various processes in the
Furnace and Rolling Mills, the metal is
ready to be made into cookers, fires, irons
and many other “homely” things.
The outer and inner cases of the Cookers
are made out of these metal sheets, cut,
drilled and folded. Most of this cutting
and folding is done by machines, while
some small parts are made by hand. The
inner cases are then enamelled and form
the interior of the oven.
Cast iron forms the hob, door, door frame,
base and legs, and on arriving from the
Foundry they are sent to the Grinding
Shop to be trimmed and polished.
When the door and door frame have been
fitted to the base, the outer and inner cases
are put in position, and the cooker is then
lagged with heat-insulating material, packed
in between the outer and inner sheet metal
cases. This is done in order that the heat
should be retained in the oven, and pre-
vents it from escaping into the room.
The top structure is next assembled, and
the 3-heat switches and fuses are fitted and
wired up to the oven, grill and hotplates.
The final operation here is the fitting of
the hob, and the cooker is thoroughly in-
spected by the Assembly Shop foreman
before it is taken to the Test Room, where
it is put on circuit with all switches on
“Full” for a set period of time, after
which it is tested throughout to see if the
insulation is good. It is then allowed to
cool, and the electrical connections are
again tested.
The cooker is finally cleaned and sent to
the Despatch Department where its ulti-
mate destination is decided, maybe a village

A Table Model of the “Magnet”
Cooker made of pressed steel.

in the heart of England, a City home, or
somewhere Overseas where “Magnet”
Appliances are almost as well-known as they
are here. V.N.

Unnamed: 9: Commented on factors necessary for the progress of rural electrification.
transcription:
426 	 The Electrical Age

Rural Electrification is only being made possible by the Overhead System of Transmission and Distribution, and that very hackneyed expression "bespoiling the countryside with poles and wires" has got to be lived down, for as much as the people want Electricity, the fact must not be overlooked that the Supply Authority concerned has got to see some return on the capital they have to expend.
To develop Rural Supply by means of an Underground System of Transmission and Distribution would call for such a heavy expenditure that to cover interest charges alone, it would be impossible to quote terms for current which would be a commercial proposition to the average consumer.
Without doubt the Shropshire Electric Power Company have paid particular attention to the design of their Overhead Low Pressure Distribution Lines, and there are numerous instances of villages connected, through which one could pass without noticing the existence of this so-called "unsightly method."
It is very interesting after a motor run to ask the friends that accompanied one if a certain village had telegraph wires along the road, and in almost every instance it will be found that the reply given is: "I did not notice." Well, this being so, Overhead Distribution for Electricity Supply cannot be too bad.
Mr. Legge remarked that although much progress in Rural Electrification had been made during the last few years, future developments largely depended on three important factors, namely: Reduction in cost of Overhead Transmission and Distribution; more assistance from tenants and land owners regarding Wayleave facilities; and lastly, cheaper lamps and electrical domestic appliances.
