A NEW CLOTHES DRYER.
This new " Sadia " Drying Stand over-comes the difficulties experienced during the winter and at all times in flats, in drying and airing clothes.
The main part of the stand is a box heater, loaded to 750 watts, mounted on a wooden white enamelled post. The extend-ing arms are made of wood and can be placed in any position.
The heater and arms can each be ad-justed to four different heights, so that anything from a handkerchief to a rain-soaked overcoat can be dried and aired.

Showing the "Sadia" Drying Stand in use as an Airer.

A further advantage of this Drying Stand is that it can be dismantled and the stand and arms put away, and the heater can be used separately for warming a room or dry-ing a cupboard. The heater can also be used for drying fruit and vegetables as the heating element is covered and protected.
It is a well-designed, practical and well-made article as one would expect of a " Sadia " product.

A GRAMOPHONE PICK-UP.
For those fortunate ones who possess both a Wireless Set and a Gramophone, the B.T.H. Electrical Pick-up is an excel-lent accessory.
When plugged into the low frequency amplifier of an ordinary wireless set this

B.T.H. PICK-UP AND TONE ARM

Unnamed: 9: Gave a lecture on the Electricity (Supply) Act  1926.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 429

The Electricity (Supply) Act, 1926.
Being Report of a Lecture given by Mr. E. E. Hoadley, M.I.E.E. (Electrical Engineer of Maidstone). before Members of the E.A.W.
Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley presided.
history of the Act.
In December, 1926, the above Act, with all its far-reaching consequences, came into being. The reasons for the Act go back to the earliest days of Electricity Supply, and it may be of interest to briefly sketch these reasons and the history of previous legislations in the industry of Electricity Supply. From the inception of the public supply of Electricity, up till the time of the Great War, and, indeed, later even than that, it was the opinion of a great many people engaged in the industry that one of the factors seriously hampering its expansion was the legislation which Parliament, in its wisdom, had imposed on it.
I have heard it said that only one man ever entered Parliament with good intentions, and his name was Guy Fawkes. It is now generally agreed that legislation is more often than not behind the times.
Electricity Supply up to the date of the War was governed by:—
The Electric Lighting Act of 1882.
The Amending Act of 1888.
The Electric Lighting Clauses Act of 1899.
The Electric Lighting Act of 1909.
These Acts contained many clauses that were either good or necessary, but also contained other clauses which were not sufficiently up-to-date. In other words, legislation affecting Electricity Supply in this country was rather of a parochial nature.
During the War it was brought home to the nation at large, as well as to its rulers, that a " cheap and abundant supply of Electricity " was an absolute necessity in the life of the nation, both industrially and from the domestic point of view. It is from this latter point of view that my audience this afternoon will principally consider the working and the effects of this Act.
After the War, a Committee was set up, called " The Electric Power Supply Committee " (generally known as the Williamson Committee of 1918). This Committee recommended the division of the country into areas, the appointment of Joint Boards of Control, of Generating Stations to be purchased, the best of these stations to be kept running and the supply organised on a regional basis.
A Bill brought before Parliament on these lines was very considerably modified and mutilated in its passage through Parliament, especially in the House of Lords. Although the Act of 1919 set up the Electricity Commissioners and conferred on them certain powers, it did not go far enough, and owing to the word " may " having been substituted for the word " shall " in a great number of places, and owing to the jealousy existing between Municipalities and Companies when called upon to work together, it was found practically impossible, except in very few cases, to form Joint Electricity Authorities. Hon. Secretary: Miss J. Dicks,
149, High Street, Winchester.
The Inaugural Meeting of the Hampshire Branch was held at Southampton on October 29th, 1928.
The President, the Dowager Lady Swaythling, in her opening remarks, expressed her pleasure in the fact of a Branch being started for Hampshire, stating that she was very interested, as she had recently fitted up her house with an apparatus that controlled the whole of the heating, lighting and cooking system; the installation had greatly lessened the work in the house.
Alderman Brown, the Chairman of the Southampton Electricity Dept., welcomed the formation of a Branch, and hoped that it would induce many other householders to become users.
Miss Haslett, Director of the Association, outlined its objects and described the work carried out by other Branches; she gave a most interesting lecture on the aims and objects of the Association.
The following officers were elected for the Branch:—President: The Dowager Lady Swaythling; Hon. Treasurer: Miss I. D. Sandeman, of Southampton; Hon. Secretary: Miss J. Dicks, of Winchester.
The first Council Meeting of the Hampshire Branch was held at Southampton on December 8th.

Rugby Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss N. Pedlar,
Electricity Showrooms, Little Church Street, Rugby.
A few months ago it was suggested that a Branch of the Association should be formed in Rugby, as there were so many people here interested in the Electrical Industry and also the local electrical tariff brought electricity within the reach of practically everybody.
On October 11th, the Rugby Branch was inaugurated at a very successful meeting. The Viscountess Fielding (whom we are fortunate to have for our President) took the Chair, and after the Branch had been welcomed by the Rugby Urban District Council Electricity Dept., Miss Haslett very fully explained the aims and objects of the Association.
A week later members attended, by kind invitation of the Rugby Engineering Society, a lecture given by Lieut.-Col. Vignoles, on “Electricity in the Home.” This was our first “official” appearance.
Our first works visit, which took place on November 20th, was, by courtesy of the British Thomson-Houston Co., to their Radio and Magneto Works, at Coventry. The party of 25 members who took part in this visit were met with cars at Coventry, driven out to the works, and here spent a very interesting and enjoyable time, afterwards being entertained to tea. Mr. Vinsen (the Acting works Manager) expressed his appreciation of the interest shown in the work under his supervision, and invited the Branch to pay a return visit.
We held another successful meeting on November 25th, when Mr. A. S. Kettle gave us an exceptionally interesting talk on “Fuses,” after which members spent an instructive half-hour blowing and mending fuses.
Future items on our programme include the following:—
Lectures on
“House Wiring and Tariffs,” by Mr. B. M. Butler.
“Electricity in the Home,” by Mr. B. C. Holding.
“Domestic Appliances,” by Miss D. Vaughan.
“Radio,” by Mr. B. M. Gambrell.
Visits to
The Printing Works of a local Paper.
The new Longford Power Station at Coventry.
A modern Coal Mine.
We are hoping that the Rugby Branch will be a very active one, and so promote the interests of the Association, and although we have existed, as a Branch, only since the middle of October, our membership is already between 40 and 50.
NORAH PEDLAR.

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. Klitz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, Denbighshire.
Two Inaugural Meetings were held in connection with the starting of this Branch, as the area is so far-reaching, being about 60 miles in extent, the first meeting on October 5th, at Church House, Wrexham, with Alderman Edward Hughes in the Chair, speakers were Miss Haslett and Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, and on October 6th, at the Town Hall, Llandudno, Mrs. Price White, C.C., the Chairman of the North Wales Branch, in the Chair, speakers again being Miss Haslett and Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti. Both meetings were most successful, though not so well attended as we should have liked, but as the Association was quite unknown in North Wales, we have to educate the women up to the knowledge of the work of the E.A.W.
Our membership is over 40, and we have had quite a successful two months’ work. Our programme has been a visit to new Showrooms at Abergele, with a cooking demonstration by Miss Argyle. Unnamed: 9: President of the branch; chaired the Outlet Campaign meeting session.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 435

very successful, and those who attended very much regretted their termination.
The session opened on October 4th with a meeting on the "Outlet" Campaign. Lady Brooks was in the Chair, and the speakers were Miss Haslett, three Supply Engineers, a builder, and an architect. The meeting was very well attended and the discussion was full of enthusiasm and interest. The meeting was followed by an "At Home," which was thoroughly successful.
Following this meeting was a lecture by Mr. A. P. M. Fleming, of Manchester. Mrs. Beale, Acting Vice-President, took the Chair, and the lecture, "The Romance of Electricity," fully lived up to its title. The clever way in which facts were linked up right through the ages and illustrated by slides made one realise how much thought and time must have been expended in acquiring and arranging the whole thing.
On October 23rd, members were privileged to visit the Municipal Laundry, Birmingham, where they saw the newest, most fully equipped "All-electric Laundry" in the town. Everything was done by electricity, and members were able to see a family wash begun, ironed, and aired within two hours for less than 1s. 6d. The party was very interested in the Automatic Washers and Electric Drying Cabinets.
This visit was followed by a Faraday Lecture by Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti. The members of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch of the E.A.W. joined with the members of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, making the attendance nearly 400, with Lady Brooks, our President, in the Chair. The lecture itself was one of the clearest and simplest that the women have ever heard, and at the same time most enlightening. It certainly was felt by all the women what a great privilege it was to be able to join with the I.E.E. in order to hear one of the leading scientists in the electrical world.
On November 8th and 9th, two visits were paid to an "All-electric Dairy"-50 members in each visit. This is one of the most model and up-to-date dairies in the Midlands. Members were able to view every stage of the sterilization of milk. The Bottle Washing Machine was a centre of great interest. Our host photographed each party of members, and at the conclusion of each visit every member was presented with a souvenir, containing the photographs taken.
On November 22nd Miss Partridge gave a lecture on "Womens Part in the Development of Rural Electrification." This was well attended, and all members were very pleased to learn of the great work being done by pioneer women in this direction and to know what good openings are being created for girls in the electrical industry.
A. L. HAYES.

Unnamed: 9: Honorary Secretary of the Manchester District Branch of the association.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 437

Manchester District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Foster-Jeffery, LL.B.,
6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.

Our opening meeting on October 4th had been planned as a reception by the Lord Mayor in the Town Hall, followed by an address by Mr. Llewelyn B. Atkinson, but owing to a bereavement the Lord Mayor was unable to be present, and Mr. Lamb, the City Electrical Engineer, presided.
Mr. Atkinson gave an excellent resume of the 1926 Electricity Act in an hours talk that sped like ten minutes, and many of his intent audience stored in much useful information to be released with good effect later in the family circle.
The Electrical "Outlet" Campaign Meeting on October 23rd might be called an All-Star Matinee: we had Miss Haslett up from London to tell us of the aims of the movement and to report progress, and we had three representative links in the chain that delivers electricity into our houses—Mr. Lamb, the Engineer, Mr. Halliday, the Architect, and Mr. Lightfoot, the Contractor, each in turn presenting his case, touching on the difficulties he had to meet, and all with hopeful suggestions for the future. After the meeting, Mrs. Fleming kindly invited the speakers and committee to tea at the Home and Counties Club, a privilege for which we were very grateful.
Of the visits paid this winter, the first was to our old friends, the Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical Co., to a demonstration of their Cooking and Domestic Apparatus, at Trafford Park. More than a dozen members of the recently formed North Wales Branch joined us in this visit, and Mrs. Lamb thanked the firm warmly in our name for their kindness and hospitality.
Another visit was to the Frigidaire Co., in Deansgate, on December 5th, when Mr. Jones explained the necessity of preserving food by some method, and the reasons why refrigeration is the best of these methods. Mr. Woodward showed us exactly how refrigeration is effected, and tea completed a very interesting and instructive afternoon.
The Electricity Showrooms of the Manchester Corporation were crowded on November 23rd, in spite of the bad weather, when Mrs. Flack gave a most interesting talk on "Electrical Appliances and their Uses in the Home." The array of irons, vacuum cleaners, kettles, cookers, etc., used in the demonstration added to the interest of the lecture, and question time was lively and fruitful of suggestions. Tea was doubly appreciated on so wet an afternoon, and we are grateful to the showroom staff for providing it.
The last lecture before Christmas, that given by Mr. Hall on "Electricity and Musical Reproduction," will be described in the next number.

It is fitted with a "Regulator" switch (Rheostat), by which one can obtain just the faintest glimmer up to the full power, as required.

It is fitted with a "Regulator" switch (Rheostat), by which one can obtain just the faintest glimmer up to the full power, as required.

Unnamed: 9: Undertaken to help Mrs. Harcourt Williams with honorary secretary duties.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 439

Honorary Secretary of this Branch, and each in turn has found that if the work of the Association were to grow as it should, then help must be given.
We are glad to say that Miss Foster Jeffery, LL.B., has kindly undertaken to help Mrs. Harcourt Williams with the duties of Honorary Secretary, and we trust that this friendly partnership may continue for some time to come. We are lucky to have Miss Jeffery, and extend a hearty welcome to her from all our members.
D. M. PEATTIE.
* * *
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Stemp, 1, York
Terrace, St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.

Our first meeting of the Autumn Session was a Medical Lecture of exceptional interest. We were privileged to visit Dr. Curtis Webbs Ultra-Violet Treatment Room at Imperial Square, and to hear him discourse on the effects of Artificial Sunlight and its value as a general tonic if correctly administered. We were surprised to see how, by the use of the Ultra-Violet Ray Lamp, butter could be distinguished from margarine, also the curious effect on various colours. We all thoroughly enjoyed Dr. Curtis Webbs witty and humorous chat, and were very sorry when it ended all too soon.
The " Outlet " Campaign meeting was well attended. Our President (Mrs. Atwell Lake) explained the aims and objects of the campaign. The speakers were Mr. W. J. Bache, M.I.E.E. (Electrical Engineer), Mr. T. Overbury, F.R.I.B.A., and Mr. J. Marshall, A.M.I.E.E. Each spoke from his own point of view, and all were unanimous in expressing their approval of the interest being taken by women in planning Electrical " Outlets." An interesting discussion ensued, and many points were raised, which should be of considerable help to all present.
A lecture on " Ultra-Violet Rays and Health," by Mr. B. Book-Jones, attracted a good number of members. The uses of the Ultra-Violet Ray, Infra-Red Ray and High Frequency for health purposes were fully explained. An interesting demonstration of the apparatus was given, and some members donned goggles and enjoyed a short spell of " sunshine."
A demonstration, " Cooking Christmas Fare by Electricity," by Miss A. A. Stemp, was a popular meeting. Many members were agreeably surprised at the ease with which rich Christmas cakes could be baked in an electric oven, with excellent results. It was heard declared that mince pies had never tasted so delicious!
A useful souvenir, giving all the recipes used at the demonstration, was presented to each member.
Our Electrical Engineer, Mr. W. J. Bache, was to have given us a lecture demonstration on " What an E.A.W. Member Should Know," but this had to be postponed owing to Mr. Baches illness that week.
We have still two more meetings before finishing the years programme—a visit to " The Echo " Printing Works, and a demonstration on " Cooking a Christmas Dinner by Electricity."
We are arranging an attractive programme for 1929, including visits to the New Magnet Works at Birmingham, the Ideal Home Exhibition, London, and " Bournville," Birmingham ; also some instructive lecture demonstrations.
A.A.S.
* * *
South Wales and Monmouth-
shire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. J. Tyler, Electric Service
Bureau, 27, Newport Road, Cardiff.

We are about to conclude a very interesting session, one which I think has been appreciated by most of our members.
The " Problem of Preservation of Food " and " Water Heating by Electricity," seem to be occupying the minds of most people at the present time, and the figures, charts and explanations given us when we visited Messrs. Santon, Ltd., Dock Street, Newport, gave us quite an insight into the best methods of water heating by electricity.
An extremely interesting cookery demonstration was given by Miss P. Chalker, of " Tricity," London, over one hundred members being present, after which the members were entertained to tea by the Committee.
The " Outlet " Campaign Meeting was held on Tuesday, November 25th. We had quite a good number present, but owing to the inclement weather not quite so many people turned up as we expected. Miss Haslett, in her own inimitable way, explained fully the need for the Electrical " Outlet " Campaign. She was ably supported by Mr. C. G. Morley New, Mr. J. W. Beauchamp and Mr. R. L. Booth. Mrs. C. T. Allan was in the Chair. Councillor Charles Hoare, a prominent Cardiff builder, and Mr. E. Wilmott, architect, entered into the discussion, and I must say we all thoroughly enjoyed the meeting.
We have two more interesting items on our fixture card, namely, a visit to Messrs. Metropolitan Vickers Electrical Co., Ltd.s new Showrooms ; and a film on " How a Lamp is Made " will be shown by Mr. L. A. Snow, of the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd.
Although we are losing a good number of our members through their leaving the district, we are steadily enrolling new ones.
* * *
North East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm, Carliol
House, Newcastle-on-Tyne.

The North East Coast Branch has suffered a very great loss in the death of their President, the Viscountess Grey of Falloden—it is a loss which we feel sure will be felt by the E.A.W. as a whole.

As an indication of the late Viscountess Grey’s interest in, and enthusiasm towards, our activities, she graciously consented to receive the members at a social evening held in Newcastle-upon-Tyne on October 19th. This reception was possibly one of her last appearances in public before her death, and, writing subsequent to the event, it would be untimely to lay emphasis on the pleasure and enjoyment of the members at the social evening, the success of which was assured by the presence of her late Ladyship.
Miss Turner, of Victoria Square, Newcastle, entertained the members to a delightful tea on October 23rd, and a paper was read on "Ultra-Violet Rays" by Mr. Howorth, Edinburgh. Mr. Howorth’s paper contained very valuable information on the application of Ultra-Violet Rays, and our members were convinced that if more of these meetings could be arranged they would do a great deal towards popularising the use of these health-giving rays.
On November 9th, Mr. O. L. Falconar, a principal of one of the largest firms of electrical contractors in the area, gave a lecture on "Household Electrical Repairs." Mr. Falconar presented his subject in an extremely interesting manner, and by the ease and simplicity with which he demonstrated minor electrical repairs he proved to the audience that the maintenance of electrical apparatus is not nearly so costly or apprehensive as may be at first imagined.
The visit to the Northern Counties Training College for Teachers of Domestic Subjects was very enjoyable. Unfortunately the Principal, Miss Bright, was absent through illness, but Miss Redford, Acting Principal, and her staff conducted the members round the school, and the members realised how comprehensive was the training of teachers and housekeepers. Craft in all guises, applied science and decorative art were most pleasingly shown, and a delightful tea was served by the students—with eatables well worthy of a premier school of cooking.
The year 1929 promises to be a busy one for the North East Coast Branch, and full of interest. Apart from the monthly lectures, a public meeting, to launch the "Outlet" Campaign, is to take place in the Connaught Hall. Miss M. Bondfield, M.P., will preside, and the speaker is Mrs. Willson, Past-President of the Women’s Engineering Society. We hope to have other well-known people supporting the speaker.
February 7th is to show us what can be done by an E.A.W. and E.D.A. combination. We are arranging an electrical carnival, a night filled with surprises, and any member visiting in the north at this time should apply for tickets and participate in the night of "electrical revelry." The surplus profits are to be devoted to our Hospitality Fund for next year’s Conference—a very worthy object.

success. We are much indebted to Mrs. Page

ladies out." All the members present were
anxious to hear more about this fascinating sub-
ject, and hope to bring their husbands next time,
so that speaks for itself. December 11th was
the date of our last meeting this year, when we
had a Social Evening, the members electing the
new Committee and receiving the programme
arranged for the first three months of 1929.

New Year.

The last visit was to the new showrooms of the Battersea Electricity Department, where a large party was most interested in the architectural beauties of the building and in the lovely detail work in the doors, cornices, etc. A short lecture on the growth of the Undertaking was given by Mr. H. F. J. Thompson, Deputy Electrical Engineer, and Mr. Howell spoke briefly on what the Electricity Department is doing for the housewives of Battersea. Tea was kindly provided for the party.
The Evening Lectures have been well attended, and the Socials are very popular.
In the New Year the Social Sub-Committee are arranging a special Social Afternoon, the proceeds of which will be given to the Electrical Trades Benevolent Institution, and it is hoped that a record number will attend.
The fixtures already arranged include, for the Spring, a visit to Messrs. Troughton & Youngs new Showrooms, which have been fitted with the new French Lighting Fittings, a Lecture-Demonstration at the Soho School of Cookery, a visit to the Ideal Home Exhibition, and a Luncheon at the Hotel Cecil in April, followed during the afternoon by a visit to the factories of Messrs. " M.K. " Electric, Ltd., where " Outlets " are made.

There will also be three Evening Lectures during the session.
Further particulars of these visits and of the luncheon will gladly be sent on application to the Director at Head Office. V.N

In the Model Electric Kitchen at 46, Kensington Court there is a new Floor Polisher which really does get into the corners. You are welcome to come along and see it.

THE ELECTRICITY (SUPPLY) ACT, 1926—continued.
Board is, as you know, Sir Andrew Duncan, who has achieved considerable eminence in Industrial and Legal matters. There is also a representative of the Power Companies, of Municipal Electrical Supply Undertakings, of the Coal Industry, of Labour, of Commerce, and of Banking, Finance and Industry predominating.
The initial steps in the reorganisation of the Electrical Industry subsequent to the 1926 Act are taken by the Electricity Commissioners. The Commissioners select the area to which a scheme is to be applied and prepare the details of the scheme.
The Commissioners have to be satisfied, and must likewise satisfy the Board, that a scheme in any one area will show, apart from standardisation of frequency, a saving over the cost of generation of the existing Power Stations.
The scheme for a given area, when prepared by the Electricity Commissioners, is then sent with supporting data to the Central Electricity Board for their consideration. The Board, before adopting the scheme, must publish it and give consideration to any representations made by any authorised undertakers in the area covered by the scheme. After due consideration, including representations referred to above, they may adopt a scheme with or without modification for the whole or only part of the area, as they see fit, and as may seem to them to be justifiable economically.
The scheme known as the " Scottish Scheme " was the first to be put into operation; the " South-East England Scheme " came second, since when others have followed.
As my own work has been mostly concerned with the South-East England Scheme, I will briefly refer to it. The area of the South-East England Scheme is roughly as follows:—With London as a centre, and with Peterborough to the North, Ipswich to the East, and a line running South from Peterborough to Reading and down to a point near Littlehampton.
The scheme was considerably modified after meetings between the Special Committee and the Central Board. The number of selected stations was increased, and other arrangements which would tend to improve the efficiency of the scheme were adopted.
In all these matters the local authorities receive the utmost consideration from the Central Board.
By inter-connection and co-ordination, and the erection of high transmission mains, it is hoped to eventually achieve the object of the Act, which is to cheapen the supply of electricity and to make a supply of electricity available over the greater part of the country.
Much has been written in the lay Press as to the price at which electricity will be sold, but I would suggest to members of the E.A.W. that they should not regard these notices seriously.
The first effects of the working of the Act to be felt by consumers will be a general levelling of prices; the efficient undertakings who sell cheaply will alter very little, but the consumers of the small and inefficient undertakings should at least reap some little benefit.
The working out of the Electricity (Supply) Act is a gigantic task, and it will remain for posterity to judge whether or not it was a wise piece of legislation.

The Commissioners have to be satisfied, and must likewise satisfy the Board, that a scheme in any one area will show, apart from standardisation of frequency, a saving over the cost of generation of the existing Power Stations.
The scheme for a given area, when prepared by the Electricity Commissioners, is then sent with supporting data to the Central Electricity Board for their consideration. The Board, before adopting the scheme, must publish it and give consideration to any representations made by any authorised undertakers in the area covered by the scheme. After due consideration, including representations referred to above, they may adopt a scheme with or without modification for the whole or only part of the area, as they see fit, and as may seem to them to be justifiable economically.
The scheme known as the " Scottish Scheme " was the first to be put into operation; the " South-East England Scheme " came second, since when others have followed.
As my own work has been mostly concerned with the South-East England Scheme, I will briefly refer to it. The area of the South-East England Scheme is roughly as follows:—With London as a centre, and with Peterborough to the North, Ipswich to the East, and a line running South from Peterborough to Reading and down to a point near Littlehampton.
The scheme was considerably modified after meetings between the Special Committee and the Central Board. The number of selected stations was increased, and other arrangements which would tend to improve the efficiency of the scheme were adopted.
In all these matters the local authorities receive the utmost consideration from the Central Board.
By inter-connection and co-ordination, and the erection of high transmission mains, it is hoped to eventually achieve the object of the Act, which is to cheapen the supply of electricity and to make a supply of electricity available over the greater part of the country.
Much has been written in the lay Press as to the price at which electricity will be sold, but I would suggest to members of the E.A.W. that they should not regard these notices seriously.
The first effects of the working of the Act to be felt by consumers will be a general levelling of prices; the efficient undertakings who sell cheaply will alter very little, but the consumers of the small and inefficient undertakings should at least reap some little benefit.
The working out of the Electricity (Supply) Act is a gigantic task, and it will remain for posterity to judge whether or not it was a wise piece of legislation.

The Official Journal of the Electrical Association for Women
PUBLISHED QUARTERLY
Editor
CAROLINE HASLETT
46 Kensington Court
London W.8
Vol. I. APRIL, 1929. No. 12
It is estimated that 12,000,000 people in this country are ministered to by the ether, their emotional, intellectual and spiritual life enriched mysteriously from the air.
There has been no greater achievement in the electrical age than this. Few, even of those who possess wireless sets, appreciate the power and possibilities of broadcasting.
A silent revolution has taken place in our midst. A force unseen, which steals softly through doors, and walls, and windows, travelling from the ends of the earth with the speed of lightning, has come to visit us in our homes and add to the happiness and interest of those homes.
By courtesy of "The Vote."
MRS. PHILIP SNOWDEN, J.P.
The sick, the infirm, the weary, the isolated, the poor, the illiterate, can all enjoy a bigger, brighter world than was possible to most less than ten years ago. May we be saved from the sin of taking this gift of humanity for granted.
Ethel Snowden

transcription:
EDITORIAL.

PROGRESS. When the E.A.W. came into existence just over four years ago, no one would have predicted that in such a short space of time it would have become so vast and its ramifications so varied.
It was generally felt by the small group of pioneers who started the Organisation that some avenue was needed through which the women of the country could be educated in the all-important subject of Electricity and its many Uses in our Modern Civilisation.
It took a good two years to present the E.A.W. message, but it is now no longer necessary to explain "why" and "what" the Organisation is. Branches are springing up all over the country, and hardly a week passes without a request coming from some district for a new Branch to be set up.
Obviously such a movement was needed amongst women, for it has not been the size of its staff nor its income which has made such growth possible, as a very large amount of the work is being carried on throughout the country on a purely voluntary basis.

ELECTRICITY IN THE SCHOOLS. The women of the present generation are becoming conscious of the handicap of running a modern home without an adequate knowledge of electrical methods, and are beginning to realise the need for some instruction to be given to the girl during her school life on this all-important subject.
Visits to Domestic Science Centres and Girls Schools reveal the fact that even where some such teaching is given the equipment is frequently out of date and often not properly understood.
The E.A.W. feels that here is a need for collaboration between the Educational Authorities and the Electrical Industry, and proposes to call a Conference toward the end of April of representatives of these two groups of people.
There are indications that the Headmistresses throughout the country are themselves feeling the need for some instruction on matters electrical to be given to their students.
As a first step toward tackling this problem, the E.A.W. is making a survey through out the country of the kind of Domestic Electrical Equipment, if any, which exists in Domestic Science Centres and Departments.

VARIOUS FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.
The Electrical Outlet Campaign organised by the Association just over a year ago has achieved its first object in raising discussion on this vital question of the number and position of "outlets" in the homes of the future.
The Campaign has shown that there is scope for further national activity in connec- tion with this matter, and as the result of a suggestion from the E.A.W., we understand that the British Electrical Development Association, which represents all sections of the Electrical Industry, will next year run a comprehensive campaign supplemental to our own.
As we go to Press we learn that the Lord Mayor of Newcastle will give a Civic Recep- tion to our delegates at the North East Coast Conference in July.
The April Luncheon and Ball promise to beat all previous records.
Of special interest to Members should be the Morning Session at the Hotel Cecil when reports will be given of the Progress of the work of the Association throughout the country.

The North East Coast Exhibition. :: The Lady Mayoress of Newcastle.
An Electrical Carnival on the North East Coast.
The 1929 Conference of the Electrical Association for Women, which is to be held at the North East Coast Exhibition at Newcastle from July 10th—12th, promises to be one of exceptional interest. Great preparations for the welcome of the visitors are already afoot and funds have been collected for their entertainment.
The North East Coast Exhibition, where the Conference will be held, is the largest Exhibition ever staged in the North of England.

Arts and Crafts will include decorative needlework; bookbinding and leather work; metal work in copper, brass, jewellery and enamels; lacquer and painted woodwork; carving and wood inlay; illuminating; pottery, china painting, stained glass; designs for fabrics, textiles,
A View of the Exhibition.
Special buildings are being erected, including Palaces of Engineering and Industries. Sections devoted to Art, Music and Amusements, and one very fine building is set aside solely as a Womens Section. A representative committee of women has been at work for some time arranging for the exhibits for this section, which have been divided into four classes: Fine Arts; Arts and Crafts; Domestic Science, Nurs-
wallpapers; weaving and spinning, and toys.
Lectures will constitute the Domestic Science, Nursing and Child Welfare Section, the subjects being cookery, laundry, housewifery, sick nursing, first aid, health, food and clothing. transcription:
The Electrical Age 451

municipal year, which will undoubtedly be a memorable one in the history of Newcastle. Conferences representative of the principal Scientific, Commercial and Social Organisations of the country will be held in the City, and will be attended by visitors from all parts of the British Empire, America and most of the nations of Europe. Come whence they may, all will find a kindly greeting awaiting them at the hands of the Lady Mayoress.
If Mrs. Lambert should be found lacking in her knowledge of the application of Electricity as advanced by the Electrical Association for Women, she has already shown her capabilities to make this life happier for all by her attention to music. Whether at the Great Organ, accompanying her husband in the conduct of the annual Armistice Day commemoration function, or bringing out the sweetest notes from her favourite harp, or presiding at the piano at classical concerts or community singing, she is equally "at home." It will therefore be readily appreciated that she has endeared herself to all hearts in "Canny Newcassel," which we feel confident we shall all shortly acclaim as "The Pride o the North."
An Electrical Carnival.
With a view to raising funds for the entertainment of delegates during the Conference, the North East Coast Branch of the E.A.W., together with the local branch of the E.D.A., arranged a very successful Carnival during February at the Oxford Galleries, Newcastle-on-Tyne. The company was a representative one, over a thousand people being present, and the Committee are to be heartily congratulated on the success of their efforts.
The Lady Mayoress of Newcastle received the guests, and later in the evening the Lord Mayor, the Sheriff and Lady Sheriff attended and joined in the carnival spirit that reigned the whole night through.
The programme was a comprehensive one, and included Treasure Dances, Cabaret, Shadowgraph Competitions, etc. At each supper sitting there were lucky chairs at the supper table, and programmes carrying lucky numbers were responsible for the allocation of most of the prizes. It was possible to keep the programme going to time by means of loudspeakers installed and operated by the British Thomson Houston Co., Ltd.
An interesting and spectacular part of the programme was a cabaret produced by the Misses Lazenby. They and their pupils are to be highly congratulated on the success of their efforts. Cooking "done to time and done to a turn"—picture chef with an electric cooker, table utensils complete, preparing the sweet for the evening meal, the castle puddings are put in to bake, with a quick glance at the fish and the pie in the oven. The chef falls asleep and has a nightmare. A darkened hall and slowly moving curtains reveal a cooker of immense size; the door opens and out slides a dish with a salmon. She flaps her fins, her tail, and finally flops off her dish and dances, and just manages to step back into the oven before the door closes. Then out comes a gigantic pie, the crust breaks apart and four most sprightly rabbits jump up and gambol, then four dainty castle puddings in lemon with cherry-topped heads appear and daintily do their part. The dancers disappear. The chef wakes up, looks at the clock and dishes up the meal he has prepared.
The spontaneity of the dancers, the clever by-play of a most French-like chef, and the charming costumes made the cabaret something to be remembered.
An Electrical Wedding.
At midnight the lucky programme numbers were called, and eventually thirty ladies and thirty men, the lucky holders, were standing in double file in the centre of the ballroom, and without any warning the band struck up and played Mendelssohns "Wedding March," and simultaneously from the roof was lowered a man in appropriate clerical gait but with cupids wings attached, much to the amusement of the

nine hundred and forty onlookers. This
man proceeded with a mock wedding cere-
mony, and "married" Miss Switch,

following words:—
" My deah fwiends.—We are heah for a
solemn purpose to join together—er to
weld—er to unite in matrimony our two
deah friends who are heah before me—Mr.
Plug and Miss Switch.
" These deah children are the outward
and visible symbol of two most prominent
institutions.
" On the one hand we have Mr. Plug—
this handsome and distinguished Adonis
who embodies all the attributes of complete
electrification. Of virtues he has many, of
vices, none; and, deah friends, on the other
hand we have Miss Switch, who is the per-
sonification of all that is best in this deah
land of ours—I refer to—er, electric juice
in the home. She knows—whats watt.
" Yes, I think so.
" Mr. Plug, do you take Miss Switch to
be your lifes partner for the advancement
of all things electrical, to guide her, to
give her good council whereby a great aim
may be achieved?
" Miss Switch, do you take Mr. Plug to
be your friend, philosopher and guide,
thereby making EDA and EAW two souls
with but a single thought, two hearts that
beat as one.
" If there be one in my congregation who
knows of any cause why these two should
not be united, let him speak now, or for
ever hold his peace.
" Hands up for ayes.
" Hands up for noes. Carried unan-
imously.
" EDA and EAW, with these priceless
gifts from the Electrical Industry I wed
thee."

such a success that the company present
are asking if it can be repeated each year

The Electrical Age 453
Electrify Your Home. By Lady Cowan.
Who is President of the British Womens Patriotic League.
It has been suggested that my views on the subject of domestic electrification may be of interest to readers of The Electrical Age for Women, and I trust that the following remarks will be useful to women generally.
Lady Cowan.
Electricity supply in this country has been governed by Acts of Parliament dating back as far as 1882. Parliament has long since recognised the need for the national development of electricity, in order, without doubt, to utilise to the fullest extent the natural resources of the country, and also to bring electricity within the reach of the entire population of the British Isles.
It is recognised that a cheap and abundant supply of electricity is necessary to meet the present requirements of the nation. The Electricity (Supply) Act of 1926, having now reached the Statute Book, the general electrification of England has commenced. Its first effects are already being felt in a general levelling and wholesale reduction of the cost of current, and these reductions must continue until a general economic and low rate is established, the question of price being, of course, the main factor in deciding the universal use of electricity in the home.
The home is essentially, even in these jazz days, a British womans sphere, and it is undoubtedly the aim of all British women to make their homes places of comfort. Hence the first question which presents itself is—How best can this object be attained, and by what most inexpensive method?
The first essentials in the home are: health, hygiene and comfort. Lighting and heating are, without doubt, the first which automatically suggest themselves. So far as concerns lighting, some of us will remember the old days of the tallow candle and snuffer; later the oil lamp, then the ordinary naked gas burner, followed by the incandescent upright, and, later, the inverted mantles, and, within a comparatively few number of years, the electric light, first of all in the form of carbon filament, later replaced by the ordinary tungsten filament, and, finally, by the gas-filled or half-watt lamp of to-day. It cannot be disputed that the best, the most efficient, as well as the most hygienic method of lighting is by means of electricity.
Coming now to the question of domestic heating, a hundred years or so ago homes were warmed by fires lighted in the centre of the room without any outlet for the gases. The foul atmosphere thus created was aggravated still more by the crude method of lighting. Then followed the grate using wood, peat or coal fuel. Later followed the inestimable boon of the gas fire, which probably was the first known means of heat which could be controlled

Unnamed: 9: Author providing practical hints on using electrical spring cleaning equipment.
transcription:
456 The Electrical Age
Electrical Spring Cleaning Equipment.
By Mrs. Walter Lawson.
At this time of the year every woman is searching round for efficient tools with which to
do her Spring Cleaning. In this article Mrs. Lawson gives some practical hints on this
all-important question.
Since Electricity has been tamed to our domestic use, Spring Cleaning need no longer be a bogey, and although it cannot be entirely abolished, it certainly has lost most of its terrors.
Until recently, Spring Cleaning entailed covering everything with hideous dust-sheets, and getting ourselves up in dust caps, and overalls; carpets went away to be cleaned or were beaten in the garden, in which case hands were blistered and a good proportion of the dirt swallowed. Dismal chaos reigned, accentuated by the sound of echoing footfalls on bare boards.
Now, on the contrary, anyone possessing a good vacuum cleaner can Spring Clean with a light heart. There need be no discomfort of an annual upheaval, as the dust is removed regularly, not saved up for one dread period. Neither need we be born housekeepers to make a success of Spring Cleaning with the aid of a vacuum cleaner, as we can do the tasks in almost any rotation, secure in the knowledge that there will be no dust storm when the carpet is tackled.
Now is the time to invest in a vacuum cleaner, as the bright days will soon be here, showing up all the shabbiness and dust that were hidden during the short, dark days of winter.
There are two distinct types of vacuum cleaners. The first type I shall deal with, has a hanging dust-bag of material, attached to the long handle by which the machine is guided over the carpet. In my opinion this is the better type for large houses, hotels, clubs and offices. Amongst British makes, a good example is the Magnet, made by the G.E.C.
This is a handy, medium sized model, supplied at a reasonable price. Amongst its accessories, is a special nozzle for blowing dust out of corners, or off upright surfaces (such as backs of wardrobes or sideboards), preparatory to picking it up in the ordinary way, besides the usual ones for removing by suction the dust from tops of wardrobes, and picture backs, and high shelves, without smothering everything else. There is another fixture for getting into the crevices of upholstered furniture, and a special brush for the arms and seats; thus arm-chairs, chesterfields, etc., can be cleaned without laborious beating, and without taking them out of doors. These fittings should be kept together in a special place. The Magnet Vacuum Cleaner is supplied with a wooden rack to hang them on. This is most convenient.
The Hotpoint, a subsidiary company of the B.T.H., make two machines of the first type, the Premier Duplex, and the Premier Junior, which is a baby brother
The Polisher Attachment for the Premier Duplex Cleaner, which may now be obtained also with the Premier Junior.

A Page for            Wireless.           By
    Girl Guides.                           Beatrice Shilling.

Miss Shilling, who is an Electrical Engineering Apprentice, gives practical advice to Girl
              Guides on how to construct a Home Wireless Set.

There are still a good number of families
who do not yet possess a wireless set;
many because they have not the necessary
cash, and some because they do not care
for wireless, but quite a number would
have wireless had they someone to make
the set, put up the aerial and earth, get
the wireless licence, and, after the installa-
tion, keep the batteries charged and the
set generally in order.
   This is largely because of the saving in
cash by constructing and installing the set
personally instead of paying someone else
to do it, but also because wireless is still
regarded as one of the eighth wonders of
the world, and only an experts job.  But
however difficult the theoretical side of
wireless is, the practical, as it concerns
sets for the average home, is quite simple.
   The families who have no brothers or
fathers who will make their sets can turn
to the Girl Guides, who, if they can use a
screwdriver, pliers, and a file, should be
easily able to tackle the job.
   The choice of the kind of set to be built
must be governed chiefly by local condi-
tions.  The most sure way of finding how
many valves are required to work a loud-
speaker or headphones is to make enquiries
among your neighbours who have wireless
sets.  Generally speaking, the following
reception can be expected, with an average
aerial and earth, from any of the main
B.B.C. stations or about twice this distance
from Daventry:-

Unnamed: 9: Author of article answering queries on rural electricity supply.
transcription:
The Electrical Age
461
Electricity in the Village By Margaret Partridge, B.Sc.

Miss Partridge in this article answers the query so often received from Womens Institutes and other women living in the country, as to what steps could be taken to obtain a supply of Electricity in country districts.

Scene.—A meeting of the Parkshire Federation of Womens Institutes.
Mr. Sparks, a dynamic personality, has just finished a lecture on "The Domestic Uses of Electricity." It is now question time.
The Chairwoman.—I have never listened to a more interesting address, and I have never felt more envious of our town cousins who can have the home benefits Mr. Sparks describes.
I should like to ask if we, who nearly all live in the country, may ever hope for the same advantages and in the same measure.
Answer.—There has been a marked development of rural electrification within the last few years, and now there are authorised suppliers of electricity in more than half rural England.
Question.—Does that mean that half the people of rural England will surely get electricity within the next few years?
Answer.—I would not be so optimistic as that, though it may be so. Actually the half of England covered by Electricity orders includes over two-thirds of the rural population of the country, and we may reasonably hope that the other half—except for woods, forests and heath land, will soon be included in some electricity distribution area. It must be realised, of course, that before a supply can be given there must be a demand which is likely to become remunerative.
This means that villages of about 500 inhabitants or so might expect a supply, but isolated houses could only get it by incurring additional expense on cables to bring it to the house.
Question.—What do you mean by your words "Included in a distribution area?"
Answer.—The supply of Electricity is a Public service controlled by various Acts of Parliament. Under these Acts any Local Authority, Company or person undertaking to give an electricity supply has to obtain a Special Order from the Electricity Commissioners authorising them to supply electricity in some specially defined area.
When this Order is obtained by the authorised supplier no-one else is allowed to supply current within the area, but against this the Company is compelled to give supply to anyone who requires it and to whom it is economically possible to bring it. They are not compelled to bring electricity to anyone where the cost of bringing it would not be repaid by the amount of current consumed.
Question.—The village I live in has 1,500 people. I believe it is in the area of the East Parkshire Electricity Company. Could we, as a village, do anything to get electricity fairly soon?
Answer.—Certainly, it seems as though it should be possible. I should advise you first to write and ask the Electricity Company what their plans are with regard to your village.
If they have no plans, it would be well to ascertain by canvass how many people would be likely to take supply, and then—if there are a good number ready—either petition the Company as an independent group, or better still get your local authority to do so.
Question.—How can one find out if any village is included in any Special Order?
Answer.—The nearest Municipal Electricity Undertaking will certainly know if you happen to have friends there. Failing that, write to the Electrical Association for

Unnamed: 9: Signed article about British Thomson-Houston Companys new Aldwych showrooms.
transcription:
The Electrical Age
463
“New Lamps for Old.”
A Visit to the New Showrooms of the British Thomson-Houston Company
at Aldwych, W.
“New lamps for old! New lamps for old!” Let this be our cry now when we are busy cleaning and redecorating our houses within and without. Let us see to it that we not only renew our chair covers and curtains, but that our lighting fittings are in keeping.
We have lately been re-visiting the new and up-to-date showrooms of the British Thomson Houston Company, in Aldwych, W., and were much impressed by the colouring and design of some of the new shades, floor standard lamps, and vase table lamps to be seen there. Amongst the standard lamps which particularly impressed us was one of Chinese green lacquer, with a green damask shade and silk fringe. Another, striking an entirely new note, was of waxed pine in natural colour; this would harmonise with all modern or “futurist” decoration schemes.
The vase lamp in our illustration is of jade glass, with tinted parchment shade. The density of the glass throws up the colouring, and the shade of lighter tone seems to give a fresh “May-morning” effect into the room.
The new Vase Lamp with Parchment Shade.
In the domestic apparatus section, the new B.T.H. Refrigerator seemed to us to have reached the high-water mark of perfection in design and appearance.
It is “quiet” in the real sense of the word. There are no exposed moving parts, and the operation of the unit is simple, clean and economical. It can be connected to any electric point and forgotten with the sure knowledge that perfect refrigeration will be provided the whole year round at the cost of a few pence per week.
It simplifies housekeeping as far as food supplies are concerned, besides which, pure ice for drinks or delicious frozen desserts can be quickly made and kept for immediate service.
We would suggest that everyone who is interested in having the best that electricity can give, should visit Crown House and see for themselves some of the newest ideas of design in lighting and domestic equipment.
B.S.S.
The new B.T.H. Refrigerator.

Mrs. WILFRID ASHLEY. Sir JOHN S...
THE LADY...

It is characteristic of the E.A.W. that it has succeeded in
securing the support of the most prominent people in the country.
This is essentially true of the Luncheon to be held at... At this
distinguished array of speakers, the company will consist of the
Electrical Industry and eminent representatives of...

The Luncheon will be presided over by our President,

Mrs. WILFRID ASHLEY,

who takes the greatest possible interest in the welfare
of the Association. As is well known, Mrs. Wilfrid
Ashley is an extremely busy woman, but finds time
to take an interest in many excellent movements.
Of special interest to women is the fact that she
works for a firm of decorators in London, and her
advice in connection with house decoration is sought
for by many well-known people. To listen to a lecture
by her on colour schemes and house decoration is a
sheer delight. She has always taken a great interest
in the British Film Industry and has recently joined
an English film company, where her activities lie in
working with the producer in the production of films.
In a somewhat different field she gives her practical
support to such excellent movements as the National
Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and
she is particularly interested in the National Ortho-
paedic Hospital, being the Chairman of Buttercup Day.

During her busy life Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley finds time
to interest herself in many charities, and works ener-
getically on the committees for many balls and functions
for raising money for needy and worthy objects.

One frequently sees articles from her pen in literary
and society papers, and always one can depend upon
that freshness of outlook and originality for which
Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley is so universally known.

Sir JOHN SNELL, G.B.E.,

is, we are proud to say, a Founder Member
of the E.A.W. and an ardent supporter of the
work being carried out by the Association. As
Chairman of the Electricity Commissioners, Sir
John is one of the most prominent figures in
the Electrical World. The Electricity Com-
missioners are responsible for designing and
preparing the schemes for co-ordinating the
supply of electricity throughout the country
which are eventually adopted and carried out
by the Central Electricity Board. In his work
as Chairman of the Commissioners, which brings
heavy responsibility, Sir John has the repu-
tation for always appearing patient and courteous
and displays great ability in the fulfilment of
very heavy duties which might well dismay
anyone less tactful and diplomatic.

transcription:
466
The Electrical Age
A Visit to the United States of America.
By BEATRICE JOLLEY.
Mrs. Jolley gives a fascinating picture of the way in which American Homes are built and equipped on labour-saving lines. The American Home-maker knows the value of plenty of " Outlets " in each room, so that even with the lavish use of many artistic lamps there is very little trailing flexible about the room to trip up the unwary.
In the autumn of last year I visited America with the British Delegation to the International Commission on Illumination, and on the tour and subsequently, included in my itinerary the most important Eastern cities, passing through Canada from Montreal to Vancouver, and finally down the west coast to San Francisco and Los Angeles.
During this time I was particularly anxious to ascertain how the housewife met the scarcity of labour in the home, and to what extent electrical and other labour-saving devices were used. In California, I inspected many houses and flats in the course of erection, and found that there was very close co-operation between the architect and electrical and gas undertakings, especially with regard to the kitchen arrangements. For example, in most of them the refrigerators were built into the walls, and positions arranged for dish-washing and clothes-washing machines, with points (" Outlets ") close at hand. The kitchen decorations were a source of delight and envy ; the colour schemes were carried out in the palest blue, greens, and mauves, the refrigerators, stoves and sinks all matching. It was impossible to think of a detail that was missing.
The difficulty of eliminating cooking odours in small flats and houses where the kitchen cannot be completely shut off, is overcome by a new electric ventilator, which is adjustable to any window, and by the pull of a cord is operated in either direction—drawing fresh air in, or extracting the odours. I was a guest in a typical bungalow out West, which was centrally heated and had many modern appliances. I was surprised to find that they very largely used gas for their central heating and radiators ; but all the other equipment was electrical.
They informed me, that in their case, both the gas and electric supply was under one control, and therefore there was no rivalry between them, and all their energy was absorbed in obtaining new business rather than in useless competition. In this bungalow the hot air installation pipe was connected to each room by means of a grating in the floor, and each grating could be opened separately by a touch of the

foot, and the whole system turned on or
off by a chain in the hall connected to a
pilot jet in the basement. Although there
were large windows in each room and
several doors in the lounge and dining
recess, this system was quite efficient, and
only on two occasions did we need a small
radiator for direct heat. There was very
little dust or dirt, and no fireplaces any-
where to keep clean. The rooms were
illuminated by standard and table lamps,
with a centre ceiling lamp, but this was
very seldom used. In every home we
visited we found that moveable lamps were
being used extensively; one sitting-room
had two standards and four table lamps
burning together.
There were always plenty of "outlets,"
so that even with many lamps there was
very little trailing flexible. In a modern
studio I noticed that all the lights were
arranged in pretty glass or china figures,
or behind coloured glass panels, and the
light, though subdued, gave a wonderfully
cosy appearance.
Another home in the Middle West, where
I stayed, was full of everything electrical,
that would make life easy. There were
four in family
occupying a
ordinarily,
two-storied
house, and only
very occasional
help. Again the
heating was
done by gas,
with hot water
pipes and
radiators, and a thermostatic control on
the boiler. The reason for using gas in
this case is that natural gas is available,
which is, of course, cheap.
Although the climate here was damp
and very cold, the electrical refriger-
ator was in constant use, and the fresh,
crisp lettuces as they appeared at table,
though several days old, made it seem
worth while to run the refrigerator for
them alone. The "Kitchen Aid" was
another device, which my hostess said was
her joy and pride. It would mix anything
from mayonnaise to dough for bread, and
while the lady of the house was busy else-
where, this apparatus would do the work of
another pair of hands in the kitchen. We
had on the breakfast table electric hot-
plates, coffee pot, kettle, automatic toaster
and egg boiler, and there was a novel
arrangement, about four inches by three
inches, which acted as a multiple socket,
which in turn was attached to a socket in
the wall nearest the table. The egg boiler
is of the new type, which cooks the eggs by
steam, and has no wire heating element,
using the water for this purpose, and can
be regulated to cook for long or short
periods merely by varying the quantity of
water. The toaster is one of the automatic
type, which throws out the toast and turns
off the current at the same time.
One little device in the building of this house,
which though not electrical, I should wish to
mention in passing, is a shoot, built as a cupboard
in the corner of the house, from the bedroom
floor to the basement, and into it all bed linen,
dusters, etc., can be thrown and landed in the
clothes basket in the basement, thus saving all
carrying of bundles downstairs.
In several of the showrooms there
were various electric ovens on show;
these were of two kinds, large ones
with hot plates for pans, and small
portable ovens without the top hot-
plate, the larger ones were much the
same as we have in this country, but
of the table-top variety; but amongst
the smaller ones, which are very
popular in the small flats were several
new designs.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 471
Some Spring Recipes.
By Miss Mary Mackirdy
(Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow, and Author of "Recipes for You").

The recipes in this article have been chosen as giving good results with not too much labour, and easily managed by the cook who combines the duties of hostess and cook.

To Cook a Piece of Veal.
A piece of fleshy veal is best for this dish, 2, 3 or more pounds, according to the number in the family, some young carrots and button onions, a piece of butter or fat ham or bacon, seasoning.
Heat the butter or ham in a pan, put in the veal and fry it all round, add enough water to well cover the bottom of pan, put on a close-fitting lid, and when the water boils draw to side and cook slowly for about 1 1/2 hours. It requires very little attention provided the heat is sufficiently low and the steam is kept in. Have the carrots and onions prepared, put them round the meat and cook for about 1 hour.
Serve the vegetables round the veal; reduce the liquid if necessary and pour round the veal. Other vegetables may be used.

Saute New Potatoes.
Small new potatoes, butter, seasoning.
Put the potatoes in a saucepan with sufficient butter to cover the pan, put in potatoes, scraped; the pan must have a close-fitting lid and the potatoes cooked at a slow, steady heat till tender. Before serving take off the lid and toss the potatoes in pan over heat to crisp and brown. Serve them with seasoning and a little chopped parsley sprinkled over. New carrots are delightful done in the same way.

A Delightful Salad.
This rather unusual salad is excellent for lunch or supper and quite independent of meat; the potato is the only cooked ingredient. A nice crisp lettuce, 1 or 2 apples, 1 or 2 cooked potatoes—nice mealy ones—some seeded raisins, chopped walnuts or other nuts, some good salad dressing.
Cut the apples and potatoes in dice and mix with raisins, pile up in the centre of the dish or in lettuce leaves, pour over enough dressing to moisten, sprinkle with chopped nuts.

Little Cherry Tartlets.
A quick oven is required for the pastry cases; but as they only take a few minutes, heat the oven to 400, put them in and switch off the current, or bake them when the oven is well-seasoned after something has been cooked.

Make a very good short crust with 6 ozs. flour and 4 ozs. butter or margarine, 1 oz. castor sugar, a pinch of baking powder and the yolk of one egg. The butter is rubbed into the flour, the other ingredients added with a very little water sufficient to make a stiff paste. Roll the paste about 1/4 inch thick, cut in rounds, line little flat patty tins, pressing the paste well into the tin, prick the centres and bake for a few minutes till a light brown.

Tinned or bottled cherries may be used; cook them in the liquid in which preserved, for a few minutes with sufficient sugar to sweeten and a little lemon juice; fill the cases with the fruit. To one gill of the syrup add one teaspoonful cornflour moistened with cold water, stir till boiling, pour over the cherries; serve hot or cold. The tartlets may be decorated with meringue or whipped cream; the latter only if cold.

The meringue:—Steep a small teacup castor sugar in a small pan with an eighth teacup water, when the sugar is dissolved simmer for five minutes without stirring, meantime have the white of one egg whisked very stiffly in a bowl, whisk in the boiling sugar and continue to whisk until the meringue is thick and cold. Pile it on the cases, sprinkle with sugar and decorate with a cherry.

When using fresh fruit, make a syrup with water in place of the liquid in which the cherries were preserved.

A Savoury of Eggs.
Three or four hard boiled eggs, 1 1/2 ozs. butter, 1 1/2 ozs. flour, 2 or 3 ozs. cooked ham or tongue, salt, pepper, nutmeg, 1/4 lb. spaghetti.

Cook the spaghetti in boiling salted water for 20 minutes then drain. Melt the butter, add the flour, when mixed stir in the milk and stir till boiling and smooth; add seasoning, little grated nutmeg, the whites of the eggs cut in strips and the ham chopped. Put the mixture in a fairly deep dish—not a pie dish—sieve the yolks over and put bunches of the spaghetti at each end or round as desired. Garnish with cooked mushrooms or tomatoes. Serve hot as a lunch or supper dish.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 475

An improvement on the electric iron was also displayed by the A.E.G., consisting of an apparatus fixed into the top of the iron which prevents it from becoming over-heated. As the heat increases, a small arrow moves along a short indicator, and when it reaches the maximum point the electric current is immediately and automatically cut off and the iron commences to cool. The cooling process can be easily seen by the backward movement of the arrow, so that directly the iron commences to lose heat, the current comes on again by itself.

Another very prominent firm was Messrs. Siemens-Schuckert, and amongst their novelties was an electric hot water boiler, which could be switched on during the night to heat enough water for the days needs. This is most useful in Continental countries, where the night current is appreciably cheaper. The price of this boiler complete, ranged from £8 10s. 0d. to £19 10s. 0d., according to capacity, while a boiler large enough to heat bath water was quoted at £24.

Messrs. Siemens also showed a machine which mangles and irons washing in one process. This appealed to us as being one of those articles which housewives have expected of the electrical industry for some time. Other interesting accessories by the same firm were electric ovens having three compartments for boiling, roasting, and slow heating respectively.

A novelty hot water producer, called the "Thermotor," was shown by Berlin-Charlottenburg Elektrizitats-Gesellschaft. This consisted of a small fixture which can be attached to any water tap at one end and to the electric mains at the other so that when the electricity is turned on, hot water is obtained by simply turning on water tap.

An all-purpose heating machine, costing only 14s., was displayed by Messrs. H. Richter. Amongst its many uses it heats irons, keeps food warm, boils eggs, etc., and also dries hair after washing.

Electricity Offices, Colston Avenue, Bristol.
The Inaugural Meeting of the Bristol and District Branch, at which some 150 people were present, was held at Rotary House, Bristol, on March 5th.
The President of the Branch, Lady Augusta Inskip, was unable to be present owing to illness, and Mrs. Egbert Cadbury very ably presided in her place. Mr. J. H. Inskip, the Chairman of the Bristol Electricity Department, welcomed the formation of the Branch and spoke of the great possibilities of the future in the use of electricity.
Miss C. Haslett inspired those present with an address on the aims and objects of the Association. Miss M. Partridge, B.Sc., of Exeter, also spoke on the need for electrical education in rural areas, and emphasized the fact that Bristol would shortly be the centre of supply to a large area in the West of England.
Miss A. B. Wright pointed out the need for the Association, and outlined the proposed activities for the Bristol and District Branch.
Councillor Mrs. F. E. Robinson-White proposed and Mr. J. L. Lovell (E.D.A.) seconded the resolution that a Branch be formed, which was carried unanimously. A.B.W.

Swansea and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. M. G. Davies,
3, Eden Avenue, Uplands, Swansea.
Following a preliminary meeting, a well attended inaugural Meeting was held at the Corporation Electricity Showrooms, Swansea, on January 24th, to form a Swansea and District Branch of the Electrical Association for Women.
The Branch is fortunate in having Lady Bryn Edwards as its President.
The Chairman (Mrs. J. W. Burr) opened the meeting and introduced Miss C. Haslett, the Director of the Association, to Swansea.
Mr. J. W. Burr, the Borough Electrical Engineer, in a short address welcomed the formation of the Branch in the district.
The Director, in a most interesting talk, outlined very clearly the aims and objects of the Association.
Mrs. Masters-Porter also spoke in support.
The first fixture was on February 28th, when a most interesting Cooking Demonstration and Lecture was given by Miss Weedon, of the Jackson Electric Stove Co. Miss Weedon spoke of the advantages of electricity as a cooking fuel from the point of view of both the Cook and the Housewife; it was economical, clean and reliable.
We were successful in obtaining a number of new members at this meeting.
We have two meetings during March. The first is to be a lecture on "Home Repairs of Electrical Appliances." For the other, we hope to be able to obtain the services of Mr. G. S. Francis, of E.D.A.

North Staffordshire Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries:
Miss D. Bentley, Mrs. E. M. Yeaman,
St. Georges Chambers, Kingsway, Stoke-on-Trent.
A preliminary meeting of those interested in the formation of a branch of the Electrical Association for Women was held on January 3rd, 1929, when considerable interest was shown.
The Inaugural Meeting was held on Wednesday, February 20th, when the Director gave an address on the objects of the Association.
The Lady Mayoress was present and welcomed the formation of the Branch. Alderman Mrs. Leese, President of the Branch, and Mr. Yeaman, City Electrical Engineer, also spoke. A programme of activities is being drawn up and it is felt that the movement will appeal to the ladies of Stoke-on-Trent and District.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
257, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
The meetings during the last Session were well attended and included a "Talk on Electric Wiring and Fuses," which was followed by an Open Meeting for expressions of opinion on Domestic Electrical Appliances.
The talk and demonstration, "The Telephone System from Within," by Mr. J. E. Coombs, was extremely popular.
Considerable interest was also shown in the lantern lecture, "Sunlight and Health," by Dr. Elizabeth C. Mudie, and in Mr. Martons lecture on "Radio from the House Mains." This was accompanied by three films, which were very much appreciated.
Forthcoming fixtures include a visit to the Works of Messrs. Brown & Polson, a talk on "The Preservation of Food and Automatic Electrical Refrigeration," and "The story of Broadcasting," with lantern slides.
Then there is, of course, the London One-Day Conference in April and the Three-Days Conference and Annual General Meeting at Newcastle-on-Tyne in July.

Mid-Gloucestershire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss E. Johnson,
21, Eastgate, Gloucester.
The Inaugural Meeting of the Mid-Gloucestershire Branch was held at the Guildhall, Gloucester, on February 13th.
In the absence of the Countess of Berkeley, President of the Branch, the Meeting was presided over by Mrs. H. S. Ellis, Chairman.
She was supported by the Mayor and Mayoress of Gloucester (Alderman and Mrs. J. O. Roberts).
The Mayor welcomed the formation of the Branch of the Electrical Association for Women and other speeches of welcome were given by Mr. H. S. Ellis and Mr. F. H. Corson.
The aims and objects of the Association were outlined by the Director, and Miss Partridge, B.Sc., of Exeter, spoke of the development of Electricity in Rural Districts.
It was proposed by Miss Penson, seconded by Mrs. Hill, and unanimously resolved, that a Branch of the Electrical Association for Women should be formed in Gloucester.
At the invitation of the Mayoress the company were entertained to tea.
The first visit of the Branch took place on February 20th, when eighteen members, together with members from the Cardiff, Bristol and Cheltenham Branches, visited the Magnet Works, Birmingham, by kind invitation of the General Electric Co., Ltd.

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. L. Hayes,
1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
The members of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch brought a very full Autumn Programme to a close by a visit to the Revo Electric Co., Tipton, Staffs. Members were able to see every kind of domestic apparatus being manufactured from the raw material to the finished article. A flashlight photograph was taken of all the party in the canteen, where, tired but happy, they enjoyed a welcome cup of tea.
On January 28th we paid a visit to the Central House, Electrically Equipped Canteen and Offices of the Shropshire, Worcestershire and Staffordshire Electric Power Co., at Halesowen. Here members were able to obtain knowledge with regard to Rural Electrification and the Distribution of juice to Rural Areas. A flashlight photograph was taken of the whole party and with lightning speed was developed, printed and a copy presented to each member of the party.
On February 12th, an Outlet Campaign Meeting was held to discuss the movement further. Mrs. L. A. Willson, M.B.E. (Vice-President of the E.A.W.), spoke from the builders point of view, while Mr. T. B. Martin gave a rapid survey of the Red Seal Campaign in Canada and also spoke from the manufacturers point of view. Mr. F. Forrest, M.I.E.E., Chief Assistant City Electrical Engineer, spoke from the

On February 28th, a second party of members visited the Birmingham Municipal All-Electric Wash-house, where they were able to see a family wash completed in one to two hours for 1s. 2d. to 1s. 6d.
On the same day, officials from the Birmingham and Midlands Branch joined with the West of England Branches to visit the Magnet Works of the G.E.C.
A charming lecture by Mr. J. L. G. Cooper, of E.L.M.A., on "Lighting in the Home and School" was given in Walsall for the Midland Area members, and Mrs. Beale took the chair.
At the invitation of the "Industries Fair Committee," nearly 200 members visited the Fair at Castle Bromwich and were entertained to tea on Friday, March 1st.
An interesting and informative lecture was given by Mr. K. C. Stone, M.Sc., on the "Economics of Domestic Water Heating," at the King Edwards High School for Girls, with Miss Barre, the Headmistress of the School, in the Chair.
Apparatus Classes have been started in Birmingham, Kidderminster and Walsall.
* * *
Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss D. Foster-Jeffery, LL.B.,
8, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
Since the last report the Manchester and Salford District Branch has had a varied and intriguing programme. In December, Mr. Hall, M.I.E.E., gave an interesting address on "The Electrical Recording of Music." On January 18th, 1929, we visited the new showrooms of the Salford Corporation Electricity Department, where we had a lecture on "water-heating."
We were very sorry that the influenza epidemic prevented a larger audience from attending Mr. A. P. M. Flemings address on the "Romance of Electricity." Those who were present heard the somewhat technical side of Electricity treated in a clear and altogether fascinating manner.
On February 7th we paid a visit to the Barton Power Station of the Manchester Corporation Electricity Department. This is the most up-to-date power station in England—if not in Europe—and our members had the advantage of seeing the whole procedure of the generation of electricity.
Our Annual Meeting was held on February 28th, in the Lord Mayors Parlour. Mrs. Hammer, at very short notice, travelled to Manchester and gave us an inspiring lecture on the "Public Uses of Electricity." A hearty vote of thanks was given to Mrs. Hammer and to Mrs. Nelson-Barclay, who took the chair.
* * *
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Sleep, 1, York Terrace,
St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.
Our programme for the New Year commenced very appropriately with a lecture entitled "What an E.A.W. Member should know," given by our Electrical Engineer, Mr. W. J. Bache, M.I.E.E. By means of diagrams and blackboard sketches, the electrical circuit was illustrated and reference was made to the properties of insulators and conductors. Using the familiar analogy of water, the lecturer was able to illustrate the measurement of values respecting current flow, pressure and resistance, and explained how the present units, such as ampere, volt, ohm and watt derived their names.
Mrs. C. Marshall (Vice-President) proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer for his clear and interesting explanations, which was heartily endorsed by the members.
A lecture demonstration on "Bells and Batteries" was next given by Mr. R. A. Parsons, A.M.I.E.E., Chairman of the Gloucester Branch of the E.C.A. The discussion which ensued was of much value, as it gave the lecturer an opportunity to deal with points which had previously puzzled members.
Mrs. Atwell Lake (President), on behalf of the members, proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Parsons for his simple explanations and interesting talk.
