The Electrical Age 481

fortably settled. From Birmingham Station we were con-
veyed by motor coaches to the Club House at the G.E.C.
Witton Works, where we were fortified with an excellent
lunch. Dr. A. H. Railing, in a short and witty speech of
welcome to the members, expressed pleasure on behalf of
the G.E.C. at the opportunity of entertaining three Branches
of the E.A.W.
Lady Brooks, Mrs. Atwell Lake, Mrs. Morley New and
Mrs. R. Ellis each in turn expressed thanks to the G.E.C.
on behalf of their respective Branches. We were then con-
veyed to the New Magnet Works and were intrigued to see
the many processes through which such familiar appliances
as switches, irons, kettles, cookers, etc., had to undergo
before being tested and passed. It was a tour full of in-
terest and surprises. Time was all too short, and after a
refreshing tea we were conveyed back to Birmingham
Station, where our saloon coaches awaited us. The arrange-
ments made for our comfort were much appreciated and
everybody voted it a most enjoyable and interesting day.
We also enjoyed meeting the London members at " The
Ideal Home Exhibition," which was a great success.
* * *
South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary : Mrs. J. Taylor, Electric Service Bureau.
27, Newport Road, Cardiff.
The South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch have
commenced the year well. A Cookery Demonstration, by
Miss E. S. Bunker, entitled " Tips for Tea," was held on
January 15th and 16th, with a good attendance on
both days.
On January 29th, Mr. R. L. Booth, Chairman of the
Cardiff Branch of the Electrical Contractors Association, gave
a very interesting talk on " Hints for the Housewife."
Our next fixture was a visit to the works of Messrs.
S. E. Vaughan & Co., Ltd., Dyers and Dry Cleaners,
Cardiff, which was full of interest.
On February 20th, in spite of the arctic weather con-
ditions, forty members of the South Wales and Monmouth-
shire Branch journeyed by motor coach to Gloucester, where
they were joined by several members of the Gloucester
Branch. On arrival at Birmingham we proceeded by motor
coach to the Club House of the General Electric Co., at
Witton, for lunch, afterwards going on to the new Magnet
Works for a tour of inspection, followed by tea. This visit
will be long remembered by all the members present, who
were unanimous in their praise regarding the kindness and
generosity of the General Electric Co.
We have two more items on our present programme, the
first being an address with lantern illustrations, by Mr.
J. W. Beauchamp, M.I.E.E., Engineer and General Manager
of the South Wales Electrical Power Distribution Co., on
"The Use of Electricity in the Home," and the last our
Annual General Meeting and Luncheon on March 15th at the
Royal Hotel, Cardiff.
The Branch is still flourishing, new members being
steadily enrolled. E.A.C.
* * *
North East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary : Miss Anna Holm, Carliol House.
Newcastle-on-Tyne.
January 17th. " A Man Looks in at the Kitchen," by
A. Albrecht, Esq. This proved one of the most interesting
monthly lectures the North East Coast Branch has had—a
provocative title and a good deal of matter that was worthy
of thought by E.A.W. members.
He summarised his lecture in the following words :—
" You must know what you are dissatisfied with. You
can then know what you want."
" You must have an ideal worthy of yourselves, and you
can then bend every resource to attain that end."
January 24th. A successful meeting in connection with
the Outlet Campaign was held in the Connaught Hall, New-
castle-upon-Tyne, and addressed by Miss Margaret Bond-
field, M.P., and Mrs. Laura Willson, M.B.E., the well-known
builder.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 483

Miss Bentfield enthusiastically supported the Campaign, and said that the time had arrived to do away with obsolete methods in the house, especially in the home of the working woman.

Mrs. Wilson proved how much electricity helped to solve the tasks of the woman in the home. The discussion following showed that considerable interest in the subject had been aroused.

February 7th. E.D.A.-E.A.W. Ball. Notice elsewhere.

February 20th. — "Lamp Shade Making." The idea underlying this practical demonstration was to show that with the expenditure of sums varying from pence to less than five shillings, shades can be made with little effort so that a good pleasant light can be produced throughout the house.

March 8th. Annual General Meeting. Miss Baile presided over a representative gathering. The Committee were re-elected en bloc for the ensuing year, with the addition of her secretary to fill vacancies.

Congratulations were extended to Miss Cooper Hodgson, Vice-Chairman, on her recognition in the New Years Honours List, by being awarded the M.B.E.

We are anticipating a pleasurable and busy Spring and Summer with the Conference ahead.

* * *

Ashford and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. M. Wilson, "Gleniffer Brae," Vicarage Road, Kennington, Nr. Ashford, Kent.

On January 10th we held our annual business meeting, when we were delighted to have our Director with us. Her interest in every detail of our work and her words of counsel and encouragement, coupled with the hospitality of our retiring committee, resulted in a most happy meeting.

January 19th was a red-letter day, for we held our first annual Dinner, when 100 members and friends were present. Mrs. Haslett replied in her usual breezy manner to the toast of "The Association," while Councillor Mrs. Gregory very ably proposed the toast of "The Electric Supply Industry."

February 7th, 8th and 9th, we joined the local Electrical Development Circle in an Electrical Exhibition at Ashford. Our new committee were responsible for cooking demonstrations and also for the refreshments. We were especially indebted to Mr. Lingard, of E.L.M.A., for his lecture-demonstration on "Good Home Lighting" on the evening of February 7th.

March 6th and 7th found us again helping with an Electrical Exhibition at Wye (a village about three miles from Ashford, which has lately been electrified). It was a pleasure to welcome Mrs. T. W. Cave (Vice-President of Wye Womens Institute) who opened the Exhibition, for we feel the W.I.s and the E.A.W. to be closely allied in their aims and objects.

We have visited the Victoria Co.s Flour Mills and an Iron Foundry, and we also arranged a successful Whist Drive.

We are fortunate in having as two of our Vice-Presidents Miss Brake (Headmistress of the Girls High School) and Miss Leary (Headmistress of the Girls County School), who are keenly interested in fresh careers for girls. As a result of a discussion with the Director we have now started a second class for girls over 15 years of age who are interested in electricity. As this is a pioneer class, we have limited our numbers to 22 students, but it is very gratifying to know we could have doubled this number.

Four lectures are being given on the "Theory of Electricity," after which the students take an examination before passing on to the next course of instruction. We are indebted to Mr. R. Wilson for his lectures and for the setting of the examination paper; and to Miss Brake and Miss Leary for their co-operation in the loan of rooms, apparatus, etc. The last item to report is the appointment of Mrs. S. E. Longley as Assistant Hon. Secretary.

Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. M. Wilson, "Gleniffer Brae," Vicarage Road, Kennington, Nr. Ashford, Kent.

On January 10th we held our annual business meeting, when we were delighted to have our Director with us. Her interest in every detail of our work and her words of counsel and encouragement, coupled with the hospitality of our retiring committee, resulted in a most happy meeting.

January 19th was a red-letter day, for we held our first annual Dinner, when 100 members and friends were present. Mrs. Haslett replied in her usual breezy manner to the toast of "The Association," while Councillor Mrs. Gregory very ably proposed the toast of "The Electric Supply Industry."

February 7th, 8th and 9th, we joined the local Electrical Development Circle in an Electrical Exhibition at Ashford. Our new committee were responsible for cooking demonstrations and also for the refreshments. We were especially indebted to Mr. Lingard, of E.L.M.A., for his lecture-demonstration on "Good Home Lighting" on the evening of February 7th.

March 6th and 7th found us again helping with an Electrical Exhibition at Wye (a village about three miles from Ashford, which has lately been electrified). It was a pleasure to welcome Mrs. T. W. Cave (Vice-President of Wye Womens Institute) who opened the Exhibition, for we feel the W.I.s and the E.A.W. to be closely allied in their aims and objects.

As a result of a discussion with the Director we have now started a second class for girls over 15 years of age who are interested in electricity. Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o Ingleby Motors, Ltd., Sweet Street, Leeds.
About one hundred members and friends of the Leeds and West Riding Branch gathered together at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, on March 8th, for their first Luncheon, which proved to be a great success.
The President, Lady Kathleen Pilkington, welcomed the speakers—the Lord Mayor of Leeds (Alderman D. B. Foster), although she knew very little about electricity she was keenly interested in the Association.
The Lord Mayor said that although he had only recently gone to live in a house fitted with electricity he had soon realised its advantages, and hoped it would eventually be installed in the homes of all the people. To the credit of Leeds, there were now 10,000 more people using electricity in the City than there were two years ago.
The Director emphasised the importance of electricity being taught in the schools and that modern cooking equipment should be used. She was glad the Leeds Branch had had so successful a first year, and hoped that during the next year it would at least double its membership.
Mr. Woodhouse said the Association had the support of the whole electrical industry, and that the cooperation of the women was most important, for in the domestic sphere where the women were the actual users they should be able to suggest improvements and new designs.
Mr. T. J. M. More enlivened the gathering by giving a very witty vote of thanks, which was seconded by Mrs. W. B. Woodhouse.
Other recent fixtures of the Branch were a lecture on " Electric Cookers and their many advantages," by Miss K. Rogerson, of Halifax, and a visit and tea at the Nox Electric Lamp Works, Leeds.

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. H. Klitz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, Denbighshire.
The North Wales Branch had a most enjoyable visit to the Sunlight Soap Works at Port Sunlight on February 5th. Twenty-four members made up the party and Messrs. Lever Bros. very kindly provided tea in the Lady Lever Art Gallery.
Mr. G. K. Barrett, B.Sc., A.M.I.E.E., Resident Engineer to Messrs. Electricity Distribution of North Wales and District, Ltd., gave a popular lecture, illustrated with lantern slides, upon the "Applications of Electricity," at Gresford on February 9th, and at Llandudno on February 20th.
Mr. Price F. White, Borough Electrical Engineer, Bangor, gave a lecture on "Domestic Appliances" at Llanfairfechan on February 22nd, and at Penmaenmawr on February 26th. An excellent display of electrical appliances was on view at both lectures. Conway had the opportunity of hearing Mr. White on Tuesday, March 12th, at the Town Hall.
A visit was also paid to Messrs. Courtaulds Artificial Silk Works at Flint on Wednesday, March 6th.
As a result of these lectures, the membership of the Branch has been notably increased. The efforts of the Branch are being directed towards securing a substantial representative membership in every North Wales town or village where a public electricity supply is available. We gather that the women of North Wales mean to make electricity a household word in a very real sense.
EDITH H. KLITZ.

Rugby Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss N. Pedler,
Electricity Showrooms, Little Church Street, Rugby.
The first meeting of the New Year was held on January 9th, when Mr. B. C. Holding, the Editor of "The Electrician," gave us a charming lecture on "Electricity in the Home." This was followed a fortnight later by an exceedingly interesting visit to the Printing Works of the "Rugby Advertiser," where members saw a modern electrical printing press.
A Bridge Drive, which was organised in aid of the Branch Funds, took place early in February, and was a great success, socially and financially, the prize and refreshments having been given by members.
On February 12th we held our "open meeting," when Miss D. Vaughan gave a practical lecture on Domestic Electrical Appliances.
On February 21st, by courtesy of the Coventry Corporation Electricity Department, a party of members paid a visit to the New Power Station at Longford. This was of particular interest to the Rugby Branch, as the station was constructed by the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., Rugby. Before the visit, Mr. A. S. Kettle, of the B.T.H. Co., gave a special talk on "Power Station Plant," illustrated by lantern slides.
The membership is gradually increasing, meetings and visits have been well attended, and members are enthusiastic.
N.P.

Hampshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss J. Dicks,
145, High Street, Winchester.
The first meeting of this Branch was arranged to take place on February 5th and was to have taken the form of a visit to the Southampton Municipal Works. It was unfortunate that practically all the members of the Council were victims of the influenza epidemic, and the President, The Dowager Lady Swaythling, who intended accompanying the party, also succumbed. It was, therefore, decided to postpone the meeting for a later date.

London Activities.
The Spring Programme has proved very popular, and we have been glad to see many new members at the various fixtures.
The Programme included a visit to the newly-equipped Showrooms of Messrs. Troughton & Young, at Knightsbridge, when Mr. A. B. Read gave an interesting Talk on the New French Lighting. A Lecture-Demonstration on "A Five-Course Dinner," by Miss Mabel Collins, at the Soho School of Cookery ; a Visit to the Singer Sewing Machine Co., Mr. Haseldens lecture on the "History of the Sewing Machine" was quite fascinating, as was the exhibition of Embroidery seen after tea ; the Visit to the All-Electric Restaurant Kitchen Car of the L.N.E. Railway was very popular, and Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, our President, and the Viscountess Elibank were of the party.
On January 20th a Special Social was held in aid of the E.T.B.I., and Mrs. Ll. B. Atkinson and her Social Sub-Committee are to be congratulated on the result. Five pounds raised for the Funds of the E.T.B.I.
The Evening Lectures were given by Mr. F. W. Purse, M.I.E.E., who spoke on "How Electricity is Generated in West Ham," with Lantern Slides and a Film ; Mr. A. de B. Danisthorpe gave a most interesting lecture on Wireless, and Mr. H. Bourne gave us a simple and comprehensive talk on Electric Motors.
The visit to the Ideal Home Exhibition proved to be an outstanding feature of the Session. The British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., and the Hotpoint Electric Appliance Co., Ltd., kindly invited the E.A.W. to the Exhibition and also entertained the party to luncheon and tea. The invitation was extended to the Branches also and we were delighted to have with us members from Birmingham and Midlands, Cheltenham, Cardiff, Ashford, Rugby, Gloucester and Bristol, numbering altogether over 200.
Demonstrations were given of the latest electric cooking, heating, refrigeration, and labour-saving appliances. Members were also very interested in the "Electricity through the Ages" and in the Mazdalux Electric Fountain.
After luncheon the members adjourned to the Hall of Music, by kind permission of H.M.V. Gramophone Co., and Mr. Loewe welcomed the E.A.W. party and gave an interesting address on the steadily growing appreciation of the advantages of electricity in the home.
A hearty vote of thanks to the British Thomson-Houston Co. and the Hotpoint Electric Appliance Co., and also to the Gramophone Co. was proposed by the Director, and seconded by Mrs. Beale, the newly-elected President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch. The proceedings concluded with a talk by Mr. Fenwick on "Gramophone Science versus Gramophone Guesswork."
Further activities are being arranged, but the outstanding event in the near future is the One-Day Conference in London on April 16th.

Railway was very popular, and Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, our President, and the Viscountess Elibank were of the party.

About one hundred members and friends of the Leeds and West Riding Branch gathered together at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, on March 8th, for their first Luncheon, which proved to be a great success.
The President, Lady Kathleen Pilkington, welcomed the speakers—the Lord Mayor of Leeds (Alderman D. B. Foster), although she knew very little about electricity she was keenly interested in the Association.
The Lord Mayor said that although he had only recently gone to live in a house fitted with electricity he had soon realised its advantages, and hoped it would eventually be installed in the homes of all the people. To the credit of Leeds, there were now 10,000 more people using electricity in the City than there were two years ago.
The Director emphasised the importance of electricity being taught in the schools and that modern cooking equipment should be used. She was glad the Leeds Branch had had so successful a first year, and hoped that during the next year it would at least double its membership.
Mr. Woodhouse said the Association had the support of the whole electrical industry, and that the cooperation of the women was most important, for in the domestic sphere where the women were the actual users they should be able to suggest improvements and new designs.
Mr. T. J. M. More enlivened the gathering by giving a very witty vote of thanks, which was seconded by Mrs. W. B. Woodhouse.
Other recent fixtures of the Branch were a lecture on " Electric Cookers and their many advantages," by Miss K. Rogerson, of Halifax, and a visit and tea at the Nox Electric Lamp Works, Leeds.

About one hundred members and friends of the Leeds and West Riding Branch gathered together at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, on March 8th, for their first Luncheon, which proved to be a great success.

The Lord Mayor said that although he had only recently gone to live in a house fitted with electricity he had soon realised its advantages, and hoped it would eventually be installed in the homes of all the people. To the credit of Leeds, there were now 10,000 more people using electricity in the City than there were two years ago.
The Director emphasised the importance of electricity being taught in the schools and that modern cooking equipment should be used. She was glad the Leeds Branch had had so successful a first year, and hoped that during the next year it would at least double its membership.
Mr. Woodhouse said the Association had the support of the whole electrical industry, and that the cooperation of the women was most important, for in the domestic sphere where the women were the actual users they should be able to suggest improvements and new designs.
Mr. T. J. M. More enlivened the gathering by giving a very witty vote of thanks, which was seconded by Mrs. W. B. Woodhouse.
Other recent fixtures of the Branch were a lecture on " Electric Cookers and their many advantages," by Miss K. Rogerson, of Halifax, and a visit and tea at the Nox Electric Lamp Works, Leeds.

Other recent fixtures of the Branch were a lecture on " Electric Cookers and their many advantages," by Miss K. Rogerson, of Halifax, and a visit and tea at the Nox Electric Lamp Works, Leeds.

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. H. Klitz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, Denbighshire.

Mr. G. K. Barrett, B.Sc., A.M.I.E.E., Resident Engineer to Messrs. Electricity Distribution of North Wales and District, Ltd., gave a popular lecture, illustrated with lantern slides, upon the "Applications of Electricity," at Gresford on February 9th, and at Llandudno on February 20th.
Mr. Price F. White, Borough Electrical Engineer, Bangor, gave a lecture on "Domestic Appliances" at Llanfairfechan on February 22nd, and at Penmaenmawr on February 26th. An excellent display of electrical appliances was on view at both lectures. Conway had the opportunity of hearing Mr. White on Tuesday, March 12th, at the Town Hall.
A visit was also paid to Messrs. Courtaulds Artificial Silk Works at Flint on Wednesday, March 6th.
As a result of these lectures, the membership of the Branch has been notably increased. The efforts of the Branch are being directed towards securing a substantial representative membership in every North Wales town or village where a public electricity supply is available. We gather that the women of North Wales mean to make electricity a household word in a very real sense.
EDITH H. KLITZ.

The Evening Lectures were given by Mr. F. W. Purse, M.I.E.E., who spoke on "How Electricity is Generated in West Ham," with Lantern Slides and a Film ; Mr. A. de B. Danisthorpe gave a most interesting lecture on Wireless, and Mr. H. Bourne gave us a simple and comprehensive talk on Electric Motors.
The visit to the Ideal Home Exhibition proved to be an outstanding feature of the Session. The British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., and the Hotpoint Electric Appliance Co., Ltd., kindly invited the E.A.W. to the Exhibition and also entertained the party to luncheon and tea. The invitation was extended to the Branches also and we were delighted to have with us members from Birmingham and Midlands, Cheltenham, Cardiff, Ashford, Rugby, Gloucester and Bristol, numbering altogether over 200.
Demonstrations were given of the latest electric cooking, heating, refrigeration, and labour-saving appliances. Members were also very interested in the "Electricity through the Ages" and in the Mazdalux Electric Fountain.
After luncheon the members adjourned to the Hall of Music, by kind permission of H.M.V. Gramophone Co., and Mr. Loewe welcomed the E.A.W. party and gave an interesting address on the steadily growing appreciation of the advantages of electricity in the home.
A hearty vote of thanks to the British Thomson-Houston Co. and the Hotpoint Electric Appliance Co., and also to the Gramophone Co. was proposed by the Director, and seconded by Mrs. Beale, the newly-elected President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch. The proceedings concluded with a talk by Mr. Fenwick on "Gramophone Science versus Gramophone Guesswork."
Further activities are being arranged, but the outstanding event in the near future is the One-Day Conference in London on April 16th.

484 The Electrical Age

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o Ingleby Motors, Ltd., Sweet Street, Leeds.
About one hundred members and friends of the Leeds and West Riding Branch gathered together at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, on March 8th, for their first Luncheon, which proved to be a great success.
The President, Lady Kathleen Pilkington, welcomed the speakers—the Lord Mayor of Leeds (Alderman D. B. Foster), although she knew very little about electricity she was keenly interested in the Association.
The Lord Mayor said that although he had only recently gone to live in a house fitted with electricity he had soon realised its advantages, and hoped it would eventually be installed in the homes of all the people. To the credit of Leeds, there were now 10,000 more people using electricity in the City than there were two years ago.
The Director emphasised the importance of electricity being taught in the schools and that modern cooking equipment should be used. She was glad the Leeds Branch had had so successful a first year, and hoped that during the next year it would at least double its membership.
Mr. Woodhouse said the Association had the support of the whole electrical industry, and that the cooperation of the women was most important, for in the domestic sphere where the women were the actual users they should be able to suggest improvements and new designs.
Mr. T. J. M. More enlivened the gathering by giving a very witty vote of thanks, which was seconded by Mrs. W. B. Woodhouse.
Other recent fixtures of the Branch were a lecture on " Electric Cookers and their many advantages," by Miss K. Rogerson, of Halifax, and a visit and tea at the Nox Electric Lamp Works, Leeds.

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. H. Klitz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, Denbighshire.
The North Wales Branch had a most enjoyable visit to the Sunlight Soap Works at Port Sunlight on February 5th. Twenty-four members made up the party and Messrs. Lever Bros. very kindly provided tea in the Lady Lever Art Gallery.
Mr. G. K. Barrett, B.Sc., A.M.I.E.E., Resident Engineer to Messrs. Electricity Distribution of North Wales and District, Ltd., gave a popular lecture, illustrated with lantern slides, upon the "Applications of Electricity," at Gresford on February 9th, and at Llandudno on February 20th.
Mr. Price F. White, Borough Electrical Engineer, Bangor, gave a lecture on "Domestic Appliances" at Llanfairfechan on February 22nd, and at Penmaenmawr on February 26th. An excellent display of electrical appliances was on view at both lectures. Conway had the opportunity of hearing Mr. White on Tuesday, March 12th, at the Town Hall.
A visit was also paid to Messrs. Courtaulds Artificial Silk Works at Flint on Wednesday, March 6th.
As a result of these lectures, the membership of the Branch has been notably increased. The efforts of the Branch are being directed towards securing a substantial representative membership in every North Wales town or village where a public electricity supply is available. We gather that the women of North Wales mean to make electricity a household word in a very real sense.
EDITH H. KLITZ.

Rugby Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss N. Pedler,
Electricity Showrooms, Little Church Street, Rugby.
The first meeting of the New Year was held on January 9th, when Mr. B. C. Holding, the Editor of "The Electrician," gave us a charming lecture on "Electricity in the Home." This was followed a fortnight later by an exceedingly interesting visit to the Printing Works of the "Rugby Advertiser," where members saw a modern electrical printing press.
A Bridge Drive, which was organised in aid of the Branch Funds, took place early in February, and was a great success, socially and financially, the prize and refreshments having been given by members.
On February 12th we held our "open meeting," when Miss D. Vaughan gave a practical lecture on Domestic Electrical Appliances.
On February 21st, by courtesy of the Coventry Corporation Electricity Department, a party of members paid a visit to the New Power Station at Longford. This was of particular interest to the Rugby Branch, as the station was constructed by the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., Rugby. Before the visit, Mr. A. S. Kettle, of the B.T.H. Co., gave a special talk on "Power Station Plant," illustrated by lantern slides.
The membership is gradually increasing, meetings and visits have been well attended, and members are enthusiastic.
N.P.

Hampshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss J. Dicks,
145, High Street, Winchester.
The first meeting of this Branch was arranged to take place on February 5th and was to have taken the form of a visit to the Southampton Municipal Works. It was unfortunate that practically all the members of the Council were victims of the influenza epidemic, and the President, The Dowager Lady Swaythling, who intended accompanying the party, also succumbed. It was, therefore, decided to postpone the meeting for a later date.

London Activities.
The Spring Programme has proved very popular, and we have been glad to see many new members at the various fixtures.
The Programme included a visit to the newly-equipped Showrooms of Messrs. Troughton & Young, at Knightsbridge, when Mr. A. B. Read gave an interesting Talk on the New French Lighting. A Lecture-Demonstration on "A Five-Course Dinner," by Miss Mabel Collins, at the Soho School of Cookery ; a Visit to the Singer Sewing Machine Co., Mr. Haseldens lecture on the "History of the Sewing Machine" was quite fascinating, as was the exhibition of Embroidery seen after tea ; the Visit to the All-Electric Restaurant Kitchen Car of the L.N.E. THE RIGHT HON. MARGARET BONDFIELD, J.P., M.P.
The first woman Cabinet Minister, who is to speak at the Opening Session of the Newcastle Conference, is one of the most well-known women in public life. Being compelled to earn her living at an early age, Miss Bondfield became so impressed with the need to improve the working conditions of shop assistants that she early joined the Trade Union movement, and her long association with industrial conditions in this country fits her in every way as Minister of Labour.
Miss Bondfield is a well-known personality in the world of International Labour, having been appointed Technical Adviser to the International Conference at Washington in 1919; Member of the British Delegation to Russia in 1920; and in 1924 was appointed as the first woman delegate to the International Labour Conference at Geneva.
As a public speaker she is unequalled and her enthusiasm for all progressive movements to improve the lot of the working woman is well-known.
She has already proved her interest in the use of electricity and the valuable work being carried out by the Electrical Association for Women.

JULY, 1929.
No. 13
THE RIGHT HON. MARGARET BONDFIELD, J.P., M.P.
The first woman Cabinet Minister, who is to speak at the Opening Session of the Newcastle Conference, is one of the most well-known women in public life. Being compelled to earn her living at an early age, Miss Bondfield became so impressed with the need to improve the working conditions of shop assistants that she early joined the Trade Union movement, and her long association with industrial conditions in this country fits her in every way as Minister of Labour.
Miss Bondfield is a well-known personality in the world of International Labour, having been appointed Technical Adviser to the International Conference at Washington in 1919; Member of the British Delegation to Russia in 1920; and in 1924 was appointed as the first woman delegate to the International Labour Conference at Geneva.
As a public speaker she is unequalled and her enthusiasm for all progressive movements to improve the lot of the working woman is well-known.
She has already proved her interest in the use of electricity and the valuable work being carried out by the Electrical Association for Women.

Unnamed: 10: Founder Member; promoter of association goals abroad

EDITORIAL.
NEWCASTLE-ON-TYNE—JULY 10th-12th INCLUSIVE.
Wednesday, July 10th, will see parties of E.A.W. Members travelling from all parts of the country to Newcastle to the Fourth Annual Conference of the Association.
An informal Reception by the President and Council of the North-East Coast Branch of the E.A.W. on Wednesday evening, should afford an opportunity for a renewal of many friendships and the making of new ones.
The Dinner on Friday evening, which is to be given by the local Branch, should prove very attractive, as we understand there are to be some original toasts on the Menu.
Knowing what the North-East Coast can do in the way of entertainment, there is a very enjoyable time in front of the Members attending the Conference.
* * *
AN INTERNATIONAL ELECTRICAL ASSOCIATION FOR WOMEN.
The interest which the E.A.W. has aroused in different parts of the world is evidenced by the number of overseas women who have accepted an invitation to be present at the Conference.
The speeches from the Overseas Members and the opportunities which will be afforded for an interchange of experience, will, we hope, inspire these representative women from other countries to go back and form similar Associations amongst their fellow country-women.
Great Britain is the first country in which the women have formed an Association of their own to discuss this all-important subject of Electricity, and we hope that in time many other countries will follow our lead and that the time will not be far distant when we shall have an International Federation of Electrical Associations for Women.
Already the nucleus of an Association has been formed in Australasia, where Mr. F. E. Sharp, one of our Founder Members, has been travelling and has taken the opportunity of promoting the ideals underlying the work of the E.A.W.
* * *
ELECTRICITY IN THE SCHOOLS.
The step taken by the Association to arouse interest in the all-important subject of the Teaching of Electrical Methods in Girls’ Schools has proved to be very successful. Conferences have shown that in many cases there was a somewhat wide gap between the Electrical Authorities on the one hand and the Educational Authorities on the other.
We feel that the closer co-operation between these two groups of people in their respective districts will quickly bring about the desired result.
With very few exceptions the Educational Authorities, especially the Teachers, are extremely keen on the subject, and we would appeal to all Supply Engineers and Electrical Companies to provide the very best facilities in supplying up-to-date Electrical Equipment for the Domestic Science Centres in their area.
At the Deputation received by the Board of Education on June 24th, which was arranged by the Association, we were fortunate in securing Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, F.R.S., President of the British Electrical Development Association, to speak on behalf of the Electrical Industry.

The Electrical Age 489

The Progress of the North-East Coast Exhibition.

The Activities of the Womens Section. :: Special Electrical Exhibits.
"The Hall of Light."

Over half a million people visited the North-East Coast Exhibition at Newcastle-upon-Tyne within the fortnight following its opening by H.R.H. the Prince of Wales on May 14th. A wonderful send-off this, exceeding the most sanguine expectations, and because it is in every way a very fine exhibition, thoroughly well planned and in an ideal situation, its continued success is practically assured.

The two great palaces of Engineering and Industries contain an enormous number of exhibits, which are proving absorbingly interesting to the vast crowds thronging the avenues daily, and everywhere one hears the opinion expressed that the North-East Coast has put up an Exhibition which would be remarkable at any time, but which is positively astounding in view of the very long period of industrial depression from which the north-eastern district is only now beginning to emerge. It is recognised as one of the most extensive and vigorous efforts of collective salesmanship ever attempted.

Stand-holders are agreeably surprised at the interest taken in their exhibits by people from all parts of the Kingdom and also by visitors from abroad. In many cases, definite orders are being placed, and it is hoped that considerable future business will result.

The Womens Section, of which Lady Armstrong is President, is attracting large crowds daily. Here, exhibits of womens handiwork, ancient and present day, are attractively displayed in a large hall whose decorative scheme is itself the work of members of this section. Demonstrations and lectures are given at frequent intervals and are obviously finding appreciation.

The large and handsome Palace of Arts houses what are acknowledged to be some of the finest collections of examples of the work of old and modern masters. Many of the pictures have been lent for the period of the Exhibition by the owners of private galleries in the north-east of England, and thou-

Lady Armstrong.

Unnamed: 10: Subject of a painting mentioned in the article
transcription:
490	The Electrical Age
sands of people are daily availing them- selves of the opportunity to see them under the ideal conditions which the Exhibition has rendered possible. The most popular picture is, undoubtedly, the portrait of Master Lambton, by Sir Thomas Lawrence, a picture which has been lent by the Earl of Durham. It is the portrait of a boy in a red velvet suit, and is a paint- ing of such beauty and charm as to domin- ate the whole collection of very fine eighteenth century pictures by the great masters of that period, a collection which represents an enormous sum of money. For "Master Lambton" the Earl of Dur- ham recently refused an American offer of £100,000.
Delegates to the E.A.W. Conference will find the North-East Coast Exhibition, with its beautiful buildings, lovely gardens and many and varied amusements, a most attractive place, both in conference and leisure hours.
"The Hall of Light."
Of paramount interest to the Conference Delegates will be the "Hall of Light," arranged by E.L.M.A., where interesting uses of Electric Light are shown.
The building is an example of distinctly modern architecture, with built-in lighting as an essential part, and is divided into two outer rooms and a central entrance hall.
The lighting of the ceiling and upper walls indicates the decorative possibilities of the new architectural lighting. This form of lighting is not obtained by any system of pendant units installed after the building is erected, but is actually designed
with and built into the structure. The fascinating displays set in recesses around the Hall impress still further the amazing possibilities of electric light as an adver- tising and artistic medium.
A second interior is divided into sections providing realistic settings for electric light- ing in various fields of service. The new- est designs in industrial and office lighting are shown, and every conceivable device of electric lighting for home decoration is revealed in two domestic interiors. Lumin- ous signs guide the visitor, and these silent demonstrators are assisted by Lighting Service Bureau specialists, who give advice on all illumination problems.
The first satisfactory electric lamp was developed by Sir Joseph Swan in the vicinity of Newcastle, and it is appropriate, therefore, that the Electric Lamp Manu- facturers Association should be responsible for a Hall of Light which brings to the Exhibition the pinnacle of achievement attained by the electric lamps early suc- cessor.
Another stand which will be of special interest to the Delegates will be that of the
Electrical Developments Association,
which will act as an Enquiry Bureau for members during the Conference.
Here, in addition to a lounge, will be found Cinema Films displayed from time to time, and illuminated boxes showing the various applications of Electricity.
The E.D.A. Stand is situated at the end nearest the entrance to the Hall of Indus- tries, and hence can be found by all mem- bers looking for rest and information.
* * *
"The Practical Electricians Pocket Book," price 2/6 net. Published by Odhams Press.
The New Edition of this very useful Pocket Book has been entirely re-written and brought up-to-date; the range of subjects covered is literally from Elec- trical A to Electrical Z.
For those who wish to delve more deeply into Electrical Mysteries, this book will prove very useful.
We have received from Messrs. Ferranti, Ltd., a most attractive brochure of their fires. The lovely picture reminds us very much of the Lounge at Baslow Hall, the beautiful home of Dr. and Mrs S. Z. de Ferranti.
Messrs. Electrolux, Ltd., have presented a table model of their refrigerator to the Electrical Association for Women—for the model Electric Kitchen at 46, Kensington Court, London, W.8.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 491
A New Era for the Housewife in Electrical Cookery.
THE THERMAL STORAGE COOKER.
By Mrs. Dover, B.Sc. (Lond.)
The Electrical Association for Women is always ready to provide a platform for the discussion of new Methods which might promote greater efficiency in the Home. The Thermal Storage Electric Cooker, which is used extensively in Sweden, was brought to the notice of the Association:—In order to discover whether this method of cooking would offer advantages to the British Housewife, Mrs. Dover, a member of the E.A.W., kindly undertook to carry out some experiments in her own home. The results of her experiments were given in the form of a demonstration-lecture at Kensington Court and are published below.
The great drawback hitherto in Electric Cooking has been the time required to obtain the initial heat. This has now been overcome. A cooker has been constructed in which a hot Hot-plate is always available. Besides this great asset there is an oven at the temperature of simmering connected to the hot-plate by a mechanical heat transferring device, where food can be put to cook slowly without requiring any further attention. This new part of the Electric Cooker—called the Thermal Storage Cooker—can be plugged into any outlet of the ordinary lighting installation. Used with it is a Baking Oven for roasts, cakes and pastry, which can also be plugged into any outlet.
Now I am sure you will want to know all about this new cooker, the method of cooking, the time, money and labour it is eventually going to save you. From the photograph you will see what a clean, convenient arrangement it is. But it is when the black, dome-shaped lid is lifted the cooker becomes so fascinating.
In order to avoid high load demands on the power stations, the idea of storing heat evolved electrically was conceived, and has been put into practice by storing heat in a suitably shaped iron block, surrounded by a good heat insulating material. The circular iron disc under the dome-shaped lid is the top of the iron block, and forms the Hot-plate. The iron block contains two heating elements which are supplied with electric current so as to produce an average temperature of 900° F. A thermostat (which is an instrument for controlling the temperature) is connected to the iron block and operates a mercury switch controlling the current passing through the elements. Now a point which housewives and their husbands will appreciate: when the temperature of the iron block reaches 900° F., the current is automatically switched off, and no current is used until the Hot-plate has cooled down to slightly under 900° F., then the current is automatically switched on. From the foregoing, you will see a Hot-plate is always hot and ready for you.
Oh! but I have not mentioned how rapid the heating is, and that you can have a cup of tea within five minutes of arriving downstairs in the morning, as two pints of water boil in less than three minutes. Heat has been stored in the iron block for you, and is only waiting to be transferred to the kettle of water. The kettle will probably boil before you are ready; if so, it can be raised slightly from the iron block by turning the nickel knob in the front of the stove. The water will then boil less rapidly.
The spring-hinged door in the front of the Thermal Storage Cooker closes the oven where the food is put to cook slowly, after the initial heating.

My Dear, its stupendous; of course
I dont wear those filthy pull-over things
and go about with a tureen of oil. Your
Lulu doesnt contaminate the emporium
where they boil the electricity in huge pans,
and cool it by dropping it from the top of

Im in the showroom where people
come to learn what to do with the fresh juice
when its delivered. (Juice, my Dear, is

everything at once, made just the teeniest
mistakes at first. Only the second day I
was there I was left all alone, when in
walked the most gorgeous man, my Dear,
so I said now Ill show them all what I can
do (I had my new dress on—from Isobelles)
so I shot forward and dazzled him with the
most devastating smile and he simply reeled,
my Dear, I just stunned him.
I said do let me show you our very
latest fire, its just sweet, and priceless for
lighting cigarettes (the boys had shown this
to me) think what a ghastly number of
matches you save. Of course, he would ask
me how much current the fiery thing con-
sumed, but as he didnt say juice, I knew in
a minute he hadnt the foggiest idea, so I
just said you could burn it for hours and
hours and it only used the weeniest current.
My Dear, I felt I had raised a howling
impression, for his face just skidded when
someone came in, he melted away, and later
they told me he was the Chief, a sort of
headman, in other words the boss. I could
have screamed!
Of course, I felt rather reduced but all
the men were too crushingly kind and I soon
recovered when one of them brought me a
stunning box of chocolates and I was just
submerged in them, when in comes the Chief
and with him that cat Popsie Wimble so I
just slid the chocolates like lightning under
the top of an oven and just plopped the lid
to.
My Dear, she went round all the
gadgets and stopped bang in front the very
oven and the Chief turned on a switch and
horrors the infernal old sizzler began to stew
my chocolates and there was that fiend
Popsie Wimble asking the most iniquitous
questions and she doesnt know how many
amps go to the volt. I could have fused
her.
It was years before she oozed out and
I rescued my grilled chocolates. I never
knew the beastly thing got hot there, but
the path of science is never easy and we
engineers just go on learning.
More later,
Your industrious
LULU.

The Electrical Age
A Description of a North-East Coast Switchgear Works
Messrs. A. Reyrolle & Co., Ltd., at Hebburn-on-Tyne.
At the Works of Messrs. A. Reyrolle & Co., at Hebburn-on-Tyne will be seen the manufacture of switchgear for such widely different purposes as the Coal Mine and the Home.
Of the many industrial works in the North East Coast area, not a few are known for their products far beyond their immediate locality; and one of the most renowned of these is Messrs. Reyrolles Switchgear Factory, at Hebburn-on-Tyne. It is no exaggeration to say that the firms name is a household word amongst electrical engineers all over the world; and the great quantity of switchgear sent out from the works finds its way into every country where switchgear is used at all. The beginning of what is now so great an undertaking dates back to 1886, when the late Mr. A. C. Reyrolle established a small workshop in London. Fifteen years later, in 1901, the first works were built on the present site at Hebburn-on-Tyne. They consisted of two or three small single-storey buildings, but grew to such an extent that twenty-one years later, in 1922, the available site of 5 1/2 acres was sufficiently occupied, and a new site of 4 1/2 acres began to be built upon. This was increased later on by the addition of another 5 acres for works purposes, and an adjacent sports ground 6 1/2 acres in extent, together with other land amounting to 3 1/2 acres, brings up the area at the two works to a total of 25 acres. Works extensions are still going on, and the latest additions are two large shops equipped with welding apparatus and electrically driven metal cutting and bending machines. The output from this most up-to-date factory, now employing over 2,500 people, is the greatest from any switchgear works in the United Kingdom.
Messrs. Reyrolle have been pioneers in many important departments of switchgear engineering and the kindred arts, and have had a preponderating influence on the growth of the switchgear industry as a whole. Merz-Price split-conductor and other balanced systems of protection; the adaptation of switchgear to the stringent requirements of coal mines, including the provision of boiler-plate switch-tanks, machined wide flanges giving flame-proof joints, and electrically interlocked coal-cutter control circuits; protected-type plugs and sockets with earthing facilities, making the use of portable apparatus quite safe; domestic equipment and cooker control boards—these are amongst the many things originated and developed by Messrs. Reyrolle.
The Service Table.
The cooker control board has a switch for controlling the supply of electricity to an electric oven or other cooker, and it is fitted with a red lens and a signal lamp so that indication is given when the switch is ON. It is also fitted with a neat outlet socket so that another domestic appliance, for example, an electric iron, can be easily connected up.

ticular line. To mention one item in this equipment, there is a testing transformer capable of giving half a million volts or producing a spark over 45 inches long in air.
It is only to be expected that such a progressive firm as Messrs. Reyrolle should look after the welfare of their employees, and they do this in a very up-to-date and efficient manner.
They have a very fine canteen at the Hebburn Works, comprising a self-contained range of buildings, including a large assembly hall with sitting accommodation for 250 people, three large dining rooms with accommodation for 750 people, private dining rooms for officials, kitchen, and other offices. The cooking equipment is entirely electrical, and consists of two double roasting ovens, each of an electric capacity of 11 kw, two steaming ovens, each of 5 kw, one 8-section top-plate of 13 kw, three hot cupboards with a total capacity of 24 kw, a medium-sized grill, two steaming-pans with a combined capacity of 18 kw, eight coffee and water urns of capacities varying between 6 and 10 kw each, and an electric dish-washing machine. The average number of meals served per week are 800 dinners and 400 teas. The large assembly hall, which was completed in 1927, is a well-appointed room 17 feet high, with a spring floor of polished oak so that it can be used for dancing. The lighting of this principal hall is particularly interesting, because it consists of a number of electric lights entirely hidden from view around the ceiling, and arranged to give a soft, shadowless light over the whole of the floor surface.
At the New Town Works there is another canteen with accommodation for 150 people, the kitchen for this canteen being equipped with four large coffee and water urns, each of an electrical capacity of 10 kw, and a hot cupboard of 8 1/2 kw. This canteen is intended for supplying light refreshments, and those employees who require meals are catered for at the main canteen at the Hebburn Works.

* * *

A Visit to a Co-operative Electricity Society
in Czecho-Slovakia.
By A. HONORA ENFIELD, Secretary International Co-operative Womens Guild.

Czecho-Slovakia, with its almost unlimited water supply, is doing much for the electrification of the countryside, largely through the medium of Co-operative Societies formed among the peasants themselves for the production and distribution of electricity. One of the most interesting of these is the Society of Drazice, a village on the Iser, some 30 miles from Prague, which I had the good fortune to visit during a recent stay in Czecho-Slovakia.
The Society, founded in 1900, was not originally formed for the production of electricity: its first enterprise was a mill, at which its peasant members could get their corn ground. It then occurred to them that the water power of the Iser might be used to better advantage in producing electricity which would not only drive the mill but might also be put to many other uses, and the first power station was founded not long before the war. To-day, the production and distribution of electricity is the main work of the Society, though it still has numerous other undertakings.
The Society has now 1,500 members, each of whom holds a minimum share of 400 Czech Crowns (about 30s.), and pays

Unnamed: 9: Photographer who took the picture of the Womens Day group.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 499

600 Crowns into a Reserve Fund. The members are, for the most part, peasants, but include also the workers employed in the Society, manufacturers and officials, and various towns and smaller local governing authorities. Seven rural and urban districts and three hundred parishes are covered by the operations of the Society, which distributes current to 60,000 individual consumers. The Society has now nine power stations, at all of which electricity is produced and transmitted for storage to the Central Station at Drazice, from which it is distributed to the towns or villages or direct to the individual consumers. The price to the individual consumer is about 5½d. for light and 2¾d. for power, though there are special terms varying from about ¾d. to 1d. for the supply of power to large-scale industry. Water-power only is used, as a rule, at all the stations for the production of the electricity, though some have a reserve plant run by petrol, and the Society is now co-operating with the city of Prague in the construction of a joint reservoir, in case of the failure of the water supply.

As already mentioned, the Society has a number of other productive and commercial enterprises to which its electric undertakings supply the necessary light and power, and its special interest, from the human point of view, lies in the effect which this combination of enterprises, owned and controlled by the peasants themselves and run on the most modern lines, is having in raising the whole standard of life among the population. The productive enterprises include four mills, a fruit-preserving factory, a brick works, a workshop for the repair of agricultural machinery, a chain factory, where the chains are welded by electricity, a nitrogen factory, and an estate of 100 acres on which experimental farming is being carried on. In connection with this, a research department has lately been started to test the effect of electricity upon the crops, and experiments are being worked out for the production at competitive prices of cucumbers and other vegetables out of season. Through these, and the Consumers Store and Savings Bank, also attached to the Society, the peasants are supplying most of their own needs.

Naturally, the life of the women is also being transformed. Electric light is everywhere, in every cottage; bread making, washing, ironing and butter-making are being carried out by electricity.

transcription:
500
The Electrical Age
Meals for a Week-end in the Electric Refrigerator.
By Miss MARY MACKIRDY (Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow, and Author of "Recipes for You").
This is when I really envy the women with intelligence, plus income, the others with the will to acquire a refrigerator but not the funds hope that with wider knowledge and greater demand prices will be reduced and they also will become possessors. I am certain that in the near future a refrigerator will be one of the accepted furnishings of a house and there will be no more worry as to whether the joint, cooked or uncooked, will keep fresh, no matter the degree of heat, that the butter will remain firm and the milk and cream sweet. Many of the housewifes difficulties are in regard to the keeping of food: a refrigerator will solve these.
Suggestions for Lunch, Dinner and Supper.
These suggestions are for dishes that may be kept for a considerable time in the refrigerator: they are suitable for various meals and are easily made.
Eggs in Cases.
Some eggs, some cooked vegetables, such as peas, new carrots, French beans, new potatoes, or whatever may be at hand, some good salad dressing, lettuce or cress.
Boil the eggs hard or soft, as may be desired, trim a little bit from one end so that they will stand, put in little cases—paper or china heart-shaped ones are good for this dish. Have the vegetables cut in very neat pieces, arrange round the egg, coat all with the dressing and garnish with a sprig of cress or a little lettuce leaf.
The vegetables may be varied and little pieces of cooked meat or fish added if there is anything suitable in the larder.
Mayonnaise of Cauliflower.
A nice-looking, slightly undercooked cauliflower is used for this; it should be neatly trimmed. Keep the cauliflower in the refrigerator till it is required. When to be served, stand the cauliflower on a dish, pour mayonnaise over and garnish with little tomatoes or another vegetable.
Roman Fish Salad.
Cooked fish—salmon or white fish—some hard-boiled eggs, some cooked potatoes, sufficient mayonnaise or good salad dressing to moisten, some gherkins, anchovies and pickled beet.
Put some dressing on a dish, then a layer of fish which has been flaked, some thin slices of potato and the whites of the eggs cut in strips: coat with dressing, repeat the layers, reserving a layer of sauce for the top. The mixture should be fairly flat on the dish: sieve over it, so as to cover the whole, the yolk of the eggs. Arrange round the dish gherkins cut to resemble tassels, anchovies slit to the length like a fringe and the beet cut in neat shapes.
Cream of Chicken.
This is a delicious savoury.
About 1/2 or 1 teacup finely chopped cooked chicken or chicken and ham, 1/4 pint double cream, 1 level tablespoonful powdered gelatine, 2 tablespoonfuls hot water, salt, pepper, cayenne.
Whip the cream till stiff, add the chicken, seasoning and the gelatine dissolved in the water, mix thoroughly.
The mixture may be used in various ways, it may be spread on neatly cut pieces of white or brown bread or on rounds or other shapes of cooked pastry; a good deal of mixture should be put on the bread or pastry. Garnish with salad and serve.
Peaches with Custard.
A tin of peaches, some sponge cake, some chopped almonds and cherries, some good well-flavoured jam.
Mix the cake crumbs with the other ingredients, adding enough fruit syrup or liquid from the peaches to bind all.
Dry the peaches, fill the hollows with little balls of the mixture and lay on a dish flat side down: if the peaches are fairly small put the halves together. Cover the peaches with the following custard:—1/2 pint milk, 1 oz. cornflour, sugar, flavouring, 1 or 2 eggs, carmine. Mix the cornflour and milk and stir till boiling; beat the eggs with the sugar sufficient to sweeten, beat in the cornflour and milk, add flavouring and a few drops of carmine. Decorate with fresh or crystallised fruit, or if a richer and more elaborate dish is desired, whipped cream.
Fruit Drink.
1 orange, 2 lemons, 1 pint water, 1/2 lb. sugar, some tinned peaches, some bottled cherries.
Boil the water, sugar, grated lemon and orange rind and the liquid from the peaches and cherries for about 5 minutes; strain the syrup and add the juice of the orange and lemons. Add to the syrup the peaches cut in neat pieces and the cherries, steep for several hours before using. This drink should have a good deal of fruit and may be diluted with soda or other mineral water. Other fruits may be substituted for those given.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 501
What is a Time Switch?
A Page for Girl Guides :: :: :: By Gladys F. Sharp.
Do you ever wonder? I mean something beyond the " I wonder if it will be fine for our hike on Saturday? " or " I wonder if we shall have good weather for camping?"
There must have been occasions when you have been walking along an empty street at dusk and suddenly the whole row of electric lights have leapt into brilliance. Have you stopped your tremendously inter- esting anecdote about the last district church parade long enough to wonder just what was responsible for the happening?
Have you wondered what magician operates those delightful electric signs that blink so colourfully from so many build- ings, or who are the poor unfortunates who must stay behind until the streets are quite empty and the lights can be switched off in those shop windows into which you can look long after shop hours?
Let me appease your rapidly awakening curiosity.
A wonderful instrument, called a Time Switch, performs all these duties and many others, but before telling you some more of its interesting work, here is a des- cription of the apparatus, which the illus- trations will help you to understand.
A Time Switch is simply a switch oper- ated by a clock. The simplest form which this can take is as shown in illustration No. 1. This is an ordinary alarm clock which is set in the manner you know all too well, I expect. Instead of ringing a bell, however, the action of the " alarm wind " at the back brings it into contact with an arm which knocks up the dolly of the tumbler switch and so switches off the light. This type will only switch off, and it is necessary to put the light on for yourself. so that its uses are very limited. There are others which control a whole lot of lights and which are fitted with clocks which run from eight to forty-five days without any need of re-winding. More wonderful still, is the clock that runs for ever, being automatically wound up by electricity.
Most marvellous of all is the " solar device, " by means of which the clock operates the switch year in and year out according to the time of the rising and setting of the sun, without any human interference at all. This is sheer wizardry, and had the inventors lived in the bad old days it is almost certain that they would have been burned to death at the stake.
Illustration No. 2 shows a slightly more complicated type of switch, the use of which I will explain later. You will see that it has a dial with the hours marked up to twenty-four in- stead of the usual twelve, and that one half of the face has a black band marked " night, " the plain half being marked " d a y . " There are two hands, marked re- spectively " In " and " Out . " The " In " hand is set at the time you wish your light to come on, the " Out " hand to the hour when it is required to switch off. The time pointer is at the lower right hand side of the dial, and remains stationary, the dial itself revolving.
A very simple Time Switch.
Slightly more complicated. The burglars nightmare!

504 The Electrical Age
The Newcastle Conference
OUR OVERSEAS GUESTS
The first E.A.W. Annual Conference to be organised in Newcastle promises to be a great success.
On Wednesday, July 10th, Members will be joined by over 200 women delegates from Overseas where splendid arrangements have been made by the local branch of the E.A.W.
Supporting the President, Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, will be the Deputy Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress of Newcastle and many prominent women of the North East Coast.
Interest will be added to the Conference by the presence of the Right Hon. Margaret Bondfield, P.C., M.P., J.P.
A very large gathering is being invited by the Lady Mayoress on the Opening Day.
Taken in Amsterdam by Mrs. Ll. B. Atkinson
Madame Muller-Lulefs.
One of the most interesting features of the Opening Ceremony will be the Speeches to be given by the women guests from Overseas. This is the first occasion on which women from different countries have been gathered together on one platform and we hope that the result of the Conference will be an International expression of the womans point of view on matters electrical.
From America we have three guests, Miss Sophia Malicki, who is Chairman of the Womens Committee of the Public Relations Section of the National Electric Light Association, is one of the most popular and well known women in the Electrical Industry in the United States.
The Womens Committee is organised for the purpose of formulating and putting into effect plans for the education of women of the industry on the fundamental economic principles of the electric light and power business, and the interdependence of the public and industry.
Units of the Committee are established in most of the electric service companies composing the National Electric Light Association. The total membership is about 30,000 women.
Miss Helen Norris, who will bring greetings from the Womens Division of the Electrical Association of Chicago, is Dean of the Women at the Commonwealth Edison Company of that City.

The Electrical Age 505

e, July 10th-12th, 1929
S GUESTS.
ed outside of London promises to be an unqualified
coming from all parts of Great Britain to Newcastle,
cal Branch for their welcome and entertainment.
on the platform on the Opening Day, will be the
tant representative men and women on the North-
ech of the first woman Cabinet Minister, The
Mayor to the Reception on the evening of the

Madame E. J. Waveren. Resink.

Frederick, of the U.S.A., and has translated her
book, "Household Engineering" into Dutch.
She promotes her ideals by writing and lectur-
ing and has recently given a Paper before the
IVth International Congress of Scientific Organi-
zation of Work at Paris.
Madame Van Waveren feels that Housekeeping
has become a great burden and a new point of
view is needed to solve the problem. She feels
that the principles of Emerson, Taylor and
Gilbreth might be applied to the problems of
Household Tasks.

Fraulein Käthe Böhm.

Madame Van Waverens speech at the Conference
will mainly deal with the Application of Electricity in
Rural Areas in Holland.
Madame Muller-Lulofs will, on the other hand, deal
with the tremendous strides which Electricity has made
in Amsterdam and some of the larger towns in Holland.
Madame Muller-Lulofs shares Madame Van Waverens
enthusiasm for the improvement of methods in the
home, realising that Electricity is one of the greatest
aids to bring about this improvement.
Frau Margis is very well known in Germany as an
expert on Domestic Electrification. She edits the
monthly paper, "Haushalt und Wirtschaft," and is a
very extensive writer on all subjects pertaining to the
efficient management of the home.
Frau Margis is a wide traveller and has been
appointed to represent the "Deutsche Reichskura-
torium fur Wirtschaftlichkeit" at the International
Congress of Scientific Organisation of Work in Paris.
Fraulein Käthe Böhm, who is a Diplom-Ingenieur,
was the first woman to train as an Electrical Engineer
in Austria, having studied in Vienna and taken her
Diploma in 1925.
At present she is a Household Consulting Engineer
and lectures extensively to womens organisations on
the Use of Electricity in Berlin and District.
Fraulein Böhms lecture at the Conference will deal
mainly with Electrical Accidents and their Prevention
in Households.

Unnamed: 9: Dealing with strides electricity has made in Amsterdam and Holland.

Unnamed: 9: Describes electrical installation in his house following E.A.W. national specifications.
transcription:
506
The Electrical Age
The Women’s National Specification in Practice.
A Description of “Dunottar,” Thornton Heath
Where the provision of Electrical “Outlets” is almost identical with the standard set in the
Women’s National Specification issued by the E.A.W.
Described by J. F. STANLEY, B.Sc., A.C.G.I.
Member of the Staff of the British Engineering Standards Association.
The house described in these notes was designed by Mr. A. P. Starkey, of Harrow, but the specification for the electrical installation was in my own hands. Being in a district that is supplied with electricity at the rate of less than three farthings a unit for all purposes, my wife and I decided that the house should be run on all-electric lines as far as possible, subject to certain limitations imposed by the general design of the house.
The lighting of the house is perfectly straightforward, and requires very little explanation. Lights are provided over the front and back porches, and in the larder, and I am interested to see that in the Women’s National Specification lights in these positions are recommended.
The lighting of the ingle in the drawing-room is effected by means of strip-lamps concealed behind the beam, this giving a most pleasing effect, a strong light being obtained without the lamps being visible from the body of the room.
The lights in the hall and in the landing are both controlled either from upstairs or downstairs—a very great convenience. Similarly, the light in the garage can be controlled either from the main door or from the door at the back leading on to the garden-room.
Now let us look at the “Outlets,” as the plugs and sockets are called by the E.A.W. Here again let me emphasise that nothing freakish has been attempted, my aim having been to provide just that amount of convenience that one has a right to expect in an ordinary dwelling house.
As a general principle, the “outlets” have been placed either against a chimney breast or as near a window or door as possible, so as not to spoil the appearance of the wall, and so as to leave as much clear space as possible for the furniture. In certain cases this principle has been departed from, the reason being that we had a definite disposition of furniture in mind from the outset, the plugs and sockets therefore being arranged accordingly.
“Outlets” are often spoken of as either “lighting plugs” or “power plugs,” but I prefer not to make this distinction, as many lighting plugs are used for all sorts of things other than lamps. These terms originated from the fact that the “outlets” were wired either on the lighting circuit or the power circuit, but as irons and kettles are often used off the lighting circuit, and as the “all-in” system is coming into more general use, a far more satisfactory method of classifying the “outlets” is according to their “size,” or, to put it more correctly, according to their standard current-carrying capacity.
Plugs and sockets are standardised in four “sizes,” the current-carrying capacities of these sizes being 2, 5, 15 and 30 amperes respectively. The smallest size is suitable for use with lamps, but from the point of view of mechanical strength the next larger size, namely, the 5-ampere size, is often preferred. For irons, kettles, vacuum cleaners and other small-consumption appliances, such as hair curlers, coffee pots and shaving mugs, the 5-ampere size is the best, so that in my house I adopted this size for all purposes except for electric

Unnamed: 9: She wrote this article about the Worlds Garden Toffery factory.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 509
"The Worlds Garden Toffery"
At CREMONA PARK, NEWCASTLE-UPON-TYNE.
By Anna Holm.
It would be difficult to name any industry in which Electricity does not play an important part—and in the production of food and confectionery, where cleanliness and hygiene are paramount, Electricity proves of the utmost value.
Confirmation of this may be obtained by a visit to the "Worlds Garden Toffery."
The first impression on entering the large white and blue buildings is space, airiness and spotless cleanliness. Adequate ventilation is naturally of vital importance, and the problem is solved at Cremona Park by the installation of a large number of electrically-driven ventilating fans, which exhaust the hot air and circulate cool air for the comfort of the workers.
Photo by Philipson
Aerial View of Cremona Park.
One of the Works to be visited during the Newcastle Conference.
Cremona Park, Newcastle-upon-Tyne, where Messrs. A. S. Wilkin, Limited, have established a model toffee factory amid Utopian surroundings. There are many garden cities and garden villages in the Kingdom, but Cremona Park is believed to be the only "Garden Toffery" in the world, and certainly the only place where toffee, and nothing but toffee, is manufactured under ideal conditions, in the perfect setting of a beautiful garden.
The next impression is that of well-thought-out sequence. There is no overlapping. Raw materials enter at one end of the Toffery, and after working right round the buildings, leaves as Toffee by the motor lorries at the entrance. In the raw material section are bags of cane sugar, boxes of nuts and fruit, wooden casks of dairy butter from New Zealand and Australia, barrels of treacle, more

Unnamed: 9: Delivering the Presidential Address at the Seventh Annual Conference.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 511

barrels containing full cream milk, and large churns of pure rich cream.
All these go in the making of Cremona Toffee—and Electricity helps in the making.
In the boiling rooms a number of mixers are driven individually by electric motors.
The toffee, after being boiled and mixed, is poured on to long metal tables, cooled by water running underneath, and afterwards cut into sections by means of electric cutting machines. Then, in turn, come the most fascinating machines of all—the wrapping machines. These are almost human, as they each wrap 160 pieces of toffee a minute in waxed paper, automatically cut from a long roll. The intriguing part to watch from the onlookers point of view is how the machines twist the ends of the paper after wrapping the pieces of toffee and discharge them into wire cages ready for packing.
In addition to the motive power for the wrapping of the toffee, electricity contributes its quota in the Packing Room. Cremona Toffee is sent to all parts of the world, and it arrives as fresh in the remote corners of the earth as it is when it leaves
Cremona Park. This is because it is packed in airtight tins, and special electrical apparatus has been installed to exhaust the air from the tins during the time the toffee is being packed.
At first sight, the covering of such excellent toffee as Cremona with chocolate appears to be an extravagance, but they believe in making good things better. The machine that carries out this operation takes the form of a slow-moving, endless belt, on which the toffee, after being covered with chocolate, passes through an electric refrigerator in order to harden the outer coating. It is ready for wrapping and packing by the time it reaches the end of its journey on the belt.
There are other applications of the uses of Electricity at Cremona Park of which electrically-minded visitors will take notice, and after the tour is completed they will not only appreciate that the "Worlds Garden Toffery" has been aptly named, but that Electricity has assisted very largely in achieving that industrial "ideal" into which Messrs. A. S. Wilkin, Limited, have established.

transcription:
The Electrical Age
513
ELECTRICITY IN THE SCHOOLS
Conference Convened by the Electrical Association for Women between Electrical Industry and Educational Organizations.
The survey which has been made by the E.A.W. of the kind of Domestic Electrical Equipment, if any, which exists in Domestic Science Centres and Departments, has revealed a very deplorable state of affairs.
In one or two instances, notably at Barnsley, where there is active co-operation between the Electricity Department and the Educational Department, an up-to-date electrical equipment has been installed in the local Centres.
In quite a large number of Centres there is no electrical apparatus whatever; in others there is perhaps one cooker, which is often out of date, an electric iron, and sometimes an electric washer.
It is quite clear that some action is necessary to bring about a greater co-operation between the local Education Authorities and the Electrical people concerned.
With a view to taking a first step, the Electrical Association for Women called together a Conference in London on May 8th, representative of the Electrical Industry and the Teaching World. So great was the response to the invitation that the Small Club Room at Kensington Court was hard put to it to find accommodation for all those who attended the meeting.
In addition to practically every section of the Electrical Industry, representatives were present from the Central Electricity Board, the Board of Education and the Ministry of Labour.
The Teaching World included the Association of Teachers of Domestic Subjects, the Headmistresses’ Association, the Women Science Teachers, Teachers in Technical Institutions and many individual representative men and women.
In opening the meeting, Mrs. Hammer stated that the Conference was called in order that a frank discussion might take place between representatives of the Electrical Industry and Educational Organisations with regard to the desirability of introducing some teaching on matters electrical into girls’ schools, and also to discuss the question of suitable training for girls who wish to enter the Electrical Industry.
The Director of the E.A.W. outlined the work which had already been done by the Association, and referred specially to the
By courtesy of the “Electrical Times.”

In a very excellent speech, Miss Hilda Shaw, B.Sc., representing the Association of Teachers of Domestic Subjects, outlined the needs of the Teachers and the school children, pointing out the desirability of some special instruction being given to the Teacher. She also referred to the difficulty of getting up-to-date apparatus.

Lieut.-Colonel Vignoles, of the Electrical Development Association, putting the point of view of the Industry, said that his Organisation would be pleased to help with the production of the necessary text books, with cinema films and in any other way possible.

Mrs. Wilson, of Ashford, reported on some Student Classes which had been commenced at the local High Schools and which had been extremely successful.

Finally, a resolution was passed, calling upon the Board of Education to afford facilities for the training of school teachers on this subject, and also to give its official approval to such instruction being given in girls schools. Further, that the Electrical Industry should be asked to offer every facility to the Domestic Science Centres throughout the country in regard to the installation of the necessary equipment.

As a direct outcome of the meeting the Board of Education received a Deputation on this subject on June 24th, and we feel confident that the E.A.W. has aroused a practical and very considerable amount of interest on this all-important subject.

In a very excellent speech, Miss Hilda Shaw, B.Sc., representing the Association of Teachers of Domestic Subjects, outlined the needs of the Teachers and the school children, pointing out the desirability of some special instruction being given to the Teacher. Lieut.-Colonel Vignoles, of the Electrical Development Association, putting the point of view of the Industry, said that his Organisation would be pleased to help with the production of the necessary text books, with cinema films and in any other way possible.

Mrs. Wilson, of Ashford, reported on some Student Classes which had been commenced at the local High Schools and which had been extremely successful.

Finally, a resolution was passed, calling upon the Board of Education to afford facilities for the training of school teachers on this subject, and also to give its official approval to such instruction being given in girls schools. Further, that the Electrical Industry should be asked to offer every facility to the Domestic Science Centres throughout the country in regard to the installation of the necessary equipment.

As a direct outcome of the meeting the Board of Education received a Deputation on this subject on June 24th, and we feel confident that the E.A.W. has aroused a practical and very considerable amount of interest on this all-important subject.

USEFUL HINTS
