By "ELECTRA."
ONE LAMP, TWO LIGHTS.
The Duo-Savelite, which may be described as two lamps in one, is a fascinating device for economising current consumption and eliminating all possibility of too much light in the nursery or sick room.
The lamp is made with two filaments, one of 25 watts and the other only 4 watts, and they are controlled by the chain shown in the illustration. The bulb is made of the well-known Argenta opal glass.
The Duo-Savelite is fixed into a lamp-holder in the same way as an ordinary lamp.
A further use for this new lamp during these light evenings is in the Hall. A light is generally required, though not the brilliance of the usual 40 or 60 watt lamp.
The 25 watts of the Duo-Savelite gives a very fair light, and a pull of the cord and there is just a glimmer, as of a night light.
The whole thing is very neat in appearance and not expensive in price.
PHILIPS
The Duo-Savelite, showing the cord which control the two lights in the one lamp.
THE DOME HEATER.
The Dome Heater is new and unique in design and construction. As its name implies, the four elements form a dome, instead of the horizontal or vertical bars as in the usual electric fire.
This dome disperses the heat in all directions and warms a room evenly. A three-heat switch makes for economy in use, and is a great asset when the Dome Heater is called into service for cooking operations. Consumption of electricity is 2, 1, and 1/2 unit on the respective positions of the switch.
Our illustration shows the Dome Heater with a stand placed over it, and a frying pan; but several vessels can be accommodated on the stand, and cooking operations carried out quite successfully.
The Dome Heater as a Breakfast Cooker.
Special kettles—in copper—may be obtained, which fit over the dome, and ensure quick boiling; also heat deflectors.
The Heater is well made and is a practical and interesting appliance.

Unnamed: 9: "Hon. Secretary of the Glasgow and District Branch, E.A.W."
transcription:
The Electrical Age
519
E.A.W. Branch Activities.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
We have come to the close season of July and August when most of our members are on holiday.
In September we start off with a Garden Party at "Stanely," Paisley, a lovely woodland estate, the home of Mrs. Speirs, one of our very active members. We trust to get a real army of new members as the result of this fascinating day.
For the early Autumn session we have arranged a series of Instructional Lectures for the guidance of new members in particular, who missed the early talks on Fuses, Plugs and Wiring, etc.
We are hoping to send a good contingent of members to the Newcastle Conference.

* * *

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. L. Hayes,
1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
On March 7th, 1929, the Birmingham and Midlands Branch held their third Annual Meeting at the Queens Hotel. Lady Brooks presided. The President, Lady Brooks, having completed her term of office, was presented, during the meeting, with an Electric Warming Plate by Mr. R. A. Chattock, Vice-President and wife of the City Engineer of Birmingham, on behalf of the members, as an acknowledgment and appreciation of the wonderful pioneer work done by Lady Brooks during her three years as President.
Mrs. H. K. Beale, wife of the Chairman of the Elec. Supply Committee of Birmingham, was then elected President. The Lady Mayoress proposed the adoption of the Annual Report and Financial Statement. The Hon. Secretary, Mrs. A. L. Hayes, resigned, but it was hoped that she would reconsider her decision.
Miss Haslett, who was able to be present, then proposed the adoption of the New Rules, and spoke on the work of the Association generally. Tea was then served, bringing a successful meeting to a happy close.
On the evening of the same day, the Branch held their first Ball. This proved to be very successful, both from a social and financial point of view.
On March 14th a party of members paid a visit to the Ideal Home Exhibition, Olympia, by kind invitation of the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., and the Hotpoint Electric Appliance Co., Ltd. This visit was greatly enjoyed.
On March 20th members visited the Electric Construction Co., Wolverhampton, where they saw Electrical Motors of every description in the process of manufacture.
On March 26th over 50 members visited the Printing Works of Messrs. Kenrick & Jefferson, West Bromwich. Members were much impressed with the splendid arrangements of these works.
On April 11th a visit was paid to the Birchills Power Station. This proved most interesting. Members also had the opportunity of seeing the new Anson Pumping Station.
On April 16th the party of members who attended the London luncheon, afterwards taking part in the visit to Messrs. Belling & Co., manufacturers of Electrical "Utilities," spent a very happy day.
On April 17th, Dr. A. Bryce, M.D., of Birmingham, lectured on "Health." This interesting lecture was much appreciated by the members.
On April 24th one of the most interesting visits of this session was paid to the Needle Factory at Redditch. Here they saw in the making needles of every description. Each member was presented with a very useful souvenir in the form of a Needle Case.
On May 24th a party of members visited the new Power Station at Longford, near Coventry.

Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Foster-Jeffery, LL.B.,
6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
Since our last report the Manchester Branch has heard with great regret of Mrs. Peatties removal to London. This Branch owes a very great deal to Mrs. Peattie, who has been the Magazine Secretary for over three years, and during that time she has built up the circulation of the magazine among our members until the happy state of every member taking the magazine has become almost an accomplished fact.
We regret that during her last few weeks in Manchester, Mrs. Peattie should have been so ill, and we are glad to hear that she is now getting better, and hope that good health and good fortune will attend her in the south. Of course, Manchesters loss is Londons gain, and we envy London in gaining such an untiring worker and enthusiast.
We have been very fortunate in obtaining as a successor to Mrs. Peattie, Mrs. L. B. A. Carr, who is just as keen about the welfare of the Association as was Mrs. Peattie, and we know that she will maintain and extend the excellent standard achieved by our first Magazine Secretary. We offer her our very best wishes in her work.
Our last visit of the session was paid to Messrs. Simpson & Godlees, Beelow Tissue Makers, of Swinton. The visit was well attended and much enjoyed, not only for the exceptional interest of the work but also for the extremely friendly way in which we were shown all over the works, from the recreation rooms to the most intricate piece of machinery. We were taken round in small parties, and the visit was voted quite one of the most successful ones of the year.

* * *

Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Sleep, 1, York Terrace,
St. Georges Road, Cheltenham.
The Second Annual General Meeting was held at the Town Hall on March 24th, presided over by our President, Mrs. Atwell Lake. The adoption of the annual report was proposed by Mr. W. J. Roche, who remarked that an increase in membership of 30 per cent. during the year was a healthy sign.
The Financial statement was presented by Miss Dawson Oakes and adopted on the proposition of Mrs. Chas. Marshall. After the usual business had been transacted, Miss C. Haslett gave an interesting address, and spoke of the work the Association was doing throughout the country. Miss Dawson Oakes, organiser of Domestic Science under the local Education Committee, gave an illuminating account of the Electrical equipment which had been in use at the local domestic science centres for the last four years.
The luncheon which followed at the Queens Hotel was a great success. Lack of space forbids an account of the interesting remarks made by those who proposed and responded to the toasts.
In the afternoon, Mr. G. S. Francis, of the Electrical Development Association, gave a lecture illustrated by lantern slides in his usual interesting way on "The Modern Tendencies in Architecture, Lighting and Furnishing Designs."
Three of our local Electrical Contractors who are members of the E.C.A. have each very kindly given a lecture-demonstration during the last three months.
The first, on "How a House is Wired for Electric Service," was given by Mr. J. Marshall, who had had prepared a special demonstration board, showing the various methods of wiring.
Mr. W. P. Honeywell gave an instructive account of the various methods of "Water Heating by Electricity," illustrated by charts and various water heating appliances.
"The Running Cost of Domestic Electrical Appliances" was fully explained and worked out by Mr. G. B. Bastin, who had an attractive display of Electrical Appliances.
A visit to Bournville on May 8th was much appreciated by members.
Many of our members who had the pleasure of knowing and working with Miss C. Eaton, our first Hon. Treasurer, suffered a shock on hearing of her sudden death on May 2nd. We still very much miss her cheerful and ungrudging help in our Branch.

Hon. Secretary: Miss Foster-Jeffery, LL.B.,
6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
Since our last report the Manchester Branch has heard with great regret of Mrs. Peatties removal to London. This Branch owes a very great deal to Mrs. Peattie, who has been the Magazine Secretary for over three years, and during that time she has built up the circulation of the magazine among our members until the happy state of every member taking the magazine has become almost an accomplished fact.
We regret that during her last few weeks in Manchester, Mrs. Peattie should have been so ill, and we are glad to hear that she is now getting better, and hope that good health and good fortune will attend her in the south. Of course, Manchesters loss is Londons gain, and we envy London in gaining such an untiring worker and enthusiast.
We have been very fortunate in obtaining as a successor to Mrs. Peattie, Mrs. L. B. A. Carr, who is just as keen about the welfare of the Association as was Mrs. Peattie, and we know that she will maintain and extend the excellent standard achieved by our first Magazine Secretary. Hon. Secretary: Miss A. A. Sleep, 1, York Terrace,

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
We have come to the close season of July and August when most of our members are on holiday.
In September we start off with a Garden Party at "Stanely," Paisley, a lovely woodland estate, the home of Mrs. Speirs, one of our very active members. We trust to get a real army of new members as the result of this fascinating day.
For the early Autumn session we have arranged a series of Instructional Lectures for the guidance of new members in particular, who missed the early talks on Fuses, Plugs and Wiring, etc.
We are hoping to send a good contingent of members to the Newcastle Conference.

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. A. L. Hayes,
1, Bloomfield Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
On March 7th, 1929, the Birmingham and Midlands Branch held their third Annual Meeting at the Queens Hotel. Lady Brooks presided. The President, Lady Brooks, having completed her term of office, was presented, during the meeting, with an Electric Warming Plate by Mr. R. A. Chattock, Vice-President and wife of the City Engineer of Birmingham, on behalf of the members, as an acknowledgment and appreciation of the wonderful pioneer work done by Lady Brooks during her three years as President.
Mrs. H. K. Beale, wife of the Chairman of the Elec. Supply Committee of Birmingham, was then elected President. The Lady Mayoress proposed the adoption of the Annual Report and Financial Statement. The Hon. Secretary, Mrs. A. L. Hayes, resigned, but it was hoped that she would reconsider her decision.
Miss Haslett, who was able to be present, then proposed the adoption of the New Rules, and spoke on the work of the Association generally. Tea was then served, bringing a successful meeting to a happy close.
On the evening of the same day, the Branch held their first Ball. This proved to be very successful, both from a social and financial point of view.

The Lecture to be given by Mr. J. W. Beauchamp,
mentioned in our last number, was well attended, and
proved most interesting.
Our General Meeting and the subsequent Annual
Luncheon were a great success, and we were all pleased
to have the Director with us again, and to hear from her
how our Branches are improving.
Our spring programme has proved a good one; the
Lecture on April 9th by Mr. R. S. Francis, of the E.D.A.,
on Modern Tendencies in Architectural, Furnishing and
Lighting Design, and the part Electricity Plays Therein,
was most interesting.
On April 28th we had a visit to the Cigar Factory and
Welfare Department of Messrs. J. R. Freeman & Sons, Ltd.,
Cardiff.

April 8th by Miss C. M. Burrows, of the Cardiff Electricity
Department—a cooking demonstration is always a popular
fixture.
On May 22nd we had a visit to the Cardiff Docks by
kind invitation of the Great Western Railway Co., and this
proved a most interesting and unusual fixture.
We have still two fixtures to take place—on June 13th,
the Bristol, Cheltenham and Gloucester members are visit-
ing Cardiff, when we are being entertained to a Civic
Reception and Luncheon by the Lord Mayor of Cardiff.

Co.’s Showrooms, by kind invitation of Mr. W. E. Hobbs,
the District Manager. In association with this visit we
hope to show our visitors as much of our City as possible.
Our Summer Outing takes place on June 26th, and
covers a visit to the Cable Works of Messrs. Edison Swan
Electric Co.’s Cable Works at Lydbrook, and we are looking
forward to a most enjoyable day.
All our fixtures are very well attended, keen interest
being shown by all the members.

Ashford and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. B. M. Wilson, Gleniffer Brae,
Vicarage Road, Kennington, Nr. Ashford, Kent.
A brief report of the Ashford and District Branch from
March 20th to May 31st is as follows :—
March 20th.—Lecture on Vacuum Cleaners, by Miss
May Jones. A most interesting lecture was the comment
of the members.
April 11th, 18th, 25th.—Special course of lecture-demon-
strations on Cooking, by Miss D. Vaughan. We are
greatly indebted to Miss Vaughan and the Hotpoint Electric
Appliance Company for these lectures, which were a great
help to us in understanding more about our Electric
Cookers.
May 2nd was an Open Lecture, as it was felt to be of
general interest to the public, when Dr. Scott, of Ashford,
lectured on Electricity as Applied in the Medical Pro-
fession. The Lecture was illustrated by apparatus kindly
loaned by the Ashford Hospital. This was well attended
and enjoyed by all, with a request to Dr. Scott for another
lecture soon.
May 23rd.—Mr. R. Hall (Electrical Contractor, of Ash-
ford) gave a lecture on Refrigeration. This was enjoyed
very much by the members present, who hope Mr. Hall will
give another lecture on Refrigerators.
Two Whist and one Whist Drive have also been held.
The Student Classes are still progressing, and interest
is well maintained.
We are grateful to Mrs. Knott and to Messrs. Belling
and Co. for their assistance.
B.W.

Unnamed: 10: Secretary of Leeds and West Riding Branch
transcription:
The Electrical Age
521
Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o Ingleby Motors, Ltd., Sweet Street, Leeds.
The Leeds and West Riding Branch has now closed down for the summer months, after having had an inter-esting and varied programme of Lectures and Visits during the past winter session.
Among the visits was a tour round the Neo Electric Lamp Works, Leeds, where the members were amazed to see how much goes to the making of an electric bulb. Each process, from the furnace and blowing of bulbs to the testing, sealing and packing of the lamps, was intensely interesting.
In March, Mr. S. C. Hurry, of London, gave a very good lecture and demonstration on "Electric Water Heat-ing," which was most appropriate and useful to the mem-bers in view of the coming summer months.
In April, Mr. Harry Moss, A.M.I.E.E., of Bradford, spoke on "Some more things you should know about your Wiring Installations," this being a continuation of a popular lecture he gave last year. The members very much enjoyed this address, and the useful hints Mr. Moss gave were much appreciated.
It is hoped a number of our members will be able to go to Newcastle to the Conference in July, which promises to be a great success and far too big a treat to miss.
North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. M. Kiltz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, N. Wales.
The Branch is steadily growing, our number now being 72. For the summer months we are concentrating on visits aims to interest women in the Association and to increase our membership.
In April the Director came to Colwyn Bay and addressed a meeting. The Chair was taken by Councillor Mrs. Hyde, J.P. Mrs. E. de Ferranti, our President, was on the platform, also Mr. Barnes, the Chairman of the Lighting Committee, Mr. Wilson, the Chairman of the U.D.C. of Colwyn Bay, and Mr. Smith, the Engineer.
Miss Haslett explained the objects of the Association, and as a result of the meeting several new members were enrolled.
On May 7th a party of members was shown over the Cunard Liner "Samaria" in Huskisson Dock, Liverpool. All were very interested in the equipment and size of the vessel.
Last week about thirty members met at Dolgarrog, and were shown over the Aluminium Corporation Works and North Wales Power Station. Everyone watched with keenest interest the liquid metal at boiling point being run into moulds and then taken, still hot, and rolled through heavy rollers to various thicknesses for use.
The party were afterwards entertained to tea by Mrs. Wilson, the wife of the Managing Director. Mrs. Price White proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Wilson and all the ladies who helped with the tea, and to the Engineers for kindly showing us round. Everyone spent a thoroughly enjoyable afternoon.
Our next visit is on July 23rd to Messrs. Ferrantis Works at Hollinwood—a trip will be arranged for members to go by char-a-banc to Hollinwood from Chester.
It is hoped to have a membership of at least a hundred for our first Annual Luncheon, to be held in October.

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o Ingleby Motors, Ltd., Sweet Street, Leeds.
The Leeds and West Riding Branch has now closed down for the summer months, after having had an inter-esting and varied programme of Lectures and Visits during the past winter session.
Among the visits was a tour round the Neo Electric Lamp Works, Leeds, where the members were amazed to see how much goes to the making of an electric bulb. Each process, from the furnace and blowing of bulbs to the testing, sealing and packing of the lamps, was intensely interesting.
In March, Mr. S. C. Hurry, of London, gave a very good lecture and demonstration on "Electric Water Heat-ing," which was most appropriate and useful to the mem-bers in view of the coming summer months.
In April, Mr. Harry Moss, A.M.I.E.E., of Bradford, spoke on "Some more things you should know about your Wiring Installations," this being a continuation of a popular lecture he gave last year. The members very much enjoyed this address, and the useful hints Mr. Moss gave were much appreciated.
It is hoped a number of our members will be able to go to Newcastle to the Conference in July, which promises to be a great success and far too big a treat to miss.

The Electrical Age

Rugby Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss N. Pedler,
Electricity Showrooms, Little Church Street, Rugby.
A party of members of the Rugby Branch were the guests of the Warwickshire Coal Co. when they paid a visit to the Keresley Coal Mine on March 20th. The party motored over to Keresley and were met by Mr. Jackson, the General Manager. After an exceedingly interesting tour round, which included a descent into the pit, members were entertained to tea.
A talk on Radio, by Mr. B. Gambrell, of the British Thomson Houston Co., Ltd., which was arranged for March 14th, had to be postponed owing to the illness of Mr. Gambrell, who has, however, kindly promised to give the talk in October next.
On April 10th a small but enthusiastic party of members attended the very enjoyable One-Day Conference and Luncheon held in London.
During the same month Mr. J. L. H. Cooper, of the E.L.M.A. Lighting Service Bureau, gave a most helpful talk on The Decorative Value of Light in the Home. This was accompanied by various illuminating demonstrations, and proved to be a popular subject.
The English Electric Works at Rugby were visited by a large party of members on May 15th. Mr. A. R. Law, the General Manager, very kindly gave a talk the previous evening, giving us, with the help of diagrams and models, a wonderfully clear idea of the construction of steam and water turbines and oil engines, which, he explained to the visitors, were the three prime movers in the generation of electricity. The following afternoon we spent a most interesting time in the works, seeing the various turbines in process of construction, and concluded our visit with tea.
We are now looking forward to the Newcastle Conference next month and to the very full programme which is being arranged.

North Staffordshire Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries:
Miss D. Bentley, Mrs. E. M. Yeaman,
52, Georges Chambers, Kingsway, Stoke-on-Trent.
The second meeting of the North Staffs Branch was held on March 20th, when about 30 members visited the Central Power House of the Stoke-on-Trent Corporation. After Alderman Leese, J.P. (Chairman of the Electricity Supply Committee) had welcomed the members, Mr. C. H. Yeaman, City Electrical Engineer, outlined the history and development of electricity supply in the Five Towns. At the close of the tour of the Power House tea was served to those present.
On April 18th the members had the privilege of hearing Mr. G. S. Francis, of the E.D.A., lecture on Domestic Electrification. He dealt with the applications of electricity in the home in a particularly interesting manner.
At the close of the lecture the meeting was declared open to discussion, and various members asked questions, to which the lecturer replied at some length.
A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Francis, and the wish was expressed that he might pay another visit to Stoke next year.
A particularly interesting feature was that on May 10th, when the members of the Branch visited the world famous pottery works of Messrs. Josiah Wedgwood & Sons, at Etruria. The party was conducted over the works and saw the various processes in the manufacture of the Wedgwood ware. The special interest attaching to this visit lay in the fact that Messrs. Wedgwood have an electric kiln in use, one of the first to be installed in connection with the manufacture of pottery.
A number of new members have been obtained and the meetings of the local branch appear to prove of considerable interest.

523
Swansea and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. O. Davies,
5, Eden Avenue, Uplands, Swansea.
All our meetings have been very well attended, and members are showing great interest.
A most instructive and interesting meeting was held on March 6th, when Mr. H. G. Davies, of the Corporation Electricity Department, gave a talk and demonstration on "Home Repairs of Electrical Appliances." The members have asked for this talk to be repeated next season.
On March 20th, by the kind permission of Mr. J. W. Burr, Borough Electrical Engineer, the members paid a visit to the Automative sub-station supplying power to the new Mumbles Electric Railway, where a demonstration was given of the operation of this sub-station. We were very impressed by the almost superhuman operation of the various switches and other apparatus.
At the April meeting, Mr. G. S. Francis, of E.D.A., delivered a very interesting lecture on "Modern Tendencies in Architectural, Furnishing and Lighting Design, and the Part Electricity Plays Therein." This lecture was greatly appreciated by all those present, and a hope was expressed that Mr. Francis would be able to give us another lecture during the Autumn session.
The last meeting for this session took the form of a lecture and demonstration on "Refrigeration."
We propose holding a Summer Meeting, but the arrangements for this have yet to be made.
***
Mid-Gloucestershire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss G. Johnson,
21, Eastgate Street, Gloucester.
Since our Inaugural Meeting on February 20th and the visit reported in the last journal, we have had a varied and interesting programme.
March 22nd.—Mr. Parsons, A.M.I.E.E., of Gloucester, gave a very interesting lecture-demonstration on "Bells and Indicators," in which he pointed out the simple adjustments necessary to put a faulty bell in order, and where and how to look for the trouble.
April 18th.—A fair number of members was able to attend the Luncheon and Ball at the Hotel Cecil. The visit to Messrs. Belling & Co.s Works during the afternoon was also much enjoyed.
April 19th.—Some of the artistic possibilities of Electric Light in modern civic and commercial, as well as in the home, were illustrated in the course of an instructive Lantern Lecture entitled "Modern Tendencies in Architectural Furnishing and Lighting Design, and the Part Electricity Plays Therein," by Mr. G. S. Francis, of the British Electrical Development Association.
April 26th.—By kind invitation of Edison Swan Cables, Ltd., we spent a delightful afternoon at their Lydbrook Cable Works. We received a very cordial welcome from Mr. Gait, Works Manager, on behalf of the Directors, before the party was divided into groups and proceeded to tour the Works, where rubber in its crude state is put through different processes; members were also interested in the various kinds of wire, which make up the cables.
Tea was kindly provided by the Company, and we were interested to learn that we were the first Branch of the E.A.W. to visit Lydbrook Cable Works.
May 17th.—Mr. S. C. Hurry, of the Jackson Electric Stove Co., gave a very interesting talk on the Electric Cooker, and the advantages of Electric Cooking. The questions and discussion which followed proved most instructive.
G. JOHNSON.
***
Bristol and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. R. Wright, A.C.I.S.,
Electricity Offices, Colston Avenue, Bristol.
The newly formed Bristol and District Branch believes in making a good beginning.
Its first meeting took the form of a Lantern Lecture, illustrating the important part played by Electricity in Modern Architecture, given by a representative of the British Electrical Development Association.
On April 25th members visited the Bristol Showrooms of Messrs. Electrolux, Ltd., where a highly interesting Lecture-Demonstration on Food Preservation was given.
The E.A.W. has wide interests, and Wednesday, May 22nd saw about 40 members en route for the Bristol Aeroplane Works, at Filton. By the kindness of the Directors, the visitors were piloted "behind the scenes" of one of our most modern industries, and witnessed the making of an aeroplane from the first stages to the finished machine.
One of the most notable of the future activities of the Branch is its forthcoming visit to Cardiff on June 19th, when a Civic Reception by the Lord Mayor has been arranged, to be followed by a visit to the new showrooms of the General Electric Company.
M. J. WELSHMAN.
***
London Activities.
The One-Day Conference in London on April 18th was a great success, and all the Branches, north, south, east and west, were represented.
At the meeting in the morning, presided over by Mrs. Hammer, the Director gave a report of the Associations work and progress in the past year, and the Branch Secretaries reported on the activities in their various centres. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Branches by Lady Swaythling and Mrs. Atchison.
Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, President, received the guests at the Luncheon, and presided over a gathering of nearly 400 people.
We were honoured to have as our Speakers Sir John Snell, G.B.E., Lieut.-Col. K. Edgcumbe, R.E., and The Lady Emmott, J.P.
After Luncheon, about 120 members and guests took advantage of the kind invitation of Mr. Belling and Mr. Arnold and visited their "M.K." works, at Edmonton, where "outlets" are made, and the Belling works, at Enfield, where Cookers, Fires and Water Heaters were seen in all stages of manufacture.
Motor coaches were kindly provided by Mr. Belling, and a very welcome tea was served in the Electric Canteen.
Mr. Belling welcomed the party, and gave a short account of the growth and development of the works, and a hearty vote of thanks was awarded him, his company and his staff, on the motion of Councillor Mrs. Gregory and Mrs. Hayes.
In the evening, the E.A.W. held its second Ball, when Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley again received the guests, numbering over 300.
The music was supplied by Reg. Battens Band, and the Martinoka Rag Doll Dancers, gave a novel and clever entertainment.
Both the Luncheon and Ball were held at the Hotel Cecil, and everyone voted the whole day as very enjoyable and a complete success.
Our Summer Programme opened with a Social Afternoon at the Club Room, on May 8th.
On May 29th, Mrs. Dover, B.Sc. (London), a member of the E.A.W., gave a Lecture-Demonstration on a type of cooker new to this country. This created so much interest that Mrs. Dovers Lecture is reproduced elsewhere in the Journal.
The Womens Day at the I.M.E.A. Convention at Torquay was on June 6th, and many members took part.
In the morning, Miss M. Partridge, B.Sc., gave a Lecture on "Womens Work in Connection with Rural Electrification in Devonshire." Mrs. Nithsdale-Moore presided, and a vote of thanks was proposed by Mrs. Beale, President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch, seconded by Lady Snell.
During the afternoon an interesting visit was paid to the Longpark Pottery Company, which is run electrically, and every member of the party was presented with a charming souvenir.
The party was then taken to Watcombe-in-the-Moor, where tea was served, via Bovey Tracey and Hay Tor Rocks, returning to Torquay via Ashburton.
Our last fixture was our Summer Outing, when we spent a most happy and interesting day through the kindness of our Ashford and District Branch, on Wednesday, June 12th.

Electricity Offices, Colston Avenue, Bristol.
The newly formed Bristol and District Branch believes in making a good beginning.
Its first meeting took the form of a Lantern Lecture, illustrating the important part played by Electricity in Modern Architecture, given by a representative of the British Electrical Development Association.
On April 25th members visited the Bristol Showrooms of Messrs. Electrolux, Ltd., where a highly interesting Lecture-Demonstration on Food Preservation was given.
The E.A.W. has wide interests, and Wednesday, May 22nd saw about 40 members en route for the Bristol Aeroplane Works, at Filton. By the kindness of the Directors, the visitors were piloted "behind the scenes" of one of our most modern industries, and witnessed the making of an aeroplane from the first stages to the finished machine.
One of the most notable of the future activities of the Branch is its forthcoming visit to Cardiff on June 19th, when a Civic Reception by the Lord Mayor has been arranged, to be followed by a visit to the new showrooms of the General Electric Company.
M. J. WELSHMAN.
***
London Activities.
The One-Day Conference in London on April 18th was a great success, and all the Branches, north, south, east and west, were represented.
At the meeting in the morning, presided over by Mrs. Hammer, the Director gave a report of the Associations work and progress in the past year, and the Branch Secretaries reported on the activities in their various centres. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Branches by Lady Swaythling and Mrs. Atchison.
Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, President, received the guests at the Luncheon, and presided over a gathering of nearly 400 people.
We were honoured to have as our Speakers Sir John Snell, G.B.E., Lieut.-Col. K. Edgcumbe, R.E., and The Lady Emmott, J.P.
After Luncheon, about 120 members and guests took advantage of the kind invitation of Mr. Belling and Mr. Arnold and visited their "M.K." works, at Edmonton, where "outlets" are made, and the Belling works, at Enfield, where Cookers, Fires and Water Heaters were seen in all stages of manufacture.
Motor coaches were kindly provided by Mr. Belling, and a very welcome tea was served in the Electric Canteen.
Mr. Belling welcomed the party, and gave a short account of the growth and development of the works, and a hearty vote of thanks was awarded him, his company and his staff, on the motion of Councillor Mrs. Gregory and Mrs. Hayes.
In the evening, the E.A.W. held its second Ball, when Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley again received the guests, numbering over 300.
The music was supplied by Reg. Battens Band, and the Martinoka Rag Doll Dancers, gave a novel and clever entertainment.
Both the Luncheon and Ball were held at the Hotel Cecil, and everyone voted the whole day as very enjoyable and a complete success.
Our Summer Programme opened with a Social Afternoon at the Club Room, on May 8th.
On May 29th, Mrs. Dover, B.Sc. (London), a member of the E.A.W., gave a Lecture-Demonstration on a type of cooker new to this country. This created so much interest that Mrs. Dovers Lecture is reproduced elsewhere in the Journal.
The Womens Day at the I.M.E.A. Convention at Torquay was on June 6th, and many members took part.
In the morning, Miss M. Partridge, B.Sc., gave a Lecture on "Womens Work in Connection with Rural Electrification in Devonshire." Mrs. Nithsdale-Moore presided, and a vote of thanks was proposed by Mrs. Beale, President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch, seconded by Lady Snell.
During the afternoon an interesting visit was paid to the Longpark Pottery Company, which is run electrically, and every member of the party was presented with a charming souvenir.
The party was then taken to Watcombe-in-the-Moor, where tea was served, via Bovey Tracey and Hay Tor Rocks, returning to Torquay via Ashburton.
Our last fixture was our Summer Outing, when we spent a most happy and interesting day through the kindness of our Ashford and District Branch, on Wednesday, June 12th.

Francis, of E.D.A., delivered a very interesting lecture on "Modern Tendencies in Architectural, Furnishing and Lighting Design, and the Part Electricity Plays Therein." The last meeting for this session took the form of a lecture and demonstration on "Refrigeration."
We propose holding a Summer Meeting, but the arrangements for this have yet to be made.
***
Mid-Gloucestershire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss G. Johnson,
21, Eastgate Street, Gloucester.
Since our Inaugural Meeting on February 20th and the visit reported in the last journal, we have had a varied and interesting programme.
March 22nd.—Mr. Parsons, A.M.I.E.E., of Gloucester, gave a very interesting lecture-demonstration on "Bells and Indicators," in which he pointed out the simple adjustments necessary to put a faulty bell in order, and where and how to look for the trouble.
April 18th.—A fair number of members was able to attend the Luncheon and Ball at the Hotel Cecil. The visit to Messrs. Belling & Co.s Works during the afternoon was also much enjoyed.
April 19th.—Some of the artistic possibilities of Electric Light in modern civic and commercial, as well as in the home, were illustrated in the course of an instructive Lantern Lecture entitled "Modern Tendencies in Architectural Furnishing and Lighting Design, and the Part Electricity Plays Therein," by Mr. G. S. Francis, of the British Electrical Development Association.
April 26th.—By kind invitation of Edison Swan Cables, Ltd., we spent a delightful afternoon at their Lydbrook Cable Works. We received a very cordial welcome from Mr. Gait, Works Manager, on behalf of the Directors, before the party was divided into groups and proceeded to tour the Works, where rubber in its crude state is put through different processes; members were also interested in the various kinds of wire, which make up the cables.
Tea was kindly provided by the Company, and we were interested to learn that we were the first Branch of the E.A.W. to visit Lydbrook Cable Works.
May 17th.—Mr. S. C. Hurry, of the Jackson Electric Stove Co., gave a very interesting talk on the Electric Cooker, and the advantages of Electric Cooking. The questions and discussion which followed proved most instructive.
G. JOHNSON.

During the afternoon an interesting visit was paid to the Longpark Pottery Company, which is run electrically, and every member of the party was presented with a charming souvenir.
The party was then taken to Watcombe-in-the-Moor, where tea was served, via Bovey Tracey and Hay Tor Rocks, returning to Torquay via Ashburton.
Our last fixture was our Summer Outing, when we spent a most happy and interesting day through the kindness of our Ashford and District Branch, on Wednesday, June 12th.

Electricity Offices, Colston Avenue, Bristol.
The newly formed Bristol and District Branch believes in making a good beginning.
Its first meeting took the form of a Lantern Lecture, illustrating the important part played by Electricity in Modern Architecture, given by a representative of the British Electrical Development Association.
On April 25th members visited the Bristol Showrooms of Messrs. Electrolux, Ltd., where a highly interesting Lecture-Demonstration on Food Preservation was given.
The E.A.W. has wide interests, and Wednesday, May 22nd saw about 40 members en route for the Bristol Aeroplane Works, at Filton. By the kindness of the Directors, the visitors were piloted "behind the scenes" of one of our most modern industries, and witnessed the making of an aeroplane from the first stages to the finished machine.
One of the most notable of the future activities of the Branch is its forthcoming visit to Cardiff on June 19th, when a Civic Reception by the Lord Mayor has been arranged, to be followed by a visit to the new showrooms of the General Electric Company.
M. J. WELSHMAN.
***
London Activities.
The One-Day Conference in London on April 18th was a great success, and all the Branches, north, south, east and west, were represented.
At the meeting in the morning, presided over by Mrs. Hammer, the Director gave a report of the Associations work and progress in the past year, and the Branch Secretaries reported on the activities in their various centres. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Branches by Lady Swaythling and Mrs. Atchison.
Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, President, received the guests at the Luncheon, and presided over a gathering of nearly 400 people.
We were honoured to have as our Speakers Sir John Snell, G.B.E., Lieut.-Col. K. Edgcumbe, R.E., and The Lady Emmott, J.P.
After Luncheon, about 120 members and guests took advantage of the kind invitation of Mr. Belling and Mr. Arnold and visited their "M.K." works, at Edmonton, where "outlets" are made, and the Belling works, at Enfield, where Cookers, Fires and Water Heaters were seen in all stages of manufacture.
Motor coaches were kindly provided by Mr. Belling, and a very welcome tea was served in the Electric Canteen.
Mr. Belling welcomed the party, and gave a short account of the growth and development of the works, and a hearty vote of thanks was awarded him, his company and his staff, on the motion of Councillor Mrs. Gregory and Mrs. Hayes.
In the evening, the E.A.W. held its second Ball, when Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley again received the guests, numbering over 300.
The music was supplied by Reg. Battens Band, and the Martinoka Rag Doll Dancers, gave a novel and clever entertainment.
Both the Luncheon and Ball were held at the Hotel Cecil, and everyone voted the whole day as very enjoyable and a complete success.
Our Summer Programme opened with a Social Afternoon at the Club Room, on May 8th.
On May 29th, Mrs. Dover, B.Sc. (London), a member of the E.A.W., gave a Lecture-Demonstration on a type of cooker new to this country. This created so much interest that Mrs. Dovers Lecture is reproduced elsewhere in the Journal.
The Womens Day at the I.M.E.A. Convention at Torquay was on June 6th, and many members took part.
In the morning, Miss M. Partridge, B.Sc., gave a Lecture on "Womens Work in Connection with Rural Electrification in Devonshire." Mrs. Nithsdale-Moore presided, and a vote of thanks was proposed by Mrs. Beale, President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch, seconded by Lady Snell.
During the afternoon an interesting visit was paid to the Longpark Pottery Company, which is run electrically, and every member of the party was presented with a charming souvenir.
The party was then taken to Watcombe-in-the-Moor, where tea was served, via Bovey Tracey and Hay Tor Rocks, returning to Torquay via Ashburton.
Our last fixture was our Summer Outing, when we spent a most happy and interesting day through the kindness of our Ashford and District Branch, on Wednesday, June 12th.

Swansea and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. O. Davies,
5, Eden Avenue, Uplands, Swansea.
All our meetings have been very well attended, and members are showing great interest.
A most instructive and interesting meeting was held on March 6th, when Mr. H. G. Davies, of the Corporation Electricity Department, gave a talk and demonstration on "Home Repairs of Electrical Appliances." The members have asked for this talk to be repeated next season.
On March 20th, by the kind permission of Mr. J. W. Burr, Borough Electrical Engineer, the members paid a visit to the Automative sub-station supplying power to the new Mumbles Electric Railway, where a demonstration was given of the operation of this sub-station. We were very impressed by the almost superhuman operation of the various switches and other apparatus.
At the April meeting, Mr. G. S. Francis, of E.D.A., delivered a very interesting lecture on "Modern Tendencies in Architectural, Furnishing and Lighting Design, and the Part Electricity Plays Therein." This lecture was greatly appreciated by all those present, and a hope was expressed that Mr. Francis would be able to give us another lecture during the Autumn session.
The last meeting for this session took the form of a lecture and demonstration on "Refrigeration."
We propose holding a Summer Meeting, but the arrangements for this have yet to be made.
***
Mid-Gloucestershire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss G. Johnson,
21, Eastgate Street, Gloucester.
Since our Inaugural Meeting on February 20th and the visit reported in the last journal, we have had a varied and interesting programme.
March 22nd.—Mr. Parsons, A.M.I.E.E., of Gloucester, gave a very interesting lecture-demonstration on "Bells and Indicators," in which he pointed out the simple adjustments necessary to put a faulty bell in order, and where and how to look for the trouble.
April 18th.—A fair number of members was able to attend the Luncheon and Ball at the Hotel Cecil. The visit to Messrs. Belling & Co.s Works during the afternoon was also much enjoyed.
April 19th.—Some of the artistic possibilities of Electric Light in modern civic and commercial, as well as in the home, were illustrated in the course of an instructive Lantern Lecture entitled "Modern Tendencies in Architectural Furnishing and Lighting Design, and the Part Electricity Plays Therein," by Mr. G. S. Francis, of the British Electrical Development Association.
April 26th.—By kind invitation of Edison Swan Cables, Ltd., we spent a delightful afternoon at their Lydbrook Cable Works. We received a very cordial welcome from Mr. Gait, Works Manager, on behalf of the Directors, before the party was divided into groups and proceeded to tour the Works, where rubber in its crude state is put through different processes; members were also interested in the various kinds of wire, which make up the cables.
Tea was kindly provided by the Company, and we were interested to learn that we were the first Branch of the E.A.W. to visit Lydbrook Cable Works.
May 17th.—Mr. S. C. Hurry, of the Jackson Electric Stove Co., gave a very interesting talk on the Electric Cooker, and the advantages of Electric Cooking. The questions and discussion which followed proved most instructive.
G. JOHNSON.

Hon. Secretary: Miss G. Johnson,
21, Eastgate Street, Gloucester.

S. Francis, of the British Electrical Development Association.

By the kindness of the Directors, the visitors were piloted "behind the scenes" of one of our most modern industries, and witnessed the making of an aeroplane from the first stages to the finished machine.

M. J. WELSHMAN.
***
London Activities.
The One-Day Conference in London on April 18th was a great success, and all the Branches, north, south, east and west, were represented.
At the meeting in the morning, presided over by Mrs. Hammer, the Director gave a report of the Associations work and progress in the past year, and the Branch Secretaries reported on the activities in their various centres. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Branches by Lady Swaythling and Mrs. Atchison.
Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, President, received the guests at the Luncheon, and presided over a gathering of nearly 400 people.
We were honoured to have as our Speakers Sir John Snell, G.B.E., Lieut.-Col. K. Edgcumbe, R.E., and The Lady Emmott, J.P.
After Luncheon, about 120 members and guests took advantage of the kind invitation of Mr. Belling and Mr. Arnold and visited their "M.K." works, at Edmonton, where "outlets" are made, and the Belling works, at Enfield, where Cookers, Fires and Water Heaters were seen in all stages of manufacture.
Motor coaches were kindly provided by Mr. Belling, and a very welcome tea was served in the Electric Canteen.
Mr. Belling welcomed the party, and gave a short account of the growth and development of the works, and a hearty vote of thanks was awarded him, his company and his staff, on the motion of Councillor Mrs. Gregory and Mrs. Hayes.
In the evening, the E.A.W. held its second Ball, when Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley again received the guests, numbering over 300.
The music was supplied by Reg. Battens Band, and the Martinoka Rag Doll Dancers, gave a novel and clever entertainment.
Both the Luncheon and Ball were held at the Hotel Cecil, and everyone voted the whole day as very enjoyable and a complete success.
Our Summer Programme opened with a Social Afternoon at the Club Room, on May 8th.
On May 29th, Mrs. Dover, B.Sc. (London), a member of the E.A.W., gave a Lecture-Demonstration on a type of cooker new to this country. This created so much interest that Mrs. Dovers Lecture is reproduced elsewhere in the Journal.
The Womens Day at the I.M.E.A. Convention at Torquay was on June 6th, and many members took part.
In the morning, Miss M. Partridge, B.Sc., gave a Lecture on "Womens Work in Connection with Rural Electrification in Devonshire." Mrs. Nithsdale-Moore presided, and a vote of thanks was proposed by Mrs. Beale, President of the Birmingham and Midlands Branch, seconded by Lady Snell.
During the afternoon an interesting visit was paid to the Longpark Pottery Company, which is run electrically, and every member of the party was presented with a charming souvenir.
The party was then taken to Watcombe-in-the-Moor, where tea was served, via Bovey Tracey and Hay Tor Rocks, returning to Torquay via Ashburton.
Our last fixture was our Summer Outing, when we spent a most happy and interesting day through the kindness of our Ashford and District Branch, on Wednesday, June 12th.

Unnamed: 9: Met party at Maidstone; President of the Ashford Branch.
transcription:
524 The Electrical Age

The party was met at Maidstone by Mrs. Hayward and Mrs. Wilson, President and Honorary Secretary of the Ashford Branch, and were received at the Maidstone Electricity Works by Mr. E. E. Hoadley, where a short tour of the works was made.
A short halt was made for a picnic lunch in the grounds of Leeds Castle, for which special permission had been obtained.
On arriving at Ashford, the party was welcomed by Mr. Southon, Chairman of the Ashford Urban District Council, in the Council Chamber. The members then proceeded to the Electricity Works, where everyone was very much interested in the oil plant.
The various processes of generating electricity by means of oil were explained by Mr. H. L. Wilson, the Electrical Engineer, and his assistants.
An interesting experiment has been carried out in two cottages near the works, where all the heating is done by means of the waste heat from the works.
Members then went on to the home of Mr. and Mrs. Wilson, where the Ashford members had prepared a sumptuous tea. An electrical washing-up machine was fixed up in the garden to cope with the washing-up, and created considerable interest.
A vote of thanks was proposed by Mrs. Hammer and seconded by Mr. E. E. Sharp. During the afternoon an oak tree was planted by the Director of the E.A.W., and afterwards members strolled about the lovely garden, or took part in the various games provided; tennis, ping-pong, and a shooting range, and also community singing until it was time to leave for London.
All our energies are now centred on the Fourth Annual Conference at Newcastle-on-Tyne on July 10th, 11th and 12th.
Fuller particulars appear elsewhere, and it therefore only remains to add that the North-East Coast members are preparing a real North-East Coast welcome for all the delegates.
V.S.

Unnamed: 10: author of article mentioned in editorial
transcription:
EDITORIAL.
NEWCASTLE AND AFTER.—To achieve success is one thing, but to maintain that
success and even to crown it with still greater achievement is a much more difficult
matter.
Our first Annual Conference held in the Provinces proved itself to be an outstand-
ing event, not only in the history of the E.A.W., but in the Electrical World generally.
Many well-known Electrical Engineers who looked in at the Opening Session “just to
show their interest” were so impressed with the value and importance of the Papers
given that they remained during the whole of the Session, and one heard many expres-
sions of opinion that the Papers read would compare favourably with those given at any
of the Electrical Engineering Conferences during the year.
The Overseas delegates not only gave Papers full of useful and interesting informa-
tion, but earned our admiration also by their command of the English language.
The success of the Conference was undoubtedly due to the splendid enthusiasm of the
officers and members of the North-East Coast Branch and the wonderful co-operation
which they secured from the Engineers in that District.
■ ■ ■
ELECTRICITY TARIFFS is one of the most vexed questions of the day and one
which vitally affects both the Electrical Industry and the Woman Consumer.
From the woman’s point of view, she is anxious to get her Electricity at such an
economic rate as to make it possible for her to use it unstintingly in her home.
On the other hand, it is obvious, of course, that the Engineer must meet not only the
cost of supplying Electricity, but capital and plant costs.
It would seem, however, that the Electrical Supply Industry would find it much more
profitable to sell a lot of electricity at a low price rather than a small amount at a high
price:—an economic fact discovered by many of our successful Trading Concerns.
In order to give our readers some idea of the economic problems underlying this sub-
ject we are publishing an article by Miss Margaret Partridge, B.Sc., A.M.I.E.E., which
deals with the matter in very simple everyday language.
It is our intention later on that meetings shall be held throughout the E.A.W.
Organisation, in order that the woman’s point of view can be expressed on the subject.
■ ■ ■
AN ELECTRICAL PLAY has been written for the E.A.W., and will be acted in
London and throughout the Branches during the coming year.
The chief feature of the E.A.W. work has been to interpret the vast field of Elec-
trical knowledge and achievement into the simple language which can be understood by
the “man in the street,” or, perhaps more accurately in this instance, by “the woman
in the home.”
Up to the present time this work has been carried out by means of lectures and visits
to places of electrical interest. Now, however, it is intended to embark on an entirely
new and novel form of education, through the medium of the stage.
The Autumn will also see a renewal of meetings and discussions arranged on
the important subject of Electricity in the Schools. As Dr. Ferranti stated at the recent
Deputation to the Board of Education:—“With the introduction of Wireless and Mechani-
cal and Electrical Labour-Saving Appliances in the Home, it is necessary to give girls
during their school life some idea of what Electricity is, what it can do, and how it works,
in order to clear away the mystery which generally surrounds everything electrical.”
528

Unnamed: 9: Secretary of Cheltenham Branch resigning to move to America.
transcription:
530 The Electrical Age

is knocked down, and fittings are spoilt by unsympathetic plumbers. She expects similar disorganisation of her house by an electrical contractor. The question of cost, which she imagines to be prohibitive, convinces her that electricity is not worth the trouble, and until fairly recently she was right.
Several well-known electrical manufacturers, however, realised these difficulties and designed systems known as "Surface Wiring." The basic idea underlying all these systems was the same, viz. :-that of providing a wiring system which could be put into an existing house with the minimum of cost and disturbance to decorations. The ideal elaborated from this basic idea called for a system which would be inconspicuous and neat, and at the same time efficient. This left but two alternatives: an extremely small and compact system, or a system which would harmonise with existing decorations. The first alternative has disadvantages: these are of a purely technical nature and we will not discuss them here. It has been realised that a far more efficient system may be evolved from the second principle, and in this connection the new "Ediswan" system is particularly attractive.
In this system the wires are laid behind wood channelling of ingenious design. This channelling is finished to match the decorations, and, lying flat against the wall, it is completely dust-proof. No external holding clips are visible, and unless you are looking for it, it will pass unnoticed. The accessories connected with this system, switches, ceiling roses, etc., are moulded in bakelite, and contrast very favourably with the wood blocks and ugly porcelain ceiling roses which have hitherto been employed in house wiring. The "Ediswan" ceiling rose is particularly worthy of note, as the whole fitting stands only about an inch from the ceiling and embodies a loose cord grip of exceptional strength.
With such systems available we anticipate that the householder will be far readier to consider the installation of electricity. The importance of these new systems is paramount when it is realised that they will be the means of creating a large number of new "Outlets" for using all kinds of labour-saving appliances.

MISS A. A. STEMP,
who has been the Secretary of our Cheltenham Branch since its inception, has resigned owing to her departure to America. Miss Stemp has proved herself in every way to be an ideal Branch Secretary, and it is a great loss both to the E.A.W. and the Cheltenham Branch that she has decided to go to America. However, we wish her a happy and interesting time and that she will soon come back again to this country. Miss D. Blaker has been appointed as Honorary Secretary in her place.
Miss C. Haslett has been appointed to represent the E.A.W. on the Conference on Electricity Supply in Rural Areas, convened by the Electricity Commissioners.
Miss A. A. Stemp.

Unnamed: 9: Author of the article discussing the history of sewing machines.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 531
Sewing by Electricity
By . . .
"Haselwurr."
Since our early childhood we have all been familiar with the sight of the Sewing Machine in the Home. In this article a fascinating picture is given of the history of the Sewing Machine, and how Electricity has stepped in to save labour and increase efficiency.
Like most discoveries, including Electricity, the Sewing Machine has a history which is as full of interest and of romance as any story book can tell, recounting the efforts of men of genius who spent their lives in giving the world something which would lighten toil and fatigue, and add to the comfort and happiness of all.
The pioneers of the Sewing Machine invention had little encouragement during their struggles and toil in obscurity, and often in great poverty they pursued their tasks, meeting and overcoming many obstacles; suffering also acute disappointments, but continuing undaunted because they had faith in their idea.
Fig. 1. Original type of Sewing Machine used in the middle of the nineteenth century
The growth of the Sewing Machine industry can perhaps be better realised when I tell you that whereas in 1853, or about two years after the first Singer Machine was patented, the total world sales of all makes of Sewing Machines were 2,500; at the present time well over 2,000,000 Singer Sewing Machines alone are being sold every year. It can, therefore, be justly claimed that the Singer invention has probably done more to reduce the drudgery of manual labour, and at the same time has rendered service and benefit to womankind, greater than any other single invention.
Great inventions have usually been the products of slow growth and gradual development, and the Sewing Machine is no exception to the rule, hence the long lapse of years before the introduction of the Electric Sewing Machine.
In the early stages of the first successful Sewing Machine there was bitter opposition on the part of journeyman tailors to anything providing mechanical sewing, who denounced the machine as an invasion of their rights, but I venture to say that it would be a strange world to-day if there were no Sewing Machines available for the making up of clothing, to say nothing of the many uses of the Sewing Machine in other directions. For instance, has it ever occurred to you the important part the Sewing Machine played in the Great War? Apart from the colossal amount of Army clothing and the soldiers equipment generally, think of the stitching together of tents for the battle-fields, aeroplane wings, airship covers, harness for horses, to name but a few of the hundred and one things that could not

Unnamed: 9: At the outset Mr. Singer had a hard struggle.
transcription:
532
The Electrical Age
have been provided to the extent they were but for the Sewing Machine.
Think, again, of all the hundreds of thousands of people whose sole existence depends upon constructing the Machine, shipping it, selling it, and working it, and with this thought in mind no one to-day could denounce the Machine as an unwanted invasion.
At the outset Mr. Singer had a hard struggle, and you can well imagine that he had to contend with considerable prejudice; consequently discouragements and disappointments met him at every turn, but, notwithstanding, he carried on determinedly, and slowly gained ground after he successfully produced a continuous stitching machine. That machine, however, could only be operated at from 100 to 200 stitches per minute, whereas to-day the speed of a power driven machine will attain over 4,000 stitches per minute, nearly 70 stitches per second. Even the machine you now work in your homes can, with the aid of an electric motor, account for upwards of 1,000 stitches per minute. Thus you can visualise the developments the building and perfecting of the Sewing Machine have gone through, but your conception of all its evolutions would not be complete without my telling you that at the present time the Singer Company make no less than 2,000 different varieties to fill the wants of different trades, ranging, for instance, from the making of the finest silk gowns to those of cotton and wool. Leather, canvas and rubber goods, in all their forms, are manipulated and stitched, and even the asbestos fireproof curtains, used in theatres, are stitched with asbestos thread. Paper, too, in all forms, from a pamphlet to a book, is stitched on a Singer; and, to refer to a remarkable contract, the copper brushes used in Electrical Dynamos are stitched with copper wire by the Singer Machine.
You will understand now that the ordinary family Sewing Machine is but a "drop in the ocean," so to speak, but nevertheless it fills an important role in the whole world of home sewing. It, in itself, has had many evolutions and developments, being first built in the form shown in Fig. 1, placed upon a sort of packing case, and operated by the feet with a long stick attached to heavy cogwheels, which you can imagine produced an almost unbearable noise. I might add that that case was then described as a cabinet, but which is not, I think you will agree, a very pleasing piece of furniture for the sitting room.
Fig. 2. A modern machine operated by a small electric motor which can attain 1,000 stitches per minute, as compared with the early foot-operated machines, which only attained 100/200 stitches per minute.
During the course of the last 50 years there have been many changes in the construction and style of woodwork. The present types of machine are practically noiseless in operation, speedy up to nearly 1,000 stitches per minute, and can be worked by foot motion or by electricity at a cost per hour cheaper than any other electrically driven home device.

Thus you can visualise the developments the building and perfecting of the Sewing Machine have gone through, but your conception of all its evolutions would not be complete without my telling you that at the present time the Singer Company make no less than 2,000 different varieties to fill the wants of different trades, ranging, for instance, from the making of the finest silk gowns to those of cotton and wool. Leather, canvas and rubber goods, in all their forms, are manipulated and stitched, and even the asbestos fireproof curtains, used in theatres, are stitched with asbestos thread. Paper, too, in all forms, from a pamphlet to a book, is stitched on a Singer; and, to refer to a remarkable contract, the copper brushes used in Electrical Dynamos are stitched with copper wire by the Singer Machine.
You will understand now that the ordinary family Sewing Machine is but a "drop in the ocean," so to speak, but nevertheless it fills an important role in the whole world of home sewing. It, in itself, has had many evolutions and developments, being first built in the form shown in Fig. 1, placed upon a sort of packing case, and operated by the feet with a long stick attached to heavy cogwheels, which you can imagine produced an almost unbearable noise. I might add that that case was then described as a cabinet, but which is not, I think you will agree, a very pleasing piece of furniture for the sitting room.
Fig. 2. A modern machine operated by a small electric motor which can attain 1,000 stitches per minute, as compared with the early foot-operated machines, which only attained 100/200 stitches per minute.
During the course of the last 50 years there have been many changes in the construction and style of woodwork. The present types of machine are practically noiseless in operation, speedy up to nearly 1,000 stitches per minute, and can be worked by foot motion or by electricity at a cost per hour cheaper than any other electrically driven home device.

transcription:
534
The Electrical Age
THE NEWCASTLE CONFERENCE.
The fourth Annual Conference of the E.A.W., which was held at the North-East Coast Exhibition, Newcastle-on-Tyne, during July, is a memory which will linger long in the minds of all those people who were present.
In addition to the serious side of the Conference, the social side was full of variety and charm. The Lord and Lady Mayoress of Newcastle-on-Tyne were ungrudging in the time and hospitality which they placed at the disposal of the guests.
The Exhibition Authorities, too, showed in a very practical way their pleasure at having a Women’s Conference at the Exhibition.
The Dinner, arranged by the local Branch, at the conclusion of the Conference created just that feeling of goodwill and happiness which made everyone feel how very worth while it had been to journey to Newcastle.
For those who were able to spend the week-end, however, the arrangements made by Mr. R. P. Sloan and the Directors of the Newcastle-on-Tyne Electric Supply Co., proved to be of more than exceptional interest and enjoyment.
On Saturday afternoon the Members visited the Roman Wall and were shown something of the charming historic side of the North-East Coast.
By courtesy of "The Electrical Review."
MISS ANNA HOLM,
the energetic Secretary of the North-East Coast Branch. We have made many attempts to secure her photograph, but without success. This snap was cleverly secured by Mrs. Llewellyn B. Atkinson while Miss Holm was resting against the Roman Wall.
The Opening Ceremony at the Festival Hall showed quite conclusively that women have a very definite contribution to make in the progress of the Domestic Uses of Electricity, not only in this country, but the world over.
By courtesy of "The Electrical Times."
Members embarking on the boats for the Farne Islands.

transcription:
The Electrical Age 535

On Sunday the visit to the Farne Islands, with their wonderful bird sanctuaries and unique history associated with Grace Darling, was an experience of a lifetime.
Although, unfortunately, the Minister of Labour, The Right Hon. Margaret Bondfield, M.P., could not be present owing to Parliamentary duties, the letter which she sent, and which Dr. Ferranti read to the Meeting, does, we feel, epitomise the object of the Association, which was successfully demonstrated during the Conference.
She says:—I am particularly disappointed that I am unable to be present, as I felt that there was so much to say on the subject of the Conference, "The Modern Development of Electricity as it Affects Women." When you consider how much of the time of the average woman is spent on tasks which, however useful and necessary they may be, are, in essence, mere drudgery and routine, it is obvious that a very great step forward could be taken towards a fuller, richer and more varied existence if science could be applied to domestic work equally with that in the factory. Electricity seems to me precisely the key that will one day unlock this door. We are still only at the beginning of its development in the home, and a vast field of experiment and achievement lies ahead. It is of the first importance that the ranks of those who are pushing forward with the development of domestic electricity should contain a due proportion of keen women. It is equally important that women in the homes should be stirred up to make the demand for this new servant to help them.

By courtesy of "Electricity."
Group of Members taken at the Festival Hall, North-East Coast Exhibition, with Mrs. Wilfred Ashley, President, in the front row.

As usual, the Press gave us their unstinted attention during the Conference, and the Members were photographed and caricatured in many interesting and amusing ways.
A full report of the Papers given by the Overseas Delegates on the Opening Day has been published by the Association and can be obtained on application to the office at the price of one shilling.

transcription:
536 The Electrical Age
A Talk on Tariffs. A Page
for Girl Guides.

The question of the different Tariffs (or methods of charging for Electricity) is one which frequently puzzles the Consumer. Many Committees have been appointed to discuss this important matter, but, so far, no National solution has been reached. As this is a subject which so vitally affects Women, and one which every Girl Guide should understand, we have asked Miss Partridge to describe the economics of the tariff problem, and, in her inimitable way, she has turned what might have been a very dull technical dissertation into an amusing dialogue. We hope Mr. George Bernard Shaw will approve of the intelligence shown by Miss " Lysistrata "!

Scene—A passage at the foot of the stairs of a new house in Upminster.
The Electric Meter, Fuseboxes, etc., are on the passage wall.
Dramatis Personæ:
Mrs. Jones - - - The Mistress of the House.
Miss Lysistrata - - Representative of the Upminster
(With apologies to G.B.S.) Electricity Supply Co.
Betty Jones - - - A Girl Guide, daughter of the house.

Miss Lysistrata has just taken the first quarters reading since the house has been occupied and duly entered up the meter card.
Mrs. Jones—Can you tell me how many units we have used this quarter?
Miss Lysistrata—Yes, you have used 1,950 units.
Mrs. Jones—Let me see, you charge 1 1/2 d. a unit for that. Betty, how much will that come to?
Betty (who always carries pencil and paper)—£12 3s. 9d.
Mrs. Jones—That doesnt seem much, considering that there have been seven of us at home most of the time, and all the cooking and washing to do, and fires in all the rooms except the drawing room.
Miss Lysistrata—Yes, but you have also a flat rate charge of £3, which will make the total cost come to £15 3s. 9d.
Mrs. Jones (not so pleased)—I see, however, even that is less than we paid last year at Downminster. But there we had two meters, one for light and one for power. Why was that?
Betty—Yes, and they charged us ever so much more for light than they did for cooking. Is it because it costs more to make light than it does to make heat, or is the electricity really the same for both?
Miss Lysistrata—The electricity is really exactly the same. It is only a different kind of tariff. You see, in making a charge for the current you use the Electricity Company has to consider two things. First, that they have spent about £200 on your behalf on generating plant and cable, and so on, to give you the supply, and, secondly, that every unit you use costs them some fraction of a penny in coal and oil. Then, too, there are the wages of the men in the power station, and my wages, and other similar expenses, which altogether are called working costs. The total working costs of this Company work out at 1 1/2 d. a unit, so that is the rate you are charged for current sold. It just covers the coal and oil and wages, and such like. Then the £3 a quarter, which is charged you, according to the rateable value of the house, is your proportion to pay the interest

As this is a subject which so vitally affects Women, and one which every Girl Guide should understand, we have asked Miss Partridge to describe the economics of the tariff problem, and, in her inimitable way, she has turned what might have been a very dull technical dissertation into an amusing dialogue. We hope Mr. George Bernard Shaw will approve of the intelligence shown by Miss " Lysistrata "!

Scene—A passage at the foot of the stairs of a new house in Upminster.
The Electric Meter, Fuseboxes, etc., are on the passage wall.
Dramatis Personæ:
Mrs. Jones - - - The Mistress of the House.
Miss Lysistrata - - Representative of the Upminster
(With apologies to G.B.S.) Electricity Supply Co.
Betty Jones - - - A Girl Guide, daughter of the house.

Miss Lysistrata has just taken the first quarters reading since the house has been occupied and duly entered up the meter card.
Mrs. Jones—Can you tell me how many units we have used this quarter?
Miss Lysistrata—Yes, you have used 1,950 units.
Mrs. Jones—Let me see, you charge 1 1/2 d. a unit for that. Betty, how much will that come to?
Betty (who always carries pencil and paper)—£12 3s. 9d.
Mrs. Jones—That doesnt seem much, considering that there have been seven of us at home most of the time, and all the cooking and washing to do, and fires in all the rooms except the drawing room.
Miss Lysistrata—Yes, but you have also a flat rate charge of £3, which will make the total cost come to £15 3s. 9d.
Mrs. Jones (not so pleased)—I see, however, even that is less than we paid last year at Downminster. But there we had two meters, one for light and one for power. Why was that?
Betty—Yes, and they charged us ever so much more for light than they did for cooking. Is it because it costs more to make light than it does to make heat, or is the electricity really the same for both?
Miss Lysistrata—The electricity is really exactly the same. It is only a different kind of tariff. You see, in making a charge for the current you use the Electricity Company has to consider two things. First, that they have spent about £200 on your behalf on generating plant and cable, and so on, to give you the supply, and, secondly, that every unit you use costs them some fraction of a penny in coal and oil. Then, too, there are the wages of the men in the power station, and my wages, and other similar expenses, which altogether are called working costs. The total working costs of this Company work out at 1 1/2 d. a unit, so that is the rate you are charged for current sold. It just covers the coal and oil and wages, and such like. Then the £3 a quarter, which is charged you, according to the rateable value of the house, is your proportion to pay the interest

Unnamed: 9: Discussing electricity tariffs and costs with others in dialogue.
Unnamed: 10: Character in a dialogue about electricity
transcription:
The Electrical Age 537
on all the money spent on cables and generating plant, and so on.
Mrs. Jones—That seems quite fair, and I can understand that, but I never could quite understand the two meter tariff at Downminster.
Miss Lysistrata—Well, there is some method in that, too. At Downminster you were charged 1 1/2d. for power, which covered the working cost of making the electricity, and you were charged, I think, 6d. a unit for lighting. This relatively high lighting tariff might be divided into two parts, 1 1/2d. to pay for working costs and 4 1/2d. to pay for all the money spent on cables and plant. You see, it is fairly simple for an electricity company to estimate what amount of current people are likely to use for light- ing, so that really it is nearly the same as the Upminster tariff, which we call a two- part tariff.
Betty—Are there any places where the working costs are less than they are here?
Miss Lysistrata—Oh, yes, quite a lot. In fact, there are some places where they are under a halfpenny, such as Bolton, Leeds and Sheffield, all big industrial places. There are also a lot of places where the working costs are considerably higher. Generally speaking, the smaller the place the higher the working costs.
Betty—But why, please?
Miss Lysistrata—I think you could think out some of the reasons for yourself.
Betty (thoughtfully)—Well, I suppose it takes just as clever a man to look after a little engine as it does a big one, so the wages will be about the same.
Miss Lysistrata—Thats right. Then there is another thing I think youll understand. It costs less to churn out a constant quan- tity of electricity steadily all through the day and a good part of the night than it does when you have a perpetually fluctuat- ing load. In some small towns all the plant has to be working full steam for just a few hours in the evening, when every place is lighted up, and then through the
rest of the 24 hours they still have to keep it turning round, but comparatively little electricity is used.
Mrs. Jones—Yes, I see that. Is there any other kind of tariff used in England?
Miss Lysistrata—There is one used very occasionally. Instead of having two meters you have one meter with two sets of dials. The current metered on the first set of dials is charged at a low rate and the current metered on the second set is charged at a high rate. Then for 22 hours all the current is recorded on the first set of dials, but for two hours the whole thing is switched over by a clock and the expen- sive set of dials works. This has the advantage that it makes folk more economi- cal in the evening when all the lights are on, but it is a bit difficult to explain to consumers, and the meter is expensive, so it is not a tariff worth bothering about much.
Mrs. Jones—Im always interested in costs of things and the reason why. Do you think we shall ever come to paying for electricity like we do for water—just a rate and use as much as ever we like?
Miss Lysistrata—I should think it is quite likely; in fact, the two-part tariff we use here, and in a great number of other places, is a good way on the road towards that. You see, really and truly, what current you use in a private house makes practically very little difference to the electricity company. It does cost about 1/4d. a unit in fuel for all you use, but beyond that the wages and rent and rates and capital outlay cant be reduced, because, say, you shut up your house for a month any more than the other costs of public service, police, roads, water, etc., can be reduced during the summer holidays. Many people advocate a tariff of only 1/2d. a unit with a higher standing charge.
Mrs. Jones—Which tariff do you prefer yourself?
Miss Lysistrata—Oh, I think there is a lot to be said for the two-part tariff for domes- tic supply, whether you are charged only
