Unnamed: 9: Daughter asking if her Dad committed a felony regarding electricity.
Unnamed: 10: Daughter of Mrs. Jones; Daughter of Dad
transcription:
538  The Electrical Age

½d. or 1¼d. Chiefly the advantage lies in
the use of small domestic appliances. The
little kettle, for instance, that you use by
the drawing room fire is plugged into the
same socket that you use for your standard
lamp. Now, if you were in a town like
Downminster, with its two-meter tariff, you
would be faced with a difficult problem.
Either you would have to have two outlets
by the fireplace, each wired back to a
different meter—and that might cost £1 or
£2—or if you only had one plug and that
was a lighting plug you would have to pay,
if you used the kettle, 6d. a unit for current
you were entitled to have at 1½d., or if it
were a power plug you might be tempted to
commit a felony by using it for your light.

Betty—Oh, Mum, then Im sure Dad com-
mitted a felony at Downminster that time
when he had his desk by the tall cupboard
and used the plug there for his little lamp.
Did he ought to go to prison or something?

Mrs. Jones—I suppose he did, dear. Per-
haps we had better not tell him now we are
at Upminster. He would be dreadfully
upset if he knew. Are we in any danger,
Miss Lysistrata, of committing a felony
here?

Miss Lysistrata—Oh, no. You can use
any plug for any purpose you please,
within reason. Of course, you would be
foolish if you used a 5-ampere light outlet
for your dining room fire, which is a large
one, but you would only damage your own
property if you did it, as the fittings and
cables are not large enough to carry the
current.

Mrs. Jones—I quite understand that. But
as far as the Electricity Company is con-
cerned we may use the current on our side
of the meter for any purpose we please?

Miss Lysistrata—Well, you are not allowed
to embarrass neighbouring consumers by
doing too peculiar things with your current,
making short circuits, say, or installing too
large plant ; but, as you are never likely to
do that, I think you may rest satisfied.
Remember, though, that in any case of
doubt the Electricity Company can always
help you with advice, and they are only too
ready to do so, as they want you to get the
very best service possible out of your
electricity supply.

Mrs. Jones—I am sure you have already
shown how helpful the Electricity Com-
pany can be, Miss Lysistrata, and I am
very grateful for all the information you
have given us. Good morning!

Miss Lysistrata—Good morning!
[Curtain.]

transcription:
The Electrical Age 539

USEFUL HINTS
FOR THE
HOME MAKER

By "ELECTRA."

The "Elimafuse" Small Circuit Breaker.

While we all realise the very important and necessary part which the Fuse plays in an electrical installation, we must admit that it is very trying at times when it blows and puts us in darkness or our cooker out of action just when it is required.

The appliance, the "Elimafuse," as its name implies, eliminates the need for fuses. It automatically breaks the circuit on any overload and is readjusted simply by a light finger pressure; the position of the handle or switch shows at a glance which circuit is broken. If the fault is still present, however, it will not close.

The illustration shows one type of "Elimafuse," suitable for a special appliance such as a cooker or fire.

The "Elimafuse" may be obtained for all ratings of current, from lighting to heating and cooking, and, mounted in place of any ordinary fuse-board, it is neat in appearance.

The small difference in price is more than made up by the tremendous saving in time and convenience, and one other point to be mentioned is that Insurance Companies regard it with great favour.

A Screen Fire.

In the early days of Autumn we often appreciate a small electric fire which can be switched on at odd times when it begins to get chilly, but many people dislike the appearance of a fire when it is not "on," and I am sure they would welcome the "Xeel" Screen Fire.

Showing the plaque which forms the centre medallion when this dual-appliance is used as a Screen.

It is up-to-date and attractive, and combines the efficiency of a Bowl Fire--its cheerful effect and small consumption of electricity, with an artistic Fire Screen, and the change is effected in a moment.

The "Xeel" Screen Fire may be obtained in various finishes, such as Antique Brass, Oxydised Copper and Oxydised Silver, and it is therefore easy to match any colour scheme.

She has had practical experience herself in the use of domestic electrical appliances and will be pleased to place her experience at the disposal of our readers. transcription:
540

The Electrical Age

Hints on Electric Lamps.

ANTI-GLARE LAMPS AND THEIR COST TO USE.

We have received so many requests for information about Anti-Glare Lamps and whether they are more costly to use than the ordinary clear lamps that the following notes may be of interest to other readers also.
Of all methods of illumination, it is universally agreed that where Electricity is obtainable, Electric Light far excels all others. Since the invention of the first practical electric lamp by Sir Joseph Swan, fifty years ago, we have had the carbon lamp, the metal filament vacuum lamp, and the gas-filled lamp, each one more efficient than the last both in regard to light and durability.
This bright light source, however, unless entirely screened from view, causes great discomfort and even injury to the eyes, and we complain of the " glare. " To eliminate this glare various types of obscured lamps have been devised, and a great stride forward has been made by the new " Pearl " and " Opal " lamps.
The " Pearl " lamp is frosted inside the bulb, which, while cutting out all glare, enables the outside of the bulb to remain smooth and easily cleaned.
The " Opal " lamp has a thin skin of opal glass super-imposed upon a crystal clear glass bulb. This lamp, too, has a perfectly smooth and glossy surface, and cleaning, when necessary, can be done easily with a damp cloth. The diffusion of light in an " Opal " lamp is wonderful, the whole bulb glows with an even brightness and appears to become the source of light.
There is no glare with either " Pearl " or " Opal " lamps, the sacrifice of light is almost negligible, and the mechanical strength of the lamps is not affected in any way.
And now to the question of cost. The " Pearl " lamp is the same price as the clear lamp, and the " Opal " lamp costs just a little more; but very recently further reductions have been made in the price of lamps, and if British Standard Lamps are used they have a guaranteed " life " of about one thousand hours.
Two of the popular anti-glare Lamps — the "Opal" and the "Pearl." They ensure soft, diffused light throughout the room.
In estimating how much your lamps cost to burn the following table will be found useful :
A lamp marked :
100 W. (watts) burns 10 hours for One Unit of Electricity
75 W. .. .. 13 .. .. .. .. ..
60 W. .. .. 17 .. .. .. .. ..
40 W. .. .. 25 .. .. .. .. ..
25 W. .. .. 40 .. .. .. .. ..
15 W. .. .. 67 .. .. .. .. ..
The lamps generally used for home lighting are :— " Pearl " lamps, 15, 25, 40, 60, and 100 watts, and " Opal " lamps, 40, 60, 75 and 100 watts.

Unnamed: 9: Author of the article describing a visit to glass works.
transcription:
The Electrical Age
541
Where a Fairy Tale Came True.
A Visit to the Lemington Glass Works.
By CÉCILE FRANCIS-LEWIS.
For all those who were fortunate enough to attend the Newcastle Conference there is nothing save a host of happy memories, including one which must be outstanding on account of its charm.
Let me tell you just what happened when, on the hottest of days, we visited the Lemington Glass Works. Boarding a double-decker tramcar outside the Exhibition, and endeavouring to get all the air possible, many of us were wondering as we passed through a very dreary part of the city how ever we should be able to support the heat and dust we were led to expect at the works.
The tide was low, making the river-bed look very grey as we passed along, and reflecting its drabness on the houses near. The first patch of colour was a Union Jack hanging in the centre of a strip of bunting, and we wondered why it was there. Shortly after our car stopped, and we were asked to group ourselves in front of the managers house so that a photo might be taken. All the village had turned out, and watched us with keen interest. We next visited the works proper, under the able guidance of Mr. T. W. Ferry and Mr. G. W. Barras. The entire process of the manufacture of Osram lamps, wireless valves and glass-tubes was explained, the men demonstrating each process. It was a great joy to hear all the men singing as they worked, and wonderful to think of their energy in such heat. We were so very interested in all the different things. I think we were a difficult proposition, as we "simply would not hurry." Mr. Barras, one of the finest English glass blowers, kept us spellbound whilst he blew a glass jug, complete with lip and handle, and we were only too sorry he hadnt time to blow some flowers, as he intended. Although not very ornamental, the manufacture of the pots in which the glass is melted is a very important item in connection with the successful making of glass, and it was interesting to learn that although many ways of making them have been tried, hand-made pots are still the most satisfactory. It takes nearly twelve months to build up and dry a pot, and often it will crack the first time it is heated.
We passed through the testing rooms,
By courtesy of "The Electrical Review."
A man giving a demonstration of Glass blowing for the benefit of the visitors.

transcription:
542		The Electrical Age

where the finished bulbs are examined
before they are sent out, and the show-
room, where over 300 types of Osram
lamps are displayed, ranging from 19
m/m dia. to 400 m/m dia., the larger size
being used for lighthouse and aerodrome
lighting.

Then—Hey, Presto! We were trans-
ported slap bang into Fairyland

Stepping out of the blazing sun into a
dark cavernous-looking disused Furnace
Cone we found a veritable Aladdins Cave.
It was just too wonderful. A real trans-
formation scene!

Six hundred yards of green, orange and
white material were draped to form a
tent, the centre of which was a garden
lighted with the sweetest of coloured Osram
lamps, which sent forth their bright
welcome from amongst the greenery.
Tables were laid for tea—and what a tea!
One often hears of North Country hospi-
tality, and here, indeed, was a striking
proof of it. Everyone thoroughly enjoyed
it, especially the strawberries and cream
and ices, and were very glad the cook
hadnt "washed her hands" of the whole
thing, as we heard she had threatened to
do when informed that the old Furnace
Cone, which has not been used for over
forty years, was to be used as the tea
room. After tea Mr. Ferry gave us a
short history of the works, and Mr. Barras
told us that the old Furnace Cone had
been built about 1780 by Frenchmen
brought over by the Duke of Northumber-
land, and that his own father was in
charge of the Furnace, and he had worked
in it himself as a boy. For forty years it
had been a dumping ground for all the
rubbish, and must have been an enormous
undertaking to get it clean and tidy. The

top of the Cone was open, and the cook
was afraid if it rained that everything
would be spoilt. Mr. Ferry asked each lady
to accept a souvenir of the visit, and, to
allay their curiosity, he opened two of the
parcels and showed us the contents—a
very nice morocco blotter and a red glass
flower vase made from an Osram lamp.

A vote of thanks to the Company and all
concerned for their hospitality was pro-
posed by Lady Brooks and seconded by Mr
Pinkney on behalf of his wife.

A very human touch was the welcome
given to us by the villagers. They had
(entirely on their own initiative) white-
washed their cottages and hung up the
bunting mentioned before. As I passed, a
very old woman touched my hand, and
said: "Ay, but we are glad to see yer all;
good luck to yer!" I looked up to thank
her, and saw written on a piece of brown
paper fastened to the Union Jack: "Wel-
come to the Glasswork Vistors!" Such a
welcome warms the heart, and we hope
they all enjoyed the tea they had later in
the Cone as much as we did.

August 12th, 1929, as the result of
arrangements made between The Edison

ing, Electric Refrigeration and Radio busi-

Edison Swan Electric Company, Ltd., who
will market the British Thomson-Houston
Companys products in these lines.

Unnamed: 9: Writes about autumn dishes for the electric cooker in article.
transcription:
The Electrical Age
543
Mary Mackirdy Writes about Some Autumn Dishes for the Electric Cooker.
FRUIT AND VEGETABLE DISHES.
There is a wide range of fruits and vegetables at this time, and it is well to use them, not only on account of their supply and cheapness, but for their value as food.
The more extensive use of vegetable dishes should be encouraged; so many of these are delightful for lunch or other meals, and with the addition of cheese, nuts, eggs or milk, are excellent substitutes for meat.
Vegetable cookery is a branch too often neglected in this country, and with the very great variety at our disposal this is to be deplored; the possibilities in this branch are great, but not recognised as a general rule by the cook who limits their use, only too often, as an indifferent accompaniment to a meat dish.
The chief charm of a well-cooked dish of vegetables is that it can be served alone.
Cauliflower with Braised Carrots.
The carrots may be served as a separate dish or as a garnish for the cauliflower.
Trim a good firm cauliflower and cook either by steaming or in a pan with a very little boiling water, just enough to cover well the bottom of the pan; in both cases the pan must have a close-fitting lid. When the cauliflower is tender, without being broken, put it on a hot dish, pour sauce over and garnish with the carrots or any vegetable preferred.
The sauce:—Put 1 oz. butter in a saucepan, and immediately it melts add 1 oz. flour, mix and stir in 1/2 pint milk; stir the sauce, beating it very well as it comes to boiling point. Let the sauce boil, season, take from fire and quickly stir in 1 or 2 yolks of eggs and enough lemon juice to sharpen the sauce.
The sauce may be made without yolks, and it may have the addition of some grated cheese.
Braised Carrots.
I think this is quite the nicest way to cook carrots. Prepare as many good red carrots as may be required, and cut them in strips, put into a pan with sufficient butter or margarine to cover the pan well, put a close-fitting lid on and cook, tossing them occasionally (but without taking off lid), until tender. Season and toss in some finely chopped parsley. A very little water may be added to the carrots.
If to be served without cauliflower, the carrots are delightful with tomato sauce.
Celery.
White celery cut in lengths of about 3 inches, cooked by either of the methods given for cauliflower, then served with the same sauce and garnished with poached, fried or hard-boiled eggs, is delicious as a lunch or supper dish.
Other Vegetables.
Other vegetables may be treated in the same way, and when cooked in a very small quantity of water, the water should be utilised for the sauce.
Vegetable Preserves.
Many cooks complain that vegetable preserves are not successful, but the following I consider first-rate.
Pare a marrow, cut in quarters, take out the seeds and the soft inner part, boil this and the skins with a little water for 1/2 hour, then strain. Cut the marrow in short lengths, weigh it and allow 1 lb. sugar and a half lemon to each pound of marrow, also half a teacupful of the liquid from the skins, etc. Heat the sugar, liquid, grated lemon rind and juice strained, add the marrow and boil till clear. The preserve when ready to dish may be flavoured with ginger or pineapple essence; more lemon may also be added and is an improvement, as it sharpens the rather flavourless marrow. The marrow should not be too ripe.
Put into scalded jars, cover and keep as ordinary jam.
The "Jackson Junior," a very convenient cooker for the small kitchenette, now has a Big Brother, which has a separate boiling plate and a larger hob. This makes the cooker a suitable size for three or four persons.
Apples in Syrup.
The syrup: 1/2 lb. sugar, 3 gills water, 1 lemon, 1 or 2 cloves, a little bit of stick cinnamon.
Pare the rind of the lemon very thinly, put it into a lined pan sufficiently large to hold the apples so that they do not touch, add the other ingredients with the juice of the lemon. Boil the syrup for a few minutes. Core the apples, but not too much, pare, keeping as good a shape as possible, put them into the syrup and cook, without a lid, until tender: the syrup should be ladled over them while cooking. Arrange the apples on a dish, reduce the syrup so that it forms a glaze, colour with a little carmine if desired, and pour over the apples. The apples may be served hot or cold and decorated with crystallised fruit or cream.
If very small apples are used they may be served in little pastry cases that have been cooked separately. They are glazed and decorated in the same way, and make a pretty little sweet.
My reason for giving these methods of using apples is that other fruits may be treated in the same way; for example, small pears, plums, greengages and others, also tinned fruits, may be used.

Unnamed: 9: Author describing electric lighting in her own home at Bramhope.
transcription:
544
The Electrical Age
Electric Lighting in the Home. Describing "The Croft,"
Bramhope, Yorkshire.
By Mrs. W. B. WOODHOUSE.
who says : " I think one should spend as much time and thought on choosing electrical fittings as one does on choosing furniture or decorations, because one comes to realise that electricity is not only a very good light and a very cheap light, but it is of great value in any scheme of decoration."

The Lights of Other Days.
After having been without electric light for some time and then being able to obtain it again, I think the thing that most impressed me was the great convenience of being able to go about ones home into room after room and to be able to obtain what light one wanted by turning on a switch.
When we came to live at Bramhope this house was lighted by acetylene gas, which had replaced paraffin lamps, and I expect the people who installed the acetylene lighting were very pleased with the change. The labour required for the proper care, cleaning and replacement of paraffin lamps must have been very great; the acetylene lighting did not require so much attention, though it did not always behave properly. An objectionable feature was that one had to carry matches all over the house, because even if you supplied every room with matches you would find your friends who were smokers, both men and women, would put the boxes in their pockets absent-mindedly, so that one was never safe to go about without a box of matches.

Decorative Lighting.
Then the time came when we were able to instal electric light, and, having decided generally where I would like to place the lamps, I left further decisions for a few weeks ; during that time the lamps were used without any shades because I wanted time to select just the right kind. I think one should spend as much time and thought choosing electrical fittings as one does on choosing furniture or decorations, because one comes to realise that electricity is not only a very good light and a very cheap light, but it is of great value in any scheme of decoration. Its decorative value may be made just as great as you wish by the proper choice and arrangement of fittings. The electric fittings need not cost a lot of money ; in fact, some people with a little imagination, a wire frame, and some very cheap silk, can work wonders. I myself cannot do so, and have to buy the fittings and shades, but I have spent a good deal of thought on the choice.

Methods of Lighting.
There are many ways of lighting a room. Personally, I like the use of standard lamps, as one can then light up corners or any particular spot where special illumination is wanted ; for example, a lamp placed for reading or writing or for lighting a vase of flowers or a picture.
One virtue of a standard is that, if one is alone reading, there is no need to light all the room ; the standard is placed in whatever corner of the room you like to occupy and there you have precisely the light you want.
Nowadays we can buy coloured lamps in a number of different colours, and I find the use of these lamps very pleasant when I want to alter a colour scheme. If you have bought an expensive shade in tones of pink and you want to change the decorations of your room entirely you can buy an orange or a flame-coloured lamp, which will change the pink shade into a primrose or yellow one, and so avoid the necessity for buying a new shade. Lamps can be obtained in many different colours, so that you may make many changes at very little cost.

Outlets.
In my lounge there are all sorts of lighting arrangements, except a ceiling pen-

downwards upon it to bring it out from its dark surroundings, or the light may be sent upwards through the bowl containing the flowers. All sorts of charming effects may be obtained with quite simple fittings, and there is room, I think, for a womans special knowledge of decoration in many of these applications.
The utility of electric light is its first virtue; the next, its cheapness (directly and indirectly in the saving on decoration); and the third, its beauty. I think when you study the lighting of a home electrically that many beautiful uses will occur to you and the subject will appeal to you more and more.
Electricity Generally.
I have confined my remarks to lighting, but, of course, when one has electricity in ones home the many other uses which can be made of it will, I am sure, appeal to all of you, particularly in regard to cleanliness and labour-saving. For some years I have done all my cooking electrically and I use an electric washing machine, water heaters, radiators, vacuum cleaners, flat irons and other devices. There is not one sweeping brush in the house, except the one used in the kitchen for the linoleum. The only floors where the cleaners must kneel are those of the bathroom and the kitchen.
I have used every method I know to save labour, and I believe this will appeal to all members of the E.A.W. The Association, by encouraging women to develop the design and application of electrical apparatus, will turn attention to a field in which I think many of the younger members should find a congenial and profitable occupation.
* * *
A TRAVELLING ELECTRICAL EXHIBITION.
An enterprising development has recently been carried out by the South Wales Electric Power Distribution Company.
[Image of caravan exhibition]
Elec Rev
By courtesy of "The Electrical Review."
They have fitted up a Travelling Exhibition in the form of a Caravan with Let-down Sides, and it is supplied with every kind of Domestic Electric Appliance from an iron to a cooker and refrigerator, in addition to motors and agricultural implements.
It is proposed to use this electric caravan for visiting agricultural shows and the various small towns in South Wales, and there is no doubt that the women in these districts will be very much interested, as practical demonstrations are given.
Even outlying villages which have as yet no supply of electricity will have an opportunity of seeing the electrical marvels with which townswomen are already familiar. Mr. Beauchamp and Mr. Allan, of the S.W.E.P.D. Company, who are responsible for this innovation, have arranged that for visiting these districts the Travelling Exhibition shall be towed by a special tractor, fitted with a dynamo, which will supply the electricity for practical demonstrations.

An Electric Washing Machine is not, as many suppose, a luxury for the rich, but is, on the contrary, a most practical machine, that will save its initial outlay in a very short time. It not only saves time and labour or laundry bills, but it saves very appreciably in the matter of wear and tear on the garments. We do not wear out sheets by lying on them ; shirt cuffs do not get frayed at the wrist bands by rubbing against our wrists. It is the wear and tear of abuse, the abuse suffered through antiquated cleansing processes that shorten the life of fabrics.
An Electric Washer has become a necessity in any well-ordered household, and is probably the greatest labour-saving device ever invented for the home.

The Electrical Age 551

A Visit to the Modern
Electrically Equipped Seghill Colliery.
A Glimpse of the Newcastle Conference. By Frances E. Jones.

One of the most interesting afternoons—during that never-to-be-forgotten successful Conference of the Electrical Association for Women at Newcastle—was the one spent by some of the delegates at the Seghill Collieries—one of the best of the electrically equipped collieries of Great Britain.
Three officials of the Colliery, including Major Brown, the Agent, took the delegates through the whole curriculum of the colliery day. We traversed the overground portions, coming finally to the lift, worked electrically by a mechanic from a raised platform. We saw the lifts—containing men and trolleys—at the touch of a button descend with lightning rapidity, and the return of the lift, filled with coal-laden trolleys; we went up with the trolleys over the light railway to the weighing machine, on to the check-weighing machines, on to the huge machine halls, where the coal is tilted, screened, washed, separated, etc., finally to the finished wagons of some of the best coal I have ever seen. But the women of the Electrical Association were not satisfied in seeing only the least dangerous part of the colliery life, and,

transcription:
The Electrical Age 553

after a great amount of persuasion, the officials allowed us to have the thrill of the day; but they were very reluctant. On our part we felt it was not right not to experience, a little more closely, the real life of the collier; so, with lanterns in hand, we too entered the cage lift, and down we descended into the bowels of the earth and saw for ourselves the actual coal in the pit. We realised, of course, that it was, as cream is to milk, just the very best side of the pit-life; we did not go very far along the passages underground, for the seam was a new one. We, how-ever, sensed enough to understand the dangerous work that coal-getting is; we saw the pit ponies trudging along, and the trolleys being filled.
One must say a great word of praise to the Company for the marvellous way in which they conduct the social side of their work-people. Smart looking little brick houses are for the collier and his family, to be bought by them at a sum which barely covers the cost of the bricks; tennis courts for the 20 work-girls who work in the small brick kiln, which we visited; football grounds and a miniature golf course, are all parts of their social life, and if there should be a happy com-munity of employers and employed in the country, it surely is at the Seghill Collieries.
Our afternoon was brought to a most delightful close, as we were entertained to tea by Mrs. Brown in a beautiful garden, attached to an old-world house, in bright sunlight; every kindness was shown to us by Major and Mrs. Brown and their friends. That underneath these beautiful sun-lit grounds were those dark subter-ranean passages, where men and beasts were working, gave us food for thought, and, out of that thought, came other thoughts—what wonders electricity will be able to do for the brightening of the dark places of the world!

transcription:
The Electrical Age 555
The Fourth International Congress for the Scientific
Organization of Work.
One of the most interesting Sessions of the Congress was that devoted to Scientific
House Management, which is described below by our Special Correspondent.
(PARIS, JUNE 19th-23rd, 1929).
The Fourth International Congress for
the Scientific Organisation of Work, which
was recently held in Paris, marks a for-
ward step in the evolution of household
science. Without doubt, after the indus-
trial section, that devoted to the subjects
of home management was the most inter-
esting, detailed, scientific, and followed
with greatest enthusiasm by its delegates.
Here is a brief picture of the household
section in its three aspects—physical, intel-
lectual and moral: an onlooker would have
seen an animated group, attentive, inter-
ested, averaging 80 persons from day to
day, and representing countries as widely
different in location and race as France,
Spain, Belgium, United States, Czecho-
slovakia, Poland, Italy, Holland, Bulgaria,
Peru, Germany, Switzerland, Greece, Hun-
gary and Egypt. It was remarked even by
the men how closely the women kept to
the strict schedules of their sessions.
While the reports themselves revealed the
scientific university training of the women
addressing the Congress.
The outstanding ideas presented in the
reports were as follows:—
(1) The American reports stressed
chiefly the increasing development of com-
fort and convenience in the home: im-
proved household equipment, and the
education of women in household subjects;
also the increasing aid given by industry
to the solution of household problems.
(2) The Belgian reports brought out the
importance of adding the element of
"sport" to studies of household tasks
followed with stopwatch and pedometer.
They suggested adding elements of skill,
endurance and speed—qualities of the new
age—to the traditionally uninteresting
household occupations. They cited as
examples the tests made on children of
from 13-18 years, who, by these methods,
increased their rapidity and "output" by
100 per cent.
(3) The reports from France covered
an exhaustive study of dust and its
removal. As Mme. Vézes (President of
La Ligue DOrganisation Ménagère of
France) pointed out, the problem of dust
removal is not confined to the housewife,
but is rather a matter deserving municipal
study and control. This view point—that
many household problems must be solved
and aided by the community—was further
carried out in the reports of the following
architects and engineers: MM. Ziska, Gan-
dillon, and Le Corbusier, as well as
Paulet (from Peru, S. America). They
substantially agreed that household opera-
tions must be more and more cared for by
the municipality; and cited the case of
community central heating, water supply,
garbage and dust removal by means of
inter-communicating disposal chutes; light,
heat, and power (the "big three" of the
household), furnished at low cost by
central electric stations—yes, even central
refrigerating plants, for the more perfect
control of house temperature. In short,
they showed a universal feeling that there
must be at one and the same time "an
increase of comfort in the home simul-
taneous with the suppression of manual
drudgery."
(4) The report from Holland was in the
hands of Mme. E. J. Van Waveren-
Resink, who, with Mme. Muller-Lulofs,
were recent delegates at the Newcastle
Conference. Mme. Van Waveren made
the excellent and constructive suggestion
that there be established an international
centre for the training of efficiency experts.

Unnamed: 10: Report presenter; President of the Housewives League of Berlin.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 557
International leaders should prepare a correspondence course in these subjects: the standardisation of household tasks, the choice and operation of labour-saving appliances, the rationalisation of space and house-building, the application of business principles to the management of home finances. These courses would be available to young women who had already passed their training in traditional domestic science; and these graduates would then receive a certificate as household efficiency experts, who could then advise any home manager on any problem of the home. Just as in the factory there are efficiency engineers, consulted by the manufacturer, so these women would form a new profession of "household engineers " qualified to consult with the housewife—or the manufacturer—as to the efficient installation, method or practice which should be followed in modern home engineering or management.
(5) The chief report from Germany was made by Mme. Hildegarde Margis, President of the Housewives League of Berlin. Her chief point was that the design and type of household appliance used in the home is of concern to both manufacturer and housewife alike. She urged that the Government establish standards of testing appliances, and issue a certificate or seal of approval on all household products before they are manufactured. She compared the pure food control against impure foods, and urged that a similar bureau of standards be set up by Government for the housewifes protection against inefficient and faulty appliances. An interesting report of the way efficiency is being taught in some German schools was given by Frau Silberkohl-Schulte, of Berlin. She explained how the children were taught economy of effort by means of attaching string to different pieces of furniture, so as to arrange that equipment in the most step-saving way.
(6) An intensive analysis of work in the home laundry was given by Mrs. Christine Frederick, pioneer in the field of applying the scientific principles of motion-study to household tasks. Mrs. Frederick, author of " Household Engineering " and other books on home management, and recalled as having given a series of lectures for the Electrical Association in England two years ago, brought with her a model Efficiency Laundry on a diminutive scale. This model, completely fitted with small-scale appliances of washer, ironing machine etc., and complete electric lighting, served to visually illustrate the principles of step-saving and grouped equipment as applied to the washing of clothes. Mrs. Frederick pointed out the great saving in time, effort and attention if an electrically operated washer was used, over a hand method. Electricity, said Mrs. Frederick, permitted the use of an entirely new washing principle—and it was necessary to stress the education of the woman in the use of the machine. This education should be carried on by the manufacturer, as well as by the demonstrator of the appliance.
(7) The delegate from Italy, Mme. Diez-Gasca, sent in a report calling attention to the need for estimating the value of the housewifes own time in determining the cost of any household task. If women are expected to remain at home then they should receive compensation for their work as household managers. Both the delegates from Poland, Mme. Szumlakowska and the delegate from Check, Mme. Pelantova, agreed in this view and gave numerous examples to corroborate it.
(8) Last, but not least, much of the helpfulness of the Congress was due to the splendid direction of Mlle. Paulette Bernege, the brilliant editor of " Mon Chez-Moi," and the founder of the French Ligues dOrganisation Ménagère. An admirable executive, Mlle. Bernege, marshalled her delegates and ordered the presentation of the various papers with skill and helpful comment. In her talk before the men delegates of the convention, Mlle. Bernege said in part:---

These courses would be available to young women who had already passed their training in traditional domestic science; and these graduates would then receive a certificate as household efficiency experts, who could then advise any home manager on any problem of the home. Just as in the factory there are efficiency engineers, consulted by the manufacturer, so these women would form a new profession of "household engineers " qualified to consult with the housewife—or the manufacturer—as to the efficient installation, method or practice which should be followed in modern home engineering or management.
(5) The chief report from Germany was made by Mme. Hildegarde Margis, President of the Housewives League of Berlin. Her chief point was that the design and type of household appliance used in the home is of concern to both manufacturer and housewife alike. She urged that the Government establish standards of testing appliances, and issue a certificate or seal of approval on all household products before they are manufactured. She compared the pure food control against impure foods, and urged that a similar bureau of standards be set up by Government for the housewifes protection against inefficient and faulty appliances. An interesting report of the way efficiency is being taught in some German schools was given by Frau Silberkohl-Schulte, of Berlin. She explained how the children were taught economy of effort by means of attaching string to different pieces of furniture, so as to arrange that equipment in the most step-saving way.
(6) An intensive analysis of work in the home laundry was given by Mrs. Christine Frederick, pioneer in the field of applying the scientific principles of motion-study to household tasks. Mrs. Frederick, author of " Household Engineering " and other books on home management, and recalled as having given a series of lectures for the Electrical Association in England two years ago, brought with her a model Efficiency Laundry on a diminutive scale. This model, completely fitted with small-scale appliances of washer, ironing machine etc., and complete electric lighting, served to visually illustrate the principles of step-saving and grouped equipment as applied to the washing of clothes. Mrs. Frederick pointed out the great saving in time, effort and attention if an electrically operated washer was used, over a hand method. Electricity, said Mrs. Frederick, permitted the use of an entirely new washing principle—and it was necessary to stress the education of the woman in the use of the machine. This education should be carried on by the manufacturer, as well as by the demonstrator of the appliance.
(7) The delegate from Italy, Mme. Diez-Gasca, sent in a report calling attention to the need for estimating the value of the housewifes own time in determining the cost of any household task. If women are expected to remain at home then they should receive compensation for their work as household managers. Both the delegates from Poland, Mme. Szumlakowska and the delegate from Check, Mme. Pelantova, agreed in this view and gave numerous examples to corroborate it.
(8) Last, but not least, much of the helpfulness of the Congress was due to the splendid direction of Mlle. Paulette Bernege, the brilliant editor of " Mon Chez-Moi," and the founder of the French Ligues dOrganisation Ménagère. An admirable executive, Mlle. transcription:
The Electrical Age 561
E.A.W. Branch Activities.
Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
We have had the delightful privilege of starting our Seasons activities with a Garden Party at Stanley, Renfrewshire, the lovely home in a wood-estate of Mr. and Mrs. Archibald Speirs.
Mrs. Speirs made all the arrangements for our day, the Folk Dancing on the lawn by the Glasgow Company of the Girls Guides; tennis, clock-golf, putting and bowling; tea being served in the spacious dining-room, library and billiard room.
The music for the Folk Dancing was provided electrically by the courtesy of Joseph Taylor, Esq., The Edison-Swan Co., Ltd., Glasgow.
Mr. Archibald Speirs welcomed the guests to Stanley, and wished them a very happy afternoon.
The speakers included, as mentioned, the Lady Bellhaven and Stenton, Lady Mason, Bailie Mrs. Bell, C.B.E., Miss Sellars, Miss Mackirdy, and Herbert Bell, Esq., M.I.E.E. The company numbered over 100 members.
We are very happy indeed to have had such a good send-off for the Season, and trust that this splendid function will increase our membership very substantially.
This will be followed by a visit to the Kelvin Hall Housing and Health Exhibition.
In October we visit the United Dairies Co., Ltd., one of the most up-to-date dairies in Great Britain.
After that we set out on our programme of Lectures and Talks with a Cinema Display of Electrical Films on our fourth anniversary as a branch.
The Newcastle Conference was greatly enjoyed by the Glasgow contingent of members, and has added just the zest that was needed for our particular Branch.

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. Norman Griffiths, M.Com., A.C.I.S.,
142, Woodlands Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
Phone, South 2334.
The Branch has arrangements well in hand for a number of interesting Autumn Demonstrations, Lectures and Visits. The Season opens on September 20th.
Our representative to the Newcastle Conference was Mrs. Lawson, who on her return, gave the Council an interesting and stimulating account of the various meetings.
New the report which appeared in the July issue, the Branch has lost the services of Mrs. Hayes (Secretary). Mrs. Hayes worked indefatigably to increase the interest and activity of the Branch, and she will be greatly missed.
A change has been made in the Secretariat of the Branch. The office has now been moved to "The Elms," Alvechurch. This arrangement is entirely due to the kindness of our President, Mrs. H. K. Beale, who has placed a room in her home at the disposal of the Branch. D.G.

Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Foster-Jeffery, LL.B.,
6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
After a quiet summer we are looking forward to the Autumn Session, for which a full and varied programme has been arranged.
On October 5th we are holding an American Tea, by the kindness of the Salford Corporation, at their Electricity Showrooms. We hope to meet all the members and receive many gifts.
The Luncheon at the Midland Hotel has been fixed for October 10th. We are looking forward to the pleasure of the presence of the Lady Emmett, J.P., Lady Brooks, C.B.E., J.P., and Miss C. Haslett, with the Lady Mayoress of Manchester in the chair. We hope to repeat the success of the previous Luncheons.
Many interesting visits have been arranged, including the Ford Motor Works, the B.B.C. Studio, the Exhibition of the Smoke Abatement League, and Messrs. Hans Renolds Chain Works.
Those ever-popular Cooking Demonstrations are to be held; one during the afternoon at the Showrooms of the Manchester Electricity Department, and two evening ones at the Offices of the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., and the new Showrooms of the Oldham Electricity Department respectively.
During October Mr. Francis, of E.D.A., has promised to lecture to us on "Modern Tendencies in Architectural Furnishing and Lighting Designs and the part played by Electricity therein." The title is sufficiently intriguing to ensure a good attendance. N.E.V.C.

Cheltenham Branch.
Acting Hon. Secretary: Mrs. G. F. Bache, Eythorne,
All Saints Road, Cheltenham.
Our summer programme has contained several interesting meetings, which have been well attended. On June 12th, in company with the Mid-Gloucestershire and Bristol Branches, we visited Cardiff, where the local branch Committee members met us on arrival, and acted as guides throughout the day. We first visited the magnificent National Museum of Wales, where Dr. Fox kindly explained the chief objects of interest to us. A Civic Luncheon at the invitation of the Lord and Lady Mayoress in the beautiful City Hall was much appreciated. This was followed by an inspection of the new Showrooms of the General Electric Co. Ltd. Mr. W. E. Hobbs, the Companys District Manager, and his courteous staff, showed us all the latest electrical appliances, then entertained us to a very welcome tea in the City Hall, and afterwards took us for a most interesting motor tour round the environs of Cardiff. We were very pleased to have with us Miss Haslett, who had journeyed down specially from London to join our party.
The following week we inspected Messrs. Morelands Match Factory, Gloucester, when the ingenious and fascinating processes involved in the production of an ordinary box of matches were viewed with interest.
Our next visit was the outcome of a joint invitation from the West Gloucestershire Power Co. to the Mid-Gloucestershire Branch and ourselves to visit their generating station at Lydney, in the Forest of Dean, where it is claimed that electric motors were first applied to colliery work. This generating stations proximity to the Norchard Colliery is a feature of its lay-out. The Company supplies electricity to 21 parishes in its area, and also supplies in bulk to the Gloucester, Stroud and Chepstow Undertakings. We were then conveyed through the delightful Forest of Dean to "The Grange," Newnham, where the Companys Chief Engineer, Mr. H. S. Ellis, and Mrs. Ellis kindly provided tea. We greatly admired the magnificent views over the Vale of Severn to be seen from the grounds of the house. This visit concluded the programme of a very successful and interesting half-year.
The Committee has arranged an attractive list of fixtures for the autumn, and is confidently looking forward to an increase in the membership and influence of the Branch.

South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. G. Snow, "Greengate," Lisvane,
nr. Cardiff.
On June 12th we had a very interesting and important fixture. About 100 E.A.W. Members from Bristol, Cheltenham and Mid-Gloucestershire Branches visited Cardiff.
After a visit to the National Museum of Wales, we were entertained to a Civic Luncheon by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress (Alderman W. R. Williams, J.P., and Mrs. Williams) at the City Hall. After interesting speeches by the Lord Mayor, Miss Haslett and Mr. Morley New—our City Electrical Engineer—and others, we proceeded to the new Showrooms of the General Electric Company, and were welcomed by the District Manager, Mr. W. E. Hobbs. After an interesting afternoon, we had tea at the City Hall by kind invitation of the General Electric Company.
Before proceeding home our visitors were driven around Cardiff and had pointed out to them the main places of interest.
On June 26th, fully 100 of our Members took the opportunity of visiting the Cable Works of Messrs. Edison Swan Cable Works, Ltd. at Lydbrook, Glos. Mr. F. Gale received us, and, after an interesting tour of the Works, we were entertained to tea, returning home via the Wye Valley.
Our autumn programme promises to be a very good one, and includes three social events:—
Sept. 24th.—Visit to the Power Station of the South Wales Power Distribution Co., Upper Boat, to inspect the new Travelling Demonstration Van.
Oct. 1st.—A Lecture by Mr. G. S. Francis, of the E.D.A. (London) on "The Influence of Electricity on Public Health."
Oct. 15th.—A Bridge Drive—Mr. H. Coupe, District Manager of Metropolitan-Vickers, Ltd., has kindly placed his premises at our disposal for this fixture.
Nov. 5th.—A visit to the City Lodge, Cardiff, to inspect the electrical apparatus used for patients benefit.
Nov. 20th.—A Lecture by Mr. T. Catten, of the local E.D.A., on "Furnishing your Home with Light."
Nov. 22nd.—A Dance.
Dec. 3rd.—Cooking Demonstration by the General Electric Co.

After a quiet summer we are looking forward to the Autumn Session, for which a full and varied programme has been arranged.
On October 5th we are holding an American Tea, by the kindness of the Salford Corporation, at their Electricity Showrooms. We hope to meet all the members and receive many gifts.

Cheltenham Branch.
Acting Hon. Secretary: Mrs. G. F. Bache, Eythorne,
All Saints Road, Cheltenham.

On June 12th, in company with the Mid-Gloucestershire and Bristol Branches, we visited Cardiff, where the local branch Committee members met us on arrival, and acted as guides throughout the day. We first visited the magnificent National Museum of Wales, where Dr. Fox kindly explained the chief objects of interest to us. A Civic Luncheon at the invitation of the Lord and Lady Mayoress in the beautiful City Hall was much appreciated. This was followed by an inspection of the new Showrooms of the General Electric Co. Ltd. Mr. W. E. Hobbs, the Companys District Manager, and his courteous staff, showed us all the latest electrical appliances, then entertained us to a very welcome tea in the City Hall, and afterwards took us for a most interesting motor tour round the environs of Cardiff. We were very pleased to have with us Miss Haslett, who had journeyed down specially from London to join our party.
The following week we inspected Messrs. Morelands Match Factory, Gloucester, when the ingenious and fascinating processes involved in the production of an ordinary box of matches were viewed with interest.
Our next visit was the outcome of a joint invitation from the West Gloucestershire Power Co. to the Mid-Gloucestershire Branch and ourselves to visit their generating station at Lydney, in the Forest of Dean, where it is claimed that electric motors were first applied to colliery work. This generating stations proximity to the Norchard Colliery is a feature of its lay-out. The Company supplies electricity to 21 parishes in its area, and also supplies in bulk to the Gloucester, Stroud and Chepstow Undertakings. We were then conveyed through the delightful Forest of Dean to "The Grange," Newnham, where the Companys Chief Engineer, Mr. H. S. Ellis, and Mrs. Ellis kindly provided tea. We greatly admired the magnificent views over the Vale of Severn to be seen from the grounds of the house. This visit concluded the programme of a very successful and interesting half-year.
The Committee has arranged an attractive list of fixtures for the autumn, and is confidently looking forward to an increase in the membership and influence of the Branch.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
We have had the delightful privilege of starting our Seasons activities with a Garden Party at Stanley, Renfrewshire, the lovely home in a wood-estate of Mr. and Mrs. Archibald Speirs.
Mrs. Speirs made all the arrangements for our day, the Folk Dancing on the lawn by the Glasgow Company of the Girls Guides; tennis, clock-golf, putting and bowling; tea being served in the spacious dining-room, library and billiard room.
The music for the Folk Dancing was provided electrically by the courtesy of Joseph Taylor, Esq., The Edison-Swan Co., Ltd., Glasgow.
Mr. Archibald Speirs welcomed the guests to Stanley, and wished them a very happy afternoon.
The speakers included, as mentioned, the Lady Bellhaven and Stenton, Lady Mason, Bailie Mrs. Bell, C.B.E., Miss Sellars, Miss Mackirdy, and Herbert Bell, Esq., M.I.E.E. The company numbered over 100 members.
We are very happy indeed to have had such a good send-off for the Season, and trust that this splendid function will increase our membership very substantially.
This will be followed by a visit to the Kelvin Hall Housing and Health Exhibition.
In October we visit the United Dairies Co., Ltd., one of the most up-to-date dairies in Great Britain.
After that we set out on our programme of Lectures and Talks with a Cinema Display of Electrical Films on our fourth anniversary as a branch.
The Newcastle Conference was greatly enjoyed by the Glasgow contingent of members, and has added just the zest that was needed for our particular Branch.

Cheltenham Branch.
Acting Hon. Secretary: Mrs. G. F. Bache, Eythorne,
All Saints Road, Cheltenham.
Our summer programme has contained several interesting meetings, which have been well attended. On June 12th, in company with the Mid-Gloucestershire and Bristol Branches, we visited Cardiff, where the local branch Committee members met us on arrival, and acted as guides throughout the day. We first visited the magnificent National Museum of Wales, where Dr. Fox kindly explained the chief objects of interest to us. A Civic Luncheon at the invitation of the Lord and Lady Mayoress in the beautiful City Hall was much appreciated. This was followed by an inspection of the new Showrooms of the General Electric Co. Ltd. Mr. W. E. Hobbs, the Companys District Manager, and his courteous staff, showed us all the latest electrical appliances, then entertained us to a very welcome tea in the City Hall, and afterwards took us for a most interesting motor tour round the environs of Cardiff. We were very pleased to have with us Miss Haslett, who had journeyed down specially from London to join our party.
The following week we inspected Messrs. Morelands Match Factory, Gloucester, when the ingenious and fascinating processes involved in the production of an ordinary box of matches were viewed with interest.
Our next visit was the outcome of a joint invitation from the West Gloucestershire Power Co. to the Mid-Gloucestershire Branch and ourselves to visit their generating station at Lydney, in the Forest of Dean, where it is claimed that electric motors were first applied to colliery work. This generating stations proximity to the Norchard Colliery is a feature of its lay-out. The Company supplies electricity to 21 parishes in its area, and also supplies in bulk to the Gloucester, Stroud and Chepstow Undertakings. We were then conveyed through the delightful Forest of Dean to "The Grange," Newnham, where the Companys Chief Engineer, Mr. H. S. Ellis, and Mrs. Ellis kindly provided tea. We greatly admired the magnificent views over the Vale of Severn to be seen from the grounds of the house. This visit concluded the programme of a very successful and interesting half-year.
The Committee has arranged an attractive list of fixtures for the autumn, and is confidently looking forward to an increase in the membership and influence of the Branch.

Ashford and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. B. M. Wilson, “Gleniffer Brae,”
Vicarage Road, Kennington, near Ashford, Kent.
Since our last issue the greatly-looked-for Conference at Newcastle has come and gone. Four of our members were able to attend, and the unanimous report was that it surpassed the highest expectations.
June 20th.—A round table conference was held, when members asked questions and discussed electrical problems. All present contributed to the success of the meeting, and the Council’s Engineer, Mr. H. Wilson, who was present to answer questions and give any information, was kept busy for about an hour.
The final lecture for the students on “Correct Lighting” was given by Mr. Lingard, of E.L.M.A. We are most grateful for the help we always receive from these friends.
An interesting visit also was arranged by Mr. Dowling (one of the members of our local E.D.C.) to some flats in the course of construction. This gave the students a most instructive and enjoyable afternoon, for the wiring could be seen at every stage.
Funds are few, but hopes are high, for, with the proceeds of a Rummage and Gift Sale held on September 20th, it is hoped to extend activities during the winter session. B. W.

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby, c/o Ingleby Motors, Ltd., Sweet Street, Leeds.
The Leeds and West Riding Branch has been closed down for the summer months, but is re-opening on October 10th with a Lantern Lecture by Mr. Geo. S. Francis on “Modern Tendencies in Architecture and the part Electricity plays therein.” The Electric Lamp Manufacturers’ Association have also promised to give their Lantern Lecture, “Electric Lighting and the Preservation of Eyesight.”
Other lectures on “Cookery,” “Electricity in the Home,” “Medical Electro-Apparatus,” and other subjects are being arranged, and these, interspersed with visits to various Works in the district, promise to make an interesting programme for the coming Winter.

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. M. Klitz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, N. Wales.
During the past three months North Wales has given itself up to holidays, and the activities of the Branch have on that account been restricted.
We had one very enjoyable outing, under perfect weather conditions, when two motor coaches conveyed 40 of our Members from various parts of North Wales to Manchester for Lunch, and then on to Messrs. transcription:
The Electrical Age
563
being the X-ray apparatus, which is one of the finest and
most modern installations of its kind at present in this
country. A most interesting time was spent at the Hos-
pital, greatly enhanced by X-ray demonstrations and a talk
given by Dr. Henry, a member of the Hospital staff.
A small party from Rugby attended the Newcastle
Conference in July, which was the outstanding feature of
the years programme.
We are looking forward to October, when we celebrate
the first anniversary of the Branch. This should prove a
bright opening for the Autumn Session, when we hope to
better our membership with the help of an interesting
programme.
* * *
Swansea and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. G. Davies, 5, Eden Avenue,
Uplands, Swansea.
The first Annual Summer Meeting of this Branch was
held on Thursday, July 25th. Members and their friends
numbering about 30, spent a very pleasant afternoon at
St. Madoc, Llanmadoc, Gower, by kind invitation of Mrs.
J. W. Bury (Chairman).
The party made the journey by charabanc, and were
entertained to tea, after which Miss Bury delighted the
company with a playlet entitled The Lady Interviewer,
Great credit is due for the capital way this was presented
in the evening games and sports were indulged in.
Lady Bryn Edwards (President) proposed a hearty
vote of thanks to Mrs. Bury, and this was seconded by
Mrs. W. Bevan, J.P., and carried. Altogether the affair
was a great success.
* * *
Mid-Gloucestershire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss G. Johnson,
21, Eastgate Street, Gloucester.
June 19th.—In conjunction with members from the Chel-
tenham and Bristol Branches, we visited Cardiff. This was
a memorable and enjoyable visit, including a Civic Recep-
tion and Luncheon by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress,
followed by a visit to the National Museum of Wales. We
also visited the Showrooms of the General Electric Co.,
who entertained us to tea.
July 4th.—By kind permission of the West Gloucester-
shire Power Co., Ltd., together with members from the
Cheltenham Branch we visited the Companys Power
Station at Lydney. On arrival we were cordially welcomed
by Mr. H. S. Ellis (the General Manager and Chief En-
gineer), and conducted through the Station by his Assist-
ants, who made the visit very enjoyable indeed by their
interesting explanation of what we saw. Light refresh-
ments were provided by the Company prior to our de-
parture for The Grange, Newnham-on-Severn, the home
of Mr. and Mrs. H. S. Ellis, where, after being welcomed
by Mrs. Ellis (our Chairman), we were entertained to tea
in their delightful grounds, bringing to a close a most
interesting and instructive afternoon.
This visit concluded our programme, which has been a
very successful and interesting one, for the half-year,
activities ceasing until September. Unfortunately only our
Chairman was able to attend the Annual Conference, New-
castle-on-Tyne.
* * *
North Staffordshire Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries:
Miss D. Bentley and Mrs. E. M. Yeaman,
St. Georges Chambers, Kingsway, Stoke-on-Trent.
The principal feature of the Summer programme of the
local branch of the Electrical Association for Women was
the visit to the Revo Electric Co., Ltd., on July 9th, when
about 30 members travelled to Tipton. The party was wel-
comed on arrival by Mr. Bickell. After a tour of the works,
during which the work and processes of the various depart-
ments was explained, tea was taken in the Works Canteen.
Afterwards Mr. Alderman Leese, the Chairman of the
Electricity Supply Committee of Stoke-on-Trent, who accom-
panied the party, expressed the thanks of the members
for the kindness and hospitality of the Revo Electric Co.,
Ltd., to which the Director, Mr. A. E. Felton, responded.
* * *
Bristol and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss A. B. Wright, A.C.I.S., Electricity
Offices, Colston Avenue, Bristol.
On June 18th thirty members visited the Cardiff Branch,
together with members from Cheltenham and Mid-Gloucester-
shire.

Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. G. Davies, 5, Eden Avenue,

The first Annual Summer Meeting of this Branch was
held on Thursday, July 25th. Members and their friends
numbering about 30, spent a very pleasant afternoon at
St. Madoc, Llanmadoc, Gower, by kind invitation of Mrs.
J. W. Bury (Chairman).
The party made the journey by charabanc, and were
entertained to tea, after which Miss Bury delighted the
company with a playlet entitled The Lady Interviewer,

in the evening games and sports were indulged in.

* * *
Mid-Gloucestershire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss G. Johnson,
21, Eastgate Street, Gloucester.
June 19th.—In conjunction with members from the Chel-
tenham and Bristol Branches, we visited Cardiff. This was
a memorable and enjoyable visit, including a Civic Recep-
tion and Luncheon by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress,
followed by a visit to the National Museum of Wales. We
also visited the Showrooms of the General Electric Co.,
who entertained us to tea.
July 4th.—By kind permission of the West Gloucester-
shire Power Co., Ltd., together with members from the
Cheltenham Branch we visited the Companys Power
Station at Lydney. On arrival we were cordially welcomed
by Mr. H. S. Ellis (the General Manager and Chief En-
gineer), and conducted through the Station by his Assist-
ants, who made the visit very enjoyable indeed by their
interesting explanation of what we saw. Light refresh-
ments were provided by the Company prior to our de-
parture for The Grange, Newnham-on-Severn, the home
of Mr. and Mrs. H. S. Ellis, where, after being welcomed
by Mrs. Ellis (our Chairman), we were entertained to tea
in their delightful grounds, bringing to a close a most
interesting and instructive afternoon.
This visit concluded our programme, which has been a
very successful and interesting one, for the half-year,
activities ceasing until September. Unfortunately only our
Chairman was able to attend the Annual Conference, New-
castle-on-Tyne.

North Staffordshire Branch.

St. Georges Chambers, Kingsway, Stoke-on-Trent.

local branch of the Electrical Association for Women was
the visit to the Revo Electric Co., Ltd., on July 9th, when
about 30 members travelled to Tipton. The party was wel-
comed on arrival by Mr. Bickell. After a tour of the works,
during which the work and processes of the various depart-
ments was explained, tea was taken in the Works Canteen.

Electricity Supply Committee of Stoke-on-Trent, who accom-
panied the party, expressed the thanks of the members
for the kindness and hospitality of the Revo Electric Co.,
Ltd., to which the Director, Mr. A. E. Felton, responded.

Swansea and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. G. Davies, 5, Eden Avenue,
Uplands, Swansea.
The first Annual Summer Meeting of this Branch was
held on Thursday, July 25th. Members and their friends
numbering about 30, spent a very pleasant afternoon at
St. Madoc, Llanmadoc, Gower, by kind invitation of Mrs.
J. W. Bury (Chairman).
The party made the journey by charabanc, and were
entertained to tea, after which Miss Bury delighted the
company with a playlet entitled The Lady Interviewer,
Great credit is due for the capital way this was presented
in the evening games and sports were indulged in.
Lady Bryn Edwards (President) proposed a hearty
vote of thanks to Mrs. Bury, and this was seconded by
Mrs. W. Bevan, J.P., and carried. Altogether the affair
was a great success.
* * *
Mid-Gloucestershire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss G. Johnson,
21, Eastgate Street, Gloucester.
June 19th.—In conjunction with members from the Chel-
tenham and Bristol Branches, we visited Cardiff. This was
a memorable and enjoyable visit, including a Civic Recep-
tion and Luncheon by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress,
followed by a visit to the National Museum of Wales. We
also visited the Showrooms of the General Electric Co.,
who entertained us to tea.
July 4th.—By kind permission of the West Gloucester-
shire Power Co., Ltd., together with members from the
Cheltenham Branch we visited the Companys Power
Station at Lydney. On arrival we were cordially welcomed
by Mr. H. S. Ellis (the General Manager and Chief En-
gineer), and conducted through the Station by his Assist-
ants, who made the visit very enjoyable indeed by their
interesting explanation of what we saw. Light refresh-
ments were provided by the Company prior to our de-
parture for The Grange, Newnham-on-Severn, the home
of Mr. and Mrs. H. S. Ellis, where, after being welcomed
by Mrs. Ellis (our Chairman), we were entertained to tea
in their delightful grounds, bringing to a close a most
interesting and instructive afternoon.
This visit concluded our programme, which has been a
very successful and interesting one, for the half-year,
activities ceasing until September. Unfortunately only our
Chairman was able to attend the Annual Conference, New-
castle-on-Tyne.
* * *
North Staffordshire Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries:
Miss D. Bentley and Mrs. E. M. Yeaman,
St. Georges Chambers, Kingsway, Stoke-on-Trent.
The principal feature of the Summer programme of the
local branch of the Electrical Association for Women was
the visit to the Revo Electric Co., Ltd., on July 9th, when
about 30 members travelled to Tipton. The party was wel-
comed on arrival by Mr. Bickell. After a tour of the works,
during which the work and processes of the various depart-
ments was explained, tea was taken in the Works Canteen.
Afterwards Mr. Alderman Leese, the Chairman of the
Electricity Supply Committee of Stoke-on-Trent, who accom-
panied the party, expressed the thanks of the members
for the kindness and hospitality of the Revo Electric Co.,
Ltd., to which the Director, Mr. A. E. Felton, responded.

shire.

Unnamed: 9: Promised to speak at the Opening Meeting in Bristol.
transcription:
564 The Electrical Age
An extremely interesting item of the visit was a conducted tour through the National Museum of Wales, after which the visitors were given a Civic welcome by the Lord Mayor at the City Hall.
During the afternoon a visit was paid to the Showrooms of the G.E.C., in Womanby Street.
After tea, kindly provided at the City Hall, the party were taken for a tour around the City and suburbs of Cardiff.
An attractive programme has been arranged for the coming session, including:—
The Opening Meeting of the Session at Rotary House, Bristol. Miss C. Haslett has promised to speak.
A Lecture by Dr. A. P. M. Fleming, C.B.E., M.I.E.E., entitled "Milestones in the Progress of Electricity."
An important event will be the forthcoming DANCE and WHIST DRIVE on November 25th, at Fortts Restaurant, Bristol.
A Lecture-Demonstration on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," by S. Anderson, Esq.
A Lecture-Demonstration by L. E. Buckell, Esq., on "Colour Lighting for Home Decoration."
A Lecture-Demonstration on Stage Lighting, with a selection of Dances.
An Electrical Play given by members of the B.C.E.D. Dramatic Society.
Special attention is called to the Opening Meeting of the session on October 6th, at 7.30 p.m., and the Whist Drive and Dance in November.

London Activities.
Two events of outstanding importance and interest have taken place this Summer.
Many E.A.W. Members all over the country know of the interest created in the question of giving some instruction on Electricity in Girls Schools, and at the end of June a Deputation, arranged by the Electrical Association for Women, was received by the Board of Education.
Then in July the most successful Conference was held at Newcastle-on-Tyne. From the pictures and notes given elsewhere it will be seen that not only was the Conference of the greatest possible educational interest, but it was thoroughly enjoyable also.
The weather allied itself to the kind hosts—the North-East Coast Members and their friends—and made the Newcastle Conference a memorable one to Overseas and Home Delegates.
Arrangements have been made for the Autumn and Winter, and the Programme includes:—
Visits to the Shipping, Engineering and Machinery Exhibition at Olympia; the Showrooms of Messrs. Kelvinator, Ltd., Kingsway, where a lecture will be given on "Electrical Cold that Keeps," by Mr. F. F. Kewley; Messrs. Ediswan, Ltd., where a special lecture will be given by Mr. W. J. Jones, M.Sc. (Eng.), A.M.I.E.E. Special Demonstrations and Lighting Effects are also being arranged, with Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley in the chair.
Mr. E. E. Sharp, A.M.I.E.E., who recently returned from an extensive tour in Australia and New Zealand, will lecture on some of his "Electrical Experiences in Australasia." This will be given in the Club Room, 46, Kensington Court, London, W.8.
Two Socials have been arranged by the Social Sub-Committee, one on the evening of October 23rd, with Films, and the other on the afternoon of November 14th.
A Lecture-Demonstration on "Electric Christmas Cooking," by Mr. A. Moss (Gold Medallist), will be given at the showrooms of Messrs. Berrys Electric Limited, Newman Street.
The British Electrical Development Association have kindly invited readers of the "Electrical Age" to a display of Films towards the end of December. Anyone wishing to attend is requested to write in to 46, Kensington Court, London, W.8, when a ticket will be sent.
It is with the greatest regret that we learned of the death of Mrs. E. Barnett, after only two days illness.
Mrs. Barnett was one of the earliest members of the E.A.W., and, as the Chief Woman Demonstrator for the Metro-Vick Supplies, Limited, her cheery personality and capable Lectures will be very much missed all over the country.
We wish to express our deepest sympathy with her family and many friends.

An important event will be the forthcoming DANCE and WHIST DRIVE on November 25th, at Fortts Restaurant, Bristol.
A Lecture-Demonstration on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," by S. Anderson, Esq.
A Lecture-Demonstration by L. E. Buckell, Esq., on "Colour Lighting for Home Decoration."
A Lecture-Demonstration on Stage Lighting, with a selection of Dances.
An Electrical Play given by members of the B.C.E.D. Dramatic Society.
Special attention is called to the Opening Meeting of the session on October 6th, at 7.30 p.m., and the Whist Drive and Dance in November.

London Activities.
Two events of outstanding importance and interest have taken place this Summer.
Many E.A.W. Members all over the country know of the interest created in the question of giving some instruction on Electricity in Girls Schools, and at the end of June a Deputation, arranged by the Electrical Association for Women, was received by the Board of Education.
Then in July the most successful Conference was held at Newcastle-on-Tyne. From the pictures and notes given elsewhere it will be seen that not only was the Conference of the greatest possible educational interest, but it was thoroughly enjoyable also.
The weather allied itself to the kind hosts—the North-East Coast Members and their friends—and made the Newcastle Conference a memorable one to Overseas and Home Delegates.
Arrangements have been made for the Autumn and Winter, and the Programme includes:—
Visits to the Shipping, Engineering and Machinery Exhibition at Olympia; the Showrooms of Messrs. Kelvinator, Ltd., Kingsway, where a lecture will be given on "Electrical Cold that Keeps," by Mr. F. F. Kewley; Messrs. Ediswan, Ltd., where a special lecture will be given by Mr. W. J. Jones, M.Sc. (Eng.), A.M.I.E.E. Special Demonstrations and Lighting Effects are also being arranged, with Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley in the chair.
Mr. E. E. Sharp, A.M.I.E.E., who recently returned from an extensive tour in Australia and New Zealand, will lecture on some of his "Electrical Experiences in Australasia." This will be given in the Club Room, 46, Kensington Court, London, W.8.
Two Socials have been arranged by the Social Sub-Committee, one on the evening of October 23rd, with Films, and the other on the afternoon of November 14th.
A Lecture-Demonstration on "Electric Christmas Cooking," by Mr. A. Moss (Gold Medallist), will be given at the showrooms of Messrs. Berrys Electric Limited, Newman Street.
The British Electrical Development Association have kindly invited readers of the "Electrical Age" to a display of Films towards the end of December. Anyone wishing to attend is requested to write in to 46, Kensington Court, London, W.8, when a ticket will be sent.
It is with the greatest regret that we learned of the death of Mrs. E. Barnett, after only two days illness.
Mrs. Barnett was one of the earliest members of the E.A.W., and, as the Chief Woman Demonstrator for the Metro-Vick Supplies, Limited, her cheery personality and capable Lectures will be very much missed all over the country.
We wish to express our deepest sympathy with her family and many friends.

Vol. 1. JANUARY, 1930. No. 15

Mrs. J. M. Phillips, the President of the East Devon Branch of the Electrical Association for Women, is one of the most popular women in Devonshire.

She was for five years Mayor of Honiton, being also an Alderman, Justice of the Peace and Poor Law Guardian.

Mrs. Phillips energies are by no means confined to her Civic activities, as she is Chairman of the Devon Council of Women, and her interest in the country woman is demonstrated by the fact that she has for the past three years been Chairman of the Devon Womens Institute.

That her influence is not confined to Devonshire is illustrated by the fact that she is a Member of many important Womens Committees in London, including the National Council of Women.

Amongst her wide circle of friends Mrs. Phillips is regarded as a woman of wide sympathies and exceptional business ability.

MRS. J. M. PHILLIPS, J.P.

Unnamed: 9: New Minister of Transport and enthusiast for domestic electricity use.
Unnamed: 10: Enthusiast for the cause of Electricity and domestic electricity.
transcription:
EDITORIAL.

1930—EDUCATION. The keynote for our work in 1930 would appear to be Education. The Deputation to the Board of Education organised by the Association seems to be bearing fruit, and Lecture Courses are being arranged for groups of Domestic Science Teachers all over the country.
In addition an interesting three days Course is being arranged in the Spring for Women in Electrical Showrooms, Architects and Decorators.
More than ever the special work which the E.A.W. has set itself to do is necessary—that of translating the complexities of Electrical Knowledge and Phraseology into the language of simplicity.
We have in Mr. Herbert Morrison, M.P., the new Minister of Transport, an enthusiast for the cause of Electricity and especially for the use of Electricity in the Home, and his enthusiasm is, we feel, permeating not only the various sections of the Government, but also all Electrical Organisations throughout the country.

* * *

ELECTRICITY TARIFFS.—Of all the problems which the rapid development of Electricity for Domestic Purposes has brought in its train, perhaps the most difficult of solution is that of the question of Tariffs, or the right method of charging the consumer for his supply of Electricity.
Many methods are being tried out at the moment and a Committee has recently been set up by the Electricity Commissioners to make a Report on the subject. This Committee asked for the womans point of view, which was given by a Deputation from the E.A.W.
The Deputation urged that the main points in deciding upon the type of Tariff should be simplicity and the encouragement of the consumer who is going to use Electricity for all Household purposes.
As an Association we realise that here is a very difficult question to which there is no one solution, and we are anxious to help the Electrical Engineer by giving our experience as consumers which may assist towards a satisfactory solution of the problem.

* * *

WATTS AND KILOWATTS.—The Electrical Play has now been printed and rehearsals are afoot in London and the Provinces.
“Watts in a Home,” as the Play has been christened, deals actually with the History of Electric Lighting in the Home, the story opening in 1880 and concluding in 1929.
It would seem appropriate that our first venture in the Dramatic field should be concerned with Watts. Most of us started to use Electricity in our home in the form of Watts, but progressive women are now thinking of it in terms of Kilowatts.
Already the more ambitious Members of the Dramatic Committee have in mind a Play which might be described as “The Home of Kilowatts.”

transcription:
The Electrical Age 571
Opening of a Super Power Station
Hams Hall, Birmingham.
By HARRIETT HOLMES.
Illustration of Hams Hall Power Station, showing the Cooling Towers.
T.R.H. The Duke and Duchess of York visited Birmingham on November 6th and performed the Opening Ceremony of the new Hams Hall Super Power Station at Birmingham.
This great power station is to form one of the important connecting links in connection with the grid system being carried out by the Central Electricity Board.
On approaching the power station by road from Birmingham the first objects which caught the eye of the visitor were the great cooling towers, whose outlines suggested colossal strength allied to beauty.
The power station is situated about nine miles from the centre of Birmingham and is located in the area of four of the large Midland coalfields, viz. : Staffordshire, Leicestershire, Nottinghamshire and Warwickshire.
The site, however, was mainly chosen for its water supply, as it is here that the filtered effluent from the Tame and Rea District Drainage Board Works, amounting to some 30 million gallons per day, is discharged into the River Tame. In our modern power stations water facilities are just as important as coal facilities, and the engineers concerned are to be congratulated on the stroke of genius which prompted them to use the filtered water from the Citys drainage system.
Situated as it is so many miles away from city life, this huge power station gives an impression of a silent giant willing to give forth its energy at the touch of a switch for women in their homes far away in Birmingham and the surrounding district.
A peep into the long control room, with its huge switches, left one with a feeling of awe at the way which man had tamed this wonderful force of electricity.
Mr. R. A. Chattock, City Electrical Engineer of Birmingham, and the other engineers responsible, have employed every device to produce electricity in the most economical way possible, and, amongst other things, have installed a pulverised fuel plant, which makes it possible to burn successfully and efficiently practically any type of fuel; low grade fuels, which otherwise would be regarded by collieries in the district as waste products, will be brought to the generating station at low cost, and will help in reducing the price of electricity.
England, and Birmingham in particular, might well be proud of such an achievement.
We are pleased, too, that women were honoured in such a wonderful event as the opening of this new power station, the Director and the Birmingham and Midlands Branch being invited to the ceremony.
Illustration by courtesy of "World Power."
