Unnamed: 9: Author writing about wayleaves for overhead electricity lines in villages.
transcription:
572
The Electrical Age
Wayleaves—or consents to carry the overhead electricity line over any piece of land have to be obtained for every pole or tower planted. “A little prejudice, a little misunderstanding,” Miss Partridge says, “may prevent rural development for many months or even years.”
By MARGARET PARTRIDGE, B.Sc., A.M.I.E.E.
In a pretty agricultural county in the West of England is an old-world village. It is a large village, typical of many. It boasts a beautiful old church, and it has a number of delightful houses, a few shops, some farms and one good sized works, where many of the inhabitants earn their living. Many visitors come to see this beauty spot, but few stay long, because few in these days like to pass their evenings in the light of candles or oil lamps. Ninety thousand woman hours are spent a year in the village trimming and cleaning oil lamps; one hundred-and-twenty thousand man hours or woman hours are spent a year in pumping water for the cleanliness of the village. The village would be cleaner if the factory chimney and the oil lamp were put out of use, and two hundred-and-ten thousand human hours a year would be saved if the villagers need not pump water by hand or trim and clean their oil lamps. All this the local Council know quite well, and great was the rejoicing when arrangements were made for the supply of electric light and power for the factory and houses from the nearest large town.
Just outside the village are two fair sized estates. The one belongs to a celebrated public body governed by a number of well-meaning gentlemen in London; the other belongs to a public-spirited squire, who lives in a well-kept house looking out over the wooded green pastures of his own property. The electric light main which is to feed the village must of necessity pass over one or other of the two estates. The proper way, the cheapest way, and the most inconspicuous way for the main to come would be across the estate of the public body, but—and this is the sad bit of my story—the public body wont allow a main to cross their land, even though they are offered a rent of £4,928* an acre per annum for the positions of the poles which would be planted there. The local Council, the Electricity Supply Authority, the householders of the village, all begged in vain, but the public body just refused to allow the main to come that way. The electricity undertaking was faced with three alternatives, either it might appeal for an enquiry to the Minister of Transport which would involve delay and heavy fees for the lawyers and experts, or it might re-plan the whole route and ask the owner of the other estate for his consent to cross, or, of course, it might give up the whole scheme.
They chose the second course, and as the squire was better endowed with public spirit than with pride of property he now has the pleasure of surveying from all his front windows a line of poles crossing the meadows below his house, and in a few weeks time our village will have its electricity supply. It is to be hoped that Mrs. Squire will be asked to perform the opening ceremony.
In this story everyone “lived happy ever after,” even the family who gave up their objections to an “eyesore” for the sake of their neighbours, because they learned the old, old truth, that things neat and workmanlike put up for use and not for display very soon cease to offend.
* This is paying 1/- per 9in. diameter pole per year—standard charge.

Unnamed: 9: Hypothetical figure used to illustrate historical changes in beauty standards.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 573

It is the new and unusual which is always called ugly. Things which the race have been accustomed to for generations are always thought beautiful, however much their lines depart from the accepted standards of beauty or stateliness. If Adam had had any conception of the meaning of beauty he would certainly have been shocked at the thought of clearing away the trees and dividing up the country into irregular patches of different colour bounded by banks or walls or thick grow-ing hedges; but think now how we love the fields and hedges of our agricultural districts. If Adam had been shown a picture of a windmill he would certainly have said: "Ugly, top-heavy, dispropor-tioned monster; away with it!" but time and use have endowed windmills with a traditional beauty quite hard to resist. I wonder how long before pylons will be admired for their undeniable strength and beauty of line and stateliness. Not for some time that is certain, but the time will certainly come.
The development of electricity in rural districts is only an economic possibility if the current is transmitted overhead. Wayleaves, or consents to carry the line over any piece of land have to be obtained for every pole or tower planted. The only authority empowered to compel a land-owner to grant a wayleave on any terms is the Minister of Transport, and he only does it after hearing all the arguments on both sides; on the one side why the necessity for choosing this particular field or route for the purposes of the line, and on the other what is the special inconvenience or objection to the route suggested. If Adam had been shown a picture of a windmill he would certainly have said: "Ugly, top-heavy, dispropor-tioned monster; away with it!" but time and use have endowed windmills with a traditional beauty quite hard to resist. I wonder how long before pylons will be admired for their undeniable strength and beauty of line and stateliness. Not for some time that is certain, but the time will certainly come.
The development of electricity in rural districts is only an economic possibility if the current is transmitted overhead. Wayleaves, or consents to carry the line over any piece of land have to be obtained for every pole or tower planted. The only authority empowered to compel a land-owner to grant a wayleave on any terms is the Minister of Transport, and he only does it after hearing all the arguments on both sides; on the one side why the necessity for choosing this particular field or route for the purposes of the line, and on the other what is the special inconvenience or objection to the route suggested. 574
The Electrical Age
is some ancient monument or special point of beauty to be preserved a compulsory order is seldom asked for or granted, but in other cases it is usually possible, after all methods of peaceful suasion have failed, for an electricity undertaking to get powers from the Minister to obtain compulsory wayleaves.
It should be understood that the rapidity and cheapness of rural electrical development is greatly dependant on local goodwill and public opinion. A little prejudice, a little misunderstanding, may prevent rural development for many months, or even years; but with goodwill all round and a healthy public outlook, electrical development in the country can and will go on apace, even under the existing confusing and rather out-of-date electricity laws.
Here is an opportunity for the women to foster the national common sense that in the end will over-ride the existing difficulties.

Reflections after hearing Mr. A. P. M. Flemings Lecture.
“Milestones in the Progress of Electricity.”
(BY A BRISTOL E.A.W. MEMBER).

When Offa, the Mercian,
Went for an excursion
To plunder the Severn for salmon and pike,
Said he “Will ye list all!
I covet this Bristol—
I’ll conquer the Wessex Land while on my hike.”

To-day with a story
(Tho’ not of Wars glory),
A Mercian has conquered the South with a charm.
He unfolded the history
Of modern-day mystery,
And told how a unit could cook and would warm.

The folk-lore of nations
Says weird incantations
Could summon a genii to “see the job through”;
But now magic proper,
Enshrined within copper,
Awaits on the threshold your bidding to do.

A long list of toilers
And beauty sleep spoilers
Have wrested from Nature the secrets she held.
Like Knights of the Grail,
They trekked in the trail
Of Science, and therein great visions beheld—

Vast dynamos turning,
Live currents were churning,
That shot out their tendrils from shore unto shore;
Industrial, domestic,
It all was electric,
And problems of labour were heard of no more.

There is coming, he says,
The Halcyon-days,
When he in a tele-ray pays us a visit.
He need not come nigher
Than by his own fire,
And THINK OUT the knowledge our members
solicit.

While we on our side
At home also abide,
And THINK IN the wisdom—perhaps in our
bed;
Or else like a flower
In some leafy bower
Will bask in a Sun-ray suspended o’erhead.

We left in amazement
To repair to our casement,
And ponder on what all our future would be.
Our minds being finite,
We cannot divine quite
What wonders will startle 2000 A.D.

transcription:
The Electrical Age
575
“Want to Shee Wheels go Wound.” A Page for Girl Guides.
BY GLADYS SHARP.
Describes how some modern Budges and Toddies saw the inside of an electric iron, the mysteries of the suction cleaner, and learned why water in an electric kettle became hot . . . .
In the magic world which lies between the covers of books there exist two children, by name Budge and Toddie. You may have met them and be wondering what connection they can possibly have with an article on electricity, since they existed when its uses were only faintly being guessed at.
Well, they had an unfortunate uncle, who one day showed them his watch, and was for ever after pestered with the request: “Want to shee wheels go wound.”
Now that cry, in slightly different language, is in the mouths of most people, and has been since wheels were first discovered. Small boys have pulled clocks to pieces and put them together again—with the exception of a few insignificant parts—from time immemorial. It is only the desire to “shee wheels go wound” which prompts scientists to probe into the mysteries of the world. The astronomer who gazes at the stars through a vast telescope is not so much a very learned man as a small, curious boy, wanting to see the wheels of other worlds going round.
And so it happened that the Budges and Toddies of the E.A.W. gathered together and echoed this age-old cry and a kind uncle was discovered who came, much like Santa Claus, armed with huge boxes, which contained, not toys, nor yet watches, but electric suction cleaners, hair dryers, toasters, kettles and irons of many sizes, weights and makes. These being placed before them, they were, for the moment,
quieted by the shining exteriors and wondrous patterns, but anon the cry was repeated: “Want to shee wheels go wound,” and from about him the kind uncle produced screw-drivers and pliers, and the Budges and Toddies proceeded to wreck the beautiful articles.
They exposed the soles of irons and the mysteries of suction cleaners, and the reason why water in a kettle becomes hot was a secret no longer. And as they did these things the all-wise uncle explained in very simple language the meaning of the strange things that met their eyes and told them of the things people should not attempt to do.
Would you, too, hear these things, and see, in a pen picture, some of the wonders that were unearthed by the magical screw-drivers and pliers? Read, then, an eye witness’s account.
Picture to yourself the joy of removing the handle and top cover of an iron. Inside mine was a piece of iron that closely followed the shape of the cover, and below this again was the heating element, consisting of special wire wound on mica in the shape of the iron, the whole being enclosed between two thin sheets of mica, which prevent the electricity from coming into contact with the frame of the iron and so giving a shock.
And here, by the way, the uncle paused to explain that while electricity is safer than houses even these days, it really is not wise to do your ironing electrically while you are sitting in your bath! He, so he informed us, would never think of doing

Unnamed: 9: Man explaining appliances who didnt understand hair-dryers professional use.
transcription:
576
The Electrical Age
such a thing! You see, electricity always runs to earth, and if, by any chance, there is some fault on your iron so that the electricity in it escapes from its mica covers and runs round the frame, immediately you take up the iron, if you are the nearest way to earth, it will use you. And if you are in your bath you are in contact through the water, which is a good conductor of electricity, with the water pipes, which, as you know, run straight to the ground. If you will substitute the words " electric fire " for electric iron you will see that there is wisdom at the root of the warning, which, boiled down, amounts to: never touch electrical apparatus while you are in contact with water pipes, either directly or indirectly. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred it would be quite safe, and in the hundredth there might be a fault on the apparatus and you would get a shock. Forewarned is forearmed, so dont smooth out the waves in your bath water with an electric iron!
After irons, we dissected coffee percolators and kettles and found that the elements were very much like those of the iron, with the wire wound on mica and the whole clamped to the bottom of the appliance, but brains had been at work in another direction.
Have you ever let a kettle boil dry? So have I! But it cant happen again. On any electric kettle worthy of the name is fitted some sort of gadget which switches off the electricity when the heat of the kettle becomes too great. This is mostly contrived by means of solder which melts and, in one case, releases a spring which pushes off the connector of the kettle and so breaks the electrical circuit, and, in other cases, operates a switch which has the same effect. Now, if you should talk overlong with your interesting guest you will not be greeted by a buckled, discoloured kettle when you finally remember it.
There came a slight difference of opinion at this stage. Our explicit explainer, being a man, could find no use for a hair-dryer, and imagined vaguely that all women had their hair washed by professionals. Possibly he had noticed that since the day of bobs and shingles hairdressers ride only in Rolls-Royces, and so had drawn his own conclusions! Owing to this altercation the hair-dryers were never opened up, and so remain all the more fascinating for having kept the secret of their success.

Showing the way the modern Budges and Toddies dismantled the electric iron to see how it worked
From his box this modern Father Xmas finally produced toasters; toasters that simply toast and toast and toast, regardless of everything, and toasters, good souls, which bear in mind the frailties of human nature and save many a harmless piece of white bread from assuming a delicate shade of black. Here was a real chance for the Budges and Toddies to get to work. From the depths of fine imaginations they produced the necessary bread and put it into the hole between the heating elements, for these toasters cook both sides of the bread at once. transcription:
The Electrical Age
577
ticking started, much like the clock in the alarming Peter Pan crocodile. In one model, at the end of sufficient time for the bread to toast, the delicious brown morsel was popped up, like a Jack-in-the-box, above the toaster out of reach of the heat, simply asking to be removed and eaten. In another it suddenly jumped out at the side with a " here-I-am ; arent-I-lovely " sort of expression.
But if you are one of those people who imagine you have only to turn your back for a single moment for the toast to be blackened beyond remedy, just press down the lever of one of these magic toasters and see how long it really takes. Electric Kitchen in the R.101.
for tea, etc., in addition to the 40-gallon hot water storage tank.
Having regard to the importance of weight limitation, the makers of all this Xcel apparatus, The Automatic Telephone Manufacturing Co., Ltd., are to be specially congratulated on the fact that the total weight of the completed equipment comes within 10 lbs. of the limit set by the Air Ministry.

Unnamed: 9: Author describing a visit to an electrically heated village school
transcription:
The Electrical Age
578
SCHOOLGIRLS AND ELECTRICITY.
Electricity in the Village School.
By THE EDITOR.
During a beautiful sunny day last autumn I sped over the Sussex Downs, which have now become so famous in con- nection with the Pylons con- troversy, to see a Village School which was being heated by Electricity.
Nestling in the beautiful Downs at Rottingdean, I found the Village School had an up-to-date installation of tubular heating of the "Unity" type installed in place of anthracite stoves, which had been considered by the Board of Management to be most unsatisfactory.
A visit to this Village School and a talk with the mistress and children—but especially with the caretaker—would convince many of the croakers of the value of the Pylons and Overhead Lines even on the Sussex Downs.
The school mistress and children ex- pressed their great satisfaction of the new heating, but the most interesting tribute was given by the old caretaker, who had already realised the tremendous advantage of the new system.
No longer did he need to get out of a warm bed on cold mornings to replenish the anthracite stove hours before school opened in order that the school house should be warm when the children arrived.
He also commented upon the ease with which the school could be cleaned in these days and how that now every child in the class-room is warm, whereas before only the few who could get near the anthracite stove were really happy during winter days.
The Schoolroom is heated by the Unity Tubular Heating.
The installation is thermostatically con- trolled, which also intrigued the caretaker considerably, as it was the first kind of heating which he had come across "which looked after itself."
It might be thought that such an instal- lation was expensive, but I was assured by Mr. Christie, the Brighton Electrical En- gineer, that the supply is obtained on a sliding scale from 1d. down to 1/2d. per unit, and there is little doubt that the cost of operating this installation will compare most favourably with any other method of heating class-rooms.
The ventilation of the room is greatly improved, and the atmosphere is in no way vitiated by the dry heat from closed stoves fired with coke or anthracite, the heat from which it was impossible to effectively control.
As a result of this installation two other Rottingdean boarding schools are consider- ing similar schemes for heating.

Unnamed: 9: Opened the new Varndean Municipal Secondary School for Girls school
transcription:
The Electrical Age 579
Leaving beautiful Rottingdean, my kind hosts took me on to see the new Varndean Municipal Secondary School for Girls, which was opened some three years ago under the auspices of the Brighton Education Committee by the Duchess of Atholl. This school is designed on the latest principles to afford the maximum daylight and efficient ventilation, the special feature being the domestic economy side of the instruction. Due chiefly to the enterprise of Mr. Christie and the Brighton Electricity Supply Department, the school has been equipped with a range of electric cookers, complete with meters on each circuit, and the girls are given every facility for becoming acquainted with the use of electricity for cooking and other purposes. A chat with Miss E. V. Ellis, M.A., headmistress, revealed the fact that the girls are given some instruction on electricity both in the physics laboratory and also during the housecraft course. It was interesting to find that this division of instruction on electricity had been working very smoothly and satisfactorily—this would seem a model on which all instruction on this important subject should be given to girls in the future—the physics mistress being responsible for instructing her pupils on the theory of the subject, while the practical application is taught in the housecraft centre.
Shewing the girls at work in the Varndean Secondary School, which is equipped with electrical apparatus.

Unnamed: 9: Author of the article regarding artificial production of ultra-violet rays.
transcription:
580

The Electrical Age

The Artificial Production of Ultra-Violet Rays*
By G. E. L. ROWORTH, A.M.I.E.E., C.E.E.

Now that winter is upon us with the consequent lack of natural sunlight and ultra-violet rays, this article by Mr. Roworth on the artificial production of these valuable health-giving rays will be of special interest.

As readers of this Journal are particularly interested in the electrical side of the artificial production of Ultra-Violet Rays, I shall only deal very briefly with the therapeutic and medical aspects. It is perhaps unnecessary to say that natural ultra-violet radiation comes to us from the sun, and I believe that about 17 per cent. of the total radiation known to be coming to us from the sun is in the form of what we call ultra-violet rays. As is well known, these rays emanate from that portion of the solar spectrum just beyond the violet end of the visible rays of the spectrum.
This form of energy is radiated from bodies or gases when they are at very high temperatures. The temperature of the sun is estimated at about 5,530°C. (or nearly 10,000°F.).
These rays do not penetrate the smoky air of cities, and I was reading the other day that in the city of Edinburgh a well-known doctor had made careful observations by scientific means of the ultra-violet rays from the sun over a long period, and it is a somewhat disquieting fact that between November, 1925, and March, 1926, he was unable to record any ultra-violet rays whatever from the sun. But another observer during those months was able, at Stirling, to record very small quantities of ultra-violet radiation. No wonder, therefore, that man has attempted to produce these rays artificially.
As already mentioned, very high temperatures must be employed, and the electric arc is the most convenient and suitable means, as the temperature of an electric arc is approximately 3,000°C. (or nearly 5,500°F.).
When the separated carbons of an arc lamp are rendered incandescent by the passage of an electric current, the ultra-violet radiation given off is precisely similar in nature to that received from the sun.
Instead of using ordinary carbons, however, one may substitute pencils of solid tungsten, when the output of ultra-violet radiation is much increased, current for current.
In the case of open arcs the amount of ultra-violet radiation given off is very strikingly affected by the voltage across the arc, as will appear from the following quotation from a Government publication:
"A 75 ampere arc working at 70 volts gave 70 units of ultra-violet; at 80 volts it gave 180 units; at 90 volts, 245 units; and at 95 volts, 253 units."
It will be apparent, therefore, that it is of very great importance to be able to regulate the voltage across the arc of a lamp used for producing these rays, and personally I feel that a voltmeter to read the arc voltage when installing ultra-violet arc lamps should be supplied.
Instead of open type arcs, however, one may employ the mercury vapour arc in a vacuum tube, and this tube must be of quartz, as ordinary glass would not allow the ultra-violet rays to pass.
Such a mercury-vapour arc gives a very much greater output of ultra-violet than

With regard to current consumption, the atmospheric type of mercury arc takes about 4 1/2 ampères when starting and about 2 1/4 ampères when running. The vacuum type of mercury arc takes about 9 ampères at first, which falls to about 3 ampères after five minutes; they can be used on any direct or alternating current supply from 100 V. to 500 V., of course, with a suit-able series resistance in the circuit. From 10 to as much as 75 ampères are used with carbon arc lamps, but only about 4 ampères in the case of an arc struck between pencils of solid tungsten.

The voltage across a mercury vapour arc on striking is zero, then it steadily rises till it reaches 165 in the case of the D.C. burner and 180 in the case of the A.C. burner. This takes about 5 minutes, after which treatment may be commenced.

With regard to the therapeutic uses to which these rays are put, you will perhaps have read the book by Dr. Russell, of Newcastle-on-Tyne, in which he mentions no less than 137 diseases which have been treated successfully by exposure to these rays, but it is in diseases like rickets and neurasthenia where the most startling results have been obtained, and, gener-ally, they have been found to increase body weight, to increase the rate of growth, and to improve the blood and glands where those were below normal.

The whole resistance of the body to infection is raised and a general toning up and feeling of well-being results.

The first dose is usually given for 2 1/2 minutes, at a distance of 36 inches for either adults or children, then gradually increased at each subsequent treatment. Care must be taken to measure accurately the distance of the patient from the lamp, as the law of inverse squares applies, i.e., the intensity varies inversely as the square of the distance separating lamp from patient.

So far as is known no permanent injury need be feared in the case of an over-exposure to these rays—such as would follow from an over-exposure to X-rays—I saw the report recently of a case of a man who was in the habit of exposing himself in his own bedroom for about 10 minutes daily to the rays, and who, on one occasion, fell asleep and remained exposed for 70 minutes. He suffered severely with skin eruptions, irritation, etc., and it was some 6 or 7 weeks before he was convalescent; but he recovered completely as one does from natural sunburn.

Of course, it is essential to protect the eyes during treatment with goggles fitted with glass opaque to these rays.

Ordinary window-glass obstructs the passage of these rays, and a special form of glass has now been devised called vita glass, which transmits the rays, and which has been supplied to several sanatoria.

The cost of apparatus ranges from £12 to about £60 or so, and in some places current for this purpose is supplied at the rate of 1/2d. to 1 1/4d. per Board of Trade unit, which means that a 20 minutes treatment with mercury or tungsten arc would cost about 1/2d. for current.

There is, of course, no connection what-ever between ultra-violet rays and the so-called violet ray machines which are used by hairdressers and others.

No communication on this subject would be complete without the mention of Professor Finsen, who, in 1893, first used a carbon arc lamp for artificially producing ultra-violet rays, and whose world-famed " Finsen Light " has been much used for the treatment of lupus and also of tuber-culosis.

Unnamed: 9: Miss FOSTER JEFFERY described the Smoke Abatement Exhibition at Manchester.
transcription:
584
The Electrical Age
Smoke Abatement Exhibition at Manchester.
Described by Miss FOSTER JEFFERY, LL.B.
(Hon. Sec., Manchester and Salford District Branch. E.A.W.)
I do not know whether the Smoke Abate-
ment League had any ulterior motive in
choosing Manchester as the site of their
conference, but certainly on the day that
the Manchester Branch of the E.A.W. paid
their official visit the sky was obscured by
a pall of smoke and fog the whole day
long.
And it was by no means gratifying to
learn that the main reason for our smoke-
laden atmosphere was not the occasional
black smoke from the factories, which up to
now have been held solely responsible, but
the owners and users of the domestic coal
fire.
In a lecture describing the effects of
"Domestic Smoke and the Way to Avoid
it," Mr. Arnold Marsh, M.Sc., told us that
out of each £1 spent on coal we obtain 2/-
worth of heat, create much unnecessary
labour and drudgery, and add materially
to the death roll from pneumonia and
influenza.

Unnamed: 9: Host on the very delightful day at Farne Islands.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 585

After such an indictment it was not sur-
prising that everyone visited the Hall of
Electricity to see the alternative method of
heating and cooking. This is where the
electrical method scored heavily, for
whereas the smokeless fuel and gas enthu-
siasts were able to show that you could
heat a room or cook a meal by those means,
the electricity demonstrators showed not
only how you can take the electric radiator
with you from room to room and plug it
in where you want it, but how electricity
will do your housework for you and will
clean your carpets and wash your clothes,
as well as cook the meals.

Every type of electrical appliance was
on view for us to see. The Corporation
told us of their excellent hiring terms,
which avoid that bugbear, the initial out-
lay, and the demonstrators showed us how
to get the best results at the cheapest cost.

Personally I felt that electricity is the
only solution of the domestic problem. We
saw the other methods side by side with
our own, but, by reason of its cleanliness
and convenience, electricity stood out as
the " Mothers Help " of the future.

It is to be hoped that people will realise
the danger to the community in continu-
ing to use the coal fire, and will adopt the
electric fire in the near future without the
necessity for any such Act of Parliament
as was passed in 1313, when it was decreed
that the users of sea coal should be heavily
fined for a first offence, but that on a
second offence " their furnaces should be
taken away from them and destroyed."

The Press hailed the members of the
E.A.W. as the pioneers in a " Healthy
Homes and Anti-Drudgery Campaign."
There was no E.A.W. in 1313; let us show
that to-day women will take steps to
ensure the cleanliness of their homes and
the health of the public without any need
to resort to compulsory measures passed
by Parliament.

Unnamed: 9: Author of an article discussing electrical heating methods in homes.
transcription:
586
The Electrical Age
ELECTRICAL HEATING IN THE HOME.
Panel Heating, Tubular Heating and Electric Fires.
By Mrs. WALTER LAWSON.
Last year I wrote an article on electric fires, and I am now going to deal with the more general subject of electric heating in the home, as there are several supplementary methods of electric heating coming to the fore, the chief of which are panel heating and tubular heating.
These are slow heat methods as compared with the electric fire, which is a quick heat method.
The elements are run at a much lower temperature, something below black heat, and can be placed anywhere without the least risk of fire.
Such a system is valuable where equable room temperatures are essential, and if used in conjunction with small electric fires would probably form the ideal method of heating the larger rooms of all-electric houses.
PANEL HEATING.
Up to the present this method has been used chiefly in heating schemes for big institutions and for billiard rooms, but there is no reason why it should not be generally used in all-electric houses.
Morganite Panels on Plate Heaters are dark grey in colour, but can be painted to suit ones decoration. The panels consist of a ceramic composition, in which the elements are embedded.
In order to obtain the maximum efficiency, these panels should be hung against
the wall and fixed to brackets (with special bolts) which tilt the top forwards. This counteracts the tendency of the heat to rise.
Portable Morganite radiators (these must not be confused with electric fires, which are often called radiators) can also be had for floor use in many designs, finished in enamel, or in antique brass perforated
The Dulrae PANEL Installation at the Cameo Theatre, Charing Cross Road, London.
casing, and also, if required, with wire protectors. Up to the present these are mostly in use on first-class passenger ships.
The Dulrae System of Panel Heating is embedded in plaster behind the ceiling or walls. It is of a low loading and is very effectively insulated. It has been installed in a number of private houses and offices with great success.

Unnamed: 6: maker of the Angelus electric fire
Unnamed: 9: Maker of the Angelus electric fire mentioned in the text
transcription:
The Electrical Age 587

TUBULAR HEATING.
Tubular Heating consists of heating elements enclosed in steel tubes supported at each end by metal feet. These are invaluable when placed by the side of the skirting-board, in cold corners, or under window seats, and can be had in various lengths up to 17ft., and as they can be obtained in mahogany, oak, silver, or black finish, it is easy to match ones decoration.
This tubing is also made up into portable radiators. Four short lengths of the tubing placed one above the other, with spaces between, are held in position by metal supports and feet at either end, and the whole can be lifted where required by means of a handle at the top.
These heating tubes are also made up into towel-rails. This method serves the double purpose of warming the bathroom and airing towels or clothes.
Small wall towel-rails can also be had, and in addition fixtures for the airing cupboards are obtainable.
By use of a thermostat the temperature of rooms warmed with these appliances can be automatically controlled, and kept at uniform heat; current can be saved, and the temperature can be set for any degree required.

ELECTRIC FIRES.
As regards electric fires, I only know of two new models which have come out this autumn, one is the Angelus, made by Charles Joyner, and the other is an improved model of Berrys Magicoal.
The Angelus is most artistic, and is suitable for a drawing-room or boudoir.
The electric elements which form the fire are placed low down, and in a horizontal position, while the high sides and back of silver-coloured metal terminate in a point which curves forwards and holds a partly concealed lamp, which throws a ruddy gleam on to the metal sides and back. The effect is very pretty, while the fire itself throws out a good heat.
The new Magicoal model has the imitation glass coal panel in front that we are used to associate with this make of fire, and behind that is a concealed heating element, the glow from which is reflected on to a back of beaten copper. As in last years model, a rotor on the top of a lamp, behind the glass coal panel, stimulates a natural fire-light flicker.
[Image: The new Magicoal Model referred to by Mrs. Lawson.]

The Electrical Age 587

TUBULAR HEATING.
Tubular Heating consists of heating elements enclosed in steel tubes supported at each end by metal feet. These are invaluable when placed by the side of the skirting-board, in cold corners, or under window seats, and can be had in various lengths up to 17ft., and as they can be obtained in mahogany, oak, silver, or black finish, it is easy to match ones decoration.
This tubing is also made up into portable radiators. Four short lengths of the tubing placed one above the other, with spaces between, are held in position by metal supports and feet at either end, and the whole can be lifted where required by means of a handle at the top.
These heating tubes are also made up into towel-rails. This method serves the double purpose of warming the bathroom and airing towels or clothes.
Small wall towel-rails can also be had, and in addition fixtures for the airing cupboards are obtainable.
By use of a thermostat the temperature of rooms warmed with these appliances can be automatically controlled, and kept at uniform heat; current can be saved, and the temperature can be set for any degree required.

ELECTRIC FIRES.
As regards electric fires, I only know of two new models which have come out this autumn, one is the Angelus, made by Charles Joyner, and the other is an improved model of Berrys Magicoal.
The Angelus is most artistic, and is suitable for a drawing-room or boudoir.
The electric elements which form the fire are placed low down, and in a horizontal position, while the high sides and back of silver-coloured metal terminate in a point which curves forwards and holds a partly concealed lamp, which throws a ruddy gleam on to the metal sides and back. The effect is very pretty, while the fire itself throws out a good heat.
The new Magicoal model has the imitation glass coal panel in front that we are used to associate with this make of fire, and behind that is a concealed heating element, the glow from which is reflected on to a back of beaten copper. The Electrical Age

A Psychological Home of the Future.

An account of a new Model Hygienic Home—which is, of course, electrically
equipped—designed by Miss Grace Cope, A.I.H., and opened by H.R.H. Princess
Louise, Duchess of Argyll.

Described by HILDA L. DOVER, B.Sc.

Situated in the most delightful rural country, "Stewartby," the Model Hygienic House, built and furnished under the direction of Miss Grace Cope, A.I.H., is a most charming, restful and fascinating home. This beautiful little house was formally opened by H.R.H. Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll, on a dull typical November day. But as soon as one entered the hall all thoughts of the external elements vanished. The soft electric lights and the Ferranti Electric Fires gave an air of rest and comfort, whilst the Jarrah wood floors of a mellow pinky brown colour, kept clean and polished by an electrical polisher, added to the warmth.

On the left of the porch, a sitting room, fitted with large vita-glass doors, decorated in gold and blue, invited one to rest awhile. The walls of this room had been sprayed with paint graduating from dull gold to a soft primrose as the coved ceilings were reached. In one corner of this room a reading seat lit by a soft panel of artificial light was most inviting. Additional lighting was provided by a standard lamp, fitted with a yellow nacrolaque shade. The settee and chairs were upholstered in blue, and a charming low grey wood table was just the right height from which to take ones tea. What more restful atmosphere could one desire than this whilst waiting for the gong to sound before passing into a dining room decorated in a most entrancing shade of Mediterranean blue. Here again the walls were sprayed with paint, this time blue, dark near the floor, and pale as the ceiling was reached. A little gold was sprayed on top of the blue to harmonise with the gold celanese fabric curtains. The artificial lighting was soft and becoming. It was recessed in the top of a naturally finished walnut overmantel. The fireplace was furnished with an easily removable hand-made wrought iron basket and dogs, the only coal fire in the house. There was not a picture in the house, only several panels of oriental needlework, and yet the saying "A room without pictures is like a house without windows" did not apply.

In the wall dividing the dining room from the kitchen was a large cupboard which communicated with a most efficient looking kitchen. This cupboard formed a serving hatch, and an electric cooker stood alongside it in the kitchen. The floor was covered with marbled rubber, which was curved up the walls to avoid a sharp corner and the consequent collection of dirt. The woodwork was stained yellow and red to cheer the housewife on her way; whilst the kitchen was lighted by day by a large window dressed with attractive curtains and by an opal lamp when daylight faded. Under the large window was a deep porcelain sink fitted with chromium-plated washerless taps. The taps were supplied by copper pipes with hot water from an enamel-faced coke boiler in winter and by an electric immersion heater in summer. On each side of the sink was a large draining board fitted with a rail for a tea towel. Another attractive feature to this kitchen, where the minimum movement imaginable was required, was a large

The whole of the first floor, except the bathroom, was of stained deal; in some rooms the staining cleverly represented carpets. The bathroom was covered with rubber, so one could splash to ones hearts content. Here the porcelain fittings were of a soft primrose colour with chromium-plated washerless taps. The recesses in the wall for the soap, and the electrically-heated mirror fixed in just the correct position, were great assets.
In addition to these rooms were three bedrooms with flush built-in cupboards; fixed wash basins with hot and cold water; fixed wall mirrors well illuminated on each side by candle-type electric lights; and comfortable beds with a drop pendant over each. In such a house bad tempers or sulkiness should be out of the question, but provision has been made to banish them should a day in town or a truculent tradesman have disturbed the peace. transcription:
The Electrical Age 591

Some Party Dishes for New Year Festivities.

By MARY MACKIRDY
(Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow, and Author of "Recipes for You.")

Sandwiches.
Of sandwiches there is an endless variety, but more so in America, where the possibilities of sandwiches seem to be fully understood; there is the large lunch sandwich which is a meal in itself, not the uncomfortable sandwich with its rather aggressive filling which always seemed at enmity with its surroundings, but one with all the necessaries of a meal. The most interesting of all are the wonderfully dainty sandwiches which have the appearance of a mosaic. From these, a whole loaf may be built up; the crust is taken from the loaf, which is cut in very thin slices; these are buttered and spread with various fillings, differing in colour if possible, and a contrasting colour - it may be with ginger, prunes, cress, pickled walnut, to give only a few - is arranged symmetrically on the slices. The loaf is built up covered with a damp cloth and a board or plate put on top with a weight; after a few hours the loaf is cut the reverse way, which leaves the sandwiches with the cut sides to the top; they are then cut in rounds, fingers, or as may be desired.
The same idea is carried out, but on a less elaborate scale, with thin slices of brown bread sandwiched between two slices of white, then cut in the usual fashion.

Two Delightful Sandwich Mixtures.
(1.) 2 tomatoes, skinned and chopped, 1 egg, 1/2 oz. butter, 1 oz. lean ham finely chopped, a tiny piece of onion grated, salt, pepper.
Cook the ham in the butter for a few minutes, without browning, add the other ingredients and stir over the stove until the mixture thickens. When cool spread on thin slices of buttered white or brown bread.
(2.) 1/2 teacupful sugar, 1/4 teacupful water boiled for a few minutes, 1 banana (chopped), 1 tablespoonful pine kernels or walnuts (chopped), a few dates (chopped), lemon.
Add the ingredients to the syrup and squeeze in as much lemon as gives a good sharp flavour. Use with brown or white bread.

A Sardine Savoury.
Little rounds of good pastry, a tin of sardines, 2 ozs. butter, salt, cayenne, carmine, lemon, olives, cress.
Sieve the sardines, having first taken away skin and bone, pound in the butter, seasoning, a little lemon and carmine. Put the mixture into a pointed strainer (a little one), and with the handle of a spoon press the butter through, taking it off as it comes through in tassels and arrange it, sufficient for each, on the pastry. Put a stoned olive in the centre of each and garnish with cress. The same idea may be carried out with anchovies and other garnishes.

A Marsh Mallow Sweet.
1 teacupful boiling water, 1 teacupful sugar, 1/2 oz. gelatine, 3 whites of eggs, 1 teaspoonful vanilla essence, 1 teaspoonful lemon juice, about 1/4 lb. ratafia or macaroon biscuits, 1/4 pint double cream.
Add water to gelatine, dissolve, add sugar and cool, but do not allow to set.
Whisk the whites very stiffly, add carefully the cool gelatine and flavouring, turn into a shallow tin that has been rinsed with cold water, put aside to set.
Sieve the biscuits and turn the marsh mallow right out on the crumbs, cut it in rounds or other shapes, and coat with the crumbs.
Whip the cream and pile in the centre of a pretty dish, arrange the marsh mallow round and decorate with cream, chopped pistachio nuts and crystallised fruits.
The scraps may be cut in small bits and mixed with the cream.

Little Pear Trifles.
Put the ice cream or jelly into individual dishes, then tinned or bottled pears cut in pieces; cover the top with a good custard or chocolate sauce and decorate with whipped cream.

Chocolate Sauce.
1 1/2 gills milk, 2 or 3 ozs. grated chocolate, 1 heaped teaspoonful cornflour, 1 tablespoonful sugar, 1/2 teaspoonful vanilla, 2 tablespoonfuls cream.
Put all in pan, except the cream, stir till boiling; add the cream; if ice is used, pour the sauce hot over it and serve immediately; if jelly, it must be cold.
Ice cream with hot chocolate is rather attractive and makes a delightful sweet.
Many sweets of this type are made using fruits of various kinds, custards, cream, and other mixtures, the tops being decorated with fresh or crystallised fruits, confections, whipped cream, etc.

The following recipe has been sent to us by Mrs. Dyche, of Birmingham.

WELSH SCONES.
1 lb. Flour.
6 ozs. Butter or Margarine.
4 ozs. Castor Sugar.
Currants and Milk.

Rub flour, butter and sugar all together, add currants, and mix with milk; roll out on pastry board, about 1/2 in. thickness, and cut with pastry-cutter into shapes. Bake on top of electric stove, on closed hot plates, till nicely brown, then turn with knife and repeat. Switch on at low heat, and afterwards off. Care should be taken not to overheat the plate.

OVERSEAS MEMBERS.

The E.A.W. continues to enrol numbers of Members from Australia, New Zealand, and other countries. The Director will soon need an Electric Aeroplane in order to fit in her organising work in this country and the possibility of such work Overseas!

Put the mixture into a pointed strainer (a little one), and with the handle of a spoon press the butter through, taking it off as it comes through in tassels and arrange it, sufficient for each, on the pastry. Put a stoned olive in the centre of each and garnish with cress. The same idea may be carried out with anchovies and other garnishes.

A Marsh Mallow Sweet.
1 teacupful boiling water, 1 teacupful sugar, 1/2 oz. gelatine, 3 whites of eggs, 1 teaspoonful vanilla essence, 1 teaspoonful lemon juice, about 1/4 lb. ratafia or macaroon biscuits, 1/4 pint double cream.
Add water to gelatine, dissolve, add sugar and cool, but do not allow to set.
Whisk the whites very stiffly, add carefully the cool gelatine and flavouring, turn into a shallow tin that has been rinsed with cold water, put aside to set.
Sieve the biscuits and turn the marsh mallow right out on the crumbs, cut it in rounds or other shapes, and coat with the crumbs.
Whip the cream and pile in the centre of a pretty dish, arrange the marsh mallow round and decorate with cream, chopped pistachio nuts and crystallised fruits.
The scraps may be cut in small bits and mixed with the cream.

Little Pear Trifles.
Put the ice cream or jelly into individual dishes, then tinned or bottled pears cut in pieces; cover the top with a good custard or chocolate sauce and decorate with whipped cream.

Chocolate Sauce.
1 1/2 gills milk, 2 or 3 ozs. grated chocolate, 1 heaped teaspoonful cornflour, 1 tablespoonful sugar, 1/2 teaspoonful vanilla, 2 tablespoonfuls cream.
Put all in pan, except the cream, stir till boiling; add the cream; if ice is used, pour the sauce hot over it and serve immediately; if jelly, it must be cold.
Ice cream with hot chocolate is rather attractive and makes a delightful sweet.
Many sweets of this type are made using fruits of various kinds, custards, cream, and other mixtures, the tops being decorated with fresh or crystallised fruits, confections, whipped cream, etc.

The following recipe has been sent to us by Mrs. Dyche, of Birmingham.

WELSH SCONES.
1 lb. Flour.
6 ozs. Butter or Margarine.
4 ozs. Castor Sugar.
Currants and Milk.

Rub flour, butter and sugar all together, add currants, and mix with milk; roll out on pastry board, about 1/2 in. thickness, and cut with pastry-cutter into shapes. Bake on top of electric stove, on closed hot plates, till nicely brown, then turn with knife and repeat. Switch on at low heat, and afterwards off. Care should be taken not to overheat the plate.

The Electrical Age 593
All-Electric Radio. By E. C. Ambler.

One of the chief obstacles in the path of Radio progress has been the bugbear of accumulators and batteries. Time and again one hears the would-be purchaser of a Radio set ask how long the batteries will last and is not there a set with batteries that will not need replacement or charging. The picture of the wireless enthusiast staggering to the charging station with his battery has provided many cartoonists with the material for humour, while the propensity of accumulators to run down, when particularly required for a special programme, is proverbial.

Although the idea of using electricity supply mains for providing power to operate a Radio Set was conceived and (in certain instances) carried out some years ago, it was not until comparatively recently that the advantages of mains operated sets were available to the public.

The main difficulty which was considered was the problem of A.C. mains. At first sight the design of an instrument which would provide the necessary current from D.C. mains presented no difficulty. It was soon found, however, that whereas it was a comparatively simple matter to transform and rectify A.C. mains suitably, the use of D.C. for the purpose introduced a variety of resistances, chokes and smoothing circuits to neutralise commutator ripple and other imperfections of the supply.

The first battery " eliminators," as they are called, were accordingly suitable for A.C. supply mains only. Naturally they were far from perfect, the two most prevalent troubles being " hum " and " motor-boating." " Hum " from an eliminator takes the form of a steady buzzing in the loud speaker, and it can only be cured by adjustments in the smoothing circuit being made. " Motor-boating," as the name implies, is a trouble which produces a continuous popping sound rendering pleasurable listening an impossibility. The remedies for this defect are too involved and complicated to be discussed in this article. Happily, however, in the newest eliminators these troubles are very rare.

It is a short step from adapting existing sets for mains operation, to designing a set which incorporates the necessary apparatus; but a development was forthcoming which greatly facilitated the latter operation—the introduction of the indirectly-heated cathode valve. The incorporation of this type of valve in a set does away with the necessity of rectifying the A.C. mains to heat the filaments. These wonderful valves are provided with a very small " jacket " or " heater " round the filament. This jacket is heated by passing a current through it, and the jacket in its turn heats the actual filament sufficiently to provide the necessary emission.

A typical All-British All-Electric Receiver which is supplied for use with either A.C. or D.C. mains.

An up-to-date A.C. all-electric set, then, embodies an eliminator, consisting of a transformer to reduce the voltage from the mains, a rectifier (usually a gas-filled rectifying valve) to convert the Alternating

This side of the apparatus provides the High Tension and Grid Bias currents, while the heaters of the indirectly-heated cathode valves are supplied with unrectified current from a tapping on the transformer. A D.C. set is constructed similarly, but in place of the transformer and rectifying valve resistances are used to break down the voltage, while the smoothing circuit is more elaborate.
The operation of an all-electric set is simplicity itself. To quote the words of one advertiser, you merely "Plug in, then tune in." The use of mains in Radio sets has again raised that frequently discussed (and dismissed) question of "Danger." An all-electric Radio set is no more dangerous than an electric vacuum cleaner or radiator and it is certainly as essential as either of these appliances to the attainment of comfort in the modern home.

Unnamed: 9: Author and Installation Engineer at Hendon Electric Supply Co.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 599
A Page for the Electrical Housewife.
Useful hints on fuses and other matters for the housewife who has an electric cooker.
By Mr. H. BOURNE, Installation Engineer to the Hendon Electric Supply Co.
Users of mechanical and electrical appliances may be broadly divided into two classes—those capable of helping themselves out of minor difficulties, and those who rely upon others. It is rather a remarkable fact that each type appears to get on as satisfactorily as the other, human nature being such that it is usually willing to help those who either cannot or will not help themselves. Few of us are able to resist the temptation to help the lady struggling with a muddy car tyre by the roadside on a wet day, and feel well rewarded with the smile that usually accompanies the thanks at the end of the proceedings. Those who are fortunate enough to possess electric cookers must fall within one of the two grades referred to.
To those who possess some mechanical and electrical knowledge the matter of the renewal of a blown fuse should not prove difficult, but a little advice on the subject may not be out of place. Get to know beforehand where the fuses are situated and do not commence to pull the cooker to pieces in an endeavour to discover their hiding place when one has blown. Keep suitable fuse wire handy to the cooker so that loss of time will be avoided when the failure occurs. The resourceful person who renews fuses with hairpins and metal meat skewers is not to be admired, as it is so much better and safer to have the correct size of wire available! A general hunt for the family screw-driver or pliers is not an unusual event on such occasions, whereas a screw-driver of the correct size can be purchased for a few pence and kept close at hand. Remember that each portion of the cooker has its own local fuse, one for each hotplate, one for the grill, one for the oven, and so on, and also a main fuse controlling the whole cooker. Obviously this latter will have to be a stronger fuse than the others, for it has to carry the current of the whole cooker, so that at least two sizes of fuse wire would have to be in readiness, or, if it is preferred, the smaller wire can be doubled when used in the main fuses.
A word of warning.—A little knowledge is apt to be dangerous on occasion. Everyone knows that all electrical appliances are supplied with current through two wires, one to lead the current in and one to lead it out again (some readers may have heard of the story of the Scotsman who wrote to his supply authority asking if it was true that as much current came back to the station as was sent out, and, on receiving a reply in the affirmative, wrote asking for a rebate on his account), but many consumers of electricity do not know that some switches (known as "double-pole") disconnect both these wires, whereas others ("single-pole") disconnect only one. Now, one of these wires is an innocent one, while the other can be very nasty if touched, and it sometimes happens that electrical appliances get connected so that the single-pole switch is on the innocent wire and, although the switch interrupts the flow of the current, it leaves the elements alive. Now, to hold a live element in one hand and an earthed cooker in the other is asking for trouble, so that before doing any repair to your cooker, be sure to see that the main (double-pole) switch is off. It will then be possible to go to work without the least fear of obtaining an electric shock.
Showing the position of the Fuses in a Jackson Electric Cooker.

Unnamed: 9: Joint Hon. Secretary of the Plymouth and District Branch.
transcription:
The Electrical Age
607
E.A.W. Branch Activities.
Since our last issue the following new branches have been formed: Plymouth and District, Edinburgh and District, The Hartlepools District, and East Devon.
* * *
Plymouth and District Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries: Mrs. A. L. Goodall and Miss M. Hollest, Bedford House, Bedford Terrace, Plymouth.
The inaugural meeting of the Plymouth and District Branch was held at the City Council Chamber on Friday, November 13th, 1925. The Branch is fortunate in that it has Viscountess Astor, M.P., First President of the Association, as its President, and her Ladyship presided over the meeting. Interesting speeches were also made by the Director, Mr. R. Lowell Dunstan, Chairman of the City Electricity Committee, and the Mayoress of Plymouth. The resolution to form a Branch of the Association was carried with acclamation. A short and interesting discussion followed.
At the close of the meeting some of the members of the new Branch visited the local station of the B.B.C., by kind permission of the Station Director.
Future activities will include a further visit to the B.B.C. for other members, an exhibition of electrical Christmas gifts, a Lecture by the City Engineer, a visit to the Electricity Works, and other interesting fixtures.
* * *
Edinburgh and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss M. McNicol, 32, Frederick Street, Edinburgh.
The Inaugural Meeting of the Edinburgh Branch was held on November 19th in the Gartshore Hall. The Provost attended the meeting, and Bailie Couston, presiding Chairman of Electricity Committee, presided. Miss M. G. Gowan, Vice-President, and Miss De la Cour were also on the platform. The Viscountess Elibank, President of the Branch, regretted very much her inability to be present.
The meeting was quite enthusiastic, and resolutions adopting the opening of this Branch were proposed by Mrs. T. Young, seconded by Mrs. Darby.
A whist drive was arranged, over 50 attended, and the prizes, all electrical, were presented by Mrs. Ruth, wife of the Manager of the Lothians Power Co., Musselburgh, to the successful players.
An interesting programme of fixtures has been arranged for 1926.
* * *
Hartlepools and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. D. Parker, The Cliffs, Seaton Carew, Co. Durham.
The Hartlepools and District Branch had a very cheery start. Our Inaugural Meeting took place on Friday, November 6th, during an Electrical Exhibition which was held for ten days, so that there was keen interest in all things electrical at that time.
By the kind co-operation of the Borough Electrical Engineer, the original few E.A.W. enthusiasts were able to run a café during all the Exhibition, with the hope of starting our Branch bank account with the profits, although we had an almost feverishly busy week culminating in our Inaugural Meeting, we had a very jolly time. We rejoiced when everything was cleared up and we had over £15 clear profit. The Meeting was held in the large demonstration hall at the Exhibition, and was attended by about 200 people—mostly women. We have been very fortunate in that Lady Gray has consented to be our President and also Mrs. J. W. Wilson—our only woman town councillor—Chairman of our Executive Committee. The Mayor, Alderman G. E. Hope, presided at the meeting. The Director came from London to speak to us, and we were supported by the presence of Miss Norah Balls (Newcastle), Miss Cooper Hodgson, M.B.E. (Durham) and Miss Anna Holm (Newcastle), the Chairman, Vice-Chairman and Hon. Secretary of the North-East Coast Branch. The Resolution, proposed by Lady Gray and seconded by the Mayoress, was carried, and so the eighteenth Branch of the E.A.W. was inaugurated.
Our programme begins with a very seasonable item—a demonstration of Electric Christmas Cookery by Miss Anna Holm (Newcastle) on December 2nd, which promises to be immensely popular. We hope next to visit the West Hartlepool Power Station, and then have a practical talk on Bells, Batteries and Wireless Sets by Mr. S. Tillotson in January. There are so many things everyone wants to see and hear about that the weeks seem too short to fit them all in.
H.D.P.
* * *
East Devon Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries: Miss W. L. Wilson, 181, Sidwell Street, Exeter, and Miss W. Binney, 57, Hartop Road, St. Mary Church, Torquay.
The inaugural Meeting of the East Devon Branch was held in the Castle, Exeter, on October 24th. Owing to the inclement weather, the attendance was rather smaller than was at first anticipated, but the audience was a very keen and interested one. We were fortunate in securing as principal speaker, Mrs. Workington, J.P., whose active sympathy on behalf of womens work is widely known. The speaker spoke very clearly and interestingly on the objects of the Association, and as a consequence the Secretary was able to enrol upwards of 20 members at the close of the meeting.
Up to the time of going to press, we have held two meetings. The first was a visit to the Exeter Power Station, by kind invitation of H. D. Munro, Esq., Chief Engineer, and the second a lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," by Mr. Catten, of E.L.M.A., held in the Roslin Hall Hotel, Torquay, which was very kindly loaned to us by Miss Gresham, Vice-President of the Torquay Section.
The remainder of our winter programme includes several visits to places of electrical interest in the neighbourhood, one of which is to be to the Electrical and X-Ray Department of the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital. Lectures and demonstrations are also being arranged, and we hope before the next issue of the "Electrical Age" to be able to report a substantial increase in our membership.
* * *
Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy, 211, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
All the fixtures of the Autumn Session have been well attended and appreciated by the members.
The fixtures included a visit to the United Dairies, a Talk by Mr. Alex. McKinnon on "Domestic Electrical Apparatus," a Lecture on "Modern Radio," with demonstrations, by Captain Norman Turner.
An interesting programme is being prepared for the Spring Session, and we shall be glad to forward particulars to anyone living in the Glasgow District who would be interested to receive them.
* * *
Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Sec.: Mrs. Norman Griffiths, M.Com., A.C.I.I., 148, Woodlands Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
Our opening meeting for the autumn session was a General Meeting at the Queens Hotel, followed by a discussion on "Electricity in the Schools." Miss Bassett and Miss Palmer were the speakers; Miss L. K. Barrie, M.A., Headmistress, King Edwards High School for Girls, was in the chair. There was a good discussion, and finally it was decided to send a Resolution to the Local Board of Education and a Deputation to the Electric Supply Department.
Other activities have been:—
LECTURES.
October 10th.—Joint Walsall and Wolverhampton meeting. Mr. Francis lectured on "Modern Tendencies in Architecture, Furnishing, and Lighting Design, and the part Electricity plays therein." The Mayor of Walsall most kindly took the chair for us. Light refreshments were served after the lecture.

East Devon Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries: Miss W. L. Wilson, 181, Sidwell Street, Exeter, and Miss W. Binney, 57, Hartop Road, St. Mary Church, Torquay.
The inaugural Meeting of the East Devon Branch was held in the Castle, Exeter, on October 24th. Owing to the inclement weather, the attendance was rather smaller than was at first anticipated, but the audience was a very keen and interested one. We were fortunate in securing as principal speaker, Mrs. Workington, J.P., whose active sympathy on behalf of womens work is widely known. The speaker spoke very clearly and interestingly on the objects of the Association, and as a consequence the Secretary was able to enrol upwards of 20 members at the close of the meeting.
Up to the time of going to press, we have held two meetings. The first was a visit to the Exeter Power Station, by kind invitation of H. D. Munro, Esq., Chief Engineer, and the second a lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," by Mr. Catten, of E.L.M.A., held in the Roslin Hall Hotel, Torquay, which was very kindly loaned to us by Miss Gresham, Vice-President of the Torquay Section.
The remainder of our winter programme includes several visits to places of electrical interest in the neighbourhood, one of which is to be to the Electrical and X-Ray Department of the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital. Lectures and demonstrations are also being arranged, and we hope before the next issue of the "Electrical Age" to be able to report a substantial increase in our membership.
* * *
Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy, 211, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
All the fixtures of the Autumn Session have been well attended and appreciated by the members.
The fixtures included a visit to the United Dairies, a Talk by Mr. Alex. McKinnon on "Domestic Electrical Apparatus," a Lecture on "Modern Radio," with demonstrations, by Captain Norman Turner.
An interesting programme is being prepared for the Spring Session, and we shall be glad to forward particulars to anyone living in the Glasgow District who would be interested to receive them.
* * *
Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Sec.: Mrs. Norman Griffiths, M.Com., A.C.I.I., 148, Woodlands Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
Our opening meeting for the autumn session was a General Meeting at the Queens Hotel, followed by a discussion on "Electricity in the Schools." Miss Bassett and Miss Palmer were the speakers; Miss L. K. Barrie, M.A., Headmistress, King Edwards High School for Girls, was in the chair. There was a good discussion, and finally it was decided to send a Resolution to the Local Board of Education and a Deputation to the Electric Supply Department.
Other activities have been:—
LECTURES.
October 10th.—Joint Walsall and Wolverhampton meeting. Mr. Francis lectured on "Modern Tendencies in Architecture, Furnishing, and Lighting Design, and the part Electricity plays therein." The Mayor of Walsall most kindly took the chair for us. Light refreshments were served after the lecture.

* * *
Hartlepools and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. D. Parker, The Cliffs, Seaton Carew, Co. Durham.
The Hartlepools and District Branch had a very cheery start. Our Inaugural Meeting took place on Friday, November 6th, during an Electrical Exhibition which was held for ten days, so that there was keen interest in all things electrical at that time.
By the kind co-operation of the Borough Electrical Engineer, the original few E.A.W. enthusiasts were able to run a café during all the Exhibition, with the hope of starting our Branch bank account with the profits, although we had an almost feverishly busy week culminating in our Inaugural Meeting, we had a very jolly time. We rejoiced when everything was cleared up and we had over £15 clear profit. The Meeting was held in the large demonstration hall at the Exhibition, and was attended by about 200 people—mostly women. We have been very fortunate in that Lady Gray has consented to be our President and also Mrs. J. W. Wilson—our only woman town councillor—Chairman of our Executive Committee. The Mayor, Alderman G. E. Hope, presided at the meeting. The Director came from London to speak to us, and we were supported by the presence of Miss Norah Balls (Newcastle), Miss Cooper Hodgson, M.B.E. (Durham) and Miss Anna Holm (Newcastle), the Chairman, Vice-Chairman and Hon. Secretary of the North-East Coast Branch. The Resolution, proposed by Lady Gray and seconded by the Mayoress, was carried, and so the eighteenth Branch of the E.A.W. was inaugurated.
Our programme begins with a very seasonable item—a demonstration of Electric Christmas Cookery by Miss Anna Holm (Newcastle) on December 2nd, which promises to be immensely popular. We hope next to visit the West Hartlepool Power Station, and then have a practical talk on Bells, Batteries and Wireless Sets by Mr. S. Tillotson in January. There are so many things everyone wants to see and hear about that the weeks seem too short to fit them all in.
H.D.P.

The inaugural meeting of the Plymouth and District Branch was held at the City Council Chamber on Friday, November 13th, 1925. The Branch is fortunate in that it has Viscountess Astor, M.P., First President of the Association, as its President, and her Ladyship presided over the meeting. Interesting speeches were also made by the Director, Mr. R. Lowell Dunstan, Chairman of the City Electricity Committee, and the Mayoress of Plymouth. The resolution to form a Branch of the Association was carried with acclamation. A short and interesting discussion followed.
At the close of the meeting some of the members of the new Branch visited the local station of the B.B.C., by kind permission of the Station Director.
Future activities will include a further visit to the B.B.C. for other members, an exhibition of electrical Christmas gifts, a Lecture by the City Engineer, a visit to the Electricity Works, and other interesting fixtures.
* * *
Edinburgh and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss M. McNicol, 32, Frederick Street, Edinburgh.
The Inaugural Meeting of the Edinburgh Branch was held on November 19th in the Gartshore Hall. The Provost attended the meeting, and Bailie Couston, presiding Chairman of Electricity Committee, presided. Miss M. G. Gowan, Vice-President, and Miss De la Cour were also on the platform. The Viscountess Elibank, President of the Branch, regretted very much her inability to be present.
The meeting was quite enthusiastic, and resolutions adopting the opening of this Branch were proposed by Mrs. T. Young, seconded by Mrs. Darby.
A whist drive was arranged, over 50 attended, and the prizes, all electrical, were presented by Mrs. Ruth, wife of the Manager of the Lothians Power Co., Musselburgh, to the successful players.
An interesting programme of fixtures has been arranged for 1926.
* * *
Hartlepools and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. D. Parker, The Cliffs, Seaton Carew, Co. Durham.
The Hartlepools and District Branch had a very cheery start. Our Inaugural Meeting took place on Friday, November 6th, during an Electrical Exhibition which was held for ten days, so that there was keen interest in all things electrical at that time.
By the kind co-operation of the Borough Electrical Engineer, the original few E.A.W. enthusiasts were able to run a café during all the Exhibition, with the hope of starting our Branch bank account with the profits, although we had an almost feverishly busy week culminating in our Inaugural Meeting, we had a very jolly time. We rejoiced when everything was cleared up and we had over £15 clear profit. The Meeting was held in the large demonstration hall at the Exhibition, and was attended by about 200 people—mostly women. We have been very fortunate in that Lady Gray has consented to be our President and also Mrs. J. W. Wilson—our only woman town councillor—Chairman of our Executive Committee. The Mayor, Alderman G. E. Hope, presided at the meeting. The Director came from London to speak to us, and we were supported by the presence of Miss Norah Balls (Newcastle), Miss Cooper Hodgson, M.B.E. (Durham) and Miss Anna Holm (Newcastle), the Chairman, Vice-Chairman and Hon. Secretary of the North-East Coast Branch. The Resolution, proposed by Lady Gray and seconded by the Mayoress, was carried, and so the eighteenth Branch of the E.A.W. was inaugurated.
Our programme begins with a very seasonable item—a demonstration of Electric Christmas Cookery by Miss Anna Holm (Newcastle) on December 2nd, which promises to be immensely popular. We hope next to visit the West Hartlepool Power Station, and then have a practical talk on Bells, Batteries and Wireless Sets by Mr. S. Tillotson in January. There are so many things everyone wants to see and hear about that the weeks seem too short to fit them all in.
H.D.P.
* * *
East Devon Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries: Miss W. L. Wilson, 181, Sidwell Street, Exeter, and Miss W. Binney, 57, Hartop Road, St. Mary Church, Torquay.
The inaugural Meeting of the East Devon Branch was held in the Castle, Exeter, on October 24th. Owing to the inclement weather, the attendance was rather smaller than was at first anticipated, but the audience was a very keen and interested one. We were fortunate in securing as principal speaker, Mrs. Workington, J.P., whose active sympathy on behalf of womens work is widely known. The speaker spoke very clearly and interestingly on the objects of the Association, and as a consequence the Secretary was able to enrol upwards of 20 members at the close of the meeting.
Up to the time of going to press, we have held two meetings. The first was a visit to the Exeter Power Station, by kind invitation of H. D. Munro, Esq., Chief Engineer, and the second a lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," by Mr. Catten, of E.L.M.A., held in the Roslin Hall Hotel, Torquay, which was very kindly loaned to us by Miss Gresham, Vice-President of the Torquay Section.
The remainder of our winter programme includes several visits to places of electrical interest in the neighbourhood, one of which is to be to the Electrical and X-Ray Department of the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital. Lectures and demonstrations are also being arranged, and we hope before the next issue of the "Electrical Age" to be able to report a substantial increase in our membership.
* * *
Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy, 211, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
All the fixtures of the Autumn Session have been well attended and appreciated by the members.
The fixtures included a visit to the United Dairies, a Talk by Mr. Alex. McKinnon on "Domestic Electrical Apparatus," a Lecture on "Modern Radio," with demonstrations, by Captain Norman Turner.
An interesting programme is being prepared for the Spring Session, and we shall be glad to forward particulars to anyone living in the Glasgow District who would be interested to receive them.
* * *
Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Sec.: Mrs. Norman Griffiths, M.Com., A.C.I.I., 148, Woodlands Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
Our opening meeting for the autumn session was a General Meeting at the Queens Hotel, followed by a discussion on "Electricity in the Schools." Miss Bassett and Miss Palmer were the speakers; Miss L. K. Barrie, M.A., Headmistress, King Edwards High School for Girls, was in the chair. There was a good discussion, and finally it was decided to send a Resolution to the Local Board of Education and a Deputation to the Electric Supply Department.
Other activities have been:—
LECTURES.
October 10th.—Joint Walsall and Wolverhampton meeting. Mr. Francis lectured on "Modern Tendencies in Architecture, Furnishing, and Lighting Design, and the part Electricity plays therein." The Mayor of Walsall most kindly took the chair for us. Light refreshments were served after the lecture.

Unnamed: 9: Speaker at the Birmingham and Midlands Branch opening meeting.

Hartlepools and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. H. D. Parker, The Cliffs, Seaton Carew, Co. Durham.

H.D.P.

East Devon Branch.
Joint Hon. Secretaries: Miss W. L. Wilson, 181, Sidwell Street, Exeter, and Miss W. Binney, 57, Hartop Road, St. Mary Church, Torquay.
The inaugural Meeting of the East Devon Branch was held in the Castle, Exeter, on October 24th. Owing to the inclement weather, the attendance was rather smaller than was at first anticipated, but the audience was a very keen and interested one. We were fortunate in securing as principal speaker, Mrs. Workington, J.P., whose active sympathy on behalf of womens work is widely known. The speaker spoke very clearly and interestingly on the objects of the Association, and as a consequence the Secretary was able to enrol upwards of 20 members at the close of the meeting.
Up to the time of going to press, we have held two meetings. The first was a visit to the Exeter Power Station, by kind invitation of H. D. Munro, Esq., Chief Engineer, and the second a lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," by Mr. Catten, of E.L.M.A., held in the Roslin Hall Hotel, Torquay, which was very kindly loaned to us by Miss Gresham, Vice-President of the Torquay Section.
The remainder of our winter programme includes several visits to places of electrical interest in the neighbourhood, one of which is to be to the Electrical and X-Ray Department of the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital. Lectures and demonstrations are also being arranged, and we hope before the next issue of the "Electrical Age" to be able to report a substantial increase in our membership.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy, 211, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
All the fixtures of the Autumn Session have been well attended and appreciated by the members.
The fixtures included a visit to the United Dairies, a Talk by Mr. Alex. McKinnon on "Domestic Electrical Apparatus," a Lecture on "Modern Radio," with demonstrations, by Captain Norman Turner.
An interesting programme is being prepared for the Spring Session, and we shall be glad to forward particulars to anyone living in the Glasgow District who would be interested to receive them.

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
