Unnamed: 9: Secretary who gave a lecture on Supply Undertakings and Domestic Consumer.
transcription:
608 The Electrical Age

October 21st.—“Supply Undertakings and Domestic Con-
sumer,” by Mr. E. J. Jennings, Secretary, Birmingham
Electric Supply Department. This lecture was greatly en-
joyed; excellent charts were used to make clear the varia-
tions in demand and output over a given period, and to
illustrate the constituent parts in costing. Tariffs were
also discussed.
November 19th.—“My American Tour,” by Mr. F.
Forrest. To the regret of all, Mr. Forrest had to send a
deputy at the last moment to read his paper. Mr. Lawson,
who acted in this capacity, helped us considerably to carry
the meeting through.
Discussions followed all these lectures; the average
attendance has been 40-50.
DEMONSTRATIONS.
October 13th and 14th and November 4th.—By the kind-
ness of our President in London, and of a Vice-President
(Mrs. Forrest) in November, over 150 of our members had
the pleasure of attending demonstrations on household elec-
tronic apparatus, given by Mrs. Williams and Miss Herrod,
of the western supply Department. On each occasion
members were entertained to tea, and our most cordial
thanks are due to these officers.
VISITS.
November 13th.—A most instructive afternoon was spent
at the new works of the Macintosh Cable Co., Derby.
Members were afterwards entertained to tea.
November 27th.—A visit was paid to the new showrooms
of Frigidaire, Ltd. A lecture on the general principles of
Refrigeration was given.
SOCIALS.
December 9th.—We close our Autumn activities with a
“Bridge and Whist Drive at the Grand Hotel. All profit will
be placed to the credit of a special Office Equipment Fund.
B.H.
* * *
Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secs.: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams and
Miss D. Foster Jeffery, LL.B.
This Branch has been very active during the Autumn,
and the attendance at meetings is very satisfactory.
The Session opened with an American Tea, which was
held in the Salford Corporation Showrooms, by the kindness
of the Corporation. A most enjoyable afternoon was spent,
and £13 8s. was realized.
Our members much enjoyed the visit to Messrs. Ford’s
Motor Works, where they saw the famous Ford car in all
stages of construction.
On October 14th we were very honoured to have with us
the Lady Emmett, J.P., Lady Brooks, J.P., C.B.E., and the
Mayoress at our Annual Lunch. The speeches were excellent,
and about 172 members thoroughly enjoyed the event. The
Lady Mayoress very kindly presided, and its success was
voted a great success. The following week we had a most
interesting address from Mr. Francis on “Modern Lighting
Designs,” and early in November we were shown all round
the new Manchester Studios of the B.B.C. So many people
wished to attend this meeting that we had to deal with
applications in strict order, but we hope to fix up another
visit later for those who were disappointed this time. The
visit to the Smoke Abatement Exhibition is described else-
where, but on November 20th the Manchester Corporation
gave us a most excellent cookery demonstration, showing us
how to cook Christmas fare on the different electric cookers.
This was voted one of the most attractive features we have
had. The last meeting was at “Hotpoint House,” where we
learnt not only how to cook, but how to wash and the
merits of the different vacuum cleaners.
Our last meetings before Christmas were at the new
Showrooms of the Oldham Corporation and at Messrs. Hans
Renold’s Works. To all these people we wish to express
our grateful thanks for their kind reception and information.
* * *
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss D. Blaker,
1, York Terrace, St. George’s Road, Cheltenham.
We have had some very interesting meetings during the
Autumn Session. Our first, in September, was a lecture on
“Washing by Electricity,” by Mr. W. George.
In October, Mr. H. Lingard, of E.L.M.A., lectured to us
on “Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation,” when we
learnt many useful things which I am sure will be put into
practice, if possible; the models displayed for the purpose of
comparing modern lighting with the old style caused great
interest.

October 21st.—“Supply Undertakings and Domestic Con-
sumer,” by Mr. E. J. Jennings, Secretary, Birmingham
Electric Supply Department. This lecture was greatly en-
joyed; excellent charts were used to make clear the varia-
tions in demand and output over a given period, and to
illustrate the constituent parts in costing. Tariffs were
also discussed.
November 19th.—“My American Tour,” by Mr. F.
Forrest. To the regret of all, Mr. Forrest had to send a
deputy at the last moment to read his paper. Mr. Lawson,
who acted in this capacity, helped us considerably to carry
the meeting through.
Discussions followed all these lectures; the average
attendance has been 40-50.
DEMONSTRATIONS.
October 13th and 14th and November 4th.—By the kind-
ness of our President in London, and of a Vice-President
(Mrs. Forrest) in November, over 150 of our members had
the pleasure of attending demonstrations on household elec-
tronic apparatus, given by Mrs. Williams and Miss Herrod,
of the western supply Department. On each occasion
members were entertained to tea, and our most cordial
thanks are due to these officers.
VISITS.
November 13th.—A most instructive afternoon was spent
at the new works of the Macintosh Cable Co., Derby.
Members were afterwards entertained to tea.
November 27th.—A visit was paid to the new showrooms
of Frigidaire, Ltd. A lecture on the general principles of
Refrigeration was given.
SOCIALS.
December 9th.—We close our Autumn activities with a
“Bridge and Whist Drive at the Grand Hotel. All profit will
be placed to the credit of a special Office Equipment Fund.
B.H.
* * *
Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secs.: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams and
Miss D. Foster Jeffery, LL.B.
This Branch has been very active during the Autumn,
and the attendance at meetings is very satisfactory.
The Session opened with an American Tea, which was
held in the Salford Corporation Showrooms, by the kindness
of the Corporation. A most enjoyable afternoon was spent,
and £13 8s. was realized.
Our members much enjoyed the visit to Messrs. Ford’s
Motor Works, where they saw the famous Ford car in all
stages of construction.
On October 14th we were very honoured to have with us
the Lady Emmett, J.P., Lady Brooks, J.P., C.B.E., and the
Mayoress at our Annual Lunch. The speeches were excellent,
and about 172 members thoroughly enjoyed the event. The
Lady Mayoress very kindly presided, and its success was
voted a great success. The following week we had a most
interesting address from Mr. Francis on “Modern Lighting
Designs,” and early in November we were shown all round
the new Manchester Studios of the B.B.C. So many people
wished to attend this meeting that we had to deal with
applications in strict order, but we hope to fix up another
visit later for those who were disappointed this time. The
visit to the Smoke Abatement Exhibition is described else-
where, but on November 20th the Manchester Corporation
gave us a most excellent cookery demonstration, showing us
how to cook Christmas fare on the different electric cookers.
This was voted one of the most attractive features we have
had. The last meeting was at “Hotpoint House,” where we
learnt not only how to cook, but how to wash and the
merits of the different vacuum cleaners.
Our last meetings before Christmas were at the new
Showrooms of the Oldham Corporation and at Messrs. Hans
Renold’s Works. To all these people we wish to express
our grateful thanks for their kind reception and information.
* * *
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss D. Blaker,
1, York Terrace, St. George’s Road, Cheltenham.
We have had some very interesting meetings during the
Autumn Session. Our first, in September, was a lecture on
“Washing by Electricity,” by Mr. W. George.
In October, Mr. H. Lingard, of E.L.M.A., lectured to us
on “Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation,” when we
learnt many useful things which I am sure will be put into
practice, if possible; the models displayed for the purpose of
comparing modern lighting with the old style caused great
interest.

The Premier Junior Electric Vacuum Cleaner.
MADE for the smaller house—the bunga-
low or flat. Like its elder brother—
the Premier Duplex—the PREMIER
JUNIOR has all the advantages of a motor-
driven soft bristle brush; ball bearings to
motor; three non-marring casters; easy-to-fix
bag fastener and clamp; attachments for
use on your upholstery, curtains, etc., and
weighs only seven pounds!

high-grade Vacuum Cleaner, but felt perhaps,
that the price was “just a little bit too much
at the moment.”

Miss D. Foster Jeffery, LL.B.
This Branch has been very active during the Autumn,
and the attendance at meetings is very satisfactory.
The Session opened with an American Tea, which was
held in the Salford Corporation Showrooms, by the kindness
of the Corporation. A most enjoyable afternoon was spent,
and £13 8s. was realized.
Our members much enjoyed the visit to Messrs. Ford’s
Motor Works, where they saw the famous Ford car in all
stages of construction.
On October 14th we were very honoured to have with us
the Lady Emmett, J.P., Lady Brooks, J.P., C.B.E., and the
Mayoress at our Annual Lunch. The speeches were excellent,
and about 172 members thoroughly enjoyed the event. The
Lady Mayoress very kindly presided, and its success was
voted a great success. The following week we had a most
interesting address from Mr. Francis on “Modern Lighting
Designs,” and early in November we were shown all round
the new Manchester Studios of the B.B.C. So many people
wished to attend this meeting that we had to deal with
applications in strict order, but we hope to fix up another
visit later for those who were disappointed this time. The
visit to the Smoke Abatement Exhibition is described else-
where, but on November 20th the Manchester Corporation
gave us a most excellent cookery demonstration, showing us
how to cook Christmas fare on the different electric cookers.

had. The last meeting was at “Hotpoint House,” where we
learnt not only how to cook, but how to wash and the
merits of the different vacuum cleaners.

Showrooms of the Oldham Corporation and at Messrs. Hans
Renold’s Works. To all these people we wish to express
our grateful thanks for their kind reception and information.

Unnamed: 9: Gave a lecture demonstration on Electric Table Appliances in November.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 609

On October 28th and 29th the Cheltenham Medical Spa Baths were visited. This meeting seemed to be as popular this year as the previous visit made two years ago.
On November 12th, Miss B. Vaughan, of London, gave the members a leather demonstration on "Electric Table Appliances." Miss Vaughan made her lecture most explicit and interesting. The many and varied Electrical "gadgets" displayed proved plainly that the E.A.W. were doing a great thing in moving ahead on the "Junior Campaign."
On December 3rd, Capt. G. C. Price will give a public lecture on "Wireless," which ought to prove a popular and well-attended meeting.
This will conclude the Autumn programme. The Committee are now busy preparing a most attractive and interesting programme from January to July. There will be visits; lectures; the E.D.A. film, "Country Currents"; possibly the Electrical Play; social events; and, last but not least, our third Annual Meeting and Luncheon in March, when we hope to have our Director with us.
H. B.

***

South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. G. Snow,
"Greengate," Lisvane Road, Lisvane, Glam.
Our Autumn Programme has been a good one, and all fixtures well attended.
Our visit to the Power Station of the South Wales Power Distribution Co., Upperboat, was much appreciated; also the two Lectures given by Mr. G. S. Francis, of E.D.A., and Mr. T. Catten, of E.L.M.A.
I think our most interesting fixture was our visit to the City Lodge, Cardiff, where we saw how electricity is used to relieve pain and combat disease. Mr. Ruffer, the Master, made splendid arrangements for us to see everything of interest, with the help of the Matron and Staff, the Matron entertaining us to tea.
Our social events have been most successful, and we find they bring all members together in a very friendly way.
Our Winter Programme has now been arranged, and includes lectures, demonstrations, a visit to the General Post Office, Cardiff, and an inspection of electrical appliances in the Beauty Parlours of Messrs. Burridge, Cardiff.
Last, but not least, after our Annual General Meeting on March 19th, 1930, we are holding our first Dinner. This we hope will be a great success, especially as the Director has promised to attend.

***

North-East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm,
Carliol House, Newcastle-on-Tyne.
The North-East Coast Branch has arranged an interesting Winter Programme, including attendance at the Faraday Lecture by Captain P. P. Eckersley on "Broadcasting by Electric Waves," a visit to the new Metrovick Showrooms, and a Lecture at Carliol House entitled "The Cinemas Debt to Electricity."
A specially attractive visit was that to the Northcliffe Newspapers, at Northcliffe House, Gallowgate.
The very interesting Session concluded with a Lecture by Mr. R. H. McKenzie on "The Control of Electricity in the Home."
On November 8th various officials of the North-East Coast Branch visited West Hartlepool and helped with the formation of the Hartlepools and District Branch.
Miss Norah Balls, Chairman of the North-East Coast Branch, addressed the meeting, and Miss Holm and Miss Cooper Hodgson were also present.

***

Ashford and District Branch.
Hon. Sec.: Mrs. B. M. Wilson, "Gleniffer Brae,"
Vicarage Road, Kennington, nr. Ashford, Kent.
Since the last issue of our journal we have had a full and varied programme. The Rummage Sale at the end of September was a great success, and resulted in the addition of £10 to our funds.
Again we had, by request, in October, a practical Lecture on "Fuse Mending and Meter Reading." All members read the meters and mended fuses before they left the meeting. On October 7th, Mrs. Hayward recommenced the fortnightly Whist Drives and through this social side, ten members have been interested and joined the Association. On October 23rd we were indebted to Mrs. Knott, of Messrs. Belling & Co., for a cooking Demonstration on the "Baby Belling Cooker." All users of the "Baby Belling" were invited, whether they were members of the Association or not; and on October 24th Mrs. Knott gave a cooking Demonstration at a small exhibition at Wye, near Ashford. The Committee were responsible for the refreshments, which were electrically cooked by them, and in the afternoon Mrs. Wilson explained the aims and objects of the E.A.W.
Student classes re-commenced on October 25th, and Mr. Wilson (Engineer and Manager of the U.D.C.) has again promised to give the first four lessons and to set the examination paper for the students.
In November a most enjoyable, and to us quite a fresh, Lecture was given by Mr. A. Chomley, of Ashford, on "Electricity and Musical Instruments."
On December 5th, Mr. A. E. Langley gave, by request, his second Lecture on "Wireless." This was an open lecture, and proved very popular.
We are now looking forward to the New Year, when we hold our Annual Meeting and second Annual Dinner, which the Director has promised to attend. We wish our fellow members "A Happy New Year."

***

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o Ingleby Motors, Sweet Street, Leeds.
The first half of the session 1929-30 of the Leeds and West Riding Branch has passed very successfully, commencing on October 16th with a Lantern Lecture by Mr. S. Penzer on "Modern Tendencies in Architecture, Furnishing, and Lighting Design, and the part Electricity plays therein," when Mr. Francis showed some wonderful lantern slides, and finishing with a visit to Messrs. Bryant and Mays Match Works on December 11th, where the wonders of the electrical machinery used in the making of matches were revealed.
On October 30th, a pleasant afternoon was spent at the Leeds Electricity Showrooms, where demonstrations were given on various up-to-date electric appliances, including washing machines and automatic toasters, followed by afternoon tea.
Mr. C. F. Wells, of the E.D.A., lectured on "Electricity in the Home" on November 13th, giving much useful information on radiators, cookers, washers and refrigerators, and he gave a detailed account of the cost of the running of each.
Also on November 27th Mr. S. C. Hurry gave a lecture on "Electric Cookers," and it was almost incredible that so much could be cooked at the same time in such a small oven.
After the lecture Mr. Hurry took the members across to the Hotel Metropole to see a show of Jackson cookers and radiators, etc., and then he kindly invited them to tea.
The members are now looking forward to their Annual Luncheon, which is to be held on January 21st, at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, and they have been greatly favoured by Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, F.R.S., Mr. W. B. Woodhouse and the Director having promised to speak.

***

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. H. Klitz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, N. Wales.
Our outstanding event during the Autumn Session was the celebration of our first birthday with a reception and luncheon at Colwyn Bay on November 20th. Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti (our Branch President) presided, and was supported by Dr. Ferranti, Lady Brooks, Mrs. Hyde, Mrs. Prior White and the Director, and a very large company of members and their friends. The occasion was, of course, one of speeches, or rather addresses; and these were listened to with intense interest, and are likely to be quoted from for a long time to come by those who had the pleasure of listening to them.

***

South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. G. Snow,
"Greengate," Lisvane Road, Lisvane, Glam.
Our Autumn Programme has been a good one, and all fixtures well attended.
Our visit to the Power Station of the South Wales Power Distribution Co., Upperboat, was much appreciated; also the two Lectures given by Mr. G. S. Francis, of E.D.A., and Mr. T. Catten, of E.L.M.A.
I think our most interesting fixture was our visit to the City Lodge, Cardiff, where we saw how electricity is used to relieve pain and combat disease. Mr. Ruffer, the Master, made splendid arrangements for us to see everything of interest, with the help of the Matron and Staff, the Matron entertaining us to tea.
Our social events have been most successful, and we find they bring all members together in a very friendly way.
Our Winter Programme has now been arranged, and includes lectures, demonstrations, a visit to the General Post Office, Cardiff, and an inspection of electrical appliances in the Beauty Parlours of Messrs. Burridge, Cardiff.
Last, but not least, after our Annual General Meeting on March 19th, 1930, we are holding our first Dinner. This we hope will be a great success, especially as the Director has promised to attend.

***

North-East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm,
Carliol House, Newcastle-on-Tyne.
The North-East Coast Branch has arranged an interesting Winter Programme, including attendance at the Faraday Lecture by Captain P. P. Eckersley on "Broadcasting by Electric Waves," a visit to the new Metrovick Showrooms, and a Lecture at Carliol House entitled "The Cinemas Debt to Electricity."
A specially attractive visit was that to the Northcliffe Newspapers, at Northcliffe House, Gallowgate.
The very interesting Session concluded with a Lecture by Mr. R. H. McKenzie on "The Control of Electricity in the Home."
On November 8th various officials of the North-East Coast Branch visited West Hartlepool and helped with the formation of the Hartlepools and District Branch.
Miss Norah Balls, Chairman of the North-East Coast Branch, addressed the meeting, and Miss Holm and Miss Cooper Hodgson were also present.

***

Ashford and District Branch.
Hon. Sec.: Mrs. B. M. Wilson, "Gleniffer Brae,"
Vicarage Road, Kennington, nr. Ashford, Kent.
Since the last issue of our journal we have had a full and varied programme. The Rummage Sale at the end of September was a great success, and resulted in the addition of £10 to our funds.
Again we had, by request, in October, a practical Lecture on "Fuse Mending and Meter Reading." All members read the meters and mended fuses before they left the meeting. On October 7th, Mrs. Hayward recommenced the fortnightly Whist Drives and through this social side, ten members have been interested and joined the Association. On October 23rd we were indebted to Mrs. Knott, of Messrs. Belling & Co., for a cooking Demonstration on the "Baby Belling Cooker." All users of the "Baby Belling" were invited, whether they were members of the Association or not; and on October 24th Mrs. Knott gave a cooking Demonstration at a small exhibition at Wye, near Ashford. The Committee were responsible for the refreshments, which were electrically cooked by them, and in the afternoon Mrs. Wilson explained the aims and objects of the E.A.W.
Student classes re-commenced on October 25th, and Mr. Wilson (Engineer and Manager of the U.D.C.) has again promised to give the first four lessons and to set the examination paper for the students.
In November a most enjoyable, and to us quite a fresh, Lecture was given by Mr. A. Chomley, of Ashford, on "Electricity and Musical Instruments."
On December 5th, Mr. A. E. Langley gave, by request, his second Lecture on "Wireless." This was an open lecture, and proved very popular.
We are now looking forward to the New Year, when we hold our Annual Meeting and second Annual Dinner, which the Director has promised to attend. We wish our fellow members "A Happy New Year."

***

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o Ingleby Motors, Sweet Street, Leeds.
The first half of the session 1929-30 of the Leeds and West Riding Branch has passed very successfully, commencing on October 16th with a Lantern Lecture by Mr. S. Penzer on "Modern Tendencies in Architecture, Furnishing, and Lighting Design, and the part Electricity plays therein," when Mr. Francis showed some wonderful lantern slides, and finishing with a visit to Messrs. Bryant and Mays Match Works on December 11th, where the wonders of the electrical machinery used in the making of matches were revealed.
On October 30th, a pleasant afternoon was spent at the Leeds Electricity Showrooms, where demonstrations were given on various up-to-date electric appliances, including washing machines and automatic toasters, followed by afternoon tea.
Mr. C. F. Wells, of the E.D.A., lectured on "Electricity in the Home" on November 13th, giving much useful information on radiators, cookers, washers and refrigerators, and he gave a detailed account of the cost of the running of each.
Also on November 27th Mr. S. C. Hurry gave a lecture on "Electric Cookers," and it was almost incredible that so much could be cooked at the same time in such a small oven.
After the lecture Mr. Hurry took the members across to the Hotel Metropole to see a show of Jackson cookers and radiators, etc., and then he kindly invited them to tea.
The members are now looking forward to their Annual Luncheon, which is to be held on January 21st, at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, and they have been greatly favoured by Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, F.R.S., Mr. W. B. Woodhouse and the Director having promised to speak.

***

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. H. Klitz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, N. Wales.
Our outstanding event during the Autumn Session was the celebration of our first birthday with a reception and luncheon at Colwyn Bay on November 20th. Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti (our Branch President) presided, and was supported by Dr. Ferranti, Lady Brooks, Mrs. Hyde, Mrs. Prior White and the Director, and a very large company of members and their friends. The occasion was, of course, one of speeches, or rather addresses; and these were listened to with intense interest, and are likely to be quoted from for a long time to come by those who had the pleasure of listening to them.

Penzer on "Modern Tendencies in Architecture, Furnishing, and Lighting Design, and the part Electricity plays therein," when Mr. Francis showed some wonderful lantern slides, and finishing with a visit to Messrs. Bryant and Mays Match Works on December 11th, where the wonders of the electrical machinery used in the making of matches were revealed.

Our social events have been most successful, and we find they bring all members together in a very friendly way.
Our Winter Programme has now been arranged, and includes lectures, demonstrations, a visit to the General Post Office, Cardiff, and an inspection of electrical appliances in the Beauty Parlours of Messrs. Burridge, Cardiff.
Last, but not least, after our Annual General Meeting on March 19th, 1930, we are holding our first Dinner. This we hope will be a great success, especially as the Director has promised to attend.

***

Ashford and District Branch.
Hon. Sec.: Mrs. B. M. Wilson, "Gleniffer Brae,"
Vicarage Road, Kennington, nr. Ashford, Kent.
Since the last issue of our journal we have had a full and varied programme. The Rummage Sale at the end of September was a great success, and resulted in the addition of £10 to our funds.
Again we had, by request, in October, a practical Lecture on "Fuse Mending and Meter Reading." All members read the meters and mended fuses before they left the meeting. On October 7th, Mrs. Hayward recommenced the fortnightly Whist Drives and through this social side, ten members have been interested and joined the Association. On October 23rd we were indebted to Mrs. Knott, of Messrs. Belling & Co., for a cooking Demonstration on the "Baby Belling Cooker." All users of the "Baby Belling" were invited, whether they were members of the Association or not; and on October 24th Mrs. Knott gave a cooking Demonstration at a small exhibition at Wye, near Ashford. The Committee were responsible for the refreshments, which were electrically cooked by them, and in the afternoon Mrs. Wilson explained the aims and objects of the E.A.W.
Student classes re-commenced on October 25th, and Mr. Wilson (Engineer and Manager of the U.D.C.) has again promised to give the first four lessons and to set the examination paper for the students.
In November a most enjoyable, and to us quite a fresh, Lecture was given by Mr. A. Chomley, of Ashford, on "Electricity and Musical Instruments."
On December 5th, Mr. A. E. Langley gave, by request, his second Lecture on "Wireless." This was an open lecture, and proved very popular.
We are now looking forward to the New Year, when we hold our Annual Meeting and second Annual Dinner, which the Director has promised to attend. We wish our fellow members "A Happy New Year."

The Electrical Age 609

On October 28th and 29th the Cheltenham Medical Spa Baths were visited. This meeting seemed to be as popular this year as the previous visit made two years ago.
On November 12th, Miss B. Vaughan, of London, gave the members a leather demonstration on "Electric Table Appliances." Miss Vaughan made her lecture most explicit and interesting. The many and varied Electrical "gadgets" displayed proved plainly that the E.A.W. were doing a great thing in moving ahead on the "Junior Campaign."
On December 3rd, Capt. G. C. Price will give a public lecture on "Wireless," which ought to prove a popular and well-attended meeting.
This will conclude the Autumn programme. The Committee are now busy preparing a most attractive and interesting programme from January to July. There will be visits; lectures; the E.D.A. film, "Country Currents"; possibly the Electrical Play; social events; and, last but not least, our third Annual Meeting and Luncheon in March, when we hope to have our Director with us.
H. B.

***

South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. G. Snow,
"Greengate," Lisvane Road, Lisvane, Glam.
Our Autumn Programme has been a good one, and all fixtures well attended.
Our visit to the Power Station of the South Wales Power Distribution Co., Upperboat, was much appreciated; also the two Lectures given by Mr. G. S. Francis, of E.D.A., and Mr. T. Catten, of E.L.M.A.
I think our most interesting fixture was our visit to the City Lodge, Cardiff, where we saw how electricity is used to relieve pain and combat disease. Mr. Ruffer, the Master, made splendid arrangements for us to see everything of interest, with the help of the Matron and Staff, the Matron entertaining us to tea.
Our social events have been most successful, and we find they bring all members together in a very friendly way.
Our Winter Programme has now been arranged, and includes lectures, demonstrations, a visit to the General Post Office, Cardiff, and an inspection of electrical appliances in the Beauty Parlours of Messrs. Burridge, Cardiff.
Last, but not least, after our Annual General Meeting on March 19th, 1930, we are holding our first Dinner. This we hope will be a great success, especially as the Director has promised to attend.

***

North-East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm,
Carliol House, Newcastle-on-Tyne.
The North-East Coast Branch has arranged an interesting Winter Programme, including attendance at the Faraday Lecture by Captain P. P. Eckersley on "Broadcasting by Electric Waves," a visit to the new Metrovick Showrooms, and a Lecture at Carliol House entitled "The Cinemas Debt to Electricity."
A specially attractive visit was that to the Northcliffe Newspapers, at Northcliffe House, Gallowgate.
The very interesting Session concluded with a Lecture by Mr. R. H. McKenzie on "The Control of Electricity in the Home."
On November 8th various officials of the North-East Coast Branch visited West Hartlepool and helped with the formation of the Hartlepools and District Branch.
Miss Norah Balls, Chairman of the North-East Coast Branch, addressed the meeting, and Miss Holm and Miss Cooper Hodgson were also present.

***

Ashford and District Branch.
Hon. Sec.: Mrs. B. M. Wilson, "Gleniffer Brae,"
Vicarage Road, Kennington, nr. Ashford, Kent.
Since the last issue of our journal we have had a full and varied programme. The Rummage Sale at the end of September was a great success, and resulted in the addition of £10 to our funds.
Again we had, by request, in October, a practical Lecture on "Fuse Mending and Meter Reading." All members read the meters and mended fuses before they left the meeting. On October 7th, Mrs. Hayward recommenced the fortnightly Whist Drives and through this social side, ten members have been interested and joined the Association. On October 23rd we were indebted to Mrs. Knott, of Messrs. Belling & Co., for a cooking Demonstration on the "Baby Belling Cooker." All users of the "Baby Belling" were invited, whether they were members of the Association or not; and on October 24th Mrs. Knott gave a cooking Demonstration at a small exhibition at Wye, near Ashford. The Committee were responsible for the refreshments, which were electrically cooked by them, and in the afternoon Mrs. Wilson explained the aims and objects of the E.A.W.
Student classes re-commenced on October 25th, and Mr. Wilson (Engineer and Manager of the U.D.C.) has again promised to give the first four lessons and to set the examination paper for the students.
In November a most enjoyable, and to us quite a fresh, Lecture was given by Mr. A. Chomley, of Ashford, on "Electricity and Musical Instruments."
On December 5th, Mr. A. E. Langley gave, by request, his second Lecture on "Wireless." This was an open lecture, and proved very popular.
We are now looking forward to the New Year, when we hold our Annual Meeting and second Annual Dinner, which the Director has promised to attend. We wish our fellow members "A Happy New Year."

***

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby,
c/o Ingleby Motors, Sweet Street, Leeds.
The first half of the session 1929-30 of the Leeds and West Riding Branch has passed very successfully, commencing on October 16th with a Lantern Lecture by Mr. S. Penzer on "Modern Tendencies in Architecture, Furnishing, and Lighting Design, and the part Electricity plays therein," when Mr. Francis showed some wonderful lantern slides, and finishing with a visit to Messrs. Bryant and Mays Match Works on December 11th, where the wonders of the electrical machinery used in the making of matches were revealed.
On October 30th, a pleasant afternoon was spent at the Leeds Electricity Showrooms, where demonstrations were given on various up-to-date electric appliances, including washing machines and automatic toasters, followed by afternoon tea.
Mr. C. F. Wells, of the E.D.A., lectured on "Electricity in the Home" on November 13th, giving much useful information on radiators, cookers, washers and refrigerators, and he gave a detailed account of the cost of the running of each.
Also on November 27th Mr. S. C. Hurry gave a lecture on "Electric Cookers," and it was almost incredible that so much could be cooked at the same time in such a small oven.
After the lecture Mr. Hurry took the members across to the Hotel Metropole to see a show of Jackson cookers and radiators, etc., and then he kindly invited them to tea.
The members are now looking forward to their Annual Luncheon, which is to be held on January 21st, at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, and they have been greatly favoured by Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, F.R.S., Mr. W. B. Woodhouse and the Director having promised to speak.

***

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. E. H. Klitz,
Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, N. Wales.
Our outstanding event during the Autumn Session was the celebration of our first birthday with a reception and luncheon at Colwyn Bay on November 20th. Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti (our Branch President) presided, and was supported by Dr. Ferranti, Lady Brooks, Mrs. Hyde, Mrs. Prior White and the Director, and a very large company of members and their friends. The occasion was, of course, one of speeches, or rather addresses; and these were listened to with intense interest, and are likely to be quoted from for a long time to come by those who had the pleasure of listening to them.

Unnamed: 9: Manager of the North Wales Distribution Company, amongst good friends.
transcription:
610
The Electrical Age

Our membership grows. As an instance may be quoted the little town of Llanfairfechan, whence 14 members turned up at a recent Branch visit to Messrs. Barker & Dobsons Sweet Factory at Liverpool. We have had a very well-attended Cooking Demonstration at Electricity House, Gresford, when tea was kindly provided by the North Wales Distribution Company. We number the Manager, Mr. G. E. Barrett, amongst our good friends. We also had a lecture from Mr. Francis, of E.D.A., at Wrexham. At Colwyn Bay we have also had a Whist and Bridge Drive, for which Councillor Mrs. Hyde, O.B.E., J.P., lent us the hospitality of her beautiful home. This was a very nice evening, and was a means of augmenting our Branch funds. The prizes were desirable pieces of electrical apparatus, which had been generously given to the Branch.
E.H.K.

Rugby Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Linford, 13, Cromwell Road, Rugby.

In October, when we were fortunate in having our Director with us, the British Thomson-Houston Company entertained some forty of our members to lunch and tea. A tour was made of the Works, and the official guides gave such particularly clear explanations of the various processes that the visit was a most instructive one.
The Annual General Business Meeting was held in the evening, with Viscountess Fielding in the chair, and it was then decided to inaugurate an Annual Dinner.
The first dinner of the Branch was therefore held on November 22nd, among the visitors being Mr. H. A. Law, of the English Electric Co., Mr. A. F. Young, of the British Thomson-Houston Co., and Mr. R. B. Friend, of the Rugby Urban District Council. Mid-Gloucestershire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss G. Johnson,
21, Eastgate Street, Gloucester.
October 25th.—Our Winter Programme opened with a Social Gathering in the form of an "American Tea" at the Cadena Cafes, Gloucester. This was thoroughly enjoyed, the result proving most satisfactory.

She mentioned that most progress was made where there was co-operation between the Education and Electrical Committees, or local electrical industry. An excellent musical programme was provided by Madame Maud Eaves.
On October 15th, Mr. H. R. Beasant, A.M.I.E.E., gave a talk on "How a House is Wired," touching on various types of wiring, and the tracing and remedying of faults. He brought a considerable amount of apparatus, and his lecture was so appreciated that he was asked to give a sequel before the Season is out.
On October 23rd, Mr. A. P. M. Fleming, C.B.E., M.I.E.E. (of Manchester), gave his most fascinating lecture, entitled "Milestones in the Progress of Electricity." The chair was taken by Miss G. M. Morgan, M.A.
On November 12th, Mr. Stratton Holmes, A.M.I.E.E., conducted an experimental lecture on Electricity, in which he dealt mainly with magnetic fields.
On November 29th, a very successful Dance and Whist Drive was held at Fortts Restaurant, which was attended by 120 members and friends.

London Activities.
The Autumn and Winter Session of the London Activities opened well with the visit to the Shipping, Engineering and Machinery Exhibition at Olympia, when the E.A.W. members joined the Womens Engineering Society and were welcomed by Dr. Hele Shaw and Mr. F. W. Bridges.
An interesting afternoon was spent, including a visit to the Stand of the Consolidated Pneumatic Tool Company, and the Motor Boat Section was very popular.
The visit to the showrooms of Messrs. Kelvinator, Limited, was much appreciated. Members were received by Mr. Browse, who afterwards gave a very interesting lecture on "Electrical Cold that Keeps." It was evident from the questions asked that women are keenly aware of the importance of Refrigeration and the various methods which may be used in connection with the Preservation of Foods.
The Lecture Demonstration on "Electric Christmas Cooking," held at Touchbutton House, 83, Newman Street, was an outstanding success. A Lecture on "Water Heating" was also given by Mr. Painton. Members were welcomed by Mr. R. H. Berry, and the Electrical Tea, for which Mrs. Mole had made all the cakes, was very much appreciated. The chair was taken by Mrs. Hammer, and Councillor Mrs. Gregory proposed a vote of thanks.
Many members availed themselves of the invitation from the British Electrical Development Association to the Display of Films, and an enjoyable and interesting evening was spent.
Two Lectures of special interest were given this Session, one by Mr. W. J. Jones, M.Sc. (Eng.), A.M.I.E.E., on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," with special demonstrations.
The Lecture was given at Messrs. Shoolbred, Limited, by invitation of Mr. Percy Best, Managing Director of the Store, and the chair was taken by Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley (President, E.A.W.) in her usual charming and capable manner.
By practical demonstrations, Mr. Jones showed the bad effects of Gloom and Glare, the two evils of bad lighting, and the efficient, yet non-irritating, effect of lighting by means of Pearl and Opal Lamps. Many beautiful examples of good lighting were also noticed in the furnished rooms all round.
Votes of thanks to Mr. Jones, Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley and Mr. Best were proposed by the Dowager Lady Swaythling, and seconded by Mrs. C. J. Cole, and after tea, which was much appreciated, the party was divided into small groups and conducted round the store. A special performance of the Christmas Pantomime, "Alice in Wonderland," concluded a most interesting visit.

Unnamed: 9: Gave a talk on electrical experiences in Australia and NZ.
transcription:
612 The Electrical Age

The other Lecture, by Mr. E. E. Sharp, A.M.I.E.E., was a delightful talk to members of the E.A.W., at the Club Room, 46, Kensington Court, on some of his Electrical Experiences in Australia and New Zealand.

It was very interesting to hear of the domestic electrical equipment in this far-off part of the Empire and the noble efforts of certain Supply Undertakings to provide, by means of electricity, a supply of hot water as nearly as possible comparable to the thermal springs in parts of New Zealand. The chair was taken by Mrs. Ll. B. Atkinson, and a vote of thanks to Mr. Sharp was proposed by Mrs. Jolley.

A most enjoyable and successful Social Evening was spent in the E.A.W. Club Room on Wednesday, October 23rd.

During the evening the Conferences of last summer were brought back to us by some very interesting films. The I.M.E.A. Convention, taken by Colonel Vignoles, and the E.A.W. Newcastle Conference and the W.E.S. Conference at Bedford College, taken by Mrs. Llewelyn B. Atkinson, were much appreciated, and Mrs. Atkinson’s “family” films were also much enjoyed.

Full justice was done to the excellent refreshments provided, and Mrs. Atkinson and the Social Sub-Committee are to be congratulated on the success of the first Social of this Session.

On Thursday afternoon, November 14th, a successful Social Afternoon was held in the Club Room. At the suggestion of members themselves, an interesting talk was given during the afternoon on the Electrical Appliances in the Model Electric Kitchen.

This “Kitchen Talk” was given by Miss Norvick, and provoked a valuable discussion, as a result of which members will in future conduct Demonstrations of Washing and Cooking.

———

A most successful course of three Evening Lectures by Mr. H. Bourne, of the Hendon Electric Supply Company, have been held, and are described in detail elsewhere in the magazine, in the articles by Mr. Bourne and by Miss Sharp.

———

The Surrey Branch of the Association of Teachers of Domestic Subjects again held their Annual Meeting at the E.A.W. Club Room, and at their special request Mr. R. W. Kennedy gave a lecture on “The Common-sense Handling of Electrical Appliances.” Mr. Kennedy has given a series of Lectures to the Staff of the National Training School of Cookery at the request of the Principal, Miss E. G. Clarke.

Miss M. Partridge, B.Sc., A.M.I.E.E., has been lecturing on behalf of the Association to the Women’s Institutes in different parts of the country.

Visitors and enquirers for electrical knowledge continue to visit the kitchen.

A very interesting programme has been arranged for the spring, and particulars will gladly be sent on application to the Head Office.
V.S.

A PERMANENT RECORD OF A UNIQUE OCCASION.

What Women Think
ABOUT

IN
Great Britain,
U.S.A., Holland, and Germany.

The papers read by the Overseas Delegates at the Opening Session of the E.A.W. Conference at Newcastle-on-Tyne, on July 10th, 1929, created a widespread interest, and they have been printed in an attractive Booklet.

This should be read by everyone who is interested in Electrical Development, not only in this country, but in U.S.A., Holland and Germany.

The Booklet is moderately priced, 1/- post free, and may be obtained from :—

The Electrical Age for Women,
46, Kensington Court,
London, W.8.

The
ELECTRICAL AGE
FOR WOMEN
The Official Journal of the
Electrical Association
for Women

PUBLISHED QUARTERLY
Editor
CAROLINE HASLETT
46 Kensington Court
London W.8

Vol. 1.
APRIL, 1930.
No. 16

In the passing of Dr. Sebastian Ziani de Ferranti at Zurich, on January 13th, 1930, the Engineering World, and the Electrical Industry in particular, has lost one of the men whose genius and ability has most vitally affected the progress of electrical development in this and every country.

While we mourn the loss of so sincere a friend, it will be a constant source of gratification and inspiration in all the future work of the Electrical Association for Women to know that this great Scientist and Engineer believed profoundly in the good influence which women could exert in the development of Electricity on the lines which would be of the greatest benefit to the general public.

He saw in Electricity a means whereby the work of the woman in the home could be dignified—demanding intelligence rather than hard physical labour. The universal use of Electricity was to him, not only his work and his hobby—although it was both these things—it was also a “ Gospel,” the medium through which life could be made more beautiful and simple; in other words, the substitution of intelligent leisure for unintelligent drudgery.

The women of the E.A.W. who had been fortunate to come in contact with Dr. Ferranti realised that not only was he an eminent Engineer, who had applied the Forces of Nature to the Use of Mankind, but a man who was a great believer in the power of organised womanhood to achieve the ideals for the good of the Nation which he had visualised more than a quarter of a century ago.

S. Z. de Ferranti

transcription:
EDITORIAL.

THE 1930 CONFERENCE will be held in London on May 15th and 16th, the chief Social Functions being a Luncheon on May 15th and a Ball on May 16th, both at the Park Lane Hotel.
Of special interest will be the visit to Messrs. J. Lyons & Co.s Factory at Greenford, where Members will see the part which Electricity plays in the manufacture of our food.
A visit to the Home Office Industrial Museum will provide an opportunity to see the latest methods which are employed for promoting the safety, health and welfare of industrial workers. The Exhibition, which was inaugurated in 1927 by their Majesties the King and Queen, is the first of its kind in this country, and sets out to show the best possible conditions under which industrial workers should be employed. A large part of the success of the Exhibition is due to the interest of Miss Hilda Martindale, H.M. Deputy Chief Inspector of Factories, who will receive the E.A.W. Members on their arrival.
The Institution of Electrical Engineers, with their usual courtesy, have placed their Building at the disposal of the London Executive for a Reception on the first evening of the Conference.

■ ■ ■

THE BUSINESS WOMAN AND ELECTRICITY.—It is perhaps not generally realised what an increasing part the business woman is playing in this country in electrical development. Women Builders, Architects and Decorators all realise what a very large place the use of electricity occupies in their schemes. It would be well for the Electrical Industry to realise the value of giving support and encouragement to women doing pioneering work of this kind. This remark is prompted by the fact that we have on several occasions come across instances where sections of the Electrical Industry did not think it worth their while to give necessary helpful information to women concerned with the construction and decoration of housing schemes.

■ ■ ■

WHAT OF THE COUNTRYSIDE?—Recently we have realised through the medium of the newspapers that there is an outcry about the Standards which are being erected in connection with the transmission of electricity into rural districts. While we are fully in sympathy with every attempt to preserve the beauties of our countryside, it should be realised that new development is not synonymous with ugliness. The benefits of electricity must eventually be brought within the reach of the women of the country, and those people who are agitating strongly against the transmission lines should realise that they are thus retarding what is one of the most important developments for the benefit of the countryside.
We suggest that the suppliers of electricity when about to develop a rural district should call together the members of the Womens Institutes and consult them about their plans and discuss with them possible developments, thus securing the sympathy and support of the women in whose district the supply of electricity is to be given.
The Report recently issued by the Electricity Commissioners on a Demonstration Scheme of Rural Electrification in Bedfordshire* is worthy of perusal.
"The object of this Scheme is to provide for the comprehensive and rapid electrification of a typical rural area where mixed farming is the main industry and electricity has not been previously available, so that within a period of about two years supplies for all purposes will be within the reach of practically all the inhabitants."

transcription:
618 The Electrical Age

The Edwardian period of Act II. shows the home of Tobias and Anne Jolly, with the new electric lighting. Elizabeth Tegget, now 65, is still very nervous of new inventions, and she is afraid that if she introduces the electric light into her home it might blow up.

Here we have shewn the new womans interest in Dorothy Jolly (Jean Hinchliff), who is studying architecture, and her brother, Henry Jolly (Valentine Nicholls), who is on the staff of a large works, and is eager to introduce the new up-to-date methods of lighting which they have at the Works.

The War period of 1918 occupies the stage next, and is concerned with women troubled about their men folk and the lack of food. This is a period of plenty of light, but with very poor ideas of comfort in its use.

The scene for the final act displays a charming modern room in 1929, beautifully lighted with adequate and artistic fittings.

Anne Jolly, now an old lady of 72, is full of reminiscences of the changes during the last 50 years, and is charmed with the modern conveniences of electric light, especially the little lamp by her bedside.

Helen Jolly (Ethel M. Dickinson) is delighted at having her husband home again, and is very interested in the modern development of electricity, and the really modern spirit displayed by her daughter, Mavis (Aline Jackson), who with her fiancé, Arthur (Dudley C. Apps), are determined to embark upon matrimony with an all-electric home.

The success of the play was due very largely to Jose Shannon, who not only acted as producer, but herself performed the most strenuous part.

All the players were either members of the Association or connected with the Electrical Industry, and acted with zest and interest.

The E. L. M. A. Lighting Service Bureau carried out all the lighting arrangements. The Edison Swan Electric Co., Ltd., provided the electric sound reproducing equipment; Messrs. Ferranti, Ltd., the electric fire, and Messrs. J. Shoolbred & Co., Ltd., the furniture and carpets. Our thanks are due to Mrs. Llewelyn B. Atkinson (assisted by Mrs. Neilson) for designing and making the dresses.

The play was preceded by half an hours Nonsense by Mr. T. C. Sterndale-Bennett.

The audience was both large and distinguished, many well-known people present expressing their appreciation of the play.

By courtesy of "Electrical Industries."
JOSE SHANNON.

Here we have shewn the new womans interest in Dorothy Jolly (Jean Hinchliff), who is studying architecture, and her brother, Henry Jolly (Valentine Nicholls), who is on the staff of a large works, and is eager to introduce the new up-to-date methods of lighting which they have at the Works.

The War period of 1918 occupies the stage next, and is concerned with women troubled about their men folk and the lack of food. This is a period of plenty of light, but with very poor ideas of comfort in its use.

The scene for the final act displays a charming modern room in 1929, beautifully lighted with adequate and artistic fittings.

Anne Jolly, now an old lady of 72, is full of reminiscences of the changes during the last 50 years, and is charmed with the modern conveniences of electric light, especially the little lamp by her bedside.

Helen Jolly (Ethel M. Dickinson) is delighted at having her husband home again, and is very interested in the modern development of electricity, and the really modern spirit displayed by her daughter, Mavis (Aline Jackson), who with her fiancé, Arthur (Dudley C. Apps), are determined to embark upon matrimony with an all-electric home.

The success of the play was due very largely to Jose Shannon, who not only acted as producer, but herself performed the most strenuous part.

All the players were either members of the Association or connected with the Electrical Industry, and acted with zest and interest.

The E. L. M. A. Lighting Service Bureau carried out all the lighting arrangements. The Edison Swan Electric Co., Ltd., provided the electric sound reproducing equipment; Messrs. Ferranti, Ltd., the electric fire, and Messrs. J. Shoolbred & Co., Ltd., the furniture and carpets. Our thanks are due to Mrs. Llewelyn B. Atkinson (assisted by Mrs. Neilson) for designing and making the dresses.

The play was preceded by half an hours Nonsense by Mr. T. C. Sterndale-Bennett.

The audience was both large and distinguished, many well-known people present expressing their appreciation of the play.

By courtesy of "Electrical Industries."

The War period of 1918 occupies the stage next, and is concerned with women troubled about their men folk and the lack of food. This is a period of plenty of light, but with very poor ideas of comfort in its use.

The scene for the final act displays a charming modern room in 1929, beautifully lighted with adequate and artistic fittings.

Anne Jolly, now an old lady of 72, is full of reminiscences of the changes during the last 50 years, and is charmed with the modern conveniences of electric light, especially the little lamp by her bedside.

Helen Jolly (Ethel M. Dickinson) is delighted at having her husband home again, and is very interested in the modern development of electricity, and the really modern spirit displayed by her daughter, Mavis (Aline Jackson), who with her fiancé, Arthur (Dudley C. Apps), are determined to embark upon matrimony with an all-electric home.

The success of the play was due very largely to Jose Shannon, who not only acted as producer, but herself performed the most strenuous part.

All the players were either members of the Association or connected with the Electrical Industry, and acted with zest and interest.

The E. L. M. A. Lighting Service Bureau carried out all the lighting arrangements. The Edison Swan Electric Co., Ltd., provided the electric sound reproducing equipment; Messrs. Ferranti, Ltd., the electric fire, and Messrs. J. Shoolbred & Co., Ltd., the furniture and carpets. Our thanks are due to Mrs. Llewelyn B. Atkinson (assisted by Mrs. Neilson) for designing and making the dresses.

The play was preceded by half an hours Nonsense by Mr. T. C. Sterndale-Bennett.

The audience was both large and distinguished, many well-known people present expressing their appreciation of the play.

By courtesy of "Electrical Industries."

transcription:
The Electrical Age 619
An Appreciation of
Dr. S. Z. de FERRANTI, F.R.S.
By CAROLINE HASLETT.
While women of the E.A.W. cannot fail to have realised in Dr. Ferranti an engineer of the greatest eminence, perhaps it has never been realised by the majority of women in this country how much we owe to this great man for the benefits of Electricity which we enjoy to-day. Not only was Dr. Ferranti an engineer, but he also proved himself to be a prophet, as so many theories which he outlined many years ago are just beginning to be practised in the Electrical Industry of to-day. Like the great man he was, he went on with his early work in spite of criticism and opposition, knowing of a surety that his theories and methods would one day achieve ultimate success—that success was only retarded because of the lack of vision and lethargy of other people, and to-day the lines upon which public electricity supply is being developed, not only in this country, but on the Continent, in America and throughout the world, are substantially the same as those laid down by Dr. Ferranti more than forty years ago.
Dr. Ferranti was born in Liverpool in 1864, and from his very earliest days he showed an unusual interest in Mechanics. He commenced Mechanical Drawing at a phenomenally early age, and when ten years old he compiled a very wonderful Scrap Book of Illustrations from “The Engineer ” and “ Engineering.”
While at school at Ramsgate he commenced the construction of his first Dynamo, which he eventually sold for a five pound note. Although he spent some time at University College, it would be true to say that Dr. Ferranti had to teach himself most of the knowledge which made his work possible. While still a very young man he made a motor-focussing arc lamp, which Mrs. Ferranti still has in her possession. At the end of 1883 the Company which owned Ferranti’s patents went into liquidation. Ferranti, however, succeeded in buying back the patents, and, having purchased a few tools, started manufacturing on his own account, and practically founded the great Company which is known under his name, and which to-day employs over 4,000 work-people, many of whom are

A picture of the small model Electric Cooker which Dr. Ferranti purchased in Switzerland and which was probably almost the last electrical thing which he did. The inscription on the Cooker is as follows:

for
The Electrical Association for Women
by
Dr. S. Z. de Ferranti, F.R.S.
January, 1930.

Unnamed: 7: Grosvenor Gallery Lighting Company; The Firm
Unnamed: 9: Engineer who founded the Firm and designed high pressure systems.
transcription:
620 The Electrical Age

women. About this period Mr. Ferranti became acquainted with the promoters of the Grosvenor Gallery Lighting Company. The station originated from Sir Coutts Lindsays determination to light the Grosvenor Gallery by electricity, but nemands from neighbours for current became so great that the plant soon became of considerable magnitude. The system, however, proved to be exceedingly difficult to work, and, after negotiations, Ferranti was called in at the beginning of 1886, to act as engineer to the Grosvenor Gallery Company.

The young Engineer signalled his appointment to the Grosvenor Gallery Company by immediate measures of reform, and so rapid was the progress of the Grosvenor Gallery works that in a very short time 36,000 lamps were connected.

Long before the Grosvenor Station had achieved the success already mentioned, Mr. Ferranti had laid down the principle that power generation should be done on a convenient site outside great cities, where land was cheap and water and coal were easily available. Impressed with the soundness of Ferrantis ideas, and alive to the great future of electric lighting, the owners of the Grosvenor Gallery determined to embark on an undertaking which at that time could be compared for magnitude to the building of the Great Western Railway.

While there was no insuperable difficulty in the way of securing a favourable site, the real difficulty was to find a perfectly safe means of handling the high-pressure currents involved in such a scheme. The solution which presented itself to Ferrantis mind was one which was then considered rank heresy, and was moreover entirely contrary to the Board of Trade Regulations.

A bank of Incandescent Lamps through which the first 10,000-volt current was sent on May 9th, 1888.

So satisfied, however, was this young Engineer that it was the only safe way of working that he took the responsibility of acting contrary to the Regulations so as to force home the correctness of the principle, and eventually he succeeded in laying the foundation for the tremendous work which is being carried out today, known as the Grid, under the authorisation of the Central Electricity Board.

In those days it was declared by the foremost living electricians to be an impossibility to transmit electricity at a pressure of 10,000 volts. Yet to-day the Firm which Dr. Ferranti founded is constructing Transformers which will make it possible for electricity to be transmitted at a pressure of 132,000 volts.

The Station eventually erected by the Grosvenor Gallery Company was at Deptford, and perhaps there was never before a station which provoked so much controversy. Yet when misrepresentations were

Unnamed: 4: Dr.; Past President of the Institution of Electrical Engineers; Faraday Medal recipient
Unnamed: 7: Institution of Electrical Engineers; syndicate for Niagara Falls
Unnamed: 9: Pioneer engineer responsible for many electrical inventions and Niagara scheme.
Unnamed: 10: Subject of the article; husband of Gertrude; business partner
transcription:
The Electrical Age 621

rife, and criticism was of the keenest, Ferranti, in that wonderful spirit of self-control and assurance, kept aloof and on no single occasion did he reply to his critics, having the conviction that his methods would eventually prove to be successful.
Early in his career the young Engineer had the support of Mr. Francis H. Ince, who took much interest in his work, and it was his second daughter, Gertrude, who eventually became Mrs. S. Z. de Ferranti. Married at a time when the Doctor was doing most of his difficult and arduous pioneer work, Mrs. Ferranti has always been his greatest companion and ever taken the keenest interest in the work which he was carrying out.
To endeavour to enumerate all the inventions for which Dr. Ferranti was responsible would be impossible in the compass of so short an article; suffice it to say that not only was he responsible for the invention and construction of large electrical machines, but the more humble duties of measuring current owe much to him, and everyone to-day is familiar with the Ferranti Meter.
It is perhaps not generally known that a syndicate, composed of Ferranti, Mr. Ince and Colonel Shaw, secured in about 1886 the original concessions on the Canadian side for utilising the Niagara Falls. The idea was to transmit electrical energy to Buffalo, and indeed anywhere within 500 miles. The idea, however, received little support in England, and the scheme eventually died of inanition.
In "Cassiers Magazine" for 1897, containing an interesting account of Dr. Ferrantis early work, it states:-"It is not surprising that Ferranti should have clear and distinct views on the future of Electrical Engineering. He holds that the essence of improvement lies in the cheapening of the supply to bring it within the reach of all and to adapt it to the many purposes for which it is so admirably suited. In his opinion the business of distributing electrical energy must be done on a large scale to be commercial, and to attain this we must supply a large area, not limited by the exigencies of systems, and we must do this from a site, not in the congested heart of a big city, but from a position best suited by its natural advantages to the carrying on of such an undertaking."
Thus at the early age of 32 Ferranti had envisaged the development of Electricity on a comprehensive scale, which is to-day becoming a practical possibility under the 1926 Electricity (Supply) Act.
Of his later work, more is known by the general public. He was a Past President of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, and in 1924 the Faraday Medal, the highest honour of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, was conferred upon him. It is, we feel, regrettable that his country had not thought fit to honour so great a man. Speaking of Dr. Ferranti at the time the Faraday Medal was presented, Colonel R. E. Crompton, himself a pioneer of British Electricity, said: "Ferranti, as a steam engineer, as a designer of generating machinery, of high pressure cables and of the distributing devices necessary with alternating current, was the man who did more than anyone else to start the electrical engineering profession."
Those of us who were privileged to meet him and to hear him speak will not easily forget his rich, resonant voice, his charm and modesty, and, above all, his unfailing courtesy on all occasions. To have had the privilege of knowing him in his family circle and to have seen the real delight which he took in the applications of Electricity in the home was to realise the extreme simplicity and beauty of his nature.
Both at Baslow Hall, in Derbyshire, and at the smaller home at Deganwy, North Wales, Dr. Ferranti had put his ideals for eliminating domestic drudgery by electricity into practical form.
The last picture we have of him is of a brief happy time spent with him and Mrs. Ferranti just before Christmas at Little Haldon, Deganwy, when in the absence of any domestic help the great man himself took a sheer delight in helping to cook the breakfast electrically.
The years will prove that not only the Electrical Industry owes him a very real debt, but that the woman in the home also will owe to him very largely her emancipation from household drudgery.

transcription:
622    The Electrical Age

ELECTRICITY IN THE HOSPITAL.
By GLADYS F. SHARP.

Describing a London Hospital staffed and run by women, where electricity plays an
important part in remedial and curative work.

The first woman to take a degree and practise as a doctor of medicine was Elizabeth Garrett Anderson, and to-day, in Euston Road, there stands the finest memorial to this pioneer that she could have wished. The Hospital which bears her name is run entirely by women for the treatment of women and children, and in the tiled entrance hall, from which all sound of the busy road outside is excluded as by a miracle, one sees oil paintings of many of the clever women who have been associated with the hospital.

As was to be expected, those who are carrying on the fine work of these pioneers have seen to it that all the very latest developments of science have been called in to help in the smooth running of the hospital and to aid the doctors in their fight against sickness and disease.

Electricity, the very symbol of cleanness and efficiency, is everywhere. The first use of it to meet the eye on entering the hospital is in the restful, perfectly diffused lighting, but in these days electric lighting, except in some of its most modern and eccentric forms, creates no excitement, and

so we must proceed to tour the building to discover it in a hundred and one guises, and in every one doing work of the utmost importance without fuss or bother.

Being women, even in a hospital it is the kitchen which interests us first, and here we find great baking ovens and fish fryers, with speckless interiors and exteriors and cheerful pilot lights—those red lamps which show whether the electricity is being used or not—and simply-operated switches, proving that in the study of more difficult subjects these medical women have not forgotten that the hospital is a household calling for the very finest cooking medium. In such a household cleanliness and an entire absence of fumes in the food must necessarily be of primary importance, and in this respect electricity can be of great assistance in helping to restore the patients to good health.

From the kitchen we pass through the wards and find electricity represented there by the earphones above each bed. What long, weary hours are whiled away by these

Elizabeth Garrett Anderson, the first woman to qualify in Medicine in Great Britain—in 1865. What would she think of this Hospital, which has grown from the small Dispensary which she then opened in the Euston Road for Women and Children?

Photo by courtesy of Messrs. G. Bell & Sons, publishers of "The Cause," by Ray Strachey.

To what use has electricity been put in
the operating theatre? Just look at this
light on a rise-and-fall pendant above the
operating table. The shade has a diameter
of something like two feet, and reflects
every bit of light down on to the work. The
actual lighting source looks very much like
one of those curious lamps used in a light-
house, and is shut in by glass across the
bottom of the shade. Unusual, you think,
but nothing to get really excited about.
Well, just stand under the lamp and see
how it differs from any other. Not a vestige
of a shadow anywhere! Think what a lot
of trouble would have been saved if Mr.
Darling had fitted this in his childrens
night nursery. Peter Pans shadow would
have remained outside on the window-sill
and would never have been shut up in a
drawer, causing him to come back and
search for it. Wendy would never have
been awakened and taught to fly. Perhaps,
after all, we are glad Mr. Darling never
thought of it, but just consider how much
more simple an operation becomes when
the surgeon is not hindered by his own
shadow and can move about freely without
having to consider the light.
That is marvellous ! Just step into the
lift and explore with me the modern equiv-
alent of the magic caves of story books. Here
we are beneath the level of Euston Road,
surrounded on every side by mysterious
apparatus, much more difficult to describe
than were the mere piles of precious jewels
which met the eyes of Aladdin and Ali
Baba.
Have you been ill, or does our sad winter
depress you? Come and sit under this sun-
ray lamp, with its deep silver-coloured shade
and close your eyes. Does it need a very
vivid imagination to call up a vision of a
sun-drenched banana plantation with a
camel at ease in the courtyard of the over-
seers picturesquely dilapidated house? Or
does a Spanish hacienda, with the tinkle of
a lazy guitar stirring the warm air, suit your
romantic mind better? At any rate, the
cold greyness of England is far away, the
memory of your recent illness already
erased by cheerier thoughts.

year when it seemed that our King must
lose his brave fight against his severe ill-
ness, and how at length the doctors called
electricity to their aid? Probably you heard
of ultra-violet rays for the first time then,
and remembered the name because of the
almost immediate rally that followed their
use. Here in this hospital are many
examples of ultra-violet ray apparatus—
some small pieces for local treatment,

apparent heat from the rays, and yet they
can scorch the skin badly if used indiscrim-
inately. Alarm clocks are generally used to

be switched off. This form of electrical

Unnamed: 9: The hospital mentioned in the text is named after her.
transcription:
624
The Electrical Age
number of things, from the curing of rheumatism and skin disease to the growing of new hair on heads that have long been but smooth, pink domes.
You have all, of course, heard of X-rays, whose curious habit it is to render our flesh transparent and show up our bones and organs to the curious. They are used frequently in boot shops to make sure that children are not getting shoes too small for them. It is great fun to put your hand in the rays and see how unprepossessing it looks when the nice white covering and well-manicured nails have gone, leaving only a few nasty, nobbly-looking bones. But if you have broken one of those bones, how much easier it is to ascertain the exact position of the break and make sure that the join is a perfect one !
If your baby brother swallows a pin, as baby brothers have been known to, the pin will show up plainly in the X-rays and can be operated for with comparative ease, whereas the chance of getting it up by suspending a magnet down his throat on a piece of string is very small indeed.
There is also a room in this hospital devoted to X-ray treatment, where the rays are used not for examination purposes, but actually for curing certain ailments.
Electrically, your tour of the hospital, though a little sketchy, is almost completed, but before you are ushered out into the hurly-burly of Euston Road once more, just step into this room. It contains batteries which will give light to the hospital for two hours should the electricity supply from the power station fail. Perhaps you have read, on rare occasions, in the newspapers that the electricity supply at Blank failed, and the hospital was plunged into darkness just as an operation was being performed, whereupon the surgeon carried on by candlelight or by torch-light. You will never read that about the Elizabeth Garrett Anderson Hospital. There is no worthy substitute for electricity, and no second best finds its way into this little kingdom run by women for women.
This article was written as the result of a very interesting visit by Members of the E.A.W. to the Hospital, arranged by Dr. Eva White, who represents the Medical Application of Electricity on the E.A.W. Council.

Some Electrical Novelties at the Ideal Home Exhibition.
The Electric Nursery.
One of the most attractive and popular rooms in the Pavilion of Light, erected and equipped
The Electric Nursery.
by the General Electric Company, is the Nursery, and it is of special interest that this winning design was sent in by a woman Architect, Miss Frances Barker, A.R.I.B.A., of Blackheath.
Her whole scheme has been followed in its entirety, and includes Vita Glass windows, hidden heating, and a concealed cupboard for the Nursery requisites.
The six rooms in the Pavilion are of novel design and new ideas have been incorporated in them all.
The Hall of Ideals.
The Hall of Ideals of the Ediswan Company is a very artistic and novel display designed by a well-known architect. Each room depicts the comforts and beauty which electricity can give.
" Beauty Enriched by Light."
The well-known figure of " Beauty Enriched by Light " is the centre piece of some wonderful lighting effects arranged with Mazda Lamps.

Unnamed: 9: Writes letters to Flip about her job in a showroom.
transcription:
The Electrical Age  625
IN LIGHTER VEIN.
More Letters of Lulu.
My dear Flip,
More news! Im getting along swim-
mingly here in the showroom. Still sort of
electric Mannequin. It hasnt taken your
old Lulu long to learn all the ins and outs of
electric currents, and, believe me, the kind
I represent is all ins and outs and ups and
downs.
When you have a supply put, my dear
Flip, see its the best—go in for quality as
well as quantity. Be guided by your old and
expert friend Lulu.
Our brand wiggles up and down 50 times
a sec. Think of that, my dear—incredible!
—how the boys do it without losing count
I dont know. One of them showed me a
sweet picture of one of the currents—such
sinuous curves. They go in cycles—you
know—so many to the H.P.—about 3 this
year, I believe. Quaint, isnt it?
You see the current sort of cycles back-
wards and forwards in the wire—like a
circus. Think of lights switched on and off
and then lit backwards 50 times a second.
What marvellous economy.
Think of a steak cooked up and down 50
times a second—it must be tender—(my
dear, arent I just the cutest saleswoman?).
Of course, the real work comes in knowing
what to charge for the "juice," as the boys
call it. We have a flat rate—for flats, you
know—and a two-part rate where we charge
so much for cooking current and so much
for lighting current.
The chief assistant has been hours ex-
plaining it all to me. Its so mysterious. I
asked him why the meters didnt go back-
wards when the current does this reversing
business, but I understand theres some
cunning sort of trap or ratchet affair to stop
them!
And, of course, when we deliver current
(not in plain vans, my dear) we put in an
extra wire to bring it back again. It comes
home again, slightly worse for wear, but its
brushed clean with the foulest black brushes
and sent out again. We use the same
current over and over again! And some
people say electricity isnt economical.
Thats where we have such a pull over gas
—once that beastly stuff is uncorked, its
out of the tube and off—no return tickets—
awfully unfaithful stuff.
Which reminds me of an adventure I had
the other day. Such a nice looking homely
sort of man blew into the showroom, so I
just pounced on him. It didnt take me long
to tell him all I knew.
When we came to the cooker, he said,
"Isnt gas better for cooking?" Gas—my
dear! Imagine it!
Your Lulu hadnt learnt all the talking
points for nothing! They simply sailed past
my eyes like taxis on a wet night.
"Gas," I said—waggling my nostrils like
a hound meeting a red herring on the trail
—"Gas—why, you wouldnt dream of
using gas—surely?"
"Why not?" he piped. "Think of
meat," I said, "shrinkage—loss of weight,
contraction or expansion must occur. Put
a side of beef into a gas oven—it comes out
looking like a side of lamb, but tastes like
leather. Put it into an electric oven—it
remains its full size—no loss—no shrinkage.
You recognise an old friend." Just a teeny
bit of exaggeration, my dear, but I could
see by his face it was going down well.
"And what about the fumes?" I said,
"You dont want stray therms about the
house—theyre dangerous."
Just then in popped the Chief. "Hallo,
Robinson," he said, "has the lady been
trying her hand on you?" Turning to me
he said, "I dont think youll convert Mr.
Robinson—hes the Manager of the Gas
Works!"
My dear, I felt as though my circulating
system had seized!
More later,
Your own,
LULU.

I dont know. One of them showed me a
sweet picture of one of the currents—such
sinuous curves. They go in cycles—you
know—so many to the H.P.—about 3 this
year, I believe. Quaint, isnt it?
You see the current sort of cycles back-
wards and forwards in the wire—like a
circus. Think of lights switched on and off
and then lit backwards 50 times a second.
What marvellous economy.
Think of a steak cooked up and down 50
times a second—it must be tender—(my
dear, arent I just the cutest saleswoman?).

what to charge for the "juice," as the boys
call it. We have a flat rate—for flats, you
know—and a two-part rate where we charge

for lighting current.

plaining it all to me. Its so mysterious. I
asked him why the meters didnt go back-

them!

home again, slightly worse for wear, but its
brushed clean with the foulest black brushes

people say electricity isnt economical.

out of the tube and off—no return tickets—
awfully unfaithful stuff.

the other day. Such a nice looking homely
sort of man blew into the showroom, so I
just pounced on him. It didnt take me long
