transcription:
626

The Electrical Age

WHAT DOES IT COST ?

By C. F. Wells, A.I.E.E.

So often we hear the remark—"I would like to use electricity for all purposes, but it is too costly." Here is a description of an all-electric home consisting of three adults and three children where, in addition to a small fixed annual charge, the actual cost of electricity consumed for all household purposes is £32 per annum.

The proportion of women ready to go into domestic service has, as you will all know, been declining for the past 15 years, and the households which can claim to have one or more competent servants are few and far between. In fact, most people have either to pay high wages or offer easy conditions to retain maids.

Thousands of women are to-day confronted with the task of doing all the housework as well as bringing up a family.

The solution of this problem is to electrify the home, so that housework can be done under modern conditions, and therefore with a minimum amount of drudgery. In fact, the time is coming when it will be cheaper to use electricity than not to do so. The advantages electricity offers to the modern home, such as convenience, cleanliness and the saving of work are unrivalled, and there are now in existence thousands of all-electric houses.

Believing that those in the electrical industry should not only preach but follow the slogan, "Do it electrically," I equipped our house throughout with electrical apparatus several years ago, and last year we used electricity to the exclusion of any other form of heat.

The household consists of three adults and three children, and the consumption of electricity for 1928 was 14,500 units, which cost £32. The charge for electricity is based on a fixed charge of 15% per annum of the net rateable value of the property, plus ½d. per unit.

The apparatus installed (in addition to lighting) is as follows:—3 Radiators, 1 Cooker, 1 Vacuum Cleaner, 1 Wash Boiler, 1 Rotary Washing Machine, 2 Water Heaters (one in the bathroom and one in the kitchen), 1 Iron, 1 Refrigerator, 1 Kettle, 1 Coffee Percolator.

Five meters are installed, so that a check on the various uses can be kept. It may interest you to know how the consumption of 14,500 units is made up. This is approximately as follows:—

Lighting and small appliances ... 1,600 units
Cooking ... ... ... 2,100 ..
Water Heating ... ... ... 4,000 ..
Radiators ... ... ... 6,800 ..
Total ... ... ... 14,500

The wiring of an all-electric house, and also the amount and selection of the apparatus required, calls for considerable care in order that the best and most economical results may be obtained. I will deal with this aspect under various headings.

Wiring.—You will appreciate a good installation is necessary for an all-electric house, and the consideration of this may be divided into three classes:—
(1) the lighting (which will consist of fixed lights and plugs for reading lamps);
(2) wiring for fixed apparatus, such as the cooker, refrigerator, water heater, etc.;
(3) plugs for radiators and other portable apparatus, such as vacuum cleaner, kettles, etc.

With a two-part tariff for electricity, one can afford to be a little extravagant with lighting, and the points should be well chosen and numerous, with good facilities for switching on and off at several positions for a large proportion of the lights. These additional switching arrangements are easily arranged, and only call for a little forethought when planning the installation.

* Paper read before the E.A.W. Leeds and West Riding Branch.

Unnamed: 10: daughter of Mr. and Mrs. C. F. Wells; sister of Chris
transcription:
The Electrical Age 627

Wall outlets should be planned to give the maximum convenience, and it is desir- able to have at least two in each room.

Room Heating.—The principal domestic requirement in the house is heat. It is required for a large part of the year for raising the temperature of rooms and all the year round for water heating and cooking purposes.

As a labour-saver the electric fire is unexcelled by any other type of modern heating apparatus.

There are no fumes to discolour ceilings and walls, and the ease by which radiators can be carried about enables heat to be obtained wherever you most need it and regulated as required, which ensures economy.

One cannot lay down a definite rule regarding the amount of energy required for room heating, but in choosing electric fires it will be fairly safe to make an allowance of about 1 1/4 watts per cubic foot of space to be heated.

An average household of five persons will normally use about 4,000 to 5,000 units per annum for room heating.

Cooking.—The merits of electric cooking are now well established. It is in- teresting to remember that there are more cookers per head of population in this country than there are in America. Simplicity in working and ease in obtain- ing good results make cook- ing by electricity attractive.

The heat is constant and capable of fine control, which ensures that an operation once carried out successfully can be re- peated at any time, even by the most amateur cook, but it is only by trying elec- tric cooking that its benefits can be properly realised.

The saving in weight of the food cooked is important, and enables big economies to be obtained over other methods. This claim is sometimes disputed because people do not understand the reason for the reduced shrinkage, which lies in the rapidity with which the oven temperature can be con- trolled. Half a pound of meat saved on a joint will pay the cost of current required to cook a whole meal.

Margaret and Chris, the young daughter and son of Mr. and Mrs. C. F. Wells, enjoying a few moments in front of the Electric Fire before going off to bed.

Unnamed: 9: Pioneer woman builder converting a large mansion into electric flats.
transcription:
The Electrical Age 629

A Woman Builder and Electricity.
Outlets in Every Room. Heating, Cooking and Water Heating.
Payment of Electricity by means of Slot Meters.

Mrs. L. A. Willson, M.B.E., the pioneer Woman Builder, has recently taken on a large unoccupied mansion at Walton-on-Thames, and is converting the building into flats, comprising two sets of six-roomed, four sets of four-roomed, and a series of seventeen two-roomed flats. All the flats have been extensively wired for the use of Electricity, and we are pleased to learn that heating outlets have been provided in every room; the larger flats have been equipped with a Magnet cooker, suitable for four or more persons, while the two-roomed flats each are fitted with a Magnet "Minor" cooker and three-pint copper electric kettle with automatic cut-out. The convenience of the fortunate tenants of these flats is further provided for by an electrically-heated hot water system. The larger flats have their own bathrooms, in which are installed Magnet water heaters, while the tenants of the two-roomed flats have the use of separate bathrooms, which are grouped at each end of the corridor. Hot water for each group of bathrooms is supplied by means of 30-gallon storage water heaters, thermostatically controlled, and the current used by these water heaters, of which there are three, together with that for corridor lighting throughout the building, is paid for by the owner.
By a special arrangement made with the Walton Electricity Department the owner of the flats pays to the Council the fixed charge calculated to cover the requirements of the building as a whole, while the individual tenants purchase current as they use it through a slot meter at 1 1/2d. per unit for all purposes in their own premises.

[Portrait Image]
By courtesy of "Every Woman."
Mrs. L. A. Willson, M.B.E., Vice-President of the E.A.W., and Past President of the Womens Engineering Society.

Mrs. Willson has received every encouragement and help in her work from the local Electrical Engineer, Mr. E. A. Anderson, and Mr. Edgley, the Wiring Contractor, and in a letter received from her recently she says: "Personally I am charmed by the use of Electricity, and am using it freely in a flat of my own."

[Image of a kitchen corner with a cooker]
A picture of a Magnet "Minor" Cooker in one of the two-roomed flats.

Mrs. Willson, who has carried through several extensive building schemes since she started in 1925, has had every opportunity of comparing various methods for heating and cooking, and the fact that her latest installation will be practically an all-Electric one is due very largely to her interest in the work of the Electrical Association for Women.
Of Yorkshire birth, Mrs. Willson commenced her building activities in her native town of Halifax, where she built 64 working-class houses, to be sold at £400 each.
By October, 1928, she had concluded building work to the value of about a quarter of a million pounds—a remarkable achievement.

Anderson, and Mr. Edgley, the Wiring Contractor, and in a letter received from her recently she says: "Personally I am charmed by the use of Electricity, and am using it freely in a flat of my own."

[Image of a kitchen corner with a cooker]
A picture of a Magnet "Minor" Cooker in one of the two-roomed flats.

Mrs. Willson, who has carried through several extensive building schemes since she started in 1925, has had every opportunity of comparing various methods for heating and cooking, and the fact that her latest installation will be practically an all-Electric one is due very largely to her interest in the work of the Electrical Association for Women.
Of Yorkshire birth, Mrs. Willson commenced her building activities in her native town of Halifax, where she built 64 working-class houses, to be sold at £400 each.
By October, 1928, she had concluded building work to the value of about a quarter of a million pounds—a remarkable achievement.

transcription:
630
The Electrical Age
IMPRESSIONS OF IMATRA.
By BETTY BENN (daughter of the famous publisher, Sir Ernest Benn), who gives a fascinating picture of Finlands Electricity Supply.
A four hundred mile journey by train from Helsingfors, the capital, landed us at 10 oclock on a moonlight night at Imatra, the chief beauty spot and the electrical centre of Finland. Driving from the station to the one and only hotel, we caught just a glimpse of the falls as we flashed past. First on our left a stretch of smooth black water leads up to what looked like a long high wall, brilliantly illuminated with four electric lamps, in reality the turbine house, and then on our right, as we passed over the second half of the double bridge, we saw the wonderful fall. The great black towers of the dam contrasted strongly with the phosphorescent light of the water as it rushed foaming through them. Past the open flood gates it came, a smooth, black stream; then as it crashed below on to the rocky surface of the river bed it tossed and foamed, gleaming silver in the cold moonlight. Another quick turn of the head showed us the water rushing on down the gorge, and then we had passed it all, and round the corner drew up at the door of our hotel.
The next morning dawned as sunny an autumn day as we could possibly have wished for, and it was with no little excitement that I woke with the sound of the rapids in my ears, and, hurrying out on to my balcony in the brilliant sunshine, saw the water there below me shining just the same as last night, but now with a merry sparkle as it went crashing down the narrow wooded ravine.
The beautiful wooded ravine down which the water rushes.
At 10 oclock we started out on a tour of inspection to see the power station, the water, and, if possible, the surrounding scenery. A few minutes walk found us on the bridge that spans first the rapids some fifty yards below the actual fall, and then the stream that leads to the turbine house; the stream and the rapids being divided only by a very narrow island, and meeting again a few hundred yards further down. The great dam which we now were gazing at has two of its cylinders working, and this morning, as you see in the illustration, one was half closed and the other completely open. On the right there is a passage for the timber to float down and the salmon to jump up, and on the left is the place for the third cylinder, where the water has been allowed to run during the three or four years of construction. One-third of the rivers water goes down the rapids, and two-thirds through the turbine station, but to look at the rush of turbulent water that dashed down below us, no one could imagine that so little of the total volume of water was passing down this way. We were told that the dam had been entirely closed for about ten minutes at the opening ceremony performed by the President of Finland the previous spring, and during those historic and impressive moments the bed of the rapids was seen for the first time in history, showing innumerable curiously-shaped boulders and rocks.

A new portrait of the President,
Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley,
who will preside at the Luncheon. It is always a joy
both to see and to hear the President, who is such an
asset to the work we are doing.
Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley is building a new house, in
which she intends to put her ideals into practice and
use as much electricity as possible. Not only is
Mrs. Ashley interested in the applications of electricity
to the more wealthy homes, but, writing recently in
the Evening Standard, she stated:—I look for-
ward to the day when the working-class home can
benefit by the medium of electricity, when it becomes
cheap enough to be used by the weekly wage-earner.
I should like to see the working woman able to call
electricity to her aid in her housework and weekly
washing. This is not so Utopian as it may seem, and
is one of the best uses that could ever be made of
electricity. But here, again, there is the question of
cost in connection with wiring an old house and the
purchase of electric apparatus. This declaration
shows that our President is well alive to all the
difficulties which have to be met before we can arrive
at the complete electrification of all the homes of
Great Britain.

PROGRAMME FOR MAY 15th.
11 a.m.—Annual General Meeting at the Park
Lane Hotel.
1 p.m.—Luncheon at the Park Lane Hotel.
3.30 p.m.—Visit to the Home Office Industrial
Museum.
8 p.m.—Conversazione at the Institution of
Electrical Engineers.

Herbert S. Morrison, Esq., J.P., M.P.

Mr. Herbert S. Morrison, the Minister of
Transport in the present Government, fully
endorses the objects of the Association and is
working for the time when electricity will be
accessible to all. He uses electricity in his own
home, and we are proud to number amongst
our members his wife, Mrs. Morrison.
Mr. Morrison can well visualise the need for
electrical labour-saving methods in the working-
class home, as he started life as an errand boy.
While still a comparatively young man, he has
had a wonderful career, having been Mayor of
Hackney, Leader of the L.C.C. Labour Party,
Secretary to the London Labour Party, and is
also a Justice of the Peace for the County of
London.

The Electrical Age 633

he May Luncheon.

rison, Esq., J.P., M.P. Sir Felix Pole.
et Bondfield, J.P., M.P.

Luncheon to be held in connection with the Fifth
r is assured. Our President, who has already proved
icity, will be supported by two Ministers of the Crown
Industrialist.

Sir Felix Pole.

Sir Felix Pole has had a long and varied
experience as an employer of labour, and was
for many years General Manager of the Great
Western Railway, Editor of that most popular
journal, "The Railway Review," and acted also
as Secretary to the Conciliation Boards of
his Company. He has recently become Chair-
man of Associated Electrical Industries, Ltd.,
in which capacity he will, we hope and
believe, take a great interest in the development
of electricity for domestic purposes.
Sir Felix was a most popular General Manager
and has always taken a great interest in the
welfare of the workers under his control. He
has also had considerable experience as an
industrial arbitrator, being a member of the
Industrial Court.

The Right Hon. Margaret Bondfield, J.P., M.P.

Miss Margaret Bondfield, who is the first woman in
this country to achieve Cabinet rank, was unfortunately
prevented by Parliamentary business from attending
the Newcastle Conference last year.
Miss Bondfield is a great believer in the part which
women can play in the development of electricity, and,
in a letter sent to the Director at the time of the
Newcastle Conference, she stated:—"We are still at
the beginning of electrical development in the home,
and a vast field of experiment and achievement lies
ahead. It is of the first importance that the ranks of
those who are pushing forward with the development
of domestic electricity should contain a due proportion
of keen women. It is equally important that women
in the homes should be stirred up to make the demand
for this new servant to help them. When you con-
sider how much of the time of the average woman is
spent on tasks which, however useful and necessary
they may be, are, in essence, mere drudgery and
routine, it is obvious that a very great step forward
could be taken towards a fuller, richer and more varied
existence if science could be applied to domestic work
equally with that in the factory."

The Electrical Age 635
A Possible Career for Girl Guides.
Saleswomen in Electrical Showrooms.
By HILDA L. DOVER, B.Sc., London.

It was my privilege to be present at the first practical course on Home Electrification for Women in Electrical Showrooms, Women Architects and Decorators. These lectures had been arranged by the British Electrical Development Association and the Electric Lamp Manufacturers Association in conjunction with the Electrical Association for Women. I was amazed by the number of students who had registered for the course—130 in all—many of whom had been sent by their employers and their expenses paid. One heard the Scottish accent and the Welsh intonation mingling happily, discussing the various merits of electrical appliances. They were all so keen. 

Miss C. Haslett, the Director of the Electrical Association for Women, in her opening address emphasized the growing interest of the woman public in electrical appliances, and pointed out that the women in the electrical industry should be well ahead of the women public, anticipating public needs and demands. 

The History and Geography of the Electrical Industry was touched upon by Lieut.-Colonel W. A. Vignoles, and the Modern Views of Electric Lighting were given by Mr. W. J. Jones. From ordinary lighting we were taken on to decorative lighting, and here the girl with the practical artistic bent can excel. It was pointed out that we must realise that the people who require decorative lighting are those who desire real silk damask for their upholstery, Persian carpets, and, in fact, all the expensive

transcription:
636 The Electrical Age

luxurious articles for their homes. These people are wealthy, and so with them one must think of quality rather than cost. It will be found that if their tastes are satisfied the cost will be of lesser consideration. When coloured light is used, twice as much light is required, but the cost is fully compensated by the delightful atmosphere of the room. Many entrancing effects were shown by Mr. L. E. Buckell. He pointed out that the colour present in the room should be taken into consideration, and the same colour used in lighting, or very bad effects will result. Contrasts should be used sparingly, but can be very fascinating, as was shown by a green bulb in a vase lamp which has a buff-coloured shade in an orange-lighted room. This gave a very refreshing atmosphere to the room, and emphasised the necessity for artistic taste, as an all green lighted room would be disastrous. A girl with colour lighting experience is invaluable to a householder who wishes to change the atmosphere of her house without going to the trouble of refurnishing and redecorating.

Besides colour, the influence of light on the form and appearance of a room was very ably illustrated in the Architectural Room at the E.L.M.A. Building at Savoy Hill. From the study of the position and coloured effects of lamps shop window lighting resolves itself.

It was shown how the more practical woman would find her niche in the Electrical Industry by understanding typical domestic wiring installations and by being able to execute them. It was due to the foresight of the Electrical Association for Women that the wiring specification of the

Electric Home was drawn up. By its aid the woman electrician should know the minimum number of lighting points, switches and plug points required in an efficiently-equipped electric home, and know the best positions for such in each room. Besides wiring, a handy girl should be quite easily able to remedy a defective appliance, plug, socket, or to renew a fuse. One of the merits of modern electric appliances is their simplicity—the fault usually is in the connecting flex, plug or connector.

Another attractive branch is open for the girl who is fond of cooking. Efficient cooking demonstrators, who thoroughly understand their cookers and are able to explain its merits, will always be happy in an Electric Cooker Showroom.

Women who are thinking of taking up a career in Electrical Showrooms as Saleswomen must one and all possess a pleasing personality, for however great ones technical knowledge, practical or artistic bent, it is the customers interest which is required first before advice can be given or a sale effected. This was very pointedly shown by Miss Gladys Burlton in a demonstration as a customer to a self-opiniated, highly technical salesman on the one hand, and a charming sympathetic saleswoman on the other.

There is ample scope in the Electrical Industry for saleswomen. Progress in the manufacture of electrical appliances is so rapid and methods ever-changing that an interesting and varied career awaits any woman who is keen on electrical development.

SIR ARCHIBALD PAGE.—We were pleased to see in the New Years Honours List the name of the Chief Engineer and Manager of the Central Electricity Board. Sir Archibald Page is a Past President of the Institution of Electrical Engineers and one of the men who has helped most constructively to build up the electrical industry of to-day.

MR. BERNARD C. HOLDING, who proved himself for many years a friend of the E.A.W. as Editor of "The Electrician," has resigned his post in order to take up an appointment with the International Standard Electric Corporation. He is succeeded in the Editorship of "The Electrician" by Mr. G. H. Lepper.

638

The Electrical Age

Some Attractive and Proved Recipes
for the Electric Oven.

By MARY MACKIRDY
(Lecturer, College of Domestic Science, Glasgow, and Author of "Recipes for You.")

With the advent of electric cookers the old haphazard ways are bound to give place to much more definite methods. Think of the old casual way of testing heat in a gas oven; sometimes the hand went in, sometimes the correct heat was taken for granted. The cook with a certain kind of instinct—or it might be experience—got first-rate results, but the beginner learned by heart-breaking results.

Look at the other side of the picture—the current is switched on and in 20 or 30 minutes the thermometer should register 300 to 400 degrees, the higher temperature being used for small articles with a considerable amount of moisture, such as scones, buns or cookies, and rolls or pastry. When these are put in, the current should be switched off and immediately they are cooked, which should be in a few minutes, a batch of biscuits, a rice pudding, fruit in syrup or a sponge cake may be fired, care being taken to make the change quickly, the temperature dropping with the opening of the oven door and the rush of cool air.

A piece of meat or a chicken may be treated in the same way, and many other things.

Large cakes are best put in when the thermometer registers 375°; the current is then switched to low for about 15 minutes, then switched off. It must, however, be remembered that under these conditions the oven door must not be opened.

I have given these few notes merely as suggestions. The cook with intelligence and initiative will devise rules for herself and will find it particularly helpful to keep a log book with times and temperatures.

The following simple dinner and cake will, I hope, illustrate the economical use of the oven.

A Savoury Dish of Chicken, Rabbit or Veal.
Make a very good brown sauce, joint the chicken or rabbit—the veal may be left in one piece—heat a small piece of butter in a stewpan, add the meat, and brown. When the meat has been fried, strain the sauce over it, there should be enough almost to cover, put a buttered paper on top. Put pan in oven, the temperature being 350°, switch down to medium. Have ready to put into the oven a casserole or pyrex dish of potatoes, mixed, it may be, with peas, sprigs of cauliflower or other vegetable that does not require too long cooking, a pudding, and, last of all, as the others will take no harm, a walnut cake. Switch off the current and leave for about 1 hour. The door must not be opened while they are cooking.

Brown Sauce for the Chicken.
2 teaspoonfuls vinegar, 1 oz. flour, 1 oz. bacon, piece of onion (chopped), piece of carrot and of celery (chopped), 1 tomato, 1 blade mace, 6 peppercorns, 3 gills stock or water, salt, pepper. Heat the vinegar until almost all evaporated, add the butter, when it is hot add the onion, and fry till very brown; then fry the bacon, the vegetables and the flour, add all the other ingredients, stir till boiling, simmer for half hour; strain and use.

The Vegetables.
Slice the potatoes thickly, put them into a fireproof dish with sprigs of cauliflower or whatever vegetables may be desired, a piece of butter and a very little water, just sufficient to cover the bottom of dish, season and put a lid on. Time, about 1 hour.

Eves Pudding.
1/2 lb. apples, cut in small pieces, about 2 tablespoonfuls sugar, 1 or 2 cloves or other spice. Fill a pudding dish, three parts full, putting the sugar in between two layers of apples and packing tightly. Cover the apples with the following mixture:—1 egg, its weight in sugar, in butter and in flour. Cream the butter and sugar, add the egg, well-beaten, and the flour.

Walnut Cake.
7 ozs. flour, 6 ozs. castor sugar, 2 ozs. butter, 3 yolks, 2 whites, 1/2 teacupful milk, 1/2 teacupful chopped walnuts, 1/2 teaspoonful cream of tartar, 1/4 teaspoonful carbonate of soda. Cream butter and sugar, add yolks, milk, flour, soda and cream of tartar, also the walnuts. Beat the mixture very well and mix in carefully the stiffly-beaten whites. Bake in a moderately hot oven for about 1 1/4 hours. When the cake is cool coat with American frosting.

American Frosting.
1 small teacupful castor sugar, 1 white of egg, 1/4 teacupful water, 1 teaspoonful lemon juice. Put water and sugar in a small pan, steep till sugar is dissolved, then boil for 5 minutes. Meanwhile have the white stiffly whisked in a bowl, beat in the boiling sugar, whisking vigorously all the time, and adding the lemon and any flavouring or colouring desired. Continue to whisk the frosting until it is thick and creamy, put on cake and decorate with walnuts

for their inspection. Our demonstrations are changed at different periods of the year, and include washing, cooking, refrigeration; during the winter months, lighting and heating are the chief features.
I wonder if you can imagine the intense interest displayed during a demonstration? Perhaps you would better understand if I could put down here some of the questions I am asked about the different apparatus used—such as: "Can a kettle be boiled on the toaster?" or the dear old gentleman who, looking at an early model of a Ferranti fire, asked of another: "What is it?" the reply being readily forthcoming: "Its a Dutch oven, man!"—and many, many more in a like strain, but far too numerous to mention here. Enough to shew that the time is ripe for more time and energy to be devoted to this work of propaganda in order in some measure to unveil the mystery which is generally attached to electricity and its uses.
There is no doubt that electric supply undertakings, whether owned by company or municipality, operating over an extensive district can derive the greatest benefit from the use of travelling caravan exhibitions.
It has been brought home to us that this method of demonstration has a value out of all proportion to the actual sales or business which may immediately be effected by it. In our own area, which covers some 800 square miles and is of a very scattered character, the people, both consumers and non-consumers, welcome the arrival of the caravan and the opportunity which it affords of talking to the representative of the Company—as some have expressed it, the only member of the Company they ever met previously was the man who called for their money! In this respect travelling displays will be of great value in improving the relations between consumers and the company or municipality providing the service.
This aspect of the work becomes more important as companies amalgamate and municipalities secure large territories; as the Electric Supply Organisations become larger, the management and staff are apt to become more remote from the public whom they serve.
It seems obvious that over very scattered districts, operated perhaps by companies individually too small to justify the ownership of a travelling exhibition and staff, this service might be provided for by some central body, and probably nothing could be better than a combination of the E.D.A. and the E.A.W. for this work.
As a live Member of the E.A.W., and as one of the staff of the South Wales Electrical Power Distribution Co., I am gratified to have been able to take this small part in spreading the gospel over the scattered areas of South Wales and Monmouthshire.
The winter "show," with its bright and coloured lights, making a dull corner look something like fairyland, will soon have finished—I shall be most sorry.

transcription:
646				The Electrical Age

Books Received.
" Ninth Annual Report of the Electricity Commissioners." Published by H.M. Stationery Office. Price 3/- net.
This report contains, as usual, much interesting information on the development of electricity, the principal feature being the great progress made in the preparation and carrying out of the new regional schemes for the co-ordinated development of generation and main transmission in accordance with the policy of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1926. The report also contains interesting chapters dealing with rural electrification and methods of charging for electricity to consumers.
" The Co-operative Electrification of Czecho-Slovakia." By Miss Margaret Digby (Horace Plunkett Foundation), being a Paper read before the Engineering and Scientific Association of Ireland.
Miss Digby, who was formerly with the International Co-operative Womens Guild, has written a very interesting Paper on the somewhat unique electrification schemes which have been adopted in Central Europe.
The Paper is well worthy of study by those who are responsible for rural electrification in this country.
Miss Digby, in referring to the controversy which is raging in England at the moment as to the aesthetic merits of pylons, describes their effect on Czech scenery -- " Czecho-Slovakia is a country on large lines, much of it wide rolling plains, richly cultivated and encircled with forest. In such a landscape the long swinging lines of the overhead cables give a certain air of purpose and a perspective like that of a highway." In summing up, she states :-- " The people and the Government of Czecho-Slovakia have built up in a comparatively short space a distinctive and highly successful system of electrical distribution. It is characterised by elasticity in its adaptation to varying circumstances, and by democracy not only in control, but in the system by which every consumer receives equal treatment both in supply and price, no matter where he lives or what his financial importance may be. It is all the more remarkable for being almost entirely a rural movement, cut off from the more profitable business with concentrated populations and industrial undertakings."

This is a very useful pocket book for those interested in the practical side of electricity. It is packed full with valuable data and the illustrations are especially good.

The book is written in a cheery and interest-ing manner, and would make a useful addition to any book shelf.

Eltham Housing Estate.—We have received from Mr. G. W. Keats, the Borough Electrical Engineer for Woolwich, an interesting pamphlet describing the new Eltham Housing Estate, which was formally opened some time ago by the Minister of Health. Both the streets and the houses are lighted by electricity, there being no gas on the estate. Eight hundred and forty-seven of the houses are all-electric with the exception of a slow combustion stove in the scullery. The Council have adopted a system whereby tenants can have extra heating outlets on payment of 1d. per point per week over a period of seven years. Altogether a very enterprising undertaking!

“Individual Understanding” A Layman’s Approach to Practical Philosophy.
Mr. Emile Garcke, who is one of the grand old men of the electrical industry, has sent to a large number of his friends a very interesting book containing the philosophy which he has evolved as a business man of considerable standing and long experience. We were very proud to be numbered amongst Mr. Garcke’s friends and to receive an autographed copy of what is a very wonderful contribution to modern philosophy.—Ed., “Electrical Age.”

Unnamed: 9: Hon. Secretary of the Torquay and District E.A.W. Branch, Torquay.
transcription:
648 The Electrical Age
E.A.W. Branch Activities.
TWO NEW BRANCHES.
Torquay and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Binney,
17, Hartop Road, St. Mary Church, Torquay.
The Torquay Section of the East Devon Branch has progressed so rapidly that a separate Torquay and District Branch was inaugurated on February 8th, at Roslin Hall, and formally handed over by the President, Mrs. Phillips, J.P., to Mrs. Gresham, President of the new Branch.
A most successful and enjoyable Luncheon was held after the meeting, and the Lady Emmett, J.P., President of the National Council of Women, in her speech emphasized particularly the value of Electricity to the mother of a family, by relieving her of much drudgery. She was also interested in the possibilities of employment for women in the Electrical Industry.
Other speakers and guests at the Luncheon included the Mayor and Mayoress of Torquay (Councillor and Mrs. E. H. Sermon), Mrs. Carver, Councillor and Mrs. Callard, and Mr. and Mrs. G. J. Hollyer.
The new Branch has already over sixty members, and a programme of activities for the current session has been arranged.
Bradford and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss E. Moss,
179, Manningham Lane, Bradford.
The Inaugural Meeting of the Bradford and District Branch was held on January 10th, at the Mechanics’ Institute. Lady Watson, our first President, presided over the meeting, which was very well attended. The Director addressed the meeting on the work and objects of the Association, and other interesting speeches were made by Alderman Kathleen Chambers, Vice-President, and Mr. Thos. Roles, M.I.E.E., City Electrical Engineer. The Secretary read out an apology from Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, President of the Association, who very much regretted her inability to be present, and wished the new Branch every success.
By kind permission of our City Electrical Engineer and Electricity Committee, we are able to hold our meetings at the Corporation Electricity Dept. Offices, and our first one was on February 13th, when Mr. Harry Moss, A.M.I.E.E., gave a most interesting Lecture on “Some Things you should know about your Electrical Installation,” a subject which proved very enjoyable to the large audience who attended. Following the discussion, coffee and light refreshments were very kindly provided by the Corporation Electricity Department, and several new members enrolled.
On March 3rd seats were reserved for a number of our members at a Lecture-Demonstration on Electric Cooking during a series which is being held in the Mechanics’ Institute for a fortnight. The lecture, given by Miss E. Purvis, M.C.A., Medallist, was greatly appreciated by all, and arrangements have been made for the remainder of our members to attend a similar demonstration on March 11th.
An interesting programme of fixtures has been arranged for the remainder of the Winter session.
Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
We have just had a most successful and happy Whist Drive, with nearly 200 members and friends present.
In April we are visiting the Craigpark Electric Cable Works, and in May we are having an unusual type of talk by Miss Aitken, of the College of Domestic Science, who is Dietitian in the College; the talk is “Modern Food and Feeding.”
Our Annual Summer Outing in June is not fixed yet, but we hope that it may include a visit to a Milk Research Laboratory.
A large number of our members are looking forward to the Annual Conference, to be held in London this year.
Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. Norman Griffiths, M.Com., A.C.I.I.,
148, Woodlands Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
Our Spring Programme opened with a most successful The Dansant, arranged by the Social Sub-Committee (Chairman, Mrs. Lawson). About 170 were present, and the profit—nearly £20—was placed to the credit of our office and Club-room Equipment Fund.
On January 28th, members were invited by the local Branch of the I.E.E. to attend the Faraday Lecture, which was given by Captain Eckersley, M.I.E.E.
On February 11th we held an “out of Birmingham” meeting, and 50 members visited the works of the Goodyear Tyre & Rubber Co., at Wolverhampton.
On February 27th, the Committee organising the Electrical Section of the British Industries Fair at Castle Bromwich very kindly invited us to the Fair, and entertained us to tea. Over 200 members of the E.A.W. were present—including some from the E.A.W.’s youngest Branch. A most interesting time was spent—and all members were exhorted to set their hearts on something shown at the Fair, and “not to be happy until they got it.” An admirable trade stimulus!
Our most recent activity has been the Annual Luncheon and General Meeting. This has really absorbed our energies for the last few weeks—but the result was a record. Over 500 were present. Our speakers were: Sir John Brooke, Mrs. H. K. Beale (our President), Councillor H. K. Beale, Mrs. M. L. Matthews, A.I.E.E., F. Forrest, Esq., M.I.E.E., R. Borlase Matthews, Esq., Wh. Ex., M.I.E.E., and we were happy to entertain the Lady Mayoress of Birmingham, the Mayor and Mayoress of Wolverhampton, the Mayor and Mayoress of Walsall, and the Chairmen of local Electricity Supply Undertakings.
D. GRIFFITHS.
Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secretaries: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, and Miss D. Foster Jeffery, LL.B., 6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
Our 1930 programme has been very varied and interesting. On January 17th a Cookery Demonstration was held in the Salford Electrical Showrooms. It was excellently arranged, and was well attended.
On January 29th our members were invited by the E.D.A. to attend their important discussion on the “Electric Home Campaign,” held at the Lighting Service Bureau, and in the evening of the same day we had a unique experience when we were invited by the I.E.E. students to attend their students’ lecture on “Lighting, Heating and Domestic Appliances.” We found it very refreshing and interesting to hear these young men (there being, unfortunately, no women students as yet) lecturing on domestic appliances, and there was much good-humoured heckling and discussion at the end of the lectures between our members and the students. We appreciated their invitation to attend, and hope similar joint meetings may be arranged in the future.
On February 11th, our Annual Meeting was held in the Salford Town Hall. Alderman Billington very kindly presided, and we were fortunate to have as our speaker Miss Faithfull, C.B.E. Headmistresses and teachers were specially invited, and an important step forward has been made towards Electrical education for girls, to fit them for new careers of the future.
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss D. S. Blaker,
1, York Terrace, St. George’s Road, Cheltenham.
The opening lecture this season was given by W. J. Bache, Esq., M.I.E.E. (Borough Electrical Engineer) on “How Electric Heating Appliances Work.” A short explanation of the electrical terms in most frequent use was followed by an interesting demonstration of models, and experiments which showed the members how their appliances function and how simple it was in most cases to repair them.
The E.D.A. film, “Country Currents,” was shown on February 4th at the Art Gallery.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. Norman Griffiths, M.Com., A.C.I.I.,
148, Woodlands Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
Our Spring Programme opened with a most successful The Dansant, arranged by the Social Sub-Committee (Chairman, Mrs. Lawson). About 170 were present, and the profit—nearly £20—was placed to the credit of our office and Club-room Equipment Fund.
On January 28th, members were invited by the local Branch of the I.E.E. to attend the Faraday Lecture, which was given by Captain Eckersley, M.I.E.E.
On February 11th we held an “out of Birmingham” meeting, and 50 members visited the works of the Goodyear Tyre & Rubber Co., at Wolverhampton.
On February 27th, the Committee organising the Electrical Section of the British Industries Fair at Castle Bromwich very kindly invited us to the Fair, and entertained us to tea. Over 200 members of the E.A.W. were present—including some from the E.A.W.’s youngest Branch. A most interesting time was spent—and all members were exhorted to set their hearts on something shown at the Fair, and “not to be happy until they got it.” An admirable trade stimulus!
Our most recent activity has been the Annual Luncheon and General Meeting. This has really absorbed our energies for the last few weeks—but the result was a record. Over 500 were present. Our speakers were: Sir John Brooke, Mrs. H. K. Beale (our President), Councillor H. K. Beale, Mrs. M. L. Matthews, A.I.E.E., F. Forrest, Esq., M.I.E.E., R. Borlase Matthews, Esq., Wh. Ex., M.I.E.E., and we were happy to entertain the Lady Mayoress of Birmingham, the Mayor and Mayoress of Wolverhampton, the Mayor and Mayoress of Walsall, and the Chairmen of local Electricity Supply Undertakings.
D. GRIFFITHS.
Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secretaries: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, and Miss D. Foster Jeffery, LL.B., 6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
Our 1930 programme has been very varied and interesting. On January 17th a Cookery Demonstration was held in the Salford Electrical Showrooms. It was excellently arranged, and was well attended.
On January 29th our members were invited by the E.D.A. to attend their important discussion on the “Electric Home Campaign,” held at the Lighting Service Bureau, and in the evening of the same day we had a unique experience when we were invited by the I.E.E. students to attend their students’ lecture on “Lighting, Heating and Domestic Appliances.” We found it very refreshing and interesting to hear these young men (there being, unfortunately, no women students as yet) lecturing on domestic appliances, and there was much good-humoured heckling and discussion at the end of the lectures between our members and the students. We appreciated their invitation to attend, and hope similar joint meetings may be arranged in the future.
On February 11th, our Annual Meeting was held in the Salford Town Hall. Alderman Billington very kindly presided, and we were fortunate to have as our speaker Miss Faithfull, C.B.E. Headmistresses and teachers were specially invited, and an important step forward has been made towards Electrical education for girls, to fit them for new careers of the future.

Our most recent activity has been the Annual Luncheon and General Meeting. This has really absorbed our energies for the last few weeks—but the result was a record. Over 500 were present. Ex., M.I.E.E., and we were happy to entertain the Lady Mayoress of Birmingham, the Mayor and Mayoress of Wolverhampton, the Mayor and Mayoress of Walsall, and the Chairmen of local Electricity Supply Undertakings.
D. GRIFFITHS.
Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secretaries: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, and Miss D. Foster Jeffery, LL.B., 6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
Our 1930 programme has been very varied and interesting. On January 17th a Cookery Demonstration was held in the Salford Electrical Showrooms. It was excellently arranged, and was well attended.
On January 29th our members were invited by the E.D.A. to attend their important discussion on the “Electric Home Campaign,” held at the Lighting Service Bureau, and in the evening of the same day we had a unique experience when we were invited by the I.E.E. students to attend their students’ lecture on “Lighting, Heating and Domestic Appliances.” We found it very refreshing and interesting to hear these young men (there being, unfortunately, no women students as yet) lecturing on domestic appliances, and there was much good-humoured heckling and discussion at the end of the lectures between our members and the students. We appreciated their invitation to attend, and hope similar joint meetings may be arranged in the future.
On February 11th, our Annual Meeting was held in the Salford Town Hall. Alderman Billington very kindly presided, and we were fortunate to have as our speaker Miss Faithfull, C.B.E. Headmistresses and teachers were specially invited, and an important step forward has been made towards Electrical education for girls, to fit them for new careers of the future.
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss D. S. Blaker,
1, York Terrace, St. George’s Road, Cheltenham.
The opening lecture this season was given by W. J. Bache, Esq., M.I.E.E. (Borough Electrical Engineer) on “How Electric Heating Appliances Work.” A short explanation of the electrical terms in most frequent use was followed by an interesting demonstration of models, and experiments which showed the members how their appliances function and how simple it was in most cases to repair them.
The E.D.A. film, “Country Currents,” was shown on February 4th at the Art Gallery.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,

Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. Norman Griffiths, M.Com., A.C.I.I.,
148, Woodlands Road, Moseley, Birmingham.

On February 11th we held an “out of Birmingham” meeting, and 50 members visited the works of the Goodyear Tyre & Rubber Co., at Wolverhampton.
On February 27th, the Committee organising the Electrical Section of the British Industries Fair at Castle Bromwich very kindly invited us to the Fair, and entertained us to tea. Over 200 members of the E.A.W. were present—including some from the E.A.W.’s youngest Branch. A most interesting time was spent—and all members were exhorted to set their hearts on something shown at the Fair, and “not to be happy until they got it.” An admirable trade stimulus!
Our most recent activity has been the Annual Luncheon and General Meeting. This has really absorbed our energies for the last few weeks—but the result was a record. Over 500 were present. Our speakers were: Sir John Brooke, Mrs. H. K. Beale (our President), Councillor H. K. Beale, Mrs. M. L. Matthews, A.I.E.E., F. Forrest, Esq., M.I.E.E., R. Borlase Matthews, Esq., Wh. Ex., M.I.E.E., and we were happy to entertain the Lady Mayoress of Birmingham, the Mayor and Mayoress of Wolverhampton, the Mayor and Mayoress of Walsall, and the Chairmen of local Electricity Supply Undertakings.
D. GRIFFITHS.
Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secretaries: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, and Miss D. Foster Jeffery, LL.B., 6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
Our 1930 programme has been very varied and interesting. On January 17th a Cookery Demonstration was held in the Salford Electrical Showrooms. It was excellently arranged, and was well attended.
On January 29th our members were invited by the E.D.A. to attend their important discussion on the “Electric Home Campaign,” held at the Lighting Service Bureau, and in the evening of the same day we had a unique experience when we were invited by the I.E.E. students to attend their students’ lecture on “Lighting, Heating and Domestic Appliances.” We found it very refreshing and interesting to hear these young men (there being, unfortunately, no women students as yet) lecturing on domestic appliances, and there was much good-humoured heckling and discussion at the end of the lectures between our members and the students. We appreciated their invitation to attend, and hope similar joint meetings may be arranged in the future.
On February 11th, our Annual Meeting was held in the Salford Town Hall. Alderman Billington very kindly presided, and we were fortunate to have as our speaker Miss Faithfull, C.B.E. Headmistresses and teachers were specially invited, and an important step forward has been made towards Electrical education for girls, to fit them for new careers of the future.

Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.

Manchester and Salford District Branch.

The Director addressed the meeting on the work and objects of the Association, and other interesting speeches were made by Alderman Kathleen Chambers, Vice-President, and Mr. Thos. Roles, M.I.E.E., City Electrical Engineer. The Secretary read out an apology from Mrs. Wilfrid Ashley, President of the Association, who very much regretted her inability to be present, and wished the new Branch every success.
By kind permission of our City Electrical Engineer and Electricity Committee, we are able to hold our meetings at the Corporation Electricity Dept. Offices, and our first one was on February 13th, when Mr. Harry Moss, A.M.I.E.E., gave a most interesting Lecture on “Some Things you should know about your Electrical Installation,” a subject which proved very enjoyable to the large audience who attended. Following the discussion, coffee and light refreshments were very kindly provided by the Corporation Electricity Department, and several new members enrolled.
On March 3rd seats were reserved for a number of our members at a Lecture-Demonstration on Electric Cooking during a series which is being held in the Mechanics’ Institute for a fortnight. The lecture, given by Miss E. Purvis, M.C.A., Medallist, was greatly appreciated by all, and arrangements have been made for the remainder of our members to attend a similar demonstration on March 11th.
An interesting programme of fixtures has been arranged for the remainder of the Winter session.
Glasgow and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss R. F. Kennedy,
251, Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow.
We have just had a most successful and happy Whist Drive, with nearly 200 members and friends present.
In April we are visiting the Craigpark Electric Cable Works, and in May we are having an unusual type of talk by Miss Aitken, of the College of Domestic Science, who is Dietitian in the College; the talk is “Modern Food and Feeding.”
Our Annual Summer Outing in June is not fixed yet, but we hope that it may include a visit to a Milk Research Laboratory.
A large number of our members are looking forward to the Annual Conference, to be held in London this year.
Birmingham and Midlands Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. Norman Griffiths, M.Com., A.C.I.I.,
148, Woodlands Road, Moseley, Birmingham.
Our Spring Programme opened with a most successful The Dansant, arranged by the Social Sub-Committee (Chairman, Mrs. Lawson). About 170 were present, and the profit—nearly £20—was placed to the credit of our office and Club-room Equipment Fund.
On January 28th, members were invited by the local Branch of the I.E.E. to attend the Faraday Lecture, which was given by Captain Eckersley, M.I.E.E.
On February 11th we held an “out of Birmingham” meeting, and 50 members visited the works of the Goodyear Tyre & Rubber Co., at Wolverhampton.
On February 27th, the Committee organising the Electrical Section of the British Industries Fair at Castle Bromwich very kindly invited us to the Fair, and entertained us to tea. Over 200 members of the E.A.W. were present—including some from the E.A.W.’s youngest Branch. A most interesting time was spent—and all members were exhorted to set their hearts on something shown at the Fair, and “not to be happy until they got it.” An admirable trade stimulus!
Our most recent activity has been the Annual Luncheon and General Meeting. This has really absorbed our energies for the last few weeks—but the result was a record. Over 500 were present. Our speakers were: Sir John Brooke, Mrs. H. K. Beale (our President), Councillor H. K. Beale, Mrs. M. L. Matthews, A.I.E.E., F. Forrest, Esq., M.I.E.E., R. Borlase Matthews, Esq., Wh. Ex., M.I.E.E., and we were happy to entertain the Lady Mayoress of Birmingham, the Mayor and Mayoress of Wolverhampton, the Mayor and Mayoress of Walsall, and the Chairmen of local Electricity Supply Undertakings.
D. GRIFFITHS.
Manchester and Salford District Branch.
Hon. Secretaries: Mrs. J. Harcourt Williams, and Miss D. Foster Jeffery, LL.B., 6, St. Anns Passage, Manchester.
Our 1930 programme has been very varied and interesting. On January 17th a Cookery Demonstration was held in the Salford Electrical Showrooms. It was excellently arranged, and was well attended.
On January 29th our members were invited by the E.D.A. to attend their important discussion on the “Electric Home Campaign,” held at the Lighting Service Bureau, and in the evening of the same day we had a unique experience when we were invited by the I.E.E. students to attend their students’ lecture on “Lighting, Heating and Domestic Appliances.” We found it very refreshing and interesting to hear these young men (there being, unfortunately, no women students as yet) lecturing on domestic appliances, and there was much good-humoured heckling and discussion at the end of the lectures between our members and the students. We appreciated their invitation to attend, and hope similar joint meetings may be arranged in the future.
On February 11th, our Annual Meeting was held in the Salford Town Hall. Alderman Billington very kindly presided, and we were fortunate to have as our speaker Miss Faithfull, C.B.E. Headmistresses and teachers were specially invited, and an important step forward has been made towards Electrical education for girls, to fit them for new careers of the future.
Cheltenham Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss D. S. Blaker,
1, York Terrace, St. George’s Road, Cheltenham.
The opening lecture this season was given by W. J. Bache, Esq., M.I.E.E. (Borough Electrical Engineer) on “How Electric Heating Appliances Work.” A short explanation of the electrical terms in most frequent use was followed by an interesting demonstration of models, and experiments which showed the members how their appliances function and how simple it was in most cases to repair them.
The E.D.A. film, “Country Currents,” was shown on February 4th at the Art Gallery.

South Wales and Monmouthshire Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. G. Snow, "Greengate," Lisvane Road, Lisvane, Glam.
Our anticipation that 1930 was to be a good year for our Branch has so far been well maintained. Up to March 1st we have enrolled over 30 new members, and the interest in our Association is growing in all directions.
The visits to Benton Partridges Beauty Parlour were most interesting, and showed how electricity could be used in this sphere.
The visit to the G.P.O. was well attended, as also was the talk which Mr. G. S. Francis, of E.D.A., gave us on the Outlet Campaign on February 26th. We were very pleased that a great many new members were present, and Mr. Morley New, the City Electrical Engineer of Cardiff, took the chair.
Our Spring Programme is almost ready, and includes several interesting visits.

■ ■ ■

North-East Coast Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Miss Anna Holm, Carliol House, Newcastle-on-Tyne.
Our winter session has ended, and we are looking forward to inaugurating the fourth year of our activities by a Luncheon after the General Meeting on Friday, March 26th.
Our new President, Mrs. Hugh Middleton, J.P., O.B.E., has graciously promised to preside at our General Meeting and Luncheon. Miss Haslett will be with us, and with two prominent speakers from the North East Coast, we should have an interesting luncheon. The General Electric Company have invited all guests lunching to visit the Lemington Glass Works. With the memory of a delightful visit to Lemington during the Conference, we are sure that the afternoon will be happily spent.
The lecture on January 20th on "Glass and Glass Making" was held in conjunction with the local E.P.E.A., and proved a most interesting one.
The lecture given on February 3rd on "Electrical Apparatus—its Use and Misuse" satisfied much of the latent curiosity of our members about the common electrical apparatus in their homes.
On February 27th, Mr. Wilson, of The General Electric Company, gave a delightful talk on the manufacture of G.E.C. lamps, illustrated by a film, and in addition showed many lamps from the smallest to the largest made, and cleverly demonstrated the decorative possibilities of coloured lamps when used in the home. ANNA HOLM.

Unnamed: 9: Elected as President of the Ashford branch for two years.
transcription:
650
The Electrical Age
President for two years, resigned, but we are glad that she remains a member of the Committee. Mrs. A. J. Southam (wife of the Chairman of the Ashford Urban District Council) has kindly consented to act as President.
Mr. F. S. Button, J.P., attended our meeting, and gave us a most encouraging talk. The attendance was good, and it was evident the Association was alive and already anticipating the years work.
Mrs. Sawyer, our capable Treasurer, gave the Financial Statement, which revealed a satisfactory balance.
The second Annual Dinner was held in the evening. Our new President presided, supported by Mr. A. J. Southam, the Director, Mr. Button and others. A presentation was made to the retiring President, who charmingly acknowledged her surprise and pleasure. The usual toasts proceeded, interspersed with songs and recitations by various artists, including Mr. and Mrs. Headley, of Maidstone. All voted it a good evening.
Other interesting activities have included the following: — January 22nd. — Demonstration of Washing Machines, by Mr. Dewing; a well-attended meeting, and an interesting discussion.
February 5th. — Public Meeting. Lantern lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," by Mr. T. Catten, of the E.L.M.A. In spite of many counter-attractions there was a very good assembly.
February 26th. — A visit to Messrs. Headley Bros. Printing Works. An instructive explanation of the working of various machines, etc., was given. Tea was provided by the kindness of Mr. Headley, and a small "memento" was given to each visitor.
March 3rd. — An important meeting on "Tariffs." Councillor Mrs. Gregory, of London, gave a very lucid explanation of the subject, illustrating her remarks with some very good charts. Mr. L. P. Headley, of Ashford Chamber of Commerce, and Mr. Wilson, Engineer of the Electricity Department, were among those who took part in the discussion.
March 19th. — Members are visiting the Electricity Works to view the new engine, which was "started up" on November 22nd. This is the first super charged engine of its kind to be used on load, and was supplied by Paxman, of Colchester.

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby, c/o Ingleby Motors, Sweet Street, Leeds.
The Leeds and West Riding Branch has continued to be very successful during the latter half of the Winter Session, 1929-30, the visits and lectures being well attended.
On January 31st they held their Second Annual Luncheon, at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, which passed off very well, although great sorrow was felt at the loss of Dr. Ferranti. Lady Lawson Tancred took the chair, Miss C. Haslett, Sir Charles Wilson and Mr. W. B. Woodhouse being the principal speakers. The Luncheon was followed by the Annual General Meeting, when reports for the year were read and the Council elected.
On February 12th, Mr. Gaunt Craven gave an instructive address on "Simple Repairs to Domestic Electrical Apparatus," and demonstrated how easily many little household repairs could be done with the aid of a screwdriver, a pair of pliers and a penknife.
On March 5th, a visit was paid to the Leeds Industrial Co-operative Bakery, where the members were very interested in the electric dough-mixer and other automatic machinery, and in watching the baking of crumpets and bread, etc.; they were amazed at the quantity turned out.
On March 20th, Mr. Harry Moss, of Bradford, gave, by special request, one of his always popular lectures on "Some things you should know about your Wiring Installations," from which the members learnt many useful hints. They are now looking forward to an outing to Rowntrees Cocoa Works on April 9th.

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. R. Klitz, Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, North Wales.
The North Wales Branch has started the New Year with eighty-two members, and now that the work of the Association is becoming known, we hope at least to double that number this year.
We had a very interesting visit to the Corporation of Salfords Showrooms at Salford. Mr. Romore welcomed us and entertained us to tea. All the members were greatly interested in the novel arrangement of the showroom — the model rooms, the many styles of lighting — and particularly the model kitchen, bathroom and laundry.
We also visited the British Broadcasting Corporation Studio at Manchester, and were shown the control room and studio; at a later date we hope to have the pleasure of hearing a programme broadcast.
Mr. A. P. M. Fleming came to Wrexham and gave his very fascinating lecture, "Milestones on the Progress of Electricity," and members were afterwards entertained to tea by the kindness of the Wrexham Electricity Committee.
We have had two very successful Whist and Bridge Drives in Wrexham, when the prizes were Electrical Appliances kindly given by electrical firms and engineers.
We are visiting Port Sunlight next week, and later on Bournville Garden City. It is hoped that a contingent of members will attend the Conference in London on May 15th and 16th.

Rugby Branch.
Hon. Recording Secretary: E. J. Linford, 13, Cromwell Road, Rugby.
Since the January report parties of Rugby Branch members have visited the B.B.C. studios at Birmingham, Oatby Hall, and the works of Messrs. Cadbury and the Midland Dairies Co. respectively.
The first of a series of technical lectures covering "The Elements of Electricity," was given in February by Mr. S. Kettle to an audience of 28 members. We hope to continue this course for at least three sessions, whilst repeating the elementary classes for the benefit of new members.
In January a lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation" was given to an appreciative audience of 120 people; this meeting was thrown open to the public.
A lecture-demonstration by Mr. H. Warren, on "Talking Films" given, by courtesy of the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., in the acoustic theatre at their Works, proved so attractive that although outside admission was limited to one friend per member, the attendance numbered over 150, and many applications from non-members had to be refused owing to lack of accommodation.
A third very popular lecture was given by Mr. A. P. Young on "Pioneers in Electrical Science."
A conference between the Branch Council, representatives of the Warwickshire Educational Authorities and local Headmistresses and Domestic Science Mistresses was held on February 28th, as a result of which a resolution was forwarded to the Warwickshire Education Committee. The speaker was Miss Dawson-Grove, of Cheltenham.
A successful Bridge Drive, also held in February, assisted materially in stabilizing the Branch finances.
Although membership is still little over the hundred mark, attendance at meetings averages from thirty to forty-five, and a gratifying interest in the Association and its work is beginning to be evinced locally in various quarters.

Swansea and District Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. M. O. Davies, 5, Eden Avenue, Uplands, Swansea.
The Winter Session opened on January 21st with the Annual Meeting and Luncheon, which was held at the Hotel Central, Swansea. We were very pleased to welcome the Director on this occasion, and in responding to the toast of "The Association," which was proposed by the Mayor of Swansea, Miss Haslett made a wonderful impression on the company present. The luncheon was also attended by the Borough Electrical Engineer, Director of Education, the late Chairman of the Electricity Committee, and several other prominent local people. We were especially pleased to have Mrs. Morley New and Mrs. Snow, of Cardiff, with us.
On February 25th, a cooking lecture and demonstration was very kindly provided by Messrs. the General Electric Co. A party of twenty-five girls from the local Central Training School was present, and we were successful in enrolling a number of new members at this meeting.
Our future meetings have not yet been definitely arranged, but we hope to visit the National Oil Refineries at Llandarcy and to have a talk on "Tariffs" by Mr. J. W. Burr, Borough Electrical Engineer. Our President, Lady Bryn Edwards, has kindly invited the members to her residence at Rheola, Neath, to view the electrical appliances, etc., which she has recently had installed. The Summer Meeting will be held in June, and arrangements will be announced at a later date.

They are now looking forward to an outing to Rowntrees Cocoa Works on April 9th.

They are now looking forward to an outing to Rowntrees Cocoa Works on April 9th.

Rugby Branch.

A lecture-demonstration by Mr. H. Warren, on "Talking Films" given, by courtesy of the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., in the acoustic theatre at their Works, proved so attractive that although outside admission was limited to one friend per member, the attendance numbered over 150, and many applications from non-members had to be refused owing to lack of accommodation.
A third very popular lecture was given by Mr. A. P. Young on "Pioneers in Electrical Science."
A conference between the Branch Council, representatives of the Warwickshire Educational Authorities and local Headmistresses and Domestic Science Mistresses was held on February 28th, as a result of which a resolution was forwarded to the Warwickshire Education Committee. The second Annual Dinner was held in the evening. Our new President presided, supported by Mr. A. J. Southam, the Director, Mr. Button and others. A presentation was made to the retiring President, who charmingly acknowledged her surprise and pleasure. The usual toasts proceeded, interspersed with songs and recitations by various artists, including Mr. and Mrs. Headley, of Maidstone. All voted it a good evening.

February 5th. — Public Meeting. Lantern lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation," by Mr. T. Catten, of the E.L.M.A. In spite of many counter-attractions there was a very good assembly.
February 26th. — A visit to Messrs. Headley Bros. Printing Works. An instructive explanation of the working of various machines, etc., was given. Tea was provided by the kindness of Mr. Headley, and a small "memento" was given to each visitor.
March 3rd. — An important meeting on "Tariffs." Councillor Mrs. Gregory, of London, gave a very lucid explanation of the subject, illustrating her remarks with some very good charts. Mr. L. P. Headley, of Ashford Chamber of Commerce, and Mr. Wilson, Engineer of the Electricity Department, were among those who took part in the discussion.
March 19th. — Members are visiting the Electricity Works to view the new engine, which was "started up" on November 22nd. This is the first super charged engine of its kind to be used on load, and was supplied by Paxman, of Colchester.

Leeds and West Riding Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. P. B. Ingleby, c/o Ingleby Motors, Sweet Street, Leeds.
The Leeds and West Riding Branch has continued to be very successful during the latter half of the Winter Session, 1929-30, the visits and lectures being well attended.
On January 31st they held their Second Annual Luncheon, at the Queens Hotel, Leeds, which passed off very well, although great sorrow was felt at the loss of Dr. Ferranti. Lady Lawson Tancred took the chair, Miss C. Haslett, Sir Charles Wilson and Mr. W. B. Woodhouse being the principal speakers. The Luncheon was followed by the Annual General Meeting, when reports for the year were read and the Council elected.
On February 12th, Mr. Gaunt Craven gave an instructive address on "Simple Repairs to Domestic Electrical Apparatus," and demonstrated how easily many little household repairs could be done with the aid of a screwdriver, a pair of pliers and a penknife.
On March 5th, a visit was paid to the Leeds Industrial Co-operative Bakery, where the members were very interested in the electric dough-mixer and other automatic machinery, and in watching the baking of crumpets and bread, etc.; they were amazed at the quantity turned out.
On March 20th, Mr. Harry Moss, of Bradford, gave, by special request, one of his always popular lectures on "Some things you should know about your Wiring Installations," from which the members learnt many useful hints. They are now looking forward to an outing to Rowntrees Cocoa Works on April 9th.

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. R. Klitz, Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, North Wales.
The North Wales Branch has started the New Year with eighty-two members, and now that the work of the Association is becoming known, we hope at least to double that number this year.
We had a very interesting visit to the Corporation of Salfords Showrooms at Salford. Mr. Romore welcomed us and entertained us to tea. All the members were greatly interested in the novel arrangement of the showroom — the model rooms, the many styles of lighting — and particularly the model kitchen, bathroom and laundry.
We also visited the British Broadcasting Corporation Studio at Manchester, and were shown the control room and studio; at a later date we hope to have the pleasure of hearing a programme broadcast.
Mr. A. P. M. Fleming came to Wrexham and gave his very fascinating lecture, "Milestones on the Progress of Electricity," and members were afterwards entertained to tea by the kindness of the Wrexham Electricity Committee.
We have had two very successful Whist and Bridge Drives in Wrexham, when the prizes were Electrical Appliances kindly given by electrical firms and engineers.
We are visiting Port Sunlight next week, and later on Bournville Garden City. It is hoped that a contingent of members will attend the Conference in London on May 15th and 16th.

Rugby Branch.
Hon. Recording Secretary: E. J. Linford, 13, Cromwell Road, Rugby.
Since the January report parties of Rugby Branch members have visited the B.B.C. studios at Birmingham, Oatby Hall, and the works of Messrs. Cadbury and the Midland Dairies Co. respectively.
The first of a series of technical lectures covering "The Elements of Electricity," was given in February by Mr. S. Kettle to an audience of 28 members. We hope to continue this course for at least three sessions, whilst repeating the elementary classes for the benefit of new members.
In January a lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation" was given to an appreciative audience of 120 people; this meeting was thrown open to the public.
A lecture-demonstration by Mr. H. Warren, on "Talking Films" given, by courtesy of the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., in the acoustic theatre at their Works, proved so attractive that although outside admission was limited to one friend per member, the attendance numbered over 150, and many applications from non-members had to be refused owing to lack of accommodation.
A third very popular lecture was given by Mr. A. P. Young on "Pioneers in Electrical Science."
A conference between the Branch Council, representatives of the Warwickshire Educational Authorities and local Headmistresses and Domestic Science Mistresses was held on February 28th, as a result of which a resolution was forwarded to the Warwickshire Education Committee. The speaker was Miss Dawson-Grove, of Cheltenham.
A successful Bridge Drive, also held in February, assisted materially in stabilizing the Branch finances.
Although membership is still little over the hundred mark, attendance at meetings averages from thirty to forty-five, and a gratifying interest in the Association and its work is beginning to be evinced locally in various quarters.

North Wales Branch.
Hon. Secretary: Mrs. R. Klitz, Tan-Yr-Allt, Llanddulas, North Wales.

Mr. A. P. M. Fleming came to Wrexham and gave his very fascinating lecture, "Milestones on the Progress of Electricity," and members were afterwards entertained to tea by the kindness of the Wrexham Electricity Committee.
We have had two very successful Whist and Bridge Drives in Wrexham, when the prizes were Electrical Appliances kindly given by electrical firms and engineers.
We are visiting Port Sunlight next week, and later on Bournville Garden City. It is hoped that a contingent of members will attend the Conference in London on May 15th and 16th.

Rugby Branch.
Hon. Recording Secretary: E. J. Linford, 13, Cromwell Road, Rugby.
Since the January report parties of Rugby Branch members have visited the B.B.C. studios at Birmingham, Oatby Hall, and the works of Messrs. Cadbury and the Midland Dairies Co. respectively.
The first of a series of technical lectures covering "The Elements of Electricity," was given in February by Mr. S. Kettle to an audience of 28 members. We hope to continue this course for at least three sessions, whilst repeating the elementary classes for the benefit of new members.
In January a lecture on "Electric Light and Eyesight Preservation" was given to an appreciative audience of 120 people; this meeting was thrown open to the public.
A lecture-demonstration by Mr. H. Warren, on "Talking Films" given, by courtesy of the British Thomson-Houston Co., Ltd., in the acoustic theatre at their Works, proved so attractive that although outside admission was limited to one friend per member, the attendance numbered over 150, and many applications from non-members had to be refused owing to lack of accommodation.
A third very popular lecture was given by Mr. A. P. Young on "Pioneers in Electrical Science."
A conference between the Branch Council, representatives of the Warwickshire Educational Authorities and local Headmistresses and Domestic Science Mistresses was held on February 28th, as a result of which a resolution was forwarded to the Warwickshire Education Committee. The speaker was Miss Dawson-Grove, of Cheltenham.
A successful Bridge Drive, also held in February, assisted materially in stabilizing the Branch finances.
Although membership is still little over the hundred mark, attendance at meetings averages from thirty to forty-five, and a gratifying interest in the Association and its work is beginning to be evinced locally in various quarters.
